en: Dharma is the foundation of the entire world;
this is the Prajnapathshala Mandala Granthamala Mimamsa Kosha.
Third Part (U-Ja): Editor's Preface.
Kevalānandasarasvatī Vijayā Daśamī, Thursday, Śaka 1876. Publisher’s Preface.

We hope that the hearts of those who love the divine language (Sanskrit), whose very life-breath is the perception of truth, who have exerted themselves in the science of the six duties and logic (*anvīkṣikī*), and especially those of mature intellect whose minds are devoted to the lightness of Mīmāṃsā and Tarka, will experience great joy through this third part of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsākoṣa* being published, which was compiled by our venerable teacher Kevalānandasarasvatī.

Indeed, although my venerable teachers have entered their seventy-eighth year and possess wrinkles and grey hair, their memory, intellect, and physical vigor remain as powerful even now through the majesty of the meditative concentration (samādhi) attained by the practice of yoga; they are thus capable of fathoming the depths of the profound ocean of Mīmāṃsā. For this very reason, we believe that we shall be able to complete the publication of all the parts intended for publication only in the presence of our venerable teachers.

We offer our deepest gratitude for the favor shown by the Bombay Vidyalaya, which has assisted us in the publication of this volume by providing five hundred rupees; we greatly rejoice in its kindness.
Vijayā Daśamī.
Lakṣmaṇa Śāstrī Jośī, Tarkatīrtha, President of the Prājña Pāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala, and Chief Editor of the Dharmakośa.

This is a treasury of topics (*viṣayakoṣa*), not a treasury of words nor a treasury of sentences; rather, it is a treasury of subjects.
Herein, the subjects expounded in the source texts (*ākaragrantha*) and the topical treatises (*prakaraṇagrantha*) of the Mīmāṃsā system have been arranged according to alphabetical order.
Composition according to the sequence of phonemes occurs in two ways: from a gross perspective and from a subtle perspective.
Of these, the former is easily understood for the apprehension of the meaning by speakers, while the latter is somewhat more difficult.
In this regard, the gross perspective was adopted for both the first and second parts.
In this third part, the first [view] alone was accepted at the beginning;
however, toward the end, in certain sections, the second view was accepted. From here onwards, only the second is accepted because of its purity.
To clarify the meaning, a small portion is cited here: the *bindu* beginning with "jaimineḥ paratantrāpatteḥ," and another *bindu* beginning with "jaimineḥ paratantrāpatteḥ.
In both cases, the syllables "jaimineḥ parata" are identical, so there is no need for deliberation on that point; however, later on, in one place it is "trāpa" and in the other it is "ntratāpa.
This being the case, the sequence of these two must be considered.
In this context, *atra* is a short syllable (*hrasva*) and *trā* is a long syllable (*dīrgha*).
That the short comes first and the long follows is the gross sequence.
Accordingly, the anusvāra (*bindu*) in *tantrāpatteḥ* should be placed first as *tantrāpatteḥ*, while it is placed last as *tantrāpatteḥ*; such is the easy path.

Upon careful examination, however, there is a difference in wording between "tantrāpatteḥ" and "tantra+āpatteḥ," while in the second case, there is a difference in wording between "tantra+tva+āpatteḥ.
This being so, it is our view that "tantrāpatteḥ" should be placed first and "tantratvāpatteḥ" afterwards;
or else, as in the cases of "avaghātānvāyaḥ" and "avaghātādidharmāḥ," there are two distinct points.

In this case, the syllables “avaghā” are indeed identical. Following that, there is the short *ta* and then the long *tā*. From a superficial perspective, one might first insert the dot (*bindu*) for “avaghātānvāyaḥ” and subsequently insert the dot for “avaghātādidharmāḥ. However, because of the word division in “avaghātādi” and because the vowel *a* precedes the *na*, the dot for “avaghātādidharmāḥ” should be inserted first, followed by “avaghātānvāyaḥ.”
This is the general direction.

Although this *Mīmāṃsā-koṣa* is a treasury of subjects (*viṣaya*), nevertheless, because it comprises hundreds of thousands of entries and because the vast majority of these subjects are interrelated, they must be arranged according to the alphabetical order. Thus, since the alphabetical order is difficult to manage, the work must be composed by adopting that very order. In this regard, regarding the two methods [of arrangement], the second method just mentioned has been adopted at the end of the third volume; it has already been stated that this same method will be adopted in the fourth and subsequent volumes because of its purity.
However, there may be some slight lapses on the part of the commentators here; nevertheless, we hope that connoisseurs, out of their partiality for purity, will accept a certain amount of difficulty.

Regarding the number of topics (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth: in this third part, there are 164 Bhāṣya topics, 21 Saṃkarṣa topics, 126 topics from Kevalānandī’s commentary, 5 Tautātika topics, 309 Nyāyas, and 310 Laghusiddhāntākṣas.

Now, beginning from the first section, there are 456 *mādhyādhikaraṇas*, 147 *saṃkarṣādhikaraṇas*, 283 *kevalānandīvṛttyadhikaraṇas*, 20 *tautātikādhikaraṇas*, 626 *nyāyas*, and 9,323 *laghusiddhāntākṣepas*.

Furthermore, the sūtra "kāraṇād abhyāvṛttiḥ" (5.2.13) has been interpreted by the authors of the Bhāṣya in two ways: as a subsidiary sūtra (*guṇasūtra*) for the first section under the heading "the principle of sequential performance according to individual items" (*padārthānusamayanyāya*), and as a sūtra for the second section under the heading "the principle of sequential performance according to sections" (*kāṇḍānusamayanyāya*). Regarding this, the *Śāṣṭhīṭīkā* on the sūtra "kāraṇād abhyāvṛttiḥ" should have been included only in the first section and not in the second; however, our inclusion of it in the second section under the principle of *kāṇḍānusamaya* was incorrect.
The principle of *padārthānusamaya* (performing each constituent act in its entirety before proceeding to the next) will follow according to the sequence of the syllables.
In that regard, the *Ṭupṭīkā* should be consulted as follows:

Nevertheless, recalling the proverb, "What is not to be will not be, and what is to be cannot be otherwise," I am now inserting the corrigenda for the third part alone.
This should also be noted: in the first part, the section on "Transgression" (*atikramādhikaraṇa*) has been concluded.
Therein, two sūtras were combined into a single section according to the Bhāṣya;

however, in the detailed [commentary], a division was made such that the thirteenth section is established by the sūtra "But in the case of ritual action" (*karmārthe tu*), while the fourteenth section is established by the sūtra "And because of designation" (*vyapadeśācca*).

In accordance with that, in this third part, under the heading "What is here? (*kim atra*) and so forth within the section on the *uparaveṣ* vessels in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, we have introduced only the sūtra "And because of the designation" (*vyapadeśācca*), along with its respective Bhāṣya and Vārttika, specifically as the section on transgression (*atikramādhikaraṇa*), while placing the knots of Viśvaṇḍana and Śaṅkara prior to them. Regarding the titles of the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa-śīrṣaka*), the distinction here is that while they are arranged according to alphabetical order in the *Mīmāṃsākoṣa*, they are presented here according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).

However, those very [terms] which appear there according to the order of their phonemes (varṇakrama) appear here according to the order of their recitation (pāṭhakrama). It is our view that by arranging them in both these ways, there would be great benefit for the readers. Furthermore, among the headings (śīrṣaka), some would be technical terms (pāribhāṣika), while others would indicate the subject matter of the section (adhikaraṇārtha).

Although both types [of names] indeed convey the meaning of a *adhikaraṇa*, nevertheless, there is a distinction: in the case of technical (*pāribhāṣika*) names, the comprehension of the meaning involves difficulty, whereas in the other cases, there is an absence of such difficulty.
[Objection: Well then, technical names should not be introduced here at all. [Reply: True.

Nevertheless, even within the Mīmāṃsā itself, in the foundational treatises (*ākaragrantha*), technical names for *adhikaraṇas* are designated here and there; furthermore, in the *Dharmaśāstra* and other fields, the conventional usage is exclusively by means of technical names.
Therefore, technical (paribhāṣika) names must necessarily be assigned.
Since some topics do not have a recognized technical name, in those cases a non-technical name is appropriate to be assigned; thus, there is an inclusion of both types.
Furthermore, here we shall provide a demonstration of the subject matter of each respective chapter and section (pāda), as well as a demonstration of the connection between the chapters and sections.
The demonstration of the connection between the topics (*adhikaraṇasaṃgati*) will occur in the commentary (*koṣa*) itself.
Of the Mīmāṃsā, which is an auxiliary limb (*upāṅga*) of the Veda, there are twenty-one chapters (*adhyāya*).
Among these, the final four chapters constitute a distinct treatise named Brahmamīmāṃsā; this is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the venerable and worshipful [Śaṅkara].

For this very reason, at the end of the Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa, there is a double repetition: "It exists, because it occurs at another time, as in the case of the *yājyā-saṃpreṣa*, as in the case of the *yājyā-saṃpreṣa*. Such a repetition of words and so forth does not occur in the *Ṣoḍaśalakṣaṇī*.

However, in the Brahma-mīmāṃsā, the repetition of words at the conclusion of the first, second, and third chapters is well known as indicating the end of those chapters, while the placement of the sūtra at the end of the fourth chapter is well known as indicating the conclusion of the entire treatise.
In this Dharmamīmāṃsā, however, there are sixteen chapters;
among them, the first consists of twelve chapters, known as the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇī*.
The four subsequent chapters constitute the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* (or *Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa*).
Within the twelve-chapter work (*Dvādaśalakṣaṇī*), the third, sixth, and tenth chapters each have eight sections (*caraṇas*), while the remaining chapters have four each.
In the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* as well, the first chapter likewise has exactly four sections.
In that regard, there are 936 topics (*adhikaraṇas*) in the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇī* through the summation of the *varṇaka*s and so forth, and 342 in the *Saṃkarṣa*. By summation, there are 1,278 topics.
However, in his own work titled *Mīmāṃsāsārasaṃgraha*, a treatise consisting of verses, Śrī Śaṅkarabhaṭṭa has demonstrated more than a thousand topics even within the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇī* alone.

For this very reason, in the *Nyāyanirṇaya*, his commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā*, Śrīmad Ānandagiri refers to the twelve-chapter work as the "Thousandfold Logic" (*Nyāyasāhasrī*). Furthermore, Sāyaṇa Mādhavācārya provides the names of the twelve chapters along with their respective subjects in a meaningful verse in the introduction to the *Nyāyavistara*: "Proof (*pramāṇa*), difference (*bheda*), subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*), application (*prayukti*), and order (*krama*);
Entitlement (*adhikāra*), extended application (*atideśa*), both in general and in particular."
Inference (ūha), sublation (bādha), the principal ritual (tantra), and the incidental application (prasaṅga) have been set forth in their proper order.
Thus [ends the summary]. In the first chapter, there is a definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the subject matter of Dharma.
In the second, there is a definition of the distinction and non-distinction of ritual acts (*karma*).

In the third [book], the relationship of subsidiary and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣi-bhāva*) is defined; in the fourth, the relationship of the employed and the employer (*prayojya-prayojaka-bhāva*); in the fifth, the order (*krama*); in the sixth, the qualification (*adhikāra*); in the seventh, extended application in general (*sāmānyātideśa*); in the eighth, specific extended application (*viśeṣātideśa*); in the ninth, modification (*ūha*); in the tenth, sublation (*bādha*); in the eleventh, the common ritual procedure (*tantra*) and its repetition (*āvāpa*); and in the twelfth, incidental application (*prasaṅga*).

Thus, the names of the chapters, beginning with "Means of Knowledge" (*pramāṇa*), are given as "The Definition of Means of Knowledge" (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), "The Definition of Distinction" (*bheda-lakṣaṇa*), and so forth.
This has been written by us for the purpose of demonstrating the twelve topics (*adhikaraṇa*) according to the sequence of their headings;
it will be printed here itself in the third volume of the *Mīmāṃsā-kośa*.

In truth, although there is no doubt that this will eventually be published at the end of the entire *Kośa*, nevertheless, as I enter my seventy-eighth year, it would not be right to wait for the completion of the whole *Mīmāṃsā-kośa*; therefore, its printing has been decided upon now.

In the preceding quarter, the order [of performance] was determined by means of *śruti* and other authorities. Now begins the third quarter of the fifth [book]. Just as in the two preceding quarters the order based on various constituent elements was considered, in this quarter the order based on repetition is considered; thus it constitutes a distinct quarter.

With respect to the sequence based on distinct entities, because the sequence produced by repetition is more subtle, both immediate succession (*ānantarya*) and non-immediate succession (*vi-prakṛṣṭatā*) are examined.

In the introduction [to the section], there is the determination of the number eleven (*aikādaśya*) regarding the repetition of the five *prayāja* offerings and so forth, as well as the determination of the absence of repetition (*anāvṛtti*) regarding the *adābhya* cup and the *citriya* sacrifice, and so on.
Sūtras 5.3.1–2 state that this principle applies to the *prayāja* offerings and the like.

And because that [offering] is connected with the deficiency of the substance mentioned in the preceding section, there is an immediate sequence to the subsequent section.

Now begins the sixth quarter (*pāda*) of the sixth chapter. Regarding the Soma sacrifice: in the preceding quarters, the qualification regarding the archetypal forms (*prakṛti*) was primarily investigated; here, however, the qualification regarding the modified forms (*vikṛti*) is primarily investigated. Thus, there is a sequence based on the distinction between different quarters.

6|6|3|16–23: Topic: In the *sattra* sacrifice, only Brāhmaṇas are entitled [to participate].

In the Caturhotṛ-homa and other such rites, there is no entitlement for one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni). This is the subject matter of the section.

Soma: Since it first ascends to the intellect of one whose mind is clear, an extended application (*atideśa*) based on that is to be formulated after deliberating upon the *pāda* [of the *sūtra*], as it would otherwise be purposeless; therefore, the delayed extended application by means of the *nāman* [name] is introduced in the third [section].

Now begins the ninth chapter. Bhāṣya: We shall now set forth the definition of *ūha* (modification). *Ūha* is threefold, pertaining to the domain of mantras, *sāmans*, and ritual preparations (*saṃskāra*).

other matters as well will be addressed by way of introduction and as a relevant digression.

Now begins the sixth quarter of the tenth chapter.

The distinction of this section [pāda] is due to the fact that here there is sublation (*bādha*) based on another injunction (*vidhyantara*), whereas previously it was based on the authority of a direct statement (*vacana*). Alternatively, the distinction of the section is because the sublation regarding the *Sāman* is primarily investigated here.

Furthermore, the connection with the subsequent section is well-established because, while in the previous case there was a lack of conformity even though it belonged to the same chapter (*adhyāya*), here it is stated that it belongs to the very first part of the chapter on sacrifice (*yajñādhyāya*).

Now, let it be understood that since the sublation (*bādha*) discussed here pertains to the *Soma* sacrifice consisting of a single day (*ekāha*), this constitutes a different section (*pādāntaratva*).

Now begins the eighth quarter of the tenth chapter.

Because the three types of *soma-bādha* (exclusion of Soma) have been described, and after the examination of the two unclear cases—namely, those based on the loss of purpose (*arthalopa*) and those not based on a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—there follows, in this section (*pāda*), the primary examination of the first type of exclusion (*atisṛṣṭa-pratiṣedha-nibandhana*).
Thus, there is a distinction between sections (*pādāntaratva*) for the sake of continuity (*ānantarya*).

Now begins the eleventh chapter. [Bhāṣya:
Now, the characteristics of *tantra* (extension) and *āvāpa* (insertion), which constitute the measure of application, are considered in the eleventh chapter based on the knowledge of those measures.

Since the determination of the extent of application regarding the matters taught and those extended by analogy, as well as the determination of the limits of restrictive rules (*avadhāraṇa*) and so forth, depends upon that [knowledge of measures], its commencement follows immediately after that.
Therefore,

the purpose of this section is to investigate whether the performance of common auxiliary rites for many actions— which are enjoined by a single injunction of application and which act in concert— is done *tantra*-wise (once), or by repetition (*āvṛtti*, i.e., *āvāpa*). Otherwise, it would not be possible to determine the exact extent of the constituent elements to be performed in the Soma sacrifices, both in their archetypal forms and their modified variants.

Therefore, the investigation here does not concern merely the enumeration of measures; rather, it concerns the relationship of cause and effect between the two results—namely, the determination of the number of ritual elements (*padārtha*) which is the fruit of the chapter on sublation (*bādhādhyāya*), and the means for that determination. Thus, this inquiry proceeds within the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The subject matter of the chapter is threefold: the system of results (*phalatantra*), the system of ritual elements (*padārthatantra*), and the system of performance (*anuṣṭhānatantra*).

Although the system is common to both direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*), nevertheless, sublation has the measure of subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) as its result, while the system has the measure of the performance (*prayoga*) as its result.

And so, after the *parimāṇa-phalaka* (the section concerning the measure) has been determined in the tenth book (*Daśama Adhyāya*), the eleventh [book] is considered because it shares the commonality of having the measure of application as its result; therein, the *tantra* (the principle of simultaneous performance) is examined.
Now, in the first quarter (*pāda*) of the eleventh [book], the introduction to *tantra* is described.

Now begins the second quarter (*pāda*) of the eleventh book.

In the preceding section (*pāda*), the principle of common performance (*tantratā*) regarding those elements whose purpose is solely the primary sacrifice was investigated. Here, however, the principle of common performance regarding those elements whose purpose serves both the subsidiaries and the primary sacrifice is investigated primarily; thus, it constitutes a different section (*pādāntaratva*).

Furthermore, because the principle of common performance regarding the performance itself is established here, its immediate succession to the principles of common performance regarding place and so forth should be understood.

Now begins the third quarter of the eleventh book.

In the preceding quarter, it was primarily established that factors such as time (*kāla*) and so forth function as *tantra* (common to all) with respect to both subsidiaries and primaries when they are not [specifically] restricted.

Now, as an exception (*apavāda*) to that, having introduced the case where the subsidiary and the primary have different times, the commonality (*tantratva*) of subsidiaries despite differences in place and time is being demonstrated; thus there is a change of quarters and no immediate sequence.

11.3.2: The establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) is the common framework (tantra) for all rites; it is not performed separately for each individual rite.

Now begins the fourth quarter (pāda) of the eleventh chapter.

In the first two quarters of this book (*soma*), where the distinctions and non-distinctions of place, time, and agent are explicit, the *tantrāvāpa* (common application and separate application) concerning those subjects have been examined.

Now, in the case where distinctions and non-distinctions are not explicit but must be understood through the presence or absence of *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee), the *tantrāvāpa* concerning that subject is considered; thus there is both a difference between the quarters and immediate succession.
In the third and fourth quarters, *āvāpa* is elaborated under the name of "examples" (*udāharaṇa*).
11|4|1–3: In the Rājasūya sacrifice, the subsidiary rites such as the Āgnāvaiṣṇava and others, which are associated with distinct sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), are to be performed separately.

Mīmāṃsākoṣa: Titles of Adhikaraṇas, Chapter 12.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Bhāṣya: Now the definition of *prasaṅga* (incidental application) is explained.
Dvup: Since [the performance of the *iṣṭi*] is established through the principle of *tantrāvāpa* (shared performance), this twelfth chapter is commenced as an exception (*apavāda*) to that.
A different kind of "extent" (iyattā) arises through *prasaṅga*.
O Soma, although *tantra* is also a relationship between cause and effect, nevertheless, the determination of *prasaṅga* depends upon the determination of *tantra*.

Consequently, since the *prayāja* and other such rites possess a specific nature as being consumed, and since the *tantra*—characterized by assisting multiple primary acts with a single place, time, and agent—is established even when the specific details are being grasped, it is possible for one thing to be an assistant to many. Therefore, because *prasaṅga* is the cause for determining [the application] here, its immediate succession is appropriate.

In reality, however, even a *prasaṅga* (extended application) is not possible without the non-difference of place (*deśa*) and other factors; thus, since *tantra* (common performance) depends upon place and so forth, it should be understood that even between *tantra* and *prasaṅga*, a relationship of cause and effect is possible.
Now begins the first quarter of the twelfth chapter:
Section 12.1.1–2, concerning the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
12.1.3–7: The principle of the *pauroḍāśika* sacrifice; 12.1.8–9: The principle of the *saumika* altar;

12.1.10–11: *Prasaṅga* (extension/application): [the rule that] in the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the sacrificial ladles (*juhū*) and other implements belonging to the *dākṣiṇā* [sacrifice] are not used for the *savanīya-puroḍāśa* and other offerings, because they are already provided with the vessels belonging to the *saumika* [sacrifice].

12.1.17 The principle of staying awake. 12.1.18 In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, during the southern sacrificial area (dakṣiṇavihāra), the mantras must be held separately by the Pratiprasthātṛ priest.
12.1.19 The establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) need not be performed in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice for the sake of the initiatory offerings (dīkṣaṇīyā) and subsequent rites.

12|1|24-28: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the *agnyādhāna* (establishment of the sacred fires) need not be performed even for the purpose of securing the deities (*devatā-parigraha*) during the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and subsequent rites. 12|1|29: There is accomplishment through *prasaṅga*; the *patnīsaṃyājana* (rite involving the wives) at the Soma-pressing (*adhiṣavaṇa*) is accomplished by the *patnīsaṃyājana* belonging to the Soma sacrifice itself.

12.1.30 The principle of eating forest-grown food (*āraṇyabhojananyāya*). 12.1.31–32 The non-establishment of incidental proof (*prasaṅgasiddhi*); the consumption of the *saumika* vow-food is not [included] among the consumption of the remnants of the *aiṣṭika* sacrifice. 12.1.33 The principle of the *saumika* sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
12.1.34: There is no application of the *saumikī dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee of the Soma sacrifice) to the portions consumed as remnants of the *agniṣṭoma*.

12.1.46–47: The section concerning the mantras for joining and carrying [the sacrificial post].
Now begins the second quarter (pāda) of the twelfth chapter.

Soma: In the preceding section (*pāda*), since a word occurs within the middle of a *tantra*, the application (*prasaṅga*) of its suffixes (*ājñā*) therein was established as being equal to that which arises from the middle of a *tantra*. Now, the application (*prasaṅga*) which does not fall within the middle of a *tantra* is primarily expounded; thus, there is a difference between the sections (*pādāntaratva*). Furthermore, when there is occurrence within the middle of a *tantra*, the application arises immediately (*ānantarya*); however, in its absence, it arises with delay.
12.2.1–7: The Section on the Vihāra (Separation).
12.2.8–10: In the Savanīya animal sacrifice, the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) must be offered.
12.2.11: In the Savanīya cakes, there is no invocation of the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation).

12|2|14–18: The principle of the midnight offering (*niśīthinyāya*).
12|2|19–21: The re-performance of the *ārambhaṇīyā* rite in the modified forms (*vikṛti*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, such as the *saurya* sacrifice and others.
12|2|22 The principle of further favor (*bhūyo'nugraha-nyāya*). 12|2|23–24 The principle of the offering to Agni and Viṣṇu (*āgnāvaiṣṇava-nyāya*).
12|2|25 The principle of the conflict between the subordinate and the quality (*aṅgaguṇavirodha-nyāya*).

12|2|26: In the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices involving animal offerings (*pāśuka*), when the characteristics of both the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are not present, the performance [of the former] does not take place.

12|2|27–29: In the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices involving animal offerings, when there is a conflict between the specific characteristics of the enclosing stick (*paridhi*) and those of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the characteristics of the post are not to be performed.
12|2|30–32: The principle of the *savanīya* and other [offerings].

12.2.33: When the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*) share the same ritual procedure (*samānatantra*), the requirements of the archetype are fulfilled by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*) through the procedure of the ectype. This is a hypothetical investigation (*kṛtvācintā*). 12.2.34: The principle of the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice (*āgrayaṇeṣṭinyāya*).

12.2.35: In the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, there is no restriction regarding the Vaiśvadeva ritual procedure based on the [precedent of] the Aindravaiśvadeva offerings, due to the specific nature of the earth-offering. This is the principle of the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi (the second).

Now begins the third quarter of the twelfth chapter. Regarding Soma: now the discussion on *prasaṅga* (incidental application) is introduced by means of the combination (*samuccaya*) of modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*). And in this quarter, *samuccaya* is primarily expounded.

Furthermore, because this section concludes with the determination of exceptions (*apavāda*) following from the preceding discussion (*prasaṅga*), it constitutes a separate chapter (*pādāntaratva*) and follows immediately after the previous one (*ānantarya*).
In this chapter, there is an investigation into the combination (*samuccaya*) of options (*vikalpa*) regarding indistinct objects.
[Sūtras 12.3.1–2] In the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, there is a combination of the *vāsas* (garment) belonging to the *agrāyaṇa* cup and the *vāsas* belonging to the *vasatīvarī* water.
12.3.3–8: The Section on the Irrevocable (*anivārya-adhikaraṇam*).
12.3.9: The combination (*samuccaya*) of qualities with distinct functions within a single ritual action.
12.3.10–15: The Section on Optionality (*vikalpa-adhikaraṇam*).
12.3.16: There is an optionality among expiatory rites intended for the determination of specific faults. 12.3.17: The section concerning their cumulative application (*samuccaya*).
12.3.18–19: Even during periods when study is prohibited (*anadhyāya*), etc., there is the employment of mantras at the time of performing the ritual action.
12.3.20–22: The Section on the Accentuation of Colloquial Speech (*bhāṣāsvarādhikaraṇa*).
12.3.23–24: In a sacrifice, the colloquial accent (*bhāṣika-svara*) should be employed for those mantras originating from the Brāhmaṇas.
12.3.25: How is the commencement of the ritual action performed at the end of a mantra within the mantras?
12.3.26–27: In the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) during the *vasordhārā* offering, the commencement of the ritual action coincides with the end of the mantra.

12.3.28: In the foundational rite (*ādhāra*), the commencement of the ritual action coincides with the end of the mantra. 12.3.29: There is an option (*vikalpa*) among the instrumental mantras that serve a single purpose.
12.3.30: There is a combination (samuccaya) of the mantras prescribed by number in the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana).

12.3.31–35: There is an option (vikalpa) regarding the mantras enjoined in the Brāhmaṇa. 12.3.36–38: There is a combination (samuccaya) of the mantras belonging to the office of the Hotṛ priest (hautra).
Now begins the fourth quarter of the twelfth chapter.

Regarding the Soma sacrifice: following the consideration of the combination and option of rites concerning non-evident objects, there is a consideration of those same matters regarding evident objects; hence it constitutes a different quarter and follows immediately after the previous one. (12.4.1–2) In the case of mantras that contain prayers for equal blessings, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of their recitations (*japa*).
12|4|3–4: An option between two pairs of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras in the ritual dedicated to Indra and Bṛhaspati.
12|4|5–7: The principle of the purchase of Soma (*somakrayanyāya*). 12|4|8: The principle of the secondary, the auxiliary, and the principal (*upaśayājudasamukhyanyāya*).
12.4.9: There is an option regarding the number of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) at the *āghāna* ceremony.
12.4.10–16: In a group of eleven or more animals, there is an option regarding the tails (*jāghanī*) used in the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
12.4.17–25: The taking of the fire in the pan (*ukhya agni*) by means of a desirable fire consisting of a burning tree-top and so forth, as part of the *agnicayana* ritual.

12|4|26–27: The fire for a desired rite (*kāmyāgni*) taken from the top of a burning tree as prescribed in the section on the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) does not possess the status of the *āhavanīya* fire.

12|4|28–29: For the fire for a desired rite taken from the top of a burning tree as prescribed in the piling of the fire-altar, there is an omission of the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as the formal installation (*ādhāna*).
12|4|30–31: The fire in the pan (*ukhya-agni*) belonging to the piling of the fire-altar is not to be maintained permanently.

12|4|32: In both the *satra* and *ahīna* sacrifices, the rites beginning with the *śukrānvārambhaṇa* are to be performed by a single sacrificer (*yajamāna*). 12|4|33: In the *ahīna*, the rites beginning with the *śukrānvārambhaṇa* must be performed by some one sacrificer.
12|4|34: In the *satra*, the rites beginning with the *śukrānvārambhaṇa* must necessarily be performed by the *gṛhapati* (the householder).
12|4|35–41: In the *sattra* sacrifice, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the sacrificers are for the benefit of all sacrificers.

This is the sequence of the headings of the sections (*adhikaraṇa-śīrṣaka*) in the *Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa*.
[Just now, the headings of the twelve sections (*adhikaraṇa*) of the *Pūrva* [Mīmāṃsā-sūtra] have been presented according to the order of recitation.
Now, in order to remedy the deficiency, the headings of the sections of the *Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa* are presented according to the order of recitation.
These headings are found at the beginning of the written manuscript of the *Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa*.]
These very [topics] will be presented here, refined by means of certain changes in wording and by filling in omissions;

it should be understood that the first four chapters from the thirteenth onward will be shown therein using numbers one, two, and four respectively. Furthermore, the numbers here will indicate the chapter (*adhyāya*), the quarter (*pāda*), and the section (*adhikaraṇa*).
The headings of the topics (*adhikaraṇa-śīrṣaka*) from the [Treatise] on the Sixteen Characteristics (*Ṣoḍaśalakṣaṇī*) are also set forth hereafter in alphabetical order:
1.1.1: The injunction regarding the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call (*anuvaṣaṭkāra-vidhi*). 1.1.2: The substance for the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed the remnant of the preceding [offering].

1|1|12 The *śamitṛ* (the immolator) is one and the same.

Mīmāṃsākośa 7.

1|1|13 The Piṇḍapitṛyajña for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni) should be performed in the Aupāsana fire.

1|4|32: The direction "Strew with the carriers" (*vāhaiḥ stṛṇīhi*) is intended for the sake of the *soma*.
1|4|33 In the passage “May you separate according to your respective portions,” only the two sacrificial cakes (*piṇḍa*) are to be addressed.
1|4|34 In the passage “This is for Agni; this is for Agni and Soma,” the designation of the deities refers specifically to the two distinct cakes.
1|4|35 In a group of sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), the modification (*ūha*) must be made as follows: “May you separate according to your respective portions.”

Section headings in alphabetical order [57];
section headings in alphabetical order.

[From here onwards, the headings of the topics (*adhikaraṇa-śīrṣaka*) found in the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇī* and those found in the four sections (*caturlakṣaṇī*) of the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* are combined and arranged according to alphabetical order.]

In this regard, although the headings (*śīrṣaka*) were originally arranged according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), the principal terms therein are first presented, and the remaining words are then rearranged accordingly; they are inserted by doubling the original extent compared to the previous arrangement. It should be noted that it is not intended for the ancient texts to remain solely in their original written form. This being the case, the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) may be obtained through various methods as desired.

Although the four chapters of the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* should actually be indicated by the numbers 13–16, we have nevertheless designated the chapters as 1, 2, 3, and 4. Where the term "Saṃkarṣa. is placed at the beginning of a number, that heading belongs to the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*, and therein the chapter, pāda, and adhikaraṇa numbers are inserted. However, where only the numbers are inserted without the word "Saṃkarṣa," the heading should be understood as belonging to the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇī*.

In this [work], only the chapter (adhyāya), section (pāda), and topic (adhikaraṇa) numbers are indicated; the sūtra numbers have not been included. Regarding the order of the letters of the three components, however, it should be observed that in the introduction to the third part, the first method—which consists of a simple alphabetical order—was adopted, rather than the second, which follows the tradition of the school (śākhā). The Aśvadāma sacrifice is both optional (kāmya) and obligatory (nitya) by virtue of its distinct connection (saṃyogapṛthaktva).
