10.6.21) In both cases, because of drinking from both, [it is] speckled butter. (12.18)
"If both [meanings] were intended to be expressed, the sentence would be contradicted" (Bhāṣya 2.2.12.27, p.
557). This is the maxim "a rope with a noose on both ends";
it applies when there are defects in both positions.

The form *svāśā* should be understood as derived either from the root *spaś* belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*, meaning "to touch," or from the root *spaś* belonging to the *curādigaṇa*, meaning "to seize" or "to contract. This is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the two rules: "A rope has loops on both sides" (*saupabhayataḥ pāśā rajjur bhavati*) and "After a long vowel, the suffixes *su*, *ti*, and *si*, when not followed by another consonant, are elided" (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*).

However, the form *pāśā* ending in *ṭā* (i.e., *pāśā*) without the *s*-suffix, as in the expression "a rope with loops on both sides" (*ubhayataḥ pāśā rajjuḥ*), is indeed incorrect, because it contradicts the aforementioned *Mahābhāṣya*.
Because of the lexicographical definition "the word *pāśa* [is used] in the senses of 'noose' (*bandhana*) and 'word' (*śabda*)," the word *pāśa* is masculine.

(However, this is incorrect; for even though the word *pāśa* is masculine, in the compound *ubhayataḥ-pāśāḥ*, the entire compound can properly take a feminine gender because it functions as an adjective qualifying a rope (*rajju*) via a *bahuvrīhi* construction. It must be stated, however, that the substitution [of *ā* for *a*] would not occur.)
Thus [it is] absolute.

Just as a deer or other animal, having entered a snare or rope set at both ends for the purpose of catching it, is unable to go away by any path whatsoever—so it is with the *sāhasī*. (406) Furthermore, the state of being an *atirātra* on both sides is in some cases an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of its being a *satra*.
The gift of animals with teeth in both jaws, such as horses and the like, is not [permitted] in the Viśvajit sacrifice.

Bhāṣya 6.7.3.4: Among the Northerners, the giving, receiving, and selling of those with teeth in both jaws—namely, the giving of such animals as horses—is improper conduct. (The giving of those animals, such as horses, which have teeth in both jaws.)

Or [it may be argued]: because both are drunk, the curd (*dadhi*) should also be indicated by the term *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter), since in the *nigamas* (invocatory formulas) the act of drinking is used as an indicator.

In the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "He performs the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) with *pṛṣadājya*. And in the archetype (*prakṛti*), one observes in the invocation formula (*āvāhana-nigada*): "Bring the gods who drink the clarified butter (*ājyapa*)."
And that [procedure] is obtained here by the rule of extension (*codaka*).
Regarding the inquiry as to how the specific direction (*nirdeśa*) should be made therein, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

"When *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter) is the oblation, should there be a mention of both the curd and the butter in the ritual formulas (*nigama*), such that one must say, 'O drinkers of curd and butter, come hither'? Why? Because both are drunk—since both the curd and the butter are offered with reference to the deity—and because in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the act of drinking serves as the basis for the designation."
In this case as well, since both [the curd and the ghee] are subject to falling, it is logical that both should be indicated.
Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that one should say "of the curd and the ghee-drinkers.
But it is not so, because they exist for the sake of another, due to their status as lords of the sacrifice (yajñapati).

The word "or" (vā) in the sūtra sets aside the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) that has been reached. It is not the case that both [the agent and the object] need to be expressed, because [the suffixes] serve another purpose; namely, they serve as indicators (upalakṣaṇa) for the substance that is to be caused to fall.
In that case, once the drinkers of the clarified butter (*ājyapa*) have been characterized by one [mantra], it is redundant for another to characterize them.

This is because of the status of being the "lord of the sacrifice" (*yajñapati*), just as in the archetype ritual regarding the *iḍā* offering, in the passage "those who [protect] this sacrifice and those who increase the lord of the sacrifice," the term "lord of the sacrifice" is used for the sake of bestowing [benefits] upon human priests, not for its own sake; it is employed according to the principle that [words] are used in their primary sense unless otherwise restricted.
Therefore, one should simply say "the gods who drink the clarified butter," and not "the gods who drink curd and clarified butter."
Or rather, it may refer to the invocation (āvāhana), because it is for that purpose.

It would also be an elliptical designation (upalakṣaṇa) for the curd; one should have said "curd and ghee-drinkers," because the invocation is for that purpose, namely, for the sake of reminding the deities of the drinking.
In that case, although there is already a vessel, there is also something else to be drunk.

Therefore, for the sake of following the injunction (*codaka*), another drink—curd (*dadhi*)—should be indicated as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇya*). Consequently, it should be stated as "the drinking of curd and clarified butter" (*dadhyājyapān*).
Thus, again, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
"Or rather not, because it is a word denoting a consecration (*saṃskāra*). By means of the word "or" (*vā*), the proponent (*siddhāntin*) sets aside the doubt and speaks.
It must not be said that curd is not an indicator [of the substance].
Since "curd" is a term denoting a preparatory refinement (*saṃskāra*), *pṛṣadājya* is clarified butter (*ājya*) characterized by the refinement of speckles (*pṛṣat*).
And this refinement in the form of speckles is produced by means of curd.
Therefore, the word denoting the curd and the speckled quality serves as the primary meaning.
The curd is for the sake of another [rite], not for being poured out.
Consequently, the curd is not to be characterized [as a mere subordinate element].
Or rather, it may be so, because of the mention of the substance;
that is, it would be an indication of the curd—thus the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) speaks again.
"Because of the mention of the substance" means because of the mention of the substance which is the primary element.
"In he takes the *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter); this substance consists of both clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) and curd (*dadhi*). Thus, the curd is mentioned as being equal to the clarified butter.
Therefore, one should say "the drinkers of curd and clarified butter" (*dadhyājyapān*).

However, because the curd is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), the cows should be called "drinkers of clarified butter" (*ājyapāḥ*), since the scriptural statement (*śruti*) establishes the primacy of the clarified butter.
Dispelling a doubt with the word "tu" (but), the proponent says:
"The *ājyapā*-invocations (*nigama*) should be used. This means that the invocations containing the word "ājya" (clarified butter) should be the *ājyapā*-invocations.

One should say, "Bring the gods who drink the clarified butter (ājyapān)," and not "Bring the gods who drink curd and clarified butter (dadhyājyapān)," because the curd is subordinate. As for the statement, "He takes the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya)"; this substance is indeed just clarified butter and curd combined.

Regarding the mixture of clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*) from both [milk and curds], because of the statement "when there is an equalization of both," it follows that the curd is equal to the clarified butter (*ājya*) and thus constitutes the primary substance.
That is not so.
For in the act of taking up [the substance], that [curd] is equal to the clarified butter (ājya), but not in the sacrifice.
Indeed, the sacrifice is heard to be performed with variegated clarified butter in the scriptural injunction: "He sacrifices with speckled clarified butter" (*pṛṣadājyena yajati*).
Because this scriptural statement has clarified butter as its primary element, the curd possesses the status of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), not the status of a primary element (*pradhāna*).
Therefore, curd should not be treated as a mere secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Alternatively, curd may be the primary element in the clarified butter (*ājya*), because of its connection with both the first and the last [offerings].
In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He performs the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) with speckled clarified butter (*pṛṣadājya*)."
And in the case of the *ubhayasāman* [rite], it is like the *viśvajit*;
in the *ubhayasāman* [rite] such as the *saṃsava*, there is a combined application (*samuccaya*) of the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* [sāmans] specifically in the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*.
And in the *ubhayasāman*, it is thus because of the attainment of a single purpose.
The *saṃsava*, *gosava*, and *apaciti* sacrifices are rituals characterized by both *sāmans*.
In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the properties of the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara* are already present and are extended here by the force of the injunction (*codaka*).

Regarding this, in the inquiry as to whether both sets of properties should be performed in a ritual possessing both *sāmans*, or whether there is a fixed restriction (*vyavasthā*), the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In a sacrifice such as the *saṃsava*, where both the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* are used as *sāmans* (the "ubhayasāman"), the characteristics of both should apply, just as in the case of the *Kaṇvarathantara* mentioned in the preceding section.
This is because both the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara* result in the same purpose, namely the performance of the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*.
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "in the *Kaṇvarathantara* and in the *saṃsava*, etc. serves to include both cases.
By the word "evaṃ" (thus), only the state of possessing both properties (*ubhayadharmatva*) is to be understood.
Alternatively, there may be a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) based on its own specific purpose, as in the case of the *prakṛti* sacrifice.

Having set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that in sacrifices such as the *saṃsava* and *gosava*, where both *sāmans* are employed, the properties of both the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* must be performed—the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of the word "va" (or).

The ritual properties (dharmas) of both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara should not be performed when they are combined; rather, there should be a fixed allocation such that the Rathantara-properties apply to the Rathantara and the Bṛhat-properties apply to the Bṛhat. This is because these properties serve their own specific purposes: the Rathantara-properties are for the sake of the Rathantara, and the Bṛhat-properties are for the sake of the Bṛhat. Furthermore, these properties belong to the two Sāmans, not to the Pṛṣṭha-stotra.
Therefore, when the Rathantara is employed, the properties of the Rathantara should be performed; and when the Bṛhat is employed, the properties of the Bṛhat [should be performed].
Thus, there is a fixed determination of the properties, just as in the archetype (prakṛti). "As in the archetype" means like in the original model.
This is the established conclusion (siddhānta). [Question:
In what cases? [Answer: In the case of the *ubhayasāman*, there should be an optional contingent rite (*naimittika*) because of its equality;
for in the *saṃsava*, *gosava*, *apaciti*, and so forth, it is heard in scripture: "One should perform both the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*."
It is heard in the scripture that two separate rites based on the *rathaṃtara* and the *bṛhat* [sāmans] are to be performed:
"One should use a *pratipad* containing the word *upara* for a sacrifice having the *rathaṃtara-pṛṣṭha*, and one containing the word *agni* for a sacrifice having the *bṛhat-pṛṣṭha*.
The verse "We sing near you" (*upāsme gāyat*) contains the word *upa*, and the verse "The yoked voices of Agni" (*prayujo vāco agniyaḥ*) contains the word *agni*.

This being the case, when both *sāmans*—the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathantara*—are present in a performance such as the *Saṃsava*, since two fixed *pratipads* would apply to both equally and their simultaneous combination is impossible, the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie view) is that the selection of the *pratipad* occasioned by the *Bṛhat* and that occasioned by the *Rathantara* should be performed alternatively.
Alternatively, it should be restricted by the principal [element].
Now, he states another alternative view:
The *upavatī* opening verse (*pratipad*) should be restricted by the *rathantara*, which is the primary one studied first;
primacy is the reason for this definitive selection.
Therefore, in a sacrifice where both *sāmans* are employed, the *upavatī* opening verse occasioned by the *rathantara* is to be adopted.

The word "vā" (or) serves to exclude the alternative view. Or rather, because the cause [for the application] is established, the ritual act should belong to that which is connected with the sacrifice. He states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Because of the mutual exclusion—due to the contradiction between the *nimitta* (the causal condition) of the *rathantara* and the *bṛhat* [sāmans]—it is impossible to adopt or employ both the *upavatī* and the *agniyavatī* as the *pratipad*.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there should be the recitation of some mantra connected to the sacrifice, which has the mere *pṛṣṭha* [sāman] as its *nimitta*, serving as the *pratipad*.
The word "or" (*vā*) serves to exclude the alternative position.

In a sacrifice characterized by both *sāmans*—such as the *saṃsava*, *gosava*, and *apaciti*—there should be a division between the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* like that in the *viśvajit*. Just as in the *viśvajit* with all *pṛṣṭha* stotras, one *rathaṃtara* enters into the function of the *pṛṣṭha* while the others enter into the function of the *parisāman*, so too in the *saṃsava* and other such rites, one of the two should be assigned to the function of the *pṛṣṭha* and the other to the function of the *parisāman*; this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Or it is for the sake of the *pṛṣṭha* [laud], because it has that as its purpose.
The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
There is no division of the two *sāmans*.
Rather, both Sāmans should serve the purpose of the subsequent rite;
for that is the purpose of the injunction "one should employ both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara," since it concerns the Sāmans themselves.
Therefore, both are enjoined as embellishments (*saṃskāra*) of the *ṛc*.
Both [chants] are to be sung upon those very same verses;
this is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
Furthermore, because the injunction is for the whole, the sublation of the extended application (codaka) is not a fault.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

In the *saṃsava* and *gosava* sacrifices where both *sāmans* are used, both the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara* perform the function of the *pṛṣṭha* chant, as is evident from the observation of an indicative mark.

From the statement regarding the difference in the *nidhana*—"The *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* indeed have a great *pṛṣṭha*; the sacrifice is completed when the *nidhana* is reached; it is not brought together if there is no great *pṛṣṭha*, for there would be confusion here"—this indicative mark shows that they occupy a single location.

Likewise, another indicative mark is the statement, "The *rathaṃtara* is indeed the forenoon, and the *bṛhat* is the afternoon," which shows their co-location due to their connection with a single day.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that both are to be placed in the position of the *pṛṣṭha*.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "Having consecrated [the fire], he subsequently offers the Vaimṛdha cake at the Paurṇamāsī.

Regarding this, there arises an inquiry: Is the Vaimṛdha an auxiliary to both sacrifices, with its connection to the Paurṇamāsī serving merely to indicate the time, or is it connected to both through the distinct purposes of the two parts?
In this discussion, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view is as follows: the Vaimṛdha is for the sake of both; that is, it is an auxiliary to the Darśa and an auxiliary to the Paurṇamāsa.
If it is argued that [this applies] because it is recited in the context of both,
we say no, because the word is one and the same.
When the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been established by the preceding sūtra, he refutes it:
the *Vaimṛdha* is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to both [the New and Full Moon sacrifices].
This is because of the unity of the word; that is, because the injunctive term "he offers subsequently" (*anunirvapati*) is singular.
For in a single sentence, one word cannot simultaneously enjoin a connection for the *vaimṛdha* sacrifice with both the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and the time of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).
Therefore, the *ulūkhala* and *musala* are not auxiliary parts of both; [rather], there is the upward-singing (*ūrdhvagāna*) of the two.

If this [Smṛti] were not preceded by human intellect and were equal to the Veda, then it would be accepted;
but if it were composed by a person, then it is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And where that which is not intended to be performed should not be employed;
yet there is the word "intended to be performed" (cikīrṣita). Therefore, modification (ūha) is obligatory.
That [view] has the aforementioned defect.
Commentary: This statement of yours is subject to the aforementioned defect. By you yourself, while describing the reason, this defect has been stated: "the modification (ūha) is intended.
And this [statement] that "the modification is intended" applies to that which is non-eternal (anitya).
As it has been said: "The word *cikīrṣita* occurs when something is desired; for the suffix *san* is prescribed in the sense of desire.
It is replied: True, it is desired to do [it], provided that it is actually performed; only then does it become something desired to be done.
Therefore, Āditya says:
As for what was stated— that [the practice] is established by tradition (smṛti)— this tradition is not an authoritative means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
For this [application] has its root in direct observation.
Indeed, there is a scriptural statement: "He sings the Rathantara upon the kavatī verses.
Therefore, because of this statement of extended application (atideśa), it must be sung according to the very principle [of the original]; thus, the first cognition is based on the explicit word.
Regarding this, there is this traditional teaching (smṛti):
"Therefore, it is not authoritative; the modification (ūha) is artificial.
What is the purpose [of this discussion]? It is so that even that which contradicts logic may be considered authoritative, as was the case in the prima facie argument (pūrva-pakṣa).

If, then, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that what contradicts logic is invalid (*apramāṇa*), [the opponent] objects—(criticizing the *siddhānta* stated in the Bhāṣya)—"that which has been stated as having the aforementioned defect.
How so? [The example is: "One sings the *rathaṃtara* on the *kavatī* verses. Because of its presence in the *kavatī* verses, it is not something produced (*akṛtaka*).
The *rathaṃtara* chant itself is certainly not artificial. Even the extended injunction, "One sings the *rathaṃtara* on the *kavatī* verses," is likewise not artificial.
Therefore, we do not perceive anything artificial whatsoever in the treatise on modification (*ūhagrantha*).
To this it is replied:
regarding the *rathaṃtara* chant being sung upon the *kavati* verses, the first effort made by a person toward the production of the melody is artificial (*kṛtaka*).

While the *rathaṃtara* melody is observed in the *abhilāvī* verse through direct scriptural recitation (*samāmnāya*), it is applied to other [verses]—namely, the *kavatis*—by virtue of the power of extended application (*atideśa*).

Just as the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) by living beings is something produced (*kṛtaka*), so too here, the performance of the *rathaṃtara* [sāman] in the *kavatī* verses is performed by a person himself due to the force of the injunction, and is not established by the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*).
Soma [says]: "The meaning of the sūtra is that some consider the *sāmans*—namely the *ūha-sāmans* which have become mantras—to be non-eternal.
The *Ūha-grantha* is of human origin; [it is] the motivator of *ūha*.
[The objection]: "Is this *ūha* text of human origin or not?
The first [alternative] follows because it is similar to the *Sāman* chants of the Vedas; the latter [alternative] follows from the force of the injunction.

[Bhāṭṭa]: Or rather, when considering whether this specific type of text called *ūha*, which is recited by the Sāma singers, is of human origin or not of human origin, the reasons for the non-human origin of the Veda—namely, the absence of any memory of an author—are equally applicable here as well.

Otherwise, because that [reason] would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), even the Veda would fail to attain the status of being authorless (*apauruṣeya*). Furthermore, the preservation of the study and teaching of one's own recitation (*svādhyāya*) is equal [in both cases], and the designation "ūha" can also be understood as a conventional term (*rūḍha*). Otherwise, if one were to accept authorship merely on the basis of a designation despite the absence of a remembered author, then the Veda itself would incur the status of being authored due to designations such as "Kāṭhaka" and so forth. Therefore, the *ūha* text is authorless.

This being the position reached, [we reply]: since the designation is justified by the very nature of reasoning (*tarka*)—as per the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that "ūha means deliberation" (*vitarka*)—there is no evidence for it being a conventional term (*rūḍhi*).

Furthermore, in the *Ūhagrantha* (the section on modification), after extending the application (*atideśa*) from the *Yonigāna* (the source-text) via such statements as "he sings it not according to the source," "he sings it on the subsequent verses," and so forth, the texts are recited there for the sake of ease, even though they ought to be recited in the *Nidhana* and other sections.

Furthermore, since the status of being a *yoni* (source-text) for all Sāmans in general is unestablished, it would follow that the extension (*atideśa*) of the status of being an *uttarā* and so forth to those [Sāmans] would be impossible; thus, such an attempt would result in futility. Therefore, the very fact of there being no remembrance of an author—qualified by the absence of any stronger evidence proving authorship—is what establishes the lack of authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*). Consequently, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) [in our argument]. And although the *ṛc*s and *sāmans* situated therein are indeed non-authored (*apauruṣeya*) in their essential form, nevertheless, the method of composing the specific *sāman*s in the *uttarā*s and so forth, as established by logical principle, is authored (*pauruṣeya*).

For this very reason, the observance of rules regarding days suitable for study (*svādhyāya*) and those unsuitable (*anadhyāya*), and so forth, is established as otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*), since these pertain specifically to the *Ṛgveda* and other such texts.
Furthermore, the absence of a recollection of an author is also explained by the absence of any need to postulate a foundational scripture (*mūlaśruti*).
For in the case of the Smṛtis concerning mantras and the like, a recollection of an author is necessary in order to postulate a specific scripture as the source for those mantras and other elements.
In the present case, however, because it is rooted in logic (*nyāyamūlaka*), there is no harm to the mind even in its absence.

For this very reason, when there is a conflict with a general principle (*sāmānyanyāya*), this [particular rule] lacks authority; it does not, like other *smṛtis*, lead to the postulation of a foundational *śruti* by merely casting the principle itself into a semblance (*ābhāsīkaraṇa*).
It is for this reason that the subsequent discussion regarding the principle concerning the *Sāman* chants is also consistent.
Maṇḍana: "The *ūha* (adaptation) is performed by means of the three [Vedas].
Śaṅkara: "The *ūha*-text would not be eternal.

The Grammarians maintain that grammar is also for the sake of the knowledge of *ūha*, according to the statement: "Protection (*rakṣā*), adaptation (*ūha*), traditional addition (*āgama*), brevity (*laghu*), and absence of doubt (*asaṃdeha*) are the purposes [of grammar]."
The Mahābhāṣya.
Regarding this, the author of the Mīmāṃsā-vārttika says: "Even for the sake of modification (*ūha*), grammar is not purposeful when there is doubt;
for modification is established from other sources as well, and thus there is no distinction between what is modified and what is not."

Just as the distinction between *ūha* (modification) and *anūha* (non-modification) does not depend on grammar because it is established by Mīmāṃsā, so too the very nature of *ūha* is established in both the world and the Veda; this is the meaning.
Su., page 209.
The means of knowledge consisting of modification (*ūha*), known as "displacement from its place" (*sthānāpatti*), is one [of the six means].
Maṇi, p. 13. The eleven types of factors that necessitate modification (*ūhaprayojaka*) are now described.
As it has been said: "That which serves the primary purpose, that which serves two purposes, that which is impossible for itself, and that which is possible for another."

The motivator of modification (*ūhaprayojaka*) indicates the function of the word *girā*—namely, the words for the *pravara*, the name, and so forth—by means of the rule: "One should not say *girā-girā*. (4)

For when the word *irā* is prohibited, its function is indicated as being desirous of a means; and since that [function] is thus indicated, there is an injunction for the word *irā* which is itself desirous of the goal to be accomplished. Indeed, the sentence cannot enjoin the word *irā* as a means to that [function] unless it is [itself] a word that expresses the function.

For there can be no syntactic unity between that which is not expressed by words and that which is expressed by words; therefore, in this case, it is an inference from its own word (*svaśabdānumāna*).
However, the distinction is that in the case of the *paridhi*, its own word is indeed directly recited in the scripture.

(5) "One should offer at this time when speech occurs, namely when the six-day period consisting of *pṛṣṭha* chants is completed"—by means of this completion (*saṃsthā*), a prohibition is indicated, for that which has been completed is not something to be performed. And by this prohibition, as before, the action [of offering] is indicated.
Once that is indicated, the *maghavan-saṃpratiṣṭhāna* is enjoined.
Thus, in this case, the word "own" (*sva*) functions through *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* (indication by indication).
This example of "the consumption of clarified butter" (*ghṛtāśana*) has been refuted by the author of the Vārttika.
For "completion" (*saṃsthā*) means termination; there can be no completion of what has not occurred, nor can there be the non-existence of what has already been completed.

Therefore, since it is understood from both the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the syntactical connection (*vākya*) that [the two acts] are purificatory rites for a man who has performed the *ṣaḍaha* sacrifice, how could they possibly be for the sake of the fruit of the *ṣaḍaha*?
Consequently, it was stated that one must search for another example;
and regarding that, we say the following:

In the sixth [section] (6.1.11), it was stated regarding the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit for the purpose of recovering a stolen cow": since the term *āgoraṇa* denotes the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to steal, the Viśvajit occurs for one who performs the Viśvajit-sacrifice when that resolve exists, not for one who does not perform it.
Therefore, this is an illustration of an injunction [applying] in the absence [of the primary motive].
Thus concludes the exposition of the eleven types of factors that necessitate modification (*ūha*).
There is no status as mantra for the *ūha*, *pravara*, and names.
"Those not recited in the tradition are not mantras, for the distinction [of mantras] applies only to those recited in the tradition.
Commentary: Regarding *ūha*, *pravara*, and names, there is a doubt: are they mantras or not?
They are mantras because they are expressive.
This being the position, we reply:
in the case of those [texts] not mentioned [in the Vedic corpus], there can be no status as *mantra* even though they possess denotative power.
Denotative power is not the cause for the status of a *mantra*; what then? It is their application in a specific ritual context (*abhimuktaprayoga*).
Those which are not called "mantras" by the learned are not mantras;
furthermore, such things as these do not exist in the collection of mantras (mantrasāmnāya).
Therefore, they are excluded.

The purpose [of this discussion] is that whatever expiation (prāyaścitta) is prescribed for a mantra being omitted, it applies there even when no mantra is present—or rather, there is an adaptation (ūha), such as: "I offer what is pleasing to Sūrya.
Likewise, where the lineage of the sacrificer (ārṣeya) is recited, that is the pravara.
That in which there is the mention of the names of the sacrificer, his body, and so forth, is a name-designation (*nāmadheya*), as in the *Subrahmaṇyā* formula,
where there is the modification (*ūha*) of the *pravara* and the names.

Regarding examples such as "Devadatta sacrifices," since these would also be classified as mantras due to the definition [given] in the verse "likewise in the case of water" and because they occur within the midst of mantras, it is said: "Those among the texts being recited for private study (svādhyāya) in which a mantra-word is remembered are mantras;
for this is established as the defining characteristic of mantras."
Furthermore, when a single word is modified, does the entire [mantra] become a mantra in this way, or only the modified word?
It follows that it is the entire [mantra]. This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Why? Because the word "mantra" is employed with reference to that which is distinguished by its specific sequence of vowels, consonants, and so forth; if it were otherwise, its meaning would not be understood.

If [the opponent argues that] the distinctness consisting in being recognized as such at the time of tradition cannot be identified as "mantra-ness" even in some part [of the text], yet one still accepts the existence of that [mantra-ness] in a single portion, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of everything being a mantra, because there is no difference in the nature of being a mantra everywhere. (He states the purpose of the prima facie view: Therefore, since mantra-ness is absent even upon the removal of a single phoneme, all ritual functions cease.

(He elaborates on this very point: Therefore, just as there is the obligation to perform expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the destruction of that [day] occurring throughout all the Vedic branches (*śākhā*), so too, since specific words are prescribed by way of being the subject matter of mantras and meters (*chandas*), one must employ worldly words by including them within those mantras through the extraction of all meters from even a single word or a part thereof.

Regarding its modification (*ūha*), there is one purpose: that when the cause for modification pertains not only to a single modified constituent of the sentence, but rather to all its constituents, there is no requirement for the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by the loss of a mantra.
Furthermore, regarding the rule *Pāṇini* 3.1.71, *mantra-śvetavah-okthya-ṛg-yajur-ṣiñca*, [the Vārttika] states:

"In the case of *śvetavāh* and others, the suffix *ḍas* should be stated in place of *yasya*. This means that where word-status (*padatva*) is about to occur, the suffix *ḍas* should be stated as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇpin*.
One who possesses white horses is *śvetavāh*.
One who recites hymns (*ukthas*) in both ways is an *ukthaśā*; thus, a sacrificer is an *ukthaśā*, [and in the dual] *ukthaśāsau*, [in the plural] *ukthaśāsaḥ*.
That which is offered, given, or cut into pieces in front is a *puroḍāśa*.

By such statements as these, all those specific words that are recorded in tradition—whether as objects of mantras, such as "the white horse," "the Uktha-sacrificer," and "the sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśa*); or as objects of Vedic meters, such as "Mātariśvan brought Agnihotra from heaven," "Āditya," and "Imām agṛbhṇan"—are absent [from common speech]. Therefore, one must employ worldly usage for terms such as "white horse," "sacrificial cake," "he brought," "fire," and "they seized.
Thus, the second purpose has been stated. (He states the established conclusion: To this we reply.
It is only that much which is without a mantra.
Why? Because of the *ākṛtis*—namely, the *ūha*, the *pravara*, and the names.

This section (adhikaraṇa) is intended to state that, because an *ṛk* lacks the status of being a Brāhmaṇa—due to its not being accepted as such and its lack of the purpose of an injunction—it pertains to the Veda as recited in the context of mantras;
thus, it serves as a counter-argument to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arising from the sūtra on Soma and its injunctions (*taccodaka*). This is the connection (*saṃgati*).

In the mantra beginning with "I offer the *juhū* to Agni," the term "Sūrya" and so forth—which is substituted as "to Sūrya" in modified rites (*vikṛti*) such as those dedicated to Sūrya—is what is intended here by the word "modification" (*ūha*).
Likewise, in the mantra "Agni is the divine Hotṛ," the insertion of the sacrificer's ancestral lineage, such as "like Yuvanāśva, like Agniveśya, like Āṅgirasa," is the *pravara*.

In the *subrahmaṇyā-nigada*, the names of the sacrificer’s father and ancestors—which are inserted as follows: "the son of Asurabhraśarman sacrifices," "the grandson of Somanāthayajñaśarman sacrifices," "the great-grandson of Sureśvarayajñaśarman sacrifices," and "the son of Mairamadā sacrifices"—are intended by the term "name" (*nāmadheya*).
(This is the *pitāputrīya* principle regarding the *ṛjupāṇa* section, 1238, concerning the *ṛc* and *yajus* mantras.)

"One should simply say, 'May they enjoy the clarified butter and the oblation,'" because this concluding statement establishes that the *uditahoma* (offering after sunrise) is the rule; thus, there is an option.

However, in the present case, because another scriptural injunction—namely, "He says [the mantra] over the oblation"—establishes the restriction, both the formulas "with the oblation" (*sahaviṣā*) and "without the oblation" (*ahaviṣā*) possess the status of mandatory injunctions.
(Saṃkarṣa 4.1.10)

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: since both the injunctions—"he sacrifices with the *yājyā*" and "it is offered with the *vaṣaṭ*-call"—are understood to have the purpose of offering, and because they serve a single purpose, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between them according to the principle of the *ṛgjuṣāṇa* section (*ṛgjuṣāṇādhikaraṇanyāya*).
(Saṃkarṣa 4.1.3).
[Furthermore,] the word *pṛṣṭha* in the expression "he stands near with the *pṛṣṭhas*" denotes a substance, namely the *ṛc*.

The definition of the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman* has been stated both directly and indirectly; it is now considered here whether the qualification for [the study of] the Veda (*śruti*) should apply to those who have already been born [into the lineage].

Because the words *ṛc*, *yajus*, and *sāman* are employed in the Vedas—as in the verse "By the Ṛks, the God moves at dawn in heaven"—and because of the plural usage in the phrase "not devoid of Vedas" (*vedairaśūnyaḥ*), the application of the word *ṛc* and others is clearly evident in the Veda (Sūtra-bhāṣya, p.
1504). Furthermore, the Ṛg and Yajus mantras are employed in ritual action with their specific musical intonations (*tāna-svara*).
"There should be an option because the purpose is one; for both serve that same purpose.
(9.2.8.30) Section 3. Bhāṣya: In this regard, some students of the Taittirīya recension study [the text] with a single accent, while others study it with four accents.

He said: "As for those who study by means of the fourfold accents (*cātuḥsvarya*), do they produce some other accent in addition to the acute (*udātta*), the grave (*anudātta*), and the circumflex (*svarita*)? No," he replied. "Their accents are exactly the same as those of others. What then do they do? They recite one additional accent (*kharāntara*) after what has been spoken."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is there a combination (*samuccaya*) of the *Taittirīya* and other [recensions], or is there an option (*vikalpa*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Because all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) must be brought together, there is a combination according to the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*).
This being the case, we reply:
there should be an option (vikalpa) because the purpose is one.
The single purpose for all of them—the Taittirīyas and the rest—is the accomplishment of the study [of the Veda].
Therefore, it is an option. There should be an application [of the rule] based on the statement.
The commentary: This statement, "the *tāna* [is used] in the sacrificial rite," is equivalent to a traditional text (*smṛti*).
Therefore, the recitation should be performed using a single tone (*ekaśruti*).
Now, one might ask: for what purpose is there a traditional recitation (*samāmnāya*) among the Taittirīyas and others? It is said in reply:
it will serve the purpose of bringing about the comprehension of the meaning.
The term *soma-tānaḥ* is a designation of the ancient teachers based on the *ekaśruti* (monotone) recitation.

There is no direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) specifying the accents that establishes the mantras as being knowers of the ritual action, such that—due to conflict with it—a Smṛti rule would be sublated; rather, the status of the mantras as auxiliary elements of the ritual (*karmāṅgatva*) is established through their being qualified by the accents, because they depend upon the injunction for the study of accents and because this is supported by reasoning.

Furthermore, the reasoning (which establishes the principle of "cognition across all branches" [sarvaśākhā-pratyaya] and supports the combination of accents) is weaker than the Smṛti; thus, the inference of the Veda is concluded without modification (*niṣpannūha*).

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*); that is, whatever accent belongs to the first member remains, and the final acute accent (*antodātta*) characteristic of a compound does not apply.

For example, in "sthūlapṛṣṭhīm" and similar cases, the determination of the *bahuvrīhi* is made by observing the original accent of the first member, the word "sthūla," which is characterized by a final acute. Furthermore, this rule regarding monotony (*ekaśruti*) applies to contexts other than those involving *japa* mantras and the like.

According to the Pāṇinian Smṛti rule, "In the sacrificial ritual, [the mantra] is recited in the *ekaśruti* mode, except for the *japa*, the *sāman*, and the *nyūṅkha*" (1.2.34), the mantra used in a sacrificial act should be in the *ekaśruti* mode; however, it is not *ekaśruti* in the case of the *nyūṅkha* (the syllable *oṃ*) occurring in specific branches of recitation (*japa*) nor in the *sāman*.
In the case of *japa* and similar acts, the application is indeed with the fourfold intonation (*cātuḥsvarya*).

And thus, regarding the use of the fourfold intonation (*cātuḥsvarya*) by modern ritualists (*yājñika*) even in the case of formulas belonging to the Adhvaryu and Yajamāna priests—such as "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" (*agnaye juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*)—which are *karaṇa-mantras* and so forth distinct from the *japa-mantra* and the Sun, the source [of this practice] must be sought.

On this interpretation, the terms *ṛk* and *sāman* in the Sūtra must somehow be explained as referring to the fourfold intonation and the like. As Viśvarūpa states: "The Taittirīyas and others [employ] either a combination, an option, or indeed only the *tāna* [intonation]."
From the application [of the rule], these two [Sāman-mantras] are excluded, because there is no statement [to that effect] in the Smṛti.
The Bhaṭṭa [commentator] says: By extension from the Sāman-mantras, the Ṛk and Yajus mantras are devoid of musical accent (svara).
For those two are studied in some places with the fourfold musical accents: acute (udātta), grave (anudātta), circumflex (svarita), and protracted (pracaya).
In some other recensional branch (*śākhāntara*), those same [notes] are designated as *taittirīya*, excluding the *pracaya*.
In that case, there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*) between the two, just as there is regarding the modes of chanting (*gītiprakāra*).

Nor can it be argued that both are sublated because the *tāna* accent is prescribed by the traditional law (*smṛti*) stating: "The *tāna* [is used] in sacrificial rites, and the *ajapa* in non-Vedic *sāmans*."
This should not be said.

For the accents (*svara*), which pervade the injunction for Vedic study, are established by the authority of effort as residing in the mantras that serve as means for various sacrificial precedents (*kratupūrva*) through recitation and so forth; therefore, they cannot be sublated by *smṛti*.

Otherwise, since [mantras] such as "Agnirmūrdhā" would, according to *smṛti*, be employed in the worship of the nine Brahmas (*navamabrāhmaumārcana*) [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.300], they would fail to become subordinate elements (*aṅga*) of the Āgneyī and other sacrifices due to their position in the sequence (*krama*) and other factors.

Nor does this result in the [mantras] becoming subordinate parts (*aṅga*) of the *navagraha-homa* (the oblation to the nine planets); for their application (*viniyoga*) is established by syntactical connection (*vākya*) through the very expectancy of the *saurya* sacrifice— or rather, the expectancy of the *navagraha-homa*— since the definition of an *ṛc* applies to the *ṛg* and *yajus* mantras.
In the present case, however, because it contradicts the Vedic accent (*śrauta-svara*) and because there is no traditional recollection (*asmṛti*) of such a rule, [the Smṛti] lacks authority.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: when the Vedic accent, which has been taught by the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), stands in need of a purpose, two purposes are understood from its occurrence in the recitation of mantras as assisted by context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors, through the connection "whatever one desires, that one should perform.
One purpose is its determination of the specific meaning prior to the time of performance.

Nor is there an absence of contradiction merely because one has previously retained a specific meaning, since the essence of a mantra lies in its application at the time of performance; for even if a specific meaning is understood from the injunction (*vidhi*), there would arise the possibility of non-application due to doubt as to whether that specific meaning is actually what is conveyed by the mantra at the time of performance.

Therefore, for the sake of determining the meaning of a mantra, an application such as "in a *bahuvrīhi*, the first member retains its original accent" (*bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*) must take place prior to the performance.
Furthermore, even if a meaning has been previously determined, there may be a lapse in memory during the course of the performance, necessitating a renewed determination.
And even at a time other than that [specific ritual moment], the occurrence of the accentuation is established precisely because it belongs to the Mantra system (*mantranaya*).

Since the utterance of the accentuation is accomplished through the very utterance of the mantra, it is not the case that the accentuation serves as a determining factor merely by its own recollection.
Thus, in this way, the two-fold application of the accentuation to the *ṛc* would be established through context (*prakaraṇa*) and other such means.

And in that regard, because the rule prescribing the *tāna* accent in the performance of a sacrifice (*yajña-prayoga*) sublates [other rules] through its specific form (*viśeṣa-rūpa*), the general form of the context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth is postulated only as being capable of determining the inclusion of the performance. However, in cases such as the singing out of tune (*visvaraṇa*) during the performance, the mere recollection of the accent itself constitutes the extension toward a specific meaning.

And here, since the *tāna* lacks utility for a specific meaning, even though it serves a purpose, it sublates the *Taittirīya* and other [recensions] solely by virtue of occurring within a single mantra.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of repeating the mantra in accordance with the subordinate qualities (*guṇa*).

By the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) expressed in the phrase "except for *ajapa*" and so forth, there is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for *japa* and other such acts according to the *Taittirīya* and other schools.
*Japas* are those mantras enjoined by the injunctions of the root *jap*.
The *nyūṅkha* syllables are specific types of mantras (consisting of the vowel *o* in the form of anudātta, etc. used in the case of the *śakvarī* verses. Bhaṭṭa, 9.2.7, Section 3.
Maṇḍana: "In ritual acts, there is a single recitation of the mantra."

Regarding the word *vā*: in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, during the seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*), there is a traditional injunction for the sacrificer to choose [the priests] for the purpose of employing the *yajyā* verses.

Among those [offerings], there is a *yājyā* for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and two options for it have been prescribed: its handover to the *hotṛ*, or its recitation by himself. In that regard, when he sacrifices himself, there arises a doubt: is the *vaṣaṭkāra* and the consumption resulting from it excluded, or not? [The answer is: they are not excluded, because of the explicit scriptural statement.
Furthermore, the removal of one thing does not entail the removal of another, because there is no connection between them.
For what is heard in the scripture is the removal of the *yājyā* alone, not the removal of the *vaṣaṭkāra* alone.
Therefore, even when the *yājyā* is removed, the selection of the *hotṛ* is not removed; likewise, the *bhakṣa* (the act of consuming) is also not removed.

But surely, when he sacrifices for himself, there is no removal at all, because of the statement, "The *yājyā* belongs to the sacrificer. However, when he intends [to sacrifice] for another, then there is a removal.
Therefore, it must be considered in this way: upon the removal of the *yājyā*, is the portion (*bhakṣa*) removed from the sacrificer, or not?
It is said:
"The *yājyā*, the *bhakṣa*, and the *vaṣaṭkāra* are established for the Hotṛ by virtue of his designation (*samākhyā*).
However, the removal [of these] from him is heard in the text: 'He causes the sacrificer to sacrifice' (*yajamānaṃ yājayati*)."

(This is the reasoning of the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa]: Because of the designation "hotṛ," everything was previously established as belonging to the *hotṛ* prior to this statement, "The *yājyā* belongs to the sacrificer.
In that context, by means of this statement, only the *yājyā* is made related to the sacrificer, whereas the *vaṣaṭkāra* and so forth remain as they were, belonging to the *hotṛ*.

If, however, it were explained as "removing [the duties] from the sacrificer," then since only the *yājyā* would have been assigned to him, the phrase "removing" would imply there is nothing else to remove; consequently, because there would be no possibility of assigning the *vaṣaṭkāra* and so forth [to the sacrificer], there would be no suspicion at all regarding such a removal.

Therefore, since the phrase "the *yājyā* of the sacrificer" refers merely to the *yājyā* itself, and because there is no relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*) between the *vaṣaṭkāra* and the *yājyā* due to their absolute difference, the *hotṛ* priest should consume [the portion] after uttering the *vaṣaṭ* over the *yājyā* being recited by the sacrificer.
For the consumption is caused by the *vaṣaṭkāra*, not by the *yājyā*; thus [the *yājyā*] is set aside for the sacrificer, because the cause [of the *hotṛ*'s consumption] has arrived.
Commentary: The portion for consumption (bhakṣa) should belong to those who have sacrificed.
Why? Because of the arrival of the cause.
The cause of the consumption is the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call.
And he does not arrive at the *yājyā* while it is being recited;
for thus it is heard in scripture: "He utters the *vaṣaṭ* over the *yājyā*.
But was it not said that the Hotṛ utters the *vaṣaṭ* over the *yājyā* even when it is being employed by the sacrificer?
This is not the correct concentration.
One must sacrifice without drawing breath; the sacrifice is performed with the *vaṣaṭ* call, not by the *yājyā* verse alone.
Therefore, the sacrificer must not draw breath until the *vaṣaṭ* call.

If another were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call, the sacrificer would be excluded from the ritual and would not perform the sacrifice. Furthermore, he is enjoined to perform the sacrifice itself, not merely to recite the *yājyā* verse; for in the injunction "having sat down himself, he sacrifices," there is a prescription for the performance of the sacrifice along with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*). Or rather—if only this much were heard, namely, "the *yājyā* belongs to the sacrificer," then perhaps the consumption [of the oblation] might sometimes not be removed.
In this case, however, it is heard thus: "He sacrifices himself on the Niṣadha.
And because the offering of the oblation is performed by means of the *vaṣaṭ*-call, the sacrifice is not accomplished by the *yājyā* alone.
Likewise, regarding the injunction "he sacrifices without pausing," one must not pause from the beginning of the *yājyā* until the purpose of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is completed.
And this [concomitance] is possible only when the *yājyā* and the *vaṣaṭkāra* have a single agent, not otherwise.

Therefore, since the *vaṣaṭkāra* and the consumption [of the offering] belong wherever there is a *yājyā*, it is understood that even in the absence of identity [of the agent], there is no removal [of these elements] due to their inherent connection. Furthermore, because the *pravara* (invocation of ancestors) has already commenced, it is not to be omitted.
Commentary: Now, as for what was said—that just as the *pravara* (ancestral lineage) is not removed, so too the *bhakṣa* (the portion to be consumed) is not removed—it is replied:
the *pravara* is not removed because it is impossible [to do so].
For how could that which has already passed be removed by the Hotṛ? And if it were performed when the opportunity has elapsed, it would be defective for the sacrificer;
nor can that which is defective ever accomplish its purpose.
In this case, it is not obtained through extension (codaka). It might be argued: "That which is possible is obtained through extension, but that which is impossible is not extended.
This is the archetype (prakṛti); whatever kind of injunction for a new rite (apūrva) has been stated, it should be performed in exactly that manner if it is possible.

If it cannot be performed [in one place], then it should be performed wherever it can be performed; not where it would be defective. Therefore, it is logical that there should be no omission of the *pravara*, but not of the *bhakṣa*.
Or rather—as for the argument that "the *pravara* [is the cause]," it is said in response:
"The *pravara* is not exclusively restricted to the time of the *yājyā*;
however, because the act of eating is yet to occur, the assumption of its removal is possible."
That name is subject to removal because it can be removed and applied elsewhere;

however, at the time of removing the *pravara* (the ancestral invocation), it is not possible to remove the *hotṛ*, nor is the selection of the *varaṇa* (the choosing) endowed with its proper qualities possible for the sacrificer once the time has passed.
But in the case of the *bhakṣa* (the consumption), both are possible.
Therefore, there is a disparity between the examples here in the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtuyāja*s).
(Having thus explained according to the Bhāṣya, [the author], wishing to explain otherwise:)
First, let us address the objection to the Bhāṣya—) this must be stated here:

why is it that the removal of the *pravara* (ancestral invocation) cannot be performed there, when all ritual procedures (*kalpa*) are commenced after having been determined from one or the other source right from the beginning?
Indeed, it is possible to determine at the very moment of the *pravara* whether the sacrificer will recite the *yājyā* or whether the *hotṛ* priest will.
And when it has been thus determined, the choice of one or the other shall be made.

For if this recitation of the *yājyā* were contingent (*naimittika*), like the sacrifice to Viṣṇu-Ukrama—as prescribed in the passage: "One who has rivals should offer a *caru* to the Viśvedevas; having placed it on the sacrificial grass, he should scatter it with a wooden sword and a shovel, saying, 'I scatter this one and that one,' and he should meditate upon whomsoever he hates; whatever falls below or sticks to the shovel, that he offers to Viṣṇu Ukrama" (see *Tarkapāda*, Third Section, Sūtra 10.1.1)—then, prior to the occurrence of the contingency, since its existence would not yet be determined, it might not even cause the selection (*pravaraṇa*) to be performed.
Furthermore, this [injunction] is able to restrict the choice of the *varaṇa* (selection) from the very beginning,
provided that it is not possible to remove the *hotṛ*. How could the *hotṛ* be removed, when his own *yājyā* must necessarily be performed?

There is no separate choosing (*varaṇa*) for this purpose, such that its removal might be suspected. Indeed, it is possible—and even proper—to perform a single choosing by way of a common ritual application (*tantra*) even for the sake of a thousand *yājyā* verses. Therefore, since it is performed at the very beginning for the sake of the entire performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is a *tantra*, because no distinction is perceived.

If it is argued that performing the *adhāva* at a time other than that of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) renders the rite defective, this too is refuted by the rule "and when there is an omission of a subordinate element, the primary remains" (10.1.2.164).
Furthermore, in that case, there is no specific difference in the performance between the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modified form (*vikṛti*).

If it were held that everything must be performed exactly as prescribed in the archetype, that would contradict the section on "capacity for all" (6.1.2.18–20), where it was stated that it is indeed possible to accomplish [the rite] according to the proper time.
Therefore, the Sūtra must be interpreted in this way: by accepting the proximity of this [element], there is no removal of one thing upon the removal of another for some other reason.
This much was previously illustrated.
Now, however, he says: "Because it has already begun, there is no removal of that which is pre-eminent."

The intention is that [the procedure] has been undertaken for the sake of another *yājyā*. Therefore, even if the sacrificer himself speaks or gives the *praisha*, the *pravaraṇa* must still take place in the same manner.
However, there is this much difference: namely, that he does not proceed according to this *yājyā* in the same way as he does with the *vaṣaṭkāra* and the *bhakṣaṇa*.
Śabara: [Objection: "The injunction for the removal of the *yājyā* is expressed as 'the *yājyā* of the sacrificer';
since the *vaṣaṭkāra* is distinct from the *yājyā*, it is removed. To this, we reply: "The status of being the sacrificer (*yaṣṭṛtva*) is heard directly from the explicit scriptural statement."
And it is born complete through the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance;

Soma: [Objection] Since the [performance of the sacrifice] together with its auxiliary parts was stated in the midst of the discussion on the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the subsequent consideration of the consumption (*bhakṣa*) by the master (*svāmin*) constitutes a break in the sequence of topics (*peṭikābheda*). And this would constitute a lack of logical connection (*asaṃgati*). [Response] That is not so.

I shall explain [the connection]: because the investigation regarding the mention of "flesh" (*āmiṣa*) is common to both the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the previously stated connection is untenable due to the difference in the categories (*peṭikābheda*).

Therefore, just as the scripture concerning performance (*anuṣṭhāna-śāstra*) fulfills its purpose merely through the ignorance of a person attached to a single [view], so too, since the scripture stating "the sacrificer's *yājyā*" fulfills its purpose merely by the removal of the *yājyā*, there is no removal of the consumption (*bhakṣa*).
This is the connection [of the argument] based on the counter-objection (*pratyavasthāna*) [using a] simile.
Thus say others.
But surely, this deliberation applies when the sacrificer recites the *yājyā*.

Furthermore, the sacrificer’s role as the performer of the *yājyā* is not obtained from the statement "the *yājyā* of the sacrificer" (*yajamānasya yājyā*), because the connection between that statement and the command is surrendered by the injunction "he intends [it], saying, 'O Hotṛ, recite the *yājyā*' (*hotaretadyaja*)."

Therefore, it is as follows: the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) established only the assumption that the sentence "or he himself sacrifices" refers solely to the *yājyā* (offering verse), and not the demonstration that the sentence "the *yājyā* belongs to the sacrificer" [refers to it]. Thus it is so.

The sentence "Or, having sat down himself, he sacrifices" (svayaṃ vā niṣadya yajati) does not establish a connection with the *yājyā* that was not already established by another source; rather, the connection of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) with the *yājyā*, which was indeed established by the rule "the *yājyā* belongs to the sacrificer," was set aside by the rule "he says [to the Hotṛ], 'O Hotṛ, recite the offering prayer'"; this same connection is then restored by the rule "or, having sat down himself, he sacrifices."

And since the counter-exception follows the primary application, it is possible for the statement "the *yājyā* belongs to the sacrificer" (*yajamānasya yājyā*)—which establishes that the [injunction] applies to the *yājyā* in general—to serve as a basis for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
As for the meaning of the Sūtra: just as in the case of the *ṛtuyāja* offerings, [there is] the exclusion of the *ṛtuyāja* itself by oneself... [1246] ...the exclusion of the *ṛtuyāja*.

Just as the *pravara*—characterized by the selection [of priests] for the purpose of reciting the *yājyā*—is not removed when the *yājyā* is removed, so too is the *makṣa* (the eating of the portion). This is because the selection of the priests for the *ṛtuyāja* offerings benefits all *yājyās* through a single performance (*tantra*). Thus, while the selection of the sacrificer is necessarily required for the sake of that one *yājyā* which has been assigned to the Hotṛ, the selection of the Hotṛ must also necessarily be performed for the sake of other *yājyās*; therefore, there is no removal of that Hotṛ. This distinction regarding the *pravara* should be understood in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). 17. In that case, regarding the recitation of the *yājyā* by oneself, there is the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance and the consumption [of the Soma].

Regarding the inquiry as to whether he alone is the performer or the Hotṛ priest, it is observed that by virtue of the direct statement of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīśruti*), only the *yājyā* (offering verse) of the sacrificer is heard, and not the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance; for that [utterance] is distinct from the *yājyā*, according to the injunction: "He utters the *vaṣaṭ* over the *yājyā*.

Therefore, since the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is governed by the name [of the office], the Hotṛ alone is the performer; consequently, the consumption [of the remnant] resulting from that [utterance] belongs to him alone.
As for the statement "or himself," that does not enjoin the status of being the performer of the sacrifice, since that is already established by the principal sentence itself.

Nor does it enjoin the status of being the performer of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance that reveals the sacrifice, for if it were a separate injunction (*vidhyantara*), it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Therefore, since the first sentence enjoins the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) regarding the *yājyā*, and the second enjoins his role as the prompter (*preṣaka*), the performance of the purpose of the prompt is logically untenable; thus, by the very fact that the option regarding the *yājyā* arises, and because the status of being the performer of the sacrifice is established even by the mere recitation of the *yājyā*, this third [sentence] is indeed a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
Furthermore, the term "certainty" (*niścaya*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), as the state of being seated during the *yājyā* is already obtained from a general injunction.
The statement "he sacrifices without pausing" (*anavān yajati*) refers to another *yājyā* verse.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the correct conclusion is as follows]: because of the hearing of the verb (*ākhyāta*) and because the word "or" (*vā*) would otherwise be inexplicable, the third [sentence] alone is the injunction; the first, however, is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

Consequently, since the status of being the primary performer of the sacrifice belongs to him alone by virtue of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance at the end of the *yājyā*, the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance also belongs to him alone. This is because, rather than subverting both the common agency of the *yājyā* and the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance and the requirement of non-pausing, it is more logical to subvert only one thing—the fact that the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance has the Hotṛ as its agent—which is established solely by the evidence of the name (*samākhyā*).
And thus, even when explained as an injunction (*vidhi*), there is no fault whatsoever;
consequently, the consumption [of the soma] occasioned by the *vaṣaṭ*-call also belongs to him alone.

14. Maṇḍana: "The *yājyā*-reciter should utter the *vaṣaṭ*. Śaṅkara: "The one who causes the *yājyā*s to be recited is the most excellent. The *adhvaryu* should not divide the *ṛtuyāja* precepts, but rather the *maitrāvaruṇa*.
Saṃkarṣa 2.3.13: The *ṛtuyājyā* verses belong only to the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), not to the two subsequent pressings;
however, the *prasthitayājyā* verses belong to all three.
Saṃkarṣa 2.3.13: In the *ṛtuyājyā* verses, the portion consisting of the *praiṣa* (direction) is to be omitted.

In the *ṛtugraha* [libations], after reciting the *praisha* (directions) beginning with "O Hotṛ, since Indra... and ending with "O Hotṛ, sacrifice," it is traditionally taught that "they sacrifice by means of the *praisha*.

In that case as well, although the application would initially seem to follow the recited order—joining the two portions of the *yejāmaham* formula known as *pradāna* (offering) with the two final portions of the *ṛtuyāja* sacrifices—the actual practice involves joining them at the end of those two portions, because the words "Hotṛ" and "sacrifice" (*yajati*) are not syntactically connected within the original *mantra*.

(Saṃkarṣa 2.4.125). Furthermore, the performance of the *ṛtuyāja* offerings, which serve a secondary purpose (*guṇārtha*), occurs during the *sattra* session of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
Bhāṣya 10.2.16.2: In the case of the ṛtuyāja offerings and the gift of gold, which serve two purposes, there is no sublation in the *sattra* sacrifice.
There should be performance of those that are merely ritual duties (*dharmamātra*).
Commentary: There is the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), regarding which it is said, "Those desiring prosperity should undertake the twelve-day sacrifice."

In that context, there are certain mere ritual elements (dharmamātra) obtained through extended application (codaka), such as the exclusion of the Ṛtuyāja offerings and the gift of gold to the Ātreya. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should these mere ritual elements be performed, or not?

What is established? It has been stated (10.2.10) that because the *sattra* is self-performing (*svayaṃ-kartṛka*), the choosing of priests (*varaṇa*) and the giving of fees (*dāna*) are excluded; nor is there any other scriptural injunction stating that these must be performed.
To the extent that something is heard in scripture, all of that is authoritative; to the same extent is the fault in assuming what is not heard.
Therefore, they should not be performed.
This being the case, we reply:
there should be an action for those who possess merely the quality (dharma-mātra).
If the choosing or the giving does not serve a visible purpose, then even when performed by one seeking heaven, it incurs no contradiction.
Therefore, the ritual action should be performed for the sake of favoring the injunction (*codaka*).
Soma—this is the connection [of the example].
Regarding the *ṛtuyājyā* verses, such as "O Hotṛ, Indra, from all the gods, from the earth... and so forth.

Exclusion of the Ṛtuyāja: 1247. The selection of other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) such as the *hotṛ* and others [is required]; because it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*), it must be performed even in a *sattra* sacrifice.
In the Sūtra, the phrase "mere ritual duties" means those whose purpose is invisible.
Viśvarūpa says: "One should not perform the *ṛtuyājyā* and *āhuti* offerings in *satra* sacrifices;
or rather, one may perform them, for there is no taint [of sin]. For the sake of dharma, let both be performed.
The *ṛtuyājyā* and the *iṣṭi*—these two are the *vairaṇa*.

Bhaṭṭa: Since the choosing (*varaṇa*) and the hiring (*bharaṇa*) in the *sattra* sacrifice serve a visible purpose, when their omission has been stated, the example is merely illustrative; for that choosing of the *ṛtuyājyā* priests and the gift to the descendant of Atri (*ātreyāya dāna*), which serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), must indeed be performed in the *sattra*.
For when [the rule] is heard in the context of the *soma* sacrifice, the choosing of the *ṛtuyājyā* priests again serves only an invisible purpose.
The same applies to the statement, "He gives gold to the descendant of Atri."
For in this case, a dual injunction based on a reference to the gift mentioned incidentally is not possible, as that would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, a distinct gift must necessarily be enjoined.

Furthermore, regarding the officiating priests other than those specifically prescribed by rules such as "the Hotṛ priest is a Vaiśvāmitra," the assumption of an injunction for being an Ātreya is untenable; because when the requirement is satisfied by the gift itself—which is independent of the aforementioned injunctions due to its own inherent purpose—there can be no connection with a gift that depends upon the assumption of an injunction, since the latter would lack causal efficacy.

Nor should it be argued that, since the injunction is possible for the sake of merely knowing the specific Ātreya who has reached the status of a *pakṣin* (one belonging to the category), there is no alternative injunction regarding the Ātreya even for me.

For, in cases such as "he offers the oblation placing gold in between," since the gift serves the visible purpose of the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the gold already employed, there is no evidence for its serving the purpose of hiring such a priest.
Therefore, due to the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*), this gift is solely for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

For this very reason, the principle of Ātreya (3.2.8)—which applies to the case of the priest Ātreya who is endowed with divine power—is not applicable here. This is because the principle does not apply, as there is no established [prior] cognition (*aklṛpti*) of Ātreya as being delimited by the status of being a means to a transcendental result (*apūrva-sādhanatā*). Maṇḍana: "In a sacrificial session (*sattra*), the gift produces an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Śaṅkara: "In a sacrificial session, the gift is for the sake of an unseen purpose."

27. The Principle of the Priesthood (*ṛtviktva-nyāya*): "Just as the seasonal signs themselves manifest their respective characteristics at the change of seasons, so too do the actions of embodied beings manifest according to their own nature.

(Manu 1.130, Medhātithi’s commentary). "Just as various kinds of seasonal signs are seen to appear repeatedly in each season, even so do the dispositions [of beings] recur at the beginnings of the Yugas."
Thus [it is said].
(Śāṃbhā. 1.3.30; Brahma Sūtra). This is the nature of the reasoning (*nyāya*).

According to the logic of the seasonal signs (*ṛtuliṅganyāya*), there would follow the consequence of eternality regarding the emergence of entities possessing identical names, powers, functions, and substances in every creation.
"Just as those very seasons return every year distinguished by the same characteristics, so it is also with regard to creation.

(Vākyapadīya 1.2.1.10, p. 126). Although the basis for the application of the designation "ṛtvij" (priest) is performing a sacrifice during the [proper] season (*ṛtu*), nevertheless, in the statement "there are seventeen priests for the Romanian *adhvara*," the *camasādhvaryus* do not possess the status of being *ṛtvij*s.
VI. 3.1.16: "The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is only one, namely the *adhvaryu*.
This is an injunction of restriction (*niyamavidhi*), stating: "In the *agnihotra*, for the sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) of the *agnihotra*, there is only one officiating priest.
4.2.9: "The fruit belongs to the officiating priest, because [the action] is purposeful even when performed by means of [him]."

In the context of the fire-installation (*agnyādheya*) within the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the following kindling mantras (*indhana-mantra*) are recited: "O Agni, may splendor be mine among the people; may we, kindling thee, nourish our bodies.
May the quarters bow down to me; may there be well-being through thee. O first one, may we conquer the *pūtanā*s. Thus they are chanted.
This is the mantra for the performance of the *agnyādhāna* (establishment of the sacred fires).
Regarding this, the fruit—such as the increase of luster (*varcas*), nourishment (*poṣaṇa*), burning away of sins (*dihan*), and mental clarity (*manana*)—has been stated.
Thus, regarding the fruits mentioned in such *karaṇa-mantras*, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) should pray for them for himself alone, not for the patron (*svāmin*).
Why? Because it is purposeful. The word *mama* (mine) occurring in the mantra "O Agni, [grant] splendor to me" becomes meaningful only when it refers to the fruit of the Adhvaryu priest himself;
if it were intended to refer to the fruit of the sacrificer (*svāmin*), the word *mama* would be redundant.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the fruit mentioned in the instrument-mantra belongs only to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) who recites that instrument-mantra.
"Or rather, it belongs to the master, because it is for his purpose.
By using the word "or," he sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The term "priest" (*ṛtvij*) is understood to follow here as well.
One should invoke the fruit for the master by means of the mantra used for the appointment of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), because that [mantra] is for his sake; that is,
because the ritual action is for the sake of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
Even in the case of the mantra, "May splendor (*varcas*) be mine," the splendor belongs to the sacrificer;
he designates it as "mine" by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the fruit mentioned in the instrumental mantra belongs to the sacrificer alone.
"And because of the observation of an indicative mark.

This sūtra provides another reason for the stated conclusion. The explanatory passage (arthavāda), "Whatever benediction the officiating priests pronounce, it belongs to the sacrificer alone," shows that the fruit has the sacrificer as its purpose.

From this observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is established that the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) prays for the fruit for the sacrificer alone, not for himself. For how could a priest be someone who is hated? [As it is said: "The officiating priest and the teacher are not to be transgressed against."
Bhāṣya 10.2.16.4: Other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) join in the singing;
the officiating priests act according to their prescribed duties.
"In the *pṛṣṭhya* [rite], [the singing] is not for those with the *satri*s" (10.2.14.42).
"The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) sing along" is stated in the archetype (*prakṛti*) (10.2.18).
"The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) sing along" is stated in the thousand-year sacrifice (*sahasrasaṃvatsara*).

8|1|11|18: Regarding the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), when they have been employed in one performance, they may be selected for another performance either as those same individuals or others, according to one's wish; however, there is no loss of their ritual efficacy (*yātayāmatva*) due to this. The number of officiating priests to be chosen should correspond to the requirements of the specific rite to be performed.
In that case, by implication, there would be no restriction on the number of performers, as there is no specific distinction.
The Bhāṣya states: "In that regard, since they are proclaimed [as optional] among the performers, there would be no restriction on the number of performers.
Why? Because there is no specific distinction."

No specific rule regarding the number of performers is prescribed in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). Its extent is determined by the purpose; it prescribes as many as are required to complete the performance of the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Or rather, there is no fixed rule, as the act of hiring (*parikraya*) can be accomplished by employing either one or two.

Alternatively, since the common grammatical coreference (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) applies when the performers are equal in relation to the fruit, this would apply to the entire performance as it stands; therefore, only that which is specifically enjoined here by the rule for hiring through the *adhvara* [priest] should be set aside.
And since that [result] arises from a single agent performing whatever action he does, it is not the case that a plurality [of agents] should be sublated.
Moreover, due to the difference in scriptural statements (*śrutibheda*), there would be [distinct rites] for each name.
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: "As many names of agents as are heard in connection with the ritual acts, so many [agents] are to be chosen; they are distinct."

From the hearing of those names, [the following functions are assigned]: "The *puroḍāśadhuḥ* partakes," "The *pratiprasthātṛ* offers the *manthin*," "The *neṣṭṛ* leads the wives forward," and "The *unnetṛ* draws up both the cups.

Likewise: "The *prastotṛ* chants the *prastāva*," "The *udgātṛ* sings the *udgītha*," "The *pratihartṛ* performs the *pratihāra*," "The *subrahmaṇya* recites the *subrahmaṇyā*," "The *hotṛ* recites the *prātaranuvāka*," "The *maitrāvaruṇa* gives the directions and recites the responses," "The *acchāvāka* performs the sacrifice (*yajati*)," and "The *grāvastut* recites the *āvastotrīyā*."
Such is the purpose regarding the ritual action.
Therefore, you must certainly choose these [materials] exactly as they have been prescribed;
no other substance exists apart from these.
Even that which is not taught by the direct statement (*vākya*) is understood through the name (*samākhyā*);
therefore, it is said that [the injunction] prescribes just so many [elements].

Or rather—by means of an injunction of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) associated with ritual acts whose performers are restricted by distinct names, the inclusion of just that many [elements] is established as being enjoined.
The designation of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) follows the specific duties to be performed;
the officiating priests [are those who] fall within the midst of the ritual performance.

And as for the principle "because of the connection with the origin," just as it is capable of making known a difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*), so too must distinct agents be adopted according to their respective designations (*samākhyā*) even when there is a difference in the acts.
If it is argued that this is because a single agent [performs] different acts, the Bhāṣya states: "If this is what is being asserted, then one should say no more than this."
In that regard,
when it is intended that "this person shall perform that action," he becomes denotable by that word;
even though he is one, he may be designated by many names according to the many objects he is to perform.
Therefore, there is no fixed rule;
or rather—these designations are observed to apply to things currently undergoing activity.
Since they are not understood from common worldly usage, they are distinguished as being produced effects, like the term "upādi."

And therefore, just like the *pātra* and other vessels, one who performs the various duties of the *hautra* and so forth will be designated by the terms "hautra" and so on; it is exactly thus, and not at the time of the origin of the persons.
Bhāṣya: This is not so; [the designation occurs] at the time of the origin of the persons.
When persons are being produced [for a ritual], their designations differ, as in: "He chooses the Brahman," "He chooses the Hotṛ," "He chooses the Udgātṛ," "He chooses the Adhvaryu," and so forth.
Therefore, there is a purpose for those various names in the ritual;
they must necessarily be chosen.
Therefore, the mention of these [priests] in the context of their selection is not an injunction, because there is no other purpose for it.
