The Veda would not say that so many [priests] are to be chosen; otherwise, it would be entirely meaningless.
If it is possible to indicate a specific number, then this specific number of that [sacrifice] is understood; for that purpose, this statement exists.
Therefore, sixteen performers should be chosen, and the Soma sacrifice should consist of that many performers.
The same applies to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Or rather—if these designations were heard either at the time of the application of the ritual action or at a time subsequent to it—then they would not differ [in their function].
However, *varaṇa* (the formal invitation) is a request for the purpose of setting in motion those who are already fully engaged.
In this regard, there are these [passages] beginning with "He chooses the Brahman priest.
Nor is any other cause perceived at that time by which a difference in designation (*samākhyā*) could arise.

Furthermore, these acts of choosing (*varaṇa*) themselves differ according to the scriptural texts—such as "You alone are one" (which is a repetition) and "In connection with the hearing of a subordinate quality"—up until the very end of the scripture.
Therefore, in this case, the distinction among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are to be selected is also of that same measure.

Furthermore, since the designations (*samākhyā*) were not previously perceived and because they are treated as established even when there is no [actual] time [for their application], it is understood that they are caused solely by the act of selection (*varaṇa*).
And from the distinction of the cause, the distinction of the effect is established.
Furthermore, because it has already been perceived, it is not possible to describe a single agent again and again;
for that which has already been apprehended once cannot be apprehended again.

Because they possess the status of being supplementary to the original injunction of production (*utpattivākya*), and because there is no possibility of an option (*vikalpa*) [in this case], it is not possible to combine another choosing with that very same choosing.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the choosings are distinct.

And all of them are grasped by the performance-injunction (*prayogavacana*), which prescribes them simultaneously—just like the cups for Indra-Vāyu and the others—rather than prescribing them successively.
And by virtue of that [specific] selection, all [of them] are understood as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Therefore, the distinction among the officiating priests is established up until their formal selection (*varaṇa*).

As for what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—"Therefore, the mention of these in the context of their selection is not an injunction," and so forth—that is incorrect, because a selection that has not been prescribed would not be applicable.

Nor can it be the case that the result of these components of the sentence—being imagined as a single sentence—is merely to convey a number of means that are easily understood and innumerable. Therefore, one must establish that the suffixes [denote] the number of the objects taught by the injunctions, such as the *varaṇa* (choosing) and so forth;
there is nothing [to be gained] by such a prescribed [interpretation].

The meaning of the Soma-sūtra is as follows: In that case, since the status of being an agent exists, the number of agents would be determined by the effects—that is, as many as are required to accomplish the functions of the senses—but there is no restrictive rule stating "there must be exactly this many," because there is no specific qualification [to limit it]. As for the word *vi* (in the compound *vikraya*), it means: "Or let there be no restriction on the number of agents in a purchase; no, for there is no such restriction, because in the meaning of the sentence, there are indeed only that many."

Bhaṭṭa: When the question arises as to how many [priests] there are, since the respective duties are enjoined under the designations of Adhvaryu and so forth, one should understand that there are exactly as many as are enjoined for each specific rite. Thus, there is only one Adhvaryu at the Āgnīdhra; four in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; five in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; and twenty-six in the Soma sacrifice.

Nor should it be argued that, because only one person is engaged through the method of hiring (parikraya), he alone will receive those various designations—such as "the group of five" and so on—based on the performance of those respective duties.

The status of designations (*saṃjñā*) as being caused by ritual action has already been refuted by such statements as "he chooses the *adhvaryu*," because they do not have ritual action as their cause. Rather, [the application of these terms] is caused by specific acts of choosing—either being produced by those respective acts of choosing, or being caused by a specific quality of the *adhvaryu* produced by the aforementioned injunction; for even when the act of choosing has been performed, the term *adhvaryu* is not applied if the intention "may I be the *adhvaryu*" is absent.

In reality, however, since even the Adhvaryu’s [status] consists of a momentary state of certainty, the specific conceit (*abhimāna*) produced by that is the sole cause. And because that [conceit] exists even in a *sattra* sacrifice, even in the absence of formal selection (*varaṇa*), the status of being an Adhvaryu arises simply through desire.
Consequently, the use of the word "Hotṛ" before the selection is justified in the archetype (*prakṛti*) as well, according to the rule: "The Hotṛ recites the *sāmidhenī* verses.
For this very reason, the Prābhākara view—that "the status of being an Adhvaryu must be accepted as arising from the act of selection"—is refuted.

Even in the case of the *ṛtuyāja*, it is like the selection [of priests] (*varaṇa*); for even if one were to adopt the position of selection, there is no lack of evidence for a plurality of agents, since the respective conceits of identity would be established for each individual. This is because the repeated acts of selection enjoined by their respective injunctions—such as "he selects the *adhvaryu*" and "he selects the *brahmā*"—would be inexplicable unless there were a difference in the persons to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*). For selection (*varaṇa*) is indeed a solicitation intended to induce the activity of a person who has not yet engaged; and that cannot possibly apply to a single person more than once.
Furthermore, since distinct preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*) are enjoined for their respective specific functions, there is no room for a doubt regarding optionality (*vikalpa*).
In the case of the statement, "There are four priests (*ṛtvij*) at the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," this is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Consequently, the injunction "he chooses the priests" (*ṛtvijo vṛṇīte*) is also not an original injunction (*vidhi*) for the act of choosing itself.

If that were the case, the frequent restatement "the officiating priests" (*ṛtvijaḥ*) would be untenable; rather, it is a restatement of the mere selection (*varaṇa*) for the purpose of honoring them, intended for the subsequent rites of the priests and for the injunction of their respective duties.

Therefore, as many selections as there are—whether worldly or accompanied by mantras—so many are the officiating priests. [In the context of] the assignment of fees, the officiating priests have the master as the seventeenth.

And the patron (yajamāna), being deluded and acting out of faith, accepts them accordingly; thus there is a rule that they are to be accepted by means of selection (*varaṇa*) itself, accompanied by a specific assignment of fees (*bhṛti-nirdeśa*).
(Sūtra 3.7, p. 35). The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who perform the central rites are the Brahman, the Patron, the Hotṛ, and the Udgātṛ.
(p. 1243). In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the officiating priests are distinct from the Patron.

VI. 10|6|25. "The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), with the sacrificer as the fifth, consume the *iḍā* [portion] at the New and Full Moon sacrifices. (Bhāṣya 12|1|15|32). The officiating priests are those who sacrifice during the proper seasons and those who perform the duties of the *adhvaryu* and so forth. Who are they? Those who are capable of performing them, for there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) for those lacking such capability.
And who are capable? Those who are learned.
Even among them, according to the authority of the Smṛti, those who are Brāhmaṇas; furthermore, the specific qualification is "those who have been selected by formal invitation."

Vārttika 3.7.123, p. 1097: "He makes the officiating priests wear [the garment]"—this is the introductory statement (upapattivākya). Pāṇini 5.1.12: By means of this [rule], all the *ṛtvij* priests indeed proceed wearing red turbans and red garments, not only the *udgātṛ*s;
and in the *vājapeya* sacrifice, they wear golden garlands, not only the *adhvaryu*s.
Bhāṣya 3.8.12: At the Soma sacrifice, there are seventeen officiating priests (ṛtvij):
the Adhvaryu, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, and the Unnetṛ;
the Brahman, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Agnīdh, and the Potṛ.
The Hotṛ, Maitrāvaruṇa, Acchāvāka, and Grāvastut;
the Udgātṛ, Prastotṛ, Pratihartṛ, and Subrahmaṇyā;
and the Sadasya and the ten Camasādhvaryus—these are not [considered] Ṛtviks.
And the Sadas-member [is chosen] by the sacrificer.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the officiating priests (ṛtvij) have the master as the seventeenth.
The master is the seventeenth, because of the commonality of the ritual action.
The Commentary states: It has been said that "the Sadasya is one of the officiating priests," and they are all headed by the Brahman priest.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the Sadasya the seventeenth among them, or is it the Gṛhapati (the householder)?
What, then, is the established position? That he is a *sadasya*.
For he is a performer of the ritual action, whereas the other is the master.
And whoever is a laborer (karmakara) must be hired;
and the officiating priests (ṛtvij) are hired.
Therefore, the seventeenth member is the Sadasya, who is an officiating priest.
Moreover, they prescribe for him a *camasa* and a choice (*varaṇa*).
A priest is to be chosen, not the master [of the sacrifice].
Therefore, the *sadasya* is the seventeenth.
This being the position reached, it is said:
"The master is the seventeenth because of the commonality of the ritual action.
The master should be their seventeenth.
Why? Because of the commonality of the ritual action (*karmasāmānya*): in a sacrifice, the performers are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*);
and in a sacrifice, the performer is the householder (*gṛhapati*). Therefore, he is an officiating priest because of the commonality of the sacrificial action.
As it has been stated: "They prescribe him; they prescribe his cup and his choosing; therefore the Sadasya is the seventeenth.
It is replied:
They prescribe those [functions] for the Brahman priest alone; both the choosing and the cup belong to the Brahman priest alone.
For he (the master) is present in the sacrificial assembly;
therefore, the masters are seventeen.
Or rather—because sixteen are mentioned in the passages concerning initiation and the sacrificial fee, that many [are determined].
It is not known which of them is the *sadasya*.
Only the *sadasya*, the *yajamāna*, and the *camasādhvaryus* remain.
Since the *camasādhvaryus* are of equal status [to the others], there is no authority for excluding either one; thus, it is uncertain whether it is the *sadasya* or the *yajamāna*.

In this regard, since it would follow that the *sadasya* (the assistant priest) is included because of the commonality of being a ritual performer (*karmakara*), it is stated: "There should be seventeen masters (*svāmin*).

But how is it that, having previously not accepted the status of the masters as being based on the performance of the sacrificial rite (*ṛtuyajana-karman*), one now asserts their status as priests (*ṛtvij*) on the basis of that same commonality? Furthermore, because of its connection with the originative injunction (*utpatti-saṃyoga*)—as in "he chooses the *sadasya*"—there is a distinction [of the *sadasya*] from the *adhvaryu* and others.

Moreover, a conventional meaning for the word "Brahman" as a part [of a whole] is not possible, as it is set aside by the conventional meaning of the whole [term "Brahman" referring to the Brahman priest].
Furthermore, it is not possible to enjoin or prescribe a further choosing (*varaṇa*) of the Brahman priest, because the same consequence would apply to the Adhvaryu and others as well.
Moreover, in all instances such as the invitation (*upahava*), his mantra is recited apart from the mantra of the Brahman;
in that case, one would have to resort to an improper option (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, even with respect to the word *camasa*, the mention of the Brahman priest is not applicable by means of the word *sadasya*.
Moreover, there must necessarily be a supervisor (*upadraṣṭṛ*) established by implication as the *sadasya*;
and he too can be said to "sacrifice in the ritual" because of his oversight.
All the sacrificial priests choose him individually;
therefore, it is improper that he be excluded from the assembly (sadasya). It is said in reply:
"In this context, there is no exclusion of the *sadasya* from being an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*);
rather, his fulfillment is designated as that of a *camasādhvaryu*. For the *sadasya* must indeed be chosen separately."

Furthermore, the Brahman priest is not designated by the term *sadasya* (member of the assembly), because when there is a seasonal sacrifice (*ṛtuyajana*), one is restricted to being an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) only through formal selection (*varaṇa*).

Moreover, since neither his connection to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇābhāga*) nor his initiation (*dikṣā*) is mentioned in the scriptural injunctions, he is not called an "officiating priest. Just as the *camasādhvaryus* are not called "officiating priests" despite having both formal selection and a connection to the seasonal sacrifice—due to the absence of these two specific causes—the same applies here.
As for the patron (*svāmin*), although he lacks formal selection, all other requirements are present; therefore, it is logical that he possesses the status of an officiating priest.

As for the statement that "even the *sadasya* performs the sacrifice because of his supervision," this is due solely to the force of the scriptural injunction (*vacana-sāmarthya*) when [the *sadasya*] dies; however, there is no ritual element (*padārtha*) dependent upon him by virtue of which he could have such a designation.
Furthermore, supervision is not an indefinite ritual element of the priests, as the priests are "with the master as the seventeenth" (*svāmi-saptadaśāḥ*). (1251) [End of section on] the priests.
There is no such category of entity by which a specific distinction regarding this [person] could be restricted by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the statement "the master is the seventeenth" is appropriate only when there is indeed an assembly (*sadas*).
As for that which was said by the author of the Bhāṣya, intended to exclude the *sadasya*, it should be disregarded as an excessive statement intended to exclude his status as a priest (*ṛtvij*).

Regarding the Soma—since the meaning "only certain priests, not all" in the context of selecting seventeen [priests] is unstable, there is a connection (*saṃgati*) based on the cause-and-effect relationship (*hetuhetumadbhāva*) because the seventeenth is selected for that purpose of performing the ritual.

Indeed, the mere performance of items used in a sacrifice does not constitute officiating at a sacrifice (*ṛtuyajana*), as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as the sale of hair; rather, it is the complete performance of the ritual and the inspection of what has been done and what remains to be done. Furthermore, even if one is a constituent part of the sacrifice, if one is not employed in the performance of the whole, one is not officiating at the sacrifice. Viśvarūpa says: "Whether in the *Sadasya* or the sacrificer, it is called *sāsada* because of its being held."
The officiating priests perform [the rite] for the master;
therefore,
the *sadasya* (presiding member) belongs to the seventeenth [category], according to the Bhaṭṭa school.
This being the prima facie view—because there is a separate selection (*varaṇa*) for him and because of the injunction regarding the *camasa* cup—it is concluded as follows:

Since no specific duties to be performed by the *sadasya* are heard [in the scripture], and since it is understood that the act of selection has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) by assuming a breach of the principle of single application (*sakṛnnayāya*), the *sadasya* is merely optional; thus, the scriptural mention of "seventeen" is also optional. In a *satra*, the *sadasya* who undergoes initiation (*dīkṣā*) is himself the seventeenth among the masters (*svāmin*). Even if he were a mere ritual agent (*karmakara*), the wife does not become the seventeenth, because there is no evidence to justify accepting a discrepancy in gender within the cognition of requirement (*apekṣābuddhi*).
Maṇḍana: "The master is the seventeenth! Śaṃkara: "The master is considered the seventeenth.

According to the indications of the instruction and the designation [of the ritual], each of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) must perform his own respective duty. (Bhāṣya 3.7.14–12). The consumption of the *prāśitra* and other portions must be performed by the officiating priests alone.
6|4|3|4–9: The *camasādhvaryu* priests are to be chosen by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), not by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
(In the world, however, at the time of the great choosing, the sacrificer himself chooses them.

3|7|10|25: "He gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests. Regarding this, some maintain that the plurality inherent in the object of the action (*uddeśya*) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).

The recipient [of the sacrificial fee]. Vi. 10.1.12: Regarding the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) for the officiating priests (ṛtvij), whatever portion belongs to each, that much should be assigned by the sacrificer himself after having divided it; it is not to be taken as a gift from others.
Bhāṣya 10.3.12.50–52: The seller of Soma is indeed distinct from the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
3.7.15.13: The *camasādhvaryu* priests are distinct from the officiating priests.
3.7.10.25: The singers (*upagātṛ*) are not different from the officiating priests.
The officiating priests (ṛtvij) also possess the status of performers of indeterminate ritual acts due to specific designation (viśeṣa-samākhyā).
There is a sublation of general designation (sāmānya-samākhyā) by specific designation.
Its indication is provided by the designation of instruction (upadeśa-samākhyāna).
The Commentary (Bhāṣya): Is this the general rule—that everything designated by a name must be performed by those persons designated by that same name?
We say: no.
There is a specific instruction because of a particular designation.
The instruction is as follows: "Therefore, the Maitrāvaruṇa gives the direction and also recites the response. The designation *pautrīyā* refers to the office of the Neṣṭṛ;
this is an exception to the [general] designation.

Or rather—specific designation (*samākhyā*) also sublates [the general rule] because it functions more swiftly than even specific scriptural statement (*śruti*). This is supported by the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).

The Commentary states: "In the case of the rule, 'Where one should listen to the Hotṛ reciting the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*),' this shows that the Hotṛ, who is indicated by designation, is present at the morning litany belonging to the Hotṛ."

Likewise, there is this indicative mark (*liṅga*): "The *udgītha* belongs to the *udgātṛ*s, the *ṛc*s to the *ukthaśaṃsin*s, and the *pratigara* to the *adhvaryu*s. This shows a distinction based on technical designation (*samākhyā*). Similarly, there is also this indicative mark: "He who knows the property of the *adhvaryu* becomes possessed of his own property."
"This indeed is the Adhvaryu's own [duty], that he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*," thus it shows the restriction established by the general designation (*samākhyā*).
The word "indeed" (*vā*) indicates that this is a sign specifically for the application based on the general designation;
however, in the case of a specific designation, something else must be observed.

Soma: The Prābhākaras have explained this sūtra as a separate section (*adhikaraṇa*) solely for the purpose of demonstrating the sublation of a general designation (*sāmānyasamākhyā*) by specific verbal designations (*vacana-viśeṣasamākhyā*).
That is untenable;

because the weakness of a designation relative to a verbal statement, and of a general [designation] relative to a specific one, is established elsewhere, there would be no possibility for the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) to arise here.
Therefore, this [sūtra] is indeed a supplement to the present section (adhikaraṇa).

As for the meaning of the sūtra: "There would be a fixed distribution of ritual actions because of its connection with that, since the connection itself is purposeful. This refers to the connection with persons such as the *adhvaryu*—that is to say, the designation (*samākhyāna*) of the *adhvaryu* and so forth—which was introduced in the preceding sūtra.
There is a specification of that [connection] by means of instruction, i.e., by statement, and by specific designation.
The meaning is:
the essential point; an exception.
That is to say.
The propitiation of the officiating priests (ṛtvij),
or the fee for the officiating priests— this has been included within the previous section.

Bhaṭṭa: And this general rule (*utsarga*)—derived from such statements as "the *yājyā* belongs to the sacrificer" (*yajamānasya yājyā*)—is set aside by a specific injunction (*viśeṣaśāstra*), such as "the *potrīya* and *neṣṭrīya* [recitations] belong to the sacrificer" (*potrīyaṃ neṣṭrīyaṃ yājamānam*). Nor does this lead to the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*) based on the maxim of "being obstructed by purposelessness" (*ānarthakyapratihata-nyāya*), because in such cases the general rule would otherwise result in futility; for, just as in the first performance of the sacrifice, when the *potṛ* and others are incapable, the scope of the rule is appropriately restricted.

In reality, however, because the designations such as *hautra* (pertaining to the Hotṛ priest) function through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), they serve as the prescribers of the *hautra* duties and so forth by taking as their defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) the fact that the action is prescribed in the Ṛgveda. Similarly, the passage "whatever is prior [to the offering to Agni-Soma]" serves as the prescriber of the *upāṃśutva* (whispering) by taking as its defining characteristic the state of occurring prior to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice through the aforementioned relationship. Consequently, there is no defect even if that [characteristic] is absent in certain constituent parts (*padārtha*).

For this very reason, in cases such as the optional fire-installation (*kāmyādhāna*) performed with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇāhita*), although the sacrificer alone is the agent, there is no inconsistency whatsoever regarding the designation.
21. Maṇḍana: "And it would be established by scriptural statement.
Śaṅkara:
[This refers to] the red turbans and so forth of the officiating priests (ṛtvij), as well as the gift to the officiating priests.
In the Śyena sacrifice, the red turban and other such attributes belong to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and not exclusively to the Udgātṛ and others.
The selection of the priests occurs at the Ṛtupayas; indeed, it is only at the Ṛtupayas that their selection takes place, as it is so prescribed in the hall of those [who perform them].
Saṃkarṣa 3.4.11:
The selection of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is for the purpose of purchase;
however, in the case of the *satre*, because all are sacrificers (*yajamāna*) and because purchase is impossible, there is no selection.
The selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice serves a visible purpose, namely, to cause them to submit [to the ritual].
The selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is performed by Dakṣa for those priests who are the utterers of the *vaṣaṭ* call, not for all of them.
(Saṃkarṣa 3.4.9).
The selection of the officiating priests is for all of them, and it is done with ordinary worldly speech, not with Vedic speech in the case of the Hotṛ and Maitrāvaruṇa.
The selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in the Soma sacrifice is performed with mantras beginning with "agnihotrāḥ";
and that [selection] is for the purpose of the purchase (*kraya*). (Vi.

The specific number of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) must be determined according to the rites performed during the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu*). Some of these duties are as follows: "The *purodhar* distributes [the portions]," "The *pratiprasthātṛ* offers the oblation with fire," "The *neṣṭṛ* leads the wife forward," "The *unnetṛ* draws up the cups," "The *prastotṛ* chants the *prastāva*," "The *udgātṛ* sings the *udgītha*," "The *pratihartṛ* chants the *pratihāra*," "The *subrahmaṇya* invokes the *subrahmaṇyā* formula," "The *hotṛ* recites the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*)," "The *maitrāvaruṇa* gives the directions (*preṣya*)," "The *acchāvāka* [performs his duty]," and "The *grāvastut* recites the verses for the pressing-stones (*grāvastuti*)," and so forth.
In the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, a combination of officiating priests is prescribed, beginning with: "He who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu," and so forth.
[He is the Potṛ. He who is the Udgātṛ is the Neṣṭṛ; he is the Acchāvāka.]
He who is Maitrāvaruṇa is the Brahman priest; he is the Pratihartṛ.
He who is the Prastotṛ is the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; he is the Grāvastut.
He who is the Pratiprasthātṛ is the Agnīdh; he is the Unnetṛ.
A householder is truly a householder; a priest of the Subrahmaṇyā litany is truly a priest of the Subrahmaṇyā litany.
He is one who seeks the truth. (18|4|10) Bhā. 3|8|10|12|
The right to eat the *sāmnāyya* belongs to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) together with the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), but not to the *sadasya*.
For it is the sacrificer who performs the act consisting of renunciation; thus, his status as an officiating priest is established. (Vi.
3.7.18). Furthermore, there is no *saumendra caru* for the officiating priests when they rinse their mouths after consuming the *soma*.
"He belongs to the sacrificer alone" (3.4.14).
The rule that the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) wear golden garlands at the *vājapeya* sacrifice is stated in the Yajurveda;
however, it does not apply to the *adhvaryu* priests alone.
3|8|15. By the appointment of other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice is to be performed by each [priest] individually.
"The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*) must not be transgressed against" is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*), not a duty of the ritual act (*karmadharma*).

Because of the absence of connection with ritual action and the absence of context. Bhāṣya 11.2.12.35. Regarding the bestowing of boons during the laying down of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks, which is the work of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*):
if it is obtained through the scripturally prescribed purchase (*parikraya*), then the agency belongs to the sacrificer himself.

If [the officiating priest] is not obtained, then there is a worldly means (laukika upāya). Vā. 3.8.12. The fruit consisting of the implements, mantras, and so forth, which are useful for the ritual action, goes to the officiating priest (ṛtvij), or [it goes to him] because of the absence of distress. Bhā. 3.8.14.29–30. The status of being an officiating priest (ṛtviktva) belongs only to Brāhmaṇas, not to Rājanyas or Vaiśyas.
Bhāṣya 12.4.25.42–47: Priesthood (*ṛtviktva*) is characterized by fitness, which is established through study and hearing [the scriptures].

Vārttika 3.7.6.13, p. 1098: Priesthood belongs only to those who are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) in a *satra* sacrifice. Vi. 10.6.15: Only one who is fit for the office of the Brahman priest has the status of a priest when performing sacrifices during the ritual season; it does not apply to all who sacrifice during the season, nor is it necessarily present in every case.
Or [as stated in] PMS 3.7.137: *ṛtviktvaniyamakanyāyaḥ* (The principle of the restriction to the office of the priest).
"He worships the Āgnīdhra altar with an *āgneyī* [verse].

And although it is possible that the verses already present (*prakṛta*) are restricted to the *āgneyī* class by way of the *vāhuniyama* rule, such a restriction could still occur through another function (*kāryāntara*), even if there were no connection with the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma via the medium of the stotra.

Even though [the mantra] is employed at the beginning of the *stotra* in the Āgneyī [rite], the connection with the *apūrva* (transcendental result) is understood precisely because it is recited separately within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
This very principle applies to the rule regarding the number of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in the consumption of the *brahmaudana* (as in the injunction "one should feed four Brāhmaṇas," etc.).
Bhāṣya 3.8.18: "The gift to the officiating priest should be merely for the sake of merit (*dharmamātra*), on account of the capacity of the verb 'to give' (*dadāti*)."
It is heard in the scripture: "He gives the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether that gift is merely a religious duty (dharma) or for the purpose of hiring (parikraya), the author states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): The giving to the priests—the bestowing of the sacrificial fee upon the officiants—would be merely a religious duty, intended solely for spiritual merit (adṛṣṭārtha).
By the force of the word "gives," the scriptural statement "he gives" is established.
In the Maitrāvaruṇī sacrifice, a thousand is heard as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for a small ritual;
and in the Ṛtapeya, only a single Soma-cup is heard as the fee for a great ritual.
A staff, two sandals, and a dry skin-bag (as a leather vessel)—
this is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) given to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); such is the rule regarding the fees for the officiating priests as heard in the *Śruti*.
For hiring by means of a staff or similar instruments is not possible;
therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that giving is merely a religious duty (dharma).
Or rather, it is for the purpose of hiring, because of its connection with ritual action, as is seen in the world.

The word "vā" (or) is for the purpose of refuting the previously stated prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). It is heard in scripture: "He gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests. That sacrificial fee is not merely a religious duty (*dharma*); rather, it must be for the purpose of hiring (*parikraya*).
The mention of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is intended with reference to the connection with action—that is, the connection as an agent together with the ritual act.
The term *ṛtvij* (priest) is applied by virtue of being the performer of the sacrifice, as in the statement, "They sacrifice during the season.
Furthermore, it is heard in scripture: "He gives the sacrificial fee to the priests."
And thus, because the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is heard [in the scripture] in connection with ritual action, it is understood that its purpose is for the sake of hiring (*parikraya*).

This is like the case in the world: just as in the world, even when wood and other materials are being carried, what is given is mentioned as being for the sake of hiring, even though it serves merely to gratify the person.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the sacrifice as well, the giving of the sacrificial fee is for the purpose of hiring.

Even if someone does not consider the deliberation regarding the deficiency or excess of the ritual act, the giving of excessive or deficient sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the "dry curse" (*śuṣkā śapathā*), and so forth will still occur because of the explicitness of the scriptural injunctions;
this is also because there are statements connected with the sacrificial fee.
The proponent states another reason for his conclusion.

From the scriptural statement, "The officiating priests (ṛtvij) carry out [the rites] joined with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā)," and from this indicative mark (liṅga), it follows that the giving of the sacrificial fee at a sacrifice is for the purpose of hiring the officiating priests, not for the sake of merit (dharma).
Nor can one be substituted by another through hiring, because the ritual action is for the sake of another.

There is no substitution by another means, such as friendship (sāma) and so forth, for an officiating priest in a rite like the New Moon sacrifice (darśa), once he has been hired. This is the conclusion.
Because ritual action exists for the sake of another, and indeed action must be performed for the sake of another, and that another does not perform it for the sake of another without being hired;
therefore, the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in a sacrifice is solely for the purpose of hiring the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
This is also because of the scriptural statement regarding hiring.

He states another reason: "The initiated priests, having been purchased by the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), perform the sacrifice for the uninitiated. From this statement regarding their being purchased—specifically from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the mention of the priests as being "purchased"—it is understood that the giving of the sacrificial fee at the sacrifice is for the purpose of purchase.
Furthermore, because it will come into existence [at that time], [the verbal roots] *dā* (to give) and *van* (to ask/beg) [apply].
*Dā* means to give; *van* means to beg.
In this context, *san* means wealth;
the solicitation of that wealth which is to be honored is *sani*;
and the wealth obtained through such solicitation is *sanibandha*.
In that case, where there is a specific basis, it is considered "for the sake of prosperity.

[The text states: "Sacrifice was not attained by the deities; having become [prosperity], they attained it through sacrifice. When one seeks *dhṛti* (support/prosperity), it is for the prosperity of the sacrifice; for twelve nights, being consecrated (*dikṣita*), he seeks prosperity.

This expression regarding prosperity refers to that which is begged for the purpose of the sacrifice—namely, to pay the sacrificial priests (*ṛtvij*) and to accomplish other requirements for the sacrifice.
And when prosperity is bestowed upon the laborers in an infinite measure, that is what is being described.
Therefore, the gift to the officiating priests is for the purpose of hiring them;
this is also because of their praise as those who perform the ritual acts.

This is heard from the comparison of the priests with a wood-cutter: "Just as a wood-cutter, who is not his own master but is hired for the purpose of cutting, is engaged in the performance of work, so indeed are these priests of the sacrifice. By this comparison with the wood-cutter, it is shown that the gift [of dakṣiṇā] is for the purpose of hiring; for just as a wood-cutter—one who carries wood—is supported by material wealth through the act of cutting trees, which is the basis of his livelihood, and thus remains engaged in the performance of work such as felling trees, so too are the priests. Thus, it demonstrates that the giving is for the sake of purchase (parikraya).

Thus, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) at the sacrifice is for the purpose of hiring them. Who are the officiating priests? There is no restriction regarding the priests; however, there is a restriction regarding the sacrificial fees, because of their connection with the Vedic revelation (śruti).
Commentary: It has been established that the officiating priests (ṛtvij) are similar to the *sat*.
Now this is considered: who are those who are similar to the *sat*? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Ignorance [of the specific identity].
This being the case, we reply:
there is indeed a restriction by means of the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), because of their connection with the Vedic text;
they are restricted through their association with the sacrificial fees.
For it is thus handed down in tradition: "He gives the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests.
Having stated this, in the sentence concerning the flow of giving the fee, specific individuals are heard mentioned:
"He gives to the Arthīṣṭha," then to the Brahman, then to the Adhvaryu, and to such-and-such others—only certain distinguished persons being mentioned.

Thus, those who are heard of [in the texts] are indeed the officiating priests (ṛtvij); therefore, no others besides them can be eligible. This is the restriction regarding the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Or rather—when it might be argued that some among those under discussion are equal [to the others], it is replied:
the restriction follows from the use of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
And that gift of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā-dāna*), which has come down through tradition, is seen to belong to the *adhvaryu* and the other priests, but not to the *camasādhvaryus*.

Even though it may be thought that the performance [of the ritual] by six priests cannot be established as a rule, nevertheless, there exists a state of expectancy for specific details similar to those [already mentioned]; that very state is accepted here by the Veda as an established fact.
Therefore, the determination belongs to us alone: "Surely these are the *ṛtvij*s. Thus, the word *ṛtvij* [establishes] the restriction regarding the priests. (1256) *ṛtvikśabdaḥ* (the word *ṛtvij*).

And having stated that "you are the sacrificers" because of the application of the initiation rite (*dīkṣā*) to them—the commentary says: "Having declared thus, 'Those who are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are the sacrificers,' [the text] shows the initiation in the sentence concerning the sequence of initiation for the Brahman priest and the others.
How so?
"Having initiated the Gṛhapati, the Adhvaryu initiates the Brahman, then the Udgātṛ, and then the Hotṛ.
Then the Prati-prasthātṛ, having initiated him [the Gṛhapati], initiates the Adhvaryu, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin for the Brahman, the Prastotṛ for the Udgātṛ, and the Maitrāvaruṇa for the Hotṛ.
Then the Neṣṭṛ, having initiated him [the Gṛhapati], initiates the third group: the Āgnīdhra for the Brahman, the Pratihartṛ for the Udgātṛ, and the Acchāvāka for the Hotṛ."
Then, having initiated that *ṛtvij*, he initiates those who have a share in the feet: the *potṛ* for the *brahman*, the *subrahmaṇya* for the *udgātṛ*, and the *āvastut* for the *hotṛ*.
Then, having initiated that *ṛtvij*, he initiates the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*; or alternatively, a religious student (*brahmacārin*) sent by his teacher.
Thus it is said.
And initiation (*dīkṣā*) is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer.
Therefore, there are seventeen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), beginning with the Brahman.

Or rather, by restricting the word which is a characteristic mark of the sacrificer—namely, "those who are the officiating priests, they are the sacrificers"—and by restating initiation as a refinement of the sacrificer in relation to the Brahman and others in due order, [the text] shows that both of these [initiation and being a sacrificer] apply to them.

Therefore, the status of being an officiating priest (*ṛtviktva*) belongs only to those who are fit for the office of Brahman and the other priests and who perform sacrifices during the ritual season, not to everyone; and it is precisely with respect to them that the production of the ritual (*ṛtu-janana*) serves as the basis for the application of the word.
Likewise, the word "cow" (*go*) applies to an object possessing a dewlap and so forth.

Just as the word *dhyāyā*—being prescribed [by Pāṇini 3.1.129] specifically for the *sāmidhenī* verses—is restricted by that very limitation to those alone, such that it is determined that it does not denote other verses even if they are being meditated upon (*dhīyamānāsu*), in the same way, it must be understood that the word applies only to those who sacrifice during the ritual season, but it does not necessarily apply to everyone.

The connection [of this section] is by way of an objection (*pratyavasthāna*): because all [the priests] possess the status of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) through their participation in the various applications of the Soma sacrifice, the previously stated absence of the status of officiating priest for all [of them] is unestablished.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: since it is declared along with the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) that "he gives the fee to the officiating priests," "he gives to the *Āgnīdhra*," and "he gives to the *Brahman*," and because these statements conclude with the terms "to the *Āgnīdhra*" and "to the *Brahman* priest" (*ṛtvije*), there is a connection consisting of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word "officiating priest" (*ṛtvij*) and the specific titles. Therefore, the rule must be that the status of officiating priest belongs only to those beginning with the *Āgnīdhra*.

"Even those who are not specifically enumerated, or who might be considered as such, are [excluded] particularly regarding the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the initiation (*dīkṣā*). It should be understood that there is a restrictive rule:
only the sixteen priests beginning with the *adhvaryu* mentioned in the *dīkṣā*-text are [intended], and not the *camasādhvaryus*."

Bhaṭṭa: When the question arises as to who these seventeen are, since the text begins with "He gives the sacrificial fee to the priests" and then mentions only sixteen by saying "He gives to the Āgnīdhra," etc., only they possess the status of priests (*ṛtvij*).

For this very reason, in the *sattra* sacrifice, because the sacrificers themselves are the priests, we hear of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for those very individuals together with the [original] sacrificer.
Thus, sixteen are first established.
Maṇḍana: "But those [deities] are Brahmā and the others, not anyone else.
Śaṅkara: "Their sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) are fixed.

Since the husband is designated as the officiant (ṛtvij) according to the logic of the priestly office, the terms "master" (svāmin), "wife" (patnī), and "sacrificer" (yajamāna) would be untenable; therefore, their status as agents is based on a joint function (nyāsaja-vṛtti).

*Bindu* 6.1.4. The nature of the *ṛtvik*-principle: "For the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) perform the ritual acts because they have been hired; however, they do not possess what is called the status of being the performer of the sacrifice (*yajña-kartṛtva*).

It is the patron (*yajamāna*) who sacrifices (*yajate*). The status of being a wife (*patnī-tva*) belongs to the one who takes the hand (*pāṇigrāha*), according to the rule: "The husband [attains] the status of wife through connection with the sacrifice" (*patyur yajñasaṃyoge*). Thus, the status of being the performer of the sacrifice belongs to those two (the patron and the wife).

Ke.: The term *ṛtvij* (sacrificial priest) is a name applied only to certain individuals by virtue of its etymological and conventional meaning (*yogarūḍhi*). Vi. 3.1.16. All the purposes served by the priests are connected with the sacrificer.
Vā. 3.1.138. The fruit of the priests, consisting of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), is obtained even without those [purificatory rites].

Or [it may be so]. In the section concerning the means of establishing the status of a *ṛtvij* (sacrificial priest), the author of the Bhāṣya has cited the scriptural statement: "He chooses the Brahman priest.
According to the Śāstra, this duty (*dharma*) belongs to both the *ṛtvij* and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

The word *ṛtvij* (priest) is of two kinds: that which is based on the occasion of generating a sacrifice (*ṛtu-janana-nimitta*), and that which is based on the occasion of selection and maintenance (*varaṇa-bharaṇa-nimitta*).
The word *ṛtvij* does not apply to every performer of all sacrificial acts, but rather to exactly seventeen.

Because of their performance of ritual action, everyone [engaged] therein possesses the status of an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), as there is no distinction. Commentary: Regarding those persons who are mentioned in connection with the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, are they all officiating priests, or only some among them? What is the prima facie view? All of them.
Why? Because of the performance of the ritual action.
All perform the means of sacrifice;
therefore, all sacrifice during the season.
And those who sacrifice during the ritual season are the *ṛtvij*s (priests).
No specific distinction is adopted such that "only these sacrifice during the ritual season are *ṛtvij*s" and "these are not.
Therefore, all possess the status of being *ṛtvij*s.
But surely an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) is heard: "There are seventeen priests for the Soma sacrifice.
It is replied:
since there are many faults in an exclusive specification, this will be a non-exclusive injunction (*anuvāda*).

Indeed, the word *ṛtvij*, being derived as a *nipātana* (irregular formation) according to Pāṇini 3.1.94, functions by means of a suffix connected to a subordinate term (*upapada*); thus, "those who sacrifice at the proper time" (*ṛtau yajanti*) are *ṛtvijaḥ*.
If for this reason they become *ṛtvijaḥ*, then alas, since that [condition] is common to all, it follows accordingly that the status of being an *ṛtvij* would accrue to everyone.
Therefore, the statement that "four, five, six, seventeen," and so forth, are its "parts" (*avayava*) is merely an exception (*apavāda*) intended for the purpose of praise.
Or rather, not all [are included], because of the specific enumeration.
Commentary: Or rather, not all [are included].
Why? Because of the specific enumeration.
For it is heard thus: "There are seventeen, seventeen priests for the gentle *adhvara* sacrifice.

This is not an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding many [priests] who are already established, nor is it a restatement (*anuvāda*) because there is no purpose [for such a restatement], and if it were not even an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), it would entail the assumption of distinctness and the sublation of what is already established.
It is said:
the abandonment of its own meaning is not a fault, because [the meaning] has already been obtained; and the assumption of another purpose does not follow from the suffix.
When many people are known to be officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), it is stated again: "There are seventeen officiating priests."
By this, the inclusion of the term "officiant" (*ṛtvij*) by means of seventeen [names] is further clarified, while it is not clarified by more than that; from this, the following is understood.
When the connection of the term "officiant" with the person is being clarified again by means of seventeen [names], it is understood that those in excess of seventeen have been excluded.
In that regard, is the connection with the seventeen intended, or is it the exclusion of the additional ones?
Since the connection with the seventeen [priests] lacks a governing purpose, it is understood that the exclusion of those in excess is intended.
He says: "But surely the word 'ṛtvij' (priest) is not applied to those who are being prohibited."
Since it is impossible to negate the actual nature of the word *ṛtvij* (priest), its function is what is negated.
For example, when one says, "This is not my son," the meaning is that the functions of a son do not apply to him.

Thus, this prohibition of more than seventeen [priests] which is understood from the sense of the text should be seen as pertaining to their functional role (*kārya*), not to their essential nature (*svarūpa*). If it is argued that "the act of choosing (*varaṇa*) must be accepted because it is the ground for the application of the term [‘ṛtvij’]," then in this view, since the use of the word is established through the connection with the ritual action itself, the other [view] holds that because the essential nature is prohibited, the function based upon it is also difficult to prohibit; therefore, he asks: how could those who sacrifice during the season not possess the status of officiating priests (*ṛtviktva*)?

But the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntavādī), desiring to state the answer according to the true nature of things, begins with the words, "In that case, this [term] is of two kinds," and so forth.
If this were merely etymological (yaugika), then it would not be excluded from anything;
however, this is a word denoting a technical refinement (saṃskāra).
For *saṃskāra* consists of choosing (*varaṇa*) and supporting (*bharaṇa*).
Those for whom these two do not exist will not be denoted by that term, even though they are connected with the ritual action.
And those acts of choosing and supporting are performed by the sacrificer for the seventeen [priests] alone.

And because they are the cause of that [designation], the word *ṛtvij* is a restatement (*anuvāda*) in the passage "those seventeen are the priests" (*saptadaśa ṛtvijaḥ*). It is a single compound word.

However, the statement "In this sacrificial rite there are seventeen priests" is a restatement of the whole (the aggregate), just like [the rule] "one priest" (*ekaṃ ṛtvijaḥ*) at *Pāṇini* 3.1.7.16.32, which— due to a specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) from the word *ṛtvij*— is understood as referring to the whole.

Otherwise, if it were an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), the status of being the cause for performing the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtuyajana*)— which is understood by way of their respective positions— would have to be abandoned, as that would entail the three defects [of *parisaṃkhyā*]. Furthermore,
there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a form of priestly office (*ṛtviktva*) that is not directly perceived.
It is not possible [to determine this].

(Nyāyasūtra 3.2.16, p. 33, p. 1097). Priest (*ṛtvij*): For this very reason, the basis for the application of the word "priest" is either the act of choosing (*varaṇa*) itself or that same principle—the performance of sacrifice during the ritual season (*ṛtu*).
The view that it is a *nimitta* (occasioning cause) is rejected, because there is no evidence for assuming a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*).
The purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) belong to the character of all the priests.

[This is] because of the distinction between the veils (*varaṇa*) of Brahman and the others, and because it would entail the postulation of multiple unseen potencies (*adṛṣṭa-śakti*). However, if one accepts that the capacity [to veil] belongs only to the all-pervading attribute (*vyāpaka-dharma*) of the veil itself, then in the case of "the king's man," the subordinate element (*śeṣin*)... [is established].
Bhāva: [It is so called] because of its connection with action—that is, because of its connection with the fruit of the principal action.
The meaning is that it refers to the principal actions, as in the injunction: "One desiring heaven should perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices."
Nor [is it established] by two [auxiliaries].
However, the requirement for an auxiliary (*aṅgākāṅkṣā*) is satisfied even by a single auxiliary.
This being the case, the purpose (*prayojana*) consists in the assistance (*upakāra*) resulting from the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*).
And the fruit would be without the defect of verbal expression;
there would be no defect of the injunctive word.
A "verbal defect" is the defect of a word, namely its futility.
That purpose in which there is no verbal defect is "free from verbal defects" (*aśabdadoṣa*).
Therefore, even if not all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) are performed, there is no consequence of the absence of the fruit.
If it is argued that [the fruit is absent] because of the non-performance of even one part:
The proponent (siddhāntin) further objects:
"This is not correct, because of the unity of the word (ekaśabdya).
'Ekaśabdya' is the state of having a single word for all those primary acts as well as their subsidiaries, wherein one and the same word is the prescriptive injunction."
The single term "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices" is the instructor of the performance of both the principal rites and the subsidiaries such as the Samid-yāgas;
by that term, the connection with the result is established.
Therefore, the result belongs only to that which is accompanied by all its constituent parts.

And since there is a difference in meaning, it has been stated that [the text] serves to establish the deities for the injunctions regarding the meditation on the word-meanings (*padārtha-dhyāna*). Therefore, what is the point of the fivefold repetition of "he sacrifices, he sacrifices" (*yajati yajati*), which is established by the second-case endings and does not serve that purpose? It would be meaningless.

"The deities are enjoined by means of words such as *dādi*," because it must be stated that, just like a mantra, each utterance constitutes a distinct act, as in the expression "he sacrifices to Viṣṇu."

Since the deity is also enjoined by means of the second case-ending (accusative) in such instances, this [principle] is merely general. For those [acts] which are embraced by the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), which are not directly connected to the primary purpose (*asamaveta*), and which serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*),
the word *yajati*— when repeated five times— is established as referring to a single act, namely the *samidh*-sacrifice, precisely because its purpose is invisible.
Alternatively,

in accordance with the *prābhākara* view, the action— either in the form of the *samit*-bhāvanā or in the form of the *upāṃśuyāja*-bhāvanā— is established by the verbal suffix itself, once the action has been enjoined as delimited by the name "samit," just as in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Thus it is said.
This being the position reached, it is replied:

this would indeed be so if, through recognition and its opposite, the mere object were the cause of the restatement (anuvāda) because the deities such as Tanūnapāt are designated by way of restating that [object]; what then? There will be the state of possessing a requirement for restatement.
Nor should it be asked how it constitutes a name; for that [name-status] occurs when there is the attainment of something already established as a subordinate element of the injunction.

For instance, in the case of the mantra "bhāvāḥ samiddhayah svāhā," because the name *samiddha* functions as a designation for that which is enjoined (*vidhātṛtvena*), it is the *bhāvanā* itself— motivated by the connection with the deity indicated by the words of the mantra— that connects with the meaning of the verbal root in the injunction.
And this being so, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
It is appropriate [to say that the deity is enjoined by the word].

However, when it is connected with a meaning that is already established (*upapadyārtha*), then the deityhood derived from the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*)—which is enjoined by a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) regarding Tanūnapāt and other deities—is weaker.
One must state that, for fear of excessive complexity (*gaurava*), the verbal root-meaning is abandoned and the injunction is made solely for the sake of the established meaning.
He connects precisely the deity who has been kindled by the words of the mantra.

In that case, since there is a possibility of the meaning being appropriate for the injunction, the deities such as Tanūnapāt are enjoined by way of restating (anuvāda) the knowledge of the root-meaning as delimited by the [mantric] expression.

It desires to be performed like [the sacrifice] of Manu; and that desire is not a cause for setting aside the injunction, according to the maxim: "The injunction is not set aside by a desire for the meaning of the verbal root."
It fulfills [the requirement].
However, if there is the attainment of a suitable and possible object fit for the injunction, nor [is it fulfilled] because of the status of the deity as being kindled by the words of the mantra;
therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*) among the deities.

There is recognition of the meaning of the verbal root; therefore, it is established everywhere that [the word] prescribes only the meaning of the verbal root, as in the case of the *samid*-sacrifice, where [it is said]:
"Svāhā to Tanūnapāt" (*tanūṃ*). It is indeed the meaning of the verbal root that is enjoined.

Nor are there injunctions here, such as the mantras beginning with "He does not cause to fall, [therefore he is] Tanūnapāt," which are recited in their fixed order; for one does not perceive anything therein that is suitable for being enjoined. To explain: the state of being an object of injunction is indeed perceived individually in each case, including in those sentences concerning Tanūnapāt and the others.

Is it as a substance (*dravyatvena*)? Or as a deity (*devatātvena*)? Nor is it the case that there is an injunction of an action delimited by a name, where the form of Tanūnapāt and so forth serves as the basis for obtaining a deity through the wording of a mantra (*māntravarṇika*). No such substance is well-known in the world.
Nor is the second [alternative]—[the accusative case]—appropriate.
But how can there be an injunction of a quality? This would indeed be possible if, in the word *yajati*, it were possible to convey the deity by means of that [suffix];
for instance, in "he sacrifices to Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇuṃ yajati*), since it is proximate to the action under discussion, it could function as such an object of prescription.
In such cases, one resorts to that [interpretation] out of necessity (*agatyā*).
And here, there is no other possible way;
for if [the injunction] were not to enjoin even a quality (*guṇa*), the sentence would be entirely purposeless.
Since there is no appearance of a deity based on the wording of a mantra, it would be a name by way of the principle of "that substance" (taddravyanyāya).
Therefore, disregarding the attainment [of a deity] through the wording of a mantra, [the term is applied] to the *samidh* sacrifice under discussion,
because that is logical.
Therefore, in this context, the injunction repeated in each subsequent sentence serves precisely to enjoin optional deities for the subsequent offerings;
its power being exhausted, it enjoins the *bhāvanā* itself as colored by the meaning of the verbal root.
As it has been said: "Alternatively, by means of the sentences concerning the *samidh* and so forth, [the injunction] applies to the *upāṃśuyāja* alone."

The verbal suffix first enjoins the action according to its capacity; there is no optionality regarding the deities expressed by the words of the mantras, such as Samit and others. However, when another [means] is incapable, it requires that which has not yet been mentioned.
"They are prescribed," it is said;
nor is there any contradiction with the sequence of the *upāṃśuyāja* injunction.

Nor is the prescription of what has already been prescribed purposeless; since it serves a purpose by manifesting the deities of the subsequent [offerings], such as the *samidh* and others, there is no contradiction in the cognition [of the injunction], and thus there is indeed a distinction between the acts.
Nor is there [a fault] here because of the existence [of the word];
for where deities such as Viṣṇu exist, it is as stated.
With respect to the present tense, one should say that there is simply no such thing as a "disruption" (vyadhāna), and thus there will be meaningfulness (arthavattva).
In this view, the *bhāṣya*—which states, "The *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are made five times;
this armor (*varman*) is indeed prepared for the sacrifice; what single *apūrva* do the words 'he sacrifices' enjoin?"—is to be interpreted as follows.

The meaning is that a single sentence concerning the *upāṃśuyāja*—namely, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) beginning with "for the sake of sacrifice through a name, for the self, for victory"—enjoins a new injunction (*apūrva*) and supports it.

By means of the name, the injunction of the fivefold form is determined; for the injunction and the eulogy (*stuti*) share a single object. Nor should it be said [that the deity is known] "by that suffix, by the dative case, or by the wording of the mantra," because [in this case] they do not apply.

As for the statement: "Whether the word *samit* and so forth is considered a quality (*guṇa*) or a name (*nāmadheya*), the connection with a deity is present there; however, each subsequent [interpretation] is weaker than the preceding."
[If it] were so, then since the distinction [between them] would already exist by those two alone, what will repetition accomplish here?

Thus it is stated [in Vākyapadīya, p. 533] that this applies only to mantras ending in the dative case. In that context, because the words *samit* and so forth are displaced and intended to convey a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), there is a repetition of the same [mantra], since there is a distinction of ritual acts (*karmabheda*).
First of all, a quality that is already possible cannot be a differentiator.
Nor can it be the name [of the rite].

For in this way, the repetition of what is already one would serve the purpose of specification, since there exists a verbal root (*ākhyāta*) belonging to an injunction (*vidhi*) that has no other purpose.
For in this case,
there would not be the repetition [of the rule] resulting from the application of the principle of "established otherwise" (anyathāsiddhi).

Just as in the case of "With the *udbhid* [sacrifice]," "He offers the *samidhs*," "He offers to *tanūnapāt*," "He offers to the *iḍas*," and "One desiring cattle should sacrifice"— wherein there is the repetition of the injunctive verb (*vidhyākhyāta*) through the fivefold use of the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) for the sake of enjoining the *barhis* offering and the *svāhākāra* offering as part of the very same contextually established Jyotiṣṭoma, even though these are enjoined with the fruit of cattle which is not distinct [from the primary result].
The word *yajati* has been previously employed [in other contexts].
Here, there is no difference in the verbal form;
however, due to its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), it constitutes a distinct ritual action.
What then? It belongs to the quality alone, because of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

There is a fivefold repetition of the single word *yajati*. Since that [quality] is already occupied by this name, it is impossible for another name to enter; therefore, in that case, it is merely a name.
Like a different word, it would be a differentiator through its action;
yet here, the differentiator is by means of a single word "yajati" (he sacrifices),
whereas in this case, it is by the verbal suffix itself, which possesses no other formative element.

As for what was stated: since it is impossible for that very same [action] to be enjoined by the word *yajati* when heard again—unless it be another action—it follows that the repetition of the injunctive verb (*vidhyākhyāta*) itself [effects the distinction]. Because there is no distinction [otherwise], the repeated hearing would be purposeless; thus, once the fact of differentiation is established, it is settled that the name [of the rite] serves precisely that purpose.
For indeed, it would be so;
however, for that which possesses a purpose, there is no perceived difference between each repetition, but not so at the outset.
As it has been said: "In general, a connection with the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) must be accepted [as the basis for differentiation].
Therefore, even by means of repetition (abhyāsa), the distinction between ritual acts (karmabheda) is established."
Name is not desired [as primary], for it is subject to dependence on another;
therefore, first, its divisions—
namely the five beginning with *samit*— are prescribed according to the injunctions as they are called.
Why? Because it is the cause of differentiation.
"No," [it says] in the Vārttika (p. 467).

And as for the statement, "In this way, the repeated mention of the same thing must be for the purpose of qualification," if that were so, then just as there is a distinction [of acts] due to repetition, so too [is there a distinction] in the case of "He offers the *samidh*s."
This is the logical principle (*nyāya*).
It should be observed under the section on "Repetition" (*abhyāsādhikaraṇa*) in the *Bhinnanyāya*.
(212) Thus, because of the scriptural mention of the plural number, a distinction based on number also follows.

It must be stated that there is also an addition by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the portion of the impeller (*codaka*). For the number residing in the action is not different from the action itself.

According to the principle "the repetition of the same [action] is thus" (*ekasyaivaṃ punaḥśrutiḥ*), it differentiates [the actions], just as in the cases: "He offers three oblations" and "Twelve, twelve."
Another ritual action: "And he offers these as oblations," [Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa] 10.1.7.12–7.13.
But here, however: "To the fuel-sticks, svāhā!

To the *iḍmīyas*, svāhā!"—in this way, according to the rule "In the case of a single [action], when there is a prior connection with a scriptural mention of a quality" (JS 2.1.23), the application of the name occurs through the connection with a deity indicated by the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*).
Thus they conclude, following the literal force of the scripture.
But when one [entity] possesses both [qualities], even though it is a single thing, there is no restriction regarding number, such as the expression of plurality.
"One or two or more priests (ṛtvij) should be chosen;
for even in the case of a single person, titles such as 'Hotṛ' and 'Adhvaryu' would be justified by the difference in their functions, since they perform those respective distinct tasks.
If this is argued, it is not so.
"Because a restriction regarding number is observed in the originative injunctions for the production of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Thus [it is stated] in the two Nyāya-sūtras.
[Question: "Is it true that (in the case of the *ṛtviks*, the term) 'śramitā' indicates an increase in number, but not in those who are being produced?"
As for the non-occurrence that is perceived in those cases, it is accounted for by the principle "because of the difference in actions for a single person" (*ekasya karmabhedāt*).

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) considers that the designations such as *hotṛ* and so forth will likewise apply to that very same person (the sacrificer himself) through that same principle of "because of the difference in actions for a single person. (*Bhāṣya* 3.1.13.9).
Or [the following applies]: Vārttika 3.1.18.

Since the word *śamitṛ* (slaughterer) is based on its connection with a specific ritual function (*karmayoga*), it is applicable to the Brahmin priests mentioned in the context according to the maxim "of one [person], due to the difference of functions" (Pāṇini 3.1.123). Therefore, there is no possibility of a non-Brahmin attaining the status of a *śamitṛ*. Sūtra.

"Because of the conjunction with one [deity] in one [instance], the other statement is unestablished. Now, as for the further reason stated by the proponent— that the text "it is not ground" indicates grinding in the case of a dual-deity offering, and that the text "half is ground, half is ungrounded for the dual-deity offering" indicates it is for the sake of the deity— [this is addressed as follows].
To this it is replied:
what was stated as the second reason, namely "the subsequent statement," means that since grinding is not otherwise established, this statement serves as its injunction;
nor does this constitute a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

When there is an alternative view, the injunction of multiple meanings is resolved by resorting to that alternative. However, when no alternative exists, one must accept a sentence with multiple meanings in order to avoid the contingency of [the word] being used merely for the sake of pronunciation.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that grinding does not apply in the case of an offering to two deities.

In the discussion regarding the analysis of the *puṣpa* [offering], under the sūtra "Because of the connection with one [deity] in a single [instance]" (3.2.139), he will state that the mention of *aindrāpauṣṇa* and other such offerings—which have deities associated with *puṣpa*—is not intended (i.e., they are excluded).
See Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 647. The section "Because of the connection with one in a single [instance]" should be consulted in the *Vindu* as the "Pūṣā-adhikaraṇa."
Regarding the state of being a single-potsherd (ekakapālatā) in a single ritual action, there is an option for its inclusion.
The meaning of the sūtra, however, is that among all the single-potsherds, the single-potsherd dedicated to the Viśvedevas serves as the archetype (prakṛti).

This being the case, regarding the *sarvahoma* (complete offering) and the *aparyāpti* (insufficiency) of the single-potherd cake for Heaven and Earth (*dyāvā-pṛthivya*) at the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, these two observations are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of the ritual rule belonging to the *Vaiśvadeva* [offering], not an original (*apūrva*) rule. Therefore, because of the observation of the complete offering and insufficiency at the *Āgrayaṇa*, the *Vaiśvadeva* alone is the archetype (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, in the *saumika avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), there is a scriptural injunction for the single-potherd cake for Varuṇa (*vāruṇa*) to have the offering of two portions made only once.

Because of the scriptural statement, there is a double offering at the principal oblation (*pradhānahoma*), and then a single offering again for the *sviṣṭakṛt*; thus, there is a total of two offerings—one double and one single—and this is the distinction.

Therefore, regarding the single offering at the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), because of the statement, "He offers twice from the cake baked on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*)," there is no contradiction even in the case of the Vaiśvadeva *ekakapāla* in its archetypal form (*prakṛti*).
Consequently, the Vaiśvadeva *ekakapāla* alone is the archetype of all *ekakapāla* cakes.

Nevertheless, regarding the distinction among the Vāruṇapraghāsikas— namely, that "the ladles are made of gold or of *śamī* wood"— the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the single-pother vessel (*ekakapāla*) belonging to the Vāruṇapraghāsika are extended (*atideśa*) to the single-pother vessel of the Sākamedha sacrifice by way of that [Vāruṇapraghāsika] context, and not directly from the properties of the Vaiśvadevika single-pother vessel. This is because the principle of the introductory section (Jaimini Sūtra 7.1.5.23), which states "that which is obtainable elsewhere is not prescribed," defines the nature of the rule that what is already known does not need to be enjoined again.

And this is known from the *Bhaṭṭa* text (*Mīmāṃsā-nyāya-prakāśa*, 7.1.6): "And because, in the case where [the rule of extended application] for the first [Sākamedha sacrifice]—which is to be numbered as five—is present, there is an absence of that principle of this section which would otherwise be obtainable from another source.
Ke.:

In the case of the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) offering to Heaven and Earth, there is the displacement (*vidhvanta*) of the first potsherd belonging to the eight-potsherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) dedicated to Agni.

Bhāṣya 10.1.9.16: Regarding the single-potsherd (ekakapāla) offering in the Sākamedha sacrifice, there is an extension of the ritual details (*dharmātideśa*) from the Varuṇapraghāsa single-potsherd offering.
These are the single-potsherd ritual details:
having adorned [the vessel], having filled [it], "it is to be sacrificed silently" (*upāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ*), and so forth.
7|1|5|23: "He offers the *sarvahuta*"; "He offers without leaving anything remaining.
7|1|10|26: But in the *avabhṛtha* [concluding bath] alone, there is a double-portioning (*dviravadāna*) of the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*).
Bhāṣya 7|1|5|3: There is an extension (*atideśa*) of the properties of the *ekakapāla* belonging to the *varuṇapraghāsa* to the *ekakapāla* of the *sākamedha* and the *vaiśvakarmaṇa*.

Because the *svitkārā* (the sound 'svit') is prescribed only for the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*), there is also the omission of the subsequent mantra; this is the view of Bhaṭṭa [in Bhāṣya 10.4.20].
The same applies to the single potsherd and the Indra-Agni offerings.
At the Vaiśvadeva parvan, a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth (dyāvāpṛthivya) is prescribed.
At the Varuṇapraghāsas, a cake on one potsherd for Ka (kāya) is prescribed, as well as a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni (aindrāgna).

Then, at the Sākamedhas, having prescribed a cake on one potsherd for Viśvakarman and a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni, [the text] states: "This is the Brāhmaṇa for the Aindrāgna, this is the Brāhmaṇa for the Ekakapāla; and that which is the Brāhmaṇa for the other [is the same]."
In this regard, here is the sūtra of the established doctrine (*siddhāntasūtra*):
The cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) and that dedicated to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*)—these two alone should be treated in the same manner as those [cakes] numbered five.
And thus, here too, there is a direct extension (*kaṇṭhātideśa*) of everything, including the injunctions and the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
The word "ca" (and) serves to indicate the illustrative example mentioned in the preceding section;
this is an extended application (*atideśa*).
Of what?

In the case of the *ekakapāla* (single-pot-sherd) offerings to Indra-Agni among the *Sākamedha* sacrifices, and the *vāruṇapraghāsika-ekakapāla* and *aindrāgna* offerings within the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices— due to the extension (*atideśa*) from the section on injunctions and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning the year-long rite—
the status of an *arthavāda* as a "model performance" (*parakṛti*) consists in its being a Vedic statement that possesses a single agent and a purposeful application. (Bhāṣya 7.1.4.22).
"In the case of a single action, there is no option because of the indivisibility resulting from the unity of the injunction.
Thus it is heard in scripture: "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya."

Furthermore, there are two instances of touching the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) in the archetype: "One should touch the full moon sacrifice with the *Caturhotṛ* formula, and the new moon sacrifice with the *Pañcahotṛ* formula.

When the oblation has been placed upon the altar, on the full moon day, the Adhvaryu touches it with his hand turned downward, using the mantra known as the *Caturhotṛ*, beginning with "The earth is the Hotṛ."
At the New Moon sacrifice, however, one touches [the offering] with the mantra known as the Pañcahotṛ, beginning with "Agnir hotā" (Agni is the Hotṛ).
Now, when the two solar offerings are employed at the Full Moon sacrifice, they are to be touched with the Caturhotṛ mantra.

And when the solar offering is employed at the New Moon sacrifice, it is to be touched with the Pañcahotṛ mantra. Regarding the inquiry as to whether there is an option between the two mantras in both cases, the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) against the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the application of the mantras is determined by the specific occasion (*bhavya-vyavasthā*), even though this was not explicitly stated in the Sūtra.
In a single ritual action—namely, the one solar (*saurya*) rite—there would be an option (*vikalpa*) between the two mantras for touching.

For, because the injunction is one—since the injunction “one should offer the *caru* oblation to Sūrya” is singular—the action is one, and thus there is no division between the two mantras for touching; rather, their combination (*samuccaya*) would follow.
And that is not possible because they serve the same purpose.
Therefore, the established conclusion is that there is an option (*vikalpa*). Regarding a single ritual action in the *Ekatrika* sacrifice:

here, in the performance of the *Saurya* sacrifice on the full moon day, the touching (*abhimarśana*) is performed with the *Caturhotṛ* formula alone; whereas in the performance of the *Saurya* sacrifice on the new moon day, it is performed with the *Pañcahotṛ* formula alone. Thus, the application (*viniyoga*) consists precisely in this fixed distribution (*vyavasthā*) between the two mantras.

We consider it logical that the general [view] is indeed a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), while the specific distinction lies in its being a "fixed conceptual construction" (*vyavasthitavikalpa*).
As for the established doctrine of conceptual construction (*vikalpasiddhānta*), it is necessarily based on that very [distinction].
(Ke.)

By the principle of the eighth section (*adhikaraṇa*), namely, “In the case of a single ritual, there is indeed an option because the injunction is one,” when the evening and morning *homās*—characterized by the *abhi* and *sūrya* mantras—are obtained as options in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), [that restriction applies].

As stated on page 788 of the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*: even though there is no distinction in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*), when there is a difference in the rituals, according to the principle “in the case of a single ritual,” since the extension of the ritual details (*vidhyanta-atideśa*) for one sacrifice enjoined by the sentences concerning the *aindravāyava* and others occurs optionally in the modified sacrifice, the properties (*dharma*) of that one [sacrifice] apply optionally.
The sacrifice should be performed once; the distinction is that when there is unity of action, it follows the original model (yathāprakṛti).
Page 807.
Because the auxiliary elements (guṇas) are prescribed for a single action, the entire action [should be performed] as such.
Since many qualities are prescribed—that is, enjoined—for a single action, there should be the performance of all those actions.
