Just as in the case of the *āghāra* libation, because of the injunctions "he pours straight," "he pours continuously," and "he pours eastward," there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of straightness, continuity, and eastward direction; so it is in other cases as well—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
(Ke.)

In the statement “because they are prescribed for a single action” (*ekakarmaṇi śiṣṭatvāt*), a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of straightness, upwardness, self-length, and continuity is stated regarding the substratum (*ādhāra*).
Bāla. p. 179:
there is an option (*vikalpa*) among the ritual formulas (*karaṇamantra*) that perform a single function.
Bhāṣya 12.1.21–129: There is an option (*vikalpa*) among qualities that serve a single purpose regarding a single action.

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the procedure for the animals dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatyapaśu*)—which possess properties of the same class—should be performed for the sake of favoring the number one thousand.

The state of being a single performance (*ekatantratva*) occurs when those possessing the ritual procedure (*tantriṇām*), which are enjoined by a single sentence, share the same place, time, and agent, as in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, and likewise in the Citrā sacrifice. However, in those cases where [the rites] are enjoined by separate sentences, there must be a distinction of the performance (*tantrabheda*).
Bhāṣya 12.1.11.
On one side there are two, on the other side there is one; for those who belong to both lineages (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*), there is the choice of the *ārṣeya* (the ancestral seer).
Saṃkarṣa. 3.4.8.

According to the view that "both [are] in one [place]," there is an absence of the requirement that a certainty whose qualifier has a specific delimitor (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka*) as its mode must be the cause of a cognition of qualified qualification (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyajñāna*).
Maṇi, p. 15:
It is not contradictory for that which is subordinate in one context to be primary in another;
for example, although the deity is subordinate with respect to the animal victim, it is primary with respect to the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) offered to that animal.

By the maxim "two in one," if both the number six and the unexpressed number [of subsidiaries] were admitted as being connected to the ritual action (*karman*), then upon admitting a distinction [between them], there would be the contingency of [the subsidiary] becoming part of the primary action itself—as in the case of the *ṣaṭtriṃśadrātra* sacrifice where it is said, "there are six days, there are four. (Bhāṭṭa 8.1.3) In the archetype (*prakṛti*), just like the location and so forth which are expressed, the concomitance (*sāhitya*) of the subsidiary and the primary is also admitted as a qualification in the performance of the primary by means of the maxim "two in one"; thus, the injunction for performance (*prayogavidhi*) prescribes the performance as qualified by all its specific attributes.

The maxim is: "What is determined in one place regarding the meaning of a branch [of scripture] applies likewise elsewhere. When, among various opposing doctrines, that which is established by powerful reasoning, scriptural authority, and consensus is refuted in one instance as being contrary to one's own position, then all the remaining [opposing views] are considered refuted by that very [refutation]. (Sāṅkhyasūtra-bhāṣya 2.58)
The *ekatrika* sacrifice:
because of the interchanging of the number one and the number three, there is a certain sacrifice named *ekatrika*.

It is heard [in scripture] as follows: "Now, the *ekatrika*: for it, the *vahiṣpavamāna* chant is on one verse; the *hotṛ*'s *rājya* chant is on three verses; the *maitrāvaruṇa*'s chant is on one verse; the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*'s chant is on three verses; the *acchāvāka*'s chant is on one verse; and the *mādhyaṃdina-pavamāna* chant is on three verses."
VI. 10.1.2: In the Ekatrika sacrifice, the chanting is performed on a triplet of verses (*tuce*).
In the Ekatrika sacrifice, by the triple repetition of a single verse, the Trika-stoma-ṣṭoma is formed.
In a *trika-stotra*, there should be a *dhurya* [stotra].
The Commentary states: There is a *kratu* (sacrificial session) called the *ekatrika*: "Now, the *ekatrika*: its *vahiṣpavamāna* is on one [verse], the *hotṛ*'s *rājya* on three;
the *maitrāvaruṇa*'s on one, the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*'s on three."
"In one [verse] for the Acchāvāka priest, and in three [verses] for the Mādhyandina Pavamāna.
However, there are Sāmans associated with the *dhur* verses.
Regarding these, a doubt arises: are they to be sung over a triplet (*tuca*) of verses, or over a single verse?
What is established? The *trika* hymn-form (*stoma*) should belong to the triplet (*tuca*) among the *pṛṣṭha*-sāmans.
Thus, a rule that establishes the triplet and excludes other possibilities is inferred.
Therefore, it should be sung upon the triplet.
In the Ekatrika sacrifice;
that is, in the Ekatrika, whether in the *ṛc*s and so forth, or in a single [verse], because the property of repetition belongs to the *stoma*.
The Commentary: Or rather, it should be sung upon a single verse.
For in that case, the quality of repetition belongs to the *stoma*, on the authority of the scriptural statement:
"They praise with the *dhurs* repeated," and "He worships with the *pṛṣṭhas* after they have been repeated."
Why should one not follow this statement?

[The rule is] that among the *dhuri* *sāmans*, the singing should be performed on a single verse (*ṛc*). Soma says: Since it follows the original sequence (*prākṛta-krama*), here too, because it is original, it is logical that it should remain as it was.
Thus, the connection with the example is appropriate.
The *sāmans* that consist of modifications of the *gāyatrī* are expressed by the word *durgāṇa*, because of the statement:
"The *dhurs* of the *gāyatra* are modifications of the chant."

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: "That *dhurya* [chant], which is the *trikastoma* occurring in the midst of the *dhūrgāna* stotra, should be performed upon the *tuca*s. Vi [the commentary] states: "'It should be on the *tuca*'; thus, the *dhūrgāna* would be on a single [verse], as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Or rather, it should be on the *tuca*, because by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the repetition is enjoined for two [verses]."
Bhaṭṭa: In the archetype sacrifice (*prakṛti*), some stotras are to be performed with triple-chanting (*tri-stoma*) on different verses (*dhur*), while others are not so performed.

Now, regarding this *ekatrika* sacrifice, there arises the question: in the case of those stotras where triple-chanting on different verses is prescribed, should the chanting be performed on three distinct verses, or should it be performed on a single verse alone through repetition so as to achieve the state of having a triple-stoma? Upon reflection, for the sake of following the injunction that extends the model sacrifice (*codaka*), the chanting should be performed on three distinct verses.

Nor should it be argued that in the section on the *ekatrika* sacrifice, because of the injunction "they praise with the *dhurs* repeated," there is an absence [of the *ekatrika*] due to the prescription of the repetition of only a single verse;
for this statement is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to refer to the repetition of the *sāman*.
To explain: first of all, this does not enjoin the repetition by means of the *stoma* alone, because that would result in such repetition even when the chanting is not performed on the *dhurs*.

If "in the *dhurs*" were a qualification [of the act of praising], it would result in a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭoddeśa*). Furthermore, if repetition were enjoined with reference to the hymns of praise (*stotra*), it would follow that only those [specific] hymns themselves must be repeated; however, there is no evidence for the repetition of a single verse (*ṛc*) alone.

Therefore, the connection with repetition must be enjoined specifically with respect to the singing of the *dhurs*, while accepting that the word "one should praise" (*stuvīta*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Since that [repetition] is already established by the general rule (*codaka*) which prescribes the singing of the *tuca* (three-verse unit), this sentence is merely a restatement; thus, the singing should be performed on three distinct [verses].

This being the case, since it would otherwise result in the entire sentence becoming purposeless, repetition is enjoined by this [text] specifically with reference to the *stotra* when the *dhur* verses function as the occasion (*nimitta*). This is because the locative case expresses the status of being the occasion. Since the occasion is precisely the distinction inherent in the sacrifice, and because the occasion is the chanting on the *dhur* verses which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *stotra* that serves as the object of the injunction, there is no possibility of the repetition applying to other *stotras*. Furthermore, because a *stotra* consists essentially in the glorification of qualities (*guṇasaṃkīrtana*), it is denoted by the verbal root [√stu]; therefore, the injunction for repetition is made specifically with reference to that [type of *stotra*].

Therefore, because the subject matter (*uddeśya*) consists of the clarified butter (*ājya*), the *luptṛpta* verses, and so forth—arising from the context of defining their characteristics—there is no contingency of the entire [verse] being repeated.

Furthermore, since this is a hymn (*stotra*) consisting of the glorification of qualities, and since that cannot be accomplished without the repetition of the *ṛc*, the state of having a threefold hymn (*trikastomaka*) must be achieved through the repetition of a single verse (*ṛc*). Consequently, in the case of a threefold hymn (*trikastomaka*), the requirement for the singing of triplets (*tṛca*) on the *dhur* verses—which would otherwise be established as distinct units—is set aside. However, it should be understood that in the case of a single-hymn (*ekastomaka*), there is indeed the singing of triplets.
Maṇḍana: "It should be in the first verse of the *sāman* chant. Śaṅkara: "The chanting is on the first verse of a single *ṛc*.

In the *Ekatrika* sacrifice, on the day of the *Mādhyandina-pavamāna*, for the purpose of chanting, the entire first triplet (*tṛca*) alone is to be taken, and not the first three verses of three separate triplets.
Regarding the *ekatrika* sacrifice on the middle day, beginning with the *tuc* verses, because the meters have become the revealed texts (*śruti*).
There is a sacrifice called the *ekatrika*: "Now this is the *ekatrika*; for it, the *bahiṣpavamāna* is on one [verse], and the *hotṛrājya* is on three."
The *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is performed on one verse; the *hotṛrājya* chant is performed on three verses.
The *maitrāvaruṇa* chant is on one verse; the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* chant is on three verses. The *acchāvāka* chant is on one verse; the *mādhyandina-pavamāna* chant is on three verses.
Thus, in this Ekatrika sacrifice, on the Mādhyaṃdina Pavamāna, the chanting should take place upon the first verses of the triplets (tṛca), which constitute the *stotriyas*.

This is because the meters (*chandas*) are the primary basis for the ritual; for in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is stated: "The Mādhyaṃdina Pavamāna has three Sāmans and consists of triplets of meters (*trikchandas*)," referring to the three meters named Gāyatrī, Bṛhatī, and Triṣṭubh, which have become the very essence of the Śruti.
Those [details] obtained through the rule of transfer (codaka) can be integrated here if the singing is performed on the *tṛca* verses.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the singing is to be done on the *tṛca* verses and so forth.
Alternatively, it should be at the beginning, because that is the logical principle and the other [position] is merely inferential.

In the *ekatrika* sacrifice, which is a specific type of ritual (*kratu*), the measurement (*māna*) is indeed at the very beginning—the first triplet (*tṛca*)—of the *pavamāna* chant on the middle day (*mādhyaṃdinapavamāna*).
This is because of that principle (*tannyāyatvāt*); that is, the principle concerning the potsherds (*kapāla*) mentioned in the preceding section.

That which belongs to the chanting of the *mādhyaṃdinapavamāna* is "made of that" (*tanmayya*); the state of being so is "that-principle-ness" (*tannyāyatva*), and it is from that [principle] [that the conclusion follows].
The previously stated principle is: "When there is the grasping of a single part of things that follow a sequence, the application begins from the beginning.
By that very principle, the determination here is also made.
As for the other, namely that which was stated in the passage: "The *mādhyandina-pavamāna* [stotra] has the *triṣṭubh* as its meter and is the insertion (*āvāpa*)."

Regarding unity: since the favoring of the meter is obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) when there is a quality of an animal sacrifice dedicated to a single deity, it is of inferential nature.

Furthermore, because the favor of the *chandas* (meter) prevails over the favor of the sequence, the singing (*gāna*) must take place in the first *ṛc* of the triplet alone; it does not apply to the first verses of all three triplets. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
And this follows the original placement (*yathāniveśam*), as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), since there is only a modification of the number.

In the *ekatrika*—a specific type of sacrifice—on the day of the *mādhyaṃdina-pavamāna*, the singing (*gāna*) occurs only in the first [set] according to the arrangement and sequence, and not in all three *ṛcas* of the first [section].
It is "as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*), meaning just as it was in the archetype, so it is here as well.

Now, if one accepts compliance with the sequence, it has been stated that "the *mādhyaṃdina-pavamāna* insertion consists of triple-chanted verses" (*trikchandas*). To this, he says: "There is no contradiction regarding the state of having triple chants. To that, he replies:
The modification would be of the mere number of the triad, not of the meter nor of the sequence;
for the preservation of the sequence is primary, while that of the meters is secondary.
Therefore, the established conclusion is that the singing occurs only upon the first triplet of verses.

In the case of "one should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni-Soma" (*agnīṣomīyaṃ paśumālabheta*), singularity is intended to be significant (Bhāṣya 4.1.1.11–16). In the case of "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), singularity is not intended to be significant (3.1.7.14–15).
Singularity is properly subject to injunction by way of the factor (*kāraka*) [of the object] because it is connected to the action [in the sentence "the cup"]. (Regarding the word *graham*).
[This is the prima facie view.
Su. pṛ. 1014. ❖ "That which is associated with singleness [applies] to one [vessel], because of its connection with the Vedic text.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "He cleanses the *daśāpavitra* filter over the cup (*graha*)."
In the Agnihotra, it is said: "He cooks the clarified butter for Agni";
likewise, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is said: "He carries fire around the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).

Regarding this, a discussion arises as to whether this [act] pertains to one cup (graha) and one cake, or to all the cups and indeed to all the cakes; therein, he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
The sweeping, the removal of grass, and the carrying of fire around [the vessel] would be connected with singularity.
Because of the connection with the Vedic text (śruti) of the singular, it is proper that the injunction applies to one alone, since there is a connection with the Vedic text of the singular form;
for in the statement "He sweeps the cup" (grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi), the act of sweeping is connected to only one cup.
The same applies to other examples as well.
Or rather, it belongs to all [of them], for a definition is not distinguished by its specific character.
The word "or" (vā) is intended to set aside the prima facie position.
The cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) must be performed for all the *grahas*, not for just one.

This is because "being a *graha*" (*grahatva*) functions as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), because it establishes the entirety [of the class], or because it serves as the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*).
Having characterized the substance by means of the universal (*jāti*) of "grahatva," the cleansing and other rites are enjoined.

Since the characteristic of greatness is indeed common and identical across all vessels (*graha*), therefore all the vessels are to be wiped; for all of them, the grass-blades are to be placed [on the fire], and all the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are to be carried around with fire. This is because the singularity residing in the subject is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).
But when [a quality] is enjoined for the sake of another, it should be understood according to the scriptural text.

that is the five-fold portion, like the omentum (vapā). [This refers to] the singular term *medhapati*.
There is an injunction regarding the *vapā* (omentum) by way of its designation as having the function of the original [archetypal] offering.

Therefore, in the second view, it should be understood that the injunction serves to ensure the constant accomplishment of the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvadāna*), and that the portion consisting of the cuttings is for the purpose of preparing the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) and for the purpose of avoiding the violation of the principle of "single movement" (*ekaprasaratā*).

(10.1.18) For, by the statement "The *vapā* must be prepared as a five-fold cutting," there is a necessity for an injunction of another cutting that has taken over the function of the original, due to the fear of violating the principle of single movement.

10|1|2: In the passage "Pūṣan is indeed toothless," there is no injunction for grinding with reference to the sacrifice indicated by the word *bhāga* (share), because that would result in a violation of the principle of single-unitary expression (*ekaprasaratā*).
3|1|12: Regarding *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter), only the quality of being speckled is enjoined with reference to the *ājya* (butter).

Alternatively, out of fear of breaking the unity of the single syntactical extension (*ekaprasaratā*), this [rule] applies by way of extended application (*atideśa*) to that which is qualified by being subsequent; whereas when it applies previously, the injunction has as its sole result the state of being subsequent.
10.1.25. Just like a single portion, there is no two-fold portion for the Maitrāvaruṇa in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice regarding the *Āgnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice.
Bhāṣya 10.7.20–21. The maxim: "Ritual acts are performed with a single mantra."
(Those for which there is only one mantra as the instrument [of performance] are called *ekamantra*.
This means that for a single ritual act, there is only one mantra serving as its instrument.
Satyāṣāḍha Śrautasūtra 1.1.14. The twenty-one mantras beginning with "With the fires and the waters" (*agniyenubhiḥ*, Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.8) are the *saṃbhārayajus* formulas.

When a section (*anuvāka*) has been completed (and there remains a need for further mantras), a repetition must be performed, according to the principle that "ritual acts consist of single mantras" (Satyāṣāḍha Śrautasūtra 2.8.19). In that regard, in the case of the *Kahoḍa* and other such sections, this libation (*tarpaṇa*) should be performed according to the sense of the context; one should perform the libation for every individual sentence.
"Ritual acts [performed] with a single mantra," according to this principle.

*Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra*, Nārāyaṇa-vṛtti 3.4.4. "With the formula 'Homage be to all,' one of the three [priests] places the serpent's head [in the fire-altar construction], because of the principle that 'ritual acts [performed] with a single mantra'.
*Satyāṣāḍha Śrauta Sūtra* 11.1.63. For she is indeed purified by a single [act].
It is perceived in a variegated form,
produced from a composite mass of impressions consisting of objects and so forth.

By this principle, although [the qualities] such as *aruṇa* (red) are understood sequentially, they are experienced as entering into a single relation with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) of purchase simultaneously when they are situated in one place. (Ratna. 6.1.5.22, Section 2). The *sāmans* such as *rathantara* and *vṛhat* should be situated in one place in a sacrifice, just like the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). Just as these *sāmans* are situated in one place, they should be sung in a single *ṛc* verse, not in a triplet (*tṛca*).
It is like the *svādhyāya*.
Just as at the time of *svādhyāya* [the verses] are sung in a single *ṛc*, so it is here. That which is both one and an *ṛc* is a "single-verse" (*ekarca*).
According to Pāṇini 5.4.74 (*ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe*), the suffix *a* is applied to a compound ending in *ṛc*, *pura*, *ap*, *dhur*, or *pathin* (provided it does not relate to *akṣa*).
However, this does not apply to a compound where *dhur* signifies a "yoke" in relation to an axle (*akṣa*).
Thus, the suffix *a* is applied.
The neuter gender [of *ekarcasthāni*] is due to its inclusion in the *ardharca* group. Those which stand upon a single ṛc are "standing on a single ṛc" (*ekarcasthāni*).
This is the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*).
Or rather, [the Sāmans] are to be sung on a triplet (tuca), because of the observation of indicative marks.
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
Just as the Sāmans are to be sung on a triplet, not on a single verse (ekarca).

This is because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating: "One chants the *prastāva* of the first verse with the syllable *adha*, and of the two following verses with the syllable *dhi*.
Indeed, such a designation as "of the first" and "of the two following" would not be possible without a triplet of verses (*ṛcaṃ*).

Furthermore, the statement, "A single *sāman* is performed for a triplet as the hymn of praise (*stotrīya*)," serves as evidence there even as an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) by its very meaning.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *sāmans* should be sung according to the triplet (*tṛca*).
[In this case], the assumption of multiple characteristics (*anekalakṣaṇā*) sublates the assumption of a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇā*).

For example, in the tenth [book] regarding the phrase "the sound of a chariot" (*rathaghoṣaṇa*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that it is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*), which would entail the assumption of two word-characteristics; however, in that [concluding] position, it resides in the first word alone, and that alone is logical—this is the established conclusion.

*Bāla.*, p. 143: "The rule that the singular number [denotes] one is merely a general tendency (*prāyika*), because it is subject to exceptions in the case of words such as *dāra* (wife/wives). *Bṛhatī.*, pp. 130–131: "If it is asked, 'How can a word ending in the singular number be expressive of many?'—it will be understood by way of being a collective whole (*samudāyatayā*).

*Bhāṣya* 2.1.3, p. 479: "For there indeed exist words ending in the singular number that refer to many things when they depend upon a collective whole (*samudāyāpekṣa*), such as *yūyam* (you all), *vanam* (forest), *kulam* (family), and *parigada* (a type of plant)."

The words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* are terms whose meanings are known through the statements of the learned (Vedic sages). (2.1.3, p. 480). In the case of two animal sacrifices (*dvipaśuyāga*) as a modified form (*vikṛti*), there is a modification (*ūha*) from the singular and plural forms ending in the word for "animal" (*paśu*) to the dual form.
Bhāṣya 9.3.4:
In the case of a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*), there is a modification (*ūha*) of the singular form of the word *medhapati*.
Bhāṣya 9.3.144: When the animal is dedicated to multiple deities (*bahudaivatya*), there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the singular form of the word *medhapati* and the dual form.

A single sentence (ekavākya): In the section on syntactic unity (ekavākyatādhikaraṇa), a "single sentence" refers to as many words as accomplish a single purpose; these constitute one sentence. (Bhāṣya 2.1.2.27, p. 560). Two distinct meanings cannot be enjoined within a single sentence.

Page 331, 1|4|2|3: A modification (*vipariṇāma*) occurring within a single sentence is lighter [in weight] than even another *sādepi* (assimilation), because the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with that [sentence] is direct (*pratyakṣa*), whereas [the unity] with the other is indirect (*parokṣā*). Bhāṣya 3|4|8|24: When those enjoined as a single sentence share the same place, time, and agent, there exists a single performance (*ekatanttratva*).
As in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, and as in the case of the Citrā sacrifice (Bhāṣya 1.2.1.2, p.
2215). Syntactic unity arises by virtue of mutual expectancy; that which is perceived first expects what follows to be either consistent with itself or additional to it.
Vārttika 3.1.12, p. 806: "And syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) occurs when there is a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), and not otherwise.

That [relationship] also occurs either through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) among words ending in the same case-suffix, or through non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) as the relation between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), or as the relation between the subordinate and the principal (*śeṣaśeṣibhāva*). (3.4.4.13, p. 123). "There is no syntactic unity with the injunction (*vidhi*)," it is said, because of the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*); in that case, the form of syntactic unity is sublated.
Bhāṣya 3.4.119: For when [a word] is uttered immediately after [another], there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).
Indeed, a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is able to qualify a cognition (*vijñāna*) only when it is connected with what immediately precedes it, not when it is separated by an interval.

Therefore, as long as a clear unity is perceived among the words while they are being heard, there is syntactical unity (ekavākyatā) to that extent. It is established that this alone is the definition of a sentence, even in cases where worldly speech and mantras differ.

Vārttika 2.1.4.16, p. 445: "Not [with] another purpose" means that even when connected with a cognition, syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) does not occur when there is the possibility of a connection with something else, as in the case of: "The king's wife; Devadatta's man. Bhāṣya 3.8.16.11: "And there would not be syntactic unity with me in the village."

When there is syntactic unity with one [word], then for that which has no further expectancy toward it, syntactic unity with another is not postulated. (1.1.2, p. 1642). Nor does syntactic unity occur with that which is not present in the mind; the meaning of a sentence is produced by two proximate word-meanings, not by either one alone.

The very purpose of the traditional recitation (samāmnāya) being in close proximity [to one another] is this: how might it produce a cognition qualified by both word-meanings? For a sentence-meaning can only be established when there is a cognition of immediate sequence; and through the utterance of unrelated words, such immediate sequence is not cognized.

Therefore, there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with that which is separated [by an interval]. (3.1.1.21, p. 734). Indeed, when two independent injunctions, each lacking the requirement of the other, are prescribed as being mutually connected, there can be no syntactic unity because of the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*). For the mode of expression of the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*) is one that concludes with only that much [the primary act], whereas the mode of expression of the scriptural text (*śruti*) is different, as it follows the state of being subordinate to another.

Bhāṣya 3.4.19: There is no syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) between a word that functions as an injunction and one that does not, by way of the relationship of qualifier and qualified; for instance, in the phrase "of the goat's omentum" (*chāgasya vapāyāḥ*), the word "goat" (*chāga*) is a qualifier of the omentum (*vapā*). 6.1.8.13: When words are understood through their constituent word-meanings, the overall sense is conveyed; this is established in common worldly usage, and there is no need there for the basis of syntactic unity.

For if the sentence were like the word—that is, if the sentence itself were a single entity—then, because the sentence-meaning would follow that unity, the sentence-meaning too would sometimes be perceived as a single unit.

However, when the word-meanings have been expressed by distinct words that are mutually independent, and the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises solely from the connection between those meanings without depending on the operation of the words themselves, it is at that point that we determine that so many words constitute a single sentence. At that time, we do not perceive any operation belonging either to the sentence or to its unity.

2|1|14 (p. 445): When it is possible to achieve syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with a perceptible injunction in some way, it is not proper to assume a syntactic unity with that which is imperceptible. For if that were the case, there would be the postulation of many unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, he will state that syntactic unity arises from having a single purpose (*arthakatva*).
Bhāṣya on 3.1.1, p. 5. Section on Unity of Sentence (*Ekavākyatādhikaraṇa*):
"Because of the unity of purpose, there is one sentence, provided that upon division there would be mutual expectancy.

Commentary: Now, among these *yajus* mantras that are thrown into the ritual, how is it understood that "this is one *yajus*"? To the extent of the collection of words by which the sacrifice is performed, that much collection of words constitutes one *yajus*.
And by how much is it sacrificed? It is called a "sentence" because it must express as much as is necessary to manifest the assistance to the action.
By that [criterion], it is stated: "A sentence is one because of the unity of its meaning.
For this reason, there is the state of being a single sentence; therefore, a collection of words having a single meaning is a sentence.
And if, when being analyzed, a word remains expectant [of further syntactic connection], what is the example? "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ.
But surely each individual word has its own single meaning.
True; however, it does not stand in need of further specification regarding its division.

In that case, the unity of meaning is not established, because there is a multiplicity of word-meanings. And it has already been stated that a collection of words possesses no separate meaning of its own.

In the section concerning "unity of meaning" (*ekavākyatādhikaraṇa*), although it is heard that the meaning of a sentence is either a distinction (*bheda*) or a relation (*saṃsarga*), even so, there would be no single unified purpose (*ekārthatā*).
Because there is a multiplicity of words, substances, and conjunctions,
it is appropriate [that they share] a single purpose;
for example, the phrase "of the god" (*devasya tvā*) serves to manifest the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*).
A collection of words of this extent which expresses that specific [meaning] is a sentence (*vākya*).

Now, one might object: "In the case of *devasya tvā savituḥ prasave nirvapāmi* (I offer you at the impulse of the god Savitṛ), this is one sentence; then *aśvinorbāhubhyāṃ nirvapāmi* (I offer with the arms of the Aśvins) is another; thus there are many sentences here.
But such *anuṣaṅga* (supplying an ellipsis) does not occur."
If [the mantra] "I offer" were subordinate (guṇabhūta), then it would have to apply to each principal act.
Furthermore, the offering is not expressed for the sake of the mantras beginning with "devasya tvā";
for if the means of accomplishment were primary, the statement would serve no visible purpose (adṛṣṭārthatā).
Furthermore, since the primary act is the pouring out (nirvāpa), its visible purpose is the manifestation of that pouring out;
this [purpose] is said to be qualified by all those [subsidiary acts] previously described.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
And just as a word is qualified by another word, so it has been stated in the sūtra *tadbhūtānām* (1.1.25).
Therefore, a single sentence is the means for accomplishing the sacrifice.
To that extent, the statement consisting of the Yajus-mantras is considered fit to be spoken.
For I am indeed the speaker of the sentence; that which is capable of accomplishing the task becomes [the sentence] for me, neither deficient nor redundant—it is known by that alone.
And as to what kind it is, the definition is: "having a single purpose and being expectant. If it is such, then it is one.
That which exceeds this [unit] is said to be a different sentence and a different *yajus*.

Thus, in all cases, by the inclusion of words capable of supporting a single meaning both before and after [a given unit], and by the exclusion of words incapable [of such support], distinct *yajus* formulas are determined.
Therefore, since the definition of a single sentence implies, by necessity, the definitions of the division of *yajus* formulas and the division of sentences, he says: "And for this reason."

"What is the example?"—thus he asks, taking the word *artha* to mean "that which expresses the denotation," because he anticipates the impossibility of the two definitions coexisting [in a single sentence]. For it has been stated: "The unity of meaning (*ekārthya*) would belong to a word; that [unity] does not exist where there is expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*). A collection of expectant parts is not found in such cases as *tathyau* and so forth."

For a word (*pada*) may have a single meaning consisting of its form (*ākṛti*), but there is no mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) among its constituent parts—the phonemes (*varṇa*), the base (*prakṛti*), and the suffix (*pratyaya*)—because they lack the capacity to produce the cognition of meaning individually. Words, like other composite entities, expect one another when divided; however, these [constituents] do not share a single meaning, because the properties of each individual word differ, and because a distinct, separate meaning is well-established for the collection as a whole. Therefore, since there is no object to be characterized (*lakṣya*), this is not a valid definition (*alakṣaṇa*). To this extent, the objection in the Bhāṣya, "What is the example? is most appropriate.

With the intention that the word *artha* in the Sūtra expresses the purpose—meaning with the intention that it denotes the purpose (*prayojana*)—[the author cites] "devasya tvā" (in the Bhāṣya). [The opponent] says "But... to reveal his own view:

when there is no single sentence-meaning as a distinct division separate from the meanings of the individual words, then the very properties of those respective word-meanings, by virtue of their proximity, would constitute their exclusion (*bheda*) and conjunction (*saṃsarga*). Therefore, he says: "Even so, there would be no unity of meaning (*ekārthatā*)."
How is it that "difference" (bheda) consists in the mutual exclusion of categories? And since that [exclusion] resides in each individual category, how is it apprehended?

In the view that the word-meaning consists of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), since all individual instances [of cows, etc. are already denoted by the word "cow" itself, words such as "white" need only express the exclusion of [cows] that are black and so forth from the object.
Since their relation is included within the word-meaning itself, it does not constitute the sentence-meaning; thus, their difference is apprehended as subordinate to that [relation].

And just as the word "cow" is differentiated from "black" and so forth by the word "white," so too the word "white"—which has been excluded from "horse" and so forth by the word "cow"—is likewise differentiated; for there is no proof for this [notion of] identity, since the exclusions (vyavaccheda) are distinct. Alternatively, if one were to grasp the generality of difference, it would follow that the meaning of every sentence is one and the same. But when the meanings of words themselves, as possessing distinctions, constitute the sentence-meaning, then their plurality is established.
Likewise, "non-association" (asaṃsarga) is also the mutual non-coloration of word-meanings;
since that too exists in each individual [meaning], unity is not perceived.

In the view that the universal (*ākṛti*) is the word-meaning, when "whiteness" and "cowness" are denoted in their own forms—according to the technical rule that the genus together with the individual appears in its own form—their mutual implication (*itaretarānuñjana*) by virtue of proximity constitutes the sentence-meaning, which is a distinction established through the sense.
And this, whether it be the relation of whiteness to cowness or the relation of cowness to whiteness, is perceived as manifold because it is fully subsumed within each individual instance.

Although it might be understood as a unity because the same connection exists in both cases within a single word, nevertheless, in the case of multiple words, the two words are perceived through each respective form of connection with which they are joined; thus, there is multiplicity.
Furthermore: "Because of the primacy of the objects [of cognition], it is only the properties (*dharma*) that are experienced;
it is not by resorting to unity that [the property] is differentiated from the difference of the substrata (*dharmin*)."

For as long as a single purpose is not accepted, independent word-meanings cannot be brought into a state of unity; thus, they experience difference and connection separately. For this reason also [the sentence-meaning is distinct]. And although, because the *ākṛti* (form) is the word-meaning, difference itself is not intended as the sentence-meaning, nevertheless it was put forward by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) merely as a hypothetical alternative. The explanation of the intention of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is appropriate because the word *artha* denotes "purpose."

This being the case, some object is primary, while others are mentioned as its qualifiers. Furthermore, because all [objects] are distinguished by that [primary one] and are connected with it, it can also be said that there is only a single distinction or connection.

Therefore, since it is shown to be inherent in the ritual action (*karma-samavāyin*), it is established that the entire collection of words—such as "from the whole cloth" (*aśeṣavastra*) and so forth, which manifest the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) qualified by those objects, and the mantra beginning with "O God, thee, the knowing one" (*devasya tvā savituḥ*) and so forth—has a single purpose. This is the illustrative example.

But the opponent, not knowing that the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is the primary element, asks: "Is it not the case here [in the mantra] *devasya tvā*? (as stated in the Bhāṣya). The proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) says: "If the pouring out were to be supplied by ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) here, then it would be so.

And that ellipsis would occur only as a subordinate element (*guṇabhāva*); however, this [mantra] does not have the status of a subordinate element because it possesses its own purpose, and because Savitṛ and the others are not connected to the ritual action (*akarmasamavāya*). Thus, they share a single purpose."
Section on Unity of Statement (Ekavākyatādhikaraṇa): Why are both [unity and sentence] defined by the Sūtra?

And in cases such as "The staff has broken, or let him divide [it]," although there is a distinct cognition [of the parts], those things which, when combined, possess a single purpose, [are considered a single sentence] because they lack that capacity [individually].

Because the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), which serves as the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*) in these two cases, is one, there is an absolute mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) among the individual parts; thus, their status as being "inexpressible" [as separate sentences] is established.
Therefore, for the purpose of pervading them with the nature of a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*), that [expectancy] belongs to the two [verbs] which are otherwise distinct.

Alternatively, "mutual expectancy when divided" is a qualifier characterized by the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭatāphala*) arising from the non-connection of the word-meanings, given that they possess a single unified purpose (*saṃhataikaprayojanatva*).
It does not exist without a pleasant [place], because the accomplishment of independent activity occurs only through each individual [word].
[In the sequence] "He makes a seat;

sit upon that," there is mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) in this syntactic connection. Therefore, even though there is mutual expectancy, because they are distinct sentences due to the division of expectancy, the qualification [of one by the other] occurs only through the implication of the other by means of that very division of expectancy.

15. Regarding "the state of being a designation" (*abhidhātva*): he shows this in the counter-example by saying "it is said. Maṇḍana states: "In this context, that which is expectant and has a single meaning constitutes a single sentence."

A single purpose, namely the illumination of the method for dividing the *puroḍāśa*, is observed for those [formulas] that are independent [of one another]. Regarding the *nivāpa* offering, Śaṅkara also raises the objection concerning the diversity of divisions: "The measure belongs to the *yajus* and the *manas*.
That is, it belongs to the *yajus* mantra.

Because there is no application of a specific qualifier after they have been combined, [the principle of] *anuṣaṅga* (syntactic connection) is proposed for that which is employed repeatedly—as in "the *yajus* is not broken," and so forth. Since there is no fault [in this], it is set forth. To that, the reply is: first of all, there is no basis for a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) among those [words] that are independent.

Since the substratum of the *yajus* has been defined, we shall explain later that there is a multiplicity of actions even due to the difference in their means (*sādhana*). Now, as an incidental discussion, this is begun for the sake of distinction [in the section on *ṣaṅga*], to determine how far the *yajus* extends across a collection of words—taking as an example from the *ṣaṅgādhikaraṇa* the phrase "punātu tisraḥ" (may he purify the three)—with the statement: "Nor is it sufficient in only some," and so forth, beginning with "Its distinction arises from the difference in the factors of action" (*kāraka-bheda*) and so on.
Regarding the predominance of the means (*sādhana-prādhānya*), it is stated on page 120: "But it is indeed sufficient within the sentence itself."

This distinction is made because [the former] is not a constituent part of the ritual action (*karma*); thus, it is "not-yajus" (*anāyajurṣman*). Likewise, the nature of being a *mantra* should be understood as residing in the sentence, since the word "mantra" is applied to it; therefore, there is a single purpose due to the general manifestation [of its meaning].
That alone is sufficient for that [definition]. Consequently, it is established that the state of being a *yajus* resides in the sentence as a whole.

Although the word "sit" (sīda) requires a preceding element, because the purpose is distinct, there is a separate sentence-status (*vākyāntaratva*) based on the unity of meaning characterized by a divided expectancy (*vibhajyamānākāṅkṣatva*).
Therefore, they constitute a definition only when combined. Thus, the extent of a *yajus* was considered by way of its being a sentence.
2|1|16|18. *Soma*—the occasion; the connection (*saṃgati*).

The purpose: as long as there is a single *yajuḥ* characterized by the capacity to form a single sentence (*ekavākyopagamanasāmarthya*), which is the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the word, so long must that entire unit be employed at the time of performance, and not merely a portion of it. (Bālamanoramā, p. 9). Thus, in this sūtra, the word "sentence" (*vākya*) refers to the *yajuḥ*.

In the Sūtra, regarding the word *yajus*, although there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) based on the substratum when the milk is to be employed in the *āmīkṣā* offering, the term "sentence" (*vākya*) is used to indicate the aforementioned purpose, as in the case of "saṃ te prāṇo vātena" (Vi. 2.1.18). It is not a lack of skill on the part of the author of the Sūtras that he uses the term "unity" (*eka-*) [in this context]; for syntactic unity exists through *anuṣaṅga* (supplying a missing word) in the mantras for the *upadhāna* (placing of bricks) at the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, such as the sentence "yā te agne" and "devasya tvā. Thus, there is no contradiction in the unity [of the *yajus*].
Regarding "agne'yāśayā" and so forth (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.16):
there is syntactic unity [of the mantra], yet because the factor that establishes its oneness is difficult to comprehend, there is a sense of distinctness.

In the case of a split [of a sentence], by way of an extension (*anuṣaṅga*), in the *dīkṣā-mantra* of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice—such as "punaḥ... punātu" and so forth—even though there is a mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*), unity of purpose (*ekārthatva*) is the determining factor. Therefore, through this, the status of being a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) is established for the Yajus formula, based on its having a single purpose. (2.1.17)

"Or you [may say]: according to PMS 2.1.47 (p. 560), syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is sufficient for as many words as constitute a sentence; this is not possible between two names without some connection (*upapatti*).
That much is sufficient, but it does not apply to a collection of sentences."

Regarding its application (viniyoga): [see] 2|1|14|24, p. 740. There is syntactic unity (ekavākyatva), fitness (yogyatva), and [the absence of] unfitness. Furthermore, syntactic unity (vākyatva) exists where there is a single meaning, as well as mutual expectancy (sākāṅkṣatva). These are the factors that effect application. Syntactic unity consists in having a single object of cognition despite the words being divided; and intermediate context (avāntaraprakaraṇa) is stronger than great context (mahāprakaraṇa). These are the means of application. Syntactic unity is the state of having a single purpose, even when the words are distinct.

3|1|14|24, p. 740: In the case of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), there is everywhere an absence of more than one principal qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*), because any other would be weak. This [unity] is rooted in expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). 3|1|14|24, p. 829: Furthermore, in cases such as *gām anayeta* ("one should lead the cow"), since the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) which serves as the principal qualificand is singular, syntactic unity with multiple subordinate elements is not possible without causes such as [repetition or other indicators].
That is so;

for in the sentences concerning the *darśa-pūrṇamāsa* oblations (page 1023), there is no lack of distinctness in the objects of cognition regarding the various *bhāvanās*, since they are not enjoined as a single unit. Thus, there is no syntactic unity (*aikavākyatva*) between the two sentences concerning rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*).
The *brāhmaṇa* is injunctive.

Unity of sentence (*ekavākyatva*) [is like] two fruits on a single stalk; a mantra that does not enjoin [an action]. Bhāṣya 10.8.10.20: And since these [sentences], when divided (such as "One should sacrifice a white [animal] to Vāyu," etc.), have words that require further semantic connection, the unity of sentence is logically established.
2|3|5|14. "In the cognition of their own meaning, compounds possess expectancy;
therefore, the unity of sentences arises again by bringing them together. (Regarding the object to be enjoined at the outset), Vākyapadīya 2.114–134, p. 166.

The intention is that even when the mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) among the word-meanings (*padārtha*) has reached its conclusion, the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) among the sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*) through mutual dependence is not contradictory.

This is because the suffix *-tva* expresses a relationship; specifically, in relation to the relationship between the subordinate (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*), there is the subordinate’s dependence on the principal, and the principal’s dependence on the subordinate.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the meaning is that there arises a single syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) through the formation of one great sentence-meaning by combining sentences—even those whose own meanings are already complete—by virtue of the primary rites such as the Āgneya having a single fruit, and the subsidiaries being related to a single contribution toward the performance.
When such a single syntactic unity is possible, it is improper to accept them as separate injunctions that would result in multiple connections and distinct sentences.
This is the nature of the maxim: "If one does not posit another [meaning], etc. (10.8.4.7). Page 525.

Su. Pṛ. 62. The definition of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is given in the Sūtra: "A single sentence consists in a single meaning, provided that there is expectancy if it were divided" (*arthakatvādekaṃ vākyaṃ sākāṅkṣaṃ cedvibhāge syāt*). That which, when divided, possesses expectancy, and when undivided, has a single meaning—that is a single sentence.
The term "single meaning" (*ekārtham*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as "A pleasant seat for you—sit upon it.
The phrase "expectancy if divided" (*vibhāge sākāṅkṣam*) is stated to exclude over-extension to the pair of mantras: "May Bhaga divide you two; may Pūṣan divide you two."
VI. 2.1.14. Because a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is improper when a single unified sentence (*ekavākyatva*) is possible.

*Parākrama*: p. 51, l. 1. The principle is that those [words or phrases] which have attained the status of forming a single sentence convey a single meaning collectively. "Collectively" (*saṃbhūya*) means having combined; that is to say, they convey [the sense] together with the assistance of one another.

Just as the sentences concerning the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* oblations possess syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) by virtue of accomplishing the purpose of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, so too does such an application (*prasaṅga*) occur in various instances.

For example, since this [Brahman] is of the nature of the one, non-dual Brahman, those scriptural passages that establish Hari, Hara, and others as being that Brahman do not constitute valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is the summary.
*Sāhasī*, 130: Regarding the statement "the *ṣoḍaśin* is twenty-onefold," when the *ṣoḍaśin* is repeated twenty-one times, there is no repetition of the *naiśoka* verses.
(In the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, all the *stotras* consist of twenty-one [verses]).
Bhāṣya 2.2.5.24, Section 2. The *ekaviṃśa* *stoma* is used on the day and night of the fourth day.

Vi. 7.3.90. The *ekaviṃśa* *stoma* is prescribed as an optional (*kāmya*) element for the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant in the *atirātra* sacrifice, according to the injunction: "One desiring offspring should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the *atirātra* consisting of twenty-one [verses]."
5|3|4. The *viṣṭuti* (recitation pattern) of the twenty-one-fold hymn (*ekaviṃśa-stoma*) is thus handed down in the tradition:
"He utters the *hiṃ*-call seven times; he [recites] with three [verses], he with three, he with one.
He utters the *hiṃ*-call seven times; he with one, he with three, he with three."
"Whichever [verse] one performs first, that [one] thrice, that [one] once, and that [one] thrice"—this is the third section (varṇaka) of 9.2.6.
Its meaning is as follows: in the first round (paryāya), the first verse is recited three times, the second verse three times, and the third verse once; thus it becomes seven [recitations].

Then, in the second round, there are seven: the first [group] once, the second three times, and the third three times. In the third round, there are likewise seven: the first three times, the second once, and the third three times.
In total, there are twenty-one.

In the case of the *ekaviṃśa* Atirātra, regarding the addition [of stotras] to complete the required number, the rule here is determined solely by the sequence of the recited text (*sammāmmā-pāṭha-krama*).
(Bhāṣya 5.1.13, Section 2). In the *ekaviṃśa* Atirātra characterized by the *viṣṭut-stoma*, there is an increase through the addition of Sāmans, not through repetition.
(Vivaraṇa 10.5.16). In the *ekaviṃśa* Atirātra, the four *tudu* chants of the *vidvat* [stomas] are to be inserted after the *paryāya*, not before the *bahiṣpavamāna*.
5|3|4. A single object is understood through a single injunction.

Vi. 5|2|3. Because of the indication by a single case-ending, we understand [the relationship] even without grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in the example "a blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*).
Thus someone has said (Bhāṣya 3.1.6.2, p. 685):

"By the principle that 'the qualification by another belongs to that which is already qualified by one,' the connection with the number four must be stated as belonging to that which is already qualified by the number six.
Consequently, even though there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*), the number four is only one, which brings about repetition."
Bhāṭṭa 8.3.3: When two things have the same object, the general is sublated by the particular.
Vārttika: This is the maxim of the two fruits on a single stalk.

In the case of restrictive injunction (*niyama*) and exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), there is an attainment by implication through the connection of threshing with rice, based on their mutual dependence according to the maxim of the two fruits on a single stalk (*ekavṛnta-nyāya*).
*Rasāyana*, p. 138.
[The phrase] "two fruits on a single stalk" (refers to) either the single-stoma sacrifice.
The maxim of the two fruits on a single stalk (*ekavṛntagataphaladvayanyāya*) is clear.
Amara states: "A *vṛnta* is the stalk that binds the flower.
This was stated in the tenth chapter of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, in the treatment of the figure of speech known as *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

For it is said: "śleṣa (paronomasia) occurs where, as if there were a semantic paronomasia (*artha-śleṣa*), a difference in meaning arises from a difference in words due to the non-difference in effort of pronunciation caused by the non-difference of vowels; this is śleṣa according to the maxim of two fruits on a single stalk.
— Sāhasī.

The state of being multiple words is sublated by the state of being a single word, as in the section on grammar (Bālamanoramā, p. 140). Through connection with a single word, either by way of a restatement of a collective whole or by bringing about the status of a collective, [the unity is established], as in: "He who, knowing thus, performs the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice."
Vārttika 2.2.14, p. 463: The status of being the referent of multiple words is sublated by the status of being the referent of a single word, because it has not [otherwise] been established.
Vārttika 3.1.14, p. 860: "The eleven-day sacrifice consists of eleven animals, one of which is a white-footed, fat-tailed animal" (the twelfth animal among the eleven).
In the Aśvamedha and the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices:
*pelvaḥ* means one whose testicles have fallen away;
*ekaśitipāt* refers to one who has one white (*śiti*) foot.

There is elision of the word *pāda* [in a compound] when preceded by a numeral or the word *su* (Pāṇini 5.4.140). [This applies to] the dual number (vi. 8.1.7). This is *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one member). That which expresses mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is the basis for the *dvandva* compound; that same principle applies to *ekaśeṣa* as well.

However, this is the distinction: in one case both the word and its meaning are distinct, while in the other the meanings are distinct but the word is one and the same. (Vākyapadīya 6.1.5.22, p. 1366). *Ekaśruti*, *pracya*, and *tāna* are synonyms.
*Ekaśruti* is the fourth accent, distinct from the acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*).

In the performance of the *yājyā* and other such elements, the recitation is by means of *tāna* alone; there is neither a combination nor an option between the three accents (*svaras*) and *tāna*. (Vi. 6.1.2, Varṇaka 3). *Ekaśrutitva* is the state of the syllables contained within a mantra having a single type of accent. (Saṃkarṣa. 4.3.3). A connection with a single [common] conjunction establishes an extended application (*atideśa*) even when devoid of any other purpose.

Bhāṭṭa 8.1.13: According to the maxim that "the knowledge of one related thing brings about the recollection of another related thing," the word *apaśu*—which ends in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*)—functions, in accordance with the syntactic requirement of excluding cattle and horses, as a means of presenting the absence of excellence (*prāśastya*) pertaining to cattle and horses, even within the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "cattle are [true] animals. Consequently, from the understanding of the excellence pertaining to cattle and horses, the deprecation (*nindā*) of goats and other such animals is understood.
(Mīmāṃsākośa 162; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 1.4.16.26, p. 284). From the knowledge of one related thing, there arises the recollection of another related thing.
The maxim "the perception of one related thing causes the recollection of another related thing" (mami. pṛ.

78) means that just as the sight of an elephant's tusk serves to recall the elephant, and likewise the sight of an elephant-driver recalls the elephant, so too the cognition of a river and such things serves to recall its related banks and so forth. This is the underlying sense. Sāhasī. 91: By the maxim "the recollection of one related thing through the perception of another related thing," when the primary meaning (pravāha) arises from the word *gaṅgā* through its direct denotative power (*śakti*), the secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) arises because of its connection with that [primary meaning].

278: "The recollection of the preceding word-meaning in its entirety is that which causes the immediate recollection of the subsequent word-meaning, according to the maxim: 'The perception of one related thing [causes the recollection of the other]'" (ekasaṃbandhidarśanād itara-saṃbandhismaraṇanyāyaḥ).

Bhāṭṭa 5.1.6: The Principle of Perceiving One Related Member (*ekasaṃbandhidarśananyāya*). In the *Nyāyasudhā* and other works, it is stated that the word "animal" (*paśu*) is accepted as referring to the excellence (*prāśastya*) inherent in cows and horses, and that by means of the negative particle (*nañ*), its absence is predicated in the case of goats and the like. If, in that context, the presentation of the excellence belonging to cows and horses is intended through the principle of perceiving one related member, then—because that [excellence] is not directly expressed by words (*aśābdatvāt*)—there would be an impossibility of its syntactic connection (*anvaya*) either with the word or with the meaning.

Kau. 1|4|16|26: By the maxim that "the recollection of one related thing brings about the recollection of another related thing," when the word *siṃha* (lion) is uttered, the lion is apprehended through its own power (*śakti*), which brings to mind the qualities residing in it.

Through that same maxim, by the very fact of making known the possession of similar qualities, once such possession of qualities is known, there is no obstacle presented to the justification of the verbal cognition (*śabdabodha*) of the aforementioned kind arising from the word *siṃha*.
1|4|13|23, p. 275: Or rather, because of the connection with the sacrifice (*ṛtu*) of a single *stoma*.

In the passage, "He who, having performed this Agniṣṭoma, should sacrifice with another [rite]," it is understood that by the word *anya* (other), there is a reference to the sacrificial rites (*kratavaḥ*) which are modifications (*vikāra*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether this reference to the modifications of the Jyotiṣṭoma applies only to those with a single *stoma*, or to all of them—whether they have one or many *stomas*—the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

It would be a reference by the word *anya* to the "single-*stoma*" rite, such as the Abhiplava and others; for a "single-*stoma*" rite is one in which there is only one *stoma*, such as the Triṣṭut and so forth.

Through the connection with the seasons, by such passages as, "That which is indeed the *trivṛt* [stoma] which attains this sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*), it kindles that; that which is the *pañcadaśa* [stoma] (which attains this sacrificial rite), it [kindles] that," the connection of each single-stoma with a specific season is shown by means of the word *ekahāyanī*.
Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that this injunction applies only to those sacrifices consisting of a single stoma;
the word "vā" (or) serves to exclude other alternatives.
In this regard, the reading elsewhere is either "ekastomato vā" or "ekastome vā."

Or rather, [the praise] applies to all the specific injunctions (*codanā*) regarding the *stomas*. Rejecting by means of the word "or" (*vā*) what was established by the previous *sūtra*, he states the final position (*siddhānta*).
"Injunction" (*codanā*), "utterance" (*ukti*), and "discourse" (*vāda*) are synonymous.

There would be an injunction for all [the sacrifices], both those with a single *stoma* such as the *agniṣṭut* and so forth, and those with multiple *stomas* such as the *ukthya* and so forth; that is, there would be a statement, meaning that the word "other" would apply to them. Because there is no distinction—since there is no difference in the inclusion of both those with a single *stoma* and those with multiple *stomas* by the term "other"—the statement, "He who indeed approaches another sacrifice with his own *trivṛt* [stoma] kindles it," may be a statement regarding the single *stoma*, yet it would serve as praise for all *stomas* alike.

It is said that the ritual elements (*dharma*) practiced in the archetype (*prakṛti*), which are extended to the ectype (*vikṛti*) by the rule of transfer (*codaka*), are easily understood because they have been previously experienced; thus, [the word *anya*] "kindles" or "illuminates" them. However, in the absence of such practice, there would be no correct illumination due to the lack of comprehension of the aphorism (*sūtra*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that all modifications of the *jyotiṣṭoma*—whether involving a single or multiple *stomas*—are enjoined by the word *anya*.

"Because there is no distinction in the injunction (*codanā*)," meaning that because the word "other" (*anya*) occurring in the injunction applies without distinction to both those sacrifices characterized by a single *stoma* and those characterized by multiple *stomas*—this is the explanation according to the *Ekapaḍī*.
It is explained as a single compound in both the *Subodhinī* and the *Kutūhala*. Ke.

[explains] that this section, "Or rather, of the single-stoma sacrifice, because of its connection with the ritual season," should be seen in the *Bindu* as referring to the modifications of the *agniṣṭoma*, whether they consist of one or many *stomas*.

It has been established in the *Pādyamikā* section (*adhikaraṇa*)—namely, "Or [the quality] belongs to the single-stoma sacrifice, because of its connection with the rite" (JS 3.3.14)—that it is reasonable to interpret a specific statement in the concluding portion (*aupasaṃhārika*) in accordance with the specific procedure introduced at the beginning.

*Parimala* 4.4.123–24: The sacrifices characterized by a single *stoma* (*ekastomaka*) are those such as "The *agniṣṭoma* is threefold (*trivṛt*)" and "The *ukthya* is fifteenfold (*pañcadaśa*)," and so forth.
Regarding both those sacrifices that have a single *stoma* and those that have multiple *stomas*, there is the statement "now by the last one.
Bhāṣya 5.3.15.43–44: For all modifications of the *agniṣṭoma*, whether they possess a single *stoma* or multiple *stomas*, the time is characterized by the *agniṣṭoma*.

5|3|15|43–44. Even when there is only a single oblation, the offering of the five-portioned rice (*pañcaśarāva*) must be performed for both the morning and evening milk-offerings of the *darśa* sacrifice;
this is to be seen in the section (*adhikaraṇa*) on the *ārtitanyāya* in the *Bindu*.
Mā. 6|4|122–23. The giving of a one-year-old animal to an enemy is merely a religious duty (*dharmamātra*), not for the purpose of a sacrificial fee (*parikrayārtha*).
This [is for] one who is not an officiating priest (*anṛtvij*).
At the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara in the *kapālābhihoma*;
therein, this is the gift.
Bhāṣya 10.2.16.47: "He buys with a one-year-old [cow]" (*ekahāyanā krīṇāti*) is an injunction restricting the substance (*dravyaniyamavidhi*). Bālamanoramā, p.

24: Since it is determined that the one-year-old cow is for the purpose of purchase alone, it is understood that even its leading [to the place of sacrifice], which is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to it, serves that same purpose alone.
Bhāṭṭa 4.1.120:
The one-year-old oxen, their birth, the anointing of the dice, the foot-stamping, and the foot-oblation are not the motivating factors; rather, it is the purchase of Soma alone that is the motivator.

When a one-year-old cow is being led for the purpose of purchase and, by chance, falls into a pit, the act of picking her up is not for the purpose of anointing the axle, nor does that [act] apply again to the purchase of Soma in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
(Bhāṭṭa 4.1.120). The "Principle of the One-Year-Old Cow" (ekahāyanīnyāya) should be consulted under the entry "Aruṇānyāya" at Ke.

It must be stated that because the *vrīhi* rice and the *apūpa* cake are mentioned in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the fact that *paryagnikaraṇa* (the act of carrying fire around) serves as their means of accomplishment follows from being established by scripture.

However, even in that case, since it is not a motive (*aprayojaka*) according to the principle of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī-nyāya*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its omission (*lopa*) in the absence of those [rice and cake].

According to the logic of the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow), even though the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is enjoined as having rice as its material cause (*prakṛti*), the cake could be accomplished by taking any substance whatsoever; however, since the omission of the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire) would be improper, this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is unsatisfactory.
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 638). Both the words *ekahāyanī* and *pañcākṣī* denote a single substance due to their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
(Vārttika 3.1.6–22, p. 673). The word *ekahāyanī*, being enjoined in connection with the purchase (*kraya*), would be like something unknown [if it were not already established].

Just as in the case of [the word] "knower" when connected with the word "aruṇā," so too, although the word *ekahāyanī* has fulfilled its purpose by being connected with the verb *krīṇāti* (he buys), it cannot enter into a connection with another word in the absence of [such a need]. Nevertheless, because the word *aruṇā* would otherwise be meaningless if it lacked a connection with another word, it enters into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the word *ekahāyanī*. *Bhāṣya* 3.1.12, p. 691. The word *ekahāyanī*, though having its purpose fulfilled by being connected with the verb *krīṇāti*, is not capable of forming a connection with another word in the absence of [that necessity].
(Nevertheless,) since the word *aruṇā* would be purposeless if it did not manifest a connection with another word, it accepts syntactic unity with the word *ekahāyanī*.
[Objection: But was it not said that [the word *aruṇā*] is for the purpose of connecting with the action, not for the purpose of connecting with [the substance]? [Reply:
We say that it is for the purpose of connecting with both, in order to avoid the word *aruṇā* being rendered meaningless.
Otherwise, [the purpose] would already have been accomplished [by the other connection].
The meaning of the word *ekahāyanī* in the eleventh chapter can be established in another way as well;
for example, irrigation channels are constructed by the Śālvas, and from them water is drunk and used for ritual sipping (*upaspṛśyate*).

Similarly here as well, the word *ekahāyanī*, being uttered for the purpose of establishing a connection with the act of purchasing (*kraya*), is construed together with the word *aruṇā* (red); nothing is thereby impaired. Therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). [3.1.12, p. 689]. This is an inquiry into whether the word *ekahāyanī* is connected with the verb *krīṇāti* (to buy) or with the word *aruṇā*; this should be seen under the section titled "The Aruṇā-nyāya" in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya.

Certain words such as *ekahāyanī* and others, while denoting substances associated with specific times, function by indicating [the animal's] age. (Vārttika 3.1.6.12, p. 679). The maxim states: "For a solitary thesis (*pratijñā*) cannot establish what has been proposed.
(The meaning is that a mere thesis, devoid of both the reason (*hetu*) and the pervasion (*vyāpti*), is unable to prove the matter proposed.)

(Ke. Sāhasrī. 148. There should be a single performance (*tantra*) for the subsequent [offerings] because they are characterized by oneness. Regarding the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice, it has been stated that there is no distinction in the fire (*agni*) for the preceding offerings;
now, since the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings are to be performed in the Gārhapatya fire, there should be a single performance for them as well, because they are characterized by oneness.
The *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings belonging to both the southern and northern sacrificial halls have only one single *gārhapatya* fire, namely Agni.
Because there is only one [fire], there should be a *tantra* (common procedure) for the subsequent oblations;
such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Or rather, [they are] different, because of the difference in their agents. The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) says:
by the word "or" (vā), he sets aside the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
Even though there is only one fire, because there is a difference of performers (*kartṛbheda*), the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings should be separate—that is, distinct.

Those intended for the southern sacrificial area (*dakṣiṇavihāra*) are to be performed by the *pratiprasthātṛ*, while those intended for the northern sacrificial area (*uttaravihāra*) are to be performed by the *adhvaryu*.

According to the opinion of Someśvara, this is a restorative injunction (*pratiprasavavidhi*) concerning the scope excluded by the restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) that "there are indeed eleven portions (*avadāna*) of the animal."
*Bāla.*, p. 16: The enumeration of these [eleven] ignorances (*ajñāna*) is given in the *Agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice.
*Bhāṣya* 10.2.13–19: A collection of eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) is called the *yūpaikādaśinī*.
Among them, the eleventh post situated to the south is named the *upaśaya*.
In that [context], the sacrificial post-consecrations such as *vyāna* and so forth do not exist above the *uccaya*.
(Vi. 7.1.13). The eleventh [chapter] begins for the purpose of investigating the applicability (*prayogyatā*) by means of the method of *tantra* and *āvāpa*. (Ṭupṭīkā 7.1.11, p.
1524). It will be stated in the eleventh [chapter] that the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) and the primary rites (*pradhāna*) are enjoined by a single performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*).
Bhāṭṭa 5.1.1: At the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina-savana), there is a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) for Savanīya consisting of eleven potsherds (ekādaśapāla). Ke:
Regarding the eleven-potsherd cake for Indra, the ritual procedure (vidhvanta) of the medicinal herb (auṣadha) and the cake for Agni applies.
Mā 8.1.17–34: In the eleven-night sacrifice (ekādaśarātra), the piling of the fire-altar (cayana) can be performed.
Bhāṣya 10.5:
The eleven-night sacrifices, beginning with the two-night sacrifice, possess the nature of the *Iṣṭi* because they are enjoined by the verbal root *yajati*.

Bhāṣya 8.2.16–26: In the eleventh section (*adhikaraṇa*), it was established that because the word in the form of *yajati* is employed, the conjunction (*sāhitya*) of the *Āgneya* and other offerings is intended.

*Bāla*, p. 168. The subject matter of the eleventh chapter: "The introduction to the *tantra*, the *tantra* and the *āvāpa*, the expansion of the *tantra*, and the expansion of the *āvāpa*—these are the sections (*pādas*) of the eleventh chapter.
In the first section, the introduction to the *tantra* is described.
In the second [chapter], the tantra and the āvāpa were briefly stated;
in the third, the tantra was elaborated upon with numerous examples;
and in the fourth, the āvāpa was likewise demonstrated.
VI. Introduction. Verse 23: The subject matter of the eleventh chapter.
Therein, the definition of *tantra* has already been stated: "That which is common is *tantra*.
Here, the word "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) expresses the inclusion of particulars.
And thus, when there is a perception of distinction (*viśeṣagrahaṇa*), there occurs the state of being the motivator of a contingency (*prasaṅga-prayojakatva*).
The meaning is that when there is a perception of distinction, the performance is governed by a single execution (*sakṛdanuṣṭhāna*).

Furthermore, the perception of distinction is sevenfold: 1) from the desire for a result (*phalakāmanā*), 2) from a causal occasion (*nimitta*), 3) from form (*rūpa*), 4) from number (*saṃkhyā*), 5) from time (*kāla*), 6) from mantras (*mantra*), and 7) from differences among performers (*kartṛbheda*).
The *tantra* (extended application) is of two kinds: that of principal rites and that of subordinate elements.
For example, it occurs in the case of the *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice and the *prājāpatya* offerings within the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

In both of these cases, there is no mention of a specific substance (*sattva*) as previously stated; for in the first instance, there is no specification regarding the desire for heaven, and in the second, there is no specification regarding the means of assistance to the instrument (*karaṇa*).

For here, as in the case of the obligatory *agnihotra* being subsumed by the optional *agnihotra*, there is no mention of a specific distinction regarding the desire [for results]. Nor is there a mention of a specific distinction based on a causal occasion (*nimitta*) in the two examples cited from the *Tantra*, such as when the requirement for the substance of water for washing (*pādya*) is fulfilled through incidental application (*prasaṅga*) in the two means prescribed for the Vaiśya occasion. Furthermore, in the two examples from the *Tantra*, there is no mention of a specific distinction based on the form consisting of substance and deity, such as in the case of the animal sacrifice where it is said, "He performs the after-sacrifices (*anuyāja*) with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*)," [as opposed to] the after-sacrifices performed with mere clarified butter (*ājya*).

The subject matter of the eleventh chapter (1292): An investigation into the subject matter of the eleventh chapter [concerning] the establishment by extension (*prasaṅga*) of the *anuyāja* offerings belonging to the sacrificial cake (*pauroḍāśika*), which involve substances.

Furthermore, in the two previously cited examples from the Tantras, there is no mention of either a specific number or a specific time, such as in the case of the *pāśuka* (animal sacrifice) *prayājas*, where it is said, "They perform the *prayājas* while the animal stands," and thus they are performed while the animal is standing, even though eleven in number—as in "He performs eleven *prayājas*"—and in contrast to the five *prayājas* prescribed for the *pauroḍāśika* (cake-offering) by the rule, "They perform the *prayājas* when the oblations have been placed," which are performed at a time subsequent to the placing of the oblations; [in these cases, the *prayājas* are established through *prasaṅga* (incidental application) of the extended rules].

Furthermore, in the two previously cited examples from the *Tantra*, there is no apprehension of a distinction based on either the mantra or the agent; just as in the case of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice, where—due to the extended application (*atideśa*) from the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice—the *praiṣa* (direction) is performed once, and thus the *tantra* (common procedure) serves as a contributory factor (*prasaṅga-upakāritva*) for the knowers of the *savanīya* oblations who are devoid of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest, because the direction is performed by the Hotṛ priest for the consecrated animal and the sacrificer for the pressed offerings.

Therefore, it is established that when there is an apprehension of distinction in seven ways, there is a *tantra*; and in the apprehension of distinction in these seven ways, [the commonality] becomes the motivator (*prayojaka*).
For them, even the *utpattyapūrva* (the intermediate apūrva of production) is not the direct motivator for what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because it is not itself an effect (*kārya*).
Indeed, the *utpattyapūrva* is not the end to be achieved; rather, through it, the *paramāpūrva* (the ultimate apūrva) is achieved.

And that which is not an effect cannot be a motivator; thus, only the *paramāpūrva* is the motivator of the rituals by means of its intermediaries. Similarly, in the context of rites performed for specific desires (*kāmādhikāra*), the fruit (*phala*) also motivates the means (*sādhana*) by means of the *apūrva*.
But that is not the case, because no such medium is possible.

For if even the *paramāpūrva* (the ultimate transcendental result) were unable to function as an independent motivator (*prayojaka*) like the *utpattyapūrva* (the origination-apūrva), then it would have to serve as the medium for that very motivator, the fruit (*phala*).
