Why, then, should it—being itself a primary effect (*kārya*), being immediate with respect to the fruit, and being perceived first in relation to the fruit—wait for the mediation of a remote *paramāpūrva* whose connection to the fruit is not even perceived? For the status of the fruit as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is derived from its very nature (*aupādānika*).

Because it is dependent upon the relationship between the specific *niyoga* (obligation) and the specifically qualified *niyojya* (the person to be impelled), its status as being apprehended last is indeed logical.

Now, one might object: "In the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), since the object of the rite is that which serves as the instrument for the fruit, the state of being accomplished through the *niyoga* must necessarily be preceded by its being accomplished through the fruit.
Surely you have not previously reflected properly even upon the determination [of the agent] according to his capacity.

For in that case, when it is determined that the fruit is accomplished by the ritual action independently of being accomplished by an injunction (*niyoga*), the very nature of the *apūrva*—namely its designation as the primary element and so forth—is already demonstrated.

Therefore, because of its inherent capacity for instigation (*prayukti*) and because there is no other intervening factor, the injunction itself cannot serve as a medium for the ritual action to instigate the fruit; this is because the fruit is not instigated by anything other than that [injunction].

For the *utpattyapūrvas* (origination-apūrvas), because they are themselves not the end to be accomplished (*kārya*), it is logical that they possess the status of being effects (*kāryatva*) as they are employed as means for the accomplishment of the supreme *apūrva*. Thus, they serve as the medium (*dvāra*) for the supreme *apūrva*, which is the motivator of the ritual action; therefore, the supreme *apūrva* is indeed the effect. And since that [supreme *apūrva*] cannot be accomplished without the intermediate *apūrvas*, those too must be performed. Since those [intermediate *apūrvas*] are established dependent upon the ritual action, the ritual action itself must also be performed. It is by this sequence that the *apūrva* becomes the instigator of the performance of the means.

Nor is the necessity of the *apūrva* dependent upon the necessity of the fruit (*phala*), because the *apūrva* itself is what is to be accomplished (*kārya*). And how could that which is not the motivator (*prayojaka*) of one thing become the motivator of another through its mediation? This being so, it is established that even in the case of a mandate for a desired result (*kāmādhikāra*), the motivator is the injunction (*vidhi*) alone; there is no difference in the conceptualization of the motivator between the occasional (*naimittika*) and the desired (*kāma*) mandates.

On the contrary, even in the case of a mandate for a desired result, there would be three additional factors: the nature of the *apūrva*, the status of being a means to the fruit, and [the status of being] a duty.
The status of the sacrifice as the means to that [result] must be postulated, yet its being the motivator (*prayojakatva*) is exactly the same.
As for the postulation (*kalpanā*), it occurs to both the result and the *apūrva* in either of the two positions; or rather, in both cases, the postulation of the *apūrva* is precisely the same.

In the context of rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya-adhikāra*), however, there is this distinction: it is unestablished that the *apūrva* has the nature of being the means to the fruit, and both the fact that the sacrifice is the means to that *apūrva* and the fact that the sacrifice is the means to the fruit must be postulated.

Even if one were to grant that no such postulation is required in the context of rites for specific desires, nevertheless, the *apūrva*—as the substratum (*dharmin*)—must have its nature as the means to the fruit postulated, and the sacrifice’s status as the means to that [apūrva] must also be postulated.
In the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*), however, [the relationship is between] the action-form of the task (*kārya*) and the established substratum (*dharmin*).
It would be merely a motivator (*prayojaka*); therefore, it is better that it be occasional (*naimittika*).
For the abandonment of what is established by worldly consensus (*loka-siddha*) necessarily involves a contradiction with scripture (*śruti-bādha*).

Consequently, because it does not contradict scripture and because of the parsimony of conceptualization (*kalpanā-lāghava*), it is more appropriate that it be occasional rather than a qualification based on desire (*kāma-adhikāra*).

But how can that which lacks the word *yat* (the relative pronoun) function as a condition (*nimitta*)? We do not say that its status as a condition is based on direct scriptural statement (*śruta*); rather, just as in the case of the *jañjabhyamāna* (one who is yawning), because the person is enjoined (*niyojya*) as qualified by a desire, the status of the desire as a condition is inferred by implication. Furthermore, the presence of the word *yat* does not constitute the definition of a condition; therefore, in this case, that [status] is established through other means, as it resides in the object of reference (*uddeśya*).
For the word "yat" (that which) expresses merely that which is to be designated (*uddeśya*), not its status as a cause (*nimittatva*).

Since the person possessing a house fire or similar condition is designated as the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*) as qualified by an attribute that is not itself to be performed (*anupādeyaviśeṣaṇa*), it is said that the burning—which serves as that qualifying attribute—functions as a cause in a secondary sense (*ārthika*).

And since even for a person desiring a fruit, the designation remains the same because they too are the one to be enjoined, it is logical that the desire for that fruit also functions as a cause in the same way.

Furthermore, since expressions such as "He who desires offspring, he who desires cattle" and "If one should desire that Parjanya be rainy," etc., are heard many times, there is no distinction whatsoever regarding their being intended to signify a causal occasion (*nimitta*).
Now, an objection is raised: the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites are obligatory (*nitya*); they cannot become occasional (*naimittika*).
If they were to be performed as a rule, then the injunctions for occasional rites would be rendered purposeless.
If, on the other hand, performance occurs only when there is a specific cause consisting of a portion of that [desire], then the injunction for lifelong performance would be rendered meaningless.
Therefore, it is argued that the qualification based on desire alone is logical.
To this, it is replied: "No."
For if the statement were common to both positions, then meaningfulness might be relied upon in this particular position.
But here, by means of a multitude of arguments such as the non-sublation of direct scriptural authority (*śruti*), it is determined that [the act] is indeed a cause (*nimitta*).

If, in that case, one of the two becomes purposeless, let it be so; for what is called "purposelessness" is not included within the category of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consisting of scripture.
Whatever possesses a discernible purpose, that alone is [to be accepted];
but for that which is understood to be purposeless, that very [absence of purpose] is superior.

For the repetition of the performance is purposeful, as in the case of the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice; however, it is not possible to assume a different meaning [for the word "life"]. Alternatively, since the performance of the occasional rite extends over the entire duration of one's life, it is enjoined by the "as long as one lives" (yāvajjīva) statement through indirect indication (lakṣaṇā).
For that [repetition] is worldly, whereas the assumption of a different meaning for the optative suffix (liṅ) occurs only here.
Therefore, it is not logical that desire (*kāma*) should be the governing factor (*adhikāra*).

Alternatively, let the view of the author of the *Vārttika*, which is established in the Sūtras and their commentaries, be adopted: "The efficient force (*bhāvanā*) delimited by sacrifice and the like, being subject to injunction and requiring an object desired by the person, brings about heaven and so forth through the sentence and thereby adopts them as its result; it does not take [the desire] as a causal occasion (*nimitta*), because that is not required."

For in that case, the status of sacrifice and the like as instrumental causes (*karaṇatva*) is possible through the mediation of a postulated *apūrva* (unseen potency), just as firewood, the act of rubbing, and so forth serve as means for cooking rice through the mediation of burning and smearing; or just as the group of six sacrifices beginning with the *Āgneya* serves as means for the ultimate *apūrva* through the mediation of the originating *apūrvas*; or just as the act of sprinkling water and so forth serves as a means for the hundredfold cutting [of the enemy].
Thus, everything becomes well-established.
In the case of the *Saurya* and other such rites, the desire for a result is established as the occasioning cause (*nimitta*).
For in that case, no word at all has been brought forward to establish a unity of meaning.

Or, let it be granted that in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other such rites, there is a focus on the fruit because of the existence of the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*). But in the case of rites such as the Saurya sacrifice, where there is no such scriptural injunction for a permanent obligation (*nitya*), why should a focus on the fruit be accepted merely to avoid the charge of meaninglessness? Or perhaps this is the intended meaning: "In the case of the Darśa and others, it has been determined that the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is what is to be expressed."
Do not fear that it has resorted elsewhere, even though it is marked by the signs of desire.

First, regarding the avoidance of the futility of the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*): when it is established that in passages such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," the word *kāma* (desire) has the purpose of indicating a result, then—since an injunction of what must be done for one who desires [a result] would be untenable if the means were not that which accomplishes it, and since a rite that perishes in a moment cannot possibly be its means—the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is understood to denote a durable action distinct from the ritual act itself. Once this is realized, because the hearing of the optative suffix in rites such as the *Saurya* sacrifice shows no partiality toward either the ritual act or anything distinct from it, it is logical that it refers to a result, given that the very nature of desire is directed toward an object.
We say: "No.
For the scriptural mention of the name is a mark of difference that is not sublated;
however, the scriptural mention consisting of the identical word-form is a sublater even of that."

Although the optative suffix (*liṅ*) denotes, by the rule of denotation, a general "task" (*kārya*) common to both its usage in worldly contexts regarding actions and its usage in Vedic injunctions such as those for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices regarding the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*), it nevertheless cannot—by virtue of the optative suffix itself—be prevented from being connected specifically with the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), which is presented by the same word. This is because, when the general term requires a specific instance, that which is presented by the same word through the means of direct statement (*śruti*) characterized by co-referentiality (*samānapadopādāna*) is connected as the specific [object], and it cannot be set aside by another word presented by a different term, owing to the inherent nature of desire (*kāmanā*) which serves as its qualifier.
For the suffix (*pratyaya*), as soon as it is uttered, expresses its own meaning as a universal (*sāmānya*) that conforms precisely to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).

As it has been said: "The case-ending (*vibhakti*), such as the accusative, being uttered after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), is a qualifier (*viśeṣaka*) of the meaning of the nominal stem" (Bhāṣya on Pāṇini 2.3.46, p. 99).
Therefore, even though there is no difference in the act of denotation (*abhidhāna*), gender (*liṅga*) is grasped solely due to the conflict with the audible form of the word (*padaśruti*).
The Prābhākaras conclude as follows:
"They indeed hold that if the *apūrva* were the denoted meaning, the action would be merely indicated by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).
However, because of the fault of having multiple meanings, neither of the two can be the denoted meaning."

For when, due to the impossibility of a person enjoined who desires a fruit (*phalakāmin*), the *apūrva*—which is something over and above the action—is established as the denotation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), then it is not easy to maintain that the action itself is also its denotation; for it is improper to assume multiple meanings [for a single word], and because the cognition of the action is possible even through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Indeed, since the status of the *apūrva* as the object to be accomplished is invariably concomitant with the status of the action as the object to be accomplished, once this is understood from the word, it brings the action to mind; thus, there is no possibility of it being the direct denotation.

Furthermore, in the case of the *saurya* sacrifice and others, there is no cause for secondary indication; therefore, the *apūrva* alone is denoted by the optative suffixes and other such terms in their respective contexts.

Therefore, it is not logical to accept that [the word] has the nature of denoting the object (*nimitta*) by means of its aspect as the desire (*kāmanā*). [To this, the opponent replies: "This is merely their dogmatic assertion," which those who follow valid authority do not believe.
For it is said: "The fault of having multiple meanings arises from the defect of having multiple powers for a single word."
Regarding the two [the optative suffix *liṅ* and the imperative suffix *loṭ*]: their denotability is established through common cognition.

First of all, ordinary people do not consider the *liṅ* (or by extension the *loṭ*) in expressions such as "bring the cow" to be a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), but rather to be primary (*mukhya*) in its meaning.

In that case, if the action to be performed were denoted by the primary function, then the assumption of incapacity would arise, and consequently, its status as a secondary indication would have to be accepted; however, this is not the case, because the primary status is justified in both instances by the single capacity to denote the mere action to be performed.

For polysemy (anekārthatva) does not occur by way of its own nature due to the fault of postulating multiple potencies for another meaning; lest there be such a fault, let it be determined that denotability [of the word] applies to the obligatory (*nitya*) and other rites, because various types of obligatory and optional rites are under discussion.

Therefore, just as those [rites] possess denotability through their fitness to be characterized by the nature of being an effect (*kāryatva*), so too will action (*kriyā*), though it is wretched, possess denotability through its connection with that [nature].
He says: "Not by a single potency in the form of action..."
An investigation into the subject matter of the eleventh chapter:

indeed, in the investigation of the subject matter of the eleventh chapter, it is precisely the qualification consisting of its necessity for performance that must be established through indicative marks (*liṅga*) due to the application of the archetype (*prakṛti*).

But since the *apūrva* has not been previously established by anything else, its very nature—qualified by the necessity of being performed (*kartavyatā*)—must be denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) alone; thus, there is no possibility of [the word] functioning in more than one way. If it denotes the qualified entity, then it would denote the *apūrva* itself and not the action.
On the other hand, if it denotes the qualifier, then it would denote the action alone and not the *apūrva*.
This is not so;

this word denotes only a qualified [entity]. When it is directed toward an action, since the nature of that [action] is already obtained from the verbal root itself, it becomes directed toward the qualifier.

For example, in the expression "the staff-bearer recites the *preṣas*," although the word "staff-bearer" denotes a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭābhidhāyī*), it nevertheless refers to the qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇapara*) without recourse to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Likewise, when a word denoting an action (*kāryavacana*) is employed in reference to an activity, it attains the status of referring to the qualifying attribute of "being an action" (*kāryatvarūpaviśeṣaṇaparatva*) by virtue of its primary denotative function (*śrutivṛtta*); it does not thereby involve figurative indication. Thus, in both cases, the meaning is primary (*mukhya*). As for the one who says: "But if this were so, then even in the context of optional desires (*kāmādhikāra*), since [the result] would be denoted by the same word [as the action], the theory of denoting the *apūrva* (unseen potency) would collapse."

"Therefore, since it was understood that the word expresses something unprecedented (*apūrva*) due to its connection with the person to be enjoined who desires [the result], then the fact that the action is indicated only figuratively (*lākṣaṇikatva*) in order to fulfill that [unprecedented result] is also established.
He should be instructed as follows: "Alas! Have you not heard: 'For those who eat stones become the seal-stones of the Lord'? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.13.18).

For how could one who, on account of its connection with the person to be impelled (*niyojya*), understands the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as denoting a specific task in the form of an action, yet directs it toward the *apūrva*—how could such a person not be capable of directing that same suffix, which denotes a general [task], toward the *apūrva*?

Therefore, although it denotes the general sense of "that which is to be done" (*kartavyatā*), where there is the status of being the person to be impelled for one desiring a fruit, it expresses the *apūrva* by virtue of that [connection]; elsewhere, however, due to its inclusion within the same word, it denotes the action (*kriyā*).

Since the word *liṅ* expresses a general property (*sāmānya*), just as it applies to the *apūrvas*, so too should its denotability be accepted for the action (*kriyā*) as well; why is this not admitted?
If it is argued that this is because of a difference in the nature of their "to-be-done-ness" (*kartavyatā*), we say no, because that [difference] does not exist.

In this regard, one might think: "The state of being something to be accomplished (*kṛtyadeyatā*) is the 'to-be-done-ness' denoted by *liṅ*, and since all *apūrvas* are characterized by that, it is logical that they are denoted by it."

"But since ritual action (*kriyā*) is directed toward a result and is not an end in itself, its 'mode of performance' (*itikartavyatā*) consists in that [result]; thus, due to this difference in the mode of performance, it is impossible for it to be the primary subject matter (*abhidheyatva*).
This is not so, because of the difference in the mode of performance.

Although in common worldly practice, actions such as bringing a cow are not understood as being independently "to be performed" (*kartavyatā*), nevertheless, in the Veda, sacrificial rites such as the *saurya* will possess precisely such a status of being "to be performed."
For the optative suffix (*liṅ*), when uttered in co-utterance with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), denotes an independent action and conveys that very same [action] as such.
If it is argued that "the status of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*) in that manner has never been previously understood in the case of a worldly action," we say no;
for what has been understood in the case of the mandate (*niyoga*) by virtue of which it is accepted?
If it is argued that even though [the duty] is not understood through worldly means, such a duty of his is understood from the Veda alone, then the same applies to action as well.
Now, one might object: how can the Veda establish the duty of an action that is of the nature of suffering and contradicts direct perception? [We reply:
For the Lord, whose essence is not of a single flavor due to His own conceit (*abhimāna*), the duty [of such an action] would not be contradicted by other means of knowledge.

Furthermore, that [niyoga] itself, being achievable only through the expenditure of much wealth and effort, is nothing but a source of suffering and cannot therefore serve as the intended object (*uddeśyatā*) of a conscious agent's activity.

Just as its status as something to be performed (*kartavyatā*) arises from the Vedic injunction (*āmnāya*), which is eternally independent [of human motives], so too will it be for ritual action (*kriyā*).

Moreover, since *niyoga* is distinct from the attainment of pleasure or the avoidance of pain, its status as an end to be accomplished (*kāryatva*) independently—like that of ritual action—is not tenable.
For action (*kṛti*), which consists of the effort of bodily movement, must have as its object that very thing for the sake of which it is preceded by desire;
and since desire has as its object only pleasure or the avoidance of pain, it too has those alone as its objects.
Therefore, it is not tenable for the *apūrva* (unseen potency) to be the primary objective, as was explained in the *Śaktinirṇaya*.

Furthermore, you cannot maintain that the "ought-to-be-done" (kartavyatā) of an action consists in its being pervaded by an effort directed toward another end, for that would entail the consequence of [the agent's] desire being the cause.

Your view is that since it is understood in the world that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote action and its effect, there is an exclusion of qualifiers consisting of the form of action; yet in the Veda, it is understood—merely through the co-occurrence with the word "desire" (*kāma*)—that they terminate in the *apūrva*. In that case, if this "to-be-done-ness" (*kartavyatā*), which consists in being pervaded by an activity directed toward another purpose, is understood as having action as its object, then alas! even in the Veda, one must postulate that they terminate in the *apūrva* without abandoning that [action], and thus your desired primacy of the *apūrva* is contradicted.
For co-utterance with the term *svargakāma* (desiring heaven) is an obstacle only to a specific [action] in the form of a ritual act, but not to its status as subordinate to another [purpose].
Therefore, since in both worldly and Vedic usage there is the expression of an action subordinate to something else, there is no polysemy.
On the contrary, co-utterance with the term *sarvakāma* (desiring all objects) is understood in exactly this same way.
For that which denotes an independent action, like the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others, must be asked: "What is your authority for this?
If he should say, "The co-occurrence with the person to be enjoined who desires the fruit...
[this is the subject of the discussion in the eleventh chapter].
Regarding the investigation of the meaning of the eleventh chapter:

[if it is argued] that "from the co-utterance (*vyāhāra*), a purpose distinct from the action is established as being subordinate to another," one should reply to this: "No, because that serves to prove the opposite.
For the co-occurrence with the word "desire" (*kāma*) is a means of proof only for denoting a purpose subordinate to another, not for independence.

For he, desiring heaven, is capable of understanding that action as subordinate to that [heaven] by virtue of its being desired; for this reason, it is accepted that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others denote an *apūrva* (unseen potency) conducive to that [heaven], rather than denoting the performance of an action connected with being a means to that [heaven]. So how can there be an acceptance of primacy that contradicts one's own authority?

Now, even if something is in fact conducive to the fruit, it need not be expressed by the word in that way; but does it follow from this that what is considered primary must be expressed? For there is not even a grain of evidence for such primacy.

Moreover, due to the very connection with the word denoting the person to be impelled (niyojya), it must be inferred in this way: that form of the task (kārya) which a seeker of a result is capable of understanding as "this is my task" must be what is expressed.

For elsewhere than in the *kāma-adhikāra* sentences, the *liṅ* suffix lacks the capacity to denote a primary action that is otherwise unknown; on the contrary, it has the capacity to denote an action known from common worldly usage as being subordinate. Thus, to say that the very same *liṅ* suffix denotes that [action] as the primary element in the *apūrva*—by virtue of its being the subject of application and its subordinate nature—while contradicting both worldly usage and its own authoritative scope, is indeed laughable.

"Because it is based on worldly usage, because it possesses its own means of knowledge, and because its object is the purposeful result, the apūrva has no other purpose; its primacy cannot be derived from anything else."

By this, the view that words such as "cow" denote their own meanings as related to an action (*kāryānvita*) is refuted; for while expressions such as "bring the cow" employ words in relation to what is to be done (*kārya*), expressions such as "there are fruits on the bank of the river" employ them in relation to an established fact (*siddhārtha*). Since words like "cow" denote their own meanings as related merely to any object that is desired, proximate, and capable—features common to both types of usage—their denotation of what is related to an action is set aside.

In the case of the *ekādaśina* animals,

Nor should it be argued that, since everything is already established there and there by means of extended application (*atideśa*), the restatement of that rule (*tadvidhi*) would be redundant;

for the purpose of that restatement is to restrict (*parisaṃkhyā*) the eleven sets of animals (*ekādaśinaḥ*)—which are obtained through extended application across all *sūtas*—to the ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*).

Nor does this constitute the same fault [of redundancy], because according to the principle of the *niṣādasthapati* section, that [restriction] is not a defect when considered in relation to the indication of time (*kālalakṣaṇa*).

In reality, however, since the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice—whose application is possible everywhere through extended injunction (*atideśa*)—is established by the rule of distribution (*vihāra-vidhi*) as consisting of five animals each for the twelve days, its numerical restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*) is already accomplished. Thus, there is no pointlessness in enjoining the *ekādaśinī* for the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* days where it was previously unobtained. Consequently, because it is logical that an accessory (*guṇa*) should repeat with each primary (*pradhāna*), the complete *ekādaśinī* is performed on the *prāyaṇīya* day and the complete one on the *udayanīya* day; therefore, it is not to be employed by dividing it [between the two].
And in the *daśarātra* sacrifice, since there is no modification (*ūha*) even for the five [sets] of ten animals that exceed the single [set], such is their statement regarding that matter.

This being the position reached, this is not an "exclusionary injunction" (*aprāpta-parisaṃkhyā*), because it is impossible for the injunction for the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* [days] to produce a state of lack of expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*) regarding the other Soma-sacrifices through its own rule; thus, that injunction would act as a blocker of the extended application (*atideśa*) in those cases.

Therefore, in all instances, that very cognition (*citti*)—in order to avoid its own futility—indicates an exclusionary restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*) regarding the others; it is by means of such a method that this becomes an injunction of exclusion.

Nor does this constitute an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction), because there is no evidence for a sequence of priority between two animals that are simultaneously active independently of one another; otherwise, even the injunction regarding rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth would result in being a restrictive injunction (*niyama-vidhi*). Furthermore, in rites such as the *prāyaṇīya*, since one animal is already obtained through the rule for the distribution of the two sets of animals (*payovihāra*), if ten were prescribed there instead, it would result in an inconsistency with the term *ekādaśina* ("consisting of eleven").

Furthermore, these and other such objections regarding the basis for the fruit being the time (*kāla*)— namely, that it would be a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) rather than the object of reference (*uddeśya*)—
are to be considered as equally applicable to the theory of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore,
it is better to assume indication of time within the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself.

In reality, however, the locative status (*adhikaraṇatva*) denoted by the seventh case is twofold: temporal and spatial; for we observe its usage even in a temporal sense, as in "on the full moon day" (*paurṇamāsyām*).

Consequently, when the seventh case denotes temporal locus, because the *Prāyaṇīya* and *Udayanīya* rites connect with it through their association with temporal adjuncts (*kālopādhi*), there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of time either.
For this very reason, according to the view that "mere birth is the temporal adjunct," there is no indication in the expression "the cloth [exists] in the jar by way of a temporal relation."

Therefore, since the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* sacrifices—which serve as temporal qualifiers for the injunction regarding the set of eleven animals (*ekādaśinī*)—are intended to be taken together as a compound (*dvandva*), the eleven animals, though subsidiary to all twelve days, must be performed on both occasions.
In this way, even the archetypal rule (*codaka*) that extends to the subsidiaries of the ten-day period (*daśarātra*) is not sublated.

Likewise, in the case of the *vihāra* arrangement, because the word "daily" (*anvaham*) prescribes only the time, the *ekādaśinī* that is subsidiary to all the days must be performed separately on each day.

However, it is not the case that one animal is assigned to each individual *ekasutā* (single-day sacrifice), because that would result in the sublation of the injunction for obtaining ten animals (*daśapaśu-prāpti*).

For this very reason, even when there is a modification involving only one *ekasutā* within the ten-day period, and although the time in the form of the original position (*prakṛtasthāna*) for the *ekādaśī* is absent, the application of the entire set of eleven animals (*sakalaikādaśinī*) in both cases is contradictory according to the maxim "when a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is omitted, the principal (*mukhya*) remains" (Jaimini Sūtra 10.2.23). Furthermore, by combining the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* sacrifices, there are five animals at the *prāyaṇīya* and six at the *udayanīya*, since the remaining final animal must be performed right there.

The Commentary states: regarding the difference in deities, in the case of the *ekādaśina* offerings where the presentations (*pradāna*) are distinct, the *yājyā* verses ending in the *ardharca* are distinct. Among these, if there is a specific rule—that for whichever presentation a *yājyā* verse ending in the *ardharca* has been made, that [verse] is for the sake of that [specific offering].

Therefore, there is a distinction of ritual procedures (*tantra*). Soma—[this is] the connection [established] by way of a prior exception (*pūrvapavāda*). Vi— "If one desires [to perform] the *vasāhoma* sacrifice within the *ekādaśinī* ritual procedure..."
The *tantra* is [defined] by its feasibility; the distinction [between types of tantra] is due to the purpose of the offering.

Bhaṭṭa: However, even in cases where there is a single deity (*ekadevatākatva*), since it will be stated later that in the case of animals of the same class (*sajātīya-paśu*) the cooking is performed together with the marking of the signs, the *vasā-homa* (fat-oblation) must be performed separately despite the fat being mixed. For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), because the time of the half-verse of the *yājyā* has already been utilized for the purpose of the *yājyā*, it lacks the status of being for the purpose of the *vasā-homa*. Consequently, it is understood that the time of the half-verse of the *yājyā*—which was employed by another [rite]—is merely a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) for the *vasā-homa* produced as a by-product (*anuṣṣiddha*) of the animal sacrifice.
At the conclusion of each respective *yājyā*, the *vasā-homa* (offering of the fat) must be performed for each animal produced as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of that respective *yājyā*.

It should not be argued that because the *vasā* is mixed together, the requirement for its disposal (*pratipatti*) is fulfilled by a single performance, and thus—despite the fact that distinct portions are taken at different times—the purpose is accomplished through *prasaṅga* (extension of benefit) from the service rendered to one, making a repetition unnecessary. This is because the assistance generated by the offering exists for each individual case.

Even though [the substances] are mixed, because the remainder remains undifferentiated at once, the deity who distinguishes milk from water accepts only the portions belonging to their respective sacrifices; for, since the portions belonging to other sacrifices have been offered as a single undifferentiated whole, they are not to be discarded. Thus, even in the case of accepting portions from other sacrifices, the requirement that they be of the same time as that specific sacrifice is fulfilled by the subsequent disposal (*pratipatti*) of those portions. Therefore, the consumption of those [remnants] is logically established.

Therefore, since the visible benefit produced by the agent in the form of the *pratipatti* (disposal) is logically accounted for as being a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to another [rite], and because no unseen benefit (*adṛṣṭa-upakāra*) arising from a restrictive rule (*niyama*) exists—since even that would be destroyed by the *apūrva* of the sacrifice itself—the performance must indeed be repeated by virtue of its being the agent of the *pratipatti*-effect.

However, where there is a difference in cooking due to the animal being of a different species, and thus the cooking is performed separately, then because the fat (*vasā*) is not mixed, it is clear that there is a distinction between the offerings to the Aṣṭrins and the deities. Maṇḍana says: "In that case, however, the fat is separate."
"In that case, there is a distinction based on the deity.
Śaṅkara says: "The distinction is held to be based on the difference in time. The distinction refers to the various oblations (*vasā-homa*).
There should be a rotation of the *vyanīkā* as in the case of the *ekādaśina*.
In the *gavām ayana* sacrificial session (*satra*), the *vyanīkā* is obtained by extension (*codaka*) from the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*).
And in that context, because of the greater number of days, a rotation of the *vyanīkā* must be performed.
And that rotation of the *vyanīkā* should be like that of the *ekādaśinī*.
Just as in the *Gavāmayana* sacrifice the *ekādaśinī* animals are repeated like a "measuring-stick" (*daṇḍakalita*), so too the *vyanīkā* should be rotated like a "measuring-stick.
When one *vyanīkā* consisting of nine days has been performed, it must be performed again in that very same manner and sequence, and so on repeatedly.
Just as a special punishment for the seizure of fields and so forth is fully applied again and again, so it is here;
such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
[This is] like the case of the eleven [animals], namely the sacrificial animals beginning with the *ekādaśina*. 1309. *Ekādaśinādipaśu* (The sacrificial animals beginning with the *ekādaśina*).
"Or rather, there is an increase in position because the number is not directly perceived.
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the prima facie view.
There should be an increase in position, not like a "repeated-stick" (daṇḍakalita) sequence.
Because the number of nine days is not perceptible, the number of the days is not perceived.

Those days whose number is perceptible are "perceptible-numbered" (*pratyakṣasaṃkhyāni*); since they are not like that, they are "imperceptible-numbered" (*apratyakṣasaṃkhyāni*), due to the existence of that state.
The mention of "days" (*ahar*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), not for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhāna*).
The precedence is prescribed;
therefore, an extension of the position must be made.
For each [cup], starting from the first, which has the Aindravāyava as its initial [deity], an extension of that first position must be performed.
For there are nine days of the *vyūḍha-vyanīkā* sacrifice, and in those [days] of the *dvādaśāha*, nine leadings (*agratā*) are prescribed in sequence.
However, in the *gavāmayana*, all the days are divided into nine parts, and in each twenty-day section, one leading is to be performed in sequence.

In the first twenty-day section, there is the leading of the *aindravāyava*; in the second twenty, the leading of the *śukra*; in the third twenty, the leading of the *āgrayaṇa*; and in the fourth twenty, again the leading of the *aindravāyava*. In this manner, there is an expansion of the positions.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Furthermore, because the *āgrayaṇa* cup is seen at the repetition of the *pṛṣṭha* chant, upon the thirty-second repetition, the *aindravāyava* cup would occur again.
Now, he states another reason for the established conclusion and a fault in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the milking.

When there is a reversal on the northern wing, that is, a reversal of the *pṛṣṭha* section in reverse order, the *aindravāyava* cup is seen at the end of the thirty-third day of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) because of the reversal; thus, it is included within the reversal through the expansion of its position. However, if the reversal were like a "staff-measured" repetition (*daṇḍakalita*), then the *aindravāyava* would occur again [at the beginning], and the *aindravāyava* would consequently fall on the thirty-third day, which is improper.
Therefore, it is established that there is indeed an expansion of position (*sthānavivṛddhi*).

For instance, in the view that the position [of the cups] increases, in the Gavāmayana sacrifice, because there is no contradiction with the scripturally prescribed precedence of the Aindravāyava cup for the first two days, the *vyanīkā* sequence proceeds from the very beginning and is completed within the first fortnight divided into nine parts (180 ÷ 9 = 20).
Then, at the end of the first part of the subsequent fortnight—which proceeds in reverse order—at the thirty-third day (on the sixth day), the precedence of the Āgrayaṇa cup occurs.
This is what is meant by the statement: "Because the Āgrayaṇa is seen at the thirty-third [day] upon the repetition of the *pṛṣṭha* days."

But in the case of the "returning like a staff" (daṇḍakalitavat) model, for the latter fortnight which proceeds in reverse order, the state of having the cup for Indra and Vāyu first (aindravāyavāgratā) would apply to the thirty-third day of that latter fortnight.

Thus, the *vyanīkā* arrangement, being inserted into the former fortnight, occurs after excluding the first two days; for those two days, there is the state of having the cup for Indra and Vāyu first.

According to the *daṇḍakalitapakṣa* (the "stick-whirled" method) of calculation based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since there is no *aindravāyavāgratā* (the state of having the cup for Indra and Vāyu as the first) on the second day, seven days remain when the *vyanīkā* (the alternating sequence of cups), which is to be inserted into the remaining days and repeated nineteen times (*180 - 2 = 178 = [9 × 19 = 171 + 7]*),
is applied. Among those, the *aindravāyavāgratā* occurs on the seventh day,
and at that point, the first half of the cycle is completed.
The *vyatīkā* [section], however, is not yet completed; it must be brought to completion.

Then follows the *viṣuvant*, beginning with the *śukra* cup; then the first *kharasāman*, beginning with the *āgrayaṇa* cup; then the second *kharasāman*, beginning with the *aindravāyava* cup; then the third *kharasāman*, beginning with the *śukra* cup; then the *viśvajit*, beginning with the *āgrayaṇa* cup; then the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) is performed in reverse order.
The first day of that initial [sacrifice] is the Trayastriṃśa; it follows that the Aindravāyava cup comes first.
Such a scriptural observation would not be possible if the repetition were like the "beating of a staff" (daṇḍakalita).
Therefore, this has been stated again: "It should be the Aindravāyava."
This should be seen under the heading "The arrangement of the days in the Gavāmayana.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the rotation of the *vyanīkā* occurs through the expansion of the positions;
however, according to a specific scriptural injunction (*vacana*), this rotation applies to the sets of eleven animals (*ekādaśina*).
As for what was stated by the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) as an illustrative example—"like the eleven [animals]"—that is incorrect.

In the case of the eleven animals, there would be a transposition (*parivṛtti*) and a shifting of the order (*vāpana*), because of the scriptural injunction: "In the subsequent days, one should lead forward the Agneya animal first.
That [transposition], occurring in the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), enters into the Gavāmayana.
And thus, the illustrative example is dissimilar.
Therefore, the *vyanīkā* array is increased only by position,
because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

From the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it follows that in the *Gavāmayana* sacrifice, the eleven animals (*ekādaśinaḥ paśavaḥ*) revolve like a measuring rod (*daṇḍakalitavat*). This is indicated by the passage: "The eleven animals are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*); when days are exceeded by means of the sets of eleven, they are [exceeded] as animals. When there is an increase in the position (*sthāna*), there is no excess;
however, in the case of revolving like a measuring rod, there may be either a deficiency or an excess.
Therefore, it is logical that the repetition of the eleven animals occurs like a "measured stick" (daṇḍakalita);
however, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *vyanīkā* arrangement occurs solely through the expansion of their positions.
In the case of the eleven animals and so forth, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the tails (*jāghanī*) during the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
The modification of the substance, however, would apply to the meaning of the preceding verse; likewise, there is a restriction in the case of an option, because of its predominance.
In the case of the eleven animals and so forth, [the rule applies] to the eleven animals and so forth; the Kṣatriya is dedicated to Indra.
The effect of action inheres [in it].
What, then, is that? It is the formative force (*saṃskāra*).
For that is produced by action.
Furthermore, neither this boiled milk nor the curd has been used anywhere;
that for which they were procured—the sacrifice—has not yet been performed.
Therefore, by means of that substance, the tail, and the two items, curd and boiled milk, there should be a primary ritual act (*arthakarma*), not a disposal (*pratipatti*).
Soma: In the previous case, since the substance (the one-year-old cow and so forth) was a subordinate factor (*guṇa*), let there be an option (*vikalpa*).
But here, since the tails (*jāghanī*) are to be disposed of (*pratipādyatayā*), their combination (*samuccaya*) is appropriate; such is the connection.
Bhaṭṭa Rudradatta states that the word *jāghanī* denotes the tail.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: Even though there is a modification characterized by a restrictive rule regarding the *jāghanī* (tail) substance—a substance derived from the sacrificial animal—it is a primary act (*arthakarma*) because it possesses the nature of the archetype (*prakṛti*). Since an option would otherwise arise due to its being a primary act, this is for the purpose of restriction; furthermore, a re-enactment (*punarvidhāna*) serves to restrict [the choice] according to what has been established. As will be explained later: "Is there a combination of *jāghanīs* or not? Or rather, like the *guda* (intestines), it is not so.
Because in the archetype it is an act for the purpose of restriction, it is thus."

Bhāṭṭa: Regarding the question of whether there is a combination (*samuccaya*) or an option (*vikalpa*) of the *jāghanī* (tail) among the animals for which the *nīrājanā* (purificatory rite) is extended by analogy—at least in the case of the *darśa* sacrifice, since the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are *arthakarma* (primary acts), there is no dispute that the *jāghanī* functions as a subordinate element (*guṇabhāva*) alongside the clarified butter (*ājya*) by way of option.

Furthermore, since the same [procedure] applies by extension (*atideśa*) even in the case of the *daikṣa* sacrifice, the statement heard again—"He performs the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with the tail" (*jāghanyā patnīsaṃyājaṃ yajati*)—is, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), intended merely to exclude the clarified butter (*ājya*), and not for the purpose of enjoining the *patnīsaṃyājas* as having the tail as their disposal (*pratipatti*). Even though the tail requires disposal here, it is untenable to assume that the *patnīsaṃyājas* serve as its disposal on the grounds of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), because the *patnīsaṃyājas* would otherwise be performing a function not inherent to their original archetype (*aprākṛta-kārya*).

For this very reason, even if this statement were intended merely as a restrictive rule (niyama), one should not entertain the doubt—raised by Pārthasārathi—that, according to the logic of the sprinkling of the remnants of the *prājāpatya* offerings (*prājāja-śeṣābhighāraṇa*), the restriction itself should be assumed to serve the purpose of purifying the tail (*jāghanī*). This is because the restriction itself already has a well-established purpose in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Furthermore, the suggestion that, in the manner described by me, one should assume an injunction for a different disposal (*pratipatti*) specifically for the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, is not even worth considering.

Therefore, by this statement, since it merely establishes a restriction (*niyamamātra*) regarding the intended refinement (*saṃskāra*) which is already obtained as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*), and because there is no other means of comprehension (*pratipattyantara*) due to the requirement of parsimony in the adoption [of the word], and because that [number] present [in the context] possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even when the animal is taken as the primary object, only a single thing to be numbered (*ekasaṃkhyeya*) is to be grasped optionally (*vikalpena*).
Maṇḍana says: "And the tail (*jāghanī*) is optional. Śaṅkara says: "There is a combination (*samuccaya*) among the tails."
"No;

because of the unity of purpose, it should be restricted, as in the previous case, for the modification is indeed [governed by] the procedure. Since the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) applies by extension (*atideśa*) to each individual modification such as the *saurya* sacrifice, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the eighth chapter, "Because of the unity of purpose" (*aikādaśya*), is maintained. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 730).

"The principle is that a collection of words constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) based on their having a single purpose (*aikārthya*). He states this because the statement of the author of the *Kalpasūtra*, "The beginning of the latter is the indicator of the end of the former," is itself rooted in the principle that "a collection of words constitutes a single syntactical unit based on having a single purpose. Thus, he explains the nature of that definition. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 683)
Furthermore, the statement "the beginning of the subsequent [section] is the characteristic of the preceding limit" is not a Vedic injunction;

rather, it is called a "characteristic of logic" because it was stated by the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* regarding the application (*viniyoga*) of the *Āmnāya* and the *Brāhmaṇas* according to logical principle.

The two *vidhṛtis* are made of *ikṣu* stalks, according to the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) [which states they are] "made of *ikṣu* stalks" (*ikṣuyavavāmike*), meaning "made of leaves" (*patrātmike*).
And from the remainder of the sentence, they are made of *kāśa* grass.
Śābarabhāṣya 1.3.5, p. 35.
The ritualists, however, take them as being made of sugarcane leaves.
Who [says this]? "The two *vidhūtis* are made of sugarcane;
those two are established in the world as being composed of sugarcane parts, and likewise in the Veda, they are made of the roots of *kāśa* grass."

Vārttika 1.3.4, p. 222: "If the word *aikṣyavī* abandons its well-known etymological meaning (*avayavaprasiddhi*) in favor of its established usage as a conventional whole (*samudāyaprasiddhi*) in Vedic literature, then the very purpose of the operation of the grammatical treatise—namely, the comprehension [of the correct form]—is already accomplished.

However, on p. 223, it is concluded that because the established usage of the word *aikṣyavī* as a whole is stronger, and because its etymological meaning is difficult to find in common worldly usage, it must be determined to be derived from *kāśamūla*."
Su. Pṛ. 218:
"Even though it is established that the selection of the substance for the animal-offering (*paśugraha*) is optional—meaning one may choose either this or that goat (chāga)—" Bāla. Pṛ. 157.
Tradition (*aitihya*): "Vaiśravaṇa is in the banyan tree"—this tradition is not a means of valid cognition (*pramiti-karaṇa*).
Even so, it is included within scripture (*āgama*).
Maṇi, p. 62:
"The reddish-brown animal dedicated to Indra is the seventh among the eleven animals;
it is used in both the Aśvamedha and the Jyotiṣṭoma."
The bull dedicated to Indra is the third animal in the Carakasautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
Satyāṣāḍha states: "A bull, a ram, or a goat dedicated to Indra."
The cake for Indra on eleven potsherds belongs to the king (the Kṣatriya), as in the Rājasūya sacrifice.
The cup for Indra is the archetype for the other cups.

And that very [sacrifice] possesses common characteristics (*sadharmaka*); those [sacrifices] not belonging to Indra (*anaindra*) and not belonging to the Maruts (*amarka*) possess common characteristics by virtue of the *codaka* (the extended application).
Vi. 3.1.16: "The Kṣatriya is one for whom Indra is the deity" (*aindro rājanyaḥ*).
Here, by virtue of being for Indra...

"The Kṣatriya belongs to Indra" (AitB 2.24). When the cup for Indra and Vāyu is being offered, the Kṣatriya is praised as "belonging to Indra. Thus, the word "Indra" is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), not an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
Mā. 1.4.12.1–2: "Is it that 'in the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice, a bull dedicated to Indra (aindro vṛṣṇiḥ) is to be offered'? (Regarding the seasonal animal as belonging to the Savanīya).
"Soma dedicated to Indra is both drawn and measured;
therefore, in [the cups] dedicated to Indra there is Soma, but in those not dedicated to Indra, there is no Soma at all."
Thus, all the characteristics of Soma apply only to those [vessels] dedicated to Indra;
the others are without such characteristics and remain expectant.
But how is it that Soma dedicated to Indra is drawn when [the deity] has already been produced? From the wording of the mantra.
The mantra beginning with "For Indra, thee, accompanied by the Vasus" is capable of denoting Soma dedicated to Indra, and not any other.
Therefore, the Soma belongs to Indra;
consequently, the ritual properties of Soma apply to those [offerings] dedicated to Indra.

But other offerings are expectant; therefore, according to the principle that "they will receive the ritual properties," the mantra must be modified (ūhitavya) according to the respective deity. Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 3.1.1.129.
"In the *aveṣṭi* sacrifices, which are part of the *rājasūya*, there is a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, and a bull is the sacrificial fee" (Bhāṭṭadīpikā 11.4.13).

In such injunctions as "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra," the extension of the properties (*atideśa*) of the archetypal *puroḍāśa* applies, and not the extension of the properties of the *sānnāyya* (milk-offering), because the similarity of the deity and the similarity of the oblation are more powerful [grounds for extension].
VI. 8.1.17: "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra.
In this case, if there is no specific statement [regarding the time of result], the fruit is of this world; but if there is such a statement, it is of the next world.
4.3.12: A sacrifice for a specific desire, such as "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra," must be performed out of that very desire.
In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, one takes up the Aindra draught after it has been offered.
Bhāṣya 3.5.1.14.
There is neither the status of being an archetype (*prakṛti*) nor the status of being an ectype (*vikṛti*) for those [libations] dedicated to Indra and those not dedicated to Indra.

Thus, there is no [recitation of] the *ahaḥ* formula in the offerings not dedicated to Indra. Therefore, the consumption of those offerings not dedicated to Indra is performed without a mantra (this being a hypothetical discussion). Vi. 3.1.17.
In the case of the eleven-potherd offering for Indra consisting of grain, there is the displacement of the *āgneya* sacrificial cake.
Bhāṣya 8.1.17.32–34; Bālakrīḍā p. 141: In the *aindra* sacrificial cake, the displacement pertaining to the *sānnāyya* (milk-offering) is set aside by the displacement pertaining to the *āgneya*.
In the consumption of the cup belonging to Indra (aindracamasa), the deity Agni, who is associated with the *vaṣaṭ* call, is to be indicated.
[Vi.
3.2.16] Regarding the injunction "He takes the draught for Indra and Vāyu," what is intended is that he intends it for both Indra and Vāyu.
In that case, since it is not logical for one to resolve [upon an action] without a sacrifice, a sacrifice must be postulated.
Bhāṣya 2.1.6.18; Mīmāṃsākośa 165.

Even when there is a connection with a specific desire (*kāmasaṃyoga*), the drawing of the *aindravāyava* cup, which is established by its textual position (*pāṭhaprāpta*), must be performed in its own place and not from the very beginning of the sequence.
However, in the case of a connection with a specific desire, there would be a displacement to the beginning due to the explicit scriptural statement (*vacana*).

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: Now, regarding the connection with a specific desire, there is a scriptural statement concerning the *aindravāyava*: "One who desires that offspring may be produced in the proper order should draw the cups beginning with the *aindravāyava*."

In this regard, is there a withdrawal from the very beginning of everything, or is there a taking up of that which stands in its own sequence? What is the prima facie view? By the preceding section (17), it was established that it is "that which stands in its own sequence.
This being the position reached, we reply:
But in connection with a specific desire (*kāmasaṃyoga*), there should be a withdrawal from the very beginning of everything.
Why? Because of the scriptural statement (*vacana*).

For there is indeed a scriptural statement: "One who desires that offspring may be arranged in their proper order should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu. This [statement] is purposeful when there is a displacement from the very beginning, provided that priority (*agratā*) is being enjoined.
If the drawing of the cups were being enjoined without reference to priority, it would not produce any specific modification in the performance.

"Therefore, there is a withdrawal from the very beginning. [Objection: "Or rather, because of the connection with the self (ātman), that treatise on desire (kāmaśāstra) would be connected to those regions, due to its connection with what is desired.
Commentary: This is not so; namely, that which was stated—that there is a withdrawal from the very beginning—is incorrect.
In the case of grasping that which stands in its own sequence, there will be favor toward the sequence;
therefore, it is said "of that which stands in its own sequence.
As for what was stated—that because of the mention of priority, there is a withdrawal from the beginning—that is not correct.
This is the instruction regarding those [soma-offerings] where the Aindravāyava cup comes first among the sequence of cups;
it is accomplished by the drawing of those cups that are associated with it and have it as their first.
In this way, the direct Vedic statement (śruti) is upheld; for in your view, it would be a syntactical connection (vākya), and a direct statement is more authoritative than a syntactical connection.
Now, regarding what was stated—that [the injunction] does not produce a specific modification of activity in the act of taking—it is because it follows upon a conjunction (*saṃyogapṛṣṭhakatvāt*).
Here, there is one conjunction with a desire for the obligatory rite: "one should accomplish the desire by means of the taking."
There is another constant connection: "One should take those cups which are for Indra and Vāyu.
Therefore, there is no distinction in the application [of the rule].
Consequently, this is a means for fulfilling a desire when connected with that specific location.
Therefore, the mention [of the order] refers to that which remains in its own sequence.
Soma: In that case, let there be a displacement from the beginning; thus, the connection arises from the act of rising (*utthāna*).

[Objection: But if the priority were enjoined for the sake of a specific desire (*kāma*), then the statement—"Speech indeed is this [cup], namely the Aindravāyava; since the Aindravāyava cups are drawn"—would be purposeless.
If it is argued that since the cups (*graha*) themselves are enjoined for the sake of the fruit,
and because the cup for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava-graha*)—

which has already obtained its purpose through the context (*prakaraṇa*)— would otherwise, by virtue of the syntactical statement (*vākya*), be understood as being solely for the sake of the fruit, the explicit mention [of the fruit] is meaningful as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).
Not so;

for even in the absence of being a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), there is no pointlessness to the scriptural statement, since the quality of the optional rite (*kāmyaguṇa*)—namely, the sharpness of the parrot’s beak (*śukāgramatva*) and so forth—attains the status of being dependent on the *dhārāgraha* (the stream-draught) by its very presence.
In reality, however, it is not possible for the sentence beginning with "Speech indeed" (*vāgvai*) to function as a counter-exception.

Vi— "In the place of one's own [cup], the Aindravāyava cup may optionally come first; according to this injunction, the Vaiçirādi is first, and the last is for the sake of a desire. Bhaṭṭa— Within that very intermediate context (of the Jyotiṣṭoma and others), it is heard: "One who desires that offspring may be produced in due order should draw the cups beginning with the Aindravāyava. Regarding the inquiry as to whether the fruit [mentioned] is produced by the quality of *agratā* (priority) or indeed produced by the act of drawing (*grahaṇa*), and considering its utility for sublation (*bādha*), it is [concluded] that, according to the principle of the section on the desire for sensory power (*indriyakāmādhikaraṇa*, 2.1.11), it is produced by the quality alone.

Furthermore, where a quality such as the *godohana* vessel is enjoined because it is absolutely unestablished (*atyantāprāpti*), the principle of the *indriyakāmādhikaraṇa* applies, since the connection with the fruit belongs to that which is enjoined.

However, where both the quality and the verbal root-meaning are established from another source, it must be stated that—according to the principle of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*—the connection with the fruit belongs to the verbal root-meaning alone.
If that were the case, then even the staff, being already established by the injunction "He offers with curds" (*dadhnā juhoti*), would have to be said to possess a connection with the fruit.

Nor can there be a connection with the fruit [of the action] based on the understanding that it is something to be enjoined, out of fear that its optional nature would lead to the contingency of being merely a partial restatement (*pākṣikānuvāda*); for in the present case as well, there is no understanding of the *aindravāyavāgratva* (the state of having the cup for Indra-Vāyu first) as being optional, given that it is determined by the occasion of the *bṛhatsāman* chant and the form of the *śukrāgratva* (having the *śukra* cup first) according to the desire-based mantras.

Therefore, the connection of curd and so forth with the fruit must be stated solely for the purpose of conveying the meaning of the word denoting the quality. And this is the same in the present case as well; thus, it is the *aindravāyavāgratva* itself that is enjoined with reference to the fruit.

And in that context, since the quality of having the cup for Indra and Vāyu as the first (*aindravāyavāgratva*) is what is to be enjoined, its acquisition [in the sequence] occurs simply from the textual order (*pāṭha*) relative to the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa, because otherwise it would result in not being an object of injunction.

Since it is understood that the injunction applies only in relation to the cups for Upāṃśu and Antaryāma, the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) is set aside by the larger context (*mahāprakaraṇa*); therefore, all the cups (*sarvagraha*) constitute the substratum, and there is a "drawing back" (*pratikarṣa*) of the cup for Indra and Vāyu to the very beginning of all. This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In reality, however, since the quality of having the *aindravāyava* cup first (*aindravāyavāgratva*), which is obtained through recitation and other means as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*), can logically serve as a means to a result (*phalārtha*) by virtue of its sequence [with the *āditya* cup], and because there is an intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), the *āghāra* libation alone serves as the substratum (*āśraya*).

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: since the word expressing the quality—the phrase "the cups with the *aindravāyava* first"—is already fulfilled by its function as the definition (*avacchedaka*) of that which is to be enjoined, namely, the state of being produced from the vessel (*yapātra-janyatva*), the principle of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* (JS 2.1.1–4) does not apply here.
Regarding the cup for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava*), there is an exception concerning the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa (*maitrāvaruṇa*).
The status of being a cup for Indra and Vāyu and so forth is the defining characteristic of that class; nothing else.
This very point is also the purpose for including the term expressive of a quality in the passage, "Speech indeed is this [cup] which belongs to Indra and Vāyu.

For this reason, wherever a term expressive of a quality does not yield such a purpose, there—such as in the case of curds (*dadhi*) and so forth—there is only a connection between the quality and the result.

Consequently, the connection with the result applies only to the cups drawn from the stream (*dhārā-graha*); the phrase "those beginning with the cup for Indra and Vāyu" (*aindravāyavāgrān*), however, is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already possible.

For this very reason, in the second prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the occasional (*naimittika*) precedence of the *śukra* cup, because two contradictory qualities cannot be grasped simultaneously as belonging to their respective bases. In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, even when the cups intended for progeny are employed, the occasional precedence of the *śukra* cup and the optional (*kāmya*) precedence of the *manthin* cup and others are not mutually contradictory; this is the purpose [of the discussion].
Maṇḍana states: "Even in the case of an optional rite, there is no restriction from all the cups."
First, the drawing back [of the sequence].
Śaṅkara says: "Likewise, in the case of desire, there is precedence for that.
This means that the performance of the *aindravāyava* cup takes place before the cups dedicated to Mitra-Varuṇa and the others.
Because of the statement regarding the precedence of the Aindravāyava cup, there should be a displacement [of it] to the beginning.
The Commentary: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "Speech indeed is the Aindravāyava; when the cups are drawn beginning with the Aindravāyava, one secures speech itself.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: should there be a displacement of the Aindravāyava to the very beginning, such that it is to be drawn prior to the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups; or is its drawing to be prior to the Śukra and Manthin cups?
What is established? That there is a displacement of the Aindravāyava cup to the very beginning.

Why? Because of the mention of "beginning" (*agratā*). Here, "beginning" is what is being enjoined by the statement, "He draws the Aindravāyava first," meaning that one should place the Aindravāyava at the head of these [cups].
Since there is no distinction, all [cups] must indeed be made Aindravāyava.
If the displacement were not performed from the beginning, the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups would not be Aindravāyava.
However, when the displacement is performed from the beginning, all [the cups] become Aindravāyava.
And here, the precedence of the Aindravāyava cup is not being enjoined.

If it were enjoined, then with respect to those [cups] enumerated, the act of establishing the precedence of the Aindravāyava would have to be performed [repeatedly]. Furthermore, if the precedence of the Aindravāyava is stated as a property (dharma) of other cups, then that property must be performed for all of them; thus, there would be a displacement [of the sequence] from the beginning.

But how, then, is it understood that "this entire thing is the ritual act (dharma)"? From the injunction: "One should make [the cups] for Indra and Vāyu. Here, the necessity of performing the drawing of the cup (graha) is not being stated; rather, it is heard [in the scripture]: "Those cups are to be drawn."
It is understood that preeminence (*agratā*) is for the sake of others (*parārtha*), not for one's own sake (*svārtha*).
Therefore, there should be a withdrawal (*pratikarṣa*) from all initial positions.

Alternatively, because there is no distinction in the nature of the factors (*dharma*), it is stated that those which are foremost possess their own intrinsic nature (*ātmatva*) within their respective places according to the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Commentary: The phrase "also" (api ca) serves to exclude the previous position.
There would not be a withdrawal from all [the preceding elements];
rather, there is the inclusion of that which occupies its own place.
Why? Because here the state of being "that-first" (tadgratā) is not enjoined;
for in that case, the syntactical connection (vākya) would be favored. What then? The taking up of those [cups] is what is enjoined.
For it is thus supported by scripture (*śruti*):

"If the *Soma* sacrifice has the *Rathantara* as its *Sāman*, then those cups (*graha*) which are prescribed as beginning with the *Aindravāyava* are enjoined to be taken according to this specific sequence—that is, starting with the *Aindravāyava*—thereby prescribing the ritual details (*dharma*) for those very cups under discussion.

Since the injunction regarding the taking of the cups refers to those cups that begin with the *Aindravāyava* in their own respective positions, there is no displacement (*pratikarṣa*) of all [the cups] to the beginning."
And because of the connection with a stream.
The Commentary states: Furthermore, there is a connection with a stream in the sentences concerning the Aindravāyava and other cups, namely, "He draws [the soma] with another uninterrupted stream.
Therefore, those are cup-drawings by means of a stream.
With reference to that [cup], the act of taking (*grahaṇa*) is enjoined.

Soma: Just as in the previous case, by the force of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, there was the status of being an independent means of preparation (*praṇayana*), so too here, by the force of the *bahuvrīhi* compound alone, it is appropriate that the properties of all cups (*sarvagrahadharma*) are obtained; thus the connection is established.
Vi: "In place of that [cup] which is before the *upāṃśu*, the *aindravāyava* cup should be."

[Objection: "In this case, it must be the first [instance] because of the injunction for non-stream [soma]. [Reply: "Not so, because it effects the attainment of what was not previously obtained through connection with the stream. Bhaṭṭa: Having prescribed the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups as non-stream [soma] cups in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, [the text] states at the beginning of the series of stream-cups, such as the Aindravāyava and Maitrāvaruṇa: "Speech indeed is this Aindravāyava; when the Aindravāyava cups are drawn, they proceed following speech itself."

In this regard, when considering whether the text prescribes an extraction (*apakarṣa*) of the Aindravāyava cup before the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups—despite its performance having already been established by the textual order following the Maitrāvaruṇa cup—or whether it does not: since the direct evidence here, consisting of the injunctions "He takes the Aindravāyava" and "He takes the Maitrāvaruṇa," cannot logically function as a mere restatement of the cups already established in brief, the Aindravāyava must be enjoined by this text precisely because it was not yet obtained in its proper place among all the cups under discussion.

For this very reason, by the term "precedence" (*agraha*), only those cups dedicated to Mitra-Varuṇa and others are not meant; for there is no evidence for such a restriction, and because their precedence is already established by the mere recitation of the text.
Consequently, the precedence of the cup for Indra-Vāyu is enjoined even with respect to the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups.

Furthermore, although it follows from logic alone that the [Aindravāyava] cup must be placed only when the *Rathaṃtara* is the *sāman*, even if it cannot be included because its being first due to the *Śukra* cup is contingent (*naimittika*) and thus contradicts the state of having many *sāmans*, nevertheless, it is prescribed as a contingent rule by the text "if the *Rathaṃtara* is the *sāman*. And its purpose, as in the final established view (*siddhānta*), is the non-application of that rule in cases such as the *Kaṇvarathaṃtara*.
Therefore, the Aindravāyava cup is to be made the first of all.

This being the case, because of the desire to enjoin merely the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it is the *grahaṇa* (the act of taking) itself that is enjoined here as the name [of the sacrifice], since otherwise there would result a third type of injunction by way of the location of the *grahaṇa*.

Nor is there any possibility of enjoining what has already been enjoined; for when an injunction regarding a particular qualifier of a specific grammatical factor (*kāraka*) has been made, there is no obstacle to an injunction regarding another property (*dharma*) of that very same particular, even if it involves a further qualification of that factor.

For, by such injunctions as "He takes the draught for Indra and Vāyu," there is an injunction regarding those various individual extractions due to the prescription of heterogeneous extractions; however, by this [present injunction], there is an injunction regarding those various extractions characterized by a generality (*vaijātya*) that pervades the aforementioned state of being established in those extractions.

And it is established that this generality (*vaijātya*) is the delimitor of the status of being the object of an injunction (*vidheyatāvacchedakatva*) for that which is assisted by the mode of the first injunction in its specific form.

Furthermore, this [injunction] does not apply in common to the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups and others; for if it were interpreted as referring merely to the cups under discussion, then this [subsequent] definition following the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma would result in redundancy, and the restatement "beginning with the Aindravāyava" would be untenable. Moreover, the purposes of the injunctions—which will be explained later—consisting of general attributes, would be impossible if they did not apply to the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma.
Therefore, there is a concise injunction of those specific Aindravāyava and other cup-drawings that have already been prescribed.

Among those [cups], the precedence of the Aindravāyava cup is established by the order of the recitation (pāṭha); thus, because of the restatement (anuvāda) "the Aindravāyava is first," there is no retroactive application (pratikarṣa) of the Aindravāyava to the very beginning of the entire sequence. Furthermore, the purpose of the concise injunction is the establishment of a subordinate context (avāntara-prakaraṇa) for those very cups, by way of generating a specific expectancy.

Consequently, in the sentences preceding them—such as "he draws with a stream" (anyā dhārayā gṛhṇāti)—since the verb *gṛhṇāti* (he draws) refers back to those same cups, the injunction of properties such as "stream" and so forth applies only to them, and not to the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups.
And for this reason, the status of these two as the substrata (*āśraya*) is established.

Furthermore, another purpose is that in the injunction regarding the optional (*kāmya*) drawing of the cups, it will be stated in the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*) that "these alone [are the substrata] when connected with a desire.
Moreover, in the case of the fruits of qualities (*guṇaphala*) dependent on the drawing of the cups, the status of these alone as the substrata is established; such is the *tantra*.
