The Aindrāma twelve-cake offering—1319—the consumption of Soma by the Aindrāmas.

There is an extension (*atideśa*) of the section containing the injunctions along with their explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) regarding the single potsherds (*ekakapāla*) belonging to the *Aindrāgna* offerings at the *Sākamedha* and the *Cāturmāsya* festivals, from the section concerning the twelve-potsherd offering to Indra.

(Bhāṣya 7.1.4.22). Just as in the case of the *Aindrāgna* sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), there is no fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*) even though Agni is associated with it, so too in the *Somāpauṣṇa* cooked rice (*caru*), there is no grinding (*peṣaṇa*) even though Pūṣan is associated with it.

Ke. 3|1|5|14. Regarding the *aindrāgna* [offering]: just as the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*) does not apply to the *aindrāgna* because it has mixed deities, so too the *upāṃśuyāja* cannot be designated by the term *agnīṣomīya*, since it may also belong to Viṣṇu and others.
Some hold that even the modifications (*vikāra*) of the *aindrāgna* occur only prior to the Soma sacrifice.
In reality, however, the time for those modifications is not fixed.
According to the Bhaṭṭa school,
the *aindrāgna* sacrifice is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *aindrasomīya*, because [in the latter] Indra is the enjoyer of the oblation (*sukh*).

Thus, in the case of the offerings to Indra-Viṣṇu, Indra-Pūṣan, Indra-Bṛhaspati, and so forth, they are indeed modifications (*vikṛti*) of the offering to Indra-Agni (*aindrāma*). Bāla. pṛ. 120. The repeated mention of the Āgneya in the injunction "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni is offered at the new moon" is intended to prescribe the offering to Indra-Agni (Bhā. 2.3.14–29). Due to the sequence of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses in the offerings to Indra-Agni and Viśvedevas, there is no restriction of the Viśvedeva procedure (*tantra*) upon the Āgneya;
this is the principle of the Āgneya sacrifice.
12.2.15.36–37. Regarding the mantra for consuming the Soma dedicated to Indra and Agni in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice:
it should apply to the offering to Indra and Agni because of the presence of its indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Commentary: This being the case, the matter is now considered.
There is a Soma offering for Indra and Agni there, according to the injunction: "He draws the Aindrāma cup.

Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the consumption [of the Soma] accompanied by a mantra, or is it without a mantra? What is the prima facie view? It should be with a mantra in the case of the Aindrāma.
For one whose deity is Indra-Agni, there is no Indra [as a separate recipient];
yet it is possible to designate that [soma] as "drunk by Indra" (indrapīta).
For that which has been drunk by Indra without any intervening [deity] is what is called "drunk by Indra."
Of that [Soma], the portion for Indra and Agni was drunk by Indra;
therefore, there is consumption accompanied by a mantra.

Or rather—[this section] is intended to state its pervasiveness, having first raised as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) the absence of mantras on the grounds that the application of modified mantras is appropriate when consuming Soma dedicated to Indra in conjunction with another deity, since that [absence of mantras] applies to all [Soma] not dedicated to Indra.

(Su. Pṛ. 1199. Now, where Indra is the deity accompanied by another, there arises a doubt: does the designation "drunk by Indra" apply there or not? We say that it does apply. Why? Because Indra’s status as a deity is not described by virtue of his having drunk [the soma]; rather, he is designated by name because of his connection with that [act of drinking].
Thus, even when [the deity] is incapable [of drinking], the designation is established.

For in the case of *āgneya*, the sacrificer is mentioned as a qualifier; and since that [term] is taken by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) as referring to something independent of anything else, it does not convey something dependent. Here, however, in the term *indrapīta*, the operation of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is the qualifier.
And when both [portions] are being conceived together, each is distinguished by some specific part.
Whichever has whatever function, it is perceived as the drinker thereof.

(Since the *bhāṣya* passage "for that which has another part" is disconnected from the preceding *bhāṣya*, considering it to be displaced, he first explains the *bhāṣya* passage "of that, in the case of Indra-Agni": Therefore, regarding the offering to Indra-Agni, it can be said that in the *pīvo-vṛdhī* [verse], one half is drunk by Indra and one half is drunk by Agni.

(The commentary *yasya hi*, which was previously set aside, is now explained: Nor is Indra’s drinking [of the Soma] direct in the case of what is currently present; rather, the designation is made by way of the portions offered into the fire.
Furthermore, there is no fixed measure for that [offering], such that one could be designated as having "drunk this much.
Therefore, since the specific qualification is established, the consumption is accompanied by the mantra.
Or [it may be] in one [vessel], like the separation from another deity.
Commentary: It is not drunk by Indra through another part; nor does it become drunk by him merely because it is drunk by a part of Indra.
Therefore, this is a technical term (*lakṣaṇaśabda*) meaning "drunk by him. It refers to that which has been intended with reference to Indra—that of which Indra is the deity.

And just as there is no connection for a word that requires a complement with a second [word] such as *tat*, so too a compound such as *indrapīta* is not possible for that which still requires a complement.

As it has been said: "Or rather, there is a fixed rule because of the connection with the purpose" (3.1.15.27). An objection is raised: "But surely this point was already established by that [previous] section; for what purpose is it stated again?
It is replied:
Whatever has been deliberated there is already established; how then can it be deliberated upon again? [The objection is: "There is no connection with a deity for that which is expectant.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that here there is no connection with a deity at all. The final view (*siddhānta*) is that here there is a connection with mere drinking; where it is drunk by two, there the connection with the deity is through one of them.
Therefore, there is a redundancy.
Or rather—true, if the deity’s act of drinking were the qualification here for being "clear," then even the offering to Indra-Agni would be included;
however, for us, the deity does not drink.

What then? It is employed solely as the object of a conceptual resolution (*saṃkalpa*). Furthermore, in a mixed conceptual resolution, the designation of either one [of the two] is not possible, because a compound does not apply to dependent terms when they possess such a [mixed] nature.

Therefore, just as in the case of the fourfold division of the *āgneya* [cake], because the scope here is exclusively the deity Indra, a designation as belonging to both deities is impossible; thus, there is an exclusion of the mantra.
By this very point, the qualification is not redundant.

As for what the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) thinks—that "deity-hood is not the qualification here; rather, it is the state of being a vessel involved in the preparation, and that exists in each [portion] individually"—the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) counters that, since the primary sense of "being a vessel" is impossible, it is the deity itself that is indicated by this term (and not the state of being a vessel).

Even though the primary status of being a "vessel" (pātratva) might belong to the deity, nevertheless, it is impossible to say that the substance has been drunk by [the deity]. For that Soma which has already been drunk is not designated in this manner; nor does its being drunk by Indra constitute its being "drunk by Indra. Indeed, it is the Soma residing in the cup (*camasa*) that is designated as being "pleasing to Indra," and that [residing in the cup] is not what was drunk by Indra.
Because it has become the object of the oblation, there is the designation "drunk by Indra" (indrapīta).
Therefore, since the quality that must necessarily be distinguished is expressed, each [portion] intended for Indra is "drunk by Indra.
Consequently, it follows that the deity itself is the defining characteristic (upalakṣaṇa).

Furthermore, it is not possible to figuratively attribute the state of having been drunk (*pītatva*) to that which has entered the *soma* offered into the fire, because the designation is justified by the intention (*saṃkalpa*) which possesses the nature of an initial undertaking.

For even when only one part is being offered, this entire substance, being renounced for the sake of the deity, accomplishes the sacrifice; therefore, just as in the case of the root *nir-vap*, the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is precisely what is meant here by the root *pā* (to drink).
Consequently, because it is the means for the Indra-sacrifice, and by virtue of the force of the cognition "drunk by Indra," there is the exclusion of the [other] mantra.
Śabara: "Therefore, there should be a mantra for the consumption [of the soma] in offerings to Indra-Agni and others.
This would indeed be so if there were drinking; however, it will be stated that such drinking does not exist.
Just as in the case of the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*), there is an absence of a mantra in offerings to Indra-Agni and others."

Soma: The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is that the mantra should apply even to the *aindrāma* [offering], because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is present there as well. Viśvarūpa: "Should the consumption of the *aindrāma* and other offerings be accompanied by a mantra or without a mantra? Since the quality of being 'drunk by Indra' (*aindrapītatva*) is possible in the case of the *aindrāma*, it should be accompanied by the mantra."
Drinking is not appropriate for one who is bodiless, but giving is mixed [in nature]. This mantra, however, applies to the mixed [act]; this [other act] is without a mantra.
Bhaṭṭa: Such being the case, there is further deliberation.

Even in the case of the *aindrāgna* [offering], when there is repetition, the consumption is accompanied by the mantra "of that which was drunk by Indra" (*indrapītasya*). Although the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) occurs through the functions of depositing (*nyāsa*) and reciting (*japya*), the drinking—or rather, the acceptance indicated by the word "drunk" (*pīta*)—occurs individually. Therefore, it can be designated according to its specific occurrence, as in the expression "the mother of Ḍiṣṭha. Since the relinquishment pertains to the entire collection of what has been offered and what is being offered, whereas the consumption pertains only to the portion of the offering currently being consumed, there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the state of having been relinquished by the word "drunk."

Therefore, since it does not fall within the scope of the fourth *karaṇādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the instruments of action), its consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) must also be accompanied by a mantra.

This being the position reached, [we reply]: It is true that the word "drunk" (*pīta*) indicates acceptance (*svīkāra*), because drinking is prohibited in the ninth book [of the Jaiminīya-sūtras], and because, according to your own reasoning, it is impossible to indicate "relinquishment" (*tyāga*).

However, as for acceptance—which is to be inferred from the act of touching the feet of the gods and others—it must be inferred as qualified by the fact of having been offered (*hutatva*); thus, the indication [by the word "drunk"] is appropriate.

Nevertheless, because it is more parsimonious to assume that [the term] refers only to that which subsists collectively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), and because there is no evidence for its subsisting in each individual part, it is established that the fourth vessel (*caturtha-karaṇa*) is the object; thus, its consumption is not accompanied by a mantra.
Maṇḍana says: "That which is drunk by Indra is not desired by Indra. Śaṅkara says: "The [cup] belonging to Indra is not [drunk] by me as one who has drunk of Indra's [portion]."

In the discussions concerning the fourth case-ending, the "drunk by Indra" (*indrapīta*), the entry of *Pūṣan*, and the portions (*bhāga*), there is no capacity for terms such as *āgneya* (dedicated to Agni) to denote sacrifices like the *aindrāgnīṣomīya* (dedicated to Indra-Agni-Soma) which have deities other than Agni alone; thus, they are not included.
The modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as those dedicated to Indra-Agni and others, being designated by their own names, are to be performed on either the full moon or the new moon day.
"Because of the statement, 'He who [performs] with an *iṣṭi* or an animal sacrifice'...

(Bhāṣya 5.4.7.24). The optional rites (*kāmyāni karmāṇi*) dedicated to Indra and others are prescribed; in that very same order, those [rites] belonging to those respective deities, which are designated as optional and provided with *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses, are applied respectively to those very same optional *iṣṭis*.
However, the indicative marks (*liṅga*) do not apply solely to the ritual action of that very [deity] by bypassing the sequence [of the text].
Regarding the *aindrābārhaspatya* rite among the *aindrāma* and others... [1322]... in the *aindrābārhaspatya* ritual.

According to the astrologers Dhūrta, Svāmī, and others, following the performance of the *prakṛti* (archetype) rites on the day of the *āvartana* and the preceding *saṃdhi*, the performance of the *vikṛti* (ectype) rites occurs on that very same day (*saṃcidina*). This is because terms such as "Paurṇamāsī" denote the specific moment of the conjunction (*parvan*) of the moon. As stated in the Gobhila Sūtra: "That which is the greatest distance between the sun and the moon is the Paurṇamāsī; that which is the closest proximity is the Amāvāsyā."

And therefore, since the terms *paurṇamāsī* (full moon) and *amāvāsyā* (new moon) denote only a day-and-night delimited by proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*) or distance (*viprakarṣa*), and since that [delimitation] occurs on the second day during the two *pūrvāhṇas*, the performance of the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice) takes place precisely then. Furthermore, that cannot be before the *prakṛti* (archetypal sacrifice), because, as the *prakṛti* has a perceptible time (*dṛṣṭakāla*), it would follow that its requirements are already fulfilled through *prasaṅga* (incidental benefit) in the *vikṛti*. Hence, it is said that, having no other recourse, one must simply accept the morning time (*prātaḥkāla*).

In this regard, based on the explanatory passage (arthavāda) beginning with, "The nights of the half-month of King Soma were the courtesans; he did not approach them on the new moon day or the full moon day," and according to what is well-known even among commoners through the *Jyotiṣa* and other sciences regarding the lunar days (*tithi*) such as the full moon,
there is the principle of Indra (the *aindrīnyāya*).
The nature of the *aindrī* principle is explained as follows: "This *aindrī* [verse] should belong to the Gārhapatya fire.
Whether it refers to the primary Indra or to Indra in a secondary sense, let it apply to the primary one, as before.
In one case, there is a secondary (gauṇa) application because the mantra itself is a restatement;
therefore, in the act of worshiping [the Gārhapatya fire], the mantra is enjoined by direct Vedic statement (śruti).

Bhaṭṭa: However, where there exists a statement that indicates the intention toward a secondary meaning—such as "With the mantra *na kadā cana starīrasi*, she worships the Gārhapatya"—there the application is indeed to the Gārhapatya fire in its secondary sense.

Now, since the opening statement "Aindrā" (belonging to Indra) is sustained by the primary force of the *taddhita* suffix, the secondary accusative case (*dvitīyā*) must, in accordance with that, be understood through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as denoting the counter-correlative [of the action], namely, "standing near the Gārhapatya fire.

Thus, the mantra—which primarily expresses the subordinate element—possesses the capacity to reveal Indra either through secondary indication (*gauṇī*) based on similarity to the means of sacrifice, or through connection with the householder (*gṛhapati*).

Alternatively, let it be that due to its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the fire itself is the object (*karman*) with respect to the act of standing near denoted by the verbal root; however, it is not the object with respect to the expression accomplished by the mantra, because that [expression] is not directly stated by the word.
And there is no "dependence on mantras" (*upānamantrakaraṇa*).
Regarding desirable actions such as the *Citrā* sacrifice, their fruit is experienced in this life (*aihika*) provided there is no obstruction.
In that regard, [the soul is] common to all, because there is no distinction.
Section 2. Commentary: Or rather, it is thus.
The performance of optional rites (*kāmyāni karmāṇi*) consists of bringing about specific results, as in:

"One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya"; "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni"; "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *Citrayā* [Iṣṭi]"; and "One desiring a village should offer the *Sāṃkramaṇī* oblation to the Viśvedevas.
Thus it is said.
Regarding these, there is a doubt:
are the objects of desire (kāmāḥ) here in this world, or in the world beyond? What is the prima facie position?
In that case, the objects of desire (kāmāḥ) exist in that other world, because there is no distinction [between them and those in this world];
just as heaven [is not distinct from the earthly realm], so too are these [objects of desire].
For the fruit, such as cattle and the like, is not perceived immediately after the ritual action has been completed.
And that which is perceived immediately after something is understood to arise from that [preceding thing].
For example, at whatever time there is kneading, it is easy to obtain the resulting product at that same time.
And as for that which is perceived at a different time, its cause is likewise directly perceptible as being something else entirely.
However, there is no reason whatsoever for the assumption of a body other than the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

Therefore, it should be understood that in this case, the fruit—consisting of the acquisition of sense organs and so forth, which is capable of being connected with the state of an animal—is produced from the ritual action whose fruit is the animal itself.
For that [scripture] demonstrates it thus:
Kaikaya, intending to perform a sacrifice, said to Dālbhya Suvāca:
"Perform for me this sacrifice which is capable of establishing sovereignty over a kingdom.
He replied:

"O gentle one, the handing over of a kingdom is certainly not the fruit [of Vedic study]; rather, sacrifices are undertaken for the sake of that [specific] desire," thus [the text] shows that they have fruits in another birth.
Therefore, optional rites have fruits in another birth;
or else, there is the attainment of yoga, because of the suitability of the purpose.
Commentary: Herein alone is the accomplishment of their yoga;
its production through [the present] birth is not possible.
It is not understood from this that "he who desires cattle should perform it by means of this sacrifice," because it is not possible in this life.
As for the claim that "it is not perceived immediately thereafter," that is not so; it is not apprehended through perception or inference,
but its comprehension occurs through verbal testimony.
As for the claim that there is another cause at a later time, this is not a fault;
there will be both that [other cause] and this one as well.
And regarding the statement, "For the sake of such-and-such a desire sacrifices are undertaken," it is said in response to this:
Such is the opinion of this seer:
"In this world, I do not cause you to sacrifice with that which has its fruit here; rather, I shall cause you to sacrifice with that which has its fruit in the next world.
Therefore, this [objection] is refuted.
Ḍa—(He states the established conclusion: There is no fixed rule that the attainment of sons, cattle, and so forth occurs either in this world or in the next.
Why? Because the means for those things desired, such as sons and the like, is prescribed [in scripture].
And when the means has been performed, the end must necessarily follow.
In that regard, sometimes unwholesome karma was performed in a previous birth, and that is what must be experienced.

Therefore, what was done in a previous birth is experienced [in this one]. In that case, if the demerit (*adharma*) committed in another life is powerful, then the fruit [will arise] in this very birth (due to the absence of any obstacle).
If, however, [the result] has not yet been exhausted, then the means for establishing that connection is postponed.
There is indeed an injunctive word stating "there will be a fruit," but there is no evidence whatsoever for its immediate succession; therefore, there is no fixed rule.
As for heaven, it occurs only in another birth.
For that is unsurpassed bliss and conforms to one's karma; thus, it cannot be experienced in this present life,
since in this world a person experiences pleasure and pain moment by moment.
And it has been stated that mere pleasure is not the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Furthermore, even for a mere living being, there is very slight pleasure arising from such things as scratching;
yet a mere living being does not perform the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Therefore, [heaven] is inherent [to the self] because it is common to all living beings.
However, a different location (distinct from the place of action) is postulated because it would otherwise be impossible for it to be experienced as unsurpassed bliss.
And that [change of location] is not possible for the immortal person; therefore, heaven occurs only in another birth.
Śā— "Receiving gifts and so forth are seen as causes for [rebirth as] cattle and the like;
[the sacrifice of] Citrā and the like are causes for other [results].
Because they initiate the body, Citrā and the like possess the nature of being causes for the fruit."
Thus, [the opponent argues that] animals and the like belong solely to the world beyond.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"The very fact that the animal and so forth are things to be accomplished (sādhya) is what is expressed by the word."
The restrictive term "either there or here" does not exist; rather,
it is the fact that the fruits have the commencement of a body as their primary manifestation that serves as the proof for their ripening (*vipāka*).

Those karmas for which the falling away from the previous body has already occurred are experienced here as "prior" (prāgbhāsa); other [karmas] are experienced in another existence. Destiny (daiva) and human effort (puruṣakāra) are the two causes, beginning with the latter.
Therefore, this [is the case].

12. Soma: Here, in the Bhāṣya, after explaining the two sūtras—"tatra sarvair aviśeṣāt" and "yogasiddhir vārthasya yogatvāt"—both in terms of simultaneity and non-simultaneity, they are further explained as referring to the present and future lives by means of the words "evaṃ vā" and so forth. In that context, at the beginning of another exposition (varṇaka), the author of the work follows the Bhāṣya exactly with the words "evaṃ vā."
The state of being both pertaining to this world and the next (*aihikāmuṣmikatva*) is written everywhere by the author of the *Śāstradīpikā* (*Oṣadhinā*).

However, here, due to a deliberate variation, it should be understood that the sūtra of the established conclusion (*siddhāntasūtra*), “Or there is the perfection of yoga (*yogasiddhir vā*),” has been written.
Regarding the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) and others:

having stated that they serve the purpose of all fruits by way of alternation (*paryāyeṇa*), we now consider, as a relevant consequence (*prasaṅgāt*), whether those fruits belong to this life (*aihika*) or the next life (*āmuṣmika*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: "In this case too, there would be the attainment of the connection with these fruits, and not [only] in the next life, because it is not understood that the fruit (*artha*) is necessarily connected to arising in another birth."
[Objection: "In the case of the *citrayā* sacrifice, would the animals necessarily belong to that very same person, or not?
[Response: The first position [is correct], because it is equivalent to heaven (*svarga*) and because it produces a body."
"In the case of the Citrā sacrifice, however, no restriction is heard in scripture, nor can one be inferred;
for when the causal connection is not obstructed by the activity of the person and other factors, the result would follow.
No restriction is heard regarding the production of a body through the Citrā."

12. Commentary: Or rather, heaven is indeed exclusively pertaining to the next world, as it is said: "That pleasure which is unmixed with suffering, not immediately swallowed up by it, and brought about by desire—that is the locus of the term 'heaven'."

This is because that [result], understood from the completion of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) as consisting of unsurpassed joy, is connected with birth; furthermore, it is well known from mantras, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth, that it is to be experienced in a specific location.
On the other hand, cattle, sons, and the like pertain both to this world and the next, and not exclusively to the next world alone.
Even in those cases, they belong to the next world only when there exists demerit (*durita*) that obstructs their enjoyment.
In the absence of that [result], there is indeed only a result pertaining to this life (*aihikatva*).

Nor is there any restrictive factor to suggest that actions achieve their results solely through the medium of generating a body, which would necessitate their being exclusively otherworldly (*āmuṣmikatva*).

Nor do these actions have an exclusively worldly result, for even when sons, cattle, sovereignty, and so forth exist in this birth—or even when one possesses the capacity for them—the desire "may I have those in another birth" is difficult to deny.
Therefore, even for those who are about to die, the Citrā sacrifice must indeed be performed for the sake of the afterlife.
However, where there is desire for results such as [supernatural] vision that pertain only to this world, there it possesses exclusively a worldly character.
Or, let it be granted that even for vision and the like, if such a desire exists, it possesses a dual nature.

However, the state of having results pertaining solely to this world (*kevalaihikatva*) is to be understood in the case of the purity of the son and so forth, as well as in the case of the *āhavanīya* fire and other such rites.
(Section 9, Variant 2). Maṇḍana: "The fruit [is obtained] either here or there.
(12) Śaṅkara: "[The fruit] is even that of the next world, such as cattle and so forth."
12. O. One desiring vigor (*ojas*) should cause [the sacrificer] to perform the *triṇava* *atirātra* sacrifice.
Bhā.

Regarding the principle of warp and woof (*otaprotanyāya*): this has been explained in detail in the commentary on the verse, “In me all this is woven, like clusters of gems upon a thread” (Bhagavad Gītā 7.7).
[The word] *sāhyī* [is used]. 916. Rice (*odana*) exists even without grinding.
One may certainly grind it if desired; however, it might become flour (*piṣṭaka*), or gruel (*yavāgu*), or parched grain (*khalati* / *khala*).
Bhāṣya 10.1.1250: "Rice in five bowls" (*pañcaśarāva odanaḥ*); this is the expiation even when one of the two milch cows is lost at the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*).

6|4|6|22–23. Regarding the statement "Or *odana*, because it is that which has been employed" (10|1|10|44), since it is being established in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the word *caru* denotes *odana*— because the word *odana* is a specific term for that which is cooked with rice as its material and is consecrated by the *sāvitṛ* mantra, and because the word *caru* specifically denotes that which is characterized by having rice as its material and ends with the *sāvitṛ* consecration— the sūtra of the tenth book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras], however, is intended to establish the pervasion of the word *caru* as referring to the cooking vessel (*sthālī*).

In the expression "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), either the capacity for the object (*karmaśakti*) being expressed, or the operation of the prompted agent (*prayojyavyāpāra*) which is implied, or simply the operation of the prompted agent alone—which may itself imply the operation of the prompter—is intended to be signified. (This is [an example] extracted from the Vārttika.)
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 2.1.1.1, pp.
377–378: In the *saurya* sacrifice, the original oblation (*prākṛtahaviḥ*) is set aside by the rice (*odana*), which is denoted by the word *caru*.

(Bhāṣya 10.1.10.36–46). This is because, even when a word is dependent [on another], we observe the indication of distinct application, usage, and sequence in such cases as "One desiring rice should cook" and "One should fetch firewood," and so forth.

Thus, at the beginning of creation, the Blessed One, having created the world of moving and non-moving beings as well as dharma and adharma, established the relationship between each specific word and its respective object through conventional usage; then, having composed the Vedas intended to convey dharma and adharma, he taught them to Hiraṇyagarbha and others, who in turn taught them to others—in this manner, there is a continuous tradition of understanding.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: since the absence of comprehension of the meaning upon the first hearing is satisfactorily explained by its being rooted in the knowledge of an eternal relationship, there is no evidence for postulating such a [new] meaning. Furthermore, because it is established by experience that the world is uniform from beginning to end, there is no destruction at the start of a creation; and since even the Mantras, Arthavādas, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas depend upon human relationships, they are of human origin—just like any other composed work—and thus lack the capacity for authority regarding supersensuous matters. Consequently, the existence of a Creator (*sadgati*) established by such non-authoritative sources is utterly remote.
Therefore, it is not possible for the relationship between words and their meanings to be established at the time of creation and so forth.

In the case of an innate [term], its origin is by way of its own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*). Even in the absence of the word "cow," when words such as *dhenu* (milch cow) are heard—which frequently denote qualities like being a milch cow—there would be a sublation (*bādha*) of the substance obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal transfer rule), which is a modification of the goat-substance. This is because it is improper to resort to a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for words like *dhenu* that are directly heard in the scripture, since they are not something produced [by the ritual].
Therefore, in this context, the offering (*ālambha*) is of cows alone, characterized by qualities such as being milch cows, and not of goats.
The giving of milk preceded by the spreading [of grass] is *dhāna*. Ke.:

It is possible to understand "intrinsic connection" (*autpattikatva*) only in the case of an object already known through another means of valid cognition; however, in this case, intrinsic connection cannot be understood as a linguistic usage preceded by the comprehension of the word.

*Bṛhatī*, p. 255. The maxim of the primacy of the meaning of the suffix as the general rule (*autsargika-pratyayārtha-prādhānya-nyāya*): Even when the agent is subordinate, since the primacy of that which constitutes the meaning of the suffix—namely, the action (*bhāva*)—is not relinquished, the maxim of the primacy of the agent would not be set aside even in cases where the agent is intended to be primary. However, if the agent were the very meaning of the suffix, then because the primacy of the agent itself would not be relinquished, the maxim of the general rule would indeed be set aside.
Su. 1372–73: Because of the non-sublation of the primacy of *bhāvanā*—which constitutes the meaning of the suffix—by virtue of adopting the general rule that the meaning of the suffix is primary.

The *Audamedhi-nyāya*. 1336. The *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa*.
The Principle of Audameghi:

The nature [of the rule] is as follows—one whose father is well-known as Audamegha refers to his own son as "Audameghi," even without explicitly stating that he is not the self (the father). One who has a well-known father [named] Audamegha understands that the person [referred to as Audameghi] is his father, even though he is not explicitly named.

Bhāṣya 3.5.8.26: Regarding the acceptance that the names beginning with *adhyardha* (such as *audameghi*) are based on ritual action (*karmanimittatva*), according to the principle of *Audameghi* (Su.
3.7, p. 27). For the *Chandoga-pravacana* is designated by the term *audgātra*;

since the ritual action is connected to that [designation], and the persons connected to it perform the practice prescribed by the original text, they can be understood as "udgātṛs" according to the principle of *Audameghi*.
But surely this principle was refuted in the discussion on the *avedhya* (the non-piercing)?
It is said [in reply]: "In this case, the term *udgātṛ* is indeed secondary (*gauṇa*), because a primary *udgātṛ* is impossible.

(Vārttika 3.5.8.26). Since in the Draviḍa country the referent of the word *rājan* is understood as being of the nature of a Kṣatriya, the *audamedhi*-principle does not apply; therefore, one should not assume the verbal formulation that "a king is the performer of royal duties" (*rājya-kartā rājā*) based on the presumption (*arthāpatti*) that the word *rājan* would otherwise be inexplicable due to its connection with royal functions.

Su. p. 107: The sentence beginning with "The sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood; the Udumbara is indeed strength" is heard in the context of the modified animal sacrifice, "One desiring cattle should offer a Soma-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifice lasting three months.

Su. p. 71: Even such explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) as "The sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood; the Udumbara is strength; cattle are strength; by means of strength he obtains for him strength and cattle; for the sake of bestowing strength" are authoritative regarding Dharma because they are merely laudatory.
Vi. 1.2.12: A cup made of Udumbara wood is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) at the Ṛtapeya sacrifice.
"He is to be given to a dear Brahmin of the same lineage (*sagotra*).
And he (the gift) supersedes the entire sacrificial fee (*ṛtudakṣiṇā*) [of the model sacrifice].
Bhāṣya 10.3.1.9–18. By virtue of being heard as made of *udumbara* wood, there is the supersession of the original [wood] and so forth in the case of the animal dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan.

[The passage] would be an injunction because it conveys something not previously known (*apūrvatvāt*); for a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) is purposeless. Commentary: Here, those explanatory statements (*arthavādas*) that appear as if they were injunctions (*vidhi*) are the examples.
"The sacrificial post is made of *udumbara* wood; the *udumbara* is strength (*ūrj*); cattle are strength; by means of strength he obtains strength for him, [and] cattle, for the sake of strength."
Is this an injunction (*vidhi*) that must be performed, or is it a mere praise (*stuti*) of that [injunction]?
What, then, is the prima facie position? It should be an injunction because it conveys something not previously known; for a mere statement [of fact] would be purposeless.
In the case of such types of passages, there should be an injunction of a result (*phala-vidhi*).
For a result is indeed understood; thus, it will enjoin a previously unknown matter. Otherwise, it would be a mere statement of praise and would be purposeless.
In that case, the meaning would be exactly the same as what was heard from the Teacher.
Furthermore, the purpose "for the sake of strength" (*ūrjāvaddhe*) is heard [in the text],
yet there is no word whatsoever to indicate that this meaning is commendable.
But praise is understood through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And direct statement (*śruti*) is more authoritative than figurative indication.

Or rather—thus, with respect to those things that oppose meaninglessness, narrative, and so forth (the word "and so forth" including purposelessness and being for the sake of an unseen result), which have these as their opposites and contradictories.
(Su. Pṛ. 67) In the *arthavādas*, those things opposed to injunctions are considered by means of an improper method (*anyāya*).

Why is there doubt? (He sets forth the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] by way of a fourfold uncertainty regarding the doubt: For in the preceding case, because their own literal meaning was not useful, it was accepted that they convey praise through remote indication (*dūralakṣita*). But if that [indication] were blocked, then even praise would be rendered useless.

Furthermore, the injunction (*vidhi*) cannot belong to anything else in any way whatsoever; however, as was stated previously, the incitement (*prarocanā*) may somehow arise even from a portion of the injunction. Moreover, the injunction is the primary element, while the praise (*stuti*) is its subordinate member (*aṅga*).
In that case, it is logical that [the word] should indeed qualify the principal [element],
for the explanatory passage (arthavāda) proceeds only after the injunctive portion (vidhyuddeśa) has been completed;
therein, the components of the productive operation (bhāvanā) converge precisely according to their sequence.

Thinking that the fruit is to be attained specifically through the primary and non-primary [aspects], and so forth, he says "because of its being something not previously known" (*apūrvatvāt*); and in comparison to that, he considers mere praise to be purposeless.

But surely, such an inquiry as to whether this kind of thing is a "rule prescribing a fruit" (*phalavidhi*) or an "explanatory passage" (*arthavāda*) will occur in the fourth book under the sūtra "In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and rituals" (*dravyasaṃskārakarmasu*, 4.1.1); therefore, it should not be introduced here.

If it is argued that the mind [is what is meant] there, then since the meaning has already been conveyed by that, an inquiry should properly be directed to that very point rather than this being called a redundancy. (He refutes this resolution: This is true; however, if another solution can be found by waiting for that time, then we shall seek it there. But if it can be stated right here, then even if it is said now, the fault is slight.

(Though there is no need for repetition, he refutes [the opponent's view] by setting forth four alternative positions: Regarding this, others say that while in the former case there was merely a rejection of an injunction regarding a result, here it is for the sake of meaningfulness;
as he will state there, "It should be an explanatory passage (arthavāda)," that should be understood as being merely a rejection of an injunction.
That is incorrect.

Since, because they are injunctions of results (*phalavidhi*), the possibility of their being purposeless would follow for those [passages] that have deviated [from the status of injunction], the fact that they serve as praise (*stuti*) was established by the very same preceding section (1.2.12); and this has been demonstrated in the case of such expressions as "His face shines" (1.2.15).

Others, however, say: "It is appropriate that [passages] such as 'Wind is indeed the swiftest' are praises; furthermore, just as [passages] such as 'Bestow vigor' are employed because they constitute injunctions of results (*phalavidhi*), so too are the statements of praise despite their apparent contradiction. Thus, let them be injunctions at will, by which the contradiction—arising from the fact that [the result] occurs at a later time—is somehow removed. This is the commencement of this section (*adhikaraṇa*). That too is incorrect.
Moreover, the reason for our acceptance—that there is clearly no contradiction in the Veda—would then be rendered redundant.

However, in the body of the *adhikaraṇa* [concerning the *parṇamaya*], that very same point [is maintained as being non-different from the body of the *parṇamaya-adhikaraṇa*]; furthermore, no contradiction has been resolved by the sūtra "But it is a figurative statement" (*guṇavādastu*, 1.2.10). Moreover, the answer will once again be merely that much.

(Another method may be possible—) therefore, because it is mentioned without distinction in "Or it may be an injunction" (*vidhirvā syāt*, 1.2.19), and because the mention of the hearing of a fruit occurs in the fourth [section].

Others maintain: "In this [context], those [passages] that consist of injunctions regarding substances, qualities, actions, and so forth in their entirety; whereas in that [other context], only those consisting of injunctions regarding results serve as examples.

Accordingly, [the sūtras] "An injunction is sometimes purposeless" (1.2.23), "And its occurrence within a specific context" (24), and "The horse is born from water, the reed grows from water," as well as "That which is burnt," are cited as examples.
Otherwise, if one were to introduce them merely as injunctions of results, that would be entirely inconsistent.

(He refutes: "In this case as well, since that [previous rule] has a specific scope (*viśeṣaviṣayatva*), this [present rule] would concern a matter not yet covered; however, since by this [present rule] there is a general differentiation (*sāmānyato vivecanā*) regarding all objects, it is indeed a mere repetition. (He anticipates another alternative: "For this reason, some cite examples here only for injunctions concerning substances (*dravya*) and so forth, and not for injunctions concerning results (*phala*). Having set aside the example given by the author of the Bhāṣya, another example must be provided."
To this we reply: Why must two distinct topics (*adhikaraṇa*) necessarily be established, such that this specific arrangement of examples is resorted to?

For a topic does not become divided merely because of a difference in examples; otherwise, there would be no repetition even in cases where [the subject matter] remains fixed, as in the case of the distinction between the *lā* affixes and the *audumbara* rule.
Rather, it is the status of being the object of a logical principle (*nyāya*) that constitutes the nature of a topic, and that alone is the reason for its non-repetition.

Even regarding the various types of substances (*dravya*) and so forth, not all have been examined here: some were discussed in the *Tat-siddhi-sūna* (1.4.12–23), some in the *Nītātādhikaraṇa* (3.4.1), others by way of *parakṛti* and *purākalpa* in the sixth book (6.1.12) starting with "And that which they praise" (*yac ca stuvate*); those concerning the unity of purpose (*arthakatvādhikaraṇya*) in the ninth book (9.2.8), and those in the form of injunctions for *jatilagava* and *gavīdhuka* in the tenth book (10.8.4).

(He states two alternative views: Therefore, one should simply say that there is no fault of tautology; or else, the undertaking is repeated because some particular aspect of the very same principle is being refined in this instance.

(One of the four modes has been stated. He states the second: Or rather, as clearly explained in the *Sudhā*, the diversity of subject matter (*viṣaya-nānātva*) should be described in this way: here, by means of the refutation of the view that [passages] similar to injunctions in form are exclusively injunctions, their status as *arthavādas* is established.

As for the renewed commencement [of the discussion] in the fourth [section], its intention in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the injunctions whose fruits are enjoined—such as the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice—is as follows: when there is a requirement for a fruit in an injunction established through an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the application-injunction (*prayogavacana*) provides an alternative possibility; therefore, that [application-injunction] itself is more proximate. Furthermore, for that which already has an established relationship, it is easy to establish merely a specific detail. Otherwise, one would have to postulate both the relationship itself and its mode of assistance (*upakārakatva*). Thus, the prima facie view holds that [the fruit] belongs to the domain of the injunction of the fruit, just like the "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth in the case of the *Rātrisatra*.

Since another purpose can somehow be obtained, it is not logical for a single [passage] to have multiple meanings; therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is indeed an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
By this, the injunctions regarding the *nīcais-tā* (lower tone) and so forth are explained as being [merely] explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
Alternatively, those deliberations are to be understood as having been conducted by first establishing the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa*.
For what indeed would be the remainder (*śeṣa*) of that which is already established by an injunction?

Having deliberated whether it belongs to the sacrifice (*kratu*) or to the person (*puruṣa*), and so forth, the conclusion is reached here through an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Similarly, regarding *parakṛti* and *purākalpa*, it was considered whether [the rule] applies to those of that specific lineage (*gotra*) or to all men.
Thus, the deliberation regarding the ninth and tenth [sections] is concluded by means of the principle of *ūha* (adaptation) and *bādha* (sublation).
However, the discussion concerning their establishment is merely for the purpose of praising their qualities (*guṇavāda*).
(Now he states the third method: Alternatively, where there are various fruits resulting from praise through a distinct injunction of results (*phalavidhi*), that constitutes the example here.
Just as in this very context, there is praise in the statement "The *udumbara* tree is strength; cattle are strength," while the result is expressed by the phrase "May I bestow strength upon myself.

However, where the result or the praise is stated by that much alone, those cases belong to the fourth [category]. (Because of dissatisfaction even with this, he states a fourth type: Alternatively, since two reasons are taught there under the heading "because of being for the sake of another" (4.1.1), and because of the usage based on well-known reasons, those for whom the meaning of "being for the sake of another" is already understood serve as examples, such as: "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood..."
For here, the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood must be enjoined by means of the mention of the *juhū*, because it is incapable of an independent connection with a result.
For everywhere, when a quality is enjoined for the sake of a result— as in the case of the *audumbara* section— it [requires] some [substantive].

It requires a substratum (*āśraya*), and that substratum cannot be obtained through another context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, if in this case the statement "one should bring about the fruit by means of being made of *parṇa*-wood" were to be supplied, then when the requirement arises—"by what [substratum] is it supported? (the analysis of the compound being *kasyāśritena*)—what could possibly be connected? If one says "the *juhū* ladle," no; for that would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
That [quality] also does not acquire its status as an action prior [to the sentence], nor does it become independent of expectation;
furthermore, there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its connection with an action.

Therefore, since the [intended] syntactical construction cannot be maintained, one must abandon this interpretation and resort to the other: "One should effect the *juhū* ladle by means of being made of *parṇa* wood."

In that context, regarding the statement "he offers with the *juhū*," since its purpose is established by the context (*prakaraṇa*), there exists an expectancy for the specific material prescribed for that [sacrificial ladle]. As soon as the class-property of being made of *parṇa*-wood is brought forward, because the [ladle] would otherwise remain without a known purpose, one accepts that [property] which was previously unknown.
Consequently, once that expectancy has been satisfied, there is no ground for assuming a result within that very sentence; thus, its status as an *arthavāda* is logical.

Here, however, the quality of being made of *udumbara* wood, as heard in the modified context (in the passage: "one should sacrifice a three-year-old [animal] dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan"), is cited as the example.
Furthermore, its subservience to another (pārārthya) is not established, such that it could become the subject matter of the fourth section [of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtras].
Why? Because here, one cannot enjoin a genus when the form has not yet been established.

If it were so, then—since the requirement for the form would necessarily have been fulfilled by the already established auxiliaries such as the "being" (bhūta) and so forth—the [genus] would have no further expectancy.
Therefore, since that [subordinate] arises for the sake of that [principal], how could there be an injunction for it? Consequently, the injunction applies to the fruit.

Furthermore, as for the requirement of a substratum (*āśraya*), that too is set aside by the inclusion of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) obtained through the transfer-rule (*atideśa*) from the archetypal rite (*prakṛti-karman*); thus, it remains unestablished.

Therefore, because it would necessarily result in a connection with the fruit prior to its being subordinate to another, this must be refuted by another line of reasoning; hence, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is commenced.

Among the four methods for avoiding redundancy that have been stated, he expresses his preference for the first principle presented—namely, "in some cases, something is made known by something else"—as follows: This is the preferred view; both the sentence concerning the *audumbara* wood and the sentence concerning the *juhū* ladle serve as examples.
How so? Because there is no redundancy due to the consideration of different aspects of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).
For the relationship between the end to be accomplished and the means is possible only when both are presented as being mutually suitable, and not otherwise.

In that context, having disregarded or, alternatively, having accepted the investigation into the means of accomplishment (*sādhanasādhana*), there was an investigation into the constituent part alone: "Can such a word denoting desire (*kāmaśabda*), which is devoid of a specific substance and expresses a connection with a present result, cause one to understand [the injunction] as being fruitful, or not?
Here, however, taking up the objective constituent (*sādhyāṃśa*)—or, alternatively, having accepted it—the *Audumbara* section [is introduced].

An investigation into the components of the means alone: "Are substance, quality, and action presented as a means toward something by such [an injunction] that is devoid of an inquiry into the injunction itself? Or not?
Whatever is presented in its own nature becomes connected with that which is introduced by another word, provided it stands in need of a specific counter-correlative (*pratiyogi*).

In that context, when it is determined that "this is the end to be accomplished" (*sādhya*), the remaining element is understood as the "means" (*sādhana*) by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*); and likewise, by the application of the means. Thus, both components must be defined according to their essential nature.

Thus, when the constituent part of the means (*sādhanāṃśa*) is being examined here, whatever contact there is with the constituent part of the result (*phalāṃśa*) should be understood as occurring by way of a causal connection (*hetutva*) on account of the discussion of accomplishment (*siddhi*) in the fourth [chapter].
Likewise, where there is a reflection upon the constituent part of the means, that is established here; and where it occurs later, there is no redundancy.

Now, if this is the case, one might object that since this is an investigation into the location of the injunction (*vidhideśa*), it does not connect with the section concerning explanatory passages (*arthavādādhikaraṇa*).
This is not a fault, because it determines the meaning in its entirety.
For if this [statement] were understood from the preceding [text] as something being enjoined, then it would not be an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise).
But if it is for the purpose of praise, then it is indeed an *arthavāda*.

In this regard, the intention of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: whatever is uttered in the proximity of the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*), by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), becomes a means (*sādhana*) even if it is not explicitly stated in that specific form; just as the word "by means of sacrifice" (*yāgena*) when uttered connects [with the action], so too does the word "by means of the *audumbara* wood" (*audumbareṇa*).

In that case, what would the injunction (*vidhi*) do? It would impel the person to act; yet since that person is already impelled solely for the sake of the result, what is the use of an injunction? Alternatively, this [injunction] merely effects the connection with the result for that which has been enjoined by the *prayogavacana* (the statement of performance), or else the fifth mood (*leṭ*) will enjoin it, or it is as already stated: that it is a portion of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

Therefore, because the word "for the sake of" (*tādarthya-caturthī*) in the phrase "bestow vigor" (*ūrjam vadhāi*) already expresses the purpose, and because the result is even more clearly indicated by the word "desiring such" (*evamkāma*), it must be understood that the rule for the *audumbara* wood applies to that [result], rather than being a prescription of the result itself; for the prescription of a result is prohibited in the section concerning the nature of action (*bhāvādhikaraṇa*).
The statement "the *udumbara* is vigor" (*ūrjo 'dumbaraḥ*) is a eulogy (*stuti*).
Thus, there is no contradiction.
Therefore, since a primary injunction is possible, praise should not be understood through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā);
this is the point of the phrase "as in the world."

Commentary: If you think that praise is purposeless and is not understood through the words themselves, then let your honors consider common worldly sentences. For example: "This cow belonging to Devadatta should be purchased; for she yields much milk, has healthy offspring, and her progeny does not perish."
When it is said, "It should be purchased," people proceed [to buy]; nevertheless, because of the mention of its qualities, the buyers proceed even more so.
And the mention of qualities, such as "yielding much milk," is understood.
The same will be the case in the Veda as well.
Or rather— firstly, in the world, persons who act with deliberation do not employ even a small measure of what is to be enjoined.

And in that context, when it is prescribed that "she is to be bought," the praise [of her] by means of qualities such as "having much milk" is resorted to as the cause for a specific inclination toward action.
Furthermore, milk and the like are not injunctions regarding results, because they are objects of direct perception;
therefore, they constitute praise.
The same applies to the Veda as well.
"And because [the primary sense] is impossible according to the Vedic text, the adoption of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is not a fault.
No, because of its being prior.
The Commentary says: "This is not so."
In the world, things such as "abounding in milk" are said to refer to objects already previously known;
for these, mere cognition is not the purpose.
Therefore, praise is understood [from the statement].
People would not have faith in a doctrine that has not been previously known, just as they do not with the words of others;

rather, they are inspired precisely because it is already known. Furthermore, among Vedic matters, if one is not inspired by the injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*), one will certainly not be inspired by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
For at that time, doubt would have arisen regarding the word expressing an injunction;
yet, once one has been incited by the word of the injunction, what further purpose is served by the words of the explanatory passage (arthavāda)?
Moreover, there is a clear lack of correspondence in the Veda: the statement "bestow vigor" (*ūrjam avadadhai*) is an unfamiliar expression.
Furthermore, the causal relationship expressed in "The Udumbara tree is strength" is unestablished.

Because the Udumbara is strength, therefore the sacrificial post (yūpa) should be made of that; since the statement "the Udumbara is strength" is an untrue assertion, one might assume that there is something else equally untrue about it.
Or rather—this is not a valid example, because praise depends upon the corroboration of other means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
In the world, [people] would accept it because it is possible for such a thing to occur; however, in the Veda, they would not have faith because it would be a claim regarding something unknown.
Alternatively, if someone were to speak of something unknown even in the world, then people would certainly not have faith.
"As from a repetition" means as from a different location and so forth.
Alternatively, if it were a figurative comparison (*arthopamā*), then one would have faith in a statement whose meaning has already been understood, but not in a doctrine that is unknown.
Furthermore, these things such as "abounding in milk" do not become attractive merely by being stated; rather, it is precisely because they are known [to be true] that they are so.
In the case of the Veda, however, one who has developed doubt regarding an injunction due to the untruthfulness of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) does not proceed to act upon it.

Alternatively, he who, having bypassed the injunction (*vidhi*), seeks out the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) finds no rest in a new injunction. If there is no confidence in that [injunction]—where there is no confidence in the *codanā*—how can there be conviction in the *arthavāda*?
Thus it is said.
"Moreover, there is clearly a lack of correspondence in the Veda.
This praise is made by means of present, vigorous wealth, yet that [wealth] does not exist; thus, this would be like the mention of abundant milk where none exists.
Furthermore, the nature of food in the *udumbara* tree is unestablished as a property of the subject.

If it is argued that [the passage] is a cause because of its well-known logical concomitance (*anvaya*), such a "well-known" status does not exist either in common worldly usage or in the Veda—that "whatever is food is a sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) is nowhere established.
Therefore, since there is no corroboration, it is better that it be a mere injunction; what is the use of praise that depends upon corroboration?
To this, it has been said that it functions as a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).
The Commentary states: "The highest [status] is that of being supplementary to the denotative [word]," according to the sūtra *vidhinā tvekavākyatvāt* (JS 1.2.7).
Now, one might object: "In this case, it is understood as a statement of the fruit (*phala*), not as praise (*stuti*)."
If it were a statement of a result, it would pertain to the sacrificial post made of Udumbara wood; however, since no Udumbara post has been prescribed elsewhere,
a statement of a result in that context would be entirely purposeless.

If it is argued that there is no word consisting of praise, [we reply: although the second meaning called "praise" is not directly expressed here as having a fruit—since it would otherwise be purposeless—it is nevertheless understood. Even if it is apprehended through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it certainly possesses meaningfulness.

For even figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is worldly. But was it not said that there is no correspondence in the Veda, as in the case of "the *udumbara* tree is straight"? We reply: it is for the sake of praise (*prarocanā*) by means of a figurative description (*guṇavāda*).
Because it is used in a figurative sense, it is consistent with reality.
What is to be established? Just as food is a means for pleasure, so too is this [the Soma].
It is expressed by the word "means of pleasure"—a term denoting praise—in order to praise that which is endowed with the power to produce pleasure.
For that [the Udumbara tree] can indeed be called "strength" (*ūrj*) on account of its connection with the fruit of strength;

thus, the passage beginning with "The Udumbara is strength" forms a single syntactical unit with the words "is fit for eating strength," being an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*), not a disconnected eulogy.
Indeed, when it is simply stated that "the Udumbara is food," no quality of excellence is understood by a person.

But the phrase "for the sake of bestowing vigor" serves as an incitement (prarocanā). Thus, it is consistent that this constitutes the justification for that [injunction]. Therefore, the entire passage expresses either the fruit or the incitement.
In that case, even if there were an indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, it would still be understood all the more as being merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

How much more so, then, in the case of a statement in the present tense, which exists solely for the purpose of establishing an injunction? Furthermore, since the benefit of assisting the sacrifice is obtainable through the context (*prakaraṇa*), why should we assume a fruit from something that lacks expressive power?
If it is argued that [the direct statement] is sublated by the context (*prakaraṇa*), we say no, because there is no contradiction.
For if the direct statement and the context were to coincide in a single part, then indeed there would be sublation.

But here, the context takes up the injunction regarding the *audumbara* wood, and that injunction also takes up the incitement (*prarocanā*) provided by the words "The *udumbara* is strength" and so forth.
In that case, the mention of the *udumbara* wood as qualified by that [result] would contradict the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Therefore, since there is no mention of a result, the possibility of its inclusion through the context and other means must not be bypassed.

Furthermore, since the incitement (*prarocanā*) is established from the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), it will not be imagined as an independent explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) merely because of its isolated location.
For elsewhere, even an injunction might lead one to imagine such a thing; but here, since the injunction itself is poorly established, what will it accomplish by means of persuasion?
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which has already served the purpose of praise to function again toward a result, as is the case with [the establishment of] the *pratiṣṭhā* and so forth.
For in the case of the *rātrisatra* sacrifices, because they have no other purpose, even a cumbersome assumption is resorted to.
But here, it has been stated that the accomplishment of the purpose exists by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Furthermore, because the specific class [of wood] is required by its very suitability, it is well known that it does not exist for the sake of the fruit [of the sacrifice].
Moreover, the word "sacrificial post" (yūpa) refers only to that which is brought forward as the substratum for the ritual action;
therefore, since its subservience to another purpose is established, these are merely explanatory passages (arthavāda).
As for the claim that the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), having no further expectancy, perceives the genus (*jāti*), this will be a case of sublation (*bādha*) similar to the *śara* grass;
moreover, there is no such mode of non-existence,
since even in the optional (*kāmya*) context, that [genus] is admitted.

However, this is the distinction: for you, because it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), existence (*sattā*) is somehow brought into connection with a different object by virtue of being its locus; for me, however, because both serve the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*), they share the same object.

Furthermore, when the genus (*jāti*) is enjoined for the sake of a result, the oblation (*homa*) does not revolve in the mind as its locus in the manner that the oblation is [the locus] for curd (*dadhi*).
For that animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*) which is under discussion is indeed suitable [as the locus].
And the yoking of the animal is established by necessity through the acquisition of that [substance];

and thus, since the injunction of the connection with the fruit pertains to the oblation which has obtained the modification of curd, the coloring by curd is also established by necessity— it is for this reason that both connections are enjoined by the sentence.

Success (*siddhi*) consists in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), and not in both relations being enjoined by the sentence. In the present case, however, because the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is of an unseen nature (*adṛṣṭarūpa*) and thus non-worldly (*alaukika*), its worldly relations cannot be established; therefore, while it is possible for the sentence to enjoin only the connection with the fruit by relying on that [post], since the relation between the post and the *udumbara* wood must necessarily also be enjoined, syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is unavoidable.

Therefore, while that much suffering remains unremoved that causes pain to oneself, one who, having gathered everything together to remove it all, applies a mantra while proceeding to scratch [the itch], finds that the mantra becomes redundant (*tantra*) because no distinction is perceived.

Nor, even in that case, can there be a repetition according to the distinction of each limb—as in the logic of the *nirvāpa* mantra (1.4.14)—on account of being joined with the word *tvā*; for since the limbs have not yet been employed [individually], they do not constitute separate actions, and thus it is impossible to refer to them by means of the word *tvā*.
