Therefore, the *yoni* [the original source verse] is also a qualifying factor.
That is incorrect.

Since the *kaṇvarathantara* is prescribed in the *vaiśyastoma* as the means for accomplishing the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, its chanting must be performed upon its own source-hymn (*svayoni*), namely "O Soma, being purified, flow with your stream. For the purpose of the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, there is another *rathantara*, because it must be preceded by its own source-hymn and because it is a distinct entity for that purpose.
Commentary: There is the Vaiśyastoma sacrifice, [established by the injunction]: "A Vaiśya should sacrifice with the Vaiśyastoma.
In that context, it is heard: "The Kaṇvarathantara becomes the Pṛṣ�thastotra.

It has been stated that the Kaṇvarathantara is a modification of both [the Bṛhat and the Rathantara], according to the principle: "Because they do not belong to the archetype, and because of the contradiction, they should be restricted [to their respective places]" (9.2.16.47).

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the *kaṇvarathantara* be sung without restriction in either the *rathantara*-origin or the *bṛhat*-origin [sāman], or in the *rathantara*-origin, or else in its own origin? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? There is no restriction according to the extended application (*codaka*), for in that way there is simplicity (*lāghava*).
Therefore, the correctness of the performance [is established].
This being the case, we reply:
that which is heard as the *kaṇvarathantara*—other than the *rathantara*—for the sake of the *pṛṣṭha* [laud], that should exist in the source (*yoni*) of the *rathantara*.
For the Vaiśyastoma is preceded by the Jyotiṣṭoma.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Pṛṣṭha-stotra was performed upon the source-hymn of the Rathantara;
but was it not also performed there upon the source-hymn of the Bṛhat?
It is not so, because the *ṛcs* are divided;
here the division of the *ṛcs* is understood,
as in the expression "it is the source of the *rathantara*."
Why? Because the word "Rathantara" is heard in reference to the Kaṇvarathantara; from this it is understood that the Kaṇvarathantara is a specific variety of the Rathantara.

The term "Kaṇvarathantara" would apply to something else only if the properties of the Rathantara were not present. Since those properties do exist, its application is justified, just as in the case of a sacrificial post (yūpa).
For example: "The sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood.
Indeed, the Udumbara as the substance for the sacrificial post is not mentioned in the original archetype (prakṛti);
rather, this word is justified as being based on a specific religious merit (dharma).
In the same way here as well, the word *rathantara* occurs in the *kaṇvarathantara* by virtue of its connection with the *dharma* (characteristic) of the *rathantara*, and not otherwise.
Or rather, it occurs in its own source (*svayoni*), because it is designated by that name in its entirety.
The Commentary states: "And it is not the case that it is sung in the source of the *rathantara*."
What then? In its own source.
Why? Because it denotes everything.
For the word *rathantara* is the designator of that which is qualified by all the specific attributes.

The designation "Kaṇvarathantara" applies to the entirety [of a sāman] which possesses the *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratihāra*, *upadrava*, and *nidhana* sections, along with its specific *stoma*, *svara*, *kāla*, and *abhyāsa*.
Therefore, the *yoni* (the source verse) is also a qualifying factor.
Furthermore, if it were a different matter, the word "Rathantara" would have to be figuratively applied to the Kaṇvarathantara.
Therefore, it should be sung in its own source (*svayoni*).
[Duh]—This explanation provided by the Commentator, namely, "the word *kaṇvarathantara* refers to the *prastāva* and the following [parts]," is incorrect.
According to the rule "The designation *Sāman* applies to songs" (*gītiṣu sāmākhyā*, 2.1.36), the word *kaṇvarathantara* denotes a *Sāman*, not a *ṛc*.
In the archetype, the *rathantara* chant, which embellishes the syllables of the *ṛc*, is understood as a means for accomplishing the *pṛṣṭha* stotra;
the same applies to the *bṛhat* chant.
However, in this case, by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*, another distinct chant is enjoined as the means for accomplishing the *pṛṣṭha*.

Therefore, singing (*gīti*) serves only as a function of singing itself (in the manifestation of syllables), not as a function of the *ṛc* (because it lacks the capacity for that). And the *ṛc*, by virtue of the injunction (*codaka*), is obtained in its archetypal form (*prākṛtī*). That [archetype] must not be sublated by the modification (*vikāra*), for it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) in the archetype through its sequence and performance.
The meaning of the statement is as follows: (namely, the performance of the *sāman* alone) does not constitute a sublation of the *ṛc* by that [performance];
nor is there a sublation of the *ṛc*—which is brought forward by the *codaka*—by virtue of the capacity of the word-meaning.
This reading is found in the two manuscripts, the Dūṣaṇa and the Ratna;
however, in the Ānandāśrama edition, the reading is: "First, regarding the sentence [being set aside] by things that are not its own constituent parts (apadārtha);
nor can there be a sublation of the Ṛk verse brought forward by the *codaka* on the strength of what is not its own constituent part."
And that is not tenable; for example, the word *dhenu* [is not applied] to a goat or the like.
Indeed, the word *dhenu*, when employed, is never a cow without possessing the quality of giving milk (*godhuk*).
On the other hand, the singing of the *Kaṇvarathaṃtara* is indeed seen to be employed even with respect to other *ṛc*-verses.

(Since there is no justification for the chanting [gīti] in the two subsequent verses by means of this [first verse], and since that chanting cannot be figurative when applied elsewhere due to a lack of authoritative evidence,
it follows that the *ṛc* is obtained through the *codaka* [extended application rule].
However, it is not possible to establish this as the final conclusion.)
However, the Kaṇva and Rathantara [Sāmans] are recited in the subsequent section within the context of the Vaiśyastoma;
therefore, it is clear that they are set aside by the force of that context.
Consequently, they should be chanted in their own original sources (yoni).

The birthplace (*yoni*) of the *Bṛhat* is "tvāmiddhi," and the birthplace of the *Rathantara* is "abhi tvā śūra. This arrangement of the *Kaṇvarathantara*, which was established in the archetype (*prakṛti*), is here prescribed for the two functions of that archetypal *Sāman*.
The author of the Bhāṣya maintains that when one performs both actions, one also adopts the conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the two properties (*dharma*).

The author of the Vārttika, however, considers them to be merely optional (*vikalpa*). Since it was stated that there is no conjunction here in the archetype of the Soma sacrifice, this constitutes a relevant counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*).

The meaning of the Sūtra (according to the Bhāṣya) is as follows: In the case of the non-standard *kaṇvarathantara*, because it is a modification of that [sāman], and because it is a modification of both the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*, the properties of both should apply, since neither has been specifically set aside.
As for those properties that are mutually contradictory, they are settled by the impossibility of their simultaneous performance due to such conflict; thus, there is a fixed distribution.

According to the view of the Vārttikakāra: since the Vaidya-stoma is a modification (*vikāra*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is an option between the two praises as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Consequently, its properties—such as "the *bṛhat* is sung loudly" and "the *rathaṃtara* is sung softly"—are also subject to option.
Because these properties are mutually contradictory, [the question arises] whether the properties of both are combined in the *kaṇvarathaṃtara* or not.
According to the Bhāṣya, because it has two positions, they are combined; according to the Vārttika, because of the contradiction, the latter [option] prevails.
In the *Bhāṭṭa* [tradition], it is heard in the *Vaiśyastoma*: "The *kaṇvarathaṃtara* becomes the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra].

And since, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the term *pṛṣṭha* stands in grammatical apposition with both the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara*, and because it is in apposition with the word *pṛṣṭha*, it is established—clearly in that very section of the *Kaustubha*—that it pertains only to the *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ priest by means of the two *ṣaḍaha* days, and not to the *pṛṣṭha* stotras of the Maitrāvaruṇa and others.

Consequently, because it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara*, the application of their properties (*dharma*) is likewise beyond dispute, according to the method stated in the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the inquiry as to whether that [attainment] results from the combination (*samuccaya*) of both properties or by way of an option (*vikalpa*): although in the archetype (*prakṛti*), two sets of heterogeneous impressions (*saṃskāra*) producing two hymns of praise are obtained as options due to the difference between the *tattvadṛk* and *sāma* etc., nevertheless—in the *vaiśyastoma*, because of the unity of the *sāman* consisting of the *kaṇvarathaṃtara* and its substratum, the *ṛc* verses, etc.—there is no obstacle to the presence of the two causal factors (*prayojaka*) within a single set of seventeen impressions, or within the collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of the qualities produced thereby; thus, there is an injunction for their non-contradictory conjunction.
"In the skulls and vessels of the miserly,
the lives of others generally result in the destruction of their own welfare"—
this is the maxim.
The characteristic of a miser: "He who, out of greed, accumulates wealth while causing suffering to himself, his religious duties, and his children and wife, is known as a miser."
Thus [ends] the *Sāhasrī*. 738. The maxim of the plantain fruit (*kadalaphalanyāya*):
Just as the plantain fruit destroys its own mother, the plantain tree, so too does knowledge destroy ignorance.
The Summary: Having heard the mantra "kadā cana strīrasi," it should be employed for the worship of the Gārhapatya fire, and not for the worship of Indra by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*).
This is the section concerning Direct Assertion (*śruti*) and Indicative Power (*liṅga*).
The Golden Earring Maxim (kanakakuṇḍalanyāya):

Just as an earring produced from gold is not different from the gold itself, so too the world, which is the effect produced from Brahman as its cause, is not different from Brahman as its cause. Sāhasrī 416: By the maxim of the golden earring, Brahman alone has transformed into the form of the world.
Nīlakaṇṭha [states] that it is improper for an elder brother to subsist on wealth acquired by a younger brother (Sudhāpṛ.
186). Marrying the wife of a younger brother who has acquired [the property] is a violation of custom (Vācaspatimiśra 113/714, pp.
203–204). The maxim of the ball (kandukanyāya).
Just as a ball, though fallen, rises up by its very nature when struck by the hands, so too do those of virtuous conduct rise up.

(Sāhasrī 990). "If he should carry one [of the two] skull-bowls, he should offer a cake on one potsherd to Heaven and Earth; if he should carry two, he should offer a cake on two potsherds to the Aśvins.
This connection with the mishap is for the purpose of indicating the occasion [for the rite].
Bhāṣya 4.3.16.18–39: The potsherd (kapāla) is employed first for the purpose of baking (śrapaṇa).
Once the potsherd has been employed for baking, it remains available even for the scattering of husks (tuṣopavāpa).
Vi. 4.11.19: "Having thrown the broken potsherd into the water"—thus, the total destruction [of the potsherd] is heard in the scripture.

Bhāṣya 6.4.14.6: Regarding the potsherds (*kapāla*), which—like the cooking-pot (*kumbhī*)—are equal in number [to the horses]: "As many horses as one might receive, so many Vāruṇa-Aśva potsherds should one offer. Thus, even in the case of non-reception, Vāruṇa-Aśva sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) on potsherds are heard of in scripture as being equal in number to the horses. When those sacrificial cakes are many, a discussion arises: should their baking be performed on long potsherds, or is there a separate set of four potsherds for each sacrificial cake? It is with reference to this inquiry that he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In the case of the animal sacrifices dedicated to Prajāpati, the potsherds for the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) of equal number should follow the principle of a single performance (*tantra*), like the cooking-pot (*kumbhī*).
The baking of several sacrificial cakes should take place upon exactly four potsherds—some longer and some longest.
Or rather, there should be a separate performance for each primary offering, as in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
He states the established conclusion (siddhānta):
There should be a division of the potsherds for each principal offering and for each sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).

This is according to the archetype (prakṛti), just as in the archetype of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) there are separate potsherds for each sacrificial cake; it is so because of the force of the extended injunction (codaka).
Furthermore, there would be spreading over all [the potsherds].
According to the injunction, "He spreads the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) as far as the potsherds," the spreading of the cake is prescribed over all the potsherds belonging to it.
And that cannot be accomplished if [the rite] were performed as a single common act (tantra).

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that for all the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) to be prepared, there must be a division of the potsherds (*kapāla*) into four for each cake, so that the spreading [of flour] may occur upon them as intended. Are the potsherds separate for each cake in the New and Full Moon sacrifices? The potsherds are a sacrificial implement (*yajñāyudha*).
"He bakes [the sacrificial cake] on the potsherds" (Vi.
3.15). In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the placing of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) on the altar is performed after it has been removed from the potsherds (Bhā.

10.1.2.58). Even though the potsherd is subsidiary (śeṣatva) with respect to the scattering of the husks (tuṣopavāpa), it does not possess the status of being an instrument for that purpose (tatprayojyatva).
VI. 3.12: Regarding the breaking or the leaking of a *kapāla* (potsherd), there is a specific expiatory *homa* offering.
VI. 4.4: The placing (*upadhāna*) of the *kapālas* should not be performed in the *saurya-caru* sacrifice.

Bhāṣya 10.1.16.54: In the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is the heating (*saṃtāpana*) of the *kapālas* with the mantra: "By the heat of the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Bhṛgus, the Aṅgirases, and of Dharma—that [heat] has been placed here."
10|1|15|53 (56): The heating of the potsherds (*kapāla*) need not be performed in the *saurya* sacrificial oblation (*caru*).
10|1|15|53 (56): When a potsherd is lost, no sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) is prescribed for its recovery; one does not spend a *kārṣāpaṇa* coin to search for a single *kākinī*.
4|3|16|39. Bhāṣya 6|4|17: The baking of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) takes place on the potsherds themselves, because the cake is dependent upon them.
VI. 10|1|11. Upon those potsherds, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is placed for baking from below;
while the cake is on the potsherds, embers are heaped over them. This is the "potsherd-logic" (kapālanyāya).

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the spreading of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) upon the potsherds (*kapāla*) is performed with the mantra: "O wide one, spread out; spread yourself out widely" (ŚB 10.1.15.55).
Even when the function of the potsherd has been fulfilled, the *medana-homa* (the oblation for breaking) must still be performed (Bhāṣya 9.1.4.6).
Just as with the potsherds, so too in the case of the acceptance of a horse, [the rite] is repeated for each sacrificial cake.
Bhāṣya 11.4.11.39–41. The Principle of the Potsherds (kapālanyāya);
the Principle of the Fuel-Sticks for the Potsherds (kapālasamidhenīnyāya):
When a single component of the archetypal rite is adopted in a modified rite (vikṛti), only the first one is adopted and the others are omitted.
Regarding the sequential order, when a single part is mentioned, there may be an elision of the final portion, as in the case of traditional texts (*āgama*).

The Bhāṣya states: "The mention of a single part occurs in such expressions as 'a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth,' 'a cake on two potsherds for the Aśvins,' and 'a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu.
There is also mention of the whole, as in: 'One should offer a cake on eight potsherds for Agni.'"

Likewise, there is mention of a single part [of the sacrifice]: "One should sacrifice with a two-night rite; one should sacrifice with a three-night rite; one should sacrifice with a four-night rite; one should sacrifice with a five-night rite; one should sacrifice with a six-night rite; one should sacrifice with a seven-night rite; one should sacrifice with an eight-night rite; one should sacrifice with a nine-night rite; one should sacrifice with a ten-night rite; one should sacrifice with an eleven-night rite. There is also mention of the whole: "One should cause one who desires offspring to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite. Similarly: "He recites one *sāmidhenī* verse."
"He recites three *sāmidhenī* verses"—this is a mention of a single part.
There is also a mention of the whole: "He recites fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses.
Regarding this, there arises a doubt: is it that in all cases the first [verse] is taken up while the others are omitted, or is there an option?
Thus [the question arises]: what is the conclusion? We say that for those things possessing a sequence, there is the mention of a single part;
that is, the elision of the others and the inclusion of the first.
What is the reason? The primary is the first, and the secondary is the other.
Between the primary and the secondary, when both are joined (*lopa*), the secondary would be elided;
for the primary is that which ought to be favored.
As it has been said: "Or rather, the primary [is established] because of the prior mention, as in the world" (12.1.8.23).
It is like the case of arrivals.
Just as in assemblies and gatherings, newcomers arrive and settle down without even looking at those already seated, so too should it be understood here.
The gender is not distinctive, for that [gender] expresses the number.

The Bhāṣya states: "Now, as for what was stated by way of gender—namely, that 'this sixth day would be omitted,' which shows the omission of the sixth and not the first—that is not distinctive even in the case of an option.
For the expression 'five' constitutes a complete statement regarding the number."
That which, when excluded, completes the number by means of the first, the middle, or another [member], is the sixth.
For example, in the case of "five of the brothers are not seen," this occurs when the youngest, the eldest, or the middle one is not seen.
It should be understood in the same way here as well.
Or rather, there should be an operation from the beginning, because the commencement starts from that point; otherwise, there would be a different rule due to the specific statement.
The Commentary states: The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the previous position. An operation from the beginning is appropriate for the pervasive nature [of the rule].
Why? Because the commencement is at the beginning of that.
For the commencement is rightly placed at the very start of their sequence;
for the second [section], having been introduced by the preceding one, must be performed as the beginning.

When that [action] is performed here for the first time, it anticipates the subsequent ritual item. Furthermore, whatever ritual item remains, it must be carried out by another person who has already commenced the sequence.
Even if that [first action] is not performed at the very beginning, there is no fault of non-sequential commencement (*anuprakrama-doṣa*).
It will be so.
Therefore, in every case, those things that possess a sequence must be undertaken starting from the first; thus, one should begin with the first.
Furthermore, the cause for the first [is] to be approached.
And there is no contradiction when those [initial elements] have been performed;
even though other [elements] would be applicable by virtue of the occasion, their omission is not contradictory because the constituent parts [of the rite] are already complete.
Therefore, there is the inclusion of the first and the omission of the others.
Thus, when it has been established by logic that this is the case, wherever there is a specific scriptural statement, there the rule is applied even by removing the middle [element].
For example: "He performs the *prayāja* offerings with the remaining oblation," and "He performs the two *anuyāja* offerings with the remaining oblation.
In the absence of such a scriptural statement, the logical conclusion is that only the final element is to be omitted.

Soma: Following the determination of the sublation of the entire constituent element (*padārtha*), the sublation of a portion of that constituent element is now determined; thus, there is both a difference in the section (*pāda*) and immediate succession (*ānantarya*).

Although, in cases such as "the cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth" (*dyāvāpṛthivyamekapālam*), there is no possibility of taking a single part because the potsherds themselves are enjoined as a qualified object of action and thus lack a prior location, nevertheless, since the mantras used for placing the potsherds in the archetype—such as "Thou art firm, strike the earth" (*dhruvamasi pṛthivīṃ hana*) and "Thou art supported, strike the intermediate space" (*dhṛtamantarikṣaṃ hana*)—are extended here by analogy (*atideśa*), the expression "taking a single part" (*ekadeśagrahaṇam*) is stated with reference to those mantras. It should be understood that this same intention applies to the rule regarding the beginning, middle, and end.

Although it is heard in the *mahāpitṛyajña* that "one recites a single *sāmidhenī* verse," and since there is no recitation of other *sāmidhenīs* there, one does not take a portion of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) verses; nevertheless, it should be understood that where in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) there is no recitation of other *sāmidhenīs*, the possibility of taking a portion exists.

Nor is the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) the archetype for the two-night and other sacrifices according to Kātyāyana; rather, it is by way of its constituent parts—because the two-night sacrifice is contained within the twelve-day sacrifice, and the three-night sacrifice is likewise contained therein—and by that much alone, the requirement [of the ritual] is satisfied.

And thus, one should not say that there is no possibility of this being an illustration because there is no grasping of a single part of the archetype (*prakṛti*); for what is established here is precisely the point that the entire twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is not the archetype, but rather its first half. Furthermore, it should be understood that although this discussion belongs to the eighth book as part of the investigation into specific extended applications (*viśeṣātideśa*), it has been placed here for the sake of brevity, as it is required by the context of the *kapāla* [section].
Nor does the principle of the "intruder" (āgantunyāya) apply here.
Where the placement of a primary rite is certain, there the omission of the last element occurs by virtue of the principle of the intruder;
but here, even that is not certain, because there is no distinction among all [the rites] insofar as they are understood through the extended application (codaka).

Regarding the statement, "Or [the quality] of the primary [subject], because of the preceding [rule]" (12.2.8.23), although it is established that qualities are attributed to the primary subject (*mukhyadharmī*), here the attribution of the *first* quality to a single subject is prescribed; thus, they say, its purpose is not already covered by that [previous rule]. In the Sūtra, the term *āgamavat* means that where an adventitious element (*āgantuka*) is inserted at the end, it is like that. Viśvarūpa states: "There may be some portion of the archetypal [elements], or perhaps only the very first."
If there were no distinction, who would be the one [to attain it], since [the result] is understood from the preceding [text]?
Up to the fourth rite, one is not confused; having said, "I shall do this, I shall do that," the rites are to be performed by recollecting them in their proper sequence.

In this regard, the natural sequence is as follows: first, having properly established a particular ember with a specific piece of wood called the *upaveṣa*, one places the sacrificial cake pan (*puroḍāśapātra*) upon that ember while reciting the mantra, "Thou art firm" (*dhruvam asi*).
This sequence is obtained through the general injunction (*codaka*), and it is to be carried out exactly in that manner.
In that context, by means of the prior item—the placement of the coals—only the very first placing of the potsherd (kapāla) which occurs immediately thereafter is brought to mind;
and by that, the second [placing] is also [brought to mind].
Nor is there an absence of distinction between the first and the second, for the second is distinguished by the mantra "thou art held" (*dhṛtam asi*) and by its location in the eastern direction.
Since this is the case, and because it is improper to abandon what is well-known while accepting what is unknown, only the first part must be accepted.
The remainder is omitted due to a lack of purpose.

Bhaṭṭa: Where in the archetype (*prakṛti*) items such as the sacrificial post (*aghnyādi*), the number [of animals], or the potsherds (*kapāla*) are prescribed, there is no dispute whatsoever in the modified rite (*vikṛti*) in cases where the number remains the same.
And in the case where there is a greater number, it will be stated in the fifth [chapter] (5.1.1) as an incidental discussion;
and it will also be explained that in the *viśvā-sāmidhenī* and other such cases, there is even a specific distinction consisting of additions (*āgama*) and so forth.

In cases where the number [of items] is deficient—such as in the *tri-kapāla* (three-potsherd cake), the *sāmidhenī* verses, the *ṛc*, or the *dvirātra* sacrifice—and where there is a necessity to fulfill the number heard in the scripture by omitting certain constituent elements (*padārtha*), the omission of whichever element occurs first is determined due to the absence of a specific rule of selection (*vinigamanā-virahāt*). Nor is it correct to argue that when the primary element is to be favored, the omission must belong only to the final element; for although in the archetype (*prakṛti*) all elements to be performed are understood as "primary" according to their order of recitation (*pāṭha-krama*), in the modified rite (*vikṛti*) other elements are also to be performed, and thus the status of being "primary" relative to those others does not apply to the former.
For this very reason, because there is no unity of statement (*ekavākyatā*), even that which expresses a contradictory [meaning] arising subsequently [is not sublated].

Nor is it proper to effect the omission of the final [kapāla], because the first ordinary *kapāla* and its associated mantra exist as the means of recalling that preceding ritual act (*padārtha*), and thus, in accordance with them, that very [first act] must be performed. Since the performance of the subsequent acts—beginning immediately after the placement of the final *kapāla*—is what is enjoined, and since these subsequent acts recall the placement of the other *kapālas*, it is understood from their requirements that the placement of the final *kapāla* must also be performed. For it is never logically tenable for primary ritual acts (*padārthas*) to be sublated merely in accordance with a subordinate number (*saṃkhyā*).
This being the position reached, [the author states: "the omission of the *kapāla*..."

The *kapālanyāya*: Since, between the placing of the potsherds (*kapāla*) and the placing of the feet (*pāda*), there is no presentation of any ritual act (*padārtha*) to be performed subsequent to the placing [of the potsherds], it is impossible for there to be a rule governing the performance of the preceding acts in accordance with that [subsequent one]. However, because there exists a presenting factor for the act that precedes the first placing of the potsherd, and because that is necessarily presented, the first [act] alone must be performed as many times as the number [required]. Therefore, the other [acts] are omitted by being performed according to that number.
And thus, the indicative mark (liṅga) found in the statement, "This eighth day might be confused [with others] if one offers on five potsherds," also becomes appropriate.
Maṇḍana: "In the case of taking the word *barhis*, there is elision of the final [syllable].
Śaṃkara: "In a modification (*vikṛti*), there is elision of only the final [element]."

The Principle of the Potsherds (*kapālanyāya*): The offering on eight potsherds (*aṣṭakapāla*) is the archetype (*prakṛti*); the one-potsherd, two-potsherd, three-potsherd offerings, and so forth, are the modified forms (*vikṛti*).

In that regard, the properties belonging to the first potsherd of the eight-potsherd offering would apply to the single-potsherd offering; the properties belonging to the first two potsherds of the eight-potsherd offering would apply to the two-potsherd offering; the properties belonging to the first three potsherds of the eight-potsherd offering would apply to the three-potsherd offering, and so on.

The nature of the *kapāla* maxim is stated as: "When a portion of a sequence is mentioned, it is the mention of the first [element] and the elision of the last.

"Like the *kapāla*."

"Like the potsherds" (*kapālavat*; because there is no loss, it is like the potsherds).

10.1.1.126 (27): Like the potsherds. (Because the Audumbarī post exists for the sake of another, like the potsherds) | The maxim of the potsherds and the Sāmidhenī verses | The maxim of the potsherds.

According to the principle of the *sāmidhenī* verses regarding the eight potsherds (*aṣṭakapāla*) in the first section, in the case of the initial offerings and the mantras for shaving and so forth, the commencement [of the ritual] would logically belong to the mantra recited first (this being the prima facie view).
In the case of the "eight-potsherd" and others, the collection of eight or more potsherds constitutes a single ritual act (*padārtha*).
Therefore, in that case, there is a collective application (*samudāyānusamaya*).
Regarding the offering on the potsherds (*kapālābhihoma*) during the *patnīsaṃyāja* rites of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, there is the cake for Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds.

In that regard, the gift of a one-year-old cow is to be observed; in that case, the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is merely a matter of dharma and is not to be performed [as a regular obligation]. This is for the non-priest (*atvij*).
In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the placing of the eight potsherds for the *āgneya-puroḍāśa* constitutes a single ritual act (*padārtha*).

At the removal of the potsherds (*kapālodvāsana*) in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices, it should be performed after counting them in the manner of "one, two," and so forth, because of the scriptural injunction: "He removes them after counting for the protection of the sacrificer. Ke.: The removal of the potsherds is performed with the mantra beginning, "Those potsherds which they collect for the ritual duty (*dharma*)," and so forth.
But regarding the removal of the single potsherd: "That potsherd which the wise pile up for the sake of Dharma—let that too be released for Indra at the conclusion of the vow."
Such is the modification (*ūha*).
However, modern ritualists read, "When the ordainers pile the potsherds upon the dharma," which is utterly incorrect;
for the potsherd is not the agent of the act of piling, but rather the ordainers themselves.

But regarding the guardian of the direction: "O guardians of the directions! Those who, through their wisdom, collect these dharmas upon the skull—may they too, having fulfilled their vow, release them for Indra."
Thus the modification (*ūha*) should be performed.
By whom? By the one who, having properly placed the fire-brand (*upaveṣa*) and the charcoal for the placement of the potsherds (*kapāla-upadhāna*), performs [the rite] upon that.
The mantras beginning with “*adhruvam asi pṛthivīm hana*” and “*dhr̥tam antarikṣam hana*” are for the placing of the potsherds (*kapālopadhāna*).

When the hall has been cleared and its foundation-wood (*mūla*) has been set aside, one should not exert effort in searching for other wood for the purpose of placing the potsherds during the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*).
However, at the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), since there is no hall at all that is devoid of milking, one should not cut branches for the purpose of the *upaveṣa*.

Regarding the placing of the potsherds and the pouring [of the water]: the scattering of the husks at the time of threshing is not the motivator; however, that which occurs at the time of pouring does indeed become the motivator for the holding of the potsherds.
As for the taking up [of the potsherds], even that is not its motivator.

The Kapiñjala Section (Kapiñjalādhikaraṇa):
Regarding the *kapiñjala* birds.
Just as in this very context it is not deliberated whether the *kapiñjala* birds are to be sacrificed, or perhaps peacocks or pigeons.
For what reason? Because peacocks or pigeons are not denoted by the word *kapiñjala*. (If you say this is not so:
the usage of the word *kapiñjala* is observed for both the pigeon and the peacock.
A large pigeon is called "this is a *kapiñjala*, not a pigeon," and likewise,

Thus,
[it is said]. Therefore, that which is called "akavaḍā" or "halguḍa" would be the pigeon.

He says: the word *kapiñjala* is applied there figuratively (*bhaktyā*), and in figurative usage, the word does not denote its primary meaning.

Bhāṣya 11.1.8.138–44: The mantra "kapiñjalān ālabheta" (one should sacrifice kapiñjala birds) is intended [to prescribe] in the Aśvamedha sacrifice. Vi. 2.1.7: The mantra "kapiñjalān ālabheta" is injunctive in form.
In the phrase "kapiñjalān ālabheta," the plural number connects with the sacrifice by way of the grammatical factor (*kāraka*), and subsequently, it serves as the qualifier of the kapiñjala birds.
And likewise, the sacrifice is performed with many—specifically three—kapiñjala birds, not with two, nor with one.

What is the abandonment of the kapiñjala birds once they have been encircled by fire? (The refutation of specific doubts regarding this, however, should be seen in the Kapiñjalādhikaraṇa in the *Some*).
*Soma*, p. 145, verse 2.47: "One should offer oblations with clarified butter.

Here, because of the plural number in the word *āhutīḥ* (oblations), it should be understood that there are exactly three oblations, according to the *kapiñjala-nyāya* (the rule regarding the partridges). *Prāyaścittamayūkha*, p. 6: "Or one should eat oil-cake or even grain-particles for a year at night" (*Yājñavalkya-smṛti* 3.254). Here, in the reading "for a year at night," the [rule] must be applied according to the *kapiñjala-anvaya* (the connection with the partridge rule).
Page 59: "He chooses those who have composed mantras" is the injunction.

In this regard, since there is no fixed rule and the principle of the *kapiñjala* (partridge) rule would lead to the contingency of choosing only three out of many possible numbers, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that exactly fifty are enjoined as a single unit.
Saṃkarṣa 3.4.13: According to the *kapiñjala* rule, the plural number has its purport in the number three.

Dattakamīmāṃsāṭīkā, 72: "The established position is that in the occurrence [of a word], the number one without distinction (abhedai-katvasaṃkhyā) is manifested. Just as in the scriptural injunction regarding the *kapinjala* birds, the number three is established through reasoning (*nyāya*).

This so-called 'number one without distinction' is the existence of numbers in a state of non-differentiation, or it is the generality of number (*saṃkhyāsāmānya*) from which particularities have been abandoned."
Vai. Sāra. Kārikā 54: "Having honored the king and the pure twice-born with madhuparka... (The plural form *dvijān* [twice-born] is understood as three, according to the *kapiñjala-nyāya*.

Dattaka-candrikā 10: Regarding the consecration of a king, the mantras of *abhayā-parājitā* will be stated in their application; those [mantras] should be taken as three each by means of the plural number, according to the *kapiñjala-nyāya*).

*Nītimayūkha*, p. 5. Regarding the "Slaughter of the Kapiñjala" (*kapiñjalavadha*), the plural form found in the scriptural text—referring to the three [birds] among those who perform the hymns (specifically the *udgātṛ*s)—is established.
*Vārttika* 3.5.8.26, p. 1004. This is the *Kapiñjalādhikaraṇa*.
The plural number culminates in the sense of "three," provided there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).
Because of the plural number, there would be an option regarding the attainment of all [the birds].
The Commentary states: "It is heard in scripture: 'One should sacrifice Kapiñjala birds for the spring.
In this regard, it is deliberated: should three, four, or five be sacrificed as an option, or only three?"
What is established? They are to be sacrificed according to option.
Why? Because all are obtained.
All these specific numbers are obtained by means of the plural number.
All of them are to be prescribed for him, because they are applicable in every case.
Yet they cannot coexist through conjunction (*samuccaya*), because that is impossible.
Therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
But if this is so, it follows that a single word has multiple meanings, and this is not a logical principle.
It is replied: This is true.
A resort to necessity (agatya) is taken. If a resort to necessity is taken, it should not be resorted to when a [logical] way [of interpretation] exists.
But this way does exist: that the meaning of the plural number is "three-ness" (tritva), and by connection with that, it applies even to four and so on, because three-ness exists in all of them.
This is not tenable.
If the meaning of the plural number were three, then the grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "four Brāhmaṇas" would not be possible.
For the word "Brāhmaṇas" has three as its referent, while "four" has four; a coreferential relationship between these two cannot obtain.
It is not the case that "there are four";
thus, in all instances, it will occur through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*),
just as one says, "the banyan tree is the field."
For the number three can indeed indicate [the presence of] four and so on through association;
thus it is established, and a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is resorted to.
What can be done? It is resorted to out of necessity.
When another interpretation is possible, it should not be resorted to.

And such an interpretation exists: that plurality is the meaning of the plural number. For all of them are indeed many; thus, there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) by the very force of the scriptural statement.
If multiplicity were to be understood, what is that multiplicity? It is said: multiplicity is increase; it is accumulation;
the meaning is excess.
How so? [The root] *vṛh*tiḥ.
This [root] has the meaning "to increase. To it, the suffix *u* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules: "and there is elision [of the *ṛ*] of *vṛh*."
[Uṇādi Sūtra 275.
According to the *Kaumudī*, the suffix *is* is carried over from the preceding sūtra.
Therein, the word *bahiḥ* is derived; the word *bahu* is not.]
The etymology of the word *bahu*, however, is shown in the *Amarakośa-ṭīkā* by Rāma and Āśrama as follows:
"From the root *baṃh* (or *bah*), meaning 'to increase' (*bhvādi* 633), [the suffix] *u* is applied according to the rule *laghivardhorlopaśca* (*uṇādi* 30); its form is *bahu*.
*Bahu* means 'grown' or 'excessive'."
And all these are superior by way of logic;
therefore, all are designated as "many.
Now, one might object: is it not the case that "many" and "superior" are relative terms?
For that which is indeed much becomes "not much" in relation to something else.
True, it is so;
however, that which is much in relation to one thing is not itself "not much" in relation to that very same thing.

For example, the Northern Kurus are called "northern" in relation to the Southern Kurus; yet there are no other regions to the north of them that do not exist, and nevertheless, by virtue of their relative position, they do not lose their status as being "northern. In the same way, three sides obtain the state of being "many" (plural) in relation to the duality [of two], and yet they do not cease to be those very same sides even when considered from the perspective of four or more. How, then, is it known that the plurality of three sides depends upon duality? It is said:
Relative dependence, first of all, occurs among things of the same class; for example, when it is said, "Devadatta is strong," this is not said in relation to an elephant or a lion.
What then? It is in relation to men of his own kind. In the same way, number also acquires plurality only by depending on another number.

In that regard, singularity is not required at all, because the plural number is observed for two things and is seen in all [cases] among those who follow the rules of logic. Therefore, it is understood that [the plural] depends on duality;
and that [duality] is apprehended by means of the plural number.
Why? Because it exists when that exists, and it does not exist when that does not exist.
When that exists—in the case of three or more—it occurs; and when that does not exist—in the case of two or one—it does not occur.
Thus, the designation "plural" (*bahuvacana*) is etymologically significant.
And there is the statement of the learned authorities: "The plural number [is used] for many" (Pāṇini 1.4.21).
If the meaning of the plural were simply three, one would have said "the plural is used for three," because that would be more concise and free from ambiguity.
Therefore, these are "many" in relation to duality.
Therefore, the plurality of the three and so forth remains.
This being the case, no single word has multiple meanings, and since all [the words] possess plurality, there is no usage whatsoever by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). It is thus applied.
The term *nirupada* (without remainder) is applied to three;
however, in the case of four and so forth, it is used with a remainder (*sopada*), as in "four Brāhmaṇas.
But that is false.
In all three cases, it is used with an accompanying term (*sopada*),
as in "the three worlds" and "the three Vedas.

If the number three were to convey its meaning without an accompanying term (*nirupapada*), then this very inquiry would not have arisen regarding the injunction, "One should offer *kapiñjala* birds to Vasanta."
Just as in this very case, one does not deliberate whether the *kapiñjala* birds to be sacrificed are peacocks or pigeons;
for what reason? Because neither peacocks nor pigeons are denoted by the word *kapiñjala*.
Likewise here, if the plural number were to denote only the number three and no other numbers, then this deliberation would not occur, just as in the previous case.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā*: Regarding the passage "In the spring, one should sacrifice *kapiñjala* birds," this is the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) view.
Just as the word *akṣa* is used in a general sense for dice-playing and other such activities, so too the plural number (*bahuvacana*) functions in a general sense with respect to three or more.
Alternatively, it applies where singularity and duality do not exist.
In this view, this term is used in its general sense.
Even in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), this alone is the meaning of the word; it does not follow the strict logical rule (*nyāya*).
If it is argued that such usage is observed [in scripture], [we reply:]...
The Commentary: Now it might be argued that the use of the plural number is observed in cases such as "four" and so forth, as in the expression "four Brāhmaṇas. To this, the investigation [proceeds]:
and it is exactly so.
The Commentary states: Here too, the word *kapiñjala* is observed to be used for both a pigeon (*kapota*) and a peacock (*mayūra*).
It is said: "This is a large pigeon; this *kapiñjala* is not a [common] pigeon."
Likewise, [one might say] "this is a small peacock, this is a *kapiñjala*, not a peacock.
[The meaning is that the name *kapiñjala* applies to both a large pigeon and a small peacock.
If you argue that this is done figuratively (*bhaktyā*), [we reply:]...
The Commentary says: He replies:
The word "kapiñjala" is used there figuratively (bhaktyā), and in a figurative usage, no doubt arises regarding the primary meaning of the word.
Likewise in the other case.
The Commentary states: "In the other case as well, the term 'four Brāhmaṇas' is employed by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā)," as has been explained.
And when a word is used through secondary indication, there arises no doubt regarding its primary meaning.
Furthermore, the number belonging to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is expressed by the suffix (*vacana*), as in the case of "brāhmaṇāḥ" (Brāhmaṇas).
Or rather, it is the meaning of the nominal stem itself, as in the case of "dvau" (two) and "ekaḥ" (one).
And "three-ness" (*tritva*) is neither the meaning of the nominal stem nor its number.
Therefore, the plural form "four" would not be applicable. Now, it might be argued:
"Within the four, there exists a three that constitutes a constituent part; the plural is used in reference to that."
Duality also exists there, as does unity.
Granted, for this very reason, the dual number and the singular number might be urged;
therefore, the use of the plural number in the case of four and so forth is not due to the presence of the number three.
The plural number is used for them precisely because of their multiplicity;
therefore, all [the birds] are [to be sacrificed] according to the principle of the *kapiñjala* section concerning the benefit of others.
The section concerning the *kapiñjala* birds establishes that the meaning of the plural number extends to the limit [of the group].
If all [the birds] were the intended meaning, then by the injunction "one should sacrifice the *kapiñjala* birds," all of them would be obtained.
Therefore, there is an option;
or rather, the first [alternative] should be restricted, otherwise there would be a transgression of the cause.
Commentary: Or rather, plurality should be restricted to three.
What is the reason? For no one who takes four ever fails to take three; this is because:
The scripture is known as the *anugata*;
and since there are three things to be adopted, from where would the meaning of the word [arise]? It is heard that this belongs to many.
And many [beings] are to be sacrificed.
This being so, there would be a transgression of the rule.
Furthermore, if there were some other reason for not adopting [the practice] exactly as it was heard, then there would be a transgression.

There is no such thing as a case where many ritual procedures (*kalpa*) are heard of, some of which are light and others heavy; rather, because the performance of the heavy ritual procedure is common [to both], it is inferred that from its performance there arises a greater fruit.
For example: "one should give one, six should be given, twelve should be given, twenty-four should be given."
But here, with respect to the mantras which are instruments, there is the maxim of the single elbow-socket.
The maxim of the elbow and the wrist (*kaphoṇiguṇḍanyāya*).
Amarasimha states: "The *bhujagrāha* [forearm] is the *doḥ* [arm], while the *kaphoṇi* is the *kūrpara* [elbow].

Just as one might write with the expectation of finding a sweetmeat (*guḍa*) at the elbow—the joint in the middle of the arm—even though no such sweetmeat exists, this maxim applies where there is a distinction in activity due to identification with something, even when that thing does not actually exist.

This is reckless (sāhasī). For in the *Parṇamayī-Adhikaraṇa* (Su. p. 490), it will be refuted that "being a means to an end" (*sādhyatva*) is based solely on the evidence of mere co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) independent of any injunction (*vidhi*).
This will be like the case of a woolen blanket (*kambala-narṇija*);
for by washing (*narṇija*), one accomplishes both: the cleansing of the blanket and the cleanliness of the feet.

Saṃkarṣa 4.4.3: The maxim of the "ornament on the hand" (*karakaṇṭhanyāya*). Even though the word *kaṇṭha* denotes an ornament of the hand, when the word *kara* is used prior to it, just as at the time of usage it is expressed as being related to the hand, so too this maxim applies where a term is used to indicate the relationship of another thing to that [primary object] at that specific time.

207. The *sāhasī* [rite] consists of the worship of stationary deities (*sthāvaradevatā*) such as the *karapūjākā* and others, performed according to the traditions of one's own respective lineage (*kulāgata*). This is called *āhūnīyaibuka*, and it is practiced by those of the South (*dākṣiṇātya*).
VI. 1.3.8. *Karaṇa*:—The *karaṇa* is one born from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother.
VI. 6.1.12. *Karaṇa*:—A substance possessing the power for an action, or the power residing in that [substance].
Vākyapadīya 1.4.12, p. 322. *Karaṇa*:—"That which is designated as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the accomplishment of something."
The expectation of assistance for that [injunction] does not obstruct its own capacity;
for there is no such means of action (karaṇa) in either the world or the Veda which lacks a desire for assistance in its status as the "manner of performance" (itikartavyatā).
"And because it is not restricted to being a substitute, it may function as an instrument (*karaṇa*) itself,
whether through the distinction between external and internal or always by virtue of the speaker's intention.
(Since [the sense] is observed everywhere— in the case of a wheel and so forth— to manifest its object like a lamp, it does not incur incapacity by being invariably dependent on an auxiliary.)

On the contrary, instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) consists precisely in the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*); in the absence of that, it is not established, because the dependence upon it is necessary for every instrument.
He provides an example: "For someone pointed out by darkness might even say:
'What use is this eye of mine? That which was seen by me was seen by means of the lamp.'"
However, for the blind,

there is no perception of form and so forth even with thousands of directions of vision; therefore, because it is the uncommon cause [for the perception of form] through the conjunction of the body, self, and mind, the eye is the illuminator.
And because consciousness is its essence, the eye is considered an instrument (*karaṇa*).
[See] *Stotrāvalī*, p. 507–08; *Saṃbandhavārttika*, p. 507–08. An instrument is an active, sustaining cause.
*Maṇiprabhā*, p. 19. For sacrifice is indeed the instrument.

Even *udbhid* and the like are instruments (*karaṇa*) because they are indicated by the instrumental case; in that context, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "by means of the sacrifice" as "by means of the *udbhid*" is appropriate.

Bhāṣya 1.4.12, p. 324. It was stated in the *Indriyakāmādhikaraṇa* (Vārttika 3.6.1643, p. 1069) that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is not connected with an instrument. An instrument does not require an auxiliary (*anugrāhaka*) due to incapacity.
Regarding the *karaṇa-mantras* that have a single purpose: why [is the addition] at the end of the *karaṇa-mantras*? Because of their conjunction (*saṃnipāta*).
These are indeed *karaṇa-mantras*.

And it has been stated that the commencement of the ritual action coincides with the end of the mantra for all instruments: "Because mantras have the purpose of indicating the action, the commencement of the ritual action should coincide with the end of the mantra" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 12.3.10–25). Furthermore, without an option [to choose], it would be impossible to effect the coincidence of the commencement of the action with the end of every single mantra. Is this a scriptural injunction? No; rather, it is a logical principle (*nyāya*), because it serves the purpose of explaining everything.

If it is thus, then that mantra is said to be "all" even in the case of a conjunction (*samuccaya*); in that case as well, the purpose of the statement is fulfilled. However, when an action has been performed by one, the employment of a second is purposeless; this occurs when there is a single effect.
Therefore, there is [the principle of] having a single effect and so forth.
And that has already been stated [in the rule]: "But those with a single purpose are to be combined optionally" (12.3.4.10).
Therefore, this sūtra regarding their attainment is for the sake of the subsequent deliberation.
Soma [says]: The connection is for the purpose of depending upon the conjunction of the ritual actions and so forth at the end of the previously mentioned mantras.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: there should be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the mantras because they serve the purpose of performing a single action; this is due to their being "conjoined" (*saṃnipātin*), that is, because they are by nature intended to be brought together with the ritual action and so forth, since it is impossible for all the mantras to be conjoined with the action and so forth without such an option. [The commentary] says: "For mantras that have a single purpose, such as purification (*pūyādi*), there is either simultaneity (*sāhitya*) or an option. The first [position, simultaneity], is untenable because of the impossibility [of performance]; it is not so, because the conjunction occurs at the end of the mantra."
Bhāṭṭa:
Thus, having concluded the discussion on the application (*prasaṅga*) of mantras that have been introduced, we shall now proceed with the specific investigation regarding mantras themselves.
Those which are *karaṇa-mantras* (instrumental mantras) serve the purpose of illuminating a single ritual action.

Regarding the statement "or let him distribute the offerings," and so forth—since there are many such [options], one is established by the exclusion of the other through the logic of rice and barley (*vrīhi-yava-nyāya*).

Nor can there be a combination (*samuccaya*), because even though [the mantra] has already been revealed, its revelation cannot occur again; for since revelation is an act of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), once the performance is accomplished either simultaneously or sequentially, another revelation serves no further purpose. Maṇḍana [says]: "In the case of a mantra-sentence with a single purpose, there would be an option."
Śaṅkara says: "The mantras are to be conceptualized as instruments (*karaṇa*).
In the case of instrumental mantras, the commencement of the ritual action occurs at the end of the mantra.

Because mantras have the purpose of conveying meaning, the conjunction with the beginning of the action should take place at the end of the mantra, since the entire [mantra] serves the purpose of expression."
Commentary: Those mantras that serve as instruments for the performance of ritual acts—such as, "For food, thee! (with which he cuts), and "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, thee!
(with which he takes up)—for these, the conjunction with the beginning of the rite occurs at the end of the mantra, in whichever rite they are employed.
What is the reason? Because the purpose of every utterance is to convey meaning.
Every mantra effects the purpose of its verbal expression.
What, then, is the purpose of a mantra’s verbal expression? It is the presentation of the ritual object at the time of performance.

It is understood that the ritual object presented by the mantra is to be performed, due to the capacity of the mantra’s traditional recitation (*āmnāna*) for that purpose and because of its formulation.
Someone says, "He takes it," or "He pours it out.
And that is the point of application for the mantra;
once applied, it remains sufficient as long as it does not fall away.
Therefore, in the case of instrumental mantras, there is a conjunction of the ritual action at the end of the mantra.
It effects that which is to be manifested by the instrumental mantra; while the action is being performed, there is a conjunction of the rite at the end of the mantra.

Śaṅkara says: "One should perform the ritual action at the end of the mantra. Oṃ! In some cases, the fruit manifested by the *karaṇa-mantra* belongs even to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), where the fruit is for the sake of the ritual action;
or where, among the subordinate acts (*upāṅga*), there is the designation "together with that" (*tano saha*).
Bhāṣya 3.8.14.29–30: "The fruit manifested by the mantra of the instrument belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).
The third case ending occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expressing an instrument. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.18, p. 324). "The third case ending expresses the instrument. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.18).

Vārttika 4.4.1.1, p. 322: "Oṃ. For those [words] employed with the instrumental case-ending, the status of being a means to the fruit is logical, because otherwise their utility in every respect would be untenable.
Sūtra 1.2.4.35, p. 153: "Oṃ. Because the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) is distinct from the *karaṇa* (the instrument).
Sūtra 2.2.1.126, p. 550: "Oṃ. Whatever kind of meaning the word *karaṇa* expresses, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is indeed expressive of that very same thing."

For by means of a primary derivative (*kṛdanta*), it is precisely a substance (*dravya*) qualified by a factor of action (*kāraka*) that is expressed, and not an isolated power (*śakti*) as is the case with a case-ending (*vibhakti*). And thus, we observe the connection of other factors of action, such as in the expressions "the instrument," "by the instrument," and "for the instrument. Otherwise, because the substance would be already governed by the single factor of action denoted by the case-ending itself, it could not enter into a connection with another factor of action.

But for *śakti* (power), there is no other object of power (*śakya*). Therefore, because it denotes a substance (*dravya*) qualified by power, it is appropriate for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that expresses the meaning of the word "instrument" (*karaṇa*).

Oṃ. In accordance with the requirement for an instrument (*karaṇa*), an auxiliary (*aṅga*) that provides assistance must be postulated. Furthermore, an instrument, being a single entity whose nature is the awakening of its own power, requires only a single unified assistance as an auxiliary.
However, its status as an auxiliary is established through the distinction of mediating factors (*dvāra*).
VI.1.12: "Om; being recited by way of favoring the instrument (*karaṇa*), it requires the ritual properties (*dharma*). (Ṭupṭīkā 9.1.12, p.
1637): "Om; in the world, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is seen to be that which favors the instrument; it ought to be exactly so here as well."
7|1|1|2, p. 1626: Oṃ. The instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) are required by the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).
Among these, the instrument is connected with the fruit.
Oṃ. Both the instrument and the procedure are first connected with the *apūrva*.

Subsequently, there is a mutual connection between them by way of the relationship of subordinate and principal. (Vi. 7.1.1) The connection between the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is according to the principle of the *aruṇā* section.
*karoti* means "the manifestation of what was previously non-existent.
"Oṃ, [the root] *kṛ* [is used] in sacrifices for all verbal roots," as they say: "(The roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* have one and the same meaning). Vārttika 2.1.11, p. 380.

*Sudhā* (p. 565): "Having divided his army and appointed generals, Indra, whose actions are directed toward the ultimate goal, then deployed his forces against the enemies, just as one performing sacrifices employs all the ritual implements. *Oṃ karoti:* The term *karoti* refers to the causal factor (*pratyaya*) which is the vehicle-like activity conducive to that [action], remaining steadfast in the fruit whose nature is origination (*utpatti*).

And thus, if one does not act in this way, there would be the fault of [the verb] having a common object (*samānārthakatva*); or if one does not strive [to avoid it], there would be the consequence of it being transitive (*sakarmakatva*), as well as the charge of inconsistency.
Oṃ. The root *kṛ* (karoti) has the sense of expressing origination (*utpatti*).
Thus, it is established as permanent in the Siddhānta.
... In the Siddhānta, it must be stated that [the text] prescribes [the rite].
Sūtra-pṛ. 1187, oṃ karoti: [he performs].

The meaning of *vyāpāra* (activity) is *artha* (purpose/object). Because the root *kṛ* has the sense of "coming into being" (*bhavati*), it shares the same meaning as the causative form (*ṇijanta*) of *bhū*. (Maṇi, p. 108). [O] *karoti*: there is no action whatsoever that occurs without something being produced.
The root *karoti* is the agent of the sense of "becoming" (*bhavati*), and the object of the sense of "becoming" becomes the object of the root *karoti*. 1366.
Since the root *karoti* (to do/make) is invariably transitive, its meaning does not reach completion as long as that which is being made is not obtained.

In this regard, it is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that "the agent of the action of *bhavati* (to be) becomes the object of the root *karoti*. For instance: "That which does not have constant becoming, or that which has become constant..."
For it, like a sky-flower or space, possesses no state of being currently produced (*kriyamāṇatva*).
Indeed, only that which has already begun its manifestation or whose manifestation is possible, when employed by another agent, is determined as "being produced," and nothing else.
Accordingly, no one is ever observed making a sky-flower or space.

Even in cases such as "he makes feet" (*pādau karoti*), where the usage of the object (*karman*) is observed for things that are not yet produced, there is no deviation [from the rule], because the words "feet" and so on are employed with the intention of referring to formations (*saṃskāra*) and the like that are not yet fully realized.

Furthermore, even though the root *kṛ* possesses the sense of "producing," a commonality is understood across all instances—such as threatening (*gandhana*) or throwing (*kṣepaṇa*)—insofar as they involve the production of something previously non-existent.
Alternatively, when this [root] denotes "production," it is observed to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with finite verbal forms (*ākhyāta*) in general.
The agent (kartṛ) [is defined] in Bhāṣya 10.2.22.8: "The agent is specifically known in three ways with respect to each action:
by way of fitness (yogyatva), by way of non-prohibition (apratiṣiddha), and by way of a specific proximate word (viśeṣopapada)."
Or [as stated] on page 245, verse 13.7.16:

"Even though it is heard without qualification in the injunction 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice,' because sound and other such things—which have been examined—are incapable of being the agent due to their lack of fitness, the Vāṇika is specifically known as the agent by virtue of his fitness.
Furthermore, because of the prohibition, 'For the outcaste and the eunuch there is exclusion from the duties of the twice-born,' that which is acquired by him is understood to be unprohibited."

In the injunction “A king should sacrifice with the Rājasūya,” it is understood that the Kṣatriya is the agent by virtue of the specific qualifying term (*viśeṣopapada*). (Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 246). Furthermore, one who practices giving—which serves as the cause for the distinction [of ownership]—is also designated as the agent in the act of receiving; this is because, while the causal agent possesses diligence toward his own operation, he lacks the status of being the agent of the operation of the person being prompted. (Parākrama, 512). That factor of action whose intermediate operation the verbal root expresses primarily is the *kartṛ* (agent).

Or [as stated in] Pāṇini 3.4.143, page 917: "He whose activity is primarily denoted by the verbal root is the agent (*kartṛ*). Even though the verbal root denotes an activity that accompanies all the factors of action (*kāraka*), the activities of the other factors are subsumed under it because they are regulated by it, just as the activities of ministers are regulated by the presence of a king. (Somadeva, 10.2.19). Agents perform actions that bring about their own accomplishment.

11.4.2.4–7: "Those same [priests] or others may be the performers when there is a difference in the ritual acts.

the Soma sacrifice thus has that many performers.

Bhāṣya 8|1|13|20–22. Furthermore, the agent’s attainment of the state of being dedicated (*dīkṣāniṣṭhatva*) through the force of the restatement (*anuvāda*) is not improper, just as in the case of the word *irā*;
and thus, the status of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) is attained for the entire [Dīkṣā] passage.
Bhāṭṭa 5.1.1: This is a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) regarding the agent.

Regarding the Agnihotra, it is heard that there is only one officiating priest (ṛtvij), namely the Adhvaryu. Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, however, there are four priests: the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, the Hotṛ, and the Āgnīdhra.

"For the *yajñakratu*s of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, there are five officiating priests (*ṛtvij*): the *adhvaryu*, the *pratiprasthātṛ*, the *brahmā*, the *hotṛ*, and the *āgnīdhra*. For the *yajñakratu* of the *Paśubandha* sacrifice, there are six officiating priests:
the *adhvaryu*, the *pratiprasthātṛ*, the *hotṛ*, the *maitrāvaruṇa*, the *brahmā*, and the *āgnīdhra*."

‘There are seventeen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) for the gentle *adhvara* sacrifice-rite’: the *adhvaryu*, *pratiprasthātṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, and *unnetṛ*; the *brahmā*, *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*, *agnīdh*, and *potṛ*; the *udgātṛ*, *prastotṛ*, *pratihartṛ*, and *subrahmaṇya*; and the *hotṛ*, *maitrāvaruṇa*, *acchāvāka*, *grāvastut*, and *sadasya*. (Vi. 4.2.9, 3.17). Furthermore, it has been stated that the agent (*kartṛ*) is grasped through an absolute mental conception (*aikāntika-bhāvanā*) and in a specific form. Parimala 3.4.1344; Brahmasūtra: Since the agent possesses the possibility of experiencing the fruit [of action], there is qualification for ritual acts.
Vi. 6.1.1: By the principle that "because the agents are connected with the Vedic texts" (3.4.12), it is stated that the duration of life is a duty of the agent.
Bhāṣya.
The *tantra* (common procedure) for the performers—the Adhvaryu and the Maitrāvaruṇa—is found in the Varuṇapraghāsa rites included within the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
Bhāṣya 11.2.10–14, 44–48. Regarding the unity of the performers (*kartṛṇām aikyam*) in the primary rites such as the Āgneya and others in the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Cāturmāsya sacrifices:

according to the principle stated in the Vārttika, "In the case of a matter known from scripture regarding the performers," since the status of being a performer cannot be established in relation to a ritual act that is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*) and is merely enjoined, the connection of that [performer] with the person through the desired and predominant [result] is understood by means of the word-hearing (*padaśruti*), in order to give meaning to the direct scriptural statement (*tadabhyaśruti*).
“For conscious agents, there is eligibility regarding a matter known through scripture;
and for them, there is no injunction [to act] apart from the intention for the fruit.”

Although the agency of the performer— the agent— is merely nominal with respect to the quality of the action, nevertheless, for those who act with deliberation, it is mixed with the intention for a result.
Only such [beings] as these have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for Vedic rituals, not insentient things.
Furthermore, all these actions are joined with injunctions (*vidhi*), since even prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) are dependent on their connection with the injunctive suffix.

(Vārttika 3.4.142, p. 906). The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of the agent is an expressive scriptural statement (*viniyoktrī śruti*) in the form of a case-inflection (*kāraka-vibhakti*), as in: "The Veda, along with its six auxiliary limbs, should be studied and understood by a Brāhmaṇa without [any specific worldly] motive."

*Bāla.*, p. 44: The genitive case in the sense of the agent (*kartari ṣaṣṭhī*) is an applicatory scriptural statement (*viniyoktrī śruti*) in the form of a case-ending (*kārakavibhakti*), as in "the work of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇasya kṛtiḥ*). p. 45:

Regarding the rule—"From the verb, there is cognition of the agent and the object alone as the intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*), and number is based on that [intended meaning], but not for other factors of action (*kāraka*)"—the reason is that "intentionality (*tātparya*) is caused by the desire to express predominance (*prādhānya-vivakṣā*); and since other factors of action, like the object, possess agency only as a factual characteristic (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*), it is impossible to intend to express their predominance as a linguistic characteristic (*śabda-lakṣaṇa*)."

Su. Pṛ. 1457: "Therefore, words such as *pacati* are denoters of the agent and the object, because they function non-differently from those terms [denoting the agent and object], like the words *paktṛ* (the cooker) and *pakva* (the cooked). For functioning non-differently means having grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with those terms; this is observed in unambiguous denoters ending in primary suffixes (*kṛt*), such as in the examples: 'The cooker is Devadatta' (*paktā devadattaḥ*) and 'The rice is being cooked' (*pacyata odanaḥ*)."
And where there is no denotation of agent or object, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in the case of words such as *pāka* ("cooking") and so forth.

Vārttika 3.4.143, p. 930: "The capacity of agentive and objective *kṛt*-suffixes resides in that which is the substratum of agency."
*Maṇi*, p. 114. This is the worldly maxim known as the "comprehension of number qualified by agent and object. *Sphuṭārthā*, p.

1427: In verbal forms denoting agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*), such as "the rice cooks by itself" (*odanaḥ pacyate svayameva*), because there is an intention to express the agency and objectivity residing in the rice, the understanding is that there is a *bhāvanā* (efficient force) which is not confused with respect to its coreferentiality with the agent residing in the rice, and which possesses a fruit coreferential with the objectivity residing in the rice.

*Maṇi*, p. 114: The agent (*kartṛ*), time (*kāla*), place (*deśa*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and consecration (*saṃskāra*)—namely, the *adhvaryu* priest and others, the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) and others, the *samā* and others, the *nīya* and others, the white color (*śukla*) and others, and the threshing (*avaghāta*) and others—are employed as restrictive rules (*niyamena*) by their respective names. (In this context: the *adhvaryu* and others are the agent; the full moon day and others are the time; the *samā* and others are the place; the *nīya* and others are the substance; the white color and others are the quality; and the threshing and others are the consecration. *Kevala*, 4.2.9–123–26: But when the quality belongs to the agent, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because of its inherence in the action.
In the *prayāja* section of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in the scriptural text: “He offers while stepping forward; thus he conquers. Here, *abhikrāmam* is the suffix *ṇamul*.
Its meaning is “having stepped forward, having stepped forward.”
In the inquiry as to whether this *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) pertains only to the *prayāja* offerings or to the entire context, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) states:
First of all, the *abhikramaṇa* is a quality of the agent.
If that *abhikramaṇa* were a quality of the agent, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the sentence "He offers while stepping forward" (*abhikrāmaṃ juhoti*).

Because of the non-inherence of the action: since there is no inherence—that is, no connection—of the action of *abhikramaṇa* with the action of *juhoti*, the *abhikramaṇa* is therefore placed within the entire context (*prakaraṇa*) by way of the agent. Alternatively, if *abhikramaṇa* were a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) of the agent, then because the subsidiary acts (*ajñās*) lack a requirement for a procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*), there would be no dependence on a sub-context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*). Consequently, due to the absence of inherence with the action, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) consisting in the absence of a single-sentence unity (*ekavākyatva*) with that [context]. This is the meaning of the Sūtra according to the Vārttika.
The preceding subject matter follows the commentary.

"Because the agent's quality [of stepping forward] does not have a direct connection (*asamavāya*) with the act of instigation (*prayājakarman*), there would be no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) within that sentence"— this is the meaning of the Sūtra, according to the *Kaustubha*.
"But it would be a single sentence because of expectancy, for it is connected with what precedes. The word "but" (tu) sets aside the prima facie view.
[The opponent argues: "One offers while stepping forward"—this stepping forward does not find its place within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

However, it finds its place specifically within the *prayāja* offerings. By means of the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*), the agent approaches the *āhavanīya* fire; otherwise, he might offer with his hand from afar, having merely intended it. Therefore, the stepping forward assists the oblation.
Therefore, the application is to the *prayāja* offerings themselves.

The meaning of the words of the Sūtra is as follows: the phrase "abhikrāmam" (stepping forward) should form a single syntactical unit with the verb "juhoti" (he offers), conveying a single intended meaning.

For this reason—since the knowledge of the object produced by the preceding word "abhikrāmam" alone is incomplete and not fully concluded, it remains expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) for the subsequent word "juhoti."

Therefore, it is logical that it forms a single syntactical unit with that [the *prayāja*]. Alternatively, the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) is itself expectant of the *bhāvanā* of the *prayāja*, and thus possesses the context (*prakaraṇa*) characterized by the expectancy for the mode of performance (*itthambhāva*). Consequently, it should be construed as a single syntactical unit, integrated precisely within the *bhāvanā* of the *prayāja*.

By the previously mentioned method of bringing together [the elements], the *prakaraṇa*— characterized by the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for the manner of performance (*itthambhāva*) of the *prayāja* productive operation (*bhāvanā*)— is not yet completed. Thus,
in the case of a quality pertaining to the agent (sūtra 3.4.13), there is agency.
The first meaning follows the Bhāṣya, while the second meaning follows the Vārttika.

However, in the Kaustubha, it is stated that the sentence concerning the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward), which possesses a desire for manifestation due to the intermediate [act], should form a single syntactical unit with the sentence concerning the *prayāja* offerings.
For the manifestation is not completed by the mere initial stimulant, because it depends upon the final [stimulant]; thus the Sūtra should be explained—so it has been said.
"However, if [the quality] belongs to the agent, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda) because of the lack of inherence in the action.
In this context, although there is no syntactical split according to the definition, this was stated with the intention of expressing a mutual relationship.
Vārttika 3.6.7.22, p. 1050. "Agency": the subsidiaries and the primary acts in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are equal.
"In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there are four priests.

He will state that the subsidiaries share the same place, time, and agent as the primary rites in the passage: "But the subsidiaries [are performed] because of their subordination to the primary" (11.2.8).

The status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) is established by an explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanika vyavasthāvidhi*). For example: "Milk is the fast-food for a Brāhmaṇa, rice-gruel for a Rājanya, and meat for a Vaiśya.
Likewise: "One should perform the *Bārhadgira* as the *brahmasāman* for a Brāhmaṇa, the *Pārtharaśma* for a Rājanya, and the *Rāyovājīya* for a Vaiśya."

Regarding agency, there is a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*) based on the performer; for example, in the vow (*vrata*) of the sacrificer, there is a sequential arrangement by the Brāhmaṇas for the three mantras: "O Lord of Vow, Agni," "O Lord of Vow, Vāyu," and "O Lord of Vow, Āditya.
(This [distinction] is to be examined, since even a Brāhmaṇa may employ these three mantras.)
(ke. p. 159: Agency (*kartṛtva*) is established as that which is subject to prohibition, as in the case of "one who has not performed the *Agnihotra* sacrifice should not teach.
p. 34: Agency is the state of being a performer prior to the performance [of an action], because it is that which must be performed.
Agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the instigator of other causal factors (*kāraka*s) while oneself being instigated by those other causal factors.
The meaning of the qualified portion of the definition is "the state of generating an operation that is dependent upon other causal factors.
And this [agency] exists in the weaver and others.
This is because [the axe] generates an operation in the form of a conjunction residing in the cloth, which brings about its production.
Even in the case of an axe, since it possesses the status of an agent by virtue of generating a conjunction residing in the wood, its reality [as an instrument] is established;
for it is employed therein as the substratum of the conjunction produced by the person.
