Thus say the ancient followers of all philosophical systems (*sarvadarśanānuyāyin*). In that regard, since [the potter] is distinct from the Lord in terms of being the locus of the conjunction produced by the stick, and [the action] is distinct from the potter in terms of being produced by the stick, the position of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) is that agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the locus of the operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*).

In examples such as "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*) and "The pot comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), the definition applies because Caitra, the pot, and so forth are the substrata (*āśraya*) of the operations (*vyāpāra*) consisting of cooking, coming into being, and so on.
By the inclusion of the term "operation," there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the rice and other such things which are the substrata of the result (*phala*).

In cases such as "Caitra causes Maitra to cook" (*pācyati caitro maitreṇa*), since both the act of cooking and the meaning of the suffix *ṇic* are operations denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvartha-vyāpāra*), it is logically established that both substrata of those [operations] possess the status of agent (*kartṛtva*).
However, since [the action] is expressed by the *tiṅ*-suffix as residing in Caitra alone, that [action] is the relation for its grammatical justification (*upapatti*), and not that of Maitra.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of Maitra being the agent in the sentence "Caitra makes Maitra go" (*caitro maitraṃ gamayati*); for even in that case, such usage exists and is therefore accepted.
As for the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*), however, there is no such contingency because the designation of "object" (*karma-saṃjñā*) takes precedence by virtue of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*).

Thus, they say that in expressions such as "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*), because the activity residing in the pot is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), there is no contradiction with its status as an agent (*kartṛ*). This is not correct.

In cases such as "Caitra does not cook" (*caitro na pacati*) and "There is no pot on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭo nāsti*), there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding Caitra and others, who are the substrata of the absence of the activity denoted by the verbal root. Nor can it be said that in those instances, the cooking residing in Caitra is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the absence; for we accept that the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) takes the form: "the cooking residing in Caitra is the counter-positive of the absence," or "existence residing in the ground is the counter-positive of the absence. Otherwise, in cases like "Fire is not in the lake" (*hrade vahnir nāsti*), there would be the undesirable consequence of non-pervasion (*avyāpyāpatti*), because the counter-positive—qualified by its counter-positiveness-determiner (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*)—would be unestablished (*aprasiddha*).

Nor can that [over-extension] be avoided by accepting a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) in that case such as "the existence of the occurrence of fire is the counter-positive of the absence of both [fire and smoke]," because even so, there would be the consequence of over-extension (ativyāpti) in cases like "the pot becomes white," since the quality of whiteness is the locus of existence, and because [existence] resides in the pot. If, on the other hand, it is held that in that case both the qualifier and the qualified are loci of becoming (*bhavana*), then in instances such as "the pot occurs in the wheel" (cakre ghaṭo bhavati), the same [undesirable] consequence would apply to anything whatsoever.

Now, if that which is intended as the locus of the verbal root's meaning is called its "agent" (*kartṛ*), and since there is no such intention regarding the wheel [in the case of "the potter makes the wheel"], there is no over-extension; then, however, in cases such as "the cloth is not a pot," there would be an under-extension (*avyāpti*), because the pot and so forth—which serve as the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) in this mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*)—lack the status of being the locus of the verbal root's meaning.

Nor should it be argued that, by supplying the word "becomes" (*bhavati*) there, one accepts a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) in which the verbal root *bhū* indicates the becoming of identity (*tādātmyabhavana*) between the pot and the cloth, and such a becoming is the counter-positive of non-existence; for while this would logically establish mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), it would entail that the act of becoming—which exists in both and has both as its agent—belongs to both [the pot and the cloth].

Even so, this would result in the undesirable consequence that the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) would have to denote a thousandfold pervasion in both cases, and the usage "The pot is not the cloth" (*ghaṭo na paṭaḥ*) would be impossible.

By this, the following view is refuted: that in the expression "the pot is not a cloth," the word "pot" indicates a mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) having the pot as its counter-positive, while the negative particle (*nañ*) serves to indicate the speaker's intention; whereas in other cases, both [the word and the particle] function either by taking an implicit relation of identity (*pārśvika-abheda-sambandha*), as in "a white pot," or by functioning as qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) with respect to an elliptically supplied verb, as in "the cloth is not a pot.
For if that were the case, the very usage "the pot is not a cloth" would be impossible;
furthermore, agency could never be established in such instances as "the pot perishes."
Therefore, that which is the locus of the meaning expressed by a word whose gender is delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) possesses the status of being its agent (*kartṛ*).

This [definition] exists in cases such as *pacyate caitreṇa* ("it is cooked by Caitra") and *pacati caitraḥ* ("Caitra cooks"), because Caitra is the locus of the effort (*kṛti*) delimited by the meaning of the root, even when the passive suffix (*karmalakāra*) is employed.

In cases such as *ghaṭo bhavati* ("the pot comes into being"), the locus is indicated by the verb (*ākhyāta*), and in cases such as *ghaṭo naśyati* ("the pot perishes"), the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) is indicated by it; thus, the definition is consistent there as well.
And "being delimited" (*avacchinnatva*) is a specific type of essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*), and not [a causal relation] such as being a generator (*janakatva*).
Therefore, there is no deficiency even if [the counter-positive] and so forth do not generate destruction by way of being a counter-positive.

In cases such as "Caitra is a cooker" (*paktaḥ*) or "Caitra is a cook" (*paktā*), since the very act (*kṛti*)—which is the effort conducive to cooking—is expressed as that which possesses the connection with the suffix, his status as the agent (*kartṛtva*) is established.

In expressions such as *caitrasya pākaḥ* ("Caitra’s cooking"), although the suffix *ghañ* denotes three genders, there is no contradiction in Caitra being the agent (*kartṛ*) because the effort delimited by cooking—which is expressed by the verbal root *pac* through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—possesses all three genders; thus, its locus, Caitra, is the agent.

Alternatively, since the *ghañ* suffix expresses the action (*bhāva*) as the locus of cooking through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), while expressing the effort itself through primary denotation (*śakti*), the resulting verbal cognition is: "Cooking is that which is to be accomplished by an effort delimited by cooking.
Since the effort is construed with Caitra, the status of being the agent is established.
Since this is a residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), there is no deficiency even in the absence of agency;
moreover, its connection occurs only with the principal verb that has been supplied (*adhyāhṛta*).
This is necessary for the justification of usages such as "Caitra’s act of cooking" (*caitrasya pākakṛtiḥ*).

Even in cases such as "it was done by Caitra" (*caitreṇa kṛtaḥ*), although [the action] is not performed [by the agent at that time], there is no obstruction to Caitra’s status as the agent (*kartṛtva*) because, in reality, the verbal root expresses only the activity conducive to cooking, and he is the locus of that activity.

Similarly, in cases such as "Caitra causes Maitra to cook" (*pācyati caitro maitreṇa*), Maitra possesses the status of agent because he is the locus of the effort conducive to cooking expressed by the verbal root;
Caitra, however, possesses it precisely because he is the locus of the effort conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

In this context, because of the analysis "he causes cooking to be done" (*pākaṃ kāryati*), the meaning of the root (*nijartha*) is an operation conducive to the action of doing (*kṛti*). Thus, the definition [of the causative] is consistent. Furthermore, in cases where the object suffix (*karmalakāra*) occurs, since it is accepted that the result appears solely by way of a relation (*saṃsargavidhi*), it is not present as something denoted by the word itself; therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the boiled rice (*odana*), which is the locus of that result.

In expressions such as "the rice grains soften" (*viklidyanti taṇḍulāḥ*), because the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has the nature of characterizing the substratum of the meaning of the root, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the rice grains which possess that [softening].
Similarly, in cases such as "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*), since the verbal root indicates that the activity resides in the pot, there is no impairment of its status as an agent (*kartṛtva*).
And in the case of the "agent-as-object" (*karmakartṛ*), in this particular instance, the verbal suffix denotes the result itself.
The agency of the agent and the location, and [the agency] of the agent, the location, and the time.
The rules regarding the agent, place, and time are construed through syntactic connection (*saṃsarga*);
and there is a cognition of difference between the mental [action] and its locus.
Thus, it should be understood that both the relation of mutual connection (*svasvasambandha-anvaya*) and agency (*kartṛtva*) are established.

In the same way, expressions such as "existence (*sattā*) does not reside in a genus (*jāti*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*)" are to be explained through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth, or they are to be considered ungrammatical; this is discussed in detail elsewhere.
And in this context, for those who maintain that the third and first case endings denote the locus (*āśrayatva*), that alone is their meaning.
It should be understood, however, that everything else is obtainable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Alternatively, agency (*kartṛtva*) consists primarily in being the substratum of an action (*kṛti*), because the word "agent" (*kartṛ*) is etymologically derived from the verbal root *kṛ* (to act) combined with the suffix *tṛc*.
In other cases, the conventional usage of the term "agency" should be regarded as merely figurative.

In reality, however, because of other authorities such as "She must not be transgressed by you in matters of dharma, artha, or kāma," "In the conjunction of our husband's sacrifice" (Pāṇini 4.1.33), and "The wife and husband should pile the fires," it is understood that the ritual actions themselves possess agency just like the sacrificer. Therefore, in injunctions such as "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires in spring" and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," the hearing of the singular number—since there is no evidence for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) according to the principle of the locus of the cognition of accomplishment—indicates that the single agency belongs to both [the husband and wife] collectively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*).
And that [agency] is not merely a limited adjunct (*khaṇḍopādhi*), because that would entail contradiction;

rather, it is agency in the form of an unlimited adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) which pervades the previously mentioned limited adjuncts, and it is precisely this [agency] residing therein that constitutes oneness and so forth, as stated previously.
On this view, even though there is the status of being both object and agent, there is no contradiction regarding the nature of the fruit.

However, it is stated in the *Kaustubha* that agency (*kartṛtva*), which is the referent of the verbal suffix and consists of an indivisible attribute (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), is construed with the effort (*kṛti*) denoted by the verbal suffix itself through the relation of being the motivator of a result that is coreferential with it.
This very agency is the meaning of the instrumental case.

And in the sentence "it is cooked by Caitra" (*caitreṇa pacyate*), this [agency] is construed with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)—which is connected to the gendered [object]—either through the relation of being conducive to the activity that constitutes its own definition, or through the relation of being its definitor (*nirūpakatva*).
And this alone is the primary meaning according to the view of Kātyāyana;

it is the denotatum of the agent-terminations (*kartṛ-ākhyāta*), the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the suffix *kṛt*, and intended for the comprehension of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) caused by its connection with the verbal root.
(Rahasya, pp. 91–96).
Agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the prompter of an effort (*kṛti-prayojakatva*) or being the locus of that effort (*kṛti-samavāyitva*).
(Maṇi, p. 86). Agency is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) residing in the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).
(p. 112). Both agency and enjoyership (*bhoktṛtva*) belong to that which possesses activity, not to that which is devoid of activity.
Straightforward. Page 171. Agency (kartṛtva) exists for the sake of being an enjoyer, according to the maxim "the fruit of the scripture [accrues] to the performer" (Soma.
3.7.2). Agency is the state of being the accomplisher of the sacrificial act (vi.
According to the principle stated in the Vārttika beginning with "The status of being an agent [is established] by way of being an instrument" (Su. p.
1382): "The status of being an agent is established as an instrument, and that is what is expressed."
Ownership, however, follows thereafter as the object of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Although agency is not possible without ownership, nevertheless, once that [ownership] is obtained through another means of knowledge, the verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta-aṃśa*) denote only the portion to be performed.
Accordingly, words such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) are employed here and there for the purpose of establishing ownership.
Therefore, agency consists solely in the possession of qualities.
Vākyapadīya 3.4.4.12, p. 904. Agency is independence (svātantrya).

From the sūtra "The agent is independent" (Pāṇini 1.4.54), that meaning which is intended to be expressed as possessing independence with respect to the action shall be the agent. Independence consists in being the primary factor regarding the meaning of the verbal root.
That independent agent is of three kinds: the pure agent, the instigator, and the agent-as-object.
The first is the substratum of the activity conducive to that [result].
The second is the substratum of the result while not being the substratum of the activity. The third is the substratum of the activity conducive to that while not being the substratum of the result.

Agency (*kartṛtva*) is not, first of all, the state of being the substratum of a machine, nor is it the state of possessing mediate knowledge, desire to act, and volition directed toward its material cause, because these are absent in cases such as "the bank wishes to fall" (*kūlaṃ pipatiṣati*) and "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*).
Nor is it the state of being the instigator of other causal factors while itself not being instigated by other causal factors, since that would fail to avoid the aforementioned objections.
Rather, it is the state of being the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvartha-vyāpārāśrayatva*).

Alternatively, when a verbal suffix such as *yaṅ* (the desiderative marker) or others is not co-occurrent with [the *ātmanepada* suffix], that which is understood as possessing a property whose locus is the agent of that very suffix is the state of being the agent of that action.

In examples such as "Caitra cooks, knows, perishes," the state of being the agent of that action consists precisely in possessing an activity conducive to cooking, being the locus [of that activity], being the counter-correlative [of destruction], and so forth.
The phrase "not co-occurrent with *yaṅ* and others" is included to prevent over-extension to the object in examples such as "The rice is being cooked."

Therefore, in the cases of "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*) and "the pieces of wood cook" (*kāṣṭhāni pacanti*), agency is not contradictory even for the pot, the wood, and so forth. (Maṇi, p. 162). Agency with respect to a sacrifice (*yāgakartṛtva*) consists in being the substratum of an effort conducive to the sacrifice.
In the case of friendly rites, there is no restriction regarding the difference between the agent and the location.
Bhāṣya: There is no injunction regarding the agent, location, and time, because they are invariably present in the performance.

The agents have been stated by such [passages] as: "There is one officiating priest for the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice," "There are four officiating priests for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices," and "There are five officiating priests for the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices.
The location has been stated by such [passages] as: "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* on level ground.
The time has been stated by such [passages] as: "One should sacrifice on the full moon day with the full moon sacrifice."

Regarding these agents, places, and times, no injunction (*codanā*), nor an instigation (*vidhāna*), is made by these sentences; rather, a restatement (*anuvāda*) is made. This is because they are eternally inherent (*nityasamavāya*) in the performance (*prayoga*), that is, in the execution (*anuṣṭhāna*), since [the performance] is constant.
For indeed, no performance occurs without an agent, a place, and a time.
Therefore, it is a restatement (anuvāda).
This is the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa).
Or rather, the scriptural statement is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha).
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
It is not a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the agent, place, and time, but rather an injunction (*vidhāna*) itself.
[Objection: But was it not stated that the mention of the agent and so forth is a restatement because they are invariably present in the performance?
It is said:
that scriptural statement (śruti) serves as a restrictive rule (niyamārthā). Since there would otherwise be no restriction, the scriptural statement is intended to provide a restriction.

Regarding the performance of the Agnihotra, when one or several priests might be employed, the restrictive rule (niyama) "for the sacrificial rite of the Agnihotra, there is one priest" is stated to limit [the number] to one.

Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa), when four or more priests might be employed without restriction, the restrictive rule "for the sacrificial rite of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, there are four priests" is stated to limit the number to exactly four, including the Brahman.

In the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, when both even and uneven ground are available without restriction, the rule "one should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* on level ground" prescribes level ground.

Similarly, for the *paurṇamāsa* sacrifice, either the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) or another lunar day might be considered possible; therefore, by the injunction "one should sacrifice with the *paurṇamāsa* on the full-moon day," the time consisting of the full-moon day is prescribed as a restriction.
Thus, such scriptural statements serve the purpose of restriction (*niyama*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that this is an injunction regarding the agent, place, and time, and not a restatement (anuvāda).
What are these injunctions regarding agent, place, and time? They are for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha).
There is no injunction regarding the agent, the place, or the time, because they are invariably connected with the performance [of the rite].

Commentary: This is heard in the scriptures: "For the *pañcanakha* sacrifice, there are five officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)," "For the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there are four officiating priests," "For the *agnihotra* sacrifice, there is one officiating priest," and "For the *saumyādhvara* sacrifice, there are seventeen officiating priests.

Likewise: "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* on level ground," "One should sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva* on ground sloping toward the east," "One should sacrifice with the full-moon offering on the full-moon day," and "One should sacrifice with the new-moon offering on the new-moon day."
In this regard, there is a doubt: are the agent, place, and time being enjoined, or are they being restated?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That the agent, place, and time are not injunctions, but rather restatements.
Why? Because of their constant concomitance with the performance [of the rite].
"These [factors] are eternally inherent in the performance.
Without the agent, place, and time, the performance is not accomplished;
therefore, this is a restatement (anuvāda) of those factors already obtained through the injunction of the performance itself.
[Objection: But surely this statement will serve to prohibit [eating] poison and the like?
[Reply: No, we say.
A statement of this kind is purely injunctive; it is not prohibitive.
Therefore, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Since the faults, the agent, and the number are already implied by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), they are not enjoined;
therefore, it is a restatement.
Furthermore, the mention of "equal" (samā) does not exclude "unequal" (viṣama) and the like, because there is no prohibitive statement [to that effect].
Nor is there an exclusion of the other [options], because there is no single vowel (ekāra).
Nor is it an injunction, because it is already established.
With this intention, he said: "A statement of this kind is merely injunctive, not prohibitive" (Bhāṣya).
Or, the Śruti is for the purpose of restriction.
The Bhāṣya says: It is replied that this is not so; it is not a mere restatement (anuvāda).
A mere restatement is purposeless; if it were an injunction, it would thus bring about a new meaning. Therefore, it is an injunction.
[Objection: But surely they are already established because they are constituent parts of the performance.
[Reply: It is said:
the scriptural statement will serve the purpose of restriction.
What is this rule? It is the restriction of that which was unrestricted.
As a constituent part of the performance, all locations are applicable, but not by way of conjunction.
When it is even, it is not uneven; when it is uneven, it is not even.
This very [path] is both attained and unattained.
When it is attained, one employs the rule of the path;
therefore, even in the case of uneven fame, the rule is prescribed as equal.
Therefore, since the non-attainment of inequality occurs when there is a rule (*vidhi*), equality is prescribed.
This applies to the others as well. Consequently, it is a rule.

Since it is heard in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices that "one should sacrifice with *vrīhi* rice," the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) arises as soon as it is implied; meanwhile, the place and other such factors remain established.
Furthermore, the [occurrence of] the new and full moon festivals serves as both the occasion (*nimitta*) and the motivator (*prayojaka*).
Therefore, because the occasion is fixed, this is called a "rule" (*niyama*).

Regarding the injunctions concerning the agent, place, and time (1374): if it is argued that there is likewise a distinction of agents [in the case of the *prayāja* offerings], and if it is further argued that this applies to the *prayāja*s and so forth as well, that is not so.

For when something is obtained even without an injunction in a particular case, that which is heard [as an injunction] is designated as a "restriction" (*niyama*) because it enters into a factor that was previously unrestricted.

Nor can it be said that this is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), for that which is already established is what is restated. Therefore, the Commentary says: "The restriction of that which was unrestricted."

Śālikanātha: "Since every factor of action (*kāraka*) is obtained solely through the injunction of an act (*kriyāvidhi*), therefore it must be enjoined therein; for an injunction is purposeful only regarding what has not [otherwise] been obtained.
If the hearing of the word 'equal' (*sama*) is for the sake of precluding poison and the like,"
Exclusion by enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) would result; there is no other mode of injunction than this. Therefore, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
[The Siddhāntin says: It is not so.
There is no restriction regarding the attainment of the performance of the ritual through the injunctions for the *samad* and other offerings;
whether on level or uneven ground, the sacrifice may be performed with *soma* or with something else.
Therefore, there would be no attainment of *soma* and the rest in any case whatsoever.

"In whichever alternative there would be no possibility of obtaining *soma* and so forth even once, that injunction is established as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) because of the contingency of non-obtention. (Regarding restriction and exclusive specification, although there is no difference in the exclusion of the other, in a performance where *soma* and so forth are possible, since the scripture implies an injunction regarding non-performance, the exclusion of *viṣaya* and so forth—which would otherwise obtain—is the result. This is because [the *soma* etc. is the first to present itself; because it is proximate as the enjoined substance; and because its nature is positive, making its form lighter [than the negative exclusion]. Thus, the fulfillment of the unobtained portion is indeed the fruit.)

The cessation of [performing sacrifices on] uneven ground and so forth, however, is not the result [of the injunction], because it is the opposite of that [prescribed action] and because it is accomplished as a matter of course through the very nature of the means (*māna*).

In the case of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification), since both alternatives are eternally established, the fulfillment of an unobtained portion cannot be the result; rather, the result is simply the exclusion of the other. Thus, in the statement "one should sacrifice only on even ground," the single syllable 'eva' explains the result as the exclusion of what is unfit, but it does not exclude other fit [grounds] even in the case of *parisaṃkhyā*. Therefore, due to this difference in the results of *niyama* (restrictive rule) and *parisaṃkhyā*, [the distinction between them] is unavoidable.

The third type of injunction [in the form of a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi)]: this is the intended meaning. Regarding *soma*—due to the context of the place of the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), other places of performance that follow the same principle, as well as time, agent, rice-grains, and so forth, also come to mind; thus, there is a connection based on their attainment. However, according to the Sūtra: "There would be no injunction of the agent and so forth, but rather a mere restatement (anuvāda), because in the performance there is already a restriction regarding the commonality of the agent and the rest."
[The opponent] says: "In the injunction *yajeta same* ('one should sacrifice on level ground'), is there a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the location and so forth, or is it an injunction (*vidhi*)?
It is a restatement because [the requirement for a location] is already established by the very impossibility of performing the ritual [without one].
The mention of 'on level ground' is intended to exclude the alternative of 'on uneven ground.'"
In this case, a restriction is prescribed by means of the proportion of the portions not yet obtained.

Bhaṭṭa: In that regard, the agents such as the Adhvaryu and others, the times such as the full moon (paurṇamāsī) and others, the places such as the sacrificial ground (samā) and others, the materials such as rice (vrīhi) and others, the qualities such as whiteness and others, and the purificatory rites such as threshing (avaghāta) and others—all these are heard in their respective sentences and are enjoined because they are obtained through implication by the injunction of the ritual action itself. Thus, when the prima facie objection arises that these are not employed by the injunctions of the ritual action because they are restricted [by other means], [the reply is: as long as these are obtained through implication in an unrestricted manner, so long does the formulation of an injunction with restriction as its result, by means of a specific statement, establish restriction itself as the motive for their employment.

And every type of restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is [to be understood] by the principle of anticipating what is yet to come (*anāgatāvekṣaṇanyāya*); this has been demonstrated in the *Kaustubha* within the section on Mantras (*mantrādhikaraṇa*).

Maṇḍana states: "In a sentence concerning place and so forth, a restriction (*niyama*) is the thing to be enjoined. Śaṅkara states: "With respect to time and so forth, a restriction is the injunction."
The lifelong recitation is a duty of the performer.
As many rites as are heard of by the names of their performers, so many [performers]—namely, the officiating priests—are required to be chosen; thus they are established.
(Bhāṣya 3.7.9).
The Principle of the Agent (*kartṛnyāya*). (The Section on the Agent, 3.4.12–13).
When the agent is primary—as in the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*)—there is no object to be accomplished; therefore, there should be no requirement for the means of accomplishment.

For [the question] "by whom, for what purpose, and how" does not arise regarding the act of becoming (*bhavati*); however, when the emphasis is on the action itself (*bhāvaprādhānye*), [these questions] do arise. (Bhāṣya 1.1.4.24). There is a difference of agent (*kartṛbheda*).

In the case of the *Agnicayana* and the *Sautrāmaṇī*, because of the difference in sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇābhedāt*), a difference of agent is understood from the statement: "The fee is a mare (*vaḍavā dakṣiṇā*). This refers to the distinction between the primary and subsidiary elements.
If it is argued that there is likewise a difference of performers:

regarding the inquiry as to whether the performers in the southern and northern sacrificial enclosures (*vihāra*) during the Varuṇapraghāsa rites are distinct or whether they constitute a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
just as it was stated in the preceding section that the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) for both enclosures are distinct, so too there should be a difference of performers.
If the proponent should say, "In both cases, the agents would also be distinct because of [their association with] all [the qualities]," we reply:
No, because of inherence (samavāya).
In both ritual stations (*vihāra*), it is not the case that all the performers are distinct.

For the *hotṛ*, while remaining in his own place, is indeed capable of directing the *pratiprasthātṛ* just as he does the *adhvaryu* by reciting the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. As for the *āgnīdhra*—

If it is argued that there is thus a difference of agents, [we reply: even in the section concerning the agent (*kartṛ-adhikaraṇa*), one who is situated in the *utkara* region will perform the response to the call (*pratyāśrāvaṇa*).
Furthermore, the Brahman priest, having been initiated and remaining present in both sacrificial enclosures (*vihāra*), will grant permission after inspecting what has and has not been performed.
Therefore, these [five] constitute the framework for these sacrifices.
Because of their collective association, as stated in the injunction, "There are five officiating priests (ṛtvij) for the Cāturmāsya sacrificial rites," there is a connection with exactly five;
otherwise, there would be ten.
The Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ—these two officiating priests (ṛtvij) are distinct.
For in this way, there would be five;
however, if the Adhvaryu were also to share the same ritual procedure (tantra), there would be only four, not five.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark:
in the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, it is stated that "he gives one dakṣiṇā for the sake of both vihāras [altars] to an aged man"; this indicative mark demonstrates that there is a single agent.
Thus, the performers constitute a single unit (tantra).
"An aged person, meaning one who is old. [The opponent] says: "Because of the connection with the altar," thus says the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin).
"One foot of the Hotṛ is within the altar, another is outside the altar"—thus the connection of the Hotṛ with the altar is heard in the scripture.
Furthermore, the placement of the feet on the altar must be performed at the northern corner (uttaraśroṇī).
And that cannot be accomplished by a single Hotṛ alone, because there are two deities, one in the south and one in the north, [to whom the fruits belong].
Therefore, two Hotṛ priests must indeed be appointed. Furthermore, on account of this indicative mark (liṅga), all [the priests] would be distinct.
No, because it is merely a matter of location.
The proponent says:
This is not so.

Because it is merely a matter of location, by the statement "another [foot] within the altar" (*antarvedyanyaḥ*) and so forth, only the location is prescribed; in that location, the Hotṛ has independence, such that one of his feet should be within the altar and the other outside the altar.
A foot of the *hotṛ* priest is not prescribed as a contributing factor for the altar (*vedi*) or the two sacrificial sites (*vedī*).
Furthermore, there are indeed two feet belonging to a single *hotṛ*;
therefore, there is no requirement for two *hotṛ*s for that purpose.
Furthermore, the Hotṛ priest—or the two Hotṛs—need not stand at both altars.
Therefore, there is no difference in the performer.
Ke.
There is a difference of performers due to the difference of sacrificial fees;
and from the difference of performers, there is a difference of subsidiaries.
There is no difference in the agent in the case of the *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee) in the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice. (*Dvādaśāhikanyāya*, 1.1.4.17).
And from the difference in the agent follows a difference in the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*).

In the Rājasūya sacrifice, there is a distinction between the performers (kartṛ) due to the difference in sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) in the triad beginning with the Somāpauṣṇa and the triad beginning with the Āgnāvaiṣṇava; and because of this distinction in performers, there is a distinction in the subsidiary elements (aṅga) of the two triads.
(Vi.
1.1.4) An action becomes praiseworthy through its connection with human agents.
And that which is praiseworthy is to be established.
Bhāṣya 6.1.2.26:
"Like the agent."

Just as the long stature of the agent is not the cause for the *saṃtardana* (joining together), so too are the *saṃsthās* (sacrificial forms); for in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the purpose of *saṃtardana*, which is "for the sake of both supporting and non-supporting," there is an equal connection with the explanatory passage without distinction in the case of the *saṃsthās* as well, just as in the case of the agent's long stature.
The phrase "for the sake of support" (*ghṛtyai*) is the explanatory passage.
‘“May it be long for me, may it be firm through the pressing.

Just as the agent [is not to be indicated], so too the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is like the agent (AŚ 3.2.16–18). In the Soma consumption mantra, the deity of the *anuvaṣaṭ*-offering is not to be indicated, just as the agent [is not].
Just as the agent is not specified [by the words] "drunk by the Hotṛ" or "drunk by the Adhvaryu," so too the deity of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* should not be specified [by the word] "intended.

(Bhāṣya). Optionality of the agent: "One, two, or many may sacrifice with the *ahīna* [sacrifice]. (Bāla. p. 163). Injunction regarding the agent: An explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"This indeed is the oblation for one who has not established the sacred fires, namely this which is offered now. (Bāla. p. 163).

(6.8.1 Adhikaraṇa), p. 55, in the form of an injunction regarding the agent: the *arthavāda* states, “Thus indeed said the young student Vādhri: ‘Cook for me only the *māṣa* beans. (6.7.2 Adhikaraṇa), p. 56, this *bhāvanā* consists precisely in the general activity of the agent, and it brings that very [activity] to mind in its specific form. Vārttika 3.4.4.13, p. 917: Furthermore, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent—namely, eating—is the most internal [of all].
"Because there is no recollection of an author, the Vedas are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

[Objection: Since their purpose is fulfilled by the recollection of their meaning, the application of the term 'author' is a negation based on the non-recollection of a source; it is a delusion due to lack of respect [for the Vedas]. [Response: This is incorrect.
— Vaidyanātha, *Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī*, 1.1.8.129.
The section on the agent (*kartṛ-adhikaraṇa*). The principle of the agent (*kartṛ-nyāya*).
The principle of the expression of the agent (*kartṛ-nirdeśa-nyāya*).
Or rather—the question is: is the agent intended by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), or not?

In that regard, if he is intended, then because it is directly stated (*śruta*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), which requires a purpose, becomes for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) by means of a statement that [otherwise] its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) would be understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*).
If, on the other hand, he is not intended, then, in the absence of a conflict with the direct statement, its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice follows from the context.

Now, even though the agent is denoted, because the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) primarily expresses the efficient force (bhāvanā), the connection of that which is introduced by it—even if it is directly expressed (śrauta)—is not at all contradicted by its being for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvarthatā), since it is consistent with the context (prakaraṇa).
For two connections of equal status would indeed contradict one another, but not those that stand in the relation of subordinate and principal.

For example, in the case of the injunction "He cleanses the cup with the fringed filter," there arises no such doubt as to whether the cleansing— which has the fringed filter as its subordinate instrument— is to be connected with the filter or with the cup.
Likewise, here too, there is no contradiction in an action that has an agent as its subordinate factor being undertaken in relation to the sacrifice.
If, however, the verbal suffix were to express the predominance of the agent, then there would be a contradiction with the predominance of the sacrifice understood from the context.
Or, if the sacrifice were to possess a subordinate status just like the agent, then a contradiction regarding the coexistence of two subordinates with a single principal would be observed.
But neither of these two cases exists.

Therefore, because the Śruti [text] indicates that the agent is subordinate and the context (prakaraṇa) indicates that the sacrifice is primary, there is no contradiction due to their having different objects and thus not being co-present.
It might be argued that "in the absence of that [co-presence], there would be subordination here," but this is not so.
"Even though the agent is initially understood as subordinate within the action,
nevertheless its status as the primary factor is not subsequently negated.

Even though an action, at first requiring an instrument of accomplishment, grasps the agent as subordinate, nevertheless, at the time when that action requires a purpose, it is the agent alone who is proximate.
He is capable of bringing that [result] about;
yet even he, while attaining the status of an instrument, expects: "How will this [agent] benefit me? Thus he awaits.

Furthermore, when two things are conveyed by a single word and their mutual relationship is being established, the connection with the sacrifice is not grasped due to the remoteness [of the relationship].
Moreover, when an inherent contribution (*sāmavāyikatva*, i.e., proximity-based assistance) is possible, one should not assume an indirect contribution (*ārādupakārakatva*).

Likewise, in the case of the injunction, "Having performed the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma, he subsequently prepares the *paśupuroḍāśa* cake for Agni-Soma," since the deity is already expressed as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), and since the sacrifice has a requirement for a purpose, it is understood that the two items proximate to the term *agnīṣomīyasya*—namely, the omentum and the cake—are the objects to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*). Thus, it is not assumed that the animal (meaning the animal-sacrifice in relation to the *paśupuroḍāśa*-sacrifice) serves as a consecratory object merely as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).
For prior subordination (*guṇatva*) is not contradicted by subsequent predominance (*prādhānya*).
When the postulation of a purpose is inevitable, there must be primacy for one [of the two]; it is the same here as well.
Alternatively, the agent is denoted by the verb alone, while the status of being subordinate or primary will occur according to the sense, as desired and as appropriate.
Thus, between the two actions, the relationship of subordinate and primary is established through mutual expectation, proximity, and compatibility.
"Or rather, both [the suffixes], remaining in their specific positions by virtue of the sequence,
express the meaning of the suffix together, with the meaning of the base as a subordinate element.
Thus it is said.

Therefore, even in the case of a verb (ākhyāta), it is the agent alone— subordinated to the meaning of the verbal root— that is expressed as the primary element by both [the suffix and the root], just as in the case of a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix. Indeed,
no other rule that would serve as an exception to this general principle or traditional maxim is found either through reasoning or through tradition.
Therefore,
although the agent (kāraka) in cases such as "the cook" possesses an undisputed predominance,
nevertheless, the state of being an object to be accomplished (sādhyatva) is not attributed to the actions themselves.

And likewise, in cases such as the oneness of the person (*puruṣaikatva*) and so forth—where the *śruti* characterized by being expressed within a single word is present, yet [the meaning] is determined by the *vākya* to be for the sake of action—it will be stated: "The meaning of the *vākya* does not set aside that which has become *śruti*" (*na śrutibhūte vākyārtho bādhakaḥ*; cf. *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya* 4.1.5, p.
Therefore, here too it can be said: "The meaning of the *prakaraṇa* does not set aside that which has become *śruti*."
Furthermore: "Even if agency is indeed expressed here primarily, its status as a subordinate factor (guṇatva) must be understood as being established by implication (pāratantryataḥ).
Primary expression refers to the intended meaning (tātparya), not to the state of being a principal object (śeṣitva)."
Therefore, in this context, if the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) refers to the agent, then its subordinate status (*guṇatva*) is all the more clearly expressed;
for one who does not act is not called an "agent.
And whoever performs an action is invariably subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to that action; thus, for such a person, primacy (*prādhānya*) by way of being the principal element (*śeṣitva*) is untenable.
This must also be stated regarding the position that [the agent] is designated by the term "indifference" (*audāsīnya*).

(He refutes the second resolution: As for what was said—"The agent is expressed solely by the suffix, while the relationship of subordinate and principal will follow from the sense" (Vārttika 902.9)—even there, if the agent is expressed merely as a thing-in-itself, then, because it remains in a state of indifference, it may assume the status of either a subordinate (*aṅga*) or a principal (*aṅgin*) as desired.
But since that [agent] is denoted precisely as having the nature of a quality (*guṇa*) by virtue of its being the agent, there is no state of neutrality.

(He refutes the first solution mentioned in the verse, "Even though initially [denoted] as a quality": As for what was said—that "even though denoted as a quality, it again attains primacy through the requirement of the second case"—that too is untenable because it contradicts direct statement (*śruti*). For the agency, in the form of a synonym for a quality, is denoted by the verb itself through direct statement; if it were subsequently set aside, a contradiction with direct statement would result.

Nor does this lead to the consequence of meaninglessness through another assumption, because it is assumed in this way precisely since the possibility of a purpose is established by the context (*prakaraṇa*).

And just as when the agent is not explicitly expressed, it is sufficient for application by context without opposition, so too there is no contradiction even when it is expressed in such a form. Furthermore, a single suffix, being uttered only once, cannot simultaneously express both subordinate and primary status.

In that case, if one were to rely upon only one [of the two] while intending to express predominance, then, by setting aside the agency characterized by being the primary factor in the action, there would follow the consequence of its being an object (*karman*) because it is being attained by that [action]. Consequently, the *lakāra* suffix would be prescribed for that very [object]; and due to the application of the *yak*, *ātmanepada*, and other affixes, the verbal form would take on a different shape. Specifically, if the *lakāra* were prescribed for the object, because of the application of *yak*, *ātmanepada*, *saṃprasāraṇa*, and *sīyuṭ*, the resulting word would be something like *udyeta*, but not something like *vadet*.
Now, it might be argued: "No agent ever engages in an action without aiming at some purpose.
Therefore, agency consists solely of substance, taking the form of the instrument (*sādhaka*) and the form of the owner of the fruit of the action (*kriyāphalasvāmin*).
When both [aspects] are expressed, two expectations (*ākāṅkṣā*) arise, which will be fulfilled by the action."
That is not correct.

Why? Because agency is established as being the means of accomplishment (*sādhakatva*), and that is what is denoted [by the verbal suffix]. Ownership, however, is apprehended by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only after that.

Although agency (*kartṛtva*) is not possible without ownership (*svāmitva*), nevertheless, since that [ownership] is obtainable through other means of knowledge, the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) expresses only its unopened portion.
Thus, for the purpose of establishing ownership, the various means such as all ritual actions (*sarvakarma*) and so forth are employed in various places.
Therefore, agency is merely a subordinate quality (*guṇatva*).
And for this reason—meaning precisely this—it is so; for instance, agency is attributed even to insentient things such as wood.
Yet, in those cases, there is no aiming at a fruit; therefore, your restriction [of the definition] is untenable. Indeed, pervasion must be accepted as the defining characteristic of agency.
Furthermore, aiming for a result (*phaloddeśa*) is not all-pervasive, because it is absent in insentient things;
however, the state of being a means of accomplishment (*sādhakatva*) is all-pervasive. Therefore, that alone must be accepted [as the basis].
(He concludes with two sūtras of resolution: "Therefore, it is not at all logical that [the world] has the human goal as its purpose."
An objection must be raised against this.
To refute the third response and to address the criticism stated in the *Vārttika* beginning with "In that case, this would follow" (*vā. pṛ.* 903), he says: "To this it is replied:

although subordinacy (*śeṣatva*) is not directly expressed by the Vedic text (*śruti*), nevertheless, that very state of being a subordinate element (*upasarjanatva*) which constitutes its subordination also brings about its status as a subsidiary (*śeṣatva*)."

Therefore, for the time being, that which consists of the expression [of the purpose] is indeed the means (*upāya*); even in the case of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), that alone must be accepted as such.

Even in cases such as "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*), by virtue of the function of the word's meaning, it follows that the king and so forth possess the status of a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*); however, on the strength of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the opposite is postulated.
And this has been demonstrated in the section concerning substance (*sattvādhikaraṇa*).

And it has already been stated that something does not become the meaning of a word merely by this much. Furthermore, the word functions with respect to that very aspect of the king which is a quality (*guṇatva*) even in reality; and such an aspect exists.
How so? "The king first attains the state of being a quality (*guṇatva*) toward the Brahmins and men;
he subsequently assumes lordship (*svāmitva*). But the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) depends on one's preference.

In that context, when a man qualified by the king is intended to be expressed, then—in accordance with the meaning of the words—one must intend to express the state of being a benefactor (*upakārakatva*), even though it exists as an absolute reality.

Furthermore, when the state of being assisted (*upakāryatva*) is intended to be expressed, then—since that [state] falls under the category of a specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*)—the persons who act as the benefactors (*upakāraka*) by virtue of being the king's commands become the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*); thus, the compound *puruṣarāja* (king’s men) alone should be employed.

Since the existing word-form (*prayoga-dravya*) can apply to both meanings, why should we resort to such a cumbersome arrangement based merely on a difference of intention (*vivakṣā-bheda*), depending on the action to be described hereafter?

Therefore, when the term *nimitta* (cause) is employed in the sense of *bhūta* (actual), it is understood that in the case of "the king’s servant" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), what is intended to be expressed is precisely the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) based on the fact of providing assistance (*upakāra*).

Even in cases where the status of being a subordinate is absolutely non-existent in the owner of a cow, a slave, or the like, it should be regarded as a figurative usage (*upacarita*) because the possibility of providing assistance still exists.

Furthermore, even if "subordinate status" (*upasarjanatva*) were defined merely as being "beneficial" (*upakārakatva*) for the sake of establishing the primacy of such things [as the agent], and not as "subsidiarity" (*śeṣatva*), nevertheless, because subsidiarity alone possesses such a result, this [definition] is more closely related to it than the status of the principal (*śeṣin*); thus, it is understood precisely as a means of comprehending subsidiarity. Even in cases such as "cook" (*pācaka*), since the state of being produced by that [action] exists everywhere and the quality of being beneficial is present, actions possess subordinate status; they do not possess primacy by virtue of existing as the object to be accomplished (*nirvartya*).

[Objection: But if this were the case, then even in the instance “by means of the two winnowing-basket and pestle that have been sprinkled” (*prokṣitābhyām ulkhalamusalābhyām*), it would follow that the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is for the sake of the substance. [Reply: For whom is this undesirable? (The meaning is: it is not undesirable for us. It is not so;

for if this were the case, there would be no contradiction with the discussion [in *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 1.1.2–3] concerning whether [the sprinkling] is connected with the acts of threshing and grinding, or connected with the sacrificial cakes (*apūpa*).

How indeed is there a contradiction? For when the *tantra* (the ritual procedure) and the *yukti* (the logical application) are one thing, while the *tādarthya* (the purposefulness) is another. Since the status of being for the sake of the substance (*dravyārthatva*) is established, and since the properties (*dharmas*) are prompted by the action (*karman*), the question arises: should they be employed by the immediate effects—the striking (*hanti*) and the grinding (*piṣi*)—or by the remote effect, the *apūrva*? Furthermore, even the inquiry regarding that *tādarthya* must be viewed in this very same way, without abandoning the mortar and pestle: is this sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) for the sake of that which is the means to striking and grinding, or for the sake of that which is the means to the *apūrva*?
"Even though the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is concealed, it would not grasp the action;

however, the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), when manifested, will be grasped by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). The case-factors (*kāraka*) expressed by primary derivatives (*kṛdanta*) would be unable to grasp the action as the meaning of a noun because they are concealed, whereas those ending in nominal suffixes (*sup*) are able to do so because they are manifested."

As for the argument that because this [number] is expressed by a single word, it does not deviate from the meaning of the verbal root and thus its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice is not contradicted—this is not so. It is said: "Because it is grasped by the *kāraka* (case-role), number and the like are for the sake of the action; however, because the status of being a *kāraka* has ceased, they are sublated and become subordinate to the substance.

Number and the like might occur merely through the effort associated with a substance that has become subordinate to a *kāraka*; but these are taken away by the *kāraka*, which is the ultimate instrument of accomplishment, and are led toward the action."

But the verbal roots (*dhātvartha*) are not understood by any more powerful means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to have action as their purpose, such that their status as subordinate to the agent would be sublated.

As for the argument that because the agency is of the nature of a subordinate factor (*guṇa*), when its predominance is expressed, it necessarily results in [the agent] becoming a subordinate factor—that is incorrect.
Why? Because, according to the treatises of the Śāstra, "the entitlement (*adhikriyā*) belongs to conscious agents."
If performed according to the injunctions, these [actions] do not produce results because of the absence of a mental resolve for fruit (*phala-saṃkalpa*).
Although agency belongs to every performer simply by virtue of being an agent, nevertheless, in the case of those who act with prior reflection, that agency is mixed with a resolve for fruit.
Only such persons possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for Vedic rites, not insentient beings.
All actions, when conjoined with an injunction (*vidhi*), are [considered] unimpaired; for even prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) are dependent upon their connection with the cognition of an injunction.
Furthermore, an injunction is not possible without a sense of duty (*kartavyatā*) directed toward a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
Therefore, a person being addressed as one who must necessarily perform [the action] determines: "This action of mine will benefit me, either directly or through a succession of steps."

It is not possible for [the agent] to be a direct benefactor, nor is it obtained through being an indirect cause. Furthermore, the agent is not incapable of being refined (*saṃskāra*), because he is the primary purpose by virtue of being the substratum for the fruit of the ritual (*kratu*).
If it is asked, "What is his benefit?", it is determined in every respect that there is at least a general benefit.
By that much, its status as being for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvarthatva*) has been set aside;
and the specific determination of that [status] will be postulated as desired.
But this [postulation] is not useful.
(He concludes the third response: Therefore, [the agent] does not exist for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*).

Even though the aspect of predominance (*prādhānya*) is not explicitly expressed by the word denoting agency (*kartṛtva*), nor is it included therein, nevertheless, because it cannot otherwise be accounted for, it is established through the force of the suffix itself.

Just as the fact that heaven is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) will be inferred—even though it is not mentioned—by words such as "one who desires heaven" which denote a specific person, so too ownership (*svāmitva*) is understood from the very perception of agency on the part of a person acting intentionally out of a desire for the fruit.

In this regard, just as the predominance of the deity who is intended by the ritual act is understood solely for the purpose of establishing its status as a means (*sādhana*) of the sacrifice—and not as terminating in the nature of predominance itself—so too should its subordinate character (*guṇatva*) be viewed. For it is said: "The subordinate status of the agents is not perceived with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*);
but since they are subordinate to the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), why would the meaning of the verbal root not be subordinate to them?"
Even for one who holds that the agent is the meaning of the suffix, he too must necessarily admit *bhāvanā* on the strength of cognition;
and since it is grasped by the same suffix, it is this [bhāvanā] alone that possesses primacy and incorporates the agent, and not the meaning of the verbal root.

In that case, it will be brought forward; therefore, by the force of the context, it will be established as the meaning of the treatise (śāstra). However, being occupied with the cultivation (bhāvanā), he is unable to perform anything other than that. Indeed, the entire treatise, when its literal meaning pertains to action, accepts only that [cultivation] as its objective.
Nor is it contradictory for there to be a dual nature; it is not useless, for in that case, it brings about the self for the sake of the definition.
This is indeed the meaning of the direct statement (*śruti*), precisely because the objects are different.
If, in this context, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is employed as being subordinate only with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
Furthermore, both *śruti* (direct denotation) and *lakṣaṇā* (indication) cannot be assumed simultaneously; thus, if they were taken together at once, there would be a contradiction.
However, their utility for the purpose [of the sacrifice] is well-established.

Therefore, just as in the case of "the front one runs," here there is no contradiction: while there is subsidiarity (*guṇatva*) toward the *bhāvanā*, there is primacy (*prādhānya*) toward the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—for when the meaning of the root is mentioned, because of its inherent relationship, even though another [element] is implied, it is not [excluded] by the function [of the word].

And the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is included within both; likewise, even when another [meaning] is intended, the object consisting of the agent and its relation is understood through the power of the word.

If the word arises in that very way, why is there any contradiction? It is simply because of the restriction [of the speaker's intention] that it is not grasped as being useful [for that specific purpose]. Is this established? Or rather, one [aspect] is from the word and one is from the capacity (*sāmarthya*); and since this cognition is also applicable as a secondary quality (*guṇatva*), there is no contradiction.
In every respect, there is first the consequence of the agent's predominance; furthermore, [the agent] brings about even the conceptualization of that predominance.

And at that time, according to the principle that "the efficient force (bhāvanā) has the agent as its locus," it follows that the meaning of the verbal root would be for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha).

Moreover, this is another distinction: for the sake of establishing its own existence, the connection of a cook or the like with another action is perceived only as something already made subordinate by the mere fact that [the primary action] cannot otherwise be accomplished.

In that case, it is understood [as subordinate] and not as the primary element; thus, the predominance [of the root-meaning] would be established by the word alone without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and it would merely serve as a qualifier for the verbal root.
The comprehension of the word's meaning would occur [in this way].
For *bhāvanā* does not lead one to understand that [root-meaning] as the primary element, since the meanings of things (*vastvartha*) are of both kinds.
Regarding the section on the agent (kartṛ-adhikaraṇa),
the teachers say that neither the agent nor the object is expressed by the suffix in the sense of the agent.
Is it not the case that the verbal suffix (lakāra) is heard in both the sense of the agent and the object?
It is not heard as denoting either the agent or the object; rather, there is another statement therein: "the singular number is used for one, the dual for two, and the plural for many.
In that context, the connection is made thus: "when there is one agent," "when there are two agents," or "when there are many agents."
Thus, [the rule applies] when there is one object (*karman*).
How then? It means that the singular number is used when there is one agent (*kartṛ*), i.e., when there is oneness of the agent;
likewise for duality and plurality, as well as for the object.

When it is explained in this way, the meaning of the Sūtra is described as being consistent with worldly logic (*laukikanyāya*), and the very syllables of the Sūtra become consistent with that logic. This is indeed the traditional teaching (*āgama*): "When singularity and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings, then action (*karman*) and so forth function as qualifiers.
But is it not also the case: "When action and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings, then singularity and so forth function as qualifiers"?

It is said: For [factors] such as the ritual action (*karman*) are obtained through the force of the meaning (*arthaprāpta*); therefore, they become the expressed meanings (*sāmidheya*) of the word. However, [qualities] such as singularity (*ekatva*) are not obtained through the force of the meaning; therefore, they constitute the expressed meanings of the word itself.

Consequently, although singularity and so forth are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), nevertheless it is the qualifier itself that is denoted. Just as in the case of the statement, "The priests wearing golden garlands proceed with the sacrifice," although "wearing golden garlands" is perceived as a qualifier, nevertheless that very thing is what is enjoined.
Therefore, the meaning of the word is the singleness of the agent, not the agent itself (p.
130). Or rather: (1.913) "In all verbal forms, the agents are certainly not intended to be denoted.
As for the cognition that arises from them, it must arise from another [grammatical] connection."
In every case, when a word is uttered, many meanings are understood;

yet not all of these become its denotable meaning (*abhidheya*), because the postulation of a denotative power (*vācaka-śakti*) is not justified unless it is established that the cognition of the meaning occurs only when that specific power is present.
A meaning is indeed said to be "denoted" only where the denotative power of the word is postulated.

And where is this [unperceived entity] postulated when it is not seen? It is postulated in a case where cognition and linguistic usage would otherwise be impossible without that postulation. However, where those two are established elsewhere by means of that very object [already perceived], even though it has not been postulated there, then its non-existence can be understood through non-perception—just as in the case of class-words (*ākṛtiśabda*) with respect to individuals, and of words such as "lion" with respect to humans and the like.

Thus, here, from the utterance of the word *pañcāśat* ("fifty"), these many meanings are understood: the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the agent (*kartṛ*), its number (*saṃkhyā*), the person (*puruṣa*), the voice (*upagraha*), and the specific tense (*kāla*).

(Persons: those of the first, middle, and highest types; voices: those of the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* forms). However, the distinction between which of these belongs to the word and which belongs to the meaning is not known.

And according to this definition—"that which is understood from the sense (of the word) is the meaning of the word"—we do not perceive any indicator of the *bhāvanā* other than the word itself; for in that regard, factors such as time (*kāla*) and so forth are variable, since time, number, and the like can indeed exist even without a *bhāvanā*.

If it is argued that [the *bhāvanā*] is understood because it is invariably concomitant with the agent and the object, we say no; for then there would follow the undesirable consequence that it would be perceived as non-primary, just like a verbal root ending in a *kṛt* suffix.

If the *bhāvanā* were understood through the agent and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then it would be understood as having its own nature obscured, as in the case of words such as "cook" (*pācaka*). However, because it is perceived as the primary element, there is the undesirable consequence that it must be the denotation of the word itself. Furthermore, time and other factors are not conveyed by the *bhāvanā*, because they are seen to vary across different times, numbers, persons (*puruṣa*), and voices (*upagraha*). Thus, precisely because of this mutual variation, it is understood that time, number, and so forth cannot be conveyed [by the *bhāvanā*].

Furthermore, since the agent is understood here as being subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), and since the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) cannot be established without such an agent, [the agent] can be made known either through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or through inference (*anumāna*).

If it is argued that [this inference] is incapable because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) caused by its connection with other factors (*kāraka*), we say no; for we do not admit a deviation consisting merely of a connection with something else.
Indeed, one single relation connects itself with many in two ways: some abandon the other relatum, while others do so without abandoning the previous one.

In that regard, that which, having abandoned one thing, occurs elsewhere, becomes non-conclusive due to its deviation (*vyabhicāra*), such as [the property of] being upright with respect to both a post and a person. And in that case, there is no connection with anything else; how then can there be deviation?
What then? It is occurrence even without that [specific object].

However, that which exists elsewhere as well—existing only by way of the fulfillment of a previously understood relationship, such as the state of being a *śiṃśapā* existing within [the categories of] being a tree, being an earthy substance, and so forth—is not "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*), because its power to pervade all [instances] remains unimpaired. Furthermore, the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) residing in the causal factors (*kārakas*) does not exist in a fragmented or partial form; rather, it exists simultaneously in all of them. And this is not called "deviant," because even when it occurs elsewhere, it does not abandon its prior [universal] nature.
Therefore, all the factors of action (*kārakas*) are undoubtedly understood.

Even in cases where—due to the verb being intransitive (*akarmaka*), or because the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*) are more external [to the action]—there might be a suspicion of deviation because they are not perceived, even there it is only those [other factors] that are absent, and never the agent (*kartṛ*). For there is no action whatsoever that exists without an agent, since the commencement of action is rooted in that [agent].
Or rather, there is an even greater purpose here in its non-deviation from that [the agent]:
while other [means of knowledge] may deviate, the capacity of this [scripture] alone to convey the agent is more clearly manifested. This is what must be established.

The section concerning the agent (*kartṛ-adhikaraṇa*) is indeed for this purpose: to establish the unique status of the agent when its connection with number is to be effected [in order to demonstrate that *bhāvanā* does not deviate toward other factors of action].

However, because [the agent] is not a derivative (taddhita) [of the action], it requires an instrument; because in cases such as moving or falling, the destruction of the substratum is observed; because there is an absence of an object in intransitive verbs; and because in verbs such as "sitting," "standing," or "speaking," there is no recipient (saṃpradāna) or point of departure (apādāna), the agent alone is invariably proximate in all verbal processes (bhāvanās). Thus, it is connected with a number that is expressed by its own specific [grammatical] form (*tiruvācyā*) due to its unique status.
Furthermore, it is evident to everyone that in this context, the number understood is one that qualifies the agent, and not one residing in any other kāraka.

In this regard, if someone were to say: "Since all factors of action (*kāraka*) are equally understood [as being denoted], why is there a connection with number only for the agent (*kartṛ*), and not for the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the others as well?"—he should be told: "It is just as it is for you. If he should reply: "In my view, the agent and the number are both expressed by a single word and thus restrict each other; therefore, since the number is restricted to that which is not otherwise expressed, it must reside in the agent alone," [then the response follows].

In this regard, one must respond as follows: "Now, since the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in action) is equal [for all], what is the reason that you claim only the agent (*kartṛ*) is denoted, and not the other *kārakas*? In this case, one must necessarily take refuge in the very power of the word (*śabdaśakti*), which is to be understood through its result (*phala*), because it is from that [power] that the cognition arises. And that [cognition] is no different even in the case of the [opponent's] false position (*asatpakṣa*), since we perceive number (*saṃkhyā*) residing solely in the agent.
Therefore, such is the extent of this power; how then could it be understood from the effect?

If it is asked, "When the presence of the causal factor (*kāraka*) is equal across all *bhāvanās*, what is the cause for the restriction of [specific] capacity (*śakti*)?", the answer is: "That which has been stated—that when the status as a causal factor is equal, the expression of the agent (*kartṛ*) is the cause for the restriction of capacity. Nor can this be questioned; it has already been stated that the arrangement must be understood according to the specific effect [of each word] (as in *śakyaḥ sarvabhāvanā* etc., 2.1.15, p. 378).
Furthermore, you will first postulate a capacity for the expression of the agent, and then you will further postulate a capacity for the expression of its number.

[Objection: Surely, since that [distinction] is established by the very fact of being based on a single cognition, no further conceptualization (*kalpanā*) need be resorted to. Why? For how can a restriction be established without postulating multiple potencies (*aneka-śakti*)? Indeed, this too must necessarily be postulated: that when the same number is applicable, it expresses the number only of what has been expressed (*abhihita*), and not of what has not been expressed. For without such a potency, the opposite would be asserted: "Since the agent is expressed from that very [verbal suffix], its number should not be stated; for by that much alone, there is a distinction between those that are expressed and those that are not. Why is this so?
Moreover, that which is expressed does not become the sole cause for its grammatical determination (*vyavasthā*);

for even in the case of those [factors] that are expressed—such as the specific qualifications regarding the time of action (*bhāvanākāla*) and the inclusion [of the object]—there exists a connection with number (*saṃkhyā*) by means of that very same cognition.
Indeed, that which appears as being perceived as primary would all the more readily enter into syntactic connection (*saṃbadhnīyāt*).

If, however, it is argued that there is no connection [of number] with those [factors] due to their unsuitability (*ayogyatā*), then this is no different even in the case of other factors (*kāraka*) which are merely implied (*gamyamāna*).

If you say, "They do possess suitability for a connection with number, by virtue of which they are connected with the number expressed by another word," then the same applies to *bhāvanā* and so forth when they are expressed by words such as *bhāvayet*. Now, if it is argued that they are unsuitable here because they are non-existent (*asadbhūtatva*), that is incorrect.
This is because it is precisely the non-existence of the entity that has been questioned.
For absolute non-existence does not follow merely from a thing's unsuitability for connection with number and so forth.

In this regard, one must also accept the following: "Number, or the *bhāvanā* and other factors, expressed by such a word, are unable to enter into mutual relation. And this [objection] is equal [to our position], because what is expressed by this [word] is likewise unfit for connection with other *kārakas*.

If it is asked how there is a lack of connection [with the number], it has been stated that [the status of] being the object of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) and so forth arises through the power of the word's expressive capacity (*śabdaśakti*).

Now, one might object: "In cases such as 'the rice is cooked' (*pacyate odanaḥ*), it is observed that the object possesses a connection with the number expressed by the verbal suffix; therefore, such a connection would necessarily follow for [the object] here as well.
This is not so.
Why? [Because: "Just as even when expressed by a *tiṅ*-suffix, the action (*karman*) will not be expressed elsewhere;
likewise, its number (*saṃkhyā*) also remains fixed solely by the power of the word.

For one who thinks, "Since it is observed that the action has its number expressed by a *tiṅ*-suffix in some instances, therefore it must also have another [number] expressed in other cases," for him, because the state of being expressed by a *tiṅ*-suffix is observed in some instances, there would necessarily be expressibility [of that number] everywhere.
Now, if that [agent] somehow remains present, then number will likewise remain established; this is what must be understood. In this regard, one might argue:

"Number, being expressed as qualified by the agent, cannot be spoken of while expressing only the agent. To this it is replied: "The apprehension of a qualified object is not desired unless the qualifier has been apprehended. But when there is the expression of the expressed, no one will abandon it."
"Since a specific cognition does not arise unless its qualifier has been apprehended," that apprehension is required for the sake of the meaning;
however, nothing is impaired by the mere fact that the qualifier has not been expressed.
For if even an unexpressed qualifier, when conveyed by some other means, is sufficient to bring about the cognition of the qualifier, what need is there then for adherence to its verbal expression?

Moreover, in this case, the agent who is the object of cognition possesses the capacity for qualification through mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) alone; thus, it does not depend upon verbal expression.
This principle is established in all cognitions of qualified objects: "And they are not taught by direct perception" (PMS 1.4.19).
In that regard:

Section on the Agent (Kartradhikaraṇa) 1382–1383: When a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*) has arisen, an investigation is conducted as to whether the agent of expression is conveyed by the word itself or by something else—specifically, whether it is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). In every case, where the qualificand is established from another source, the function of the word lies with the qualifier; where the qualifier is obtained from another source, it lies with the qualificand.

And in all instances, based solely on the qualified cognition, the function of the word is postulated through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) for either one or both of the two components, namely the qualifier and the qualificand.
And that [principle of] "impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti) applies to a subject matter not obtainable through any other means;
for in this case, neither the singularity as a qualifier nor as a qualified is obtained from any other source, such that it could be postulated as non-denotable.
For if the agent were able to convey that [singularity], then by the principle of the "form" (ākṛti), that [agent] alone would be the denoted meaning.

The other [view], however, maintains that whatever is being understood (*gamyamāna*) is what is expressed; yet, because that is subject to deviation and is therefore incapable [of denoting the agent], one must necessarily resort to that which is actually denoted (*abhidheya*). Consequently, once the expressive power has been transferred there, the agent characterized as "being understood" does not become denoted, even though it possesses the status of a qualifier.
Even when singularity alone is the qualifier, that very [singularity] must necessarily be denoted first.
