If that [agent] has already been denoted, the word, its expressive power exhausted, requires the accomplishment of the agent from another source.
And since that [agent] is accomplished through the *bhāvanā*, there is no reason to postulate a denotative power for it.
Furthermore, although other factors (*kārakas*) are also perceived, their perception does not provide any assistance—nor cause any lack of assistance—to that which is not yet perceived.
In every respect, first of all, that agent who is intended is already established.
But if something else is also established, what harm is done to us? For it is by that which is not established that we are contradicted, not by the apprehension of something additional.
However, although the instruments and other factors are indeed perceived, they are not grasped by the number which seeks the agent through the power of the word's expressive capacity.
For it is not the case that whatever is perceived must necessarily be grasped;
rather, in all instances, action is performed through the grasping of that which is fit for being perceived.

Therefore, in this case, since it is established for both parties that number resides in the agent (*kartṛ*), other *kārakas*—because they are neither required nor suitable—are not understood as having a connection with it, even though they are proximate.

Nor is there any indication that those [other *kārakas*] themselves possess the expressed number denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), because in all cases, number is delimited by what is expressed by the nominal suffix (*su*).
Furthermore, this number, being perceived in its general form, does not require another correlate.

For the distinction between the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) and the nominal suffix (*sup*) has indeed been explained [in the *Vākyādhikaraṇa*, verses 355–57] as being based solely on their relative order.
That is to say, as soon as the meaning of the root is cognized, it is determined that "there must be some efficient force (*bhāvanā*) and some agent.

Consequently, when the number is expressed by the very same [suffix] that denotes the agent already previously cognized, it assumes the status of either a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or the qualified (*viśeṣya*).

"Just as the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) first relates to the agent, there is no designation of number [at that stage]; this is the reason for its transcendence [of number]. Even though there exists a specific relationship with the factors of action (*kāraka*), the efficient force first requires and grasps the agent, because the association with the other factors of action is dependent upon it."

And by way of the general form of the agent's operation (*kartṛvyāpāra*), it establishes that very [agent] in its specific aspect; however, other factors (*kāraka*) are more external (*bahiraṅgatara*), because they are connected to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), or because they are based on operations consisting of the most subordinate ritual procedures (*itikartavyatā*).
Nor is there any reason why other factors should attain number (*saṃkhyā*) by virtue of being the agency established as primary and initial.
Furthermore, that factor whose intermediate operation the verbal root expresses as primary is the agent (*kartṛ*).

In grammar as well, other *kārakas* indicate the agent alone as that which has become manifest; therefore, the number is connected with that [agent] alone, and because it is expressed, it is perceived in its specific form.

Since other *kārakas* lack such a function, their being understood—even though it exists—is, due to its disregard, as if non-existent. However, at the time of examining the ultimate reality, since they are invariably concomitant, those [other factors] are presented by the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) on equal terms; thus, they are not disregarded by any means.

Now, if this is the case—namely, if the primacy of the previously perceived [agent] is accepted when the number expressed by the *tiṅ*-suffix differs from that of the agent—then in instances such as "Let rice be cooked by you" (*odanaḥ pacyatāṃ tvayā*), the expression of the number of the object would not be obtained.
Why? Because "the action of the rice is not here presented as primary by the verbal root;
let it be so, but its status as the agent must not be the thing to be expressed, nor the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)."
In this case, the operation upon the rice (*odana*) is not primarily denoted by the verbal root, because the number of the object is expressed as something specifically perceived.
Let it not be that, due to its being characterized as the agent, it should abandon its status as an object and instead become the agent.
And precisely because it is not the agent, its operation is not the *bhāvanā*.
Therefore, even so, there is no presentation of the action (*karman*) in its specific form.

Furthermore, the human effort (*puruṣavyāpāra*) itself must necessarily be stated as primary; otherwise, if it were merely a subordinate operation, there would be no injunction (*niyoga*) for this [action] at all.
Moreover, the agency (*kartṛtva*) not constructed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapada*) would not manifest even for that which is expressed by another word.

Consequently, the instrumental case in "by you" (*tvayā*) and so forth would not occur. Alternatively, when the object possesses an operation that is not overwhelmed by [the agent's] operation, because it is not being reached (*anāpyamāna*) by that [agent], it would abandon its status as an object (*karman*) and, its own operation having become manifest, attain the very status of an agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, through the sacrifice of its own [object] identity, it is conjoined precisely with the number of the agent. Therefore...
"Even though number is expressed [by the suffix] in forms such as *pacyate* just as it is by the word *pacati*, because it is not suppressed, it would apply to the agent alone and not to the object.
(Vākyapadīya, p. 917) It is replied:
"This consequence applies even to one for whom the *kāraka* is the expressed meaning."
Nor can one person, while investigating both sides, avoid the fault that rests upon both;

for in every way, whether it be the agent or the object, that which possesses the characteristic [of being denoted] by your definition is what is brought into proximity, and it is precisely such a thing where the number is expressed.

Therefore, if even when the object (*karman*) is produced by my [action], the number belongs only to the agent (*kartṛ*), then in that case as well, there ought to be an expression of the agent. Now, if for you there is somehow no expression of the agent in that instance, then for me too there is no expression of that [number] belonging to it; thus, there is no fault. This very point must necessarily be explained and resolved in this way: "In all cases, because it is that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*), the object possesses primacy over other factors of action (*kāraka*) by virtue of its objective nature; and through its role as the object, its operation is included within the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)."

In that regard, when it is intended that this predominance be shown by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) itself, then—even though the agent possesses an operation in the form of a general and particular property denoted by gender and number as the word-meaning, and even though agency is thereby obtained—the *l*-suffix arises in relation to the object or its number, because another kind of predominance, characterized as the "thing" (*vastu*), is intended to be expressed.

However, when that [agent]—though existing—is understood as "not even existing" because it is not intended to be expressed either as a specific verbal root-meaning (*dhātuviśeṣa*) or because the intention is merely to express the predominance of the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*), then, having accepted the manifestation of the predominance of the object (*karman*) through the case-endings (*sup*), the *l*-suffix arises in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) or its number.

But for the factors of action (*kāraka*) and so forth, there is no intention to express predominance based on their actual nature (*vastulakṣaṇā*) nor even based on the word-meaning (*śabdalakṣaṇā*); therefore, they are always to be included by the term *bhāva*.
Some, however, say:

When the expressive power of the word is understood in this way—that "this [suffix] is capable of expressing the number of the agent alone, while that [suffix] is capable of expressing the number of the object alone"—then, even in the absence of another [element] such as *bhāvanā*, that very number, having been expressed as pertaining to no other [referent], takes up the agent. This is just as the word *śoṇa* (red), while expressing a quality inherent in it, implies its own substratum, "horseness," even when that [horseness] has not been conveyed by anything else.
If that were the case, then by this same logic, all [words] such as "cow" (*go*) and so forth would also result in being non-denotative.
How so? "Let it be said that here [in grammar], like that [in the world], some [word] expresses gender, number, and so forth;
that very [word], having been expressed, will subsequently cause the understanding of the cow and other objects.

If such is the extent of the word's power that is postulated, then this [power] itself expresses the quality; what further capacity need be imagined beyond that, since linguistic usage is established by the former alone?

However, in such cases as these, the connection must be understood through the employment of a single word (*ekaśabdopāttatvena*), and not by virtue of the expressive power of the word itself; therefore, even in the case of the number of the agent (*kartṛsaṃkhyā*) and so forth, that very same [expression]—namely, the expression of mere number by the *sup*-suffixes—must be accepted, because [the agent, etc. are not themselves denoted.
Regarding this, others hold the view: "Even in the case of the word 'red' (*śoṇa*), there is no denotation of the possessor of that quality without first expressing the quality itself;
for nowhere is a cognition observed that has grasped a qualifier without [first] grasping the qualified."

For how could the cognition of redness as delimited by that [horseness] arise if horseness were not being expressed, [and thus] lead one to understand the horse (the possessor of the quality) as qualified by redness?
Nor can it be said that [redness] will indicate [the horse], because of the deviation [of redness] in the case of cows and other animals.
For that which indicates must be invariably concomitant; redness, however, deviates from horseness.

However, a mere substance (*dravyamātra*) would cause [the cognition] to arise because it is exclusive (*aikāntikatva*), but not its specific quality (*viśeṣa*). Therefore, since both "horseness" (*aśvatva*) and "redness" (*raktatva*) are non-exclusive of one another and thus incapable of causing cognition, and because it is impossible to apprehend a property presented by another entity, it must be admitted that the word *śoṇa* does not denote [either of them individually]. For in that case, horseness alone has not been made exclusively known by anything through its commonality with other entities. On the other hand, it has already been stated that for the agent (*kartṛ*), there is an exclusive adoption of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) and in its specific form.

Alternatively, let it be granted that the word *śoṇa* denotes only the horse-nature (*aśvatva*), the oneness, the inherence, and the quality [redness]. Even so, it is not logical to apply the capacity of agency to number by means of that example.
If it is asked, "How can there be a cognition of the qualified object when its qualifiers have not been apprehended?"—it is said in reply:
"That by which horse-nature is accepted as the qualifier of the red [horse]..."
However, this is a distinct quality (guṇa) belonging to a different genus (jātyantara), which has come into association with that [substance] by chance.

For if it were to express mere redness, then it would require the qualification "horse" because [the genus] is capable of being expressed; whereby one might say that here too there is identity (ekātmya) with redness.

But this word, just as it is non-expressive of existence (sattā) and quality-ness (guṇatva), likewise transcends mere redness and expresses "redness" (śoṇatva) as a subordinate genus within the class of redness.
And since that [redness] exists as "horseness" [in a horse] and not in cows and the like, "horseness" is perceived; there is no doubt arising from its redness.

But what kind of redness is this—that which, being distinct from the unity of cows and others, inheres in horses and does not inhere elsewhere? It is said: "It is another quality that establishes the connection with all other qualities."

In some cases there is a specific [denotation] of the mind, and in some cases there is a general designation. First, among all classes [of objects], qualities such as black, white, and red—which follow only their own individual manifestations—are perceived through direct perception as being distinct.
Among these, in certain instances, there is a word that denotes an existing particularity.

The statement "it does not exist" implies that while the object is denotable by its mere generality (*sāmānyamātra*), it is accepted as having specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) cognizable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). However, in some cases, because specific words such as "red" (*śoṇa*) and so forth do exist, it is denoted in its specific form. Likewise, in some instances, a particular [quality] is perceived in each region through a corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*), such as "the Rohaṇika cow."
Never, however, does such a designation occur for a horse's coat when it possesses the quality of redness (*raktaguṇa*).

Therefore, "redness" (*śoṇatva*), "whiteness" (*karkatva*), "fairness" (*gauratva*), and so forth, are indeed distinct universals (*jātyantara*) belonging to horses, humans, and the like; when they are predicated, they produce a cognition even with respect to those individuals. (Whiteness-in-general that inheres in the same substrate as the universal "horseness" is the universal "whiteness-of-a-horse" [*karkatva*]; whiteness-in-general that inheres in the same substrate as the universal "humanity" is the universal "whiteness-of-a-human" [*gauratva*].)

In this way, by the two words "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is stated that *puṇḍarīkatva* (the state of being a white lotus) is a subordinate genus (*avāntarajāti*) inherent in the same entity as the quality of whiteness, while *kokanadatva* (the state of being a red lotus) is an [inherent] subordinate genus of redness, and so on.
Just as one should not suspect that the word *go* (cow) lacks denotative power with respect to those possessing dewlaps and other such features,

by this very [argument], words such as *kumāra* (youth), *karabha* (young camel), *kalabha* (young elephant), *kiśora* (colt), *vatsa* (calf), and *barkara* (kid)— which denote specific stages of age connected to particular genera— are explained as being non-denotative [of the general class], even though they include humans, horses, and so forth.

(Boyhood is a subordinate genus inherent in the same object as humanity; camel-hood is inherent in the same object as excellence; cub-hood is inherent in the same object as elephant-hood; colt-hood is inherent in the same object as horse-hood; calf-hood is inherent in the same object as cow-hood; and kid-hood is inherent in the same object as goat-hood). For it is said: "Even though childhood and the like are common, the distinctions of age are established for each genus through their respective characteristics, such as standing and so forth."

Now, as for what was said—that even in the case of [words like] "cow" and so forth, since the specific universal (*jāti*) is established merely by the denotation of number and other such properties, the universal would be undenotable with respect to that [substance]—to that we reply:
"Number does not differ according to the difference in universals in the way that redness and so forth do.
There is no denotation of both [the universal and the number] here by the word to that extent."

For if, as in the case of redness and other qualities, a distinction between the oneness and so forth residing in cows and horses were perceived by direct perception, then it might be postulated in that way.

And if, just as the nominal stem *śoṇa*—which, having no distinct parts, functions as the designator of both the quality and the substrate, and thus, while being understood through the determination of one or the other, is held to denote the quality because it does not invariably indicate horsehood due to its deviation—is established as denoting the quality; likewise, for the universal (*gotva*) and number (*saṃkhyā*), which share the same word as their designator, the status of designator would have to be determined for one of them based on its non-deviation. But that is not the case. For, insofar as number consists everywhere in the nature of delimitation, no distinction whatsoever is observed [between the universals and numbers].

Nor can it be supposed that the word consists of only those two [parts], since both function as denoters: for the nominal stem denotes the genus through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), while the case-ending denotes number.
Furthermore, there is no fault of assuming multiple meanings for a single word;
if the capacity of the multiple word were not assumed there, then one or the other would necessarily be rendered meaningless.
Furthermore, there is no mutual deviation between number and the numbered, such that the cognition of one would necessarily lead to the cognition of the other.
For it has been said: "The determination of cows and the like does not occur without number;
nor does number ever function without the numbered."

"But surely, gender is apprehended by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself; therefore, being distinct for each class (*jāti*) and functioning without deviation, it should be similar to qualities such as redness (*śoṇatva*).
This is not so.
For that which is perceived in insentient things is not indeed distinct [from the substance]."

Therefore, it does not negate that the classes such as trees (*vṛkṣa*) are denotable. Likewise, even in cases where the feminine suffix *ṅī* is perceived due to its connection with *ṭāp* and other suffixes, there too the denotability of the class (*jāti*) is determined to exist prior [to the gender].

Although suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others do not denote gender as a distinct meaning because they merely manifest it, and rather bring forth a different aspect of the very same prior denotable object (*śakya*), nevertheless, the capacity of the word-form following *ṭāp* and so on to signify the genus (*jāti*) through gender was postulated while the form was in its unmanifest state; this capacity cannot be withdrawn later.
Likewise, even in cases where masculinity or neuter-ness is manifested through connection with case-endings, the expression of the genus should be applied in exactly the same manner.

However, in cases where the gender is understood from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself—either prior to the application of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) or when that ending has already occurred—such as in the words *hastī* (elephant), *nā* (man), *devadattaḥ* (Devadatta), *śrīḥ* (fortune), *sarit* (river), *toyaṃ* (water), or *vāri* (water), there is nothing contradictory even if one accepts that [gender] is thus apprehended.
Alternatively, even without the grammatical division [of gender], when the meaning is being cognized, all sentient beings first comprehend their genus (*jāti*) without such a division.
Furthermore, "the properties of the individual, such as masculinity and so forth, are not perceived prior to that [comprehension of the genus]. (Vākyapadīya, p. 121)
Furthermore, when the genus (*jāti*) is understood, no individual (*vyakti*) is perceived [as the primary object].
Therefore, it may well be that the gender (*liṅga*) alone is what is understood through the genus, but the genus is not understood through the gender.
Moreover, since this [gender] is always subordinate, its being understood cannot prevent the genus—which is perceived as the primary element—from being the denoted meaning (*abhidheya*).
Furthermore, in words such as "cowherd" (gopa) or "cattle" (paśu), there is no manifestation of either gender as there is in the case of a genus (jāti).
Therefore, the genus is indeed the primary denotation.
And that [gender] will indeed convey the meaning wherever the gender-sign does not deviate.

Even in cases where deviation occurs (as with insentient objects), if the meaning is understood from another source, then either that [other factor] alone is the indicator, or the genus (*jāti*) assisted by it, or the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself; thus it is conceived according to one's preference.
(He concludes the refutation of the suspicion that words such as *go* [cow] are equivalent to words such as *śoṇa* [red]: Therefore, there is no equality with words like *śoṇa*.

Even in words such as *pañca* ("five") and so forth, if number were perceived—like the word *śoṇa* ("red")—as having its own nature independent of all other factors and following the agent alone, then the agent might indeed be understood through that [number]; even so, it would still remain unexpressed [by the suffix].

However, when, according to the reasoning previously stated, no distinction of number is obtained, and it is impossible to postulate infinite distinct universals (*jāti*) such as oneness and so forth for each individual object, then one must adopt the very same principle [of indirect denotation] applied to the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) regarding the agent.
Furthermore: "The cognition of the genus [horse] is not established by anything other than the red [horse] and so forth;
therefore, the affliction (defilement) resides therein, but it is not accepted as being so here [in the case of the horse itself].
If someone were to bring another horse for the sake of the red one, that [red horse] would certainly not become afflicted on its own.
Since both the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) bring about the number, it will not [itself] possess it.

And when the presence of the *bhāvanā* has been stated, the distinction [is established] (Vārttika, p. 914.16). [To explain the Commentary, he says: Therefore, because the qualification of the agent—which is not directly denoted—is logically possible through the qualification of the [verbal root's] meaning, we understand that the assumption of a denotative power [for the agent] lacks authority.

When the matter has been thus determined by reasoning, someone, pointing out a contradiction with traditional scripture (*āgama*), says in the *Bhāṣya*: "Because of the Teacher’s instruction that 'the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together,' it is understood that the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) are the meanings of the word; and this is also [known] from the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), because of the word *ca* [which implies] 'and in the sense of the agent. Furthermore, the status of being indicators (*liṅgatva*) for the agent and the object follows from the fact that they occupy the place of the substitutes (*ādeśasthānin*). But surely, since a contradiction with scripture has already been shown by the very wording of the Sūtra, this statement—'the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix'—is irrelevant."
How is there no confusion? When, according to the previous reasoning (*yady etad viśeṣeṇa*—Vākyapadīya p.

902), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) must also demonstrate the predominance of the agent, this [text] shows that both this designation and that predominance are established by tradition (*smṛti*).

Since both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) express together the agent and the object which constitute the meaning of the suffix, there is a contradiction between this [interpretation] and the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) as well as the context (*prakaraṇa*), because they denote those two [agent and object] as qualified by the action.

In that regard, in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.69)—which states that "the *l*-suffixes [occur] after transitive roots in the sense of the object and the agent, and after intransitive roots in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) and the agent"—the agent and the object are introduced as being exclusively denotable. However, in the rule *kartari śap*, there is instead the observation of only one thing to be denoted.
Furthermore, in the rule *kartari*, the locative case is one of "proximity" (*parasaptamī*).

Since an agent cannot possibly exist elsewhere than in the arrangement of the word itself, it is understood—on the grounds that [otherwise] the rule would be purposeless—that the operation applies to the word itself, according to the principle *ānarthakyāt tadbhedeṣu*.
Thus, the meaning of the rule *kartari śap* is: "when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix denoting an agent (*kartṛvācin*) stands proximate."
In every respect, the teachers of grammar have stated that the agent is the meaning of the suffix;
therefore, it is incorrect to maintain that [the agent] is not denoted at all. To this, it is replied:
"The relationship between the signified and the signifier is not taught by the Teachers;
rather, it is understood from worldly usage through the principle of inexplicability otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*).
In that case, it is only appropriate to raise an objection regarding contradiction with scripture (*āgama*) where reason (*nyāya*) and scripture have the same object."

But here, the scope of logic (*nyāya*) is entirely different—namely, "what is the expressed (*vācya*) and what is the implied (*gamyamāna*)?"—whereas the scope of the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) is entirely different: "Among those joined with a single meaning, which is the correct form and which is the corruption (*apabhraṃśa*)?

It is not logical that something belonging to a different scope should sublate something belonging to another scope, even if the latter is weak; how much less so when the distinction between the expressed and the implied is a matter of direct self-evident experience (*pratyakṣa-svasaṃvedana*).

Therefore, even if the Teachers were to say, "The agent (*kartṛ*) is the word-meaning," they would still not be worthy of respect, as their view is contradicted by the beginning and end [of the Veda].
But they do not speak in that way at all.
Is it not the case that [the truth] is indeed evident through direct perception?
True; however, this is not after having reflected upon the nature of the scriptures.
What then? [It is] by means of observing a single part.
And it is not possible to raise an objection regarding contradiction with the scripture on the basis of that alone.
Why? Because "indeed, all scriptures, together with their own other sections..."
A coherent unity (*ekavākyatā*) is extended to the instruction as follows:

"If, by examining only a portion of the scripture, one who accepts what is contrary to it were to point out a contradiction with the scripture, then even in the case of the rule 'wine must not be drunk,' one who does not perform the drinking prescribed for that specific portion would be acting in contradiction to the scripture.
Likewise, regarding distinct sentences such as 'one should offer the *agnihotra* as long as one lives,' he says that even the initiated person is impure, based on that alone."
Even in grammar, if one were to consider only the rule "there is guna for *mid*" (*mider guṇaḥ*), then the non-application of *guṇa* in the case of *midaḥ* would contradict the scripture.
Therefore, a contradiction based on a single part [of a rule] should not be raised.
And it has been said: "In other cases, the meaning of the scripture is understood through a single part."
Otherwise, even when all [the causes] are fully present, [the result] is withdrawn;
however, there is a distinction regarding the prophecy (vyākaraṇa).
For in that system, the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* is generally operative for each individual word;
therefore, any contradiction with the meaning of the complete rule "laḥ karmaṇi ca" (Pāṇini 3.4.69), which includes other constituent parts, must be avoided.

And here, by this much, the rules for suffixes (*pratyaya*) are completed: [the rules] "that which is not a suffix" (*apratyaya*), "and that which follows" (*paraśca*), "accented on the first syllable" (*ādyudāttaśca*), "sup and pit suffixes are unaccented" (*anudāttau suppitau*), "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*), "in that case, the subordinate word is situated in the locative" (*tatropapadaṃ saptamīstham*), "ku, ad, and iha" (*kudatiha*), "a dissimilar suffix may optionally occur, except in the feminine" (*vā'sarūpo'striyām*), "the *laṭ* suffix occurs in the present tense" (*vartamāne laṭ*), "the *kṛt* suffixes occur when the agent is expressed" (*kartari kṛt*), "the *la* suffixes occur in the sense of the object and, after intransitive roots, in the sense of the action itself" (*laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*), "of *la*" (*lasya*), "the *ti* group beginning with *tip*, *tas*, *jhi*, etc. [all the sūtras]," "the *ātmanepada* occurs after roots marked with an indicatory *ṅ* that have an unaccented vowel" (*anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam*), "the *parasmaipada* occurs in the remaining cases when the agent is expressed" (*śeṣāt kartari parasmaipadam*), "the second person and so forth occur when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are the subordinate words" (*yuṣmadasmadupapadādiṣu madhyamādayaḥ*), "three each of the *tiṅ* suffixes are called first, middle, and last" (*tiṅastrīṇi trīṇi prathamamadhyamottamāḥ*), "these are respectively singular, dual, and plural" (*tānyekavacanadvivacanabahuvacanānyekaśaḥ*), "the plural is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*), and "the dual and singular are used for two and one" (*dvayekayordvivacanaikavacane*)."

Furthermore, all the subsequent rules—consisting of technical definitions (*saṃjñā*), grammatical conventions (*paribhāṣā*), and so forth, as well as the treatises concerning elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), and the modification of phonemes (*varṇavikāra*)—constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*).
This unity of a single sentence occurs when there exists a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*); otherwise it would not.

Moreover, that relationship occurs either through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), involving terms ending in identical case-suffixes, or through non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), taking the form of action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*) or the relationship between the principal and the subordinate (*śeṣaśeṣī*).

Therefore, since other grammatical components (*avayava*) are irrelevant here due to their lack of utility, we shall set them aside. Instead, we shall consider the relationship between qualifier and qualified, as well as the operation of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), regarding these rules: "The suffixes [of case endings] occur with respect to the agent and the object; the singular number is used for one thing, the dual for two, and the plural for many.

In this regard, it has been established in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* that the words *na*, *bahu*, and *eka* do not denote numbers, because it is impossible for those words to function by denoting a number.

In the *Pātañjala* [Mahābhāṣya] as well, having commenced with the question "In which cases among many? and having stated the faults therein, it asserts that [the suffix] expresses number (*saṃkhyā*). This is because of the explanation: "When there is plurality (*bahutva*), [the suffix denotes] duality and singularity. When it is asked, "How can an expression be primarily expressive of a state (*bhāva*) without an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*)?", it is rightly replied: "It occurs when a quality (*guṇa*) itself is intended to be expressed as primary. For instance: "First, a certain quality is prescribed independently."

Another [type of usage] is distinguished from that by the absence of a substance as a factor. Where a quality is intended to be primary from the very beginning, there it remains restricted—without producing an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) and without grammatical coreferentiality—as in "the white of the cloth" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*).
But where a substance...

The reading in the *Pātañjala-mūla* (the *Mahābhāṣya*) is: "The meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), not the [object] itself, [is expressed] by virtue of the governing rule *anabhihite*. However, this has been restated by Bhaṭṭapāda according to its sense.
(Ke.: "But is it not also the case that when the object and so forth are the meaning of the case-ending, then singularity and so forth function as qualifiers?"
Since this is the statement of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is not to be accepted as established, but is presented as a concessionary argument (*abhyupetavāda*).

What is meant is this: even when actions and so forth, being the qualificands (*viśeṣya*), are primarily considered as the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), then oneness and the rest are still denoted as being situated as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), because it is impossible for those not already denoted to function as qualifiers, and because the distinction [of the qualifier] is established from something else.
Indeed, in such a state, the injunction has the subordinate element as its primary focus, as in the case of "red-turbaned" (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*) and similar instances.

Alternatively, by the word *artha*, "purpose" (*prayojana*) is denoted; the meaning is that even when those two [the action and the purpose] are the purpose, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is employed for that purpose. When both [types of] statements are set aside (meaning their specific domains are not specified), they are applied according to possibility: one will concern the domain of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), as previously illustrated, while the other will concern the domain of the nominal suffix (*su*). In that case, since [the suffixes] are accepted as having the object (*karman*) and so forth as their meaning.

But surely, since they are equal in being expressed by a plural number and thus possessing a uniform form across all branches, just as with verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), no expression of the *kāraka* occurs because they express specific numbers such as the object (*karman*) and so forth, the same would necessarily apply to nominal suffixes (*suP*) as well.

Consequently, there would be a contradiction with established usage in passages such as: "That which is mentioned in connection with a case-ending expressing the instrument" (*Bhāṣya* on *Pāṇini* 3.1.67, p. 679), and "For when that [suffix] is present, its cognition is observed" (*Pāṇini* 4.1.155).
(He states the resolution for those who maintain that the scope of the two grammatical traditions is fixed: Regarding this, some say:

"Even a single treatise, being divided according to its purpose and according to the distinction of its relations, will express number as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) in the case of finite verbal endings (*tiṅ*) for the sake of understanding the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), whereas it will express it as the qualified (*viśeṣya*) in the case of nominal suffixes (*sup*).

(The author himself says: "If there is dissatisfaction with this, then it is stated otherwise (Vārttika, p. 927): 'Although in this treatise [grammar] these [numbers] are not relied upon as being directly denotable (*abhidheya*),'..."
Nevertheless, for the sake of establishing [its] manifestation, it is accepted as being denotable.

For in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), even that which is not the primary denotable object is accepted as being "denotable" (*abhidheyatva*) by virtue of its function, based on technical convention (*pāribhāṣika*). However, this does not necessarily follow in common worldly usage (*loka*).

Nor is it stated in the treatise that the objects of action (*karman*) and so forth are *not* denotable at all; rather, it has already been explained that they possess specific qualifiers such as being exclusively denotable as one [of the six relations] and so on.
Therefore, these [words] attain the status of qualifiers alone. Thus, where there is no attainment of denotability through either scripture or logic, they are understood to be non-denotable.

However, where those mentioned in scripture cannot be understood as qualifiers unless they are denoted, they must, due to the lack of any other recourse, also attain the status of being denotable, even though this is obtained through logic.

Alternatively, they will be stated as being denotable by the treatise through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*). In that case, since the status of being a qualifier is established because the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is present in finite verbs (*tiṅ*), it is not necessary to admit that they are directly denotable.

Furthermore, since nominal stems (*prātipadika*), meanings, and suffixes such as *taddhita* and *kṛt* deviate with respect to both the specific grammatical relations (*ākāraka*) and other relations, and since their capacity to convey only one of these has been established, nothing else—such as the *bhāvanā* or its indicators—is present to provide that meaning. Consequently, because it is impossible to express a number qualified by a relation without first expressing the relation itself, the relation (the *kāraka*) must be denoted.

[Objection: But surely, since there is no occurrence of a mere *kāraka* (grammatical factor) used in isolation, the connection between the number and the *tiṅ*-suffixes will necessarily be possible only for those *kārakas* that have been brought forth by the *bhāvanā* expressed by the verbal root (*ākhyāta*) and then conveyed by the case-endings. [The respondent says: How can this be possible? For when, in a sentence consisting of elements with their own fixed order, the cognition of a *kāraka* is produced by a nominal stem (*subanta*)—such as "tree" (*vṛkṣam*)—which is sometimes employed before the verbal form, it cannot be established without the act of denotation (*abhidhāna*).

(He himself raises an objection: "But even in that case, since the status of being a *kāraka* is untenable prior to its connection with an action, it cannot arise through the power of being a *kāraka* until the connection with an action has been demonstrated; and only then does it attain the nature of an action. (The respondent refutes the objector: "True, so far as the speaker is concerned."

Furthermore, the hearer who first hears the word "tree" has not previously ascertained through any other means either the action or its connection [to the tree]. What then? Having understood the *kāraka* (the factor of action) from the mere word, he understands the action previously postulated by the speaker through inference or through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Otherwise, there would be a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*). Why? Because: "The *kāraka* is to be understood through the action, and likewise the action through the *kāraka*."
If even a single [cause] were independent, no root cause would be established.

"Between two related entities, one must necessarily accept that the cognition of at least one is rooted in its independence from the other. Therefore, in this case, if the *kāraka* (participant) is understood through action (*kriyā*), it must be stated by what means that action is signified.
To begin with, the nominal stem *vṛkṣa-* is not the denoter of action, because it expresses only the genus (*jāti*) characterized by having roots and so forth."
Nor is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) indicative [of the action], since it is logically possible even without an action.
Now, if it were argued that no entity is ever found to be devoid of action, and therefore some action—such as "existing" or "standing"—will necessarily be implied;

or else, as stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* (2.3.46): "The first person ending in the roots *as* or *bhū* is understood to exist even when not explicitly employed," then, because of this possession of action, the requirement for a *kāraka* will be established (and thus there is no circularity).
That is untenable.

Why? Because even when a mere action is expressed in [verbs] such as "he stands," which are intransitive (*akarmaka*), only the agent (*kartṛ*) would be expressed, while the object (*karman*) and so forth would necessarily [not be].

In this case, some general action such as "eating" might be implied by the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), yet that [stem] is not capable of implying all the factors of action (*kāraka*). Therefore, something else must be sought to bring about [the specific realization of] the object (*karman*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) does not express the action in such a way that the object would be implied;
nor has it been stated that number is capable of implying a specific action or a specific factor of action.
Therefore, there is no means of conveying action other than the cognition of the *kāraka*.
In that case, if the action were also conveyed by the *kāraka* itself, then, due to a clearly manifest circularity (*itaretarāśraya*), both would become utterly groundless.
Consequently, since there is no other recourse here, the *kāraka* must be expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*).
It must be stated that through that connection, the action of that [number] is implied.

However, when a case-inflected word (*kāraka-pada*) is employed preceded by a verbal form (*kriyāpada*), then because the action suitable for that connection has already been perceived earlier, the case-endings denote number alone, owing to the capacity of the case-inflected word to convey the *kāraka*. This would indeed be so if sentences were always employed beginning with the verb; however, their usage is established as being entirely unrestricted, as in "Look at the cow" (*gāṃ paśya*) or "The cow, look at her" (*paśya gām*).
(He concludes the demonstration that the *kāraka* is denoted by the sentence: Therefore, it is not the case that [the *kāraka*] is not denotable.
[Objection: Even so, because of its power of denotation (*abhidhānaśakti*), it must nonetheless be something not denoted. [Reply: It cannot be so.

For when the expressive power (*vācaka-śakti*) is postulated in dependence upon its connection with a preceding nominal stem (*subanta*), how could that [power] be removed in another usage? Indeed, the relationship between word and meaning is not like the wind; rather, as it has been stated in the *Ślokavārttika* (in the *Saṃbandhākṣepavāda*, verses 13–14), "the relationship is the restriction of two powers."

Now, it might be argued: "In the theory that the verbal root is employed first, since the absence of power in the case of the suffix has been determined, and since uniformity is inevitable, let it be by means of absolute power alone. This is not correct. Why? Because: "Power that is already established does not fail when its purpose has been fulfilled."
But for one who lacks faith, the desired fruit of that [action] shall be difficult to obtain.

In every case, since any given effect is observed to be characterized by the doctrine of being and non-being, and when its connection with the nature of both being and non-being is understood, a uniformity is maintained. Its existence as being (*sadbhāva*) is to be accepted, because even for those things that exist, there is no contradiction in the commencement of an effect due to obstruction, the absence of other causes, or its establishment through another means. On the other hand, for that which is non-existent, it cannot be reached even by the gods at the time of the effect; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of producing an effect without a cause. This has been stated in the *Ślokavārttika* (in the section on the Refutation of the Objection regarding Relation, verse 33) concerning the eternality of the relation.

Therefore, the imagined expressive power will function first in an application preceded by a noun; however, in the opposite case (an application preceded by a verb), it will remain indifferent. Since its nature is to seek [its object], once there is a listener, it will set about its task while refuting [the contrary] through inferential cognition.

(Therein, he concludes the systematic arrangement established by reasoning through the passage beginning with "not by the treatise" [na śāstreṇa]): Therefore, the meanings such as the object (*karman*) and so forth are established for the case-endings (*sup*).

However, because of the fixed sequence of finite verbal endings (*tiṅ*), the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) must necessarily be presented first by the root-meaning and the productive operation (*bhāvanā*); only afterwards is number understood. Thus, there is never an occasion to postulate a denotative power (*vācaka-śakti*) for the kārakas or their qualifiers.
Consequently, it is established that the agent and the object are always to be inferred.

Commentary: (pp. 930–31, 35) Now, it may be argued: "The singular number [is used] because of the oneness of the agent; the dual number because of the duality of the agents; and the plural number because of the plurality of the agents.
Therefore, it is understood that the agent is certainly the meaning of the word. To this, it is replied:
This cannot be considered an inference.
That the agent is understood precisely through the comprehension of the action to be performed is a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
and that, moreover, is not sublated by anything whatsoever.

When there is an indication in the singular number, singularity of the agent is understood; when there is an indication in the dual number, duality of the agents; and when there is an indication in the plural number, plurality of the agents.
That too is perceptual.
Which inference, then, could possibly sublate it?

Just as in a word expressing a generic form (*ākṛti*), a difference in substance (*dravyabheda*) is understood through the dual number, while in the singular number there is duality and unity, so too should it be seen here.

Or—(p. 930)—now, someone skilled in inference says: "Surely, the dual number arises from the duality of agents, the dual number [in some cases] from the duality and unity of agents, and the plural number from the plurality of agents. Therefore, the agent must certainly be the meaning of the word" (Bhāṣya).

What is the intention? It is observed that when words such as "Devadatta" and the like—which are uttered for the purpose of denoting a specific agent—are employed together with numbers such as five and so forth, they conform to that [agent] in every respect.
And this occurs because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
And grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is postulated only when two [words] have a single object.
Therefore, if Devadatta and others were expressed by the word "cooks" in a general sense, then coreferentiality with them would be obtained.
If it is argued that this will occur through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since the word is restricted to the class-form (*ākṛti*), we say no.

Because it is impossible to characterize oneness and so forth by means of the cooking that serves as their indicator; for it is only that which is inherent in the same substrate as those [qualities] that can be characterized, not that which is inherent in another.
To this, one might object: "Even acts such as placing the pot on the fire are said to be Devadatta's 'cooking' because they are associated with him."
It is true that this is said, but grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not occur by way of that [metaphorical transfer].

For words such as "cow" (*go*) or "tawny" (*aruṇa*), having first brought about the production of a form in the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) that conforms to their own nature, proceed by means of the deletion of the suffix *matup* and the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*); they thus effect coreferentiality. However, Devadatta is not understood in the form of the act of placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth, such that there could be a deletion of *matup* and a metaphorical identification.
Therefore, just as words such as "staff" do not attain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with [proper names] like Devadatta— as in "the staff is Devadatta"—

or just as expressions such as "Devadatta is the act of placing on the fire" or "Devadatta is the cooking" do not occur, so too the expression "Devadatta cooks" would not be possible. Consequently, the word *pacati* (cooks) and others are denoters of the agent and the object.
"Because it occurs in non-difference from that word, like the words 'cook' and so forth.

(The inference, however, is: "The word *pacati* denotes the agent, because it occurs in non-difference from the words denoting agents such as Devadatta, like the word *paktṛ*; [and] the word *pacyate* denotes the object, because it occurs in non-difference from the words denoting objects such as rice, like the word *paktṛ*").

For occurrence in non-difference is indeed co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that word; this is observed in the case of *kṛt*-suffixes where the denotative power is beyond doubt, as in examples such as "Devadatta is the cook" (*paktā devadattaḥ*) and "the rice is being cooked" (*pacyata odanaḥ*).

Furthermore, where there is no expression of agent or object, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed, as in the case of words such as "cooking" (*pāka*). Moreover: "Because it follows the distinction of number belonging to that [action] which is conveyed by the word *tat* (it), its denotative capacity would be exactly the same; those two examples apply here as well."

In the examples "Devadatta cooks," "Devadatta and Datta cook," and "Devadatta, Datta, Viṣṇumitra, and others cook," the very same number that is expressed by the words Devadatta and so forth when they denote the agent (*kartṛ*) is also seen in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

And wherever that [number] is seen, that [word] is observed to be expressive [of the meaning], as in "Devadatta is a cooker" (*paktā devadattaḥ*), "the two are cookers" (*paktārau*), and so on. Likewise, regarding the object (*karman*) as well, in cases such as "The rice is being cooked" (*pacyate odanaḥ*), "The two rice-dishes are being cooked" (*pacyete odanau*), "Cook the rice" (*pacodanaḥ*), and "Cook the rice and vegetables" (*pacau śākaudanau*), they will state the thesis, the example, and the illustration.

And thus the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The word *pacati* denotes the agent, because it is understood as a qualifier of the number residing in the agent, just like the word *paktṛ* in the sentence *paktā devadattaḥ* ('Devadatta is the cooker'); and the word *pacyate* denotes the object, because it is understood as a qualifier of the number residing in the object, just like the word *pakva* in the sentence *pakva odanaḥ* ('the cooked rice').
Furthermore, since those two [the agent and the object] are already expressed, they block the occurrence of case-endings;
therefore, there is a similarity [in this regard], as previously stated: "By Devadatta, it is cooked."

For this reason also, [the verbal suffix] is expressive (*vācaka*), because we observe the prevention of case-endings prescribed under the heading of "unexpressed" (*anabhihita*) kārakas, as in the examples *pacati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta cooks") and *pacyate odanaḥ* ("the rice is cooked").

For if it were not expressive, then the application of case-endings by rules such as *anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1), *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.2), and *kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.18) would not be obstructed by anything,
as in the cases *pacyate devadattena* ("by Devadatta is cooked") and *pacaty odanam* ("he cooks the rice").

Since, however, there is indeed an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), it is understood that denotative power (*vācakatva*) exists precisely through similarity with the class of agents (*paktṛpakṣasādhamryeṇa*).

Dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is the opposite of similarity; this should be demonstrated as follows: "Wherever there is no denotative power, there is also no invariable concomitance with the case-endings of the agent, as in the examples *pacyate devadattena* (Devadatta is being cooked) and *pacyate odanaḥ* (the rice is being cooked).
Furthermore, "The word is a communicator [of meaning] because it brings about cognition even when directed toward that [meaning]."
Just as the auditory faculty is the perceiver of the letter 'a', it is the perceiver of sound.

(The word *pacati-pacyate* denotes both the agent and the object, because it causes the cognition of the specific qualities of the agent and the object; for whatever causes the cognition of a specific quality of something denotes that thing, just as the sense of hearing denotes the specific form of sound—this is the formal argument. If the agent and the object were not denoted by words such as *pacati*, how could their specific quality, namely number, be expressed?
For it is a contradiction to say that "it does not denote that" while simultaneously saying "it denotes its specific quality."
For the auditory organ does not cause one to understand the specific vowel 'a' by means of the generality of sound, which is its object;
nor does a word, as a denoter, possess such a capacity to convey another meaning [indirectly].
Indeed, if it were understood through the mental impression (*bhāvanā*), then the meaning itself would be the conveyor, and not the word.
Therefore, it possesses denotative power as well (*Vākya-pada*, p. 132). Furthermore: "The relationship [of the word] with its qualifiers, as well as the agent and the object, are expressed;
for a relationship with its own qualities is not possible for that which has not yet arisen."
It is stated for this reason as well: "Because of being connected with qualifiers," as in the examples "He cooks beautifully" (*śobhanaḥ pacati*) and "It is cooked beautifully" (*śobhanaḥ pacyate*).

Wherever there is a connection with a qualifier, there the status of being denotable (*abhidheyatva*) is also observed, as in "a beautiful cooker" (*śobhanaḥ paktā*) or "a deliciously cooked [dish]" (*ramaṇīyaḥ pakkaḥ*).

However, where there is no denotability (*abhidheyatva*), there the connection with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is also not observed, as in the case of "it sits beautifully. Nor is there a connection with a qualifier for that which is merely implied (*gamyamāna*), just as fire, which is understood from the word "smoke," is not connected with [other qualifiers such as] "flaming" and so forth. All of this has already been demonstrated by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) through the passage beginning with "Now, the singular number expresses the agent and the object" (*nanu kartṛkarmavādekavacanam*, Bhāṣya p. 130, l. 1), and thus it has not been elaborated upon further.
Without this co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the state of being connected with that number would not be possible;
therefore, the position of direct denotation (*abhidhāna*) alone is logical. To this, it is replied:

As for what was stated—that "the word *pacati* and so forth is expressive [of the agent and the object] because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with them"—if the existence [of such a power] is inferred from the capacity to express, then, due to the previously mentioned refutation of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be established. This contradicts non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
Furthermore, presumptive testimony is the sole means of cognizing all capacities.
And this other possibility is not tenable;

nor is there a contradiction with inference regarding the expression of the agent and the object by words such as "pacati" (he cooks), because [such words] denote an object that is invariably concomitant with what ends in that suffix (the verbal suffix). (The meaning is: because they denote a *bhāvanā* that is invariably concomitant with the agent and the object. Whatever denotes something that is invariably concomitant with what ends in a particular suffix is not the denoter of that [suffix itself]; for example, the word "śiṃśapā" denotes the state of being a *śiṃśapā* which is restricted to the state of being a tree (it is the denoter of *śiṃśapātva*, not of *vṛkṣatva*).

Likewise, the agent and the object are not denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), because they are not abandoned when that [suffix] is denotative, and because they are cognized even without its operation, just as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) is [cognized] from the word "śiṃśapā" despite the presence of "treeness. Furthermore, it could be argued that the verbal suffix is not denotative because it is a verbal suffix, like the word "āsya-te" (it is sat). Thus, it is possible to state this as well.
Now, one might object: "The inference 'the moon is not the moon' is contrary to worldly consensus. This is not a fault.

If we were denying the capacity to signify or the capacity to be signified, then we would indeed be speaking in contradiction to the world. However, what is being negated here is the power of the signifier and the signified; and by that, there is no contradiction with worldly consensus. For the world, which achieves its purpose through the mere production of cognition, disregards the desire to express the true nature of things—such as the fitness of a thing to be understood as a denotable object. (Vākyapadīya, p. 133)

(There is a fourfold classification: for words such as "cow" (*go*), the denoted object is the universal (*jāti*); for [words like] "goer," it is the individual (*vyakti*); for prefixes (*upasarga*), the indicated meaning is the action such as "going"; and for words based on both etymological derivation and conventional usage (*yoga-rūḍha*), the referent is the state of being a lotus (*padmatva*) and so forth.

However, if one were merely to establish the well-known worldly relationship of signifier and signified (*pratyāyya-pratyāyaka*), then, because this is already accepted through the previously mentioned medium of *bhāvanā*, it would be a proof of what is already established.
Furthermore, a contradiction with common worldly experience would likewise result in that case.
Why? "The world does not desire to express that which is already established by other means;
just as, for example, the nature [of a word] is not denoted because it is already grasped by the sense of hearing."

The remaining defects of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*) should also be applied against the Grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*) by means of the previously mentioned method (Śrībhāṣya, following the sequence of the section on the eternity of sound, p. 318), through the analysis of terms such as *varṇa*, *sphoṭa*, and *jāti*, by way of the non-production of two powers, and by means of the inquiry into whether [the relation] is distinct or non-distinct.
(Sudhā, p. 1440).

Likewise, is the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) stated as the reason (*hetu*) taken in its primary sense (*śrauta*) or in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*)? First, the primary sense is established for both parties.

Why? Because we maintain that [the word] denotes mere capacity (*bhāvanā-mātra*), whereas you admit that the suffix expresses merely the factor of action (*kāraka*). For a word such as "Devadatta" denotes a substance (*dravya*) and would not express capacity.

Furthermore, the suffix, while denoting the factor of action, must denote it by means of capacity alone and not by way of the form of a substance, because the substance itself is not the factor of action.

For even by one for whom the substance (*dravya*) is the agent, a specific capacity (*śakti-viśeṣaṇa*) must necessarily be admitted as inseparable from it, because the operation of a substance devoid of such capacity is impossible. Furthermore, since the denotation of capacity is established from the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, there is no possibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word denoting a substance. Moreover, there is no word whatsoever denoting capacity that is co-uttered with a verb (*ākhyāta*), with which it could share a direct syntactic coreferentiality.
For that [word] would have to end in a case-ending denoting a *kāraka* (participant in action).

However, no such *kāraka*-case-ending is employed here. But for one who does not admit *śakti* (power) [as the *kāraka*]—for whom the substance (*dravya*) itself is the *kāraka*—since that substance which has been determined by some *kāraka*-designation does not depart from it, just as a genus (*jāti*) does not, it follows that as long as the substance exists, there would be the contingency of intending other *kārakas* for it.

Even in the view that [words denote] powers (*śakti*), there is no difference, because those powers are designated in such and such ways by the force of the speaker's intention regarding their manifestation or concealment.
However, since a substance (*dravya*) is of a single nature and lacks a causal basis for dependence, it does not admit of different intentions [of expression].
"And if the denotation of substance were intended in words ending in nominal suffixes (*su*) and verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*)," [so it is said].
Consequently, there would be a separation from gender due to its being a state of pure existence (sattva), just like a word ending in a kṛt suffix.

"Just as in words such as *pāka* (cooking) and the like, because the substance (*dravya*) is predominant, there arises a cognition of the form of a *sattva* (substance), so too it would be in the case of words ending in nominal and verbal suffixes (*sup-tiṅ*).

And consequently, just as in these very cases— such as ‘pācakaṃ brūhi’ (‘Speak to the cook’), ‘pācakena kṛtam’ (‘Done by the cook’), and ‘pācakāya dehi’ (‘Give to the cook’) — there occurs a connection with other factors of action (*kāraka*), so too in cases such as ‘pacaty odanam’ (‘He cooks rice’), there would be [the presence of] the agent (*kartṛ*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)."
Otherwise, the status of the agent (kartṛ) would result in being the locus (adhikaraṇa).

Therefore, even in the view that the two factors are the possessors of power (śaktimat), it must necessarily be accepted that the mere power (śaktimātra), having been extracted [from its substrate], is the denotation of the case-ending (sup).
For if that were so, a substance whose capacity for non-existence has been manifested by its own power would not, at that very moment, acquire a connection with another capacity.

Therefore, the non-connection with other grammatical factors (*kāraka*) and the absence of gender and number are established as having the characteristic of being primarily denotative of a substance (*dravyapradhānatva*). (He concludes that the reason—the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of that which is qualified by direct denotation—is unestablished for both parties: Consequently, the fact that the grammatical coreferentiality based on direct denotation is unestablished for both remains settled.

Now, if grammatical coreferentiality—either through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or as something exhaustive—is taken as the reason, then [the reason is] inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because coreferentiality is observed even in cases such as "The boy is a lion," where there is no relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*).

(Regarding the position that the qualification "being based on direct Vedic statement" [śrautatva] is the reason, he begins to state its lack of establishment elsewhere, because it constitutes a part of the definition of the probandum which is non-different from itself: And as for this grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on direct Vedic statement, what is its meaning? 1. "The substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) is the same" means that the denoted object (*vācya*) is the same; for there is no other meaning of the word than the substratum of the agent.

The proponent [of the established view] says: If this is so, then one must never deviate from the number that is expressed as residing in the agent. [The opponent] objects: How then is the usage "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*) to be explained?

(The Siddhāntin: It is said in reply. Now, what is logical here: is it that, for some reason, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) has been resorted to by the number, bypassing the agent; or rather, is it that the agency itself residing in the pot is intended to be expressed by that number? (In this deliberation,) we consider that the intention to express agency is the more logical.
Why? Because no other cause whatsoever is observed for bypassing the primary [meaning].

Indeed, the intention to express primacy may be applied as one desires; for when two meanings are possible in every case, it is appropriate to intend one or the other form. And it has been established previously (in the *Vākyādhikaraṇa*, verse 66 et seq. that agency with respect to its own operation is possible for all causes.
For the unity of the *kāraka* involved in the principal action is not established through agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth with respect to its own specific operation;

therefore, it is logical that this [unity] alone is intended to be expressed, and not the expression of the number of other *kārakas*. And this being the case, as for the fact that even the number of the object (*karman*)...
"By the logic of the *kartrādhikaraṇa* (Pāṇini 2.3.67), it is said that [the suffix] occurs when the substance has already been expressed.
But what is the purpose of this, since it is not observed in that way either in common usage (*loka*) or in the Veda?

Furthermore, even if there is no purpose for that [distinction] in the actual usage, it does exist in the treatise (*śāstra*). For how else could there be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) based on the assumption that those two [the agent and the object] are already expressed when there is the use of a *kāraka* term under the heading "that which is not already expressed" (*anabhihitādhikāra*)? (He concludes by demonstrating the validity of the exclusion through the acceptance of its primary status: Therefore, although in the ultimate sense it is not denoted, nevertheless, because one relies on it as if it were denoted, the case endings prescribed under the heading "that which is not already expressed" do not apply; thus, the application of the *kāraka* case endings is established.

(He refutes the reason "because it makes known its specific qualification" as being inconclusive with respect to that which stands in the fourth application: As for the argument that "it is because [the word] denotes its specific qualification" (p. 131, l. 20), that is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to words such as *śiṃśapā*.

For the word *śiṃśapā* does not denote [the universals] treeness, earthiness, substantiality, existence, or knowability; nevertheless, it denotes a particular that is qualified by those very [universals].
Thus, just as its capacity to denote a particular without denoting the universal is not contradicted, and just as in the case of the eye...
The *āya* (preparatory act) has only an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), such as the *prayāja* offerings.

However, the directly contributory (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) act is of three kinds: having a visible purpose, having an unseen purpose, and having both purposes—the latter being designated as the "substratum act" (*āśrayakarma*).

Even that which has a visible purpose is twofold: for the sake of preparing what is to be used (*bhāvya-upayoga-saṃskārārtha*) and for the sake of preparing what has already been used (*bhūta-upayoga-saṃskārārtha*).
Among those, each of the first two [categories] is of two kinds:
for the purpose of preparing the substance (*dravya-saṃskāra*) and for the purpose of preparing the deity (*devatā-saṃskāraka*).

Among these, that which has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) and is for the purpose of preparing the substance used in the ritual (*bhānyupayoga-dravya-saṃskārārtha*) is an auxiliary that assists by direct application (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), and it is of two kinds: for the purpose of preparing what is directly enjoined (*sākṣād-viniyukta-saṃskārārtha*), and for the purpose of preparing that which assists what is directly enjoined (*sākṣād-viniyuktasya yad-upakārakaṃ tatsaṃskārārtha*).
Among these, the first is, for example, "one threshes rice";
the second is, for example, "one should touch the calf.

For this very reason, Bhavadeva states in the *Paśusomādhikaraṇa* (2.1.6) that because the calf alone assists the substance that is a subsidiary to the milking which has already been enjoined, in the injunction "one should touch the calf," the act of touching (*ālambha*) serves the purpose of a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).

(With respect to substances used for living beings and those prepared for them, which serve a visible purpose, [the auxiliary] is one that assists by coming together. Subsequent performance (*pratipatti*), however, is threefold: subsequent to the primary act, prior to it, and simultaneous with it.
Among these, the first is, for example: "He throws the black antelope horn into the sacrificial pit" (*cātvāle kṛṣṇaviṣāṇāṃ prāsyati*), and so forth.
The second is, for example: "The bird will enter," and "He discards the blood."
This was established in the section [4.1.12–13] titled "In the fourth [case], the blood-sprinkling is a subsequent rite because there is no slaughter of animals.

An example of a disposal (*pratipatti*) simultaneous with the principal rite is that in the sacrifice enjoined by the *Āgneya* injunction, there is the disposal in the form of an oblation according to the rule, "He offers the fourfold portion.

For the oblation must be performed by the Adhvaryu at the moment immediately following the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call, as prescribed by the injunction, "He offers when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered."
And at that very moment, the sacrifice, impelled by the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance which brings about the completion of the sacrifice's essential form, is to be performed by the sacrificer.
This has been established in the *Vārttika* on the section concerning the "Offering of All" (*Sarvapradānādhikaraṇa*) [3.4.14]:
"But when there is the utilization of what has come into being for the sake of purifying both, there is no purifier of the substance at all."

However, that which effects the preparation (*saṃskāra*) of the deity through the utilization of an existing entity, namely the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), will be explained here as an *āśrayikarma* (a subordinate act dependent on a substrate).

Furthermore, that which is a directly contributing auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) is likewise of three kinds, just like the acts of disposal (*pratipatti*). [These are:
for the sake of preparing an existing entity for use, for the sake of preparing a vessel for use, and simultaneous with the use.
Among these, the first is as follows: [the disposal] of the burnt oblation is obtained through a rite inferred from the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).
Nor is this a mere *pratipatti* (disposal), because that which has been disposed of by the *homa* does not require another disposal for its state of being "scattered refuse" (*ākīrṇakaratva*).

Furthermore, that which is for the sake of purifying a substance intended for use is also twofold: for the sake of purifying what is directly employed, and for the sake of purifying that which assists what is directly employed.

Among these, the first is, for example: "He sprinkles the rice grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*). The second is, for example: the offering at the stump (*sthāṇvāhuti*) in the case of the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*), which serves to consecrate the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) by way of purifying the ground, the wood, and the artisan. The third is, for example: "He offers even the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) while moving it forward" (*arvāñcam*).

In the case of the archetype (*prakṛti*), however, the rule for turning over (*paryāvartana*) serves only an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). As for the action performed upon the substratum (*āśrayakarma*), which serves both visible and invisible purposes, that too is threefold: some part serves a visible purpose by way of the casting of the substance, while another part serves an invisible purpose by way of the dedication to a deity (*devatoddeśa*).
For example, the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice [serves both], because Agni Sviṣṭakṛt has no other application elsewhere.

In some cases, while having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) by way of a mere reference, it has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) by way of the casting of a substance; as, for example, the *uttama-prayāja*.

For there, according to the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantras such as "Svāhā to Agni, Svāhā to Soma," the deities who are about to be sacrificed to in the *ājyabhāga* offerings and so forth—being recognized sequentially—are the objects of refinement (*saṃskārya*).
This very point was established in the eighth book, in the section [sūtra] 10.1.7: "And in the *prayāja*, because that principle applies."

That even the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is exactly like this was established in the tenth book, in the section beginning with "If it be said that it is so even in the case of the animal sacrifice" (10.1.9). A certain foundational act (*āśrayakarma*), even if lacking the dedication to a deity, may have a visible purpose through the portion consisting of the casting of the substance; however, it acquires the status of a foundational act solely through the portion consisting of the renunciation of the substance when its purpose is invisible (*adṛṣṭārtha*). For example, in the injunction "He casts the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*," the casting of the *prastara* has a visible purpose through the mental construction of the intended deities revealed by the *sūktavāka* and the dedication to them.
Similarly, in the injunction "He places the *juhū* ladle upon the *prastara* grass-bundle," even the act of throwing the *prastara* substance onto the fire has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).
However, the mere abandonment of that [substance] therein has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Furthermore, Vedic ritual action is fourfold, by virtue of being for the sake of origination (*utpatti*), acquisition (*prāpti*), modification (*vikṛti*), and refinement (*saṃskṛti*).

Among these, the first is as follows: "He kneads with water," where the kneading is for the purpose of producing the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) lump and for the purpose of attaining heaven and so forth from the sacrifice.
The second is as follows: "He milks the cow," where the milking is for the purpose of obtaining the milk itself.
The third is as follows: "He sprinkles the rice grains," because it is for the purpose of the modification consisting of the removal of the husk.
The fourth is, for example, "he sprinkles the rice grains," because it serves the purpose of producing a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of an invisible nature (*adṛṣṭarūpa*).
Furthermore, Vedic action is fourfold: the archetype (*prakṛti*), the ectype (*vikṛti*), that which possesses both natures, and that which possesses neither nature.
Among these, the first is, for example, the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), and so forth.
The second is, for example, the *māsāgnihotra* and so forth.

The third is, for example, the *agnīṣomīya*, the *savanīya-paśu*, and so forth. For it is stated in the eighth [book] that, among the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the *agnīṣomīya* is the archetype (*prakṛti*), and the *savanīya-paśus* are its modifications (*vikṛti*). And because of the similarity of the time of the soma-pressing (*sutyā-kāla*), the *ekādaśina* animals are modifications of those; and of those, the *prājā-* [animals are modifications].
Action is twofold: action characterized by ritual injunction (*vidhi*), such as [the sacrifice] because of the similarity to the master’s herd of cattle;
and the fourth type, such as the *darvihoma* and the *nāriṣṭa* offerings.
For their novelty (*apūrvatva*) has been stated to be solely for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
The same applies to the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice and others.
Furthermore, Vedic ritual action is of two kinds: occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*).

The occasional (*naimittika*) [rite] is also of two kinds: that which has a fixed cause and that which has an unfixed cause. That which has an unfixed cause is also of two kinds: for the purpose of removing a defect and for the purpose of not removing a defect. Among these, that which has a fixed cause is, for example: "One performs the *agnihotra* as long as one lives," and "One should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma* in the spring."

Among these, the first has been established in the section concerning lifelong performance (*yāvajjīvādhikaraṇa*, 2.4.1); the second, however, was established in the sixth book in the section titled "Because of the connection with the sentence regarding the non-performance of the *Soma* sacrifice" (*somaviccāprajamaṇavākyena saṃyogāt*, 6.1.1.12).

That which is occasioned by an indefinite cause for the purpose of expiating a fault is, for example: "He who should neglect the new-moon or full-moon sacrifice shall offer an eight-potherd oblation to Pathikṛt," and "He who should neglect the new-moon or full-moon sacrifice shall offer a twelve-potherd oblation to Vaiśvānara."

Precisely because they serve the purpose of destroying defects (*doṣanirghāta*), there will be an option (*vikalpa*) between the [rites] having a single purpose and so forth, as will be stated in the section on expiations (*prāyaścitta*) in the twelfth book: "Because of being one, [there is an option] in the expiations" (12.3.16). That which is not for the purpose of destroying defects is "unrestricted" (*aniyata*); this was established in the first section of the same book (12.3.17), following the refutation of the previous rule, in the case of such injunctions as "one offers when [the vessel] is broken" (*minne juhoti*). Furthermore, optional (*kāmya*) action is also threefold: that with results in this life, that with results in the hereafter, and that with unrestricted results.

Among these, the first is as follows: "One desiring rain should sacrifice with the *Kārīrī*," and "One practicing sorcery (*abhicaran*) should sacrifice with the *Śyena*," as well as the *Jāteṣṭi* which has its fruit in the birth of a son and so forth.
For a visible result that is present is desired by everyone, not one that is not present even if it pertains to this life, much less one belonging to another birth.
