Likewise, sorcery is desired only against an enemy who is present, not against one who is not present even if he belongs to this life, much less one belonging to another birth.

In this way, even regarding purification and so forth, when a son is born to someone, that [act] is desired for him alone; it is not desired for him at another time, let alone for one belonging to another birth, even if the result pertains to this life.
An example of that which has a fruit in the hereafter is the *hotrā* sacrifice and others performed by one desiring heaven.
For heaven is not easily attainable by anyone in a human body; rather, it can be experienced through desirable enjoyments and the like, by means of both dharma and adharma.
An action with an uncertain result is, for example, "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā [offering]," and so forth.
Indeed, that the result—such as cattle—is uncertain as to whether it occurs in this life or the next was established in the fourth section on the accomplishment of yoga (4.1.11).
Furthermore, action in the form of renunciation (*nivṛtti*) is also twofold: that which has the sense of duty (*kṛtyartha*) and that which has human purpose (*puruṣārtha*).
Among these, the first is, for example: "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *Atirātra* sacrifice.
The second is, for example: "One should not harm any living beings.

That which is called *paryudāsa* (exclusion), consisting of both engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), is also twofold: pertaining to ritual action (*kṛtyartha*) and pertaining to human purpose (*puruṣārtha*).

Among these, the first is, for example: "In the *yajati* sacrifices one performs the *yeyajāmaha*, but not in the *anuyāja* sacrifices," and "One does not choose an *ārṣeya*, nor does one choose a *hotṛ*.
The second is, for example: "One should not look at the rising sun.
Thus concludes the determination of the distinctions between all ritual acts (*karma*).

this is to be seen in the word "in all verbal suffixes" (ākhyāteṣu sarveṣu).

Mīmāṃsā 4.4.13, pp. 913–940: Action is not divided even when there is a difference in substance, because [the essence of action] arises from such [definitions] as "this very movement is sacrifice" and so forth; thus, there is no harm in employing a substitute for the ritual act.
In that regard, there is only one single individual instance (*vyakti*) of the action existing upon the surface of the earth;
only its manifestation (*abhivyakti*) differs.

Alternatively, let there be no distinction between individual instances; rather, it is the classes such as the *Āgneya* and others that are distinguished by means of evidence such as different words. (Māṣṭa. 6.3.2). Action is eternally inferable.

In the inquiry as to whether that song (*gīti*) is the primary element with respect to the *ṛc* verses or a subordinate element, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
by the word "Sāman," the action— the primary action— is denoted,
because it is characterized by an injunction (*vidhi*).
In the cases of "He sings the *rathantara*" and "He sings the *bṛhat*," the characteristic or essential nature of the injunction regarding the primary action is seen in the accusative case-ending.
The word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of excluding other alternatives. Or rather, the action itself is characterized by the injunction.
That substance [is determined] by the scriptural statement, as in the case of the *pākayajña* sacrifices.
The word *sāman* denotes singing;
and that singing is not the primary element, but rather a subordinate one.
Now, what might that be toward which the song is subordinate? He says:
it would be the substance (*dravya*) serving as its substratum, namely the *ṛc*;
or rather, it would be that whose substance is the *ṛc*, i.e., the *ṛgdravya* [the Sāman].
The melody is subordinate to the substance that has the form of the *ṛc*, because of the statement: "He sings the *sāman* as mounted upon the *ṛc*.
It is like the *pākayajña*; that is, just as in the case of the *pākayajña*.

In a *pākayajña*, the material substance is verbal, consisting of parched grains (*lājāḥ*), fried grains (*dhānāḥ*), rice-grains (*taṇḍulāḥ*), and clarified butter (*ājyam*); likewise here too, the *ṛk* is the substance,
and the melody (*gīti*) is subordinate to it— this is the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*).
In that regard, there is no contradiction regarding the distinction from other substances and the spatial location.
The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view has been stated that the melody, which is the very nature of the *sāman*, is the primary element with respect to the *ṛc*.
To that, he states a specific distinction.

In that case, even when the Sāman— which rests upon the Ṛc— is accepted as the primary element, there is no contradiction in its distinction from the substance of the Ṛc (its substratum), nor is there any prohibition against its application and connection to another substance, namely another Ṛc, specifically to the "Uttarā" verse derived from the original source (*yoni*).
For an action being drawn forth by another action applies everywhere.

If one undertakes [an action] again and again, there will be fruits again and again;
through repeated practice, there is an abundance of fruit.
Because it exists as an undertaking, by means of the undertaking—that is, the application of the action—the fruit is brought into being and produced.
Thus, there is the attainment of results from the repetition of the ritual action;
just as in agriculture, when there is a repetition of cultivation by means of four-footed animals, a repetition of the fruit occurs, so it is here.
This is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
And the distinction regarding the qualification (*adhikāra*) of all [persons] is established because [the rites] are to be performed; this is the specific point.
In the final view (*siddhānta*), the next *sūtra* provides another reason:
because all optional (*kāmya*) rites are to be performed—that is, they must be practiced—repeatedly, a further qualification, namely a superior connection with the fruit, is logically established.
Therefore, the established conclusion is that there should be practice as much as one desires;
however, it might occur only once, because the purpose has been fulfilled, as in the case of the *cavet* [formula].
But the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says:

A rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya-karma*) should be performed only once; because when it is enjoined as being performed once, the injunction has fulfilled its purpose through that single performance, and because the agent, having completed the task in one instance, does not perform it again—just as the ritual implements (*yajñāṅga*) are employed only once and not repeated.
Such is the meaning of the word in common worldly usage as well.
Thus says the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).
In common worldly usage, the meaning of a word is exactly as the word [itself] indicates. For example, when told "Bring the wood," one brings it once, and not again and again;
it is just like that.
The word "ca" (and) in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) refers to another reason.

In the case of application through meditation (*adhiyā*), it is understood according to one's desire because it is not based on direct revelation (*aśrutitvāt*); thus, these would be injunctive statements (*vidhi-vacanāni*).
The word "adhiyā" sets aside the prima facie view.

When there is a connection between the purpose and the action, one who acts according to their desire is understood to have a mind that acts according to their desire during the performance. One who seeks an abundance of results performs repeatedly; one who is content performs only once.
Since it is not heard in scripture, there is no scriptural injunction regarding performing [the rite] either once or more than once.
Therefore, one who desires an abundance of results should perform optional (*kāmya*) rites as often as they desire.

Furthermore, if these were required by rule to be performed only once, then injunctions in the scriptures such as, "For those who sacrifice for the first time, there is the Gaurātirātra; for those who do so a second time, there is the Āyus," would be rendered meaningless.
Alternatively, the statements prescribing optional rites would fulfill their purpose simply by enjoining the rite and would remain indifferent as to whether it is performed once or repeatedly.
Therefore, one who desires an abundance of results should perform [the rite] even repeatedly;
likewise in other cases due to the singular number.
Regarding what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view—that it is "like the ignorant" (Sūtra 22)—he says:
Likewise, due to the singular number [used] for the ignorant;
since the single word "teacher" (upadeśaka) refers to all ignorant persons by way of dependence upon the principal among the ignorant,
the use of the plural for the ignorant is appropriate.
In the present case, however, the production of one [effect] after another in each performance is not contradictory;
thus, there is a disparity with the example.
This is because, in the case of a verbal root denoting an action (*karma*), there is the state of being an undertaking, and [the suffixes apply] when the agent is the object (*karmakartṛ*) in a verb.
In the world, action is characterized by its purpose.
Regarding what was stated by the opponent, "as in the world" (Sūtra 23), he replies:
in the world, action is characterized by its purpose; that is, it is defined by the purpose, which follows from the intended motive.
Due to the requirements of the task at hand, one who is engaged once may perform the action repeatedly, or perform it once, or not perform it at all.
However, in the present case concerning the definition of the word, it is logical that the application follows the literal meaning of the word.
Therefore, the established conclusion is that in the case of an optional rite (*kāmya-karman*), one who desires an abundance of results engages in it repeatedly.
This is the analogy of agriculture.

Thus, whether before or after [the aforementioned], there are many more persons, including the seventeen chanters (saptagātṛs) and the Soma-seller (somavikrayin).

The wife of the sacrificer—twenty in number, neither more nor less—is not authorized [here], nor is she mentioned; those regarding whom it was stated in a previous text that "others than the seven are employed in the performance of the sacrifice" are they. Of them...

The statement "ten" constitutes a distributive expression (*avayulayavāda*), wherein all [of them] would possess the status of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Why? Because of the performance of the ritual action (*karmakāryāt*).

The number of the action is proclaimed therein; in the case of the other number, the word *āvayulaya* occurs with the suffix *ya* in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāvārthaka*), as well as the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and the suffix *nu* in the sense of cognition (*buddhi*).
This is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Just as, having stated [the rule] regarding the twelve-fold vessel, it is said that "those who perform the eightfold rite,
they all perform the sacrifice"—
this refers to the ritual action in the form of a sacrifice.
The claim that "he becomes a skull-bearer" does not apply here;
therefore, because of this [absence of such] qualification, all [priests] do not possess the status of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). There is no distinction.

Regarding the *karmadhāraya* compound [in the phrase "niṣādasthapati"], since it is intended to express a relationship between an action and its fruit (*karmaphala-sambandha*), there is no possibility of it expressing a relationship because the elision of case-endings (*vibhakti-lopa*) has not even occurred in the compound. Therefore, in this context, a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound) must be understood through the word "niṣāda" itself by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Nor should it be argued that this being the case, there would be the total abolition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), because both words would then stand in apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and thus result in a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*). For it is accepted that where there is apposition through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the genitive sense, there is a genitive compound; whereas where there is apposition even without such elision (*luk*), there is a descriptive compound.

Nor should it be argued that even in this case, the analysis (*vigraha*) for *rājapuruṣa* would have to be "he is both a king and a man," because since the word *rājan* conveys a man related to a king, the analysis "the king's man" would not be possible;
for there is no genitive case in a compound, and that which has become part of a compound cannot be employed in its analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*). This objection must be addressed.
Because it would lead to an undesirable consequence here.
If it is asked, "In that case, how is even the analysis [of the compound] in 'the king's man' (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) performed?"—
it is understood that this is for the purpose of clarifying the meaning.
Otherwise, even a *karmadhāraya* compound might be possible.

Therefore, it is established that because the word "Niṣāda" would have to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the compound must indeed be a *karmadhāraya*.
Consequently, it is the Niṣāda alone who is authorized as the *sthapati* (chief).
Where there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) even without the indication of the sense of the genitive case, there is a *karmadhāraya* compound;
but where there is coreferentiality through the indication of the sense of the genitive case, there is a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*.

It has been stated that, because the genitive case in the word *niṣādasya* would necessitate a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) when taken as a locative, the *karmadhāraya* compound is stronger than the *tatpuruṣa* alternative.
An investigation into *karmadhāraya* compounds: This should be seen in the work titled *Samāsavāda* within the *Maṇi* treatise.

Bhāṣya 7.3.15 states the general rule (*utsarga*): "Every word denoting an action (*karmanāman*), when heard elsewhere [than its own primary context], is a receiver (*grāhaka*) of properties (*dharma*)."

The term *agnihotra* is a name for an action, as in: "He performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice" (Bhāṣya 1.4.14). Similarly, the word *abhijit* [is a name for an action], as in: "One should sacrifice with the *abhijit*" (1.4.19). Likewise, the word *āghāra* [is a name for an action], as in: "He pours the *āghāra* libation."
1.4.18: Likewise, the word *ājya* is the name of a specific ritual action in the form of a *stotra*, as in "the *ājya*s are fifteenfold.

1.4.13: Likewise, the word *udbhid* is the name of a ritual action, as in "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*. 1.4.11: Likewise, the word *go* [is used], as in "one should sacrifice with the *go*. 1.4.14: Likewise, the word *citrā* [is used], as in "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrā*."
1.4.13: Thus, the word *darvihoma* is the name of a *homa*.
8.1.1–2.1.6: Thus, the word *pavamāna* is the name of a specific *stotra*, as in "the *bahiṣpavamāna* consists of three *ṛc*s. 1.4.12:
Thus, the word *pṛṣṭha* [is the name of a specific *stotra*], as in "the *pṛṣṭhas* consist of seventeen [verses]."

1.4.12: Likewise, the word *balabhid* is the name of a specific sacrifice, as in "one should sacrifice with the *balabhid*. 1.4.11: Likewise, the word *vājapeya* [is the name of a sacrifice], as in "one desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the *vājapeya*. 1.4.16: Likewise, the word *viśvajit* [is the name of a sacrifice], as in "one should sacrifice with the *viśvajit*."

1|4|11, likewise the word *vaiśvadeva*: "One should sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva*. 1|4|10|13, likewise the word *śyena*: "One practicing malevolent magic (*abhicaraṇa*) should sacrifice with the *śyena*. 1|4|14, likewise the word *saṃdaṃśa*: "One practicing malevolent magic should sacrifice with the *saṃdaṃśa*."
The word *svāhākāra* is the name of the action (*karmanāmadheya*) for the fifth *prayāja*. (Vi.
10.1.17). Regarding names of actions such as *agnihotra* and others, there is the status of being an *ādeśika* [term].
However, there is no status of being an *ādeśika* for etymological terms such as *prāyaṇīya* and others, nor for terms like *vaiśvadeva* and others which denote a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

The category of action (karmapadārtha) is inferable (*anumeya*). According to the *Riju* (p. 98), the category of action is said to be "subsisting in a single substance" (*ekadravya*) because it exists in only one substance.

On page 198, it is stated that the performance of ritual action (*karmaprayoga*) occurs at all times, whether during the period of study (*adhyāya*) or the period when study is suspended (*anadhyāya*).
Moreover, there is a prohibition against study on the days of the *parvan* festivals and during the performance of ritual acts.

According to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), the performance [of study] would be required; according to the traditional law (*smṛti*), it is prohibited. And the Vedic revelation is more authoritative than the traditional law.
Bhāṣya 12.1.7.19: The fruit is brought about through the performance of action.
How is this known? Because there is no fruit prior to the performance of the action;
if it were already present, the action would be purposeless.
And it is understood from scripture that [the self] exists at a time subsequent to action.
That which did not exist prior to the action but comes into being at a time subsequent to the action is brought into manifestation by that action, like a jar.
(1.1.4.20). Regarding the relationship between action and its fruit, the action is subordinate and the fruit is primary.
This has been stated in the passage "and because of the connection with each respective object" (6.1.13).
Bhāṣya 7.4.1, p. 1569: the indication of the ripening of the fruits of action is rooted in the Veda.

Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 130: a rule concerning optional rites (*kāmya*) that pertains to the connection between action and its fruit is an injunction regarding the qualification for human goals (*puruṣārtha*), such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices."

*Bāla*, p. 14: Regarding the mantras for laying the bricks (*iṣṭakopadhāna-mantra*) of the Yājñasenīs, by the statement "This indeed is the *chandas* of the seers belonging to Agni, namely the Yājñasenīs," there is a recollection (*smṛti*).

According to the principle of the section on the *karmabhyūhastava* (1.2.39), because of its superior force and its proximity, the commencement of another rite (*karmāntara*) in the midst of a rite serves as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) for the laying of the bricks.

Nor is there a deficiency in the number of mantras, because repetition is possible—as in the case of a "stick-measurement" (daṇḍakalita)—or because the required number can be completed by those [mantras] displaced from their original positions, according to the principle of the section on the inference of ritual acts (10.1.25.8–84).
This is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). [This concludes] the section on the *vyatīkā*.

Saṃkarṣa 2.1.33: There is a distinction between the rites (*karmabheda*) due to the distinction of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇābheda*) and the distinction of performers (*kartṛbheda*). [The text states: "An offering to Agni on eight potsherds with gold as the fee; an offering to Indra on eleven potsherds with two bulls as the fee; a mixture for the Viśvedevas with a six-year-old piebald cow as the fee; a curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa with a barren cow as the fee; and a cooked rice-oblation for Bṛhaspati with a white-backed bull as the fee. Because of this distinction of sacrificial fees—and because the sacrificial fee serves to differentiate the performers—there is an understanding that there is a distinct performance for each sacrifice (*pratiyāga*), even though the substance upon which the performer stands is the same, by way of the distinction of performers involved in the performance.
Su. Pṛ. 912: "There is no difference in the action [when] a quality does not take the primary action as its substrate;
because it is a restatement of its connection, no difference is understood therein—as in the case of [the injunction]:
'One desiring sense-faculties should offer the oblation' (*dadhna indriyakāmasya juhuyāt*)."

Vārttika 2.1.12.17, p. 553: There is no differentiation of the ritual action (*karmabheda*) when the specific substance is not mentioned in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), as in "He offers the Agnihotra" and "He offers with curd," "He offers with milk. Vi. 2.1.10: There is no differentiation of the ritual action on account of names such as *Kāṭhaka* and the like.
Vārttika 3.1.12, p.

650: "The differentiation of actions (karmabheda) is the purpose of [different] names. Maṇi, p. 6: "Differentiation of actions arises from different words (śabdāntara); for example, there is a distinction between sacrifice (yāga), oblation (homa), and giving (dāna) in the expressions 'he sacrifices,' 'he offers,' and 'he gives.'"

VI. 2.1.2: From repetition (*abhyāsa*), as in "He offers the *samidh* oblation, he offers the *tanūnapāt* oblation, he offers the *iḍ* oblation, he offers the *barhis* oblation, he offers the *svāhākāra* oblation"—due to the repetition of the word *yajati*, there is a distinction among the five *prayāja* offerings.

2.1.2: From difference of context (*prakaraṇabheda*), as in "Knowing thus, one sacrifices on the full moon day" and "Knowing thus, one sacrifices on the new moon day"—there is a distinction between the sacrifices.
2.1.3: From number (*saṃkhyā*), as in "He offers three oblations"—there is a distinction between the acts of offering due to the number.

JS 2.1.6: In the case of the *Tāṇḍya* passage, "Now this is the Jyotis; now this is the Viśvajyotis; now this is the Sarvajyotis," there is a difference of ritual acts (*karmabheda*) due to the difference in names (*saṃjñābheda*).

JS 2.1.8: In the case of "The *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas; the *vājina* belongs to the Vājins," there is a difference of ritual acts due to the difference in the qualities of substance and deity (*dravyadevatāguṇabheda*).
JS 2.1.9: A difference of ritual acts does not occur when there is a difference in preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*).

"By the statement, 'He takes the mental cup for Prajāpati,' this injunction regarding the taking of the cup (*grahacodanā*) is understood as referring to the tenth day, because it prescribes a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) through the verb 'he takes. Therefore, [the mental cup] is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) for the tenth day, not an injunction for a separate day. In the case of a difference of ritual acts (*karmabheda*), the mantra must be repeated for each act, as in the case of the *āmana-homa* and others. (Mīmāṃsākośa 173; Bhāṣya 10.6.13.18). In the case of a difference of ritual acts, the mantra must be repeated for each act, as in the case of the *āmana-homa* and others.
Soma. 2.
There is no interval between actions in the context of verbal roots expressing action.

There is no other sequence within the ritual action, because a fault is heard regarding a deviation from the sequence in the statement: "Verily, something is omitted from the sacrifice when the framework of one [rite] is extended while the framework of another is already spread out" (Bhāṣya 5.1.17.131). It is like the ritual action:

"And the designation is like that of the ritual action"; just as with the principal action, there is no designation by means of the instrumental case, as in "he recites the *prauga*," "he recites the *niṣkevalya*."
Bhāṣya 2.1.28: "Like the ritual action" (*karmavat*). [The rule] "And there is a prohibition like the ritual action" (*pratiṣedhaśca karmavat*) [applies].

Since in a *sattra* sacrifice the officiating priests themselves are the sacrificers, just as the ritual action consisting of the formal selection (*varaṇa*) does not apply, so too the giving of cows and other gifts does not apply, because there is no connection with a fruit intended for oneself as the recipient.
Likewise, even a prohibition such as "neither a cow nor a garment is given here" would not apply [to the sacrificer].

[Śabara on Jaimini Sūtra 10.2.1.136 states: "But the acts pertaining to the sacrificer are like the ritual acts, because he is the principal; 'the acts pertaining to the sacrificer, however, are like the ritual acts because he is the principal due to the primacy of the sacrifice.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, purificatory rites such as shaving should pertain to the sacrificer, because the fruit of the rite—such as 'he shaves his hair and beard' and 'he cleanses his teeth'—accrues to the sacrificer, and thus the sacrificer is the principal."
"Like the primary action (karmavat): just as the principal actions belong to the person who is the sacrificer, so it is here. 3|8|2|4, "like the action":
"But the preparatory rites (saṃskāras), for the sake of the person, should be restricted according to the Veda, like the action."

Just as other ritual acts prescribed in a particular Veda are performed by a person designated by that same name, so too the purificatory rites such as shaving (vapanādi) in the Jyotiṣṭoma must be performed by the Adhvaryu; this is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa). (3|8|2|3). Ritual injunctions merely depend upon the knowledge already established through study; they do not themselves possess the power to instigate the act. (Soma. 6|8|2). "And the various types of bodies are qualities resulting from the power of karma."
"Indeed, because of the discernment through the origins of bodies, there is a distinction among individual selves. (Vākyapadīya 3.1.7.13, p.

702). Now, one might object: "Since the nature of being earth alone [in the case of bodies] excludes the pervasive earth-nature [of the Vedas], and since the exclusion of the pervaded [nature of] being a body [thereby follows], it is logical that the Vedas have their locus in names," and so forth. To this he says: "deha... (body...). Because of the discernment through the origins of bodies—that is, the diverse modes of bodies resulting from the discernment of the origins of bodies consisting of earth-atoms and the like—there are distinct types of bodies.

When this was said, [the opponent] argued that, upon investigating the commencement of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) in view of its causes, it was stated that the *guṇas* possess the power to bring about the experience of various fruits produced by the diverse actions of living beings, which do not strike at their vital points.

Consequently, the intention of the rebuttal is as follows: since pure earth exists in some cases as the material cause of the body, and since the presence of [earthly] abundance is found even in other elements, the pervasion of "bodiness" by "earthenness" is unestablished.
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 1009). Furthermore, there are certain words denoting action (*karman*), but they do not have the sense of "existence" (*bhāva*).
For example, [words such as] *dvaitin*, *traiṇika*, and so forth.
Some words have the sense of "being" (*bhāva*) and are not verbal nouns denoting action (*karmaśabda*); for instance, "being" (*bhavanaṃ*), "existence" (*bhāvaḥ*), or "coming into being" (*bhūtiḥ*).
(Bhāṣya 2.1.1, p. 386). Ordinary people employ the word *karma* in the sense of an object to be accomplished (*kāryārthe*).

*Bṛhatī*, p. 27: Having stated that [the rule] pertains to the remainder of the ritual action (*karmaśeṣa*), by means of the injunction of prohibition within the sentence, there is a distinct *uṣṇamana* every year. In the *pañcaśaradīya* *ahīna* sacrifice, according to Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 11.2.1.134–36, if it is held that [the rule] pertains to the remainder of the ritual action, then the preparation of the substance (*dravyasaṃskāra*) is purposeful, whereas the property of the fuel (*puṣadharma*) would be useless.

3|4|8|123. Since it is possible for them to serve as purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the purpose of completing the remainder of the ritual action, the mantras must be employed because they assist the rite, and not otherwise. (This is the nature of the section concerning the second hymn in the second chapter.
Su. p. 1108. The *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations are connected to ritual actions (specifically Vedic ritual actions);
they are neither independent nor are they connected to worldly activities.

Bhāṣya 3.4.15.26: In the view that [the *liṅga*] consists of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the ritual action, or the refinement of what is being offered, there would be a distinction [of the *liṅga*] due to the distinction between those [actions], as in the case of the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering in the *Sarvapṛṣṭhā-iṣṭi* where there are six [forms of] Indra. Vārttika 3.5.4.17, p. 996: The capacity of a word (*śabdasāmarthya*), which consists of the form of the meaning and serves to illuminate the purpose of the ritual action, is the *liṅga*.
Bālam Bhaṭṭa, p. 9: Because the purpose of the *tridhi* [is] the attainment of similarity with the ritual action.

Bhāṣya 10.6.12.133: Since the determination of the ritual application (*prayoga-pariccheda*) is not established without the accomplishment of the ritual action (*karma-siddhi*), once the determination of the application is established, the ritual action is thereby established.
Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 856: Having ascertained that the substance, the deity, and the action constitute the essential nature of the ritual action, the entire [ritual] is recited in the Yajurveda;
however, in the other Vedas, only the action is mentioned, while the hymns (*stotra*), liturgical recitations (*śastra*), and so forth, are studied separately.

Vākyapadīya 3.3.4.11, p. 616: In the case of a verbal expression denoting the object (*karmākhyāta*), such as *odanaḥ pacyate* ("the rice is being cooked"), the cognition is that there is an operation which brings about a result that is co-referential with the state of being the object (*karmatva*) residing in the rice-grains (*taṇḍula*). Maṇi, p. 414: Regarding the application of number (*saṃkhyā*) in the case of a verbal expression denoting the object, one should consult the note stating, "Number also [is expressed] by means of *tiP* and so forth."
The extent of karma and ignorance; an investigation into the inferability of karma.
Having heard the extent of ritual actions and knowledge, it is determined [by scripture].
However, the extent of worldly ritual actions and knowledge is determined by direct perception.
Vi. 8.2.3, Section 2. Mantras are the reminders of ritual actions and knowledge.
The fixed pronunciation [of words] is for the purpose of a restricted unseen result (*niyamādṛṣṭārtha*).
Ke. 1.2.131–53 (Vi). [Grammatical] case-endings (*karmādayaḥ*) are obtained through the sense; they do not become the denotable meanings of the word itself.
Bhā. 3.4.14.3, p. 927. In the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the conjunction of the case-endings and so forth occurs at the end of the mantra in the *āghāra* offering.

12|3|128: In the case of the *karaṇa-mantras*, there is a conjunction of the action and so forth with the end of the mantra. 12|3|125–125: In the *vasordhārā* [offering], there is a conjunction of the action and so forth with the end of the mantra.
12|3|126–27: There is no authority for the ritual action in the case of an imperfection of the command (*ājñāvaikalya*) that cannot be remedied.
Bhāṣya 6.1.10.42: There is an authority for action regarding the rectification of defects in knowledge.
6.1.9.41: An investigation into the inferability of action.

According to the general rule that "whatever is an effect (phala) must immediately follow something that has arisen," when one observes the connection between parts such as threads or the contact [of sense organs] with objects, and having determined that reaching another location is an occasional effect, one infers some antecedent cause to that which has arisen.
And in that regard, people employ the word "karma" [for it].
Nor can it be understood that the substance itself is merely accumulated,
because there would have to be recognition of it, which is not the case due to its being concealed.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that an inference contradicted by perception is possible when a non-contradictory one exists; therefore, action is inferred as something distinct from substance. Here, another [author], employing the *Paroktārthaparyālocana-laghusiddhānta*, seeks the perceptibility of action and states it as follows:

Is it not the case that action (*karman*) is not inferable, but is rather merely visible (*cākṣuṣa*), being inherent in a material substance (*rūpidravya*), because the cognition “this one is moving” depends upon the operation of the sense organs?

Accordingly, there is a sūtra in another system [the Vaiśeṣika]: “Number, dimensions, separateness, conjunction and disjunction, priority and posteriority, and action are visible because they inhere in material substances” (Kaṇāda Sūtra 4.1.11).
Now, [one might argue] that this cognition has as its object an action inferred from conjunction and disjunction.

That is untenable. Since space is beyond the reach of the senses, its conjunction with [the bird]—like the conjunction of wind and a tree—is imperceptible; therefore, due to the absence of a probans (*liṅga*), the cognition "it flies" would not arise regarding birds in flight. To this it is replied: the conjunctions and disjunctions with the rays of the sun spread across the sky are the perceptible probans; that is not so.
In the dead of night, amidst dense darkness, because there is the cognition "it moves" when lightning flashes suddenly,
and furthermore, because conjunction and disjunction exist both in the object to be moved and in the mover—
if action were to be inferred from those two, then the cognition of that [action] would also occur in the object to be moved.
Furthermore, action is that which is incompatible with its own effect;
consequently, while the action exists due to conjunction, there would be no manifestation [of the effect].
Moreover, conjunction and disjunction are capable of inferring action.

Since that [motion] too occurs only occasionally, it must depend on another cause; yet, since those two [the cognition and the action] are established from that very cause which is intended as their cause, this is merely the manifestation of a defect in reasoning.
The cognition "he moves" has the inferred action as its objective basis.
As for lightning, it is the action of motion inferred from the conjunctions and disjunctions of its constituent parts; thus, there is no lack of production [of the effect].
Nor is there an inference of motion in the object being moved (*gamya*), because the action is inherent only in the mover (*gantṛ*), which accounts for the conjunctions and disjunctions.

Nor can this be considered erroneous—that the very action being cognized produces its fruit in the goer—because no other actions are possible in the goer apart from the conjunction with the subsequent location.
It is logically consistent that the action residing in Devadatta initiates disjunction from the preceding location and conjunction with the subsequent location;
nor is there any contradiction in the present cognition expressed as "he moves."
This is with reference to a single moment of action, because a single moment lacks temporal sequence (paurvāparya).
Therefore, the determination of "presentness" in the form "this moves" is based solely on the continuum (*saṃtāna*) of moments of action.

Consequently, even when one moment has perished and another has not yet arisen, the presentness of the continuum of actions—which is delimited by a single result and remains neither begun nor completed—is not unarisen.
And this cognition arises with reference to the fruit, occurring through a succession of subsequent moments.

As it has been said: “When, from the initial contact onwards until the attainment of the fruit, the action is perceived as consisting of prior and posterior parts, then it is said to ‘exist’” (*Ślokavārttika*, Sphoṭavāda 79).
Furthermore, conjunction, disjunction, and so forth do not arise from the cause of karma alone.
For instance,
action in the feet, hands, and other limbs is held to result from the conjunction of the self and the body, assisted by an effort residing in the self.
As it has been said: "Action in the hand arises from the conjunction of the self and the body" (Kaṇāda-sūtra 5.1.1).
Conjunction initiates its effect only within the conjoined entities, just as the conjunction of parts initiates the whole.
Furthermore, conjunction and disjunction reside solely in their substrata, because they inhere even in a location that is not the substratum itself.
By that [reasoning], another action distinct from the conjunction with the self is inferred.
Nor is the rule observed there that "it produces its fruit only in its own substrate," because that [action] is something unprecedented (*apūrva*).
Therefore, even though it is an object of inference, there is no fault whatsoever.
But this is contradicted by direct perception; for,
even when investigating with great skill, those who restate the action [of throwing] do not establish it as a distinct action over and above conjunction and disjunction.

Another point is perceived. As it has been said: "For those [substances] are not perceptible" (Bhāṣya, p. 77, l. 3). Why, then, was it stated: "Having perceived that Devadatta’s arrival at another place is preceded by motion, one infers motion in the case of the sun as well"? (Bhāṣya, p. 37, l. 1); for even in the case of Devadatta, [the body] is something other [than the self].
It is said:
when motion in Devadatta has been inferred as something exceeding mere conjunction with the self, then by analogy, motion itself is inferred in the sun as well;
for in the case of Devadatta, his arrival at another location is ascertained by its temporal duration.
This is what is meant: in all cases, whether in the case of sentient beings or insentient objects, motion alone is the cause for reaching another location.
(Ṛjuvimalā, pp. 76–78). The objection that this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) with reference to an existing action (*karmānuvāda*) is refuted.
(Sūtrabhāṣya, p. 766). A distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) necessarily exists in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices.

Bhāṣya 12.2.5.63–66: A different ritual action [is established] from the Aveṣṭi by the passage beginning with "If a Brāhmaṇa," etc., which concerns the qualification for the fruit of the ritual action; [the measurements are] from the mouth [to] the distance of a span.
There, the Adhvaryu says to the sacrificer, "Insert your two hands," and asks, "What is here?
He replies, "Blessing.
The Adhvaryu responds, "May we both be there together."
Thus there is a designation for both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer.
In that context, the expression "together" indicates the inclusion of both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer.
Therefore, the fruit of the Adhvaryu is to be wished for here.
In the [sūtra] "Or else, because of the designation of another" (3.8.5.14), an example from the Brāhmaṇa was cited; here, however, by virtue of the context, one from the Mantra is given.
For there might be a doubt that if [the application] were to be inferred with difficulty, it might perhaps not be possible to infer it for both;
the reason for the inference, however, remains the simultaneous occurrence.
Thus, there is no point in [employing] both.

Now, why are both not employed together? Since even one [of them], when employed, is indeed capable of manifesting the fruit of both, then, the purpose being already established, there is no need for the employment of two agents; thus, the rule is restricted.

In the Śālikanātha-vivaraṇa and Bhaṭṭa [works], as well as in those of Maṇḍana and Śaṅkara, two sections (*adhikaraṇa*) have been accepted: "But in the case of the object of action" (*karmārthe tu*) and "And because of the designation as something else" (*nyapadeśācca*).

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated that even by means of the two sūtras, there is only one [topic]. Regarding the Soma sacrifice as well, the connection is explained: in the first case, by the previous reasoning (*pūrvanyāya*), it is established that [the fruit] goes to the sacrificer; in the second case, it is established by the principle of "dissimilarity" (*vaiṣamya*).
"Who?"—[the answer is] "Let there be no distress for me"; in whom? In the master, as before.
However, that [formula] belongs to the Adhvaryu, because it is employed for the sake of the master's ritual action.

The phrase "May there be well-being for both of us here" is appropriate when applied to the master; thus, according to the *Uśanā* scripture, it refers to both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). However, in cases such as "May I not suffer," which are enjoined by the particle *iti*, the result—consisting of the absence of suffering and so forth—is beneficial even to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) because it prevents suffering that would obstruct the sacrifice. In such instances, the genitive case in "that [result] belongs to the sacrificer" is justified even through a mediated relationship; therefore, in accordance with the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it belongs exclusively to the priest.

Thus, even in cases such as "there [they two] together," where the dual number provides the justification, the fruit belongs to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Maṇḍana [states]: "The result would not accrue to the master (*svāmin*) if there were no mental satisfaction (*asaṃtapanam*)."
"The fruit of these two is designated as *madrā*.
Śaṅkara says: 'But that which is effortless, beginning with freedom from distress (*asaṃtāpa*),' and 'and that [is] in the case of a secondary designation (*nyapadeśa*)."
(That which is designated as both) 18.
Because it is seen there in the sense of the object (*karman*).
And [the argument] regarding the original form and its modification:
the proponent states the fifth reason for the non-eternality of sound:
"Sound is non-eternal because we observe both the original form and its modification in the expression 'dadhyatra'."
Pāṇini and others teach that the letter *i* is the original form (*prakṛti*) and the letter *ya* is the modification (*vikṛti*).
That which undergoes modification is impermanent.
The letter *ca* serves to conjoin the reasons.
He states the sixth reason for the non-eternality of sound as its increase due to the multiplicity of agents; the word "and" (ca) serves to aggregate the reasons.
The increase—that is, the magnitude—of this sound is observed due to the abundance of its agents, meaning the plurality of its utterers.
Therefore, because it follows from these two reasons, sound is non-eternal due to its being produced (*kṛtakatvāt*). However, there is a common perception regarding that [magnitude].
This is the *siddhānta-sūtra* for the refutation of the first reason cited in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the non-eternality of sound.
The word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside the prima facie position.
In that regard, the perception of sound at the time following its production and its being perceived [later] are both equal [in proving non-eternality].

Furthermore, impermanence is not established by the observation of questions and answers; rather, it is the non-perception of existing objects after they have passed away. This is the *siddhānta-sūtra* intended to refute the second reason stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) for proving the impermanence of sound.
The word *param* means "furthermore" (*ity arthe*).

Regarding the object, which is sound, it is logical that there is no perception—that is, no hearing—of the eternal sound that already exists, because of the non-arrival (*anāgama*), i.e., the absence of arrival, of the manifesting agents such as the sense of hearing; for there is no connection [between them]. However, the observation of its destruction is merely an illusion.
By that [reason], impermanence is not established.
This is the final application.
This is the sūtra of the established conclusion (siddhānta) for the purpose of refuting the third reason stated by the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) which seeks to prove the impermanence of sound.
As for the other reason stated—that [the word "karoti"] is because of the word "karoti"—that refers not to the word itself, but to the employment of the word. "'Make a sound' means 'employ the word';
'Do not make a sound' means 'do not employ the word.'"
Likewise, the word *karoti* (he does/makes) also does not prove the non-eternality of sound, because it refers to an act of usage.
"Simultaneity like that of the sun"—

this is a sūtra of the established conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*) intended to refute the reason stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa-sūtra*) beginning with "and because of simultaneity in other beings."

Just as the sun, though being one, is perceived simultaneously by various people in various locations, so too would there be simultaneity in various locations for a single, eternal sound; it is indeed perceived thus.

Therefore, even though it is perceived simultaneously in various locations, neither the non-eternality nor the difference of the sound is established. This concludes the section concerning "another sound" (*śabdāntara*).

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) refutes the reason for the non-eternality of sound stated in the tenth sūtra, "prakṛtivikṛtyośca" [and because of the relationship between original form and modification].
In cases such as "dadhyatra," there is no relationship of original form and modification whatsoever;
rather, the letter *y* is a different word from the letter *i*.
Furthermore, "dadhyatra" is indeed a different word from "dadhi atra";
the letter *y* is not a modification (*vikāra*) of the letter *i*.
For this very reason, in the rule "iko yaṇ aci" (Pāṇini 6.1.77), when there is occasion for the pronunciation of an *ik*, the *yaṇ* is to be pronounced [in its place].
The grammarians explain [the rule] simply as "when *aci* follows.
Therefore, the word is not impermanent;
the increase belongs to the sound (*nāda*).
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) refutes the well-stated reason for the non-eternality of sound, namely: "And its increase [is due] to the multiplicity of its producers.

That increase of *nāda* or *dhvani* mentioned previously is not an increase of the sound (*śabda*) itself, but rather an increase of the *nāda*; it is merely an illusion that the sound becomes great because of the *dhvanis*.
Alternatively, it is simply an increase of the *nāda* alone.
There is no increase in the word-sound;
the increase in the sound is merely superimposed upon the word-sound and cannot establish it as being subject to modification.
Rather, it must be eternal, because its manifestation is for the sake of another.
By the word "tu" (but), [the author], setting aside the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the non-eternality of sound, establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that it is eternal:
Sound, such as the letter *ga* and so forth, must be eternal, because its manifestation—
that is, its utterance— is for the sake of another.
Utterance is for the purpose of making another understand.
For when an uttered sound has perished, the comprehension of meaning from it would not be possible;
since it exists for the sake of another, the word does not perish—it is known that the word is eternal.
Because of simultaneity everywhere.
This is stated as the second reason for proving the non-eternality of sound:
"Because of the simultaneity—that is, the simultaneous occurrence or simultaneous production—of the cognition of 'cowness' (gotva) in all instances of the genus 'cow'."
Because the form of the genus "cowness" (gotvākṛti) is eternal, the word is eternal;
this is due to the absence of number.
This is stated as the third reason for the established doctrine that words are eternal.

They say, "The word *go* has been uttered eight times," but they do not say, "There are eight instances of the word *go*," because [the word] is perceived there as a single entity. This concludes the chapter on the negation of the definition of a word (*kallakṣaṇapratiṣedhādhyāya*).
And thus, because number does not exist in sound, there is no difference between sounds;
and that [non-difference] is not possible without permanence. Therefore, sound is eternal, because it is independent [of causes].
In the case of cloth and other such objects, impermanence is known from causes such as the disjunction of threads or the destruction of the threads themselves.

In the case of sound, however, because there is an absence of such required causes for destruction, its permanence is understood. For a sound such as the letter *ga* is not composed of parts, such that it would be destroyed by the destruction of its parts or similar means.
Therefore, because it does not depend on a cause of destruction, sound is eternal;
furthermore, because there is no manifestation of its conjunction [with the sense organ],
this fifth reason is set forth to establish the doctrine of the eternity of sound.
*Prakhyā* means manifest appearance (*prakhyāti*), which is of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It refers to the conjunction of aerial parts (*vāyavīya-avayava-saṃyoga*) belonging to *yoga*.

Thus, according to the position that sound has air as its cause, since there is an absence of the perceptible manifestation of the conjunction of aerial parts that serves as the cause, sound does not have air as its cause; therefore, it is not non-eternal.
The reading in the *Vṛtti* is "yogasya. The meaning is as follows:

since sound—which is suitable (*yogyasya*), that is, an object of perception by the auditory faculty—is a modification of air, there would be an absence of perception; consequently, there would follow the non-existence of its being an object of knowledge for the auditory faculty. Therefore, it cannot be composed of air, and thus it must be eternal. This is the sense.
In the *Kutūhala*, however, the reading is "and because of the absence of perception of the conjunction" (*prakhyābhāvācca saṃyogasya*).
Since the conjunction of air-particles is not perceived in sound, sound does not have air as its cause.
Regarding the reading "and because of the absence of perception," the term "of the capable" (*yogyasya*) is used in the singular to denote the class.
The meaning is that there is an absence of perception—that is, manifestation—of those parts of the air which are capable [of being perceived].
The negative particle (na) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned;
it includes the resolution of the doubt.
If it is argued that while air itself is not perceived by sight, its very touch is indeed perceived by the sense of touch—
and therefore there is no perception of the air-substance in sound— this is not so;
for since there is the cognition "I touch the air," it is established as being perceptible, and thus the apprehension of the mere touch is also possible.
Nor should it be argued that there is no fault in postulating an unmanifest touch in sound;
for there is a lack of evidence for such a postulation,
and because of the observation of inferential marks [to the contrary].

The final sūtra is intended to demonstrate another reason for the established doctrine of the eternity of sound. Furthermore, there is an indicative mark [in scripture] to this effect: "Speech is manifold and eternal. This sentence, though primarily concerned with something else, reiterates the eternity of speech.
Therefore, sound is eternal. [Commentary:
The analysis of the compound is "that which is both dissimilar and eternal."
That which gives form is "rūpa," meaning the agent;
that from which form has departed is "vigatarūpā," meaning devoid of an agent.
Therefore, speech is eternal.
In the section titled *Vaidyanāthī*,

under the heading *‘karmake tatra darśanāt’* (1.1.6.16–23), the permanence of sound (*śabdanityatva*) is raised as an objection and subsequently resolved for the purpose of establishing the authority of the Veda (*vedaprāmāṇya*).
This is the section on Sound (*śabdādhikaraṇa*), consisting of eighteen sūtras (Bāla. pṛ. 7).
The cognition of the identity of the action [is established] "because of recognition everywhere, despite differences in name, form, quality, and so forth."
The cognition of being a single action does not depart from the sacrificial sheds. (PMS 2.4.1.9, p. 635)
The maxim of "pulling [the plow]":

Just as in the expression "he pulls with six oxen," the causative agency (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*) of the root *karṣ* is established by the force of the inclusion of the rule for the elision of the *ṣaṭ* suffix, so too is the application of the statement "he who accepts a horse" justified.
This is the prowess [of the grammatical system].
The principle of the "bad horse" (kallakṣanyāya).
The chapter on the negation of bad characteristics (kallakṣaṇapratiṣedhadhyāya). Who?
The chapter on the negation of auspicious marks;
the maxim of the defective horse;
and the liability of a person for transgressing a prohibition.

Because there is a single object for the prohibition, there would be an action [of eating] regarding those things that have been prohibited, since they are distinct even though they are [otherwise] without an object.
Commentary: For this is what they teach:
"One should not eat garlic, nor shall one eat leeks, nor shall one eat onions."

In this regard, there is a doubt: should one who desires a specific result not eat it, while one who is free from such desire may eat it; or rather, must it be avoided by everyone as a matter of rule? What is the prima facie view? It should not be eaten by one who seeks a result.
"For one who does not desire [the fruit], there is no restriction.
Why? Because a restriction is indeed stated as "this must not be eaten.
When this is said, two possibilities arise: either that eating must be performed, or that eating must not be performed.

If it is accepted that eating qualified by the negative particle (nañ) is what must be performed, then, having heard "non-eating," one enjoins that [non-eating] with respect to those [objects]. The negative particle qualifies the act of eating;
and because of that operation, the state of being something to be performed (kartavyatā) is connected to the negative particle.
Now, if the meaning of the negative particle (nañ) were to be construed [with the verb], then there would be an injunction by means of a sentence;
furthermore, the root *bhakṣ* (to eat) would be qualified by the negative particle.
However, direct denotation (*śruti*) is more powerful than syntactical connection (*vākya*).
Therefore, it is understood that non-eating is to be performed.
And non-eating is the absence of eating;
there can be no "to-be-performed-ness" (kartavyatā) with respect to that.
Therefore, that mental operation which occurs here is demonstrated by the means through which eating qualified by the negative particle (nañ) comes about:
first there is the connection between the negative particle and the act of eating, and then the injunction.
Just as in the case of the Prajāpati-vows, such as "One should not look at the rising sun," there is a fruit for one who performs them,
while for one who does not perform them there is neither fruit nor fault— so it is here as well.
"Because of the distinction between action and inaction.
Here, action is not being prohibited; rather, mere inaction is being taught.
For the action that is being prohibited is eating, whereas inaction is a mental resolve.

"Duṣ—(He states the prima facie view: 'The spotted [animal] should not be eaten. According to your view, this is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*); however, for me, it is merely an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). How so? By the direct audition (*śruti*) of the word as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇatayā*), the phrase 'the spotted [animal] should not be eaten' enjoins the performance of eating.

And because the negative particle (*nakāra*) is separated [from the suffix] by both the word 'spotted' and the verb 'to eat,' it does not connect with the suffix that expresses the obligation to perform."

(The word *ca* has the sense of *tu*; the word *na* is used in the sense of *iti*). Therefore, when the negative particle (*nañ*) is employed in connection with something that does not contradict the meaning of the verbal root—namely, an injunction of what is to be done—it constitutes a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) when it is conjoined with another word. [To distinguish this, he asks: "With what, then, is it connected? In that case, it is not connected with a word denoting an action (*bhāvārtha*), even one that is intended for accomplishment (*bhavyārtha*). What is the reason? Because it is not a compound (*asamāsatvāt*). When there is a compound of two nominal stems (*subanta*), a *paryudāsa* occurs, but not when there is no compound.

Therefore (because it is not a compound), that [negation] which is excluded from the word *kallakṣa* is connected with the verbal root (*bhakṣyati*, "one will eat"). In that case, because it ends in a nominal suffix (*suvantatva*), there is no compound (the meaning is that it does not occur). Consequently, since the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with *bhakṣyati*, and *bhakṣyati* as qualified by that [negation] is connected with the injunction, the non-eating qualified by *kallakṣa* and so forth must be performed by one who desires the fruit [of heaven] through the production of an injunction.
(He states another reason: Or else—
All words are connected with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).

In this context, if this [negative particle *nañ*] were to function in its own primary sense (*svārtha-vṛtta*), it would be connected with the productive urge; however, it would then exist in opposition (*virodha*) to that productive urge by way of its contrariety (since it conveys the cessation of what is contrary to it).

Therefore, because it would oppose the productive urge if functioning in its own primary sense, it abandons its primary sense and is connected as functioning through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā-vṛtta*).
A negative particle (*nañ*) alone is not capable of conveying a secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*).

Therefore, for the sake of establishing a specific secondary meaning, it is connected with the verbal root according to that same principle (by the principle stated as "there is no connection with *kal* because of the absence of a compound"). Due to the contradiction with the productive operation of meaning (*arthabhāvanā*), the negative particle (*nañ*) is instead connected with the verbal root immediately following it.
Therefore, that which is called "non-eating" is a mental operation (the *saṃkalpa*) to be performed by one who desires the result.
(While performing an action, one first forms a resolve, and only thereafter proceeds to it.

Physical actions such as touching and so forth are remote; however, the mental resolve—being common to all actions—is immediate [proximate]. Therefore, the negative particle (*nañ*), functioning through exclusion (*paryudāsa*), refers to that very resolve.)
(He states another view: Even in the case of a prohibition, one first forms a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and then desists from it.
Thus, because it is enjoined in this manner, the mental resolve is an inseparable concomitant (*nāntarīya*) in the injunction of action (or the injunction of avoidance).
(In this view, the absence of eating is conveyed by the negative particle *nañ* and the verbal root *bhakṣ*.)
It indicates its own root-intention (*saṃkalpa*), which is conjoined with the accumulation of injunctions.

However, in the former position, according to the principle of "eating" (*bhakṣyati-naya*), when the general form of the intention to eat is established by the direct statement (*śruti*) of the meaning, that very intention is not indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*) through the exclusion of the eating established by the direct statement; rather, it is established in the form of a specific injunction—this is the distinction.

Furthermore, he returns to the very first position and says: Just as in the expression "bring a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), the negative particle (*nañ*) effects the exclusion of the Brahmin caste itself, but does not state the absence of the [actual] human species (which is understood by implication);

therefore, wherever the human purpose exists—as among Kṣatriyas and others—the Brahminhood is what is excluded, and that person is brought; so too here, by the letter *na*, eating is excluded (as a direct Vedic statement).
However, that mental operation which is the basis of all actions and is permitted by the injunction is connected with the sense of "duty" because it is internal (and not excluded).
For example, in the case of "One should not look at the rising sun" (here there is an injunction regarding the mental resolve; so it is here as well).
But this much is the distinction: there (in the Prajāpati-vows), because of the cognition of an enemy, the phrase "the rising [sun]" is understood as the occasioning condition (*nimitta*).
Therefore, when the sun has risen there, the performance of the *saṃkalpa* must be done daily.

Since the scriptures possess their own inherent purpose, the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is enjoined; because those two [the scripture and the goal] are not equal, the latter serves the former, which results in the transcendence of the [ordinary] object. Commentary: The refutation of the objection regarding the description is stated therein.
It is appropriate that, within the vows of Prajāpati, a human goal is enjoined through the meaningfulness of the scriptures;
therein, a rule is taught as something to be performed,
and that which is to be performed consists of auspiciousness and the like.
That which ought not to be done results in sin.
But how can it be said that a restriction is to be observed regarding the Prajāpati-vows? It is explained:
having introduced the subject with the words "His vow," the Prajāpati-vows are traditionally recited.
And what is called a "vow" (*vrata*) is said to be the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) in the form, "I shall not do this.
What is that vow? It is the mental activity that must be performed so that one does not look at the sun when it is setting, and the maintenance of that [resolve].
Therefore, it should be understood that from that [resolve] there is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
And in that context, referring to these very [acts], it is said: "By this much one becomes unyoked from sin"; that is, by performing this much, one becomes unyoked from sin (evil).
Now, in this case, there is no coexistence of those two;
here the action is prohibited, not is non-action enjoined.
For one who eats *kalañja* does not transgress a prohibitory injunction; however,
in this case, one who gazes at the sun does not transgress an injunction,
because gazing at it is not prohibited.
A restrictive rule (niyama) is taught in that regard:
he who performs that restriction becomes connected with its fruit; this follows the logic of the prohibition against eating *kalañja*.

Although there is figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding those devoted to their husbands in the *Kalpasūtras*, in the present case there is no evidence for figurative indication; therefore, because of the similarity in being distinct from the primary [meaning], the negative particle (*nañ*), which denotes non-existence, connects with the verbal root (*bhāvanā*) itself—already qualified by its own factors—through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*).
Nor does this result in any change in the nature [of the sentence].

Even though the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) does not arise in the person, because that very [urge] is merely awakened by the suffix and there is no alteration [of its nature], for this very reason, when it has acquired the status of a negation, the productive urge does not connect with the [suffix] through the relation of being prompted (*prayojyatva*), as is the case in an injunctive sentence. Rather, since the negative particle (*nañ*) exists as a marker of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*), [the connection occurs] through its being the counter-positive of the absence prompted by itself; thus, its nature as a "turning away" (*nivartanā*) is established.

However, according to the root [text], the cognition of eating *kalañja* is the object of the cessation (*nivartanā*), because it is accepted that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others, when devoid of the negative particle (*nañ*), possess a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of cessation.

Furthermore, since the absence of activity—when prompted by oneself—is untenable without the knowledge that the object of activity is a means to an undesirable end, it is postulated that [the negative particle] generates the cognition of such an undesirable consequence.
Consequently, the qualification for the prohibition belongs to every person who is inclined toward activity due to passion.

For this very reason, since the act of eating—which is to be performed as part of the causal relationship [of the sacrifice]—is already known through natural inclination (*rāga*), once that performance occurs, there is no requirement for knowledge established by the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) regarding either the portion of its performance or the portion of its prohibition, according to the principle of being prompted (*prayojyatva*). As for the statement made in another manner in the *Naranaratna* concerning the assistance rendered by the act of turning away (*nivartanā*), that has already been refuted in the *Kaustubha* within the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*);
furthermore, the method stated by me here has been demonstrated in detail.
Maṇḍana [states]: "In the beginning, there is no indication [of a specific object] through mere negation.

Śaṃkara [states]: "[It is] the prohibition of *kalañja*. The Commentator (Śabarasvāmin) and others, having raised the doubt that the Prajāpati-vrata pertains to the ritual (*ṛtvartha*), accepted its status as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) and thereby established it as pertaining to the person (*puruṣārtha*). That too was required because the suspicion of it pertaining to the ritual—based on the chapter on the properties of gold (*hiraṇyadharma*)—is untenable in light of the prohibition against eating *kalañja*.
Bhāṭṭa 4.1.2:
In the prohibitions against eating *kalañja*, garlic, *gṛñjana*, and so forth, the fruit heard in scripture is the fear of hell;
it is not heaven.

"If one who has performed the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) should eat *kalañja* and other forbidden foods, there is no deficiency in the purchased sacrifice (*krītasattra*), because it is accomplished according to what was prescribed."
For the seasons, being related to themselves, depend upon the injunctions and prohibitions; when these are transgressed, they become defective.
However, those injunctions and prohibitions pertaining to the person are, for him, distinct from those pertaining to other seasons, just as they are for the *sadasya* priest and the *anvāhārya* fee.
Indeed, no notion of "quality" (*guṇa*) is applicable to them, such that a notion of "defect" (*vaiguṇya*) would arise upon their transgression.
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 3.4.1.23, page 912:
"The state of being a calf (*kalabhatva*) is a sub-genus of childhood (*bālya*) that inheres in the same object as the state of being an elephant (*hastitva*). — Sūcipattra, page 1411.
The word *kalabha* refers either to an elephant or denotes a specific stage of its age. (Vārttika 3.4.1.23, p.
920). A *kalā* consists of eighteen *nimeṣas*, and thirty such *kalās* constitute a *kāṣṭhā*.

Thus says Amara. Who? [In] the Kali age, all will become preponderant in unrighteousness (*adharmabhūyiṣṭha*). "By even a very small amount of dharma, a great prosperity (*abhyudaya*) will arise"—the purpose of such descriptions of the future is the knowledge of the nature of the ages (*yugasvabhāva*), the diversity in the performance of dharma and adharma, and the diversity in the ripening of their fruits. (Su. p. 128)
Due to the influence of the Kali age and the predominance of unrighteousness. (Su. p. 171).
Kalpa (the manual of ritual procedure).
Just as in the case of the *ubhaya*, both the king and the royal priest have the authority (*adhikāra*) regarding the *kulāya* sacrifice.
Mānava Śrautasūtra 6.6.12–19. [The *Kalpasūtra*: those whose ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is identical to that of the Vaiśvāmitras alone have the authority to perform the *sattra* sacrifice.
(In this context, the word *kalpa* refers to the practical application of the ritual, not to the *Śrautasūtra* itself).]

In the *Kalpasūtras*, that determination of meaning which involves the synthesis of injunctions—obtained through the method of reconciling those scattered within various sections by means of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like—is accepted as authoritative. Just as the schools (*śālā*) taught by Kaṭha and others are accepted under the designations "Kāṭhaka" and so forth, and are thus established as being non-artificial (*akṛtrima*), so too is the eternality (*nityatva*) of those texts fixed within the Vedic tradition and designated by names such as "Āśvalāyana" and so on.

Just as, in the case of the *Sāman* hymns (*sūkta*), although there are designations such as "this is the seer (*ārṣa*) of this [hymn]" and "this is the seer of that," there is no contradiction to their eternality;
so it is likewise with the Sūtra texts composed for the purpose of determining the meaning of each individual [Vedic] passage.
For instance: "No author of an Upaniṣad is remembered as a composer of Kalpasūtras;
however, whatever authorship belongs to women, all of that is equal to the authorship of the [Vedic] mantra-composers."

Just as in the passage, "As there was childhood, or Śiśu Aṅgiras was a mantra-maker among the mantra-makers," the word *mantrakṛt* (mantra-maker) is used for the one who employs the mantras; in the same way, those who employ a particular ritual manual (*kalpa*) or aphorism (*sūtra*) are designated by the title of its author on account of their having produced it.

Furthermore, in the injunction for the *brahmayajña*, after stating, "One who knows thus should study his own portion (*svādhyāya*)," the subsequent verse prescribes it as something to be recited: "Whatever [portion] one studies—whether the *yajus* formulas, the *sāmans*, the *brāhmaṇas*, the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*, or the ritual manuals (*kalpas*)"—from this it is understood that they possess the status of *ārṣa* (revealed scripture).
This is because human compositions can only be the subject of obligatory injunctions insofar as they serve as causes for merit resulting from recitation.

Furthermore, because the *Aruṇa* and *Parāśara* recensions possess the nature of *kalpa*-texts, and because all *śākhā*-holders study the *kalpa-sūtras*—which are distinct from their own specific *śākhās*—due to the strength of their tradition and authority, and because these *kalpa* works transcend other recensions (*samāmnāya*) by serving as the basis for the application of rituals (*ṛtu-viniyoga*), they are equal [to the *śruti*].
The mention of the *ārṣeya* (the lineage of seers) is understood to be eternal;

Regarding the compound *kākatālīya*, it functions as a compound denoting an action inherent in both the crow (*kāka*) and the palm fruit (*tāla*).

In both cases, the sequence of the crow’s flight and the palm fruit’s fall represents, respectively, one’s own mental agitation and the subsequent remaining of that [agitation] in solitude; thus, through an *ivārtha* compound (a compound expressing "like") involving the words *kāka* and *tāla*, which refer to the actions inherent in the crow and the palm fruit, it results that one’s own such encounter is like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit (*kākatālasamāgama*).

Immediately after such a compound, the suffix *cha* is applied to form the word *kākatālīyam* in its second sense [denoting "accidental coincidence"], according to the rule *asamāsācca taddhitāt* (Pāṇini 5.3.106), which falls under the governing heading *ive pratikṛtau* (5.3.96).

Bhaṭṭa: Those desires produced by subordinate qualities (guṇa)—such as "If he should desire, 'May Parjanya be rainy,' he should erect the Sadas shed low"—belong to the Adhvaryu priest because they reside in the person who is the locus of the measurement and so forth; and since the verb *kāmayate* (he desires) is in grammatical coordination with that [measurement], it is understood that it has the same agent. Therefore, these desires reside in the Adhvaryu alone.

For this very reason, where there is a lack of coordination, as in "For one desiring sense-power" (*indriyakāmasya*), the result belongs only to the sacrificer, because the offering known as the *praiṣa* resides in the Adhvaryu.

This being the prima facie view, [the conclusion is as follows]: because of the use of the *parasmaipada* ending in the word "should measure" (*minuyāt*), it is understood that the agent is someone other than the *adhvaryu*; thus, by overriding the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the agent is indeed the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

Even in cases such as "He who desires prosperity should praise with the Saubhara," where there is no *parasmaipada*, there is still no indication of the agent being for the sake of another (*udāttagāmitva*). This is because it would be illogical for the singing of the qualities—which serve as the means to achieve the fruit for the sacrificer—to be undertaken merely for the benefit of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Therefore, in those instances, the coreferentiality itself must be explained solely with the intention of denoting the agent who is the instigator (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*).

For this very reason, where there is no sublation of the rule regarding permanent qualities (*nityaguṇa*), or even if there is such sublation, where there is a direct scriptural statement (*vacana*), there is no defect even if the benefit goes to someone other than the owner; as in: "Whatever desire he desires for himself or for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), that he should sing out. Here, because of the hearing of the word "sacrificer" separately and the hearing of the word "or" (*vā*), the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is justified. Therefore, even if there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the ellipsis (*anupaṅga*), it is not a fault.

By the word "that" (*tam*), the optional desire residing in both [the Udgātṛ and the sacrificer] is referred to; and because the status of being sung (*udgeyatva*) is enjoined, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
