The Commentary: This is another topic of discussion.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that when accepting thousands of horses, there is a single performance of the ritual procedure (*tantra*).

The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the performance of each section in its entirety (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) must be accepted; for [the opponent] says, "Repetition [of the ritual] is due to a specific cause. However, neither the example nor the rebuttal is tenable.

In the case of the acceptance of a horse (*aśvapratigraha*) as the occasion (*nimitta*), four *kapālas* are prescribed. By the word "as many" (*yāvataḥ*), the quantity of horses is expressed; by "so many" (*tāvataḥ*), the quantity of sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) is expressed.

In one instance, the possession of the occasion is prescribed; in the other, the quantity of the occasional rite (*naimittika*) is prescribed. By the term "to Varuṇa" (*vāruṇān*), the connection with the deity is prescribed. By which [of these] is their concomitance (*sāhitya*) here prescribed?
Therefore, these applications [of the subsidiaries] are indeed separate.
However, there is only one benefit to the sacrifice (*ṛtūpakāra*), which is not itself an application.

Just as in the case of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings—even though they are joined within the same type of sacrifice—their procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is not performed collectively (*tantra*), but rather the performance of the *anuyāja* follows the completion of the *prayāja* along with its subsidiaries; so it is here as well.

For those, however, in whose text the reading is "the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s is by way of a common ritual framework (*tantra*)," and where the negative particle *na* is not read, the meaning is as follows: by the term "procedure," the accomplishment of the form [of the rite] according to the Kātyāyana rule—that is, the principle of sequential performance within a single section (*kāṇḍānusamaya*)—is expressed as the benefit to the sacrifice (*ṛtupakāra*). Just as for the *prayāja*s and other rites, even though they have distinct performances, there is only one single benefit for the sacrifice, so it is here as well.
If it is argued that by the word "vāruṇān" there is a sense of association [with other offerings], we say no;
for by this term the deity is expressed, and multiplicity is not intended therein.
Furthermore, if the multiplicity heard in the expression "vāruṇān" were intended, it would cause a division of the sacrifice, as in the case of [the injunction] "prāpnuyāt."

In that case, when there is a single acceptance of a horse, many Vāruṇa offerings would result [which is not acceptable here]. Furthermore, there is no such thing as "conjunction" (sāhitya) [of the acts]; thus, this is not a solution for both positions.
Therefore, one must look for another scriptural statement that establishes conjunction.

Soma [says]: Here, in the Bhāṣya, the sūtra "repetition because of the cause" (*kāraṇād abhyāvṛttiḥ*) is explained as having the purpose of stating the disparity between the example cited in the previous section—namely, that there is *kāṇḍānusamaya* (performance by sections) when there are many sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*)—and the present case. Furthermore, it is also explained as referring to a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), on the grounds that even when there are many sacrificial cakes, although *padārthānusamaya* (performance of individual items) would result according to the stated principle, *kāṇḍānusamaya* must instead be adopted to avoid the contingency of omitting the principal act (*pradhānalopa*).

Although four *kapalas* are prescribed as the specific measure when the gift of a horse is the occasion (*nimitta*), the quantity intended there is not actually meant to be restricted; for, by the very fact that the occasion has been established, the contingent quantity is already understood. Since the subject matter is thus already understood, the number "four" is non-restrictive (*avivakṣita*), just as the plural number in the sentence, "Having concluded the *Satra*, they should sacrifice with the *Pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*. Because it is non-restrictive, the meaning of the sentence is that the *Vāruṇī* sacrifice should be performed whenever one, two, or many horses have been given, regardless of that specific number.

And thus, because simultaneity (*sāhitya*) is not intended, there is no joint performance (*sahaprayoga*), but rather a performance by way of distinction; therefore, this [objection] was raised in the context of the *kāṇḍānusamaya* (sequential performance by sections).
Nevertheless, since there is another statement regarding simultaneity, it is established that there is a *tantra* (commonality of procedure).

Bhāṭṭa: But where there is a conflict with the primary act—as in the case of the "acceptance of horses" (*aśvapratigraha*), where one hundred or a thousand horses are given, and as many *puroḍāśas* are prescribed—if one were to perform the placing on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) for all of them and then remove them (*udāsana*) at once, they would spoil.
Therefore, in that case, there must be a sequential performance by sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) for several of the acts.

As for that which is stated here in the *Vārttika*: since the "as-many-as" (*yāvat*) nature residing in the cause is not intended to be significant, and since the "as-many-as" nature, the offering, and so forth residing in the occasional rite (*naimittaka*) are—by the logic of the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice (*10.2.13*)—not intended to be significant as they reside in the subject of the restatement (*anuvādya*), there is an absence of "conjunction" (*sāhitya*) residing in both [the cause and the effect]. Consequently, even when there are multiple horse-gifts, it is understood that the *vāruṇī-iṣṭi* must be performed through individual applications. It has been said that this example found in the *Bhāṣya* is intended to show the possibility of another statement regarding conjunction residing in both.
And that [is as follows]:

In the case of the injunction, "Having concluded the *sattra*, they should perform the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice," the intention to express simultaneity (*sāhitya*) is appropriate because plurality and so forth are established for the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* by virtue of its being performed by the same agents at the time of the conclusion.

In the present case, however, since the meaning of the word "tāvat" (so many), which corresponds to the number of the causes (*nimitta*), is not already established as a qualification of the effect (*naimittika*), it must be enjoined; therefore, even when there are multiple causes, it is entirely proper that the effects are not simultaneous.

For when there is no [restriction by] the word *tāvat* (only), it is held that when multiple causes coincide simultaneously, the occasional rite (*naimittikī iṣṭi*) is to be performed once by way of a single application (*tantra*); thus, the injunction regarding the meaning of the word *tāvat* is indeed logical.

Even in cases where, because they serve a human purpose, they do not fall within the scope of a ritual—such as touching several Caṇḍālas and so forth simultaneously, or the burning of several houses—the occasional rite is to be performed only once; however, this applies except in the case of giving away a horse during the course of a ritual performance.

Therefore, even though there is a difference between the *āgneya* and other offerings, just as the *prayāja* and other rites share a single procedure (*tantra*), and just as the *homa* shares a single procedure when several one-pot-sherd offerings (*ekapāla*) are broken simultaneously, so too does the *vāruṇī-iṣṭi* result in a single procedure (*tantratva*). Although its status as a single procedure is understood through the injunction that the number [of offerings] must equal the number of occasions (*nimitta*), its fitness as an example is indeed appropriate because its simultaneity (*sāhitya*) is understood by virtue of being encompassed by a single performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*). In that regard, in the case of remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), there is generally only the principle of "extended application" (*prasaṅga*); whereas in the case of proximate auxiliaries (*saṃnipātī*), there is generally the principle of "sequential performance of constituent elements" (*padārthānusamaya*).

Even when there is a connection with a specific desire (*kāma*), there is no drawing back (*pratikarṣa*) of the Aindravāyava cup from the very beginning of the secret rite;

rather, because it is connected to the foremost position—namely, the foremost position of those [cups] at the place of the stream—it is that which is joined with the foremost position of the stream which constitutes the injunction of the result (*kāmaśāstra*).
The desire [for a specific result] can be accomplished by means of the very same draught from the stream (*dhārāgraha*).

Because of its constant connection (*nityasaṃyoga*), even though there is here a connection with a desired result (*kāmasaṃyoga*), according to the principle of "being prompted by a connection" (*saṃyogaprayuktanyāya*), the status of being both optional (*kāmyatva*) and obligatory (*nityatva*) for the draught dedicated to Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyava*) will be established through a distinction in their respective connections.
Therefore, the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that even when connected with a desired result, the draught is to be taken from its own position in the sequence, not from the very beginning of all.

In this case, it should be understood that priority (agratā) is not being enjoined; rather, by way of restating that [priority], only the cup (graha) itself is enjoined. This is known as the "maxim of the love-stricken woman" (kāmākulakāminī-nyāya).

Just as a young woman, whose affection has been awakened by hearing of the multitude of a hero’s virtues and who is overwhelmed by passion, cannot endure the suffering of separation and performs gestures of despair because her mind is fixed on the play of love;
so too, through that intensity, her mind becomes restless.
Even when he is beheld, that sight does not attain the state of being heart-touching if it lacks a reflection upon his virtues, for it then remains merely common to all people.
But when, through the words of a teacher, one reflects upon His qualities, at that very moment there is the state of fullness.

Thus, even while the Lord of the Universe is manifest within one's own self, the manifestation of Him does not bring about the state of fullness at a time when there is an absence of reflection upon His qualities.

However, when a reflection on the Supreme Lord—characterized by omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth—arises through the words of a guru or other means, then at that very instant there is the attainment of the full tide of consciousness.
This principle is indicated in the *Sādharmya-samuccaya* (or *Sādharmya-samuccaya-vṛtti*) at the point of examining counter-objections (*pratyabhiśāda*).
[Sādṛśī 713]:

In the context of desire (*kāmādhikāra*), an injunction (*niyoga*) does not state that the sacrifice is something to be performed; rather, its status as something to be performed is established by the very result [of the desire].
*Ṛju-vivaraṇa*, page 29:

Since the scripture culminates in the accomplishment of the desired fruit within the sections concerning desires (*kāmādhikāra*), it is not the case that the injunction (*niyoga*) alone impels a person toward action for its own sake;
for since the activity of persons is drawn forth by passion (*rāga*), their engagement is established solely through the fruit.
Page 29.
And because of the word "gift" (*dāna*) in the *Kāmeṣṭi*:

"Having reached Plākṣa-prasravaṇa, they offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kāma; having given a man and a milch-cow as a fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for that [sacrifice], they go back toward the Yamunā-bhava. Thus, the *Kāmeṣṭi* is mentioned in the Sārasvata Satra.

In that context, it is stated that a straightforward gift (*ṛjivimba*) consists of giving a mare and a cow, as well as a man and a cow—specifically, a female of the equine species and a female of the human species who are "nursing" (*dhenuka*), meaning they suckle or provide milk for a child.

This is the sacrifice for desire (*kāmeṣṭi*) within the *Sārasvata-sattras*. Furthermore, it has been stated that there is no giving in a *sattra* (sacrificial session); nevertheless, because of the word "giving" (*dāna*)—that is, the word expressing giving in the phrase "having given" (*datvā*)—this must be for the purpose of hiring (*parikraya*).
Such is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
And the word "ca" (and) serves the purpose of providing the example of the *udavasānīya* [concluding rite].
Just as it has been stated that at the conclusion of the ritual (*udavasīne karmaṇi*), the gift is solely for the purpose of hiring (*parikraya*), so it is here.
Or rather, there is a scriptural statement (*vacana*) because of its existence.
By the word "or" (*vā*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is set aside.
Regarding the *kāmeṣṭi* prescribed within the *sārasvata-sattra*, there is the scriptural injunction: "Having given a male and a female calf in that [offering].
Since the *kāmeṣṭi* occurs in the midst of the *sattra* and thus shares the character of a *sattra*, purchase (*parikraya*) is not possible there, as it is prohibited for a *sattra*.

However, by the force of the scriptural statement, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that for a mare of the horse species or a female of the human species who is suckling, the gift should be performed as a mere ritual duty (dharmamātra), namely half of a cow;
this applies specifically in the Kāmeṣṭi sacrifice within the Sārasvata Satra regarding those of the horse, human, and cow species, but not otherwise.
"Having given a mare, a man, and a cow," [Vi.
There is identity of purpose between the *saubhara* and the *nidhana*.
(The *Saubhara* chant).
The rule prescribing specific *nidhana*s—namely *hīṣ*, *ūrk*, and *ū*—is based on a distinction of results.
The fact that words expressing desire for objects have as their primary purport the resulting fruit will be explained in the eleventh [chapter] and elsewhere (Su. p.
Furthermore, desire arises spontaneously from the knowledge of the beauty of the object; it does not come into being through the hearing of an injunction.
VI. 2.1.12. Desire is of two kinds: regarding the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and regarding the means (*sādhana*).
In that regard, there is no desire for heaven as something to be accomplished.
What is the reason? For everyone desires this: "May there be heaven."

By virtue of desire, [it is] "kāmya" (desirable), meaning "may this quality be mine. And while the primary desire pertains to the goal (*sādhya*), it is necessarily concomitant with respect to the means (*sādhana*), because the goal is impossible without the means.

Therefore, the desire for the means [of accomplishment] is secondary (*gauṇī*). (Duḥkha-kośa 1.1.1.14, p. 2099). Furthermore, the repeated practice of optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) is performed in accordance with that desire.
Mā. 11|1|4|20–26: For the statement regarding the sacrifice with its constituent parts (*sāṅga-yāga*) is made with reference to one who desires [a result] (*kāmin*).
Bhā. 6|6|18: Even for one who desires [a result], there is no sin in the performance of a rite intended for that desire (*kāmya-karma*).

Vi. 6|3|2: It has been stated [in the sūtra] "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer" (3|7|8|18) that one who desires [a result] is the agent of the *bhāvanā* as delimited by the means to the fruit itself.
Su. 3.8, p. 60: A sacrificial session (sattra) is prescribed for those desiring [specific results].
And these [desirers] are many indeed, being mutually independent. Thus, a performance characterized by plurality is prescribed as the object of desire.

Bhāṣya 10.6.4.45–46: Since those desiring rewards are naturally inclined toward the fruit, their engagement in ritual action proceeds solely out of that desire; thus, there is no contradiction with the prohibition "one shall not kill. Ṛjuvimalā, p. 29:

A rite performed for a specific desire must be completed even if the desire ceases midway or if the reward is obtained, because scriptural texts mention both censure and expiation [for failing to complete it].
VI. 6.3.3. When one is able to perform a desired (kāmya) rite without omission, one should perform it at that very time;
likewise, one should perform an obligatory (nitya) rite whenever one is able to do so.
VI. 6.3.2. There is a rule that a desired rite, such as the Citrā sacrifice and others, should be performed only once.
One who desires heaven and other such results repeatedly must perform the ritual application repeatedly.
(1.1.4) The *godohana* vessel and similar items are unfit to be employed in the obligatory (*nitya*) performance.

(4.3.2) That which is performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*) is stronger than that which is obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*), because its human purpose is proximate, whereas the fruit of the others is remote.

"Superior strength [belongs to the optional rite] because it acts more swiftly than even the occasional rite" (Vārttika 3.6.1.10, p. 1033). The optional rite is stronger than the obligatory rite because desire impels one to act more quickly. Vi. 12.1.13. The optional rite sublates the obligatory rite; for example, in the Agnicayana sacrifice, the obligatory [altar] is sublated by the optional [altar] made of bricks.
This is the principle that "the optional rite sublates the obligatory rite."

From the indicative mark (liṅga) itself, it follows that the fire (agni) must also have the altar (prakṛti) as its substratum, because of the proximity to the human purpose (puruṣārtha); for by the maxim that "the optional (kāmya) overrides the obligatory (nitya)," the former, being stronger due to its aim at a specific result, overrides the latter (the *uttaravedi*). This is precisely the maxim regarding the strength of the optional.
*Rasāyana*, p. 177.

The optional (*kāmya*) rite is a sublater of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite. This principle—that "the optional, due to its proximity to the human goal, sublates the obligatory"—is the same logic that will be stated in the third section (*adhikaraṇa*) under the sūtra: "But in the case of the occasional (*naimittika*), there is a modification of the archetype because of the specific nature of the performance" (3.6.1.10).
(Vārttika, p. 352)
"For every effort is for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the person; thus, that entity which requires such effort becomes more powerful" (Vākyapadīya, p.

352). This is precisely the primary principle regarding the sublation of the obligatory (*nitya*) by the optional (*kāmya*); furthermore, the optional sublates the obligatory according to the principle of the tenth section (*adhikaraṇa*), "That scriptural injunction which is without distinction" (10.8.8.16), and likewise according to the principle of the sixth section, "In case of sequence, there is weakness of the prior, as in the case of the archetype" (6.5.54).

Su. Pṛ. 488: According to the maxim that "the optional (*kāmya*) overrides the obligatory (*nitya*"), the cup (*camasa*) [used] in the performance for a specific desire (*kāmaprayoga*) has no status as a subordinate element (*anaṅgatva*) [in the regular rite]. Murāri, p. 1184: [Rituals] such as the low measurement of the sacrificial hall (*sadomaṇḍapa*) performed for a specific desire must not be carried out in the *asthiyajña* (sacrifice of the bones).
Bhā. 10.2.10.91: Vedic ritual action performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*) is of three kinds.

That which has results in this life is exemplified by such injunctions as, "One desiring rain should sacrifice with the Kārīrī. That which has results in the next life is exemplified by the Agnihotra and other rites for the sake of heaven and so forth.
That which has indefinite results is exemplified by such injunctions as, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā."
Bāla, p. 85: "Desirable [rites] (kāmyāni) have results in another birth.
Bhāṣya 4.3.1.27, Section 2:
"But the desirable [rites] are not enjoined because of the ignorance of desire, just as other [desires] are not mentioned when one [is absent]."

In the *asthiyajña* (bone-sacrifice), optional rites (*kāmyāni*) such as "If he should desire, 'May Parjanya rain,' he should erect the *sadas* shed low," and so forth, are neither prescribed nor to be performed.
For these would only be performed out of a desire on the part of the sacrificer;
for when the knowledge of that desire arises through the statement of the sacrificer, then the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) would perform them.
But since desire is impossible for the deceased, how can that which belongs to the desire of the sacrificer be performed by the officiating priests through ignorance [of his death]?
Just as, even while another sacrificer is alive, the optional rites (*kāmyāni*) cannot be performed by the priests if they are not commanded by him,
what then is the case regarding the *asthiyajña* (bone-sacrifice)?

Therefore, in the *asthiyajña* (bone-sacrifice), optional rites (*kāmyāni*) should not be performed. The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of illustration, as there is no possibility of suspecting that they ought to be performed. Who [says this]? Ke. (Kevalānanda).

A quality (guṇa) intended for a specific desire (kāmya) modifies the permanent rite; therefore, it should be integrated [into the rite] by means of the two [principles] established in the *Indriyakāmādhikaraṇa* (2.1.1) and the *Godohanādhikaraṇa* (3.6.3). A quality intended for a desired result, even though its purpose is distinct, is capable of determining the falsity of the cognition of a conflicting subsequent quality because it serves as an intermediate effect. (Vārttika 3.6.1.43, p. 1067).
"An optional quality (guṇa), when heard [in the scripture], enters into the permanent rite after having modified it"—this is the maxim.

Just as the quality of milking a cow (*godohana*) always enters into the modified form (*vikṛti*) of the carrying of water, which is normally accomplished by means of a cup (*camasa*), so too, when a primary quality is desired as a restrictive factor, it causes the number [of cups] to be modified and leads to an internal understanding [of that change]. (Vi. 3.6.16). The optional injunction for human ends (*kāmya-puruṣārtha-adhikāravidhi*) is one whose purpose is to establish a connection between the ritual action and its fruit, such as: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*). The injunction concerning the connection between a quality and its fruit (*guṇaphala-sambandha*) is one whose purpose is to establish a connection between an accessory material and its specific result, such as: "One desiring sensory power should offer an oblation with curd" (*dadhnā indriyakāmasya juhuyāt*).
According to the maxim:

"Whether optional (*kāmya*) or occasional (*naimittika*), [an injunction] enters by modifying the permanent purpose (*nitya-artha*)," even though it enters by means of an occasional application, it does not render the permanent [obligation] non-binding.

*Bhāmatī* on *Brahmasūtra* 3.4.132: "Or it is optional, as in the case of the eating of boiled rice with ghee for the Adhvaryu priest, or the rule regarding a windless place; thus, it optionally displaces the constant [requirements] of bed, seat, and food.
"Or it is optional."

Just as the performance of the fire-sacrifice (*agni-prayoga*) for the sake of heaven, by displacing the obligatory performance (*nitya-prayoga*), enters [the ritual] because there is no distinction between the two types of performance, thereby setting aside the obligatoriness of the permanent injunction; or just as the performance of the *phalacamas* (fruit-cup) displaces the obligatory *soma*-performance and enters [the ritual], since the obligatory requirement is fulfilled through the optional (*kāmya`) and occasional (*naimittika`) acts—so it is stated in the *Kalpataru* (3.4.8.32): "It is said that a quality which is optional and not taken up for the sake of the *kavya* (ancestral rite)..."

"He takes up the ritual action for the sake of the *kāmya* [desire-based] purpose, and that very same person does so for the sake of accomplishing his own goal" (Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.1.10, p. 1035). Regarding the optional *sāmidhenī* recitations at the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—such as "One desiring stability should recite twenty-one," "One desiring food should recite twenty-one," "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should recite twenty-one," "One desiring stability should recite twenty-two," and "One desiring cattle should recite twenty-six"—in these cases, one should repeat the verses as far as they are prescribed (having performed the *virāj* at the beginning and the end), and the remaining number must be completed by the introduction (*āgamana*) of additional verses.

Bhāṣya 10.1.8.26–33: Through the performance of the *agnihotra* for a specific desire (*kāmya*), the performance of the obligatory (*nitya*) *agnihotra* is accomplished by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). Bālakrīḍā, p. 132: Just as there is the production of the auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the obligatory through the optional, as in the case where the number twenty-one, which is an auxiliary of the twenty-one recitations intended for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), serves as an auxiliary for the obligatory *pāścadaśya* (the state of having fifteen).

Page 149. "The sublation of the obligatory by the optional" refers to the principle (*nyāya*) of the section [12.4.17–25] beginning with "In the *Uvāyā*, there is a combination of the optional and the obligatory.

Ke.: An instance of the inclusion of an auxiliary (*aṅgaprasaṅga*) of the occasional (*naimittika*) by the optional (*kāmya*), such as the inclusion of the twenty-one recitations—which serve the purpose of stability—as an auxiliary to the *Sāmada* chant performed for the occasion of a Vaiśya. Bāla. Page 149: Sublation of the occasional by the optional.
P. 132. In the case of the optional fire (*kāmya agni*) [produced from the tip of a tree and so forth during the *agnicayana*], there is an absence of the *āhavanīya* fire.
Bhāṣya 12.4.26–27. When there is a deficiency in the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of an optional rite, it results in fruitlessness.
Vi. 6.1.2. Even that which is taught as subsequent to the origin (*utpannaśiṣṭa*) of an optional rite possesses the power to sublate that which is taught at the time of its origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*).

Su. P. 488. Regarding optional (kāmya) action, there is practice according to one's desire: either once or many times. For the sake of an abundance of results, one performs it many times; being content, one performs it once. Thus, it is understood that one may act according to one's wish.
Bhāṣya 11.1.4.24: The characteristics of optional rites (*kāmya*) cannot belong to obligatory rites (*nitya*).

6.3.15: In the performance of optional rites, the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is not a restrictive factor, because there is no mutual expectancy due to the absence of a single unified application (*ekayoga*).
Therefore, whenever a desire or a specific occasion arises, the sacrifice enjoined for that purpose must be performed at that time.
VI. 5.3.12. For optional rites (*kāmyakarman*), if there is no obstacle, the fruit is experienced in this life; if there is an obstacle, it is experienced in the next life.
Heaven, however, is necessarily experienced only in the next life.

4|3|12. There is no commencement of optional rites (*kāmya*) by means of substitutes (*pratinidhi*). However, if some minor accessory of an optional rite that has already commenced is lost, a substitute may be employed; since that rite must necessarily be completed, its completion is performed with a modified substitute. Vārttika 3|6|1|140: In the case of both commenced optional rites and obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), when there is a deficiency of two [required elements], the completion is carried out by means of a substitute.

Just as heaven is a constant [result] in the case of a rite performed for a specific desire (kāmya-karman), as it is with the subsidiary elements of a sacrifice (yajñāṅga) that serve the purpose of the ritual (ṛtvartha),

so too in rites such as "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer a caru-oblation to Sūrya," heaven would be a constant result even in the case of a rite performed for a specific desire, namely the Viśvajit sacrifice.

However, [qualities] such as *brahmavarcasa* (spiritual luster) would certainly be obtained through the *anvācya* [formula]. Just as when wood and other items are being brought, one says, "You must also bring some vegetables," where the wood is necessarily brought, and once it is obtained, the vegetables are brought as well— so it is in this case.
Just as in the case of a subsidiary of a sacrifice, when a rite for the sake of the ritual is performed with a *godohana* vessel for one desiring cattle,
so it is also in the case of optional rites, because of the presence of desire.

In the passage "he should pour out [the water] for the sake of desire" (*kāmasya praṇayet*), regarding the sacrificial limb consisting of the pouring of water, there is the *ṛtvartha* (purpose of the sacrifice). The meaning is that it is an assistance; the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) is the benefit to the sacrifice, and that is indeed constant. Even though the acquisition of cattle is an occasional result, the purpose of the *godohana* vessel remains constant as an auxiliary (*anvācaya*). The same applies to the present case.
And when the cause has ceased, it follows from the restrictive rule (*niyamāt*).
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the following sūtra presents another reason:
even when the desire for the fruit—which is the motive for performing an action—has vanished, subsided, or ceased, a rule regarding the completion of the ritual action is observed.

In that regard, even when the desired fruit has been obtained, the rule of completing the action is justified for the sake of attaining the eternal fruit in the form of heaven; it would not be so otherwise.

In the *Kārīrī* sacrifice, which is performed for the purpose of obtaining rain, it is stated: "If it rains, one should offer the oblation immediately; if it does not rain, one should offer it on the following day.
Alternatively, the desire [for rain] is enjoined through its connection with that [sacrifice].
When the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been established by these two sūtras, he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In the case of optional ritual action (*kāmya-karma*), heaven is not the constant [result]; rather, desire alone is constant.
"Desire" (*kāma*) means that which is desired; the meaning is that it refers to the fruit expressed by the words "desire for such-and-such."
Because action is impelled by conjunction with that— that is, conjunction with desire—
and its syntactic unity with the word "desiring heaven" is inferential, whereas its unity with the word expressing the [specific] desire is direct perception;
and direct perception is stronger than inference.
Therefore, desire alone is the fruit, not heaven;
because [heaven] is subordinate as a subsidiary element (aṅga).
This is a sūtra of the final position (siddhānta) intended to demonstrate the disparity with the given example.

In the case of subsidiaries such as the *godohana* (milk-pail), since they are enjoined as subordinate elements (*guṇa*), it is appropriate that they serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).
However, in the case of the *saurya* oblation of cooked rice, there is no such injunction.
Furthermore, the restrictive rule (*niyama*) is for the sake of that [sacrifice].

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that in a non-obligatory rite such as the *saurya-caru* sacrifice, heaven is the constant fruit while the desired fruit is merely incidental (*anvācaya*), this sūtra is intended to refute the reason stated in the sūtra: "And because there is a rule when the cause has ceased" (*vīte ca kāraṇe niyamāt*). The rule regarding performance that was stated for when the cause has ceased—that rule is for its sake, for that purpose.
For what? For the apprehension of the meaning of the injunction (*śiṣṭārthavigrahaṇāya*).
If one were to begin [a rite] but not complete it, the learned would immediately censure him, saying, "This man is a coward who merely undertook the task.
Therefore, it must necessarily be completed.
Consequently, for optional rites (*kāmya*), the specific desired object alone is the fruit, and not even heaven.
In the case of optional (kāmya) rites, the fruit specifically mentioned in the scripture is to be accepted; heaven is not to be postulated [as the fruit]. (Vi.
4.3.9) In the case of an optional rite, even if the prescribed substance is unavailable, that rite must indeed be performed using another substance;
there is no omission of the rite simply because the prescribed substance is absent.

In the case of an optional rite (*kāmya*), the obligatory performance (*nityaprayoga*) is included within it. However, there is a distinction based on the Vedic text (*śruti*). According to *Ṭup-ṭīkā* 6.3.111, in an optional rite, the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*)—which is implied by the instigation (*pravartanā*)—belongs only to the principal part (*pradhāna*), and not to the subsidiary parts (*sāṅga*).
Bhāṭṭa 6.3.1, p. 250: In the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the establishment of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) are mentioned.
Bhāṣya 12.4.12–29: In the case of optional rites, the application of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga-viniyoga*) occurs only after the means [of accomplishment] has been indicated by the injunction.
Bhāṭṭa 6.3.1, p. 250: In the case of optional rites, the entitlement (*adhikāra*) belongs to one who is capable of performing all the auxiliary parts.

*Ḍup.* 6.3.111: In the case of optional rites (*kāmya*) where the result is not achieved due to the performance being deficient, there is no entitlement for one who lacks knowledge to perform them optionally. *Vi.* 6.1.10: "And likewise in the case of optional rites, because of the desire [for the fruit].

In optional rituals such as the offering to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*), the mixing of curd (*dadhi*), and the collection [of materials], there would be possession of the fruit even if some auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) are missing, just as in the case of obligatory (*nitya*) rites.
Because it is purposeful— that is, because the agent possesses a desire for the fruit produced by the principal rite—

the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that even from an obligatory rite (*nitya*) and so forth, when performed deficiently, the fruit would still arise from the optional rite (*kāmya*). The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the obligatory rites.
"It would not be so because of the lack of connection; for the injunction has the word as its authority.

Refuting with the word "tu" (but) the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya-karman*) is fruitful even when defective, just like a mandatory rite (*nitya*)—the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of the aphorism:
"In this way, there would be no fruitfulness for a defective rite performed for a specific desire."
Because the principal act alone is not connected with the fruit, but only through its relationship [with subsidiaries];
for it is established by verbal authority (*śabdapramāṇa*) that the principal act, when being enjoined, possesses the fruit only when accompanied by its subsidiaries.
Indeed, by means of verbal authority, it is understood that only the principal act together with its subsidiaries is fruitful.

Since the injunction—the performance of the primary rite together with all its subsidiaries—is established by the authority of the fruit-statement (*phalavākya*), the qualification for optional rites (*kāmya*) belongs only to one capable of performing all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). Thus it is settled.
Furthermore, there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) from the non-performance [of such rites].

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that a desirable rite (*kāmya-karman*), when performed with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), is fruitful; this is the purpose of the next sūtra, which provides another reason.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction.

In the case of an obligatory rite (*nitya-karman*), it is taught that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) if the principal part is not performed; however, in the case of a desirable rite, no such transgression is heard of in scripture regarding the non-performance of the principal part.
Since there is no transgression—that is, an absence of transgression—even when one acts without desire, the obligatory nature [of the rite] does not become optional.
Therefore, eligibility for an optional rite belongs only to one capable of performing all its constituent parts;
in optional rites, there must be a performance of all the constituent parts.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the cognitions of *nāḍikās*, *muhūrtas*, *praharas*, and so forth, as well as the cognitions of objects qualified by priority, posteriority, simultaneity, non-simultaneity, slowness, and quickness—which are all admitted to be produced by time—are distinct, it follows that a single, partless substance called "time" cannot be their cause, just like space (*ākāśa*). However, if one accepts that time—though partless—is the cause of these distinct cognitions by virtue of being delimited by the actions of the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies, then the following is established: the accumulation of the sun’s movements resulting from its crossing more than one-eighth part of the sky is a *nāḍikā*; the result of crossing more than one-sixteenth part is a *muhūrta*; and the result of crossing more than one-eighth part is a *prahara*. In this way, the causality of the cognitions of *nāḍikās* and so on is logically accounted for. Furthermore, the delimitations characterized by the greater or lesser number of solar movements relative to a counter-correlative object serve as the causes for the cognitions of objects qualified by priority and posteriority. Likewise, the delimitations of moments (the smallest units of time) serve as the causes for the cognitions of objects qualified by simultaneity and non-simultaneity. And the delimitations characterized by the greater or lesser number of solar movements occurring within the various states such as birth and so forth serve as the causes for the cognitions of objects qualified by slowness and quickness. Since there is no time apart from action, it is understood that the very action of living constitutes time.

Thus [say] those who maintain that time does not exist apart from mere action. That is not so; for it is impossible for the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies—that is, the action of motion—to serve as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of time by way of its relation to objects such as the young and the old.

However, because time is omnipresent (*sarvagata*), it is logical that it serves as the delimiter for actions associated with the sun and other celestial bodies—which possess universal visibility—and that it acts as the delimiter for objects such as the young and the old. This is because, through the cognitions of priority and posteriority (*parāparapratyaya*) among the young, the old, and so forth, time is inferred as something distinct from action; for action that is not connected to an object cannot be the cause of those cognitions of priority and so on. Thus, they also maintain that the existence of time as distinct from action is established even in those things being inferred.
But in reality, if one were to accept that time is perceptible (*pratyakṣatva*), its very establishment would be impossible.

Since notions such as "prior" and "posterior" are universal, even if one were to require their omnipresence, it is not necessary to postulate time as its cause; for this can be accounted for by the very nature of space—which, though undifferentiated in itself, acquires distinct capacities through various auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*).
However, if [time] were perceptible, then the notion "it exists" would be distinct from the notions arising from specific actions such as "the sun rises";
thus, because the notion "it exists" is cognized through the senses, a separate entity called time is established.

In a cognition that apprehends an object as emerging while delimited by past or future time—such as "the sun has risen" or "it will rise"—the entry of "presentness" is not perceived; thus, it cannot be claimed that the existence (*sattā*) is the objective support (*ālambana*) for the notion "it exists. This is because cognitions of the past and future, characterized by their distinct apprehension of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)—as in "it rose yesterday," "it will set tomorrow," "it will exist tomorrow," or "it will not set"—cannot logically have destruction or prior non-existence as their objective supports. Therefore, the objective support of existence delimited by past and future time, which appears upon reflection on the verbal root (*dhātu*), cannot be dismissed.

Furthermore, if time were not delimited, then the existence or non-existence of the sunrise and so forth would result in their being always existent or always non-existent—like space or a rabbit's horn—which would contradict their occasional perception.
Moreover, although time is inherently of a single nature, the designations of "past," "future," and "present" are established through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
For as long as a series of momentary actions delimited by a single result pervades a duration of time, that much of time is designated as "present."

Even though the moments of action (*kriyākṣaṇa*) are not simultaneous, when they are performed with a view toward a single result, there is a designation of "oneness of action" from the first moment until the attainment of the result. Thus, it is established that the "presentness" of time is conditioned by the delimitation (*avaccheda*) of an existing action; its "pastness" is conditioned by the delimitation of a destroyed action; and its "futureness" is conditioned by the delimitation of an action yet to come. Furthermore, since it is accepted that the action [of the sun] which delimits time also serves as the delimiting factor for the [other] actions being projected, there is no occurrence of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Furthermore, since even the activities of the sun and other celestial bodies are delimited by the past, future, and present times, and because time—distinct from activity and distinct from space—is established in the theory of the perceptibility of time solely through the force of a distinct cognition, their defeat is impossible.

Even for those who maintain that time is inferable, although they do not establish it as distinct from space and so forth, its distinction from activity is nonetheless established; thus, they too cannot be defeated.
