Why? Because of the statement regarding four oblations: "He gives four *kṛṣṇala* grains.
What is the intention? There are four *kṛṣṇala* grains, which are the mouthfuls of the sacrificial cake (*caru*).

Each single *kṛṣṇala* is in place of each individual portion (*avadāna*). By this, the spreading of butter (*upastaraṇa*) and the pouring over it (*abhighāraṇa*) are excluded. Accordingly, there is a scriptural statement regarding the sacrificial food: "He cuts off four *kṛṣṇalas*; this is the fourfold cutting-off (*caturavatta*)."
The benefit of that which is non-existent occurs through another object;
therefore, there is an increase of these two.
Furthermore, together with the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*), it would indeed constitute a full fourfold portion (*caturavatta*).
In that case, one should contemplate the statement regarding the material substance (*āmiṣa*).

Alternatively, the action (*kriyā*) is primary because of its connection with the measure of the principal offering; its status as a subordinate quality (*tadguṇatva*) follows from general principles.
The Commentary states: "Or rather, the action [is primary] for the sake of favoring the injunctions of those two."
For in the archetype, the measure of the primary portion is stated: "He cuts off for the deities a piece the size of a thumb-joint.
Here too, the word *kṛṣṇala* is heard as denoting a measure;
it is connected with the number four in the statement: "He cuts off four *kṛṣṇalas*."

It is not the case that those four avadānas (cuttings) are of the measure of a *kṛṣṇala*. This word *kṛṣṇala* expresses a measure of gold; it is not capable of expressing a [specific] measure [of the substance itself].
And that measure does not exclude the substance.
For a quality cannot subsist in substances belonging to a different class.
That which is the original dimension (*parimāṇa*), existing in the effect, would cause that [original] to cease;
just as in the case of the instruction: "Devadatta should be fed with this curd, ghee, vegetables, and these rice-grains; like Devadatta, [feed him] with oil."
For oil assists the meal through its oily quality; thus, for the purpose of providing that oiliness, it is capable of displacing the ordinary [fat], but not curd or boiled rice.
Likewise here, the measure serves to measure the primary portion (avadāna), but it would not displace the substance itself.
However, by virtue of the context, the measure would apply to the primary portion, not to the under-sprinkling (upastaraṇa) and the over-sprinkling (abhighāraṇa).
Therefore, there is the cessation of those two.
And because they constitute a single portion (*ekāvadāna*). The Commentary states: "It shows that for the four [kṛṣṇalas] there is a single portion, in the words: 'Four kṛṣṇalas are one portion.'"
Otherwise, there would have been four examples;
in that case, the statement of only one example would be superfluous.
For this reason as well, there is no cessation [of the rule].
Because of the equality of the number [of these] with the *āmīs* (the sacrificial portions).
The Commentary states: Now, as for what was said—that there is a mention of the *āmīs*—this is a praise of the number four.
Such is the greatness of the number four, that in a single portion (*avadāna*), there come to be four portions.

Just as in the statement, "Since the Vaiśvadeva cup is drawn at the morning pressing, one thus completes the Vaiśvadeva at the morning pressing," this is a praise of the Vaiśvadeva and not an exclusion of the other pressings;
so too here, there is a praise of the number four, and not an exclusion of the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*).
Otherwise, this non-statement of praise would be purposeless.
The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): The word "but" (*tu*) excludes this [notion of] praise consisting of the number four.

For there is no praise whatsoever of the two acts of spreading the base (*upastaraṇa*) and pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*) by means of that which is being poured (*āsicyamāna*), since those two are already present.
If it is said that [the butter] praises what is not yet present, then it is called "possessing a quality" (*guṇavat*); in that case, it is praised.
If it is argued that [the term] "attains" refers to something already existing, then it would be redundant, as has been stated; it does not refer to the act of mixing itself.
Therefore, the statement regarding the spreading and the pouring out, which concern things already existing, is indeed purposeless.
Another explanation must be provided.
But there is an option regarding the single portioning.

The Commentary states: The word "but" (tu) serves to exclude the [argument] that "there is a cessation of the under-spreading and the sprinkling because of the statement concerning the portions. Just as you say that there is a cessation of these two because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the statement concerning the portions, so too, because of the indicative mark consisting of the statement concerning the single portioning, there is no cessation of these two; thus, there is an option based on the indicative marks.
Furthermore, a variation in gender cannot definitively express the word *āti*.
For if it were applied to every modification, the repetition [of the term] would be useless, as the other oblation (*havis*) would already be implied.
Commentary: The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the expression *ātivacana*.

When the injunction regarding the *āti* (the whole) is set aside, then in the case of the four *kṛṣṇala* seeds—which are modifications of all [other] portions—the repetition would be purposeless, according to the statement: "One offers four *kṛṣṇalas* each for the sake of prosperity.
On this view, however, the repetition is justified because the other oblation is indeed a second portion (*dvitīyam avadānam*).
Alternatively, it should belong to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, since the other [interpretation] is improper.
Commentary: Now, if it is thought that this repetition of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering also belongs to me, that is not so;
for it is improper to depend upon another *sviṣṭakṛt*.
By virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), the primary sacrifice is connected with the statement; however, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering has no context of its own,
as it is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*).
Therefore, in your view, repetition would be entirely purposeless;
the spreading [of the grass] and the sprinkling [of butter] must indeed be performed.
(These two sūtras are generally printed as one, which is both correct and appropriate.)
That has been cut away by us;
the commentary (*bhāṣya*) has also been cut and adopted in accordance with that.
However, at that time, it should be seen in the very same sūtra within the marginal notes (*ṭippaṇī*) of our own Mīmāṃsā system.

(Ke. Or rather, it is non-action (*akarma*), because its purpose is cessation through non-contact; therefore, it possesses the capacity to prevent contact. Commentary: It is the non-performance of the two acts of spreading [the butter] and sprinkling [the clarified butter]. Why? Because there might otherwise be contact with the subtle particles of the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) during the act of cutting. Thus, [the purpose is] so that such contact does not occur.

In the case of the *kṛṣṇala* oblation, the spreading (*upastaraṇa*) serves to moisten the ladle, and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) ensures that the entire sacrificial substance (*havis*) falls into the fire without adhering to the ladle. However, there is no contact between the pure *kṛṣṇala* and the ladle for which the spreading and sprinkling would otherwise be performed for the sake of lubricating gold.
Therefore, since the original purpose has ceased to exist, the spreading [of the base] and the sprinkling [of clarified butter] must be omitted in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* seeds.
In this way, the scriptural statement will be justified:
"He cuts off four *kṛṣṇalas*; that is a fourfold portion for the sake of attainment."

When even the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) must be performed for the sake of the *soma* juice, then what need is there to mention the two acts of spreading the base-butter (*upastaraṇa*) and sprinkling the butter over the oblation (*abhighāraṇa*), which are not [performed] with impure substances? Thus, the connection [of the topic] has been stated. The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: because the acts of spreading the base-butter and sprinkling the butter are characterized by sweetness (*svādima*), they should be performed. Viśvarūpa states: "Should the two acts of spreading the base-butter and sprinkling the butter be performed upon those [substances], or not? There are two possibilities."
The unconditioned has an invisible purpose; it is not said that its purpose is not [to be realized].

Bhāṭṭa: In that very context, as to whether the spreading of the base (upastaraṇa) and the sprinkling (abhighāraṇa) are to be performed or not—the answer is that they must indeed be performed because, in the archetype sacrifice (prakṛti), they serve an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha). Nor should it be argued that these two are omitted in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* seeds because, according to the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*)—"He spreads the base and sprinkles; he thereby makes this an immortal oblation"—they serve the purpose of making [the offering] savory (*svādimā*), and since the *kṛṣṇalas* are inedible, that purpose is absent.
For that supplementary statement is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), as there is no actual enjoyment of the taste.

And although, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is not assumed that these [acts] have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*), but rather that their purpose is solely for the accomplishment of the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*), nevertheless, there is no omission in the *kṛṣṇala* oblation.

Nor should it be argued that, even so, because of the statement, "He cuts off four *kṛṣṇalas* each, for the sake of accomplishing the fourfold portion," which—by restating the cutting (*avadāna*)—prescribes the number four for the *kṛṣṇalas*, and by that [statement] restates the accomplishment of the fourfold portion, there is a sublation of the butter used as the means for the under-sprinkling (*upastaraṇa*) and over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) through the extension (*atideśa*) of the act of cutting from the archetype; for [the text] does not prescribe the cutting itself.
If that were the case, the repetition (*vīpsā*) and the restatement (*anuvāda*) would be untenable.

Nor can the restatement be understood according to the intention of the author of the *Sūtra*, because there is no supporting evidence; for since the fourfold cutting (*caturavatta*) is prescribed even for the *kṛṣṇala* seeds which serve as the oblation, it is possible for this [fourfold nature] to apply even to the principal [offering] itself—given that it might otherwise result in merely an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—and thus the repetition would be applicable even there.

As for the restatement regarding the accomplishment of the fourfold portion, it does not at all imply that the fourfold accomplishment applies to the cutting of the *kṛṣṇala* seeds alone, since it is achieved through the assistance of the under-sprinkling (*upastaraṇa*) and the over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*).

Furthermore, the spreading of the base (upastaraṇa) and the sprinkling of clarified butter (abhighāraṇa) must indeed be performed even for the sake of accomplishing the four-fold turning (catur-vartta). For it cannot be argued that these two are omitted in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces because they were intended as a substitute for the impossibility of cooking [the grain] in the Āhavanīya fire—due to the risk of the fine grains of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) sticking to the ladle in the archetype sacrifice; since such a sticking would not occur in the case of the *kṛṣṇalas*, they should be omitted. [This is not correct.]

If that were the case, the purpose would be accomplished by either the spreading (*upastaraṇa*) or the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) alone, resulting in the fallacy of optionality; furthermore, since contact would occur in the case of roasted grains (*dhānā*) and the like, that [non-contact] would not be achieved; and finally, if it were not for the sake of accomplishing the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) in the archetype, one could not conceive of the sprinkling as being for the sake of accomplishing the fivefold cutting (*pañcāvadāna*) and so forth in the case of the omentum (*vapā*).

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: since they serve a visible purpose, their function is precisely non-contact (*asaṃsarga*), and not the accomplishment of the fourfold portion, because that is already established in the archetype.

In the injunction "he offers with four-fold portions" (*caturvarttaṃ juhoti*), the act of throwing [the oblation] is enjoined by way of delimitation; however, the word "fourfold" (*catuḥ*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended for the spreading under (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*). Otherwise, there would be a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) and the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) due to the qualification. Consequently, since the "fourfold portion" is not established as an object to be referred to (*uddeśya*), it is even less established as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*); therefore, the spreading and sprinkling are not for the purpose of effecting that [fourfold portion]. Thus, because their purpose is merely to prevent the mixture [of the offering], they are not performed in the case of *kṛṣṇala* grains—so say the followers of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra.
In reality, however, there is no occurrence of an erroneous reading of the word *nati*;
rather, it is precisely this [word] that possesses the status of being the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the object-to-be-indicated (*uddeśyatva*).

Furthermore, because a qualified entity characterized by a relation distinct from *kārakatva* (the status of being a grammatical factor) is well-established in usage, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
For this very reason, because the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) would otherwise be untenable, one must assume an injunction for the fourfold cutting (*caturavadāna*).

For this same reason, even though the injunction for a single cutting applies to the omentum (*vapā*), the reference "even though [he is] fourfold-cutting" is consistent with the application of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) fourfold cutting;

otherwise, since only a single cutting would be required for the purpose of non-mixing (*asaṃsarga*)—namely, the under-sprinkling (*upastaraṇa*) and the over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*)—there would be the undesirable consequence of a restrictive reference (*vyavacchitti-nirdeśa*).

Therefore, just as non-mixing (*asaṃsarga*) is a purpose for the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) in the archetype, the accomplishment of the number four is also a purpose.

However, there is this distinction: non-mixing alone is the primary purpose because, like the *vaitulya* (non-redundancy), it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), whereas the number four exists only when that [non-mixing] is present.

Consequently, just as threshing and the like are not performed by one who lacks *vaitulya* despite being enjoined by a restrictive rule, but only when it is possible, so too the accomplishment of the number four through the under-spreading and sprinkling is understood to occur only when non-mixing itself serves as the purpose, and not otherwise.

And therefore, in the case of *kṛṣṇala* beans, just as the non-performance of threshing (*avaghāta*) serves the purpose of producing an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) due to a restrictive rule, so too the performance of spreading the base-butter (*upastaraṇa*) and pouring the top-butter (*abhighāraṇa*) is for the sake of achieving the number four.

Likewise, even when there is only parched grain (*dhānā*) and the like in the *savanīya* oblations, because they provide the means for achieving that [number], their performance follows the procedure of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). However, in the case of the omentum (*vapā*) and other parts, since only a connection with a few constituent parts is possible, its necessity arises for the purpose of excluding those [other parts]; thus, the notion of achieving "five-fold cutting" (*pañcāvadāna*) is also consistent with the consensus of the authors of ritual manuals (*kalpasūtrakāra*) and others.

Thus, even in a sacrifice where all oblations are offered in a single vessel (*ekakapāla*), one should understand that the rule for the fourfold cutting (*caturavatta*) and so forth applies in order to ensure the ritual perfection. Furthermore, in the *kṛṣṇala* sacrificial rice offering, there is the fourth [cutting]; and in that *kṛṣṇala* offering, the portions for the Brahmins (*brahmabhakṣa*) are also possible.

In the present case, however, since contact is impossible, it is rather the *upastaraṇa* (spreading) and *abhighāraṇa* (sprinkling) that serve as the interruptions of the possibility of such contact. Maṇḍana [states]: "There is no spreading or sprinkling in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* grains."
Śaṅkara: "There is no spreading [of the base] or pouring [of the clarified butter].
In the *kṛṣṇala* sacrifice, there is an annulment of the fourth portion (*caturthākaraṇa*).
There would be a section concerning the state of having a single meaning and so forth.
The Commentary: In this very context, the following is considered.
In the archetype (prakṛti), a distribution is prescribed: "This is for the Brahman; this is for the Hotṛ; this is for the Adhvaryu; this is for the Agnīdh."
There arises the doubt: "Is this to be performed here, or is it not to be performed?
For one who might think that it is to be performed because it is obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), this Sūtra is intended for the purpose of excluding that view.
In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the residue (*saṃsrava*) of many [offerings] is to be performed.
Since that [gift] cannot be accomplished without a distribution, a distribution is made for the sake of establishing many connections.
But here, in the case of "he bestows everything upon Brahmins," it refers to everything being given to a single person;
therefore, there is no need for a distribution.
Even if it were performed, it would not serve a visible purpose; rather, it would be performed solely for an unseen (adṛṣṭa) purpose.
Therefore, there is no "portioning out" (vyādeśa) in the *kṛṣṇala* oblation.

[Objection: Soma—If, by enjoining merely the removal, the purpose of the scriptural statement is fulfilled and thus there is no sublation of the time, then there should likewise be no sublation of the portioning out (*vyādeśa*). This is the objection raised.
[This is] the connection [of the topic].
As for the meaning of the Sūtra: because they have a single purpose, no such division as "this is for this" should be made.
Regarding the word *vi*—the first [view] is that the indications of the fourfold form exist when it is mentioned, or do they not? [The answer is: they do.
From the injunction; however, those two [the agent and the instrument] are not explicitly stated here, as they are understood through the sense of the expenditure for a manifold purpose.

Bhāṭṭa: In the archetype sacrifice (*prakṛti*), having prescribed the fourfold division of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and its distribution upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the following designation is recorded in scripture: "This is for the Brahman; this is for the Hotṛ; this is for the Adhvaryu; this is for the Agnīdh. This [designation] must be performed even in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces, because the entire [cake] is to be consumed by the Brahman alone.
Indeed, in the absence of a connection with the Hotṛ and others, designations such as "this is for the Hotṛ" would not be appropriate.
And for this reason, since there is no [portion] to be excluded, the expression "this belongs to Brahmā" is also not applicable.
Nor does this imply a lack of purpose for the fourfold division; for that division is necessary precisely because it enjoins the simultaneous consumption with all the portions that are to be avoided.

However, if it is considered that the simultaneous consumption is enjoined only with respect to those portions to be avoided at each respective time, then [the rule] would apply even to the portions remaining in the Sūtra-vessel and so forth.

However, the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is excluded because the *kṛṣṇala* seeds are too small and because there is no occasion for the fourth parting [of the hair]; this is another point.
Maṇḍana says: "There is no distribution (*vyādeśa*) in the case of the *kṛṣṇalas*.
Śaṅkara says: "In this case, there is no distribution into four parts."
In the *kṛṣṇala* oblation, the portions for the Brahman priest are to be distributed simultaneously.
In a single offering, there is joint consumption by those who eat the *brahma*-portion, because this is prescribed in the archetype.
The Commentary states: In that very context it is heard, "He offers [the oblation] to Brahman all at once.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: does this mean simultaneity (*sahatva*) or oneness-of-time (*sakṛttva*)? What is the prima facie view? It is either oneness-of-time, or simultaneity, or there is no fixed rule.
Why? Because it expresses a single mode.
The word "ekadhā" [signifies] oneness of kind; both "simultaneity" (sakṛttva) and "concomitance" (sahatva) are also [instances of] a single mode.

Likewise, he who causes cattle to reach their destination at once is said to cause them to reach it "in one way" (*ekadhā*); and he who causes them to reach it simultaneously is also said to cause them to reach it "in one way.
Therefore, either simultaneity (*sakṛttva*) or concomitance (*sahatva*) must be established.
This being the case, we reply:
it is understood that "he offers [the portion] to Brahmā in a single way.
In this manner, the disposal of both the *brahmabhakṣa* and the *atrabhakṣa* will have been accomplished.
In the other alternative, there would be no avoidance of any consumption of the *brahma-bhakṣa*.
In that case, the original injunction regarding the performance (*prayoga-vacana*) would not be observed;
for in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *bhakṣa* belongs to the *adhvaryu*.
In this case, those [portions] are indeed obtained as already separated by the injunction;

therein, the word "in one way" (*ekadhā*) is appropriate as expressing their being together. But is it not the case that here the consumption (*bhakṣa*) is based on a direct scriptural statement (*vācanika*) and is non-archetypal (*aprākṛta*), so that the archetypal separated portions do not obtain?

It is said: they do not apply because their purpose is the refinement of the person (*puruṣa-saṃskāra*), but they do apply because their purpose is the refinement of the substance (*dravya-saṃskāra*).
If they do indeed apply, for what purpose then is the statement? It is for the purpose of prescribing the means of consumption (*bhakṣopāya*).
Is it not the case that the preparation of the vessel is determined by the context or is already established by implication?
Since it is established by implication, it is a mere restatement (anuvāda).
To this, it is replied:

It is not obtained as a rule; and a rule is prescribed for the sake of restriction. [The opponent asks: "But surely, the eating here is scripturally enjoined and is non-archetypal (*aprākṛta*); therefore, the archetypal [elements], which have been expanded (*vihṛta*) [and thus belong to different times], do not obtain. What is the intention of this passage in the *Bhāṣya*? (The sense is: having stated in the previous section that there is no obtaining of the archetypal [elements] because they are for the sake of pleasure (*prīti*), how can there now be a statement regarding their obtaining?)
The reply is: these [portions] (*bhakṣas*) do not have the agent as their purpose; rather, the agent is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) here, while the portions are primary (*pradhānabhūta*).
[The word *bhakṣa* refers to] substances (*dravya*), as in "they are eaten" (*bhakṣyante*).
How then [is it that] the portion (*bhakṣa*) appears with an accusative ending—as in "the *prāśitra* here" (*prāśitram iha*)—in relation to the action?

Regarding the consumption [of the offering] in the *kṛṣṇala* oblation: 1480. In the *kṛṣṇala* oblation, the act of consumption is primary (*pradhāna*), whereas the agent—the Adhvaryu—is employed as subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the action.
This primacy is established by the word itself; however, in reality, it is understood that the substance [the *kṛṣṇala*] alone is primary.

For the black substance (*dravya*) is consecrated (*saṃskriyate*) by means of the *udaramakṣepa* rite, but this is not a consecration of the agent, Kṛṣṇa; indeed, its efficacy is not produced merely by that.
Furthermore, the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the substance occurs once its purpose has been fulfilled.
[Objection: But even in the case of a consecration of the agent, there is indeed a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭa*).

True; it has been stated that the consecration (*saṃskāra*) pertains to the substance (*dravya*), not to the agent. (Since [the substance] is already present in Kṛṣṇa, the purpose there is slight. Moreover, in the case of *soma* (which is bitter and pungent), there is absolutely no consecration [of the substance itself]; [this refers to the *pūtīka* plant, not the primary *soma*].
But harm might sometimes occur;
moreover, even if a refinement (*saṃskāra*) were to arise for the agent as well, nevertheless, a substance whose purpose has been fulfilled requires a disposal (*pratipatti*).
That [disposal] is prescribed by the scriptural statement for the agent.

Even if the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that [substance] were also to serve as the purpose of the restrictive rule (*niyama*), nevertheless, there would still be no contradiction; however, that is not what is intended [by the rule]. [In this case], the status of the substance as the primary object (*dravyārthatā*) is not lost by this much.
Therefore, it follows that the ordinary consumption portions (*bhakṣa*) belong to the *kṛṣṇala* grain; thus, the prescription of their being taken together is logically consistent.

How then is the previous section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) to be understood? To this he says: That previous four-sūtra section is [resolved] by this very principle, having been set aside as a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintā*). Soma says: Just as previously the consumption was based on the force of the scriptural statement, so too here, because the statement is common [to all], there is no such [exclusive] application; this is the connection (*saṅgati*) with what has been stated.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: Since the *brahmabhakṣas* (portions for the Brahman priest) are prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) sacrifice and occur at different times, their simultaneous offering here is enjoined by the word "ekadhā" (in one way). As stated in the Vṛtti: "The word *ekadhā* may mean either 'once' or 'simultaneously';
because there is no restrictive factor, it is indeed the latter [simultaneity], even though there is a contradiction."
The meaning of the word *ihakā* here is precisely simultaneity (*sahatva*), which takes the form of the opposite of other positions.
The Bhaṭṭa [school] maintains: In the case of the *kṛṣṇala* oblation, it is heard in scripture: "He offers to the Brahman priest *ekadhā*.

Since the word *ekadhā* is used in common parlance to denote being accomplished by a single effort, or being done once (*sakṛttva*), or occurring at one time (*ekakālatva*), or being simultaneous (*sahatva*), there arises the inquiry: what is prescribed by this? Upon reflection, since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the eating of the *iḍā*, the *prāśitra*, the fourfold division, and the portions for the *śakala* occurs at different times, by prescribing it as "once" (*sakṛt*), only the first [act] is performed, while the others are excluded.

Since there is an injunction for simultaneity (*sahatva*) for all [the participants], when the absence of a restrictive rule is reached, it is precisely because this injunction is common [to all] that— due to the lack of evidence for sublation (*bādha*) of the portions to be consumed (*bhakṣa*), which are obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) as purifiers of the oblation (*havis*)— simultaneity itself is enjoined for all. And here, simultaneity is enjoined with reference to the very vessels (*dvāra*) intended for the consumption of their respective remnants, since it will be stated later that the act of consuming occurs at different times.
And since the connection with Brahman is a restatement (*anuvāda*) because it is about to be explained, there is no specific location.
Therefore, because of the injunction of simultaneity (*sahatva*), the *āghāra* offering is merely a substitute for time. Maṇḍana says: "The word 'one' (*eka*) signifies being accompanied by another."
Śaṅkara says: "But the simultaneous recitation [of the mantra] is for the sake of a single [act].
In the case of the *kṛṣṇala* oblation, there is no contradiction regarding the consumption [of the remnant], because that is possible through the form of melting (*succhupāka*).
However, since the consumptions are for the purpose of satisfaction (*prīti*), it would constitute a ritual act (*karman*)."
Commentary: The example is the *kṛṣṇala* oblation.
In the archetype sacrifice (*prakṛti*), there are portions to be consumed (*bhakṣa*), such as the *iḍā*, the *prāśitra*, the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*), and the *śakya-vāka*.
Regarding these, a doubt arises: are those portions to be consumed in the *kṛṣṇala* oblation, or not?
What is the conclusion? They should not be performed.
For in the archetype (prakṛti), they were performed for the sake of producing satisfaction (prīti); they will thus produce that capacity.
However, gold does not produce satisfaction when it is being consumed.
Therefore, they should not be performed. [Duhkha:
This group of four sūtras beginning with "But of the eatings" (bhakṣāṇāṃ tu) establishes the point that the eatings are purificatory rites for the agent;
thus, they do not apply to the *kṛṣṇala* oblation.
Because it is not something produced by ritual action (*asaṃskāraka*).
Therefore, the consumption of gold—which was not obtained through the general injunction (*codaka*)—is prescribed by this specific statement.

Regarding this, the *Dupaṭīkā* states: "But as for that four-sūtra section (14–17) concerning the division into four parts (*caturdhākaraṇa*), it is contradicted by this principle and must be rejected."
Regarding the phrase "having performed the *kṛtvācintā*," it is stated in the *Tantraratna*:
"It might be so, because of the observation of the *nirdhāna* [the removal].
The commentary says: "It might indeed be so; there is the consumption (*bhakṣa*) of the gold."
Because of the observation of specific modes of eating:

since the rule "they shall eat making the sound *niravadyanta*" and "they shall eat making the sound *cuccupākāra*" applies when the act of eating has already been established, the scriptural text will prescribe the means for that eating. Otherwise, it would have to prescribe both the means of eating and the act of eating itself in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*), and in that case, the sentence would be split.
Therefore, the consumption [of the remnant] is obtained by the general rule (codaka).

In the *kṛṣṇala* sacrifice, there is the act of consuming; in the *kṛṣṇala* sacrifice, there is a simultaneous statement regarding the consumption of clarified butter (*ājya*), because it shares in the portion [of the offering] as in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
The Commentary states: This is not the case; that "the portions are obtained" does not mean that the [original] injunctions cease because their purpose is lost.
As for the specific statement regarding the consumption [of the offering], this will apply to the clarified butter (*ājya*) by virtue of the scriptural declaration:
"They shall consume the clarified butter without cutting it," and "They shall consume the clarified butter making the *cuccupa* sound."

The removal (*nirdhāna*) is enjoined as being in the form of *cuccu* and so forth, for one who is about to consume that which has already been obtained; thus, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Or rather, it is a statement regarding the gold (*hiraṇya*), because the clarified butter (*ājya*) is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) like the offering (*pradāna*).
The Commentary says: True, this is a statement regarding the gold, but not regarding the clarified butter.
Why? Because only this much is heard: "they shall eat," but not "this or that.
In such a case, there is a connection with that which has been specifically indicated as the subject under discussion;
and here, gold is what is indicated, not clarified butter.
How so? [In the passage] "One should offer a *caru* oblation to Prajāpati," there is the mention of "one hundred *kṛṣṇalas*.

Here, the hundred *kṛṣṇalas* are mentioned because of their connection to the ritual action (*kārya*), and the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is mentioned as a qualification of that [number], not as an independent specification in its own right.
Therefore, the *caru* alone is connected with other words, not the clarified butter.
For example, when it is said, "This staff stands on the heap of bricks; strike with it," it is understood that one strikes "with the staff," not "with the heap of bricks.
In the same way, here the word *namaḥ* (reverence) is connected with the act of eating, not with the clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Therefore, the eating belongs to the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Like the giving [of gold].
Just as the giving of those very *kṛṣṇala* seeds—which are inedible—is performed, so too should it be understood here.

Soma: [The connection is] because, just as there is no eating (*anuñjanā*) of the *upastaraṇa* and *abhighāraṇa* due to the disappearance of their purpose (*dvāralopa*), so too there is no eating of the portions (*bhakṣa*) due to the disappearance of their purpose in the form of the *tuṣi*. This is the consistency of the argument.

Vi— "There is no eating here, nor among them, because there is an absence of pleasure; it would be like an offering, based on the utterance of the sound *cuccupā*. *Cuccuyā* is the imitation of that particular sound which occurs when one eats a desired stick (*daṇḍa*) and does not accept it.
*Nirdhāna* is the complete consumption of the clarified butter (*ājya*).
According to the Bhaṭṭa school: in the archetype sacrifice (*prakṛti*), there is the eating of the remnant;
it serves the purpose of the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remnant.
This will be stated [at 10.2.9].

Furthermore, even for the purpose of the disposal of remnants (*pratipatti*), as in the case of the removal of the *prayāja* remnant [at 4.1.4], they also serve to provide strength to the agent regarding the action about to be performed; this was stated in the sixth book [at 6.4.3].
And since the disposal (*pratipatti*) is the motivator (*prayojaka*) in that case, those [acts] must indeed be performed in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces.

But when, by means of the *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical deliberation), it is established that the purpose is the satisfaction of the pure agent, then one must consider whether those [offerings] exist there or not. Since *kṛṣṇala* berries are inedible, even their purpose—satisfying the agent—is set aside due to non-performance, just as in the case of the clarified butter (*ājya*). Nor can this be a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) based on the statement, "They shall eat the gold, making the sound *cuccupa*," because here the capacity for eating belongs only to the clarified butter which serves as the medium for the gold; thus, the phrase "they shall eat the gold" means "having cast away the gold."

However, when "of gold" (*hiraṇyasya*) is not read according to the Bhāṣya, then the contact with the teeth belongs to the clarified butter (*ājya*) itself. For this very reason, the expression "in the manner of *cuccupa*" is also a restatement (*anuvāda*), since that [manner] is necessary during the consumption of clarified butter. Consequently, this consumption—which was not previously established—is either an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) or a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the clarified butter which has ceased to be a subordinate element (*avikaraṇībhūta*); therefore, the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the original consumption (*prākṛtabhakṣa*) are not to be performed therein.

This being the prima facie position (*prāpta*), the conclusion is that there is indeed the consumption of the gold itself as the primary substance (*pradhāna-dravya*), and not of the clarified butter (*ājya*). This is because the phrase "they were not cutting off" (*niravadyantaḥ*) means "not performing the crushing with the teeth. Therefore, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), this is a restorative injunction (*pratiprasava-vidhi*) specifically regarding the consumption of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). And since that [consumption] is qualified by the form of the *cuccupa* sound, it is accepted even as a fifth type of injunction through its superimposition upon the primary substance.
In reality, however, even the mention of the *cuñcupākāra* form is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the fact that it generally resembles a well-prepared bowstring.
Therefore, according to the principle of grinding (*peṣaṇanyāya*, 3.1.3), both the act of eating and its ritual properties (*bhakṣadharmāḥ*) must indeed be performed.

But upon opening the discussion as a hypothetical consideration (*kṛtvācintā*), the distinction is made that, by way of restating the already established act of eating, only contact with the teeth is prohibited.
Maṇḍana: "There is eating in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* oblation.
Śaṅkara: "But there must indeed be eating in that case, namely, in the *kṛṣṇala* oblation."

Commentary: Regarding the *kṛṣṇala* oblation, all the portions to be consumed (*bhakṣas*) are set aside simultaneously; they are to be eaten by the Brahman priest at the very time of that disposal of the remnants.
Because the individuals [who consume them] are distinct, each should have its own specific time.

Commentary: In that same context, there is a doubt: once the disposal of the remnants has been accomplished, should all the portions be eaten at one single time, or at their respective individual times?
What is established? That it is set aside for the purpose of eating.
Therefore, that which has been set aside for eating must necessarily be eaten immediately thereafter.
This being the prima facie view, we reply: because of the removal of the person, it belongs to its own time.
By excluding the person, the word becomes meaningless. In the case of the *kṛṣṇala* oblation, [the rule] does not simultaneously prevent all [of them] from their own time of consumption.

Therefore, they should be consumed at their respective times. [Regarding the *kṛṣṇala* oblation: Is there to be a simultaneous consumption of those that were offered simultaneously, or, as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), is there to be consumption at different times? (In this doubt: "Since the offering is for the purpose of consumption, therefore the consumption should also be simultaneous. [Reply: Even though the offering was made together, the consumption should be according to the time.

Therefore, because there is no injunction [to the contrary], even for those who have come together, the consumption [of the Soma] occurs at various times, just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). This is consistent with the fact that they subsist on the flowing river-like [Soma]. Viśvarūpa says: "He should consume all of that either simultaneously or at its own [proper] time."
[The phrase] "the first of all eaters" [is used] to exclude [eating] at any other time in between.
This is the meaning.

Bhaṭṭa—In considering whether the consumption by Brahmā of all the remaining [portions] gathered together simultaneously occurs all at once, or rather at their respective original times, the resolution is that because the purpose is for consumption, it is prescribed here along with this intervening rule precisely at that [original] time.

Otherwise, since the injunction would apply merely to the disposal of "all" [the soma], there would be the undesirable consequence that other persons might also consume it. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: if the injunction regarding "all" were restricted to the mere disposal, it would serve a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*); consequently, by consuming it, one would exclude others from those portions. However, even if the injunction regarding "together" (*sahatva*) were restricted to the mere disposal, it does not serve a transcendental purpose; therefore, it is logical for all of it to be disposed of to Bṛhaspati at once and then consumed by him at the respective times. Thus, there is no sublation of the original time for consumption. Maṇḍana says: "But the consumption is according to the time."
Śaṅkara says: "They are approved for their own respective times;
they are the portions to be consumed.
In the *kṛṣṇala-caru* sacrifice, all the remaining portions (*śeṣa-bhakṣāḥ*) must be brought from the other persons and handed over to the Brahman priest.
And their "universality" (sarvatva) would follow from their entitlement (*adhikāra*). The Commentary states: The example is the *kṛṣṇala* offering.
In that context, it is heard in the scripture: "He distributes everything to the Brahman priest."

In this regard, there is a doubt: does this exclusion apply only to those portions consumed by the Brahman priest, or rather to the consumption of the remnants by the persons [other than the priests]?

How is it an exclusion for the Brahman-consumers, or how is it the consumption of the remnants? If it is enjoined that "he excludes everything else for the Brahman," or if it is enjoined that "he excludes everything else for the Brahman," or if it is enjoined that "he excludes something else for the Brahman," then it is an exclusion for the Brahman-consumers.

Now, if it is enjoined that "having characterized [the portion] as 'all,' one offers it to Brahman," or if it is enjoined that "having offered it to Brahman, one characterizes it as 'all,'" then what is the conclusion regarding those who eat the remnants? It would follow that the state of being "all" applies to the portions eaten by Brahman.
Why? Because the act of offering to Brahman is already established and is not the object of the injunction;
however, the offering of the "all" is not yet established, and therefore its injunction is appropriate.
Alternatively, the entire portion belongs to this very Brahman priest.
In that case, the exclusion of one part occurs at the morning [libation], and the exclusion of another part occurs at the morning [libation];
and for that part which has not been obtained, its exclusion is now prescribed.
Therefore, the discussion concerns only those who are authorized and who consume the *brahma* [portion].
Or rather, it is a figurative application (*puruṣapanaya*) to them, because they cannot be literally designated as such.
The Commentary: The word "and" (*ca*) sets aside the previous position.
There would be a displacement of the person (*puruṣapanaya*). If it were stated thus, "Whatever he offers to the Brahman, that is all," then this entire injunction would be purposeless.
Alternatively, if it were "Whatever [is offered] to the Brahman, that he offers in its entirety," then because no specific [portion] is indicated, the word "Brahman" cannot function as a qualifier.
Furthermore, regarding the statement, "He carries away that which belongs to the Brahmin," even so, the subject would not be specified at all.
One cannot say, "He carries away that which is everything," for everything is indeed everything.
And therefore, it must be qualified.
Consequently, by the statement "he offers everything to Brahman," the connection of the entire sacrificial pap (caru) with Brahman is enjoined.
In this way, nothing is rendered purposeless.
Therefore, there is the removal of what remains for the persons.

Dūṣya: (Regarding what was said, "everything is prescribed," he says: If the word *brahma* alone is a restatement (*anuvāda*), and "everything" is what is prescribed (i.e., "whatever belongs to the *brahmán*, all that"), then in that case it is not known what "everything" is that is being prescribed. Alternatively, if the phrase "exclusion for the *brahmán*" is restated (i.e., "whatever one excludes for the *brahmán*"), even so, "everything" is not prescribed (because it is already established).
For when the exclusion of some portion occurs while another remains, then a prescription is appropriate;
but since all [the portions belonging to Brahmā] are to be consumed by him, their exclusion is already established.
(Therefore, the word "all" must indeed be prescribed.)

Furthermore, even if [it is argued that] the word *brahmaṇe* and the word *sarvam* are prescribed elsewhere as a substitute (in the sense that "whatever belongs to Brahmā, he gives away"), nevertheless, the fault of the first position also applies to this third position.

Therefore, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the word *brahmaṇe* is prescribed (neither the word *sarva*, nor the word *pariharati*; rather, having referred back to what is normally to be given away, only "that [is] for Brahmā" is thus prescribed).
In the *kṛṣṇala-caru* sacrifice, all [the rules apply]; this is the section concerning the throwing away of the black antelope horn (1483).

Just as in the preceding [section] on Soma, it was concluded according to the literal statement because there was no contradiction with the injunction, so too here; thus, the connection is established by that statement. He refutes [the objection], stating that the meaning is "he gives."

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: "all-ness" (*sarvatva*) would be the predicate to be enjoined for those portions of the *brahmā* priest, because their specific nature is already established by the general rule (*codaka*).
Therefore, "all-ness" is what is fit to be enjoined. As stated in the Vṛtti: "In the passage 'all [is] for the *brahmā*', the "all-ness" pertains to the portion of the *brahmā*."
Or rather, even for another portion, [it is said]: "That which is intended to sublate another portion...
Here, "entirety" (sarvatva) is enjoined with respect to the *brahman* priest;
let the non-eating, which belongs to oneself by virtue of the *codaka* (general rule), be sublated.

Bhaṭṭa: In that very context (*śatakṛṣṇalacarau*), it is heard in scripture: "He distributes everything to the Brahman. Therefore, whether this prescribes the distribution of the entire portion belonging to the Brahman, or prescribes the entirety of that which is to be distributed, a specific qualification is required; otherwise, the sentence would be redundant. Consequently, the connection with the Brahman is enjoined with reference to the whole.
Furthermore, since "distribution" was mentioned first as the object to be qualified in the preceding sentence, it serves as the substratum (*āśraya*).
Therefore, "he avoids" (*pariharati*) is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

For this very reason, when the action of avoiding in the preceding sentence requires an object, it must necessarily be the avoidance of that very *kṛṣṇala* remnant which was previously performed and presented as the primary element, and not the avoidance of other items such as the *ābhyañjana*.
Alternatively, the connection with Brahman is enjoined by the very act of avoidance, since it is obtained through the original context (*prakṛti*).

And because that fruit is enjoined as being connected with Brahman by way of its specific delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), even though the connection with that [fruit] is already established for the portion belonging to Brahman, the establishment of that connection for the portion belonging to another person [the sacrificer] follows; furthermore, the quality of "entirety" (*sarvatva*) is restated.

Consequently, the plural number in the phrase "they eat without leaving a remainder" (*niravadyanto bhakṣayanti*) is logical. Alternatively, due to this [establishment], the eating by other persons and so forth is optional.
There is no syntactical split (vākyabheda) because of the prescription of a specific set of dice through a previously unestablished application;
as Maṇḍana [Miśra] stated: "All the dice should belong to Brahman," [meaning they] "are to be offered."
Śaṅkara says: "All [the horns] should belong to Brahmā.

✿ The scratching with the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*) takes place during the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), beginning from the first day of initiation (*dīkṣā*) until the final day of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). And the throwing away (*prāsana*) into the *cātvāla* pit occurs on the final day, after the sacrificial fee has been given.

Bhāṣya 11.1.16.15–16: Regarding the scratching with the black antelope horn, there is a fear of defects. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), the casting away of the black antelope horn occurs after the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has been given, at the *cātvāla* pit. 4.2.16: The casting away of the black antelope horn in the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), which is a multi-day rite (*ahargaṇa*), occurs on a day other than [the first], namely not on the first day nor in the middle.
Therefore, the scratching with the black antelope horn is restricted to the entire series of sacrificial days (*ahargaṇa*).
❀ The section concerning the throwing away of the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā-prāsana-adhikaraṇa*).
The section concerning the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā-adhikaraṇa*).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the casting away of the black antelope horn is a *pratipatti* (disposal).

Since that which is connected with something at its origin is for the sake of that thing—because it serves as the means for its purification—it would be a *pratipatti* when it goes toward another purpose, because it is then a mere remnant (*śeṣa*).
Commentary: Alternatively, this may be a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).
The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that both the scratching with the horn (*viṣāṇā*) and the throwing away (*prāsana*) are equally instrumental causes.
The final (uttara-pakṣa) position is that since they reside in a single substrate, everything should be equal. [However, they are not;

because of the use of the instrumental case in "scratching," the horn has the status of a subordinate factor (*guṇa*); whereas in "throwing away," because of the use of the accusative case and because it serves its purpose elsewhere, it possesses the status of a primary factor (*pradhāna*).
Śabara: Having prescribed that "one scratches with the black antelope horn," it is heard [in the scripture]: "One throws the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the throwing into the *cātvāla* for a specific purpose (*arthakarma*), or is it a disposal (*pratipatti*)?
In that case, "there is no need for a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a substance whose purpose has already been fulfilled."
Therefore, this performance [of the ritual] does not include the *iḍā*, *sviṣṭakṛt*, and so forth.
It is said:
"Furthermore, even a substance whose purpose has been fulfilled is considered a scattered remnant (*ākīrṇakara*)."
Therefore, it is better to consider the performance [of the act] as its injunction. [Objection:

Soma—after the discussion regarding the performance of the act as a primary purpose (*arthakarma*) has been concluded, how can there be a discussion regarding the performance as a primary purpose, since such a performance is impossible? [Response:
The connection [between the topics] is established by way of this objection.

Although a discussion regarding the disposal (*pratipatti*) is also conducted in the section concerning the fire-offering (*agniprādhikaraṇa*), nevertheless, because the *soma-tila* offering—even if it were a primary action (*arthakarman*)—lacks a motivating factor due to its being a mere action of naming (*abhidhānakarman*), and because it does not extend beyond the original context (*prakṛti*), the matter is already concluded.

Regarding this Sūtra, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that the disposal (*pratipatti*) [of the horn] should be like the throwing away of the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇāprāsana*) following the infliction of punishment in the previous section. Having explained this by showing the disparity between the example cited in the prima facie view and the actual case—arguing that since the scratching of the entire body up to the end of the tail is not the function of the horn, scratching continues even after the throwing away, and thus the horn has already fulfilled its purpose, the throwing away is not a disposal—one establishes the prima facie view. Then, [the siddhāntin replies]: because of the connection with the second case ending, the throwing away is indeed a disposal.

Nor should it be argued that, for that reason alone, the throwing away (*prāsana*) must be merely a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the horn and not a disposal (*pratipatti*). If that were the case, there would be a discrepancy in the injunction "she scratches with the horn" (*viṣāṇayā kaṇḍyate*): the mere horn would be employed for the scratchings occurring prior to the throwing away, whereas for those occurring subsequent to it, the horn would have to be one already consecrated by the act of throwing away. This is the section on the throwing away of the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā-prāsanādhikaraṇa*), namely the principle of the spreading of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇajināstaraṇanyāya*).
The maxim of the spreading of the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇajināstaraṇanyāya) [145]. This follows from the context. And it is not the case that one should say, "Let the cows be kept in the house."
Just as the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), the pestle (*musala*), and the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) assist [the ritual] by means of a single common application (*tantra*),
so too let the throwing away (*prāsana*) be a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *cātvāla* pit;
and the accusative case ending [in the scriptural injunction] is [justified] in both views.
The mention of the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) and so forth [is implied], while the mortar (*ulūkhala*) is mentioned in the Sūtra.
It should be stated that [the action] occurs "when it has been husked" (*psite*). If that were the case, there would be an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of the locative case.
He indicates this so that the pestle and other implements might not be understood as mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, like the accusative case, the throwing away (*prāsana*) is a disposal (*pratipatti*).

Now, the mortar itself is considered: is it a single common element (*tantra*) [for all], or is it separate? [This is determined by whether the scratching, piercing, and winnowing] take place only prior to the throwing away (*prāsana*) of that [mortar], or otherwise.
In this regard, since there is such consideration regarding the application of the archetypal rule (*tantrāvāpa*), the fulfillment of the purpose is established through the culmination of the yoga;
thus ends the section.
This is the result of this [section] (*adhikaraṇa*).
As for the body of the section (*adhikaraṇa-śarīra*),
however, it has not been explained by the author of the Bhāṣya.
But for the teachers, it is indeed something else; and that is entirely consistent, as he says: "What is the spreading of the black antelope skin?"
The sequence beginning with the *iḍā*, the *prāśitra*, the fourth-portion-making (*caturthākaraṇa*), and the *śaṃyuvāka*,

and ending with the preparation of the rice grains (*taṇḍula-nirvṛtti*), constitutes a single ritual act (*padārtha*); this is established by the principle "that with which [the main action] is connected when there is a possibility for specific subsidiary acts."
"Prasaṅga" (meaning intermediate connection; he states the connection by way of definition):
this [section] belongs to those who say, "Because its practice is established."
There is also a difference in sequence [the difference in sequence resulting from the departure from the order of the sacrificial cake-offerings and so forth]. Furthermore,
the consumption of the *iḍā* is intended to apply to all sacrificial materials, such as bricks and the like.
It indeed exists.

But the meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: at the time of rebirth, that which is conjoined with something [is its cause], because the dharma of Viṣṇu is for the sake of that which is to be worshipped according to the rules.
It would be for that purpose alone, because being for that purpose is based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Regarding that, the commentary says: "There would be [the use] of mortars belonging to Viṣṇu."
For it is certain:
because it is employed through its connection with logical proof (*upapatti*), that [sequence] occurs when there is the possibility of another meaning.
In the case of a sequence, it is established by the order of recitation; it is possible only when there is simultaneity among the meanings of the words.
The understanding would be of a different meaning; here, the term "logical proof" (upapatti) is to be understood as following in sequence.
The items such as the lower bedding and so forth are separate objects;
this is for the purpose of illustration. Elsewhere, the departure of those who have performed their duties is considered a formal act of acceptance (*pratipatti*).
Because it is the conclusion of a state; those who know the meters say that *yati* means "cessation"—
this is the definition.

Otherwise, because there would be no attainment of the sublime, blameless, and so forth, the state of striving (*yatibhāva*)— that is, the state of being one who strives— would be interrupted; this constitutes a logical fallacy (*prasaṅga*).
"Completion" means up to that point; and "the state of a Yati" refers to the act of spreading [the grass] below.
Vi— "The throwing of the black antelope horn into the Cātvāla pit is a ritual action (arthakarma), because it is designated by its own specific term."
Therefore, it is called "purification by Viṣṇu.
Or rather, it is a ritual disposal (*pratipatti*): the former [is so called] because it possesses meaning, while the latter is so due to its utility.
Or rather, there should be only one mortar, because the act of threshing continues until the rice-grains have been produced, as that is the purpose of the action.
Therefore, the throwing out [of the husks] is a disposal (*pratipatti*).
Commentary: Or rather, there should be only one mortar used in succession.
One [says]: Bhaṭṭa— [in the context of] "he scratches with the black antelope horn" (some)—
for the ritual procedure begins from the spreading of the grass and extends up to the rice grains.
The spreading [of the grass] and so forth:

because it is postulated that the fruit belongs exclusively to the constituent part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*), and because there is no attainment of a fruit in this world [from the action itself], this is the "principle of the spreading of the black antelope skin" (*kṛṣṇajināstaraṇanyāya*), which is distinct from the principle of postulating what has already been established (*klṛptakalpanānyāya*).

If [the subsidiary acts] were considered constituent parts (*avayava*) by virtue of being auxiliaries to the remainder of the sacrifice (*yāgaśeṣa*), then there would follow the consequence of performing each act in its entirety (*anusamaya*) from the threshing (*avaghāta*) up to the grinding (*peṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, since the mantras associated with the subsidiaries, such as those recited at the time of threshing, would assist only through an invisible effect (*adṛṣṭa*), they would not attain the status of constituent parts.

Moreover, even if they were constituent parts, why would there not be individual performance (*pratyekānusamaya*)—given that the spreading of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇajina*) and so forth are enjoined and thus included within the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*), thereby achieving the parsimony of simultaneity (*sāhityalāghava*)?

If it is argued: "In this way, since the giving of the substance (*dravyadāna*) also serves to prepare the oblation (*havis*), just like the *homa*, why should there not be a sequential performance for each individual item according to the logic of grinding and threshing (3.1.13)? [Response]: No. Even though the spreading of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇajina*) and so forth are enjoined by independent injunctions, or are prompted by the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*) as subsidiary elements (*aṅga*), they are understood to be prompted through their role as subsidiaries to the threshing and other acts; therefore, the sequence follows that [of the primary acts]. Thus, there is no sequential performance for each individual item, because of the parsimony of combining them together.

In this way, even for the series of actions beginning with pouring out and ending with the removal of the wash-water, their utility lies in the result of producing the rice-grains through threshing; because they serve the purpose of threshing (*avaghāta*), they do not constitute separate entities.

For this very reason, although it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), that subsidiary act is not a separate ritual item (*padārtha*). Similarly, since the spreading of the butter (*upastaraṇa*) and so forth serve the purpose of the oblation (*homa*) by means of preventing the mixture [of the offering] within the ladle (*sruk*), they have no independent application; thus, there is no separate sequential performance (*anusamaya*).

Since the injunction for the oblation (*homa*) is prescribed by means of the delimitation (*avaccheda*) of both the substance-offering and the refinement of the sacrificial oblation (*havissaṃskāra*), it is simpler to regard the act of delimitation itself as what is to be performed.
Furthermore, because acts such as the cutting off (*avadāna*) are not conceived as having separate independent performance, they do not constitute distinct ritual categories (*padārtha*).
Therefore, the status of being a *padārtha* consists in being the object of the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) through its own independence.

For, since items such as the spreading of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇajina*) are subordinate elements (*padārthāvayavatva*) within the ritual procedure, their status as objects of application cannot be known without first knowing that they are objects of application directed toward threshing (*avaghāta*) and other such acts.

However, in the case of threshing and the like, that knowledge is not necessarily preceded by the knowledge of them being objects of application directed toward something else; for the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), by making known the impulsion (*prayukti*) toward the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) qualified by both the subsidiary and the primary, brings about the impulsion of the subsidiary through the very fact that it would otherwise be inexplicable without the impulsion of the primary.

And therefore, it is established that the cognition of the fact that something is not the object of a particular injunction exists precisely through the presence of the impossibility of that injunction otherwise; this [cognition] is a distinct category from that [injunction].

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, there is the recitation of the *klṛpti* and other mantras even for a sacrificer who possesses knowledge;

The Commentary states: In the Vājapeya, it is heard in the scripture: "He causes the sacrificer to recite the *klṛptis*"; "He causes the sacrificer to recite the *ujjitis*."

In this regard, there is a doubt: should both the knower and the ignorant be made to recite, or only the knower? What is the prima facie view? Since there is no distinction specified, both the knower and the ignorant [should recite].
To this, we reply:
"He is indeed one who knows.
Why? Because there is no one prescribed as ignorant;
for he who is ignorant is not qualified, due to a lack of capacity.
[Objection: But surely, having been trained at the time of practice, she will perform [the rite]; by virtue of her capacity, she is entitled [to the result]. [Reply:
We say no.
The performance is heard of as occurring after the study of the Veda.
The study of the Veda is not included within the *prayoga* (the performance of rituals).
Why? Because the study of the Veda is heard of as being independent of ritual acts in the statement: "Therefore, one's own portion of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied.
Given this statement, it cannot be assumed that by such injunctions as "One should offer the *agnihotra*," it is implied that "the Veda must be studied."

In that context, when only the oblation (*homa*) is enjoined, one who has studied the Veda and is capable is qualified (*adhikriyate*), not the ignorant person. But to what extent must he know so as to be considered learned and thus qualified? He who knows enough to become capable of performing the sacrifice as prescribed is qualified for that sacrifice. Now, it might be argued that because of the injunction "one should study the Veda," the entire Veda must be studied, and thus one would not be qualified for [specific rites] until the whole Veda is mastered.
It is said:
the study of the Veda must be performed for the purpose of knowing the sacrifices (*kratavaḥ*).
In that regard, when one sacrifice is to be performed, knowledge of another sacrifice does not serve a visible purpose.
Therefore, knowledge of other sacrifices need not be acquired for the sake of one's entitlement [to perform a specific rite].
A text concerning another sacrifice exists for the purpose of knowing that other sacrifice.
It is heard in scripture that the study of the entire Veda is required so that all sacrifices may be known individually.
Therefore, one who is the referent of his own word (svapadārtha) is qualified [for the ritual].
Consequently, for that which is not the referent of his own word, there is no status as an object; how then could such a person be designated?
Thus, it is correctly stated that only one who possesses knowledge (jña) is to be made to recite.
Or rather— where it is heard in the scripture, "He causes the sacrificer to recite," there is no fixed rule as to whether an ignorant person may be made to recite by the officiating priests,
or whether the learned person himself should speak, in which case the activity of the instigator would take that form.
Therefore, only an ignorant person should be made to recite.
This being the position, it is replied:
"For there is no one enjoined who is ignorant [of the Veda].

If the study of the Veda were governed solely by injunctions for specific desires (*kāmaśruti*), then one would have to be taught even at the time of the ritual performance; however, like the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*), the study is enjoined as an independent rule (*anārabhyavidhi*) in the words: "Therefore, one's own portion of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied."

And this being so, since there would be no purpose [in learning], it is already established that all ritual acts (*karmāṇi*) are grasped through mere imitation; thus, formal instruction (*śikṣaṇa*) is not employed. Furthermore, the Veda would not be "learned" (*śikṣita*). (In this context, the reading "the Veda would be unlearned" [*aśikṣito vedaḥ*] appears more appropriate; nevertheless, according to the *Klṛptyadhikaraṇa* [Jaiminisūtra 3.4.12–13], the suffix *-ken* is used.)

In the *Sudhā*, the reading "because the mantras of the *klṛpti* and so forth, due to their being established as having a specific sequence of syllables, lack the nature of the Veda for one who has studied them, and because the mantras possess the essence of the Veda only through the force of the injunction for self-study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), they merely serve as auxiliaries to ritual action" is correct exactly as it is printed (Ke.).
Therefore, those mantras which are recited prior to the ritual action attain the status of auxiliaries; thus, there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) here for one who is ignorant [of them].
And even in that case, the purposefulness of the instigator’s activity can be established through the command (*praiṣa*); for even if one has the capacity, one would not speak if not prompted.

And that state of being an instigator occurs either when [the action] is embodied, or when it is conveyed by the word, or when it is expressed as "fetch the rice"—thus, the action may be performed according to one's preference.

Regarding the Bhāṣya passage, "By knowing how much, however?", [the author] asks this in order to provide a clear demonstration that the Vaiśeṣikas and others assert a lack of qualification even with respect to their own scriptures when those have not been mastered.

In the Vaiśeṣika [sūtra], after stating at the beginning—"Now, therefore, we shall explain dharma" (1.1)—that his own treatise is for the purpose of explaining dharma, he declares that the qualification for [the pursuit of] dharma is dependent upon one's own treatise (Su.
In that context, because learning is beneficial through perception itself by way of establishing one's capacity, the Commentator says: "by whatever has been known."

Although the entire Veda is encompassed by the study of one's own recitation (*svādhyāya*), nevertheless, for one performing the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* portions of the Jyotiṣṭoma are not applicable; thus, even this does not exclude his eligibility, because his fitness is established by the very Veda used for the sacrifice.
Therefore, for such a person, the "study of one's own recitation" consists only of that much.

As for the fact that it is studied in its entirety, that is because the obligatory (*nitya*), optional (*kāmya*), and occasional (*naimittika*) rites arise at various times, so it is not known which one will be performed when.

In that regard, sometimes there arises for him either a desire to recite what has not been studied or a desire for its fruit; in such a case, because he is ignorant of it (*tadavidvatvāt*—the analysis being: *vidvān* means one who knows; *na tadvidvān* means one who does not know that; *tadavidvatvam* is the state of being such; therefore), he fails because he is unable [to perform it].

Or else, at that time, since it is impossible for one who is studying to observe the vows associated with the study, and since there would be no apprehension of such [a text] by those whose Veda-knowledge is satisfied by specific ritual acts mixed with [other] actions, there would follow the contingency of a deficiency in the rite (*vaiguṇya*).

Since the Veda is required by all injunctions that are not part of a specific context (*anārabhyavāda*) because they do not pertain to [the pursuit of] desire (*kāma*), the entire Veda must necessarily be studied during the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*).
However, if someone, being incapable, does not study the whole of it but somehow masters only the *Agnihotra*, *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, and so forth, he is not disqualified from performing those rites.
This being the case, the knowledge of a child is indeed very far removed [from such eligibility].

As for that knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), without it there is no engagement [in ritual action] at all; therefore, it must be accepted for the sake of all ritual acts. This is considered here in connection with the mantras recited by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*): "In that regard, because there is no distinction, both [the knower and the ignorant] [should perform them], or rather, the wise man himself should speak [them]."
An ignorant person, however, is not addressed [in this way], for no one who is ignorant exists in the sacrificial rite;
the settled conclusion is that eligibility belongs only to the learned and not to others.
Because of the traditional injunction "Speak! (brūhi), the addressing of this [sacrificer] is possible.

Soma: Mantras such as "May life be perfected through sacrifice" (*āyuryajñena kalpatām*) are called *klṛptis* because they are associated with the sense of perfection (*klṛpti*). Viśvarūpa: The person to be addressed is either the master (*svāmin*), both the knowledgeable and the ignorant, or the knowledgeable one alone.
Since there is no distinction [stated], it applies to both; however, because the knowledgeable one possesses mastery (*svāmitva*), one should cause that person to recite.

Bhaṭṭa: In cases such as the Vājapeya sacrifice where the scripture states, "He causes the sacrificer to recite the *klṛpti* verses," it is undisputed that the mantra belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) and the act of causing to recite (*vācana*) belongs to the officiating priest (*adhvaryu*). However, it is argued: since the term "causing to recite" (*vācana*) is well-established in the sense of instructing in the teaching of the *Gāyatrī* and so forth for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), it is understood that in the present case as well, it prescribes instruction. Furthermore, because such instruction cannot pertain to one who already possesses knowledge—since that would result in a merely invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose—it follows that, in accordance with the aforementioned rule, only one who is ignorant is entitled (*adhikārī*) to the Vājapeya and other such rites.

Therefore, although others may possess the qualification of being knowers by virtue of subsisting on the knowledge established through the injunction for the study of the *Ṛgveda*, since that is impossible in the case of the *Vājapeya* sacrifice and other such rites, the recitation must be performed by one who is ignorant [of the text].

This being the position reached, it is replied: Since the act to be considered consists merely of an activity conforming to the verbal instruction (*vacana*), even if "instruction" (*śikṣaṇa*) is understood as mere reminding (*sāraṇa*), the recitation is appropriate in the present context; for there is no evidence to necessitate the presence of ignorance (the meaning is: when there is no necessity for ignorance, it does not follow that the recitation is for the ignorant), and therefore the recitation is to be performed by one who already knows the text.
And that [instruction] is either "recite this mantra in parts" or "recite this mantra in this manner.
Maṇḍana [states]: "The *klṛpti* and other [ritual details] should be spoken by one who is learned [in them].
Śaṅkara [states]: "Only one who knows [the ritual] should speak the *klṛpti* and the *īśa*."
