the entitlement to perform the ritual action is restricted only to what is explicitly stated. For that [action], the benediction and celibacy apply only as far as they are stated, because of their inequality [with other requirements].

The Commentary states: Regarding such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," it has been stated that there is joint entitlement for both the female and the male. Now, a doubt arises: must the wife perform all the duties pertaining to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), or only those specifically mentioned, namely the benediction (*āśis*) and celibacy (*brahmacarya*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? All the duties pertaining to the sacrificer should be performed by the wife.
For she too is indeed a sacrificer, because of equality;
therefore, [the rites] belong to her entirely.
This being the position reached, we reply:
Regarding her, it should be as stated, based on the authority of the scriptural word.
There should be both the blessing and the practice of celibacy.
Why? Because they are not equal.
For a woman is indeed unequal to a man:
the sacrificer is a man who is learned, while the wife is a woman who is ignorant. What follows from this inequality?

From this it follows: regarding those scriptural injunctions concerning the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) that pertain to the purposes of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*), because they are heard as things to be adopted (*upādeya*), the gender is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*).
Therefore, in those cases, the wife (*patnī*) would not be included.
Furthermore, regarding those ritual acts accompanied by mantras (*samantraka*) that serve the purpose of the ritual, the wife would not be included because she lacks knowledge (*avidyātva*).
It will be argued that this serves as the motive for the wife's study;
but that is not so,
for even if this were the motive, the fulfillment of that [requirement] would still occur.
For there exists a man who can accomplish that [rite];
and whatever is for the sake of the sacrifice must be accomplished by anyone whatsoever.
Therefore, there is no authority for the re-authorization of the wife's study, which had been prohibited.
Therefore, even that [the wife] should not perform.
As for the blessings and the celibacy, these are subordinate to the person; they are not accomplished when performed by only one of them.
For the sacramental refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the other would otherwise be deficient.
Furthermore, the sacrificer is not heard of there as one to be adopted [as a subordinate element]. Therefore, even the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not like a direct injunction (*vidhi*).

Consequently, both the benediction (*āśis*) and the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) would belong to both [the sacrificer and his wife], just as it is stated in the *Āhnikā*: "The wife looks at the clarified butter (*ājya*)."
Therefore, because they are unequal and their ritual regulations are not the same, the wife ought to be distinct from the sacrificer.
Duh—(By the word *āśis*, the recitation of mantras such as "O Agni, giver of life, give me life" is meant;
that is improper, because it is impossible for a woman who lacks Vedic knowledge to recite mantras.)
Regarding this, he says: by the word *āśis* (benediction), the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as shaving the hair and beard are indicated.

By the word *ādi* (and so forth), the application of unguents, bathing, and other such acts are included. And the mention of shaving the hair and beard is intended to indicate all the purificatory rites performed together.
(We shall explain in the second [section] that there is no shaving of the hair or beard for the wife.
Both of these [observances] apply.
Celibacy has been stated as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), and likewise it is seen to be for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*) by means of the contextual statement.
If this were so (i.e., if it were for the sake of the sacrifice), then the study [of the Veda] mentioned here would result in a deficiency [in the rite].

Otherwise (if it were not for the sake of the sacrifice, because it would have only a personal purpose), even one who possesses that [study] would not possess the quality [required] for the sake of the sacrifice.
(Therefore, the benediction and the vow of celibacy should belong to the wife only as far as is prescribed.)
Other than that, the *yājamāna* (rites performed by the sacrificer) resides in the person alone.

How so? In that regard—in passages such as "The sacrificer touches [the animal] from behind" (*yajamāno'nvārabhate*)—because the sacrificer is being enjoined (*upādīyamānatva*), the masculine gender is intended to be significant.
Furthermore, those rites recited in the *Yājamāna-kāṇḍa* (as noted in both the printed edition and the Ratnaprabhā commentary) are likewise to be performed by the sacrificer as their agent.

(How so? In that regard, those mantras must be recited by the sacrificer alone. Why? Because he is learned (due to having studied), whereas the other [the wife] is unlearned. If it is argued that she will study because of the impossibility of otherwise [accomplishing the rite], [the author] refutes this: that [alleged] impossibility is also obviated by the sacrificer’s learning; since the sacrifice has its requirements fulfilled by his own study, the woman will not perform what is prohibited regarding study.

If, in this way, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is produced from either [the word *yajamāna*] as in "the sacrificer" (*yajamānam*), then even those ritual acts that are not accompanied by mantras will be performed by the sacrificer alone.

(He clarifies this very point: although there is no fault in them consisting of a lack of learning (*avaidyatva*), nevertheless, because the secondary derivative suffix is applicable only to the sacrificer, the performance is not carried out by the wife.

Furthermore, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in the term *yajamānam*—meaning "the ritual action of the sacrificer and the sacrificer" (*yajamānaśca yajamānā ca tayoḥ karma yajamānam*)—does not apply to the wife and the sacrificer when they have performed their respective duties, because there is no authoritative evidence for such a usage.

[The two sections concerning the *Dvādaśāha* sacrifice and the rule "only as much as is prescribed for her" (*tasyā yāvaduktam*) have been re-explained by the authors of the Vārttika in another manner.
Therein, the explanation of the second section is as follows: "All the duties of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) must be performed by both, because both possess the status of being a sacrificer."

With this intention, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): In passages such as "the sacrificer is not excluded from the *śukra*," since the sacrificer is the one to be selected (*upādeya*), his two attributes—masculinity and singularity—are intended to be expressed; therefore, only a male is to be understood [as the subject].

Furthermore, the benedictory statement ("O teacher, give this to him first") does not apply to her. Why? "Kautsa, the descendant of Kaṇva, shaves his hair and beard.

But when the purpose is not heard, there should be a modification of the archetypal [sāman], because it is a subordinate element.
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position: even when the purpose is not heard, there should be a modification of the archetypal [sāman].
For in the archetype, the sāman is a subordinate element.

This *sāman* is also heard [in scripture]. By virtue of its being a *sāman*, it ought to function as a *sāman* through its general nature as such. For example: "Curd, ghee, vegetables, and rice; Devadatta is to be fed; like Devadatta, Yajñadatta is to be fed with oil."
Although it is not explicitly stated that "oil is for the purpose of lubricating," nevertheless, oil exists only for lubrication because it is capable of that function.

Likewise, although it is not stated that "the *sāman* is for the purpose of refining the *ṛc*," nevertheless, because of its capability for that, the *sāman* must exist only for the refinement of the *ṛc*.

Regarding the phrase "but when the purpose is not heard" (*arthe tv-aśrūyamāṇe*), this sūtra was explained in the previous section as being intended to demonstrate the difference between the *śloka* and others on one hand and the *kautsa* and others on the other; furthermore, it was explained again in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) under a different section beginning with "Or thus" (*evaṃ vā*).

As stated previously, because the archetypal [rite] lacks a specific purpose, there is no accomplishment; thus, having said this, the connection of the *ktvā* suffix [is established], as in the case of the *phalārthavāda* (laudatory statement of results) in a sacrifice, like the *maṅkha*.

It has been stated [in the *Tantravārttika*] that "that [act] is either fruitless or possesses a fruit, because it is mentioned in syntactical connection with the *vājapeya*; thus, the *bṛhaspatisava* is subordinate to the *vājapeya* sacrifice.

Likewise, in the very fourth book, in the section concerning the *upaveśa* (4.2.18–19), it was said: "And by the word 'having shaved' (*parivāsya*), the gerund suffix (*ktvā*) does not indicate that shaving is for the purpose of the act of sitting down (*upaveśa*), because the second case ending (*dvitīyā*), which is stronger due to its connection with the sentence... and so forth.

The view that the *ktvā* suffix is prescribed by the rule *dhātusaṃcane vihitaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.21) for cases such as *vājapeyabṛhaspatisavābhyām saṃcayam ācchet* is the opinion of others (*paramatam*), because when the meaning of another sentence [the injunction] is established, it is improper to treat [the *saṃcaya*] as the expressed meaning [of the verbal root]. However, the rule *dhātusaṃcane pratyayāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.1) serves merely to declare grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*).
Bāla. pp. 45–46. The basis for the *ktvā* suffix is justified by the mere fact of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), just as in the expression *snātvā svapiti*.

Su. pṛ. 867. Grammarians maintain that the suffix *ktvā* has the power (*śakti*) to denote both the state of having the same agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) and the state of occurring at a prior time (*pūrvakālatva*).

Logicians (*naiyāyika*), however, hold that in expressions such as "having eaten, he goes" (*bhuktvā vrajati*), there is a cognition that the going occurs after the eating; therefore, they maintain that its power consists in denoting posteriority in time (*uttarakālatva*) and having the same agent.
Furthermore, having the same agent means that the two actions expressed by the co-occurring terms do not have different agents.

Therefore, there is the usage “The chariot stands [after] the oxen” (*ratho gāvā tiṣṭhati*). And "subsequent time" (*uttarakālatva*) should be understood as qualified by a verbal action that is to occur and which constitutes the intended object (*tātparyaviṣaya*).
Therefore, there is the usage “Then, having gone, he breathes” (*atha gatvā śvasiti*).

In expressions such as *‘mukhaṃ nyāyāya svapiti’* (“He sleeps for the sake of [re]gaining his face”), there is either a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based merely on having the same agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) or a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Some maintain that the understanding arises through the reverse order: “Having slept, [he sleeps] for the sake of [re]gaining the root.

However, in cases such as *‘darśapūrṇamāsābhyāmiṣṭvā somena yajeta’* (“Having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma”), there is the manifestation of the state of being fit for connection (*anvayayogyatva*).
*Maṇi*, p. 164: "The meaning of the suffix *ktvā* is connected with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).
*Sūkti*, p. 113: "The word *ktvā* expresses only anteriority in time and common agency; it does not express immediate succession.

It merely states that 'the initiation of the householder occurs first and that of the Brahman priest occurs later'; however, even if one were to perform a thousand ritual acts in the interval, there is no contradiction in the expression of 'prior' and 'subsequent'."

Regarding the ritual (*kratu*), Kāṣṇojini maintains that [passages such as] "those who perform these *rātris* certainly attain a firm foundation" are *phalārthavāda*s (declarations of results), like the case of the *maṅkha*. "Those who perform these *rātris*" means those sacrificers who undertake—i.e., carry out—these rites of the *sattra* type which are to be accomplished over days and nights; they indeed, with certainty, attain a firm foundation—that is, they obtain stability.
The word *rātri* here signifies a day-and-night (*ahorātra*).
From the word "they would undertake" (*upeyuḥ*), it is understood that this refers to a *sattra* sacrifice.

Here, in the inquiry as to whether these [passages] are explanatory statements of results (*phalārthavāda*) or injunctions of results (*phalavidhi*), the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The teacher Kāṣṇojini considers the phrase "they become established" (*pratitiṣṭhanti*) to be an explanatory statement of results with respect to the ritual—the action consisting of the *rātrisattra*.

Just as in the case of the *aṅkavat* [passage], where the commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the hearing of a blameless reputation and so forth in the fires possessing the *juhū* and *parṇa* ladles is like that, so too here heaven must be postulated. Regarding the fruit, Ātreya says it is based on the explicit mention; for where there is no direct scriptural statement, there would be inference.
He states the established conclusion:
regarding rituals such as the Rātrisatra, the teacher Ācārya held that results such as "they become firmly established" are actual fruits and not merely explanatory praise (arthavāda) of the fruit;
for a ritual must necessarily have a result.
And that [result] is heard in a proximate explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). It is better to assume a result that is proximate than to resort to ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).
In every way, [this is preferable].

In the case of a sacrifice, the mention of a fruit is an *arthavāda*, as in the case of the *maṅkha* [sacrifice] (Sūtra 14.9.7). For, since no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is heard of in this [Viśvajit sacrifice], there would have to be an inference of a fruit, as in the case of the Viśvajit;
but here, the fruit is indeed heard directly in the *arthavāda*.
Therefore, there is no inference [of a separate result].
Consequently, in cases such as the Rātrisatra sacrifice, the fruit is postulated as belonging to the explanatory passage (arthavāda) alone, due to the parsimony of postulation (kalpanālāghava).
Among the fires, it is praise, because they exist for the sake of another.
This is a *siddhānta-sūtra* intended to demonstrate the disparity between the examples cited by the opponent (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In the case of the fires mentioned in passages such as "They offered with the *juhū* ladle" and "with the *sruva* ladle," the statement of results—such as "he does not hear an evil report"—is indeed a direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*), because the *guhā* and other elements serve another purpose, namely, the purpose of the primary ritual.
However, this is not the case in the *Rātrisatra* sacrifices, because there they do not serve another purpose.
Therefore, the statement "they indeed become established" is a commendatory eulogy (*arthavāda*).
Consequently, the fruit mentioned here is merely figurative.
What [is the rule]? In the case of a sacrifice, the *bhāṣika* accent should be employed for those mantras originating from the Brāhmaṇa texts.
Because it follows that same principle, even what is seen [in the Vedic text] is treated in this way.

Because that is the established principle (*nyāya*), even though it is not explicitly seen, the principle is as follows:

"The word [is used] because of its form resulting from the instruction of the mantra. Or [the application of the mantra] is due to its arising from that, because it has the characteristic of being a sacred recitation (*pravacana*).

The commentary states: "Or, because it arises from that—that is, because it arises from the Brāhmaṇa—the application of the mantra would be by means of the reciter, since it has the characteristic of being a sacred recitation.
Sacred recitation is the defining characteristic of mantras."
As they are proclaimed, so they are understood; and they have arisen only within ordinary linguistic usage.
There is no authority for them outside of that.

Therefore, they should be employed exactly as they have arisen [in the Vedic text]. Soma says: the meaning of the sūtra is that even when a mantra is not found in the collection of mantras (mantrasāmnāya), the Brāhmaṇa accent does not apply by virtue of the previous principle. Mīmāṃsākośa 188.

3.4.8, p. 316). Or rather, by inference, as in the case of the sacrifice itself, there would be an abundance of fruit (*phalabhūmā*) upon repetition.
The word "vā" (or) dispels doubt.

In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, when a single performance is followed by repetition (*abhyāsa*) for those who lack knowledge, there would be an abundance of fruit—that is, a multiplicity of results. By means of inference, it is understood that prior to the performance of the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*), there was no assistance to the primary rite (*pradhāna*); however, after [the auxiliaries], it does exist. Therefore, it is recognized that the assistance is surely produced by the auxiliary; thus, if it were performed again and again, the assistance would also be produced again and again.
Just as in the case of sacrifices such as the Saurya and Āryamana, where the fruit is produced by the action, so too there is an abundance of fruit through the repetition of the action;
this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Or rather, it should be performed once, because the cause is one.
In a single performance, the auxiliary (aṅga) should be performed once, not repeatedly;
because the cause is one. The single cause of the auxiliaries is the production of the capacity for the primary act to yield its fruit.
And since that [capacity] is accomplished by performing it once, there is no further performance.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Ratna.
The Section on the Inquiry into What Subservient to the Sacrifice and What Subservient to Man.
Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into that which subserves the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and that which subserves the person (*puruṣārtha*).

The Commentary states: In the third chapter, the definition of the application of subsidiaries (*śeṣaviniyoga*) was set forth by means of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyāna*).
Here, now, that which subserves the sacrifice and that which subserves the person are to be investigated.
What is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)?

Even the investigation concerning the nature of being enjoined—characterized by being the motivator (*prayojaka*) or the non-motivator (*aprayojaka*)—is likewise merely an inquiry into what is for the sake of the sacrifice and what is for the sake of the person.
How so? [The thought is: "I am for the sake of the sacrifice," whereas the primary [element] is for the sake of the person.
The injunction regarding the fruit (phalavidhi) pertains to the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha), whereas the explanatory passage (arthavāda) pertains to the purpose of the sacrifice (kratvartha).
That which is productive (prayojaka) pertains to the purpose of the person, while that which is non-productive (aprayojaka) pertains to the purpose of the sacrifice.
Therefore, it has been stated in the aphorism that there is a desire to know (jijñāsā) concerning both the purpose of the sacrifice and the purpose of the person.
In this regard, the words *atha* and *ataḥ* were explained in the first sūtra of the first chapter.
The word *atha* refers back to the previously mentioned definition of the application of the remainder (*śeṣaviniyoga*).
The word *ataḥ* refers back to the specific inquiry into what serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
That which is for the sake of ritual action (*kratu*) is *kratvartha*;

that which is for the sake of the person (*puruṣa*) is *puruṣārtha*. The desire to know (*jijñāsā*), though it is a means to [the knowledge], is understood in the same way, since "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*) is the wish to know.

This is the introductory aphorism concerning the inquiry into what subserves the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what subserves the person (*puruṣārtha*). The *Ṭupṭīkā* states: "Once the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) has been determined by the third [book], the specific distinction is considered—namely, 'which subserves the sacrifice and which subserves the person'—since the general principle has already been established previously.
This is just as, when the general extension (*sāmānyātideśa*) has been established by the tenth [book], the specific extension (*viśeṣātideśa*) is considered by the eleventh."
Such is the distinction of characteristics.

Alternatively, having begun with the words "Now, as for the equality or inequality of the purpose" (4.1.8.22), that which constitutes the relationship between the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*) is considered here as its unique feature.
And the author of the Bhāṣya, intending this very point, said regarding the sūtra "as for the equality or inequality of the purpose": "The scope of the third [chapter] has been transcended."

And in the fifth [section] (the first Sūtra), it is stated that "in this case, which is designated by its very uniqueness, the function characterized by being non-probative and not non-probative has occurred."

In this entire chapter, the nature of *prayukti* (the motive for performance) is investigated in the following forms: when *soma* serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), its performance is prompted by the sacrifice; when it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), its performance is prompted by the person; the number one (*ekatva*) and so forth are prompted by their respective injunctions; in cases such as the *sthālīpāka*, the portion consisting of the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) is prompted solely by the *apūrva*; when there is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), the placing of the *daśā* (fringe) and so forth is prompted by the rule of placement; if the hearing of "sinless verses" (*apāpaśloka*) and the like were injunctions of results, then qualities such as being made of *parṇa*-wood would be prompted by the result; however, if they are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), they are prompted by the sacrifice; since sacrifices like the *viśvajit* lack a stated result, the motive for performance is difficult to find, but if they do possess a result, that result becomes the prompter; in the case of the phrase "having performed the New and Full Moon sacrifices," if it were merely a prescription of time, the *Soma* sacrifice would not be prompted by the New and Full Moon sacrifices; in the *Sautrāmaṇī* and similar rites, if the anointing and so forth are primary, they are prompted by themselves; when acts such as the *anumantraṇa* and the gambling (*videvana*) are equally principal, the result alone is the prompter for all of them; and if the gambling and so forth are subordinate, they are prompted by the sacrifice. In this manner, the nature of *prayukti* is deliberated upon throughout the entire chapter.

The terms *kratvartha* (subserving the sacrifice) and *puruṣārtha* (subserving the person) are appropriate as the introductory sūtra (*pratijñāsūtra*) because they concern the nature of motivation (*prayukti*).

When it is generally the case that that which subserves the person is the motivator, the word *puruṣārtha* indicates the motivator by metaphorical extension (*lakṣaṇā*), while the word *kratvartha*, expressing its opposite, indicates the non-motivator; such is the construction of the sūtra.

The Prābhākaras, however, maintain that since there is another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for understanding subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*)—namely, "appropriation" (*upādāna*) and so forth, as indicated by scripture (*śruti*) and other criteria—the fourth chapter concerns subsidiarity, application (*prayukti*), qualification (*adhikāra*), and origin (*utpatti*), all of which are accessible through the means of knowledge called appropriation.
This is not correct. For it has been said:
"One should not engage in deliberation regarding whether [an act] is for the sake of the sacrifice or for the sake of the person."
And because it would otherwise be fruitless, it must be performed; let this [rite] be carried out when there is an application [of the mantra].
In some cases, this is due to deliberation; in some, by virtue of an injunction regarding the fruit;
and in some, it is said to be because of the application [of the word] in a direct injunction.

Section 1. Bhāṭṭa: Thus, since the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) has been established and defined in relation to that which possesses the subordinate (*śeṣin*), the state of being prompted (*prayojyatva*)—as defined by the prompter—is now being defined.

In this context, although the definition of subordination is not the cause for the definition of being prompted, this is because even in the absence of a cause (*nimitta*) and so forth, there is the state of being prompted by that [cause] in the case of the occasional (*naimittika*). Furthermore, while there is the status of being a subordinate (*aṅgatva*) in terms of being a factor (*kāraka*) toward the scattering of husks (*tuṣopavāpa*) due to its pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) in the status of being a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśakalpatva*), there is an absence of being prompted by that [scattering], and thus there is also an absence of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*).

Therefore, there is no causal relationship (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) based on a restriction of the delimiters (*avacchedaka*). Nevertheless, since the determination of its subservience (*tanniṣeṣatva-nirūpaṇa*) is useful for the determination of the production [of the injunction] regarding the consumption of curd and so forth (*dadhyāyanādi-niyoga*), and because the determination of subsidiarity (*aṅgatva-nirūpaṇa*) is the cause for that determination by way of common substratum (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*), the logical connection (*saṅgati*) is established. Here, the state of being prompted (*prayojyatva*) is determined in some cases through the investigation of what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), in some cases through the door of the injunction (*vidhi*), and in some cases directly; thus, it is characterized as being prompted, for the sake of the sacrifice, or for the sake of the person.
The subject matter of this chapter is precisely the definition of that which subserves the ritual (*kratvartha*) and that which subserves the person (*puruṣārtha*).

Although the distinction between what subserves the ritual and what subserves the person is established in the third book (*adhyāya*), it is examined here as residing within specific examples for the purpose of establishing the application (*prayojya*); such is the distinction.

This is the definition of *kratvartha* and *puruṣārtha* according to the Bhāṭṭa school.

Commentary: One must state the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of what constitutes that which is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) and what constitutes that which is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
For in this way, comprehension is more concise; whereas in the case of an instruction involving "questioning and striking" (*pṛṣṭhākoṭi*), it would be more cumbersome. [To explain:

when it is necessary to touch and demonstrate each of many items lying on the ground, one must perform the "striking" (*ākoṭa*)—that is, the bending or turning over—of the questioned item; thus, there is prolixity.
To this it is said:

That object in which a person finds pleasure—that is, that thing in which a person’s pleasure arises—is the *puruṣārtha* (the human end). Why? Because the desire for it is characterized by its being an object of pursuit.
The desire for that [object] arises from the purposeful object itself, not from the scripture.
For the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) is understood from the scripture, and not otherwise.
Indeed, human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) is inseparable from pleasure and the means to pleasure; that is human purpose.

When *puruṣārtha* (that which pertains to the person) has been defined, its opposite—*kratvartha* (that which pertains to the sacrifice)—is thereby established as the definition of *kratvartha*. [The Bhāṣya] objects: "That ritual act (*padārtha*) in which, when performed, pleasure arises for the person (characterized by heaven and so forth)—that is the *puruṣārtha* act (such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa).
The desire for that [pleasure] is characterized by the purpose (*arthalakṣaṇā*)."

What is meant? If it is said that performance [of rites] is due to the desire for a result, that is incorrect; for a person does not engage in those acts which serve the purpose of the sacrifice solely by force of an injunction. [The author] replies: True.

In both cases—those pertaining to the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and those pertaining to the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*)—the relationship between the end and the means is Vedic. However, regarding the purpose of the person, the employment of the means occurs through desire, not by necessity; whereas regarding the purpose of the sacrifice, it occurs even against one's will, by necessity. Therefore, with reference to the employment of the means, it was stated: "The desire for that [result] is indicated by the purpose itself" (*tasya lipsā arthalakṣaṇā*).

Since it causes suffering, how can sacrifice be for the sake of man? It has been stated that the means is for the sake of man because of its inseparable connection with the end to be accomplished. Rite (*krama*) consists of both forms: that which is for the sake of the ritual and that which is for the sake of man.
Because of its true nature, there is the establishment of its being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).

Furthermore, regarding prohibitions for the sake of the sacrifice, they function as such because, according to the method stated, their status as things to be enjoined is for the purpose of avoiding defects in the sacrifice; it is not otherwise.

And in cases such as "not at the Atirātra," since the excellence of the sacrifice (*ṛtusādguṇya*) remains the objective even when produced by other auxiliary elements, the status [of the prohibition] as being for the sake of the sacrifice is not lost with respect to the absence of taking the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.
Thus, everything regarding the status of being the object of an injunction for permission for the sake of the sacrifice is consistent.
Maṇḍana says: "The human goal is that which is dear to man.
Śaṅkara says: "[This is] the definition of the human goal."

Su. Pṛ. 1067. Sequence (krama) is prescribed as a qualifier of the action (kriyā). Vi. 5.1.1, Varṇaka 2: There is no sequence whatsoever regulated by the order of recitation (pāṭha) and so forth in the performance of optional (kāmya) and occasional (naimittika) rites;
they are to be understood according to desire and according to the occasion.

Bhāṣya 5.1.12.23–36. *Krama* (sequence) is contiguity (*ānantarya*) consisting in the state of being immediately followed. This is related to a single counter-correlative and resides in a single locus.
For example, in the statement "Having made the *veda*, he makes the *vedi*," the contiguity relative to the making of the *veda* resides in the making of the *vedi*.

And here, since the status of being a *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice is also a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *soma* sacrifice, the qualification "immediately preceding" (*avyavahita*) is added for the purpose of excluding that.
In this context, the mere fact of occurring prior to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* is intended to establish the application of the suffix *-kvā*; however, "immediacy" is not required.

Nor does the injunction for the *soma* sacrifice depend upon that [priority], such that it would otherwise result in a different conclusion; for the injunction for the *soma* sacrifice depends on a sequence relative to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices prescribed by a separate performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*).

Therefore, in this context, only the state of being subsequent (*uttarakālatva*) is the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), not the sequence (*krama*). Furthermore, in all cases, sequence is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the subsequent constituent element (*padārtha*), because it is only there that the requirement arises: "What [element] is to be performed after me? It is not, however, an auxiliary to the preceding constituent element, as there is no such requirement as "What constituent element is to be performed after me?"—for the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites themselves serve as the qualification of the sequence by virtue of their prior occurrence. By this, the claim of certain [scholars] that sequence—which consists of the meaning of both parts—is apprehended from two constituent elements is refuted, due to a lack of evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*).
Alternatively, in cases such as "the first consumption" (*aprathamabhakṣaḥ*), primacy (*prāthamya*) is indeed a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the preceding ritual act.

Order (*krama*) is characterized by a collection of precedences and succeedances (*paurvāparya*) residing in multiple ritual acts, expressed as "after each respective act, that [subsequent one] is performed in that manner.

This position stated in the root-text is disregarded because it is not directly expressed by words (*aśābdatvāt*); furthermore, in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), when even a single ritual act is omitted, the collection of precedences and succeedances residing in all those acts becomes impossible, and there would be no resulting deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) even if the performance were carried out in a different sequence. Thus, it is set aside.
Since this sequence culminates in the purpose (*prayojana*), its commencement follows the determination of that purpose.

Regarding the desire to know that purpose, there are six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) beginning with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Their definitions will be stated on the occasion of discussing each respective one.

In this regard, the followers of the *Mūla* maintain that the scriptural order (*śrauta-krama*) is prescribed by the rule of origin (*utpatti-vidhi*), whereas the order based on meaning (*ārtha-krama*) and so forth is prescribed solely by the rule of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*).

However, in reality, in cases of scriptural order, the sequence is established by the word "and" (*ca*) and so forth; once the elements have been produced, their application (*viniyoga*) is determined by the sentence (*vākya*).
In another sequence, however, that which has arisen through meaning and so forth is applied by means of a direct statement established through context and other criteria;
in all practical applications, this occurs just like other subsidiary elements, by means of the injunction for performance itself.
This will be clarified in various places.
And it is logical that even *krama* (sequence) may be enjoined as a qualification of a ritual category (*padārtha*), just like substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth.
Bhāṭṭa 5.1.1, p. 153. *Krama* is a specific kind of extension, or rather, it consists of priority and posteriority.

In this regard, there are six means of proof (*pramāṇa*) known as: direct statement (*śruti*), meaning (*artha*), textual order (*pāṭha*), position (*sthāna*), the principal (*mukhya*), and procedure (*pravṛtti*).
In this context, *śruti* (direct scriptural statement) is a word whose primary purport is sequence (*krama*).
That [sequence] is of two kinds: that which has pure sequence as its purport, and that which has a ritual act qualified by that [sequence] as its purport.

Among these, "Having made the *veda*, one makes the *vedi*" is an example of that which has pure sequence as its purport, because the making of the *vedi* and so forth have already been enjoined by another scriptural statement.

The statement, "The first portion is for the one who utters *vaṣaṭ*," refers to an object qualified by its sequence, because it is impossible to enjoin mere sequence while restating the act of consuming, for fear of violating the principle of single-sentence unity (*ekaprasaratā*).
This direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is stronger than other means of proof, since those others function as authorities for sequence only by way of interpreting verbal expressions.

For this very reason, although the Āśvina cup is mentioned in the third position according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), it is stated that it is drawn in the tenth position because of the scriptural injunction: "The Āśvina is drawn as the tenth. However, where the determination [of order] is based on a specific purpose, that is *ārthakrama* (order based on purpose), as in the case of the *āghāra* libation and the *agnihotra* oblation.
For in this case, where the heating and cooking of the sacrificial ladles (*agnihotra-havanyādi*) for the purpose of the oblation (*homārtha*) is performed first by virtue of its practical necessity,
this [order] prevails over the order of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).

For if one were to perform the actions according to the order of the text, there would be a subversion of the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) and a subversion of its purpose, resulting in a merely transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*) effect.
And it would be so;
for there is no visible purpose served by performing [the act] immediately after the oblation.
The sequence of sentences that convey the constituent elements of the ritual is the "sequence of recitation" (pāṭhakrama).
Therefore, a sequence of word-meanings is adopted;

for in whatever order the sentences are recited, in that very same order they are studied and produce the comprehension of meaning, and from the performance of the word-meanings according to that comprehension of meaning [the ritual result follows]. And that recitation is of two kinds.
There are two types of textual order: the order of the mantra-text (*mantrapāṭha*) and the order of the Brāhmaṇa-text (*brāhmaṇapāṭha*).

Among these, the sequence that is adopted for the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) dedicated to Agni and Agni-Soma, according to the sequence of their respective *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, is based on the mantra-text.

Furthermore, this mantra-text is more authoritative than the Brāhmaṇa-text, because in the actual performance of the ritual, the mantra-sentence is more intimately connected (*antaraṅga*) than the Brāhmaṇa-sentence.

For the statement of a Brāhmaṇa fulfills its purpose by instructing "this is to be done in this manner" even outside of the actual performance; thus, it is not logically required again at the time of performance.
On the other hand, we shall explain that mantras have no other purpose than to remind one of the objects associated with the performance.

Therefore, since the sequence of the ritual performance depends upon the sequence of the [Brāhmaṇa] form, and since that sequence depends upon the sequence of the mantras, the recitation of the mantras is more internal and consequently far more powerful than the other.

For this very reason, regarding the two offerings to Agni and to Agni-Soma, although the order in which they appear in the Brāhmaṇa text places the Agnīṣomīya first and the Āgneya second, that sequence is set aside; rather, it is stated that the performance of the Āgneya comes first, followed by the Agnīṣomīya.

As for the Prayājas, the order established by the sequence of their prescriptive sentences—such as "He offers to the Samidhs" and "He offers to Tanūnapāt"—is what constitutes the order of the Brāhmaṇa text.

And here, although the Brāhmaṇa passages have fulfilled their purpose by enjoining the meaning [of the ritual], nevertheless, because there is no other means for the subjects to remember it, those very passages are accepted as the means of recollection.
Thus, they produce the remembrance of the meaning in the same order in which they were studied; therefore, it is logical that their performance should follow that very same order.

Furthermore, just as mantras serve as reminders of the actual facts in rites performed silently (*tūṣṇīṃvihita*), their sequence follows the order of the Brāhmaṇa text because they alone serve to remind one of the matters connected with the performance. The example of the *praiṣa* (directions) is cited as a hypothetical consideration (*kṛtvācintā*), since the sentences of the Brāhmaṇa do not themselves serve to remind one of the matters connected with the performance.

As the authors of the Vārttika state in the section on Arthavādas: "Sentences such as those for the *praiṣas*, having fulfilled their purpose by conveying meaning, do not attain the status of being motivators (*prayojaka*) even when their own verbal form is perceived."
Therefore, for rites accompanied by mantras, the order is according to the sequence of the mantra-text; however, for rites without mantras, the order is solely from the sequence of the Brāhmaṇa-text.

As for "order" (krama): when various items belonging to different locations in the archetype (*prakṛti*) must be performed at a single location in the modified rite (*vikṛti*) due to a scriptural injunction, that which is performed at its own location first, followed by the other two—this order is called "order by position" (*sthānakrama*).
"Place" (*sthāna*) means "proximity.

For when a rite is performed in a certain location, that very rite which was previously performed in relation to the preceding constituent element becomes proximate first; thus, its performance first is logical.

Therefore, in the *sādyaska* sacrifice, although the *agnīṣomīya*, *savanīya*, and *ānubandhya* animals are to be performed together at the place of the *savanīya*, the performance of the two *savanīya* animals comes first. This is because, at that location, immediately after the taking of the *āśvina* cup, the *savanīya* alone is proximate, while the other two follow later.
For the place of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice follows immediately after the drawing of the *āśvina* cup;

because in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is prescribed that "having drawn the *āśvina* cup, having bound the sacrificial post with the three-fold cord, one dedicates the *āgneya savanīya* animal"—thus it is performed immediately after the drawing of the *āśvina* cup.

And so, in the *sādyaska* sacrifice as well, once the *āśvina* cup has been drawn, the *savanīya* itself becomes present; therefore, its performance first on account of its position is proper, while the other two follow afterwards.
The sequence of subsidiaries that is adopted according to the sequence of the primary acts is called the *mukhyakrama* (sequence of the principal).

For if the subsidiaries are performed in the very same order as the primary acts are performed, then all of them maintain an equal distance from their respective primaries; however, if they were performed out of that order, some subsidiaries would be excessively separated from their primaries, while others would have no separation at all. This is improper, as it would result in the subversion of the "concomitance" (*sāhitya*) understood through the injunction for performance (*prayogavidhi*).
Therefore, the order of the principal acts is also the cause for the order of the subsidiaries.

For this very reason, the sprinkling of the *āgneya* oblation is performed first with the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings, and subsequently that of the *aindra* curds, because of the sequential order of the *āgneya* sacrifice and the *aindra* sacrifice.

Consequently, the sequence—first the sprinkling of the *āgneya* offering, then the *aindra* offering, then the *āgneya* sacrifice, and finally the *aindra* sacrifice—is established by the order of the principals (*mukhyakrama*).
Therefore, it is logical that the sequence for the sprinkling with the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings follows the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*).
Furthermore, this *mukhyakrama* is weaker than the order of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).
For *mukhyakrama* involves a delayed comprehension, as it depends upon the comprehension of the sequence of the principal acts, which in turn requires reliance on other means of knowledge.

The order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), however, is stronger because it depends solely on the sequence of the recited text, which is independent [of other factors], and thus does not involve such [delayed] comprehension.

For this very reason, although the *āgneya*, *upāṃśuyāja*, and *agnīṣomīya* offerings are performed in that sequence, the pouring of the clarified butter for the *upāṃśuyāja* is not performed first according to the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), because that is weaker; rather, it is performed later according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), because that is more powerful.

And this order of principal elements (mukhyakrama) is stronger than the order of performance (pravṛttikrama). For if the order of performance were adopted, there would be a great distance from the primary act for many subordinate elements; whereas if this [order of principal elements] is adopted, there is proximity.

For example, in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, first comes the performance of the Āgneya [offering], and then the Sāṃnāyya. Some of its subsidiary elements (dharmas) are performed even earlier. In that context, if one were to follow the order of procedure (*pravṛttikrama*) and perform all those subsidiary elements first, then the Āgneya subsidiaries, then the Āgneya performance itself, and finally the Sāṃnāyya performance, then there would be a separation (*viprakarṣa*) of those subsidiary elements from their own primary rites by two stages: namely, by the Āgneya subsidiaries and by the performance of the Āgneya itself.

However, when some of the *sāṃnāyya* subsidiaries are performed first, yet all others are performed immediately after the *āgneya* subsidiaries by following the order of the principal rites (*mukhyakrama*), then there is a separation of only one dissimilar element between all the *āgneya* and *sāṃnāyya* subsidiaries; for the *āgneya* subsidiaries are separated from their own principal rite only by the performance of the *āgneya* itself. Thus, there is no excessive remoteness (*viprakarṣa*). Therefore, the order of the principal rites (*mukhyakrama*) is stronger than the order of performance (*pravṛttikrama*).

When primary acts are to be performed together, and their constituent parts (aṅgas) must be executed through repetition, the sequence of the second and subsequent parts that follows the order of the items already performed is called *pravṛttikrama* (the order of commencement).
This is as seen in the case of the *prājāpatya* offerings.

For the *prājāpatyas* are enjoined to be performed at one time along with their respective accessories by the sentence, "Having performed the *vaiśvadeva*, they proceed with the *prājāpatyas*," where the use of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) indicates their status as the object of the action.
Therefore, the coordination of those primary acts and their subsidiaries, such as the preparation of the implements and so forth, must be accomplished.

Consequently, in the Prājāpatya sacrifices, after performing one ritual act (such as the preparation of the implements) in common for all, the second ritual act is to be performed. In that regard, the performance of the first ritual act should be commenced from any one animal according to one's preference.
The second category of items, however, must be performed in the very same sequence in which the first was performed.

Thus it is established that the sequence of the second set of items, which follows from the sequence of the first set of items already performed, is called the *pravṛttikrama* (sequence of performance).
In this way, the investigation into the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) has been briefly defined according to its sixfold form of sequence.

Bhāṣya 7.1.2.1, p. 1524: *Krama* (order) exists by virtue of the proximity of recitation (*pāṭhasādeśya*), because even when the ritual actions and the mantras—which serve as mutual auxiliaries—are being considered by means of the Brāhmaṇas and other texts, [namely] that the mantras studied in the *Mantra-saṃhitā* act as auxiliaries to the rituals, and the rituals are the objects of assistance for the mantras; and because, as these are reflected upon starting from the beginning, the rituals and mantras studied in the first section revolve in the mind one with another, and those studied in the second section likewise revolve with one another; thus, since this sequence cannot be denied due to its being self-evident to everyone, order is established through the proximity of recitation.

Like direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), and context (*prakaraṇa*), sequence (*krama*) also serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the relationship between subsidiary and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).
Sequence (*krama*), position (*sthāna*), and proximity (*saṃnidhi*) are synonyms,
because they share the common characteristic of being a location (*deśa*).
In certain cases, the location is common to both.
In some cases, both [mantras] are recited in the same location;
by this, the relationship of principal and subordinate (aṅgāṅgibhāva) between each pair is established.
For example, in the recitation of the consecratory mantras (anumantraṇamantra) for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, "agner aham" is recited as the first, and "dadhir asi" is recited as the second.
In that very same order, there is the rule that first comes the Āgneya sacrifice, and then the Upāṃśuyāja.
This is just as it is stated in grammar: "The designation of equals follows their respective order.

And so, according to the rule *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ*, the substitutes *ay*, *av*, *āy*, and *āv* occur in place of *e*, *o*, *ai*, and *au* respectively when followed by *a*; in the same way, this is the sequence of positions.

Some maintain that sequence (*krama*) is a distinct category (*padārtha*), because it resides in multiple things and is perceived as a conjunction. (Kaṇikā, p. 421). Sequence, which is synonymous with order (*sādeya*) or position (*sthāna*), is twofold: sequence of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeya*) and sequence of recitation (*pāṭha-sādeya*).
Furthermore, sequence of recitation is also twofold: [namely] sequential recitation (*yathākrama-pāṭha*)...
And "proximity" (saṃnidhi) as a mode of recitation— these three consist of both mutual expectancy and expectancy for the subordinate element alone.
Thus, the order [of application] is sixfold.
This very [principle] is the regulator (*viniyojaka*) known by the synonym "position" (*sthāna*).

Where one [act] is enjoined as having a fruit, and another within its own vicinity is a non-fructifying preparatory act (*ārambhakāraka*) prescribed by way of a general injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*), both must be performed independently at the same time because of their respective scriptural statements. In that case, the status of being a subordinate member (*aṅgatva*) of the fruit-bearing [act] belongs to that non-fructifying one, due to the ease of performance (*anuṣṭhānasādeśya*).

And that [order] is established by mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) when there is no prior injunction (*apūrva*) because it is a *darvihoma* possessing a fruit; however, in the case of a modification (*vikṛti*), it is established by one-sided expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*).

Where, in the Brāhmaṇa and the mantra, the injunctions for the primary acts—which have various fruits—and the injunctions for the recitation of mantras such as the *japa* occur in that very same sequence, there the order of those respective injunctions is determined by the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*) itself, since they establish the position of the respective primary injunctions.
For order (*krama*) is indeed immediate succession (*ānantarya*), or it may be regulated by the sequence [of the text].
The primary injunction for the utterance of those respective mantras is established solely by the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).

Here too, if it takes the form of a *darvī-homa* (ladle-offering) and so forth, there is a mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*); however, if it takes the form of a modification (*vikṛti*), there is expectancy of only one of the two.

Furthermore, the status of the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) as modifications is due to their being recited in proximity (*saṃnidhi-pāṭha*), since they are not enjoined by any other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Although there can be no example of "mutual requirement" (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) acting as a means of application (*viniyojaka*), nevertheless, because it serves that purpose by bringing to mind a specific *apūrva* and so forth, it is conventionally designated as a "means of application.
Thus, the applicatory power of "order" (*krama*) is established.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is set aside by the purpose (*prayojana*) and the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
