The rule of sequence, however, is now considered. Or rather: in the absence of the six means of establishing sequence, there is no fixed order.

This is as in the case of the mantras for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, which are recited in various different branches (*śākhā*), such as "I gratify Vasantam, the first of the seasons," and so on, as well as "One for me," and so forth.

Bhāṣya 5.1.13: "The means of proof for those things that indicate sequence are sixfold: direct statement (śruti), meaning (artha), textual order (pāṭha), principal action (mukhya), and commencement (pravṛtti). Maṇi, p. 13. Those things which are to be commenced must be undertaken starting from the first.
Bhāṣya 10.1.16: "Oṃ. When parts [of a word] are not apprehended due to sequential order, there is the taking up of the first and the elision of the others.
10.1.16–6: "Oṃ. This is an exception to the sequential application [stated in 3.1.123]: 'Proximity and the subsequent injunction [govern the connection].'"

Bhāṣya 3.1.124–25: "Oṃ, a penance may indeed be performed for the reversal of the sequence [in the case of the animal sacrifice to Agni-Soma and the sacrificial cake], but there is no repetition [of the rite] as a penance. If so, must a penance be performed? It is performed: one offers the 'all-penance' oblation with the mantra 'ayāś cāgne...'.
Or rather, because it is incidental, there is an absence of penance. Bhāṣya 1.2.14: "Oṃ, the principle of the reversal of sequence."

This [principle] applies where there is a reversal or inversion of the sequence regarding the distinction between what precedes and what follows. *Sāhasī* 410. "Or rather, the specific sequence is understood through the sentence in the case of the initiations in a *sattra* sacrifice. *Vi.* 5.1.1, Section 3. If it is argued that "with respect to sequence, the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) is stronger, because the determination of sequence everywhere depends upon the injunction of performance," [the reply is: no, because the injunction of performance depends upon the attainment of the constituent elements (*padārtha*), and even in that regard, it depends upon this very [sequence].
Because it subsists on the injunctions [of the *codaka*], the application-injunction (*prayogavidhi*) is stronger.
Regarding Order (*krama*) and Name (*samākhyā*): 1509. The Section on Order (*kramādhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the two [grounds of] *krama* (order) and *samākhyā* (name): in the case of *krama*, the cause for the mutual application of the subordinate (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*) is indeed established by the Veda through similarity of location.
For everywhere, a connection is conceived by means of some common location.
However, we do not perceive any similarity of location established by the Veda belonging to that which possesses a name, by which a possibility of orientation toward a connection might arise.

Or [it is said]: Vārttika 3.1.7.4, page 824. *Oṃ*. The section on Order (*kramādhikaraṇa*). Order (*krama*) is also a means of authority (*pramāṇa*) for application (*viniyoga*). And order [is determined] by similarity of location (*deśasāmānyāt*).
Commentary: Now, are these the only causes for application (*viniyoga*)? No, it is said.
What else? Order (*krama*) as well, due to similarity of position (*deśasāmānya*).
When things that possess order are taught in a sequence, an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) toward a particular property is inferred for each item at its respective turn.
"When there is a mutual expectancy, there is syntactic unity; therefore, from that [expectancy] follows the application.
What is the example here, and what is the purpose?

In the consecratory formulas (*anumantraṇa*) prescribed for sacrifices performed in sequential order, the mantra "O butter, you are named *adhi*" is recited in the sequence of the *upāṃśuyāja*. Having fulfilled its expectancy and thereby forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with it, that mantra deserves to be applied to that very sacrifice.

Likewise, there is a rite dedicated to Indra and Agni for one who has departed from his kin—meaning one whose kinsmen (*sajāta*, i.e., relatives) have gone into opposition (*viyāta*). Such a person is one who possesses rivals (*bhrātṛvyavat*).

The pair of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for that [sacrifice] is also traditionally handed down: one pair dedicated to Indra and Agni is "O Indra and Agni, the luminous realms of heaven... forward from the people," and another is "O Indra and Agni, the ninety forts... you two overcame Vṛtra.

Since the application [of these verses] is established there by means of their indicative power (*liṅga*), a specific application occurs: the former pair belongs to the first offering to Indra and Agni, and the latter to the second.
This is the example and its purpose.
Or rather—the introduction of both "order" (*krama*) and "name" (*samākhyā*) should also be made here, as with "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) and the others:
"In that regard, order is held to be of two kinds: characterized by spatial proximity (*deśasāmānya*) and proximity of recitation (*pāṭhasādeśya*). These are the causes for application (*viniyoga*)."
Even without identity of location for the performance, in whatever extent of space the primary rite (*pradhāna*) is recited in the Brāhmaṇa, the mantra occupies that very same extent.

Thus, at the time of requiring the relationship between the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the primary (*aṅgin*), proximity occurs in the intellect by virtue of occupying the same location, according to the principle of corresponding order (*yathāsaṃkhyanyāya*).
For one necessarily examines the unbroken sequence of the mantra for the first primary rite, beginning from the very start of the collection of mantras (*mantrasāmnāya*).
Consequently, the very first mantra comes first to the heart;
and since there is no reason for bypassing it, that one alone is selected.
Likewise, for a mantra that requires a principal (śeṣin), through this very process, its connection is established with the first principal.
Consequently, because that [first mantra] is satisfied [by its own object], the second and subsequent mantras must likewise be connected with the second and subsequent [offerings] respectively.

In that regard, since the *anumantraṇa* mantras for the *Āgneya* and other offerings are established as restricted by the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the *Āgneya* and so forth, he cites another example of such indicative power from the sequence of the *Upāṃśuyāja*: "Thou art named Dadhi.
[Objection: But surely, its application to all [offerings] is not understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*), and that [context] is more powerful [than indicative power].
In this case as well, the application [of the mantra] would follow.
Regarding this, some say:
because of the mention of the *upāṃśuyāja*, the curd is also included; therefore, that [curd] is what is being referred to.
However, it can be argued that the sequence [of the mantra] must indeed be accepted as subordinate, because it contradicts both the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*).

For the subsidiary nature of the remainder applies to all purposes, since it is obtained through its connection with each primary act; thus, it cannot be set aside by what is contained within the context. To this, the following reply is given: as for the other principals, such as the Āgneya and others, they do not require this [mantra], because they are already secured by other mantras that possess clear indicative marks and are established by both sequence and context.
Nor is it an option (*vikalpa*), because of the disparity arising from the fact that [the latter] has an indistinct indicative mark (*liṅga*).
If it is argued that it is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the eight purposes, we say no;
for it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) by means of the inspection of the sacrifice currently under performance.
Even though there are eight purposes, since there is another alternative for those that are independent, one does not resort to a combination (samuccaya).
Being disregarded by the Āgneya and other offerings which have already achieved their purpose, it would only be performed again through those very same [offerings] out of necessity;
however, it does have an alternative: namely, the Upāṃśuyāja.
Furthermore: "Nor indeed does a ritual procedure apply to those whose indicative marks (*liṅga*) are not recognized.
And the capacity of the word *asi* is withdrawn by its proximity [to other words].
The phrase 'Thou art named Dadhi' has an unclear indicative mark (*aspaṣṭaliṅga*)."
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to apply such a [general] context [to this specific case].

However, because these words [beginning with "ati"] have as their object the referent of *yuṣmad* (the second person), they denote what is proximate or present before one, and nothing else. Since the Upāṃśuyāja is proximate and present before one, the capacity of the expression is understood through the order [of the ritual] to have the Upāṃśuyāja as its object.
And thus, the context is indeed set aside by the indicative mark (liṅga);
this much has been explained regarding the section on the optional *yājyā* verses.
Furthermore, the sequence of performance regarding the place will also apply to the duties of the animal sacrifice (*paśudharma*) because they are for the sake of the *agnīṣomīya*.

Soma: The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: "In the application [of mantras] according to order, the authority is the commonality of place; therefore, since application is possible through the sequence of expectancy and so forth.
This concludes the section on Order (Kramādhikaraṇa). Viśvarūpa states: "Is the mantra, which has curd as its cause, to be applied as a subsidiary to the act of mixing, or not?"
Because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth are common [to many], and because there is an absence of a name (*nāmadheya*), there is no status as a subsidiary (*anaṅgatā*).
Furthermore, in this case, the lack of knowledge regarding the sequence of both mantras and ritual acts is observed.

Just as with the *prakriyā* (contextual procedure), sequence (*krama*) is an authoritative means of proof; therefore, subsidiarity arises through "correspondence according to number" (*yathāsaṃkhya*).

(He analyzes the order: "Order consists in occupying the same location, and it arises from both textual recitation and meaning. From textual recitation, there is order according to numerical sequence (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) and proximity (*saṃnidhi*). Regarding numerical sequence, it is as [assigned] given; regarding proximity, the view is that it applies to the vessels for the *sānnāyya* offering, as in the case of the mantra 'Be purified' (*śundhadhvam*)."
"Furthermore, this [act] would be of the nature of animal sacrifice (paśudharma) because it is performed by one who is about to sacrifice (īyate).
Thus, the threefold nature of the sequence (krama) is to be understood.
For the Bhāṭṭa, this is not a fifth means of proof for subsidiarity (aṅgatva)."
And that [proximity] consists in the coexistence of two sentence-meanings that are unfit to be related as "the manner of performance" (*itikartavyatā*). This unfitness is twofold:

in some cases, due to the absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), as for instance in the case of the *upahoma*s and so forth in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because the sacrifice has no further expectancy since it is already satisfied by the archetypal subsidiaries (*prākṛtāṅga*) whose assistance is already established.
In some cases, [the sequence] is due to the absence of an operative function, as in the case of mantras for recitation (*japa*) and the like.

Furthermore, since it would follow that even proximity to sacrifices and so forth would lack such [sequence] when a single sentence is possible, the sequence belongs solely to the meaning of the sentence.
This qualification is intended to exclude the possibility that *prayāja* offerings and the like would fall under the scope of "position" (*sthāna*).

And that [authoritativeness], which is synonymous with acceptability (*sādeyatā*), is of two kinds: acceptability through textual recitation (*pāṭhādeya*) and acceptability through performance (*anuṣṭhānasādeyya*).
The first is twofold: sequential recitation (*yathākramapāṭha*) and contiguous recitation (*saṃnidhipāṭha*).
Each of these three is further twofold: by way of mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) and by way of one-sided expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*).
In this context, the primary expectancy that constitutes "expectancy for both" is twofold, being distinct from the expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Among these, by virtue of the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras associated with optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) are subsidiary to those optional sacrifices.

However, by virtue of proximity (*saṃnidhi*), the mantra "śundhadhvam" (be purified), which is recited in the vicinity of the injunction for the cleansing of the *sānnāyya* vessels, is subsidiary to that act.
However, regarding the ease of performance (*anuṣṭhānasaukarya*), the properties of the animal sacrifice (*paśudharma*) belong to the right wing (*dakṣapakṣatva*).

Even though these [properties] are applied through other means of proof such as indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, and since sequence (*krama*) and the rest possess authority for subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) merely by indicating the intended meaning— namely, the characterization of being a means to an unseen result (*apūrva*)— nevertheless, distinct examples for each of the six types of sequence should be inferred from the *Kaustubha*.

In this context, regarding all six types of order (*krama*), in the case of that which assists remotely (*ārādupakāraka*), the capacity to establish a *prakaraṇa* (context) exists because the expectancy for the "how-to" (*itikartavyatā-ākāṅkṣā*) must be postulated.

Even in cases where mantras and the like assist independently of one another, although the mantra produces the sacrifice by its own nature, it does not produce it when merely restricted by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, the postulation of a *prakaraṇa*—consisting of the "how-to" in the form of generating a fitness residing in the instrument—is absolutely necessary.
For this very reason, it is weaker than those [other types of order].

However, regarding the sixfold order, since it is characterized by mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*), whereas the other orders are characterized by one-sided expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*), even there, because the proximity of the injunction (*vidhisaṃnidhāna*)—which facilitates the performance according to the order of recitation—is more immediately manifest than the other two, proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) possesses greater force between those two, due to factors such as being contained within the same textual unit (*ekagranthasthatva*). This and other points should be examined in the *Kaustubha*. Maṇḍana says: "There is application (*viniyoga*) by way of order.
Śaṅkara says: "And order may be the applicator (*viniyoktṛ*)."

"Just as here, in the secondary context (*gauṇaprakaraṇa*) known as the *mahāvikāra*, the name (*samākhyā*) and proximity (*saṃnidhi*) are set aside so that the cleansing does not apply to all vessels associated with the rite, so too has this been explained in the section on Order (*krama*) itself.

(Kau. 313|144, p. 366). [This is] the section on the non-restriction by order (*kramāniyāmādhikaraṇa*). It should be considered and examined whether, in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the duties of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) such as the *prayāja*s and others [apply]."
The favoring of the sequence is primary; that of the meters is secondary. Therefore, it should be sung upon each triplet of verses.
(Regarding the Mādhyandina-pavamāna in the Ekatrika sacrifice:
Mānava Śrautasūtra 10.1.12 states that the determination of the sequence among all ritual elements is accomplished by the order of their recitation in the text.
VI. 5|1|16. Purchase (*kraya*) is for the purpose of obtaining the *soma* which is the means of accomplishing the sacrifice.
Vārttika 3|1|6|12, p. 698. The purchase of the *soma* is enjoined in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, even though [the sacrificer] already possesses *soma*.

Bhāṣya 6|8|7|26–27. For it has been stated in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* (3|1|6) that the purchase, being connected with that which is being enjoined, does not qualify the substance being conjoined with a quality.
Vārttika 3.1.7.14, p. 715: There are two acts of purchase; one is caused by the purpose [of the sacrifice], and the other is caused by the word.
Among these, that caused by the word is the conversation with the Soma-sellers prior to the ritual efforts, at the time of procuring the means for accomplishing the sacrifice.
And the offering of the price is that which is caused by the purpose.
Bhāṣya 11.2.14–15: Purchases are distinct due to differences in the means, the substance, and the quality.
Bhaṭṭa 3.1.6: The quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) is to be applied only to the purchase, not to the entire context.
Bhāṣya 3.1.6.12, p. 696: There is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the substances for purchase pertaining to the Soma.
Bhāṣya 11.2.13–15: The leading of the *somakrayaṇī* cow is prompted by the purchase [of Soma], not by the footstep [offering] in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Vārttika 4.1.10.125: The connection with the purchase is obtained through the delimitation of the substance of the wild animal.
Vārttika 3.1.2.13, p. 752: The statement "He purchases with ten" has the purpose of enjoining a combination of purchases.

Bhāṭṭa 3.1.6: The primary act of purchasing is for the sake of the *soma*; likewise, even the ritual action is not devoid of the *soma*-dharma, remaining equal [in application] even when substitutes such as *pūtīka* are prescribed.
Bhāṣya 3.6.15.40: In the Sādyaska sacrifice, the purchase-price for Soma prescribed as a three-year-old bull sublates all the original articles of purchase.
Regarding the purchase-price for wine in the Sautrāmaṇī: "He purchases the purchasable [wine] with lead" (Bhāṣya 8.2.1.4).
However, there would be an option among the various articles of purchase because they serve the same purpose.
In the case of the ten substances for the purchase of Soma mentioned in such passages as "He purchases with a cow" and "He purchases with gold," there would be an option;
one might purchase with any single one of them,
because they serve the same purpose— that is, because they perform the same function.
Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Or rather, there is a combination (*samuccaya*), because [the quality] inheres in the substance at the time of performance.
The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie view.
There is no option (*vikalpa*) among the substances used for purchase, but rather their combination (*samuccaya*).

In the performance of the act of purchasing, the bowing down to the seller must be performed; this is because there is a conjunction of the substances, and such conjunction is necessary, since it is possible to satisfy the seller with even a single substance or others.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) according to the injunction.

The ten substances are: 1) a one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī gauḥ*), 2) gold (*hiraṇya*), 3) a goat (*ajā*), 4) a milch-cow (*dhenu*), 5) its calf (*tadvatsa*), 6) a bull (*ṛṣabha*), 7) an ox (*anaḍvān*), 8–9) a pair of cattle (*mithunau gāvau*), and 10) a garment (*vāsaḥ*).
And [the scripture] demonstrates this combination.

"He buys him with ten; the Virāj consists of ten syllables; he thus attains the Virāj"—this restatement of the purchase shows the combination (*samuccaya*) of the substances used for the purchase of Soma.
Therefore, combination is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In the section beginning "But there should be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the means of purchase, because they serve a single purpose," the combination of cows and other items for the purchase of Soma was established by logical reasoning.
This is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of two classes [of substances].

Bāla. pṛ. 166. Regarding the purchase (*krayaṇa*), however, there is an option (*vikalpa*) because they serve a single purpose; by the sūtra "In the case of purchases, there should be an option" (the better reading being "there is an option among the purchases"), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is an option among the substances used as means for the purchase of Soma.
Su. pṛ. 1103. This refers to the purchases when the distinction between separate acts of purchase is accepted.
This is because of the consequence of the [present] topic being subsumed under the previous one.

For there, having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that there should be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the substances such as goats and so forth which are the means for purchasing [Soma], the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) will be established as follows: since the substances are connected in the performance of the Soma-purchase, there is indeed a combination (*samuccaya*).

Because the primary concern is the task at hand, and considering the ease of execution, the injunctions regarding the substances are understood as being mutually dependent; therefore, there is a combination.

*Vārttika* on *Pāṇini* 3.1.6.12, p. 266: In the usage "it is done by Devadatta" (*kriyate devadattena*) or "it is done by itself" (*kriyate svayameva*), the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*), which has become subordinate, is intended to be expressed as the operation of the one being prompted (*prayojya*). *Vārttika* on *Pāṇini* 2.1.1.1, p. 378: That which is called "being in the process of being done" (*kriyamāṇatā*) begins from the movement of the causal factors (*kāraka*) following the initial resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and continues until its completion. *Vārttika* on *Pāṇini* 3.8.1.22, p. 1125: A mantra that describes an action currently being performed (*kriyamāṇānuvādī*) is, for example, the Hotṛ-priest’s recitation regarding the measurement of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*): "Young, well-clothed... (*yuvā suvāsāḥ*).

Bhāṣya 3.8.1.22, p. 1124: Mantras that describe what is being done (kriyamāṇānuvādinaḥ) reiterate an action being performed by the Adhvaryu priest, such as "The seekers of the gods anoint you at the sacrifice. This is a restatement (anuvāda);
it is sufficient for the purpose of providing a reminder to the Adhvaryu.
12.1.16.13: Mantras that describe what is being done (*kriyamāṇānuvādinaḥ*) produce the cognition "it should be done thus," whereas *karaṇa*-mantras [produce the cognition] "I am doing.
12.1.16.13: The *hotṛ*'s mantras that describe what is being done are for the purpose of reminding the *adhvaryu*.
And since a mantra intended for remembrance is incapable of acting by itself, that which has been reminded is performed for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Therefore, there is a combination of the *hautra* mantras. (12.1.16.16–38). For those who maintain that the mantras refer to the action being performed (*kriyamāṇavādinaḥ*), the purpose of the mantras is to indicate the object currently being executed. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 102). The action is cognizable through inference.
*Bṛhatī*, p. 243: It is understood that an action, once it is perceived, causes the factors of action (*kāraka*) to be known.

*Bhāṣya* 4.4.13, p. 923: Even an action, like a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, is cognized by a single cognition—such as "he moves," "he sacrifices," or "he performs the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—even when there is a difference in [the agent] such as Devadatta; thus, it does not admit of difference.
For action is not absolutely non-different from the substance, such that its unperceived difference would be possible.
But even this [distinction] belongs to that very [action], because non-deviation (*anaikāntya*) and so forth are admitted.

Soma—But where there is no sequence of differentiators such as a difference in words and so forth, there the action is indeed non-distinct; the cognition of distinction, however, is based on the difference of the agent and other factors.
Furthermore, its constant non-perception is logically accounted for by the absence of a manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*).
Consequently, like sound, action (*kriyā*) must also be eternal.
Alternatively, let it be that all actions existing throughout the three worlds constitute a single manifestation; thus, there would be identity between the *āgneya* and other such sacrifices.
At that time, one action ceases while another arises.
Furthermore, no action whatsoever is accomplished without certain factors of action (*kārakas*).
(Kārakavinā)
"Action" (*kriyā*) [is expressed] by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). (Vārttika 3.1.6.12, p.
692). The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that action is not accomplished even by some [means] without action. Action is expressed by a verbal suffix.
Bhāṣya 2.2.5.14: "Ordinary people [hold] that action (kriyā) is what is expressed by a verbal root (dhātu);
otherwise, the very designation 'verbal root' would not exist. Listen: on page 173 it says, 'Action should be understood as the mere meaning of the verbal root,' and not merely physical motion."
Ślokavārttika, Ākṛtivāda 75: Action (*kriyā*) is not merely that which inheres in space alone, nor is it accepted everywhere as being of the nature of motion.

Vākyapadīya 3.1.6.12, p. 693: In the Mīmāṃsā system, action is not the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because, according to the reasoning stated in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, the meaning of the verbal root lacks the nature of action. In our own view, since the meaning of the verbal root does not possess the nature of action, it is impossible for it to imply [the agent] as qualified by the factors of action (*kāraka*).
Soma 3.4.8: Action is not perceptible, but is inferable from subsequent conjunction following disjunction;

therefore, some hold that largeness (*mahattva*) is not the cause [of its perception]. Maṇi, p. 21: However, where action is enjoined as qualified by its own qualifier, and serves as a qualifier for another action obtained through a different sentence, there the injunctive suffix must necessarily be present.
Or: [Vārttika 3.6.7.22] "Because actions depend on a substratum" (1514). Since actions are inferable and because they depend on a substratum, there would be a separation from another substance.

This is a *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra intended to demonstrate that it is not proper to substitute one substance for another—for instance, substituting *nīvāra* grain for *vrīhi* rice—because it would result in the ritual being distinct from the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices which require *vrīhi* as their material.

(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 343). For only where a substance and so forth stand as the primary factor (*pradhāna*) with respect to an action is a prior distinction established based on that [substitution]. (Vārttika 2.1.1.1, p. 371). Furthermore, within a single action, it is impossible for one and the same thing to simultaneously possess the status of both agent and object.
Maṇi, p. 54: When an action is being enjoined, the factors of action (kārakas) possess manifested capacities;
they are connected to the action by virtue of being factors of action.
However, when an action is not being enjoined, the factors of action possess unmanifested capacities.

Vārttika 10|1|13|64: Those actions in which the fruit is understood through direct perception (or from the sentence) are "fruitful" (*phalavatyaḥ*); those Vedic [actions] for which no fruit is heard are not so. 6|1|1|12 p. 1408: Furthermore, the relationship between an action and its factors (*kāraka*) is of the nature of a potency (*śakti*). Because it is included within the instrumental case-ending, and because the meaning of the suffix is primary, the relationship—subordinate to the nominal stem—is itself enjoined as the fruit. Vārttika 2|1|1|12 p. 551: Just as words are characterized by the relation of action and factor, so too the relationship of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) and "subsidiary" (*uṣibhāva*), being included within that connection, is also verbal (*śābda*).
VI. 2|1|1. The relation between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*) is of the nature of a direct connection.
Ku. 2|1|12–14, p. 114. Because of the non-difference between action and time:

"Furthermore, the word *yāvat* is not established anywhere as denoting time; rather, it qualifies the action itself by way of its extension up to completion (as in *yāvajjīvam*, 'as long as life lasts')."

If it is argued that there is no defining characteristic because of the non-difference between action (*kriyā*) and time (*kāla*), then here the avoidance of defeat by the Vaiśeṣika would be impossible.

Furthermore, even though actions possess temporality, a certain systematic distinction exists. (Vākyapadīya 2.1.12, p. 625): "There is both difference and non-difference between action and the state of being an action."

Maṇi, p. 22: It is precisely because of the continuity (*saṃtāna*) of the moments of action (*kriyākṣaṇa*) that the basis for the present tense in the expression "this moves" is established. Krujju, p. 77: Action is inferable (*anumeyatā*).
Now, the inferability of action is being demonstrated.
In that regard, when Devadatta goes, no entity called "going" distinct from conjunction and disjunction is perceived by the senses.

But surely action is indeed perceptible; for the cognition of going and so forth, which is superimposed upon the person, is born of the senses because it exists when the senses are present, just like the perception of color and other qualities.
Not so; for such a cognition is also established as being inferential.

How so? If it is asked, "By what distinction between being perceptible (*aindriyakatva*) and being inferential (*laiṅgikatva*) is the status of being inferential not accepted?", there is indeed such a distinction.
[The opponent objects: "In the case of perceptibility, the capacity of the sense organ to grasp the operation (*kriyā*) is not postulated;

whereas in the case of being inferential, the postulation of a capacity is certain. [The author replies: No, because in the case of that which is pervaded by a universal, its capacity to function as the pervader (*vyāpakatva*) is already established.

The sense organ, however, does not possess power over generality (sāmānya); for while there is perception of a jar or similar object in some cases through conjunction, and of a ball or similar object in others, there is no perception of atoms and the like. Furthermore, through the relation of inherence in the conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya), the eye perceives color and so forth, but not taste and the like. Therefore, since the power of the sense organ exists only where there is cognition, it is more appropriate—given that this can be established even as an inference by postulating the power of the sense organ with respect to each specific object—to assume its inferential nature rather than its sensory nature. Moreover, the movement under dispute is inferable because it is an action, just like the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies.
Therefore, action is indeed only inferable.
What, then, is the mark (*liṅga*) for the inference of action? It is conjunction preceded by disjunction.

For instance, whatever is sometimes [produced] is seen to be adventitious when it arises, as for example a cloth produced from the conjunction of threads; this [conjunction] also, being adventitious, [is inferred].
By the term "adventitious" (*āgantuka*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is meant.

[Objection: But is it not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of its equality [with the inherent cause], since that [adventitious cause] lacks the status of being either an inherent cause or a non-inherent cause? [Response:
That in which the effect inheres is the inherent cause.
Furthermore, an non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) must either be inherent in the effect or inherent in the cause of the effect;
however, since there is no further inherence within inherence itself, neither of these two conditions exists [for inherence].
This is not so, because that [inherence] is also established by its being inherent in the material cause of the lump [of clay], and so forth.

And so it has been stated in the *Prakaraṇapañjikā*: "For wherever the arising of the composite occurs from its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), from that very same [cause] its genus and its common properties are also produced.
Furthermore, the moment of the inherent cause refers to the domain of inherence and its distinction; therefore, there is no other-exclusive [reason].
Now, one might object: since there is an absence of conjunction preceded by disjunction in this case, there would also be an inference of action (*karman*) in that example.
It is not so; for by means of the inference of action in one case, both disjunction and conjunction are established in both cases as well.
The pervasion (*vyāpti*) is "whatever is an effect has a cause," but it is not "wherever there is an effect, there [must] be a cause.

Furthermore, only that which is preceded by conjunction with its own location and followed by disjunction from it serves as the inferential mark (*liṅga*); however, since that is absent in the case of a post (*sthāṇu*), there is no inference of action.

Furthermore, even if a mark (*liṅga*) were present, since separation and conjunction can be accounted for by the very first action alone, there would be no need to postulate another action; consequently, the cognition "it does not move" would result [as a contradiction]. Now, is it not the case that the rule for the specific determination of action is based on the inference of action from its causes?

Since disjunction and conjunction can be accounted for simply by the conjunction of the self, which possesses effort, with the body through that very [effort], what is the use of an internal, hidden action (*karma*)? However, if it were perceptible, there would be no fault even in accepting an action in accordance with what is observed.
This is not so; for it is a fixed rule that conjunction initiates its effect either in its own substratum or in that which is inherently related (*samaveta*) to its own substratum.

Just as a cloth [arises] in its own substrates, the threads, through the conjunction of the threads; and just as magnitude [arises] in the composite whole inherent in its own substrates even when there is conjunction with the leaves as substrates; and just as the conjunction of the shuttle and the weaver’s beam [arises] in the shuttle as its own substrate, and the conjunction of the shuttle and the cloth [arises] in the cloth inherent in its own substrate—therefore, the disjunctions and conjunctions in the body and its location, which are the substrates and non-substrates respectively, are not caused by conjunction.

Consequently, from the conjunction of the self and the body, action arises in the body as its own substrate, and from that, disjunction and [subsequent] conjunction arise; thus, there is no interruption of the action.

Now, one might object: "Just as it is accepted that conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which produces its effect in its own substrate, also produces its effect in that which is inherent (*samaveta*) in its own substrate, so too should it be accepted that [the cause] produces its effect in its own substrate, or else another cause should be postulated even for that which is inherent in the substrate; why this distortion of meaning? This is not so. For, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), causality resides both in the substrate itself and in that which is inherent in the substrate; in those cases, there is no need to look for anything else regarding either of them.

Regarding the conjunction of the self and the body as a cause of disjunction and conjunction, its status as a cause is not established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), because of the absence of negative concomitance.

Although positive concomitance is established—insofar as the effect arises only when the conjunction of the self and the body exists—nevertheless, since the conjunction of the self and the body exists at all times, there is no loss of the effect in its absence.

Therefore, it must be replied that the causal relationship between cognition and the rest is established by inference—using as an example the well-known causal relationship determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—based on such reasons as "being an effect inherent in that [the self]" (*tatsamaveta-kāryatva*).

Consequently, since inference depends upon positive and negative concomitance, and since it is understood through these two that the production of an effect occurs either in its own substratum (*svāśraya*) or in what is inherent in its own substratum (*svāśraya-samaveta*), one must infer accordingly, and not that it occurs in a non-substratum (*asvāśraya*).

There is no mutual dependence between the substratum itself and that which inheres in its own substratum, because both are cognizable by the same means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, conjunction does not possess the capacity to initiate an effect in that which inheres in its own substratum; thus, it is to be inferred through action (*karman*). If it is argued that there is no restriction [that an effect must arise] "in its own substratum" because the contact between an object and a sense organ produces cognition in the self, we say no; for this restriction is governed by the nature of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), whereas the contact between an object and a sense organ is merely an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

If you argue that there is also an inconsistency regarding the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) in that very case—since the non-separation resulting from the inherent cause of the splitting of bamboo slivers occurs as a single unity, and likewise for the sky and so forth, as well as for action and the disjunctions and conjunctions of place—then let your honor understand this: it is indeed produced by the conjunction that serves as the non-inherent cause. Thus may you be enlightened.

If it is argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because the conjunction of two threads—which serves as the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa)—is the cause of a cloth that pervades many threads, we say no; for even in that case, it produces [the effect] by means of disjunction (vibhāga). To explain: the conjunction of two threads first produces a portion of the cloth in its own substratum, the pair of threads; then, through the conjunction of that produced cloth-portion with another thread, it produces another cloth-portion in its own substratum. This should be understood in the same way for subsequent cases as well. Therefore, there is no deviation.
Thus it should also be understood regarding the cloth (*vastra*) and the yarns (*tantu*).
Alternatively, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) extends only as far as the number of conjunctions that serve as non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for a single effect;
therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even in the case of a large cloth, since it shares the same effect.
Alternatively, this pervasion (vyāpti) applies only where a single entity serves as the non-inherent cause (asamavāyi-kāraṇa) for a single effect.
Since the conjunction of the body with the self possessed of effort is indeed one, there is no fault whatsoever.

Now, it may be argued that when, due to the conjunction of the body with the self possessed of effort, disjunction and conjunction arise in the body, then they likewise arise in space due to the conjunction of that space with the self possessed of effort; thus, there is no performance of an action distinct from that [conjunction].
This is not so; for the effect is simply the disjunction and conjunction of space and the body.

Therefore, since the cause [of the action] is both the conjunction of the self characterized by effort with the body and the conjunction of the self characterized by effort with a point of space, it is not the case that the action occurs in a location other than its own substratum, nor does the conjunction with a point of space produce the effect in the body, which is its own substratum.

Furthermore, the causality of the conjunction with a point of space is neither established (*klpta*) nor need it be postulated (*kalpanīya*); rather, it is the postulation of the action itself that would be required.
Therefore, it is action alone that is to be inferred in the body, and from that, disjunction and conjunction; thus everything is logically consistent.
(Praviv., pp. 35–38).
Without the persistence of action, the status of being a *kāraka* (a causal factor) would be contradicted.
Maṇi, p. 112: Without the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action), there is no possibility of connection with an action (*kriyā*).
Su., p. 751: In the absence of an action, another action should not serve as a substitute;
there is no substitute for an action itself.

Bhāṣya 6.3.1.18–19: The generation of a comprehension of syntactic connection (anvaya) without a verbal form. Maṇi, p. 112: A rule for the restriction of an action (*kriyāpratiniyamavidhi*), such as Āpastamba’s statement: "If the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should enter, [he should offer] the *vibhrāṭ* verse to Prajāpati; he should offer [it] into the *dhruvā* ladle along with the *samidh* formula.
In this case, the oblation (*homa*) is merely a location, because there is no deity (*devatā*).

When the ritual action (*kriyā*) is predominant, as in the case of one who has eaten food from a king for whom the coronation has been performed (*krītarājakabhojyānnatva*), or one who has received the *pittas* of an *āhitāgni*, there is a substitute (*pratinidhi*) prescribed for the rule "he places the *juhū* ladle in the right hand," and so forth. Similarly, when an *āhitāgni* has fallen from his status (*patita*), another rule is recorded in the Smṛtis regarding those who have reached that state: "But one should place these vessels in the two hands, or [on the ground], if the sacrificer dies in vain. Or, as in the case of the absence of twice-born guests at a *śrāddha* meal, Devala states among the various rules of dharma: "In the fire, in the cow, or in the water."

Bāla, p. 23: When the action (*kriyā*) is predominant, because it is that which is being enjoined, its qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*). But when [the action] is subordinate (*guṇabhūtā*), that which is a qualification of the predominant element is not intended to be significant.
Vārttika 6.4.6.23, p. 1442: There is a distinction of action for each case-factor (*kāraka*).
Bhāṣya 6.1.4.17: The principle is that "from a difference in action arises a difference in result.
As it is said: "In whatever manner one acts, in that same manner one obtains the fruit thereof.
(Sāhasrī).
For the suffixes *kṛt* and *suñ* are used in the sense of the repetition (*abhyāvṛtti*) of an action, not in the sense of a difference between actions.

Bhāṣya on Pāṇini 1.4.15–47. When a connection with an action in general has been established by direct statement (*śruti*), a connection with a specific [object] occurs through syntactical connection (*vākya*), as in the case of "He buys with the red [cow]," *aruṇayā krīṇāti*.
Vārttika on 3.4.1, p. 817. Words functioning as adverbs (qualifiers of an action) end in the accusative case.

An investigation into this subject is to be found in the *Bhāṭṭarahasya*, under the section "The Second [Point]" (*dvitīyā*) in the *Bindu* [of the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*], in the other part [of that work].
Ke.: Where all [elements] are qualifiers of an action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), there is no difficulty because it constitutes a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*).

Vārttika 3.6.1.22, p. 689: Those which are qualifiers of a single action, being thus enjoined, do not—by virtue of being implied by the sense (*arthād ākṣipyamāṇāni*)—divide the operation of the injunctive [element].

Furthermore, when another action is being enjoined as a qualifier, and that [primary] action is not implied because it lacks a connection with it, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) necessarily occurs, since the injunctive element remains unseparated. (PMS 2.1.9.24, p. 556).
This is because of the rule stating that "adverbs (qualifiers of actions) possess the status of an object (*karman*) and neuter gender.
Ke.: Verbal nouns such as *yāga* (sacrifice) and the like do not denote a genus (*jāti*).
Su. Pṛ. 331: According to the Vārttika school, however, even those [words] denote universals (*jāti*), because it has been stated on p.
305 that the pair of words beginning with "cow" (*gavādi*) is intended to include all nouns and verbs;
for the connection with action is accomplished by means of case-endings (*kāraka-vibhakti*).
Vārttika 3.6.1.22, p. 679: "The case-ending (vibhakti) that expresses the connection with an action is characterized as a *kāraka* (grammatical participant), such as the accusative and others;

it occurs when the connection with the action is intended to be expressed. Bhāṣya 3.1.6.12, p. 688: "The maxim: 'The accomplishment of an action belongs to great beings through their essential nature (*sattva*), not through external instruments (*upakaraṇa*')."
This too is explained in verse.
For it is said: "The pot is his birthplace, wild animals his attendants, birch bark his garment, the forest his dwelling, and roots and the like his food—such are his qualities.
Yet Agastya drank the ocean within the hollow of his hand-lotus; thus, the accomplishment of one's task depends upon inner strength (*sattva*), not upon external implements."
Thus [it is said].
100. The usage of the verb *krīṇāti* (to buy) is observed even in a negotiation for the purpose of buying; for example:
"We have bought wealth with Devadatta."
The origin [of the term] has come into being; therefore, there is its agreement.

Bhāṣya 1.1.2.159. The root *krī* (to buy) functions in the exchange of goods, whereby one's own property is transferred to another's ownership and another's property is brought under one's own ownership.
Kāśikā 3.6.12, p. 256. Or, when the King has been purchased, he cuts the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) either during the consecrations (*dīkṣā*) or [at another time].

Bhāṣya 1.1.3.13: "'One who has purchased the King (Soma) is one whose food is not to be eaten'—this prohibition is of a specific nature. Bālakrīḍā, p. 16: "'One who has purchased the King is one whose food is to be eaten'—this is an injunction of permission for the sake of human purpose (puruṣārtha).

p. 12: "'One who has purchased the King is one whose food is to be eaten'—this is of the nature of a counter-exception (pratiprasava). Thus, there arises a doubt as to whether this is not a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) regarding the dharma of the Smṛtis. The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that, having heard the Śruti text, "Therefore, when the sacrifice to Agni and Soma is completed, [the guest] must stay in the house of the sacrificer," [the Smṛti rule] is not a means of valid knowledge because it is contradictory [to the Śruti].
Bhāṣya 1.3.2.3, p. 169: The statement regarding the food being fit for consumption by one for whom a king has been purchased follows from the very sense [of the context] in the Veda.
Vārttika 1.3.13, p. 184: Therefore, the food of one who has been consecrated (īkṣita) and for whom a king has been purchased becomes fit for consumption.
Sūtra: "And this fitness for the food of one for whom a king has been purchased is Vedic."
And there is no reason whatsoever for its lack of authority;
if it does not serve a purpose here in this world, that is due to its lack of necessity.
But by what means is its status as a source of knowledge regarding other matters (arthāntara) refuted?
"That eating of food by one who has been consecrated (ikṣita), which was prohibited by other statements,
is heard of subsequently as being permitted by a rule of authorization,
when the conclusion of the Agnīṣomīya sacrifice has been proclaimed, O King."

This variation regarding time would be like the [variation] regarding the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*āśīṣaccheda*). (Vārttika, p. 1890). Just as other rules of conduct (*āpad-dharma*) arise when the primary [rule] is impossible, so too, in that very situation of distress to life, there is the eating of food from a king who has been purchased [by bribery].

p. 190: Regarding the statement that "the *kaunvāni* [offerings] are to be consumed by one for whom the king has been purchased" (1517), the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) and its refutation are intended solely to demonstrate its faultlessness insofar as no other means of comprehension is possible.

p. 199: Because it is censured, even though there is no possibility of [the food] being fit for consumption, it must nevertheless be eaten due to the requirements of worldly conduct (*lokayātrā*) and so forth.
p. 199: "'Kaunvāni bhavanti' refers to *sāman*s in a specific modification (*vikṛti*).

Vi. 10.4.11. Just as in the case of the prohibition against meditating on discarded wood and so forth, [the rites] are to be performed in the fires of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*); there is no requirement for the *pavamāneṣṭi*s in that context.

The *agnihotra*, however, occurs after the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices. Bhāṣya 5.3.1.29–25. On page 243, section 69: The word *apavāda* here refers to an exception (*bādhaka*).

As for the claim that in cases such as *kāñcī*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs even in a domain where an exception would otherwise apply—based on the maxim "in some instances, [an operation occurs] even in a domain of an exception"—that is incorrect, because it contradicts the statement in the rule *aṇ karmaṇi ca*.

For in that rule, the repetition of *aṇ* is intended to prevent its removal from the domain of exceptions; thus, when forms such as *godāyo vrajati* are stated, they should be understood as being formed by the *śaiṣika* suffix.
