There is a maxim (paribhāṣā 18) stating that "sometimes even a single portion [of a preceding rule] continues to apply.
From the preceding [rule], the word "ekayoganirdeśānām" (of those indicated by a single grammatical connection) continues to apply.
"In one case, there is a connection with the meaning;
by that [connection], the two things indicated—namely, the collective expression and the dual mention of the *dvandva*—are meant.
Thus says Kaiyaṭa on the rule *pakṣāttiḥ*.
This is obtained from the knowledge of the pratijñā (formal declaration) regarding the svarita accent for that specific portion.
This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtras "dāmahāyanāntācca" and "auto'mśasoḥ" (Śekhar, p.

(The exclusion of the negative particle *nañ* from the rule *anya-ārṣa-dhātuka-sya*, which follows from the previous rule *ne’-avadhi-kṛti*) is established by the maxim: "In some cases, even a single portion [of a preceding rule] continues to apply.
(*Śekhara*, p. 93). In certain specific ritual acts, it is heard in scripture: "They praise with the *ṛc*" and "They praise with the *sāman*.
Here, there is no option between the *ṛc* and the *sāman*; rather, one must praise with the *sāman* alone.

VI. 9.2.8, Section 1: In a certain specific ritual (the Viṣuvat), it is heard: "With this verse, 'This one, the thousandfold man,' he worships the Āhavanīya fire. This worship is to be performed by chanting the verse *asaṃsahasra* as a melody; there is no option for non-chanting. VI. 9.2.8, Section 2: In some cases, because of the sense [of the context], the repetition of the *svāhā*-utterance is not a new beginning, but rather serves to include the *svāhā*-utterances already established.
Bhāṣya 10.8.8.
Because a moment lacks succession (*paurvāparya*). *Ṛju-vimālā*, p. 77. [For details on] the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) and its refutation (*vivi.*).
For if momentariness were established for entities themselves, then that [doctrine] might indeed be proven; however, this is not the case.
For instance: its proof must be either perception or inference, because there is no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa);
for whatever is a means of valid cognition is included within these very two.

Since it is established that if [momentariness] were not included [within the object], its reality would be untenable, it follows that, in this regard, ordinary perception directed toward blue and so forth does not take momentariness as its object.
Now, one might object: "Is there not a real entity called 'momentariness' that is distinct from the blue [object]?"

For such would be the case if there were a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), as in the case of white and other colors. However, there exists no distinct causal efficiency for momentariness that is different from the causal efficiency to be established by the blue [color], which could indeed subsist through a distinction in its momentary destruction. If momentariness is [established] by the very same causal efficiency that establishes yellow and so forth, then it is in reality designated as "blue" and so on.
If it is not distinct [from the object], then momentariness must certainly be apprehended by the direct perception of blue and so forth, because of its non-difference from that [object].
This is untenable, because it does not ascend to [the level of] experience.
Indeed, experience cannot be set aside.

And that [perception] is "this is blue," but not "this is momentary. Since stability (*sthemā*) is non-different from those two, it would follow that stability—which is non-distinct from them—is also perceived therein. However, if momentariness is not established by other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), then to claim it is established by perception is mere prattle; for in that case, perception does not produce a cognition that establishes it, as it is distinct from what is established by other means of knowledge.
Because it is untenable for perception— which lacks a pervasive operation extending to a subsequent determination— to possess validity with respect to the object of purposeful activity.
It might be argued that, according to the doctrine of experience alone, blue and other [objects] exist for only a single moment.
For instance, perceptual cognition, being momentary, delimits its object as restricted by its own very moment.

Thus, for example, when a visual perception in the form of blue delimits the blue, it excludes everything that is not that [blue]; and by excluding what is not that, it also excludes yellow and other colors which do not deviate from being "not-that."

Therefore, while determining the blue object as delimited by its mere existence, it also excludes its presence at other times; and by the non-apprehension of that [presence at other times], it likewise excludes its existence at preceding and succeeding moments.
If that were not excluded, there would be no exclusion of yellow and other colors either.
And in that case, those seeking the blue object and its causal efficiency would not engage with it according to any fixed rule.
"Therefore, the momentariness of entities is established by that very experience.
This is untenable,
because indeterminate perception has as its object only the blue [color] itself.

The Doctrine of Momentary Destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) and the Refutation of Reality (*tattvabhañjana*). Indeed, the doctrine of momentary destruction perceives even that which is not of its own nature; however, its failure to perceive itself is even more remote.

Even if self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is admitted, it is merely the manifestation of the self and the non-self, and it cannot connect the self with itself or with time, nor can it connect blue with time or with a pot.
Because, by virtue of being mere indeterminate perception (*ālocana*), it does not have the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) as its object;
even if there is no interruption of those [perceptions], the establishment of blue and so forth as lasting for only a single moment is not achieved,
because indeterminate perception itself persists for two, three, or more moments, and thus its status as lasting for only a single moment is unproven.
Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that the connection of a single entity with multiple things in a successive manner is not contradictory.

Thus, it is established that perception does not have the distinction of moments as its object of appearance; therefore, mental [perception] does not have the sense-object as its domain, but rather consists solely in the grasping of whatever is presented by the senses.

[Objection: Granted that the difference between moments may not appear, but from where does their non-difference come? To this he says: "Because of the appearance of non-difference" (*vivi.*). It is precisely recognition—such as "this is that same crystal"—that establishes the persistence of the crystal.
But surely, this [cognition] cannot have as its object the stability of the crystal, characterized by its pervasion across preceding and succeeding moments?
Indeed, neither the doctrine of momentariness nor the refutation of reality [is undermined]. (1520) Neither the doctrine of momentariness nor the refutation of reality.

Since there is no other alternative when one of two [possibilities] is negated, the other must be established, things are pervaded by either successive or simultaneous causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). These two [modes], being excluded from a permanent entity, also exclude causal efficiency from it, just as the property of being a *śiṃśapā* excludes it from what is not a tree.
This is like [the exclusion of a tree] from a mountain peak consisting of a single rock.
For instance, causal efficiency cannot occur successively; for entities are observed to be engaged in causal activities precisely through their own nature.

Whatever follows the presence and absence of its effects in accordance with their own presence and absence is capable of producing those effects; and since the nature (*rūpa*) of these [entities] follows the presence and absence of the effect through its performance, that very nature is what is capable.

And since that [nature] exists in the first moment just as it does in the second and subsequent moments, it would produce the entire collection of effects arising in the second and subsequent moments in the very first moment, because there can be no delay for that which is capable. Thus, a non-momentary entity cannot have a connection with successive operations.
This might be argued:

"Even though it is incapable [of acting] by itself, it acts sequentially due to the proximity of sequential auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). This is untenable, because it cannot withstand critical analysis (*vikalpa*). Do these auxiliary causes provide some assistance (*upakāra*) to this [entity], or not? Even if they do provide assistance, is that assistance distinct from the entity, or non-distinct? If a distinct assistance is provided, then even while the nature of the entity remains present, and even while its production is possible, there would be non-perception [of the effect]—a consequence already raised.
Thus, since the effect is produced from the [pre-existing] form, it could not be the producer of that [effect].
Nor is it correct to say that the production of the effect occurs through an auxiliary assistance;
for if that assistance were to produce another assistance, it would lead to an infinite regress.
For that very reason, it follows that the entity which is assisted would not be produced by that [assistance], as has been stated.

If there were an undifferentiated assistance, then the entity itself would be what is denoted; however, that [entity] cannot be attributed to something already established in its own nature (*prakṛti*).

Alternatively, if they were not beneficial, the seed would produce the sprout even without depending on the existence of auxiliary causes, because that which is independent cannot be delayed; or else, if there were such a delay, it would not produce leaves and so forth. If it is thought that auxiliary causes may be non-beneficial, yet the seed acts only when it exists together with them—
Nor is it the case that they are not required, for without them the effect would not arise.
That is not so;
for an entity is productive of an effect by its very nature—why then does it produce it only after these [auxiliaries] have ceased? Because its form exists even prior to them.

If they are producers by way of being co-operating factors (*sahakārin*), then those [factors] alone are the producers, not the entity (*bhāva*). Or, if one thing were the producer of another by way of a different form, it would follow that even a sky-flower, by virtue of its existence, would become an object of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Nor is it correct to say that the production depends on both, because the presence or absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) conforms to the presence or absence of the two [factors], while each one individually shows deviation (*vyabhicāra*); therefore, it is not tenable that the birth [of the effect] is dependent on both.
When the cause exists in its final state, the non-perception of the production of the effect is necessarily due to the absence of deviation;
for it is not the case that an entity has arisen from its own causes with a nature such that it produces the effect after a delay of several moments of time.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that it acts with delay solely by virtue of its own nature, because this cannot withstand logical analysis.

Does its nature of causing delay cease after a brief interval of time, or does it not? If it ceases, how is it that its nature has not ceased? [This would be impossible] because a nature cannot cease. Or, if it does not cease, how can this be its nature? [It cannot], because of the conjunction of contradictory properties—namely, the states of having ceased and not having ceased.
Therefore, if it were indeed its nature [to act], it would not delay; consequently, it would follow that it fulfills its purpose immediately upon being produced.
If it does not cease, it would not produce its effect even after some time has passed,
because the nature of the entity remains in that same state.
Therefore, by this reasoning, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*) cannot occur either successively or simultaneously.
Nor is it logical for [the action] to occur simultaneously. Therefore,
whatever effect was produced by that non-momentary entity through its own nature in the first moment, all of that would have to be produced in the second and subsequent moments as well,
because its nature, which possesses the capacity to produce those effects, remains present in the second and subsequent moments.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for that which has already been produced to be produced again, if [the entity] were other [than its previous state], then for a non-momentary thing, the performance of all causal functions simultaneously by what is produced in the second and subsequent moments would not be logical.
Thus, by this line of reasoning, the capacity of a non-momentary thing to perform causal functions—whether successively or simultaneously—is not tenable.
Since existence (sattva) is excluded from the non-momentary state because of the absence of its pervader (vyāpakābhāva), it is pervaded by momentariness; thus, the proof is established.
It might be argued as follows:

Even if an entity is momentary, does it possess the nature of producing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) or not? If it does not, then it is simply non-existent. If, however, it possesses the nature of being a producer, then what use has it for auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*)? Thus, the seed would produce the sprout at that very same instant.

[Objection: Does not the moment of the seed that is immediately followed by the sprout necessarily produce the sprout? Why then is there a need for its transformation (*pariṇāma*) from the preceding momentary state?

[Reply: In that case, since all seeds belonging to that same continuum would possess the capacity to produce a sprout without distinction in their nature as seeds, the seed would produce the sprout merely by virtue of its definition. [Reply: Not so.

Due to the conjunction of preceding moments of earth, seed, wind, and so forth, another seed-moment arises, born from a succession of subsequent moments that have cognized their object; this efficient seed-moment, coexisting with efficient moments of earth and the rest, produces the sprout independently. Nor is it the case that, although it coexists with earth and the rest, it would fail to produce the effect in their absence; for if those [factors] were absent, there would be no imparting of that specific causal capacity.
Nor is it the case that earth and the other factors lack cooperative efficacy, for they produce the sprout only in conjunction with those [other causes].
[This concludes] the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) and the refutation of its reality (1521). Regarding the doctrine of momentary flux and the refutation of its reality:
even for those [factors], there is no distinction in their necessity of existing prior [to the effect], and causality consists in nothing more than that.
Nor do these dependencies themselves initiate another effect among one another, because only that [specific result] is perceived from them, and there is no deficiency in their capacity.

Nor is there a non-action on the part of the others due to the action having been performed [by one], for it is impossible to say "it is done" regarding a joint action. Furthermore, those things which possess dependency—having come together through mutual proximity while relying on their own causes—are not able to withdraw, saying, "This can be accomplished by even one of us; enough with this proximity."

Furthermore, it is not the difference in auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*) that is the cause of the difference in effects, but rather the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), because it is only when that [difference in the complex] exists that a difference in effects is observed.
Since the causal complex here is non-different, a difference in effects is impossible.

Moreover, the mutual conjunction of earth and the other factors arises from their efforts to approach one another; thus, because there is no contradiction with purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) for a momentary entity, the reason is not "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*).

Nor is it the case that, because the probandum is established for the subject (*sādhyadharmin*)—such as sound—merely through the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no statement of the reason (*ahetuvacana*).
Indeed, a pervasion that encompasses all instances cannot have the mere reason alone as its scope.

For an opponent could argue: "The existence of things being perceived has been excluded from non-momentariness; therefore, existence itself is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and does not prove momentariness."
Therefore, the pervasion (vyāpti) must be demonstrated that whatever exists—whether visible or invisible—is momentary in its true nature.

[Objection: Even so, since the pervasion regarding sound and other such subjects under dispute is established by the force of perception itself as being momentary, the reason remains as before: it is called "non-probative" (asādhana).
[Reply: Not so.

Just as, even though things such as a rabbit’s horn do not exist, the pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever exists, whether visible or invisible, is momentary" is established as a universal rule—yet rabbit’s horns and the like are not themselves momentary—so too, even if the pervasion is established despite the absence of sound and other such subjects under dispute, momentariness is not thereby proven for them. Therefore, it must indeed be shown that existence (sattva) is the means of proving their momentariness; thus, there is no lack of proof or ignorance regarding the statement of the reason (hetu).

Furthermore, do produced entities, when arising from their own causes, arise as perishable or as imperishable? If they are perishable, they vanish immediately after their emergence; thus, momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established.
If, on the other hand, they were imperishable, they would never perish at any time;
for indeed, that which is imperishable cannot possibly perish.

Blue never becomes yellow by virtue of its own cause. Nor is it tenable to claim that their destruction occurs simply through production from another cause, because this position cannot withstand analysis.
For that destruction, being produced by another cause, must be either distinct from the entity itself, or not.
Or is it non-different?
It cannot first be non-different, because of the difference in its causes; but if it were different, the entity would remain in its original state.
As before, there would be the undesirable consequence of perception and so forth.
If it is argued that, therefore, existence is concealed,
we say no.
Whether disappearance (*tirodhāna*) is distinct [from its substrate] or not, it must necessarily be an entity (*bhāva*). If it were non-distinct, a difference in causes would be untenable.

Therefore, since even non-existence (*abhāva*)—which lacks all positive form and is devoid of parts—cannot possess action, the expression "he produces non-existence" is untenable because the verb "to produce" cannot be connected with a non-existence that lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Consequently, the connection with the negative particle (*nañ*) is established as "he does not produce an entity."
And for that which does not act, being a non-agent, there is no cause; thus, there are no causes of destruction.

However, some maintain that because a thing has arisen from its own cause as something capable of enduring for two moments, it simply does not exist in the second moment by itself, and it does not require a further cause for this.

Indeed, a blue object produced from its own causes and established in its own nature does not depend upon a cause for its state of being yellow or otherwise, nor can it be questioned [as to why it changes].
Moreover, the destruction of produced entities is perceived as being non-abiding; by this, their momentariness can also be inferred.
For instance, whatever is certain to occur for something does not depend on any other cause, just as, for example, the melting of iron is certain for forms and so forth.

Since the destruction of produced entities is necessarily certain (*dhruvabhāvī*), this perception of a pervader incompatible with the [proposed] cause (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*) negates the dependence of destruction upon another cause. For necessary certainty (*dhruvabhāvitā*) is pervaded by non-dependence on another cause—which is the opposite of the dependence on another cause that is being negated—and thus it establishes non-dependence on another cause.
This, in turn, excludes its own opposite, namely dependence on another cause. To explain:
Whatever depends on other causes is not necessarily present;
for example, the dyeing of a cloth and so forth.

Likewise, if entities were to depend on another cause for their destruction rather than their own causes, then—since there would be no evidence for a rule regarding the presence of that [other cause]—not even a single produced thing would ever perish.
This destruction of momentary entities, which occurs at every stage,
indicates that they arise from their own causes as things persisting for only a single moment.
Thus, since these entities do not exist by themselves in the second moment, their momentary disintegration (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established.
Existence (*sattva*) is certainly not capable of proving momentariness, because it is an over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*) reason, as its application to momentariness cannot be established.
For instance, it is accepted that moments which have reached another instant produce an effect.
In this regard, being questioned, you must explain: does a single [cause] produce a single effect, or many? Likewise, do many [causes] produce a single effect, or many?

Not from a single [cause], for that which is called a cause is defined as the non-deviation of things that have been sequentially produced by a single effect; and since, prior to the arising of that effect,

there is the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) characterized by necessity and the refutation of [the opponent's] reality, causality itself is not the nature of existence, as is established by the experience of blue and other objects.

For that [entity] is indeed employed for various causal functions precisely by its own nature as delimited by its intrinsic essence; however, its form is not merely those various [functions] themselves. Let there not be a difference in form when it produces multiple causal functions simultaneously, and let there not be a definition of it that is dependent on others, since only its effect-ness, existence, or its specific [limited] nature is being defined.

If existence (*sattva*) were [independent] causality, then just as being an effect (*kāryatva*)—though it is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity—is in reality dependent upon a cause for its determination, so too causality (*kāraṇatva*) cannot be determined without an effect related to itself; thus, existence would not be established in its pure form. Consequently, whether one considers it from the perspective of dependence or from the perspective of destruction, the claim that "existence is an effect" would be contradicted.

And so, even if everything exists, it is nonetheless established that an entity, being of the nature of existence itself, will be experienced as the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for the cognition of that existence.
Now, even if [the entity] does not exist [at that time], nevertheless, its very nature is acquired from its own respective causes.

Although it is incapable [of acting at that moment], even if it were capable, it would be employed in various purposeful activities (arthakriyā) upon the proximity of those respective auxiliary conditions (sahakārin).

Nor is it the case that it lacks capacity because the effect is not perceived initially; for if that were so, it would follow—just as was stated—that even a donkey or similar thing would produce sprouts and the like through its conjunction with earth and other factors.

But surely, how can the two contradictory properties of being a producer and not being a producer coexist in one and the same thing? Likewise, in the very same seed, how can there be the production of a sprout and the production of its non-production—namely, the production of a stalk and so forth—which are likewise contradictory? If they are contradictory, how can there be non-difference? And if there is difference, then the world would consist of nothing but this [single entity], and thus even "manifoldness" would not exist. This, O Sage, is the reality of things according to the view of the Upamitibhavaprapañcā Kathā. If it is argued that there is non-difference because perception perceives the identity of the producing seed-form despite the observed difference in effects, we say no.
This is because the same principle applies here as well.
Indeed, even in this case, although there is a difference in the sequential effects, the nature of the seed does not depend on a substratum for its persistence (*anvaya*).
Nor can contradiction be understood merely from the presence or absence of the use of the negative particle (*nañ*), for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor is it the case that at the very moment a seed possesses productivity, it simultaneously lacks it.

Furthermore, productivity is not its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); rather, the seed is the producer, while productivity is a distinct property (*dharmabheda*), consisting either in the concurrence of other conditions or in a specific capacity (*sāmarthya*).
And this concurrence depends upon the auxiliary conditions (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*).
Nor is there no difference between the property and the property-bearer, for that [property] is distinct from it. And even though it is distinct, it is perceived because it is dependent upon it;
and its connection with it is due to their being cause and effect.

Thus it is established that even for a non-momentary entity, the performance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through either successive or simultaneous action is possible; therefore, because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful, existence (*sattva*) is an inconclusive reason and not a valid member of the proof for the momentariness of things.

As for the critique of the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) and the refutation of reality which you have proposed—namely, the dilemma as to whether entities arise by their own nature as perishable or imperishable—it is to this that we now respond.
We do not know whether there is perishability or imperishability; rather, things arise from their own causes and perish without other causes.
This means they perish when the conditions for their own destruction are present. Furthermore, destruction is non-different from the thing being destroyed, due to the identity of cause and nature.

And the distinction between intrinsic natures has already been established in the *Niyogaparīkṣā*. [Objection: "But even on this position, what happens to the entity (*bhāva*) which is distinct and real? [Reply: Nothing at all happens.
This venerable entity simply exists.

Let it be that all purposeful activities (*arthakriyā*) are set aside by the absence of those [activities]—an absence whose nature is the lack of their own essence, which arises dependent on its own causes, which possesses its own moment, and which initiates a corresponding conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). What is lost? Nor does the necessity of destruction imply a dependence on other causes, because such a premise is unproven (*asiddha*) and because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

You yourself must investigate this: is the series of shards, which is distinct from the series of the jar, necessarily occurring (*dhruvabhāvinī*) or not? If not, then the destruction of the jar is also not necessarily occurring.
Indeed, we do not perceive the destruction of the jar immediately following the moment of its division [from the potter's wheel], even when our eyes are open.

Thus, the necessity of destruction (*dhruvabhāvitā*) remains unproven. If, however, it were necessary, then even among those things that are necessarily occurring within that very series of divisions, the necessity of destruction would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because they depend on a hammer; therefore, the necessity of destruction cannot here serve to establish a pervasion (*vyāpti*) by independence, as it is capable of being negated by dependence on other causes.

Therefore, since you have rejected the inference that establishes momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), it is proven that you are establishing recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) as being uncontradicted. *Kaṇikā*, pp. 122–140.
The doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) and its refutation of reality.

[Śālikanātha: But surely, since all entities are momentary, how can sound be eternal? Furthermore, what is the proof for the momentariness of all things? Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) reveals existence at a particular time, but it does not effect the negation of [existence] at other times. Just as the perception of blue does not negate yellowness; rather, its negation occurs through the non-perception of that [yellowness].

Furthermore, time is not a substance at present, such that its negation could occur through the non-perception of something perceptible; nor do we perceive any other means of valid cognition [for it]. This is because the means of valid cognition based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) has as its object that which follows upon mere existence (*sattāmātra*). But how is the establishment of momentariness proven through the experience of mere existence? It is because a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) operates against the contrary case. For when existence is subverted in the contrary case of non-momentariness by the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), existence—being pervaded by momentariness—thereby leads to the inference of that [momentariness].
What, then, is the pervader of existence? We say it is succession and simultaneity.
For indeed, existence is nothing other than causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

An entity does not attain existence if it does not initiate some purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), because all entities are the cause of even a single moment. Furthermore, whatever is conceived as existing—even if its nature is unknown—is also capable of purposeful action by virtue of being an objective support (*ālambana*) for consciousness. Existence is defined as this capacity for purposeful action; that which performs such action is alone ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).
And this capacity is pervaded by succession and simultaneity, neither of which is possible in the case of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*).

For a permanent entity cannot perform all its causal functions simultaneously; if it did so, then in the second moment it would be devoid of causal efficiency due to the absence of any activity, and by lacking the defining characteristic of existence, it would result in its being momentary.
Nor is succession possible, for that entity is capable of performing all causal functions; why then does it initiate only one and not others, given that it is equally capable throughout?
If it is argued that it delays out of dependence on auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), [the response follows].
No;

for auxiliaries that do nothing are independent, while those that do something—whatever it is they produce—would themselves be the means of accomplishing the effect, since the effect is produced immediately after them; thus, the entity [the auxiliary] would itself be the cause.

For an entity that initiates an effect through an adventitious excellence cannot be its cause, because they are distinct; or, if there were no distinction, even the excellence would be momentary, being born at that same time.

Distinctness and non-distinction are indeed contradictory. Therefore, it is established that existence is impossible for a non-momentary thing, and thus the concomitance with mere existence proves momentariness.
Furthermore, the destruction of produced entities is inherent to their very nature; by this as well, the momentariness of jars and other things is established.
For instance: that which is certain to occur does not depend upon any other cause for those [entities] in that regard.
And the destruction of produced things is certain to occur; thus, there is the perception of a pervasion by the contradictory (viruddhavyāptopalabdhi).

For certainty of occurrence, being perceived in cases such as the falling of fruits and the like through its pervasion by the negation of dependence on another cause, establishes non-dependence—which subverts its opposite, namely dependence.

Alternatively, since the various colors and other qualities in a cloth depend upon other causes, their observed diversity proves that they are not invariably present; thus, by the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), the dependence of destruction upon other causes is excluded. Since destruction is independent and occurs spontaneously immediately after birth, momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established. Blows from a pestle and the like, however, are causes for the production of a dissimilar continuum, not for destruction itself. For the observer, the difference between moments is unperceived due to the arising of successive states that are similar to one another.

In this regard, those who observe the emergence of a dissimilar state immediately after the blow of a mallet—such as when a substance perishes—always consider that destruction [itself] to be the cause of the destruction, thinking it occurs following the blow of the mallet.
However, in ultimate reality, there are no causes of destruction whatsoever.
Furthermore, destruction cannot possibly arise from other causes such as [the action of] an agent and so forth, because of the difference in their nature.

If, however, that [destruction] were distinct [from the entity], then even when it had arisen, the entity would still be perceived as before, just as a jar is perceived after the production of a cloth.
Therefore, entities are produced from their own causes with the very nature of destruction; thus, the proof of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established.

Furthermore, even in the case of objects such as jars produced with hundreds of efforts, their destruction is observed over time through a specific decay of their constituent parts, even without blows from a mallet or similar causes. This [destruction] is not possible without some degree of "otherness" (anyatva) beginning from the moment of its accumulation; and this otherness, as it were, is perceived by direct observation itself by persons who, even after a period appropriate for the substance's age, perceive the difference between its new and old states.

Furthermore, it is not possible for a single entity such as a jar to possess multiple forms, because multiplicity and unity are contradictory; therefore, jars and other things are subject to momentary destruction. The formal argument is: "Entities under dispute are perishable in every moment because they exist, like a lamp. As for recognition, it too occurs in our view just like that of a lamp.
To this it is replied:
existence is not, first of all, the capacity for causal efficiency; for while that which exists possesses the capacity for causal efficiency, that capacity itself is not existence.
Nor is there a necessity for every entity to possess causal efficiency, since there exist things that do not produce such effects.
Furthermore, even that which is a cause of cognition is not necessarily so for everyone, because it continues to exist in its own nature even while remaining unknown.

Nor is it possible for past and future entities to serve as the objective support (*ālambana-hetu*) for the cognitions of all [beings], since it is logically untenable for non-existent things to function as causes. Moreover, if they were causes, and if they were to persist through all cognitions, then because all [entities] would be pervaded [by those cognitions], and because of their momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), a further operation would be impossible; and since existence (*sattā*) is defined by such [causal] activity, it would follow that the entire world becomes void immediately after all cognitions have occurred—thus, this [position] is trivial.

Now, the capacity of entities to perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) occurs sequentially because delay is possible through dependence on auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). And these auxiliaries produce either a distinction that is both different and non-different from the entity, or indeed something entirely distinct; for example, there is a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) in the seed when it comes into contact with soil and water. In the absence of this, the enduring seed does not previously initiate the sprout, but upon its presence, it does initiate it. Thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. [Objection: But in that case, the conjunction itself would be the cause, and not the seed.
Not so; for that sprout is seen from mere conjunction alone.

Indeed, the conjunction of earth and water does not produce the sprout. However, if the conjunction qualified by the seed is the cause, then the seed, which serves as the qualifier, must also be admitted as a cause.
However, for one who does not accept the dependence upon auxiliary causes,

his doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*)— as refuted in the *Tattvasaṅgraha* (verse 1526) under the "Refutation of the Doctrine of Momentary Flux"— [implies that] a sprout would arise from a seed situated in a granary even without depending on the conjunction of earth and water.

But surely, an entity that has reached another moment is indeed capable of producing [the effect] independently. Even though it is independent, it does not exist without its auxiliaries; therefore, it does not produce [the effect] without them.
For the seed remaining in the granary is one thing, and this [seed] conjoined with the soil is quite another, from which the sprout arises.
True;
however, this must be said here:

if that which has reached another moment and is conjoined with earth and water were the producer of the sprout, would it still produce the sprout even if it remained in the granary due to the absence of the farmer's effort?
If one objects: "For what purpose, then, would the effort of a farmer—who acts with foresight—be undertaken?
And why would the learned engage in the effort of worshipping shrines for the sake of heaven, liberation, and so forth?

Furthermore, the specification of place, time, and name would be useless, since heaven, liberation, and the like would be established solely from the cognition occurring at another moment, independent of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)."
Therefore, dependence upon auxiliary causes (sahakārin) must be accepted.

Consequently, even for an entity that is permanent, the performance of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) could occur sequentially through the sequential arrival of auxiliary causes; thus, since there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against this counter-position, existence is not invariably concomitant with momentariness, and it is therefore incapable of proving it.

Furthermore, destruction does not depend on another cause simply because it is certain to occur, for this is inconclusive (anaikāntika): we observe that in the continuum of a jar, the continuum of the potsherds—which is certain to occur—is seen to depend on other causes such as the blow of a hammer.
[Objection: But surely, if destruction were produced by another cause when the entity has already perished, then even after its destruction, the entity would still be perceived as before.
Therefore, destruction must be intrinsic (svābhāvika).
[Question: What does "intrinsic destruction" mean? [Answer: It means that destruction arises from the very nature (svabhāva) of the entity itself, not from another cause.
Now, if destruction arises from existence, the same fault applies as when it is distinct from existence, namely that there would be perception [of the object] as before.
Or, if destruction is identical with this very existence, then because destruction is imperceptible, existence too would have to be imperceptible.
Furthermore, the natures of existence and non-existence are absolutely contradictory; their coexistence in a single thing here is merely a matter of chance.

Furthermore, that which is called "destruction" is not some distinct reality; it is non-existent because it is a mere nothingness. Therefore, if a produced entity were to lack destruction, it would necessarily be eternal; thus, the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is well-established.

Therefore, even by one who does not desire it, it must be admitted that destruction is perceived as distinct from the entity itself. As for the claim that there is no difference between the preceding moment and [the subsequent state], let it be so; however, this does not imply that an enduring entity must necessarily undergo destruction at its preceding moment, for there is a lack of valid evidence [for such a necessity]. This is because various states—even those that are contradictory—can coexist simultaneously in a single substratum, while those that are not contradictory can occur sequentially.

Furthermore, for an object that has sequentially experienced new states and reached an old state, destruction through the disintegration of its parts and so forth is logical, even if it has been preserved with effort.

Nor can the momentariness of a jar or similar objects be established merely by the example of a lamp, because existence (*sattva*) is not a valid reason, as its exclusion from the contrary (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful; moreover, the thesis contradicts perception, just as [the claim of] imperceptibility contradicts perception.
Nor is that [momentariness] established by the [proposed] probandum itself.
Because a commonality of parts is impossible.

For a commonality is possible only when it is consistent [with the nature of things], and for those who maintain that everything is momentary, nothing consistent is possible; or, if such a thing were possible, there would be no universal momentariness. Therefore, since all entities are momentary, let alone sound. (Śābarabhāṣya)
"The refutation of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādakhaṇḍana*): the nature of the teacher Prabhākara is here explained.
This *Mīmāṃsājīvarakṣā* is the refutation of momentariness. Herein, the follower of the Sugata’s doctrine asserts that all entities are indeed characterized by momentary flux.

What, then, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for them in that regard? Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) certainly does not suffice to establish momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), because even for one who examines most minutely the existence of things such as pots and the like, there is no determination of their momentariness. One might think: "Momentariness is not something external to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity; therefore, through the very perception of the entity itself, direct perception directly realizes its momentariness."
The wise consider this to be a mere wishful thought;
for it is an undisputed tenet among all disputants that the determination of objects is grounded in consciousness.

Thus, this momentariness, being the very nature (svabhāva) of an entity, manifests itself through cognition; it does not exist apart from that [cognition], nor otherwise. And we do not perceive such a cognition as arising [independently];
so from where could there be an inclusion [of momentariness] within the nature of the entity?
And through the awakening to that [momentariness], there is awakening.
Now, even though momentariness has been perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it has not entered the path of certainty; therefore, it appears as if it were ungrasped.
For indeed, direct perception is not the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that [certainty].

For the Buddhists maintain that perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in cases where its operation—naturally free from conceptual construction—is followed by a subsequent conceptual cognition (*savikalpapratyaya*).
However, the claim of those seized by the delusion of their own tenets—that perception does not exist where the cognition "this has been seen" does not arise—is merely the play of verbal sophistry.

Furthermore, as for what some have said—that perceptual cognition is momentary and, by having as its object an entity characterized by its own time, makes known its momentariness—[that too is untenable].
That too is the speech of a fool;
for momentariness consists in existing for only a single moment.
It does not [occur] now by means of that condition.
It attains stability because of its indifference toward other moments;
on the contrary, perception itself, at every moment of recognition,
casts far away the notion of momentariness by conceiving of an entity as characterized by both prior and subsequent times.

Inference, moreover, which is based upon the inference of a relationship, is unable to take momentariness as its subject (pakṣa), because there is no perception of any entity together with it; for indeed,
the cognition of a relationship does not arise unless the members of that relationship have been perceived.
Followers of the Sugata’s doctrine do not consider there to be any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) other than these two;
thus, the Buddhists reject this [other view] as a mere delusion regarding space.
For they declare that momentariness is to be apprehended through inference based on the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
What, then, is that inference? It is: "Whatever exists is momentary;
and all things exist.
The essential nature (*svabhāva*) serves as the logical reason (*hetu*) when its connection is invariably concomitant with existence alone.
Just as being a *śiṃśapā* tree is concomitant with being a tree—
since the nature of being a tree is necessarily connected to being a *śiṃśapā*—
in exactly the same way, momentariness is necessarily connected to mere existence.

How, then, is the proof of its being restricted to that alone established? It is through the sixth means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), which is the non-perception of the probans in the counter-example (vipakṣa).
For in an unimpaired logical context, the non-perception of the reason subverts its existence.
Indeed, existence is the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyākāritā); there is no other such thing as existence.
And that [existence] is pervaded by succession and simultaneity, because there is no third alternative;

for these two are mutually exclusive, such that the negation of one necessarily implies the presence of the other. Furthermore, succession and simultaneity are not possible in the case of imperishable things.
But when those [two] are excluded, they exclude existence itself, just as the property of being a *śiṃśapā* excludes the property of being a tree.
And how is there an absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through either succession or simultaneity in things that are momentary? To this, they say:
For if it exists unimpaired, how could it not have the nature of producing causal efficiency?
Therefore, it must be either its own nature (*svabhāva*) or there is no other possibility.

In that regard, if the former position is accepted, since all causal efficiencies (*arthakriyā*) would be completed in a single moment, and because no further cause could then be established, the subsequent moment would result in the fallacy of being devoid of causal efficiency, thereby falling into the definition of non-existence (*asallakṣaṇa*).
[This is] the uninterrupted flow [of the argument].

However, in the case of the second alternative, no causal efficiency whatsoever arises from that [object]; thus, there is indeed the fault of it lacking the definition [of a real entity]. This concludes the section.
Even if an entity is capable by its own nature, it performs its function only at some time through the power of the assembly of auxiliary causes; in their absence, it does not do so at that time.
Even that [auxiliary] cannot withstand scrutiny under analysis.
For that auxiliary either initiates something or it does not.

Even if it initiates something, one must consider the following alternatives: is it of a nature that has acquired its existence through being the means for accomplishing a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), or is it of a nature that has not so acquired?
In the case of non-origination, the meaning of "dependence" must be explained;
for dependence toward that which does not assist [the effect] is certainly not purposeful.
And [this dependence] would have to be the very nature of the entity.
That [seed] falls away;
for that which is being sown does not possess the nature of that which is being bound [as a sprout], since the imposition of contradictory properties entails a difference [between the two].
On the view that accepts the arising of an entity, one must resort to figurative usage (*lākṣaṇikatva*).

Therefore, if one accepts that the causal efficiency (*ārambha*) is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity, then that entity must be established as such either previously [to its activity] or simultaneously with it.
For causal efficiency cannot be achieved sequentially by means of a non-momentary entity;
for that very reason, this [activity] is not a causal efficiency belonging to a jar.
Because [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists, and does not exist when that does not exist;

and there is no other mode besides these two—positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—since there is no perception of the co-inherence of two mutually contradictory properties in a single locus.

Now, as for the first alternative among the previous options: is even a momentary entity by nature capable of producing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), or is it not? [The answer to the latter] is "it is not."
In that case, there would be no dependence on a great causal agent for that which possesses an efficacious nature;
for purposeful action does not arise within the sphere of error.
Listen to the supreme secret of the Buddhists.
An entity that has reached another moment is indeed capable and produces its effect all by itself.

Why, then, does it not produce it even without its auxiliary causes? If it were a producer while being independent [of others], it must be explained what kind of "auxiliary status" could belong to those auxiliaries.
To this we reply:
as for the argument that it does not act even without auxiliary causes, that is merely a manifestation of a lack of skill regarding the Sugata’s doctrine;
for a momentary entity does not exist without its auxiliary causes.
"How will this be accomplished?
That which exists is not that [same thing].
Thus, nothing is lost.
When one is questioned as to why [the cause] does not produce [the effect] in the absence of auxiliary factors, the answer must be given in terms of the nature of the cause:
"It becomes such [a cause], and it brings [the effect] about.
Furthermore, the capacity to produce an effect consists in its being an auxiliary factor existing at another moment.

But surely, since they too are producers independent of anything else, why do they not initiate another effect? To this we reply: in this matter as well, we are powerless; let them initiate whatever they initiate—this much alone we are able to permit. Thus, for us who observe that these very [atoms] produce that very [effect], there is no admission of constituent parts (avayava).
[Objection: But surely, when one has already performed [the action], what does the other do?
This would indeed be the case if the action were performed successively;
however, in the case of simultaneous action (*sahakriyā*), the very condition "when [one] has performed" (*kṛte*) does not exist.
But surely, since that [result] is established even from a single [cause], what do the others accomplish?
This is not so;
they are not acting with foresight, such that they would deliberate in this manner.
"Even another... [is] capable of this without us;
however, we are not present here.
But they—
In this regard, it is argued that there is no cause; otherwise, it would follow that things arise without a cause.
To this, it is replied:

The difference in the effect does not arise from a difference in the simultaneous co-operating causes (*sahakārin*), but rather from a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). This point has been thoroughly investigated by those who have exerted themselves in the study of the two types of causes; it is therefore beyond my comprehension.
Consequently, even if [the entity] were momentary, there would be no room for objection based on the charge that it is incapable of being non-momentary.
For in the transformation of the succession of moments of seeds and so forth, such moments do not arise;
because immediately after the occurrence of another cause that was previously unrequired, the sprout manifests.
[Objection: Even so, the recognition "this is that very same thing" would not be possible regarding successive seeds and so forth.
Furthermore, it must be stated: when there is a contradiction with perception accompanied by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), how can mere inference (*anumāna*) be established?
Or, if it were so established, it would follow that one could infer coldness even in fire.
The resolution is stated as follows:

For those who maintain that the conventional usage of non-difference proceeds based on the non-apprehension of difference— since one is unable to reflect upon even what is seen as the similarity between the distinctness of momentary existence—
just as the conventional usage of "this is silver" occurs with respect to mother-of-pearl,
there is no distinction from the arising of inference.
Because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) would otherwise be inexplicable;
however, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is established even through the non-apprehension of difference, and thus it is faultless.
For this very reason, the elders say: "Inference is indeed stronger than even direct perception."
Thus it is said.
And we consider this alone to be correct:
that these two cognitions—"that" and "this"—are manifested as arising from a single cognition.

Furthermore, for produced entities, [perception] necessarily occurs when the sense faculty is present and directed toward its object, because there is no other cause [for it]. It does not, however, touch upon the nature of what was previously associated with it.
And the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) produced by prior experience does not possess the "this-ness" (*idantā*) that connects it with a subsequent time.
This has been explained by the case of the recognition of a flame;
moreover, the inevitable destruction of produced entities is perceived,
and from this as well, their momentary nature can be inferred.
For instance, if this [destruction] were necessarily inherent, then there would be no dependence upon other causes for it.

Since the destruction of produced things is necessarily inherent, this inference—based on the perception of a mark pervaded by a contradictory property—negates the dependence of destruction upon other causes.
For necessary inherence is established through the perception of that which possesses independence, which is the opposite of the dependence on other causes that is being negated.
And that [reason] negates its own opposite, namely the dependence upon another cause;
for those things which depend on another cause are not necessarily present,
just as the dyeing of a cloth and so forth.

Therefore, there is the perception of "invariable occurrence," which is pervaded by "independence"—the opposite of "dependence on another cause"; this very [perception] is the non-perception of "non-invariable occurrence.
Destruction does not depend on another cause.

Thus, if entities were to depend on something else for their destruction even with respect to their own causes, then, because there would be no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for a necessary presence of that other cause, nothing that has been produced would ever perish.
Since its perishability is established by its own cause, it ceases immediately after its arising; thus, momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅguratva*) is proven.
Furthermore, this must be considered:
when produced entities arise from their own causes, do they arise as inherently perishable or as inherently imperishable?
Those things which perish dissolve immediately after their arising and are thus subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgin*).
However, those whose nature is non-perishing could never perish.
Nor can their destruction arise from another cause, for that position cannot withstand logical analysis.
For when that [destruction] arises, is it non-different from the entity or different? It cannot first be non-different, because of the difference in their causes.
If it were different, then once it has arisen, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the entity being perceived as before.
Even if one imagines that it is "concealed" by it, the same dilemma applies regarding that very concealment; so enough of this over-elaboration.
On this point, some offer the following explanation:

"If those two [the perceived object and the cognition] are mutually blended at the end and grasped as one, then the perceptual cognition called 'recognition' (pratyabhijñā) obstructs the inference of momentary destruction.
However, this is not correct here.

These two cognitions, consisting of grasping and recollection, operate respectively upon the "mere-that" (tanmātra) and the "mere-this" (idantāmātra); they are not capable of manifesting the object as existing at the same time as the conjunction of both [aspects], because that would contradict experience.
For just as an object with non-distinct space and time appears as a unity, so too here, even though space and time are distinct, it flashes forth as a single unity.
And since such an emergence of consciousness cannot occur without a single cognition, this very cognition must be accepted as one.
To establish the effect as a matter of conviction, even a cause that is not [otherwise] perceived must be postulated;
however, one should not, by failing to observe the cause, consider the reversal of a clearly seen effect.

Therefore, although such a cognition cannot arise from the sense organ alone, nor from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) alone—which has acquired its birth through the intensity of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) derived from a previous experience—nevertheless, the teachers [hold] that this effect arises when those two have reached a different state through their mutual conjunction. But even this is not correct.
It is not the case that it is not perception at all.

For even though it possesses a connection with mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), its arising is dependent upon the operation of the sense faculties; and because there is no distinction between this [recognition] occurring at the time of the first encounter and those [cognitions] such as "this is the same as that" which are accepted as perception, there is no evidence whatsoever that this is a fallacy of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*).

Because there is an absence of any subsequent cognition that perceives either a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) or a defect in the cause, it cannot be maintained that this very [subsequent] inference is the subverter; for that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Indeed, as long as this [perceptual] cognition remains unsubverted, the inference itself is unable to arise; yet once the inference has arisen, this [perception] becomes subverted. Thus, the state of mutual causality is quite clear.
Furthermore, the condition of having an uncontradicted object is also a cause for the arising of inference;
otherwise, why would one not infer coldness in fire?
[Objection: But if that is so, then how is it that the oneness of flames and the like—which have been determined [by perception]—is established through inference as being distinct?
Here they proclaim the essence of the established doctrine:
all things consist of both the universal and the particular.
In this regard, while the perception of fire in a flame and the like has the universal as its object, inference has the particular as its object; thus, these two operate within distinct domains.

Since there is no contradiction between perception and inference, perception does not obstruct the emergence of inference. But how, one might ask, can a non-momentary entity perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) sequentially? To this we reply: that entity, indeed, being characterized by a specific state produced through the conjunction of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), accomplishes its respective causal efficiency only in a sequential manner.
Now, one might ask: "Is a distinction produced by the auxiliary causes that is either distinct or non-distinct [from the entity]?
And the refutations regarding this state of being subject to conceptual differentiation have already been set forth here previously.

In this case as well, those very same [arguments] serve as the determinants... unless, indeed, there were this absolute position of ours: that all things are exclusively distinct, or not distinct at all; rather, we maintain that both difference and non-difference exist in all entities.

In this regard, the objections arising from the possibility of difference have been refuted by recourse to non-difference, and those based on non-difference have been refuted by recourse to difference. But one might ask: how can these two, difference and non-difference, which are contradictory, be established together in a single place?
To this he replies: These two are not contradictory, because they are observed together.
For contradiction is characterized by the impossibility of coexistence.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the fact that non-abiding is the basis for perception;
however, this [position] is not approved by the Teachers, as it is merely "delightful when left unexamined.
For he [the Teacher] did not see that identity and difference cannot possibly coexist in one and the same place.
Because of contradiction;
for the simultaneous perception of those two is not possible. Indeed, the perception of a single form is precisely what constitutes the non-perception of difference.
The perception of a distinct form is the observation of difference.

In that case, just as one single form is perceived, so too there is no perception of a distinct form; and when a distinct form is perceived, it is not the case that the perception of a single form does not exist. Therefore, based on the distinction between difference and non-difference, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) cannot be established.

Nor is there a contradiction with recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) or inference (*anumāna*), because it is recognition itself that must be examined. For instance, in the case of mother-of-pearl, one perceives: "This is that very silver."
And since that [cognition] is indeed based on the non-apprehension of difference due to similarity, an investigation is appropriate here as well.

In that case, for one who investigates and determines an object to be momentary through the non-occurrence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it is concluded that this is a deception consisting in the occurrence of a similar subsequent [moment]. And for one who reflects, there occurs a subversion of even a cognition that has arisen through the force of inference regarding fire and so forth.

Furthermore, the perception of heat in things such as fire, though examined, cannot be accounted for otherwise; thus, there is no arising of an inference based on error (*viparyaya*). Therefore, enough with this [discussion] which has fallen into the form of a farce... Let those who have seen the further shore of the ocean of the profound and weighty systems of philosophy now state their own resolution. Regarding objects such as a jar that were first experienced, and which are subsequently perceived again after having been interrupted by concealment or other factors, there arises the cognition: "This is that very same thing."

In that case, if causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) were somehow possible even for a stable entity, then why would one postulate this delusion of non-difference based on the non-apprehension of difference?

Furthermore, causal efficiency can indeed occur sequentially even for a stable entity, provided it possesses specific qualities such as actions and so forth, which arise from particular auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
Moreover, that specific quality is indeed distinct from the entity itself, yet it is the agent of the causal efficiency.
And it is not the case that the very same entity remains as the producer of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*) after having become a mere existent; this is clear.

Thus, its status as a means (*sādhanatā*) consists precisely in its being permeated by a specific characteristic (*vidhiviśeṣa*), such that the emergence of causal efficiency occurs immediately thereafter. It is precisely through its connection with that specific characteristic that worldly people employ the conventional designation of "means" regarding entities. But how can this be a characteristic of that [entity], even if it is cast aside? Because it is inferred solely on the basis of being its substrate (*āśraya*).

But how is it that [the cognition] has that very thing as its basis? Let your honor desist, considering that [the cognition] arises from the perception of its own cause. Enough of our following you here.
Now, why is the difference between entities not inferred? We reply: because it is consistent with recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
Inference should follow what has been observed; let the occurrence of what is seen be taken into account.

Just as causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritā*) is observed, so too is this [efficacy] seen even in a stable entity (*sthāvara*); therefore, an inference consistent with that is appropriate. Consequently, since the pervader—namely, the sequence or simultaneity [of actions]—is not excluded even in a stable entity, the non-perception of the pervader is unestablished (*asiddha*). Because there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against the contrary when it is unestablished, momentariness cannot prove existence merely by its own connection [to it], because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, existence is not merely the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), but rather the fitness for connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃbandhayogyatā*). And this fitness for connection with a means of valid cognition is itself the existence of intrinsic nature (*svarūpasattā*). Therefore, there is nothing objectionable in saying that even that which does not perform a causal function exists.

Even that perception of destruction which occurs regarding an object while it is still present—being devoid of any dependence on other factors—is seen to crumble away when scrutinized, like a golden ornament [that turns out to be brass].
Now, what exactly do you venerable sirs intend by "destruction"?
If you say that destruction is "non-existence through annihilation" (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), then what, again, is this "non-existence through annihilation"?

If it is argued that the cognition regarding an entity— such as "curd does not exist in milk"— is a refutation of the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*), then the principle arising from the digit of nectar (*amṛtakalā*) must be extracted.

For there is no cognition [of the form] "it does not exist"; rather, when there is the perception of the atoms of the very form of curd—which is self-luminous—there is merely the application of the word "non-existence" to that milk. Thus, in that state, there is the apprehension of the atoms of the form of curd alone.
Nor is milk alone the cause with respect to that [effect] independently;
for even when other causes are not present, milk alone is perceived. Nor can it be said that this is a different milk altogether.
Because recognition does not prove non-difference.
[Objection: But if there were a dependence on another reason, the "being heard" (śrutābhavitva) would not be established.
From what is this "being heard" understood?

If it is argued that [destruction occurs] "from perception" (*darśanāt*), then there will necessarily be another cause for it. Nor are we fools, such that we would be afraid of such a claim. As for this further point—that even for entities that are perishable by their own causes, if destruction were dependent on another cause, then even when that distinct cause has arisen, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the entity being perceived as before—[we reply]: [This is not so. For destruction is observed to occur even in the absence of a cause, as in the case of a lamp-flame, a cloud, or a sound. Furthermore, since the very nature (*svabhāva*) of things is such that they do not persist for a second moment, what need is there for another cause? Moreover, if destruction were caused by something else, then because that cause is absent in the case of a lamp-flame and the like, those too would not be destroyed. Therefore, destruction is indeed inherent in the nature of things. And since it is impossible for a thing to exist simultaneously with its own destruction, it follows that the entity perishes immediately upon arising. Thus, the argument that "destruction is causeless" is established. As for the objection regarding the non-perception of the cause of destruction: that is unfounded, because the cause of destruction is not perceived due to its subtlety, just as the eye is not perceived by the eye itself. Alternatively, it may be that the cause of destruction is not perceived because it is not a substance (*dravya*), just as the universal (*sāmānya*) is not perceived. Or, it may be that the cause of destruction is not perceived because it is not a quality (*guṇa*), just as color is not perceived by touch. Or, it may be that the cause of destruction is not perceived because it is not a motion (*karman*), just as the mind is not perceived by the sense of touch. Or, it may be that the cause of destruction is not perceived because it is not a particularity (*viśeṣa*), just as the specific individuality (*antya-viśeṣa*) is not perceived. Or, it may be that the cause of destruction is not perceived because it is not an inherence (*samavāya*), just as the relation between a whole and its parts (*avayavāvayavin*) is not perceived. Or, it may be that the cause of destruction is not perceived because it is not a non-existence (*abhāva*), just as the prior non-existence (*prāg-abhāva*) is not perceived. Or, it may be that the cause of destruction is not perceived because it is not a negation (*pratiṣedha*), just as the mutual negation (*itaretara-abhāva*) is not perceived. Or, it may be that the cause of destruction is not perceived because it is not a substance-quality-motion-particularity-inherence-non-existence-negation, just as the absence of all these categories is not perceived. Or, it may be that the cause of destruction is not perceived because it is not a substance, nor a quality, nor a motion, nor a universal, nor a particularity, nor an inherence, nor a prior
