To this it is replied:
the principle of "the superior [element] overcomes" applies; having set aside the milk of those such as the *kṣamavatī*, [it applies to] the *khaṭvā* and so forth.
The expiation applies only when the cake is completely burnt.
For the occasion for which the scripture prescribes it has indeed been reached, namely: "the two sacrificial cakes are burnt.
This refers to the complete burning of the cake, not to its partial burning.
Nor can it be completed with a portion that is deficient, because such deficiency is unavoidable.
Now, as for what was said— that completion is observed even with a deficient oblation when that sacrifice is concluded— it is replied:
The expiation applies when the number [of offerings] is completed.
Even if that rite is concluded with another oblation, there is still an expiation; thus, there is no fault.
If it is argued that this is because of the word "oblation" (*havis*), [we reply:]...
Commentary: If it is argued that [the rite] is concluded with another oblation, this is not so;
because of the word *tad* (that).

In this context, the word *havis* (oblation) occurs in the expression, "When that oblation is completed. If [the rite] were to be completed by means of one oblation after another, the word *havis* would not be applicable.
Therefore, the word *havis* must refer to the sacrifice itself, because of its connection with the characteristic mark of that [sacrifice].
Commentary: The word *havis* (oblation) refers to that which is used in sacrifice. Therefore, "that rite should conclude" means that the ritual action denoted by the word *havis* should conclude.
Now, it may be argued that a secondary (metaphorical) sense is accepted only in the absence of a primary sense, and not otherwise.
It is said: this is simply the absence of a primary [application].
How so? Because if that ritual action were to be completed, the sentence "with that oblation" would be split.
And it would be non-expressive;
for by means of the *phala* (the fruit/remainder) the rite is completed, not by the oblation (*havis*).
Therefore, the counting is the occasion [for the action].

The phrase "that being so" (*tadvati*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). And from this restatement, it is understood that the expiation applies even when a ritual action involving other sacrificial oblations (*havis*) has been completed.
But how can the word *havis* refer to the ritual action? It is because of its association with the characteristic marks (*liṅga*) of that action.
The action connected with the oblation is understood by the word "oblation" (havis) because it possesses the designation of "oblation.
Just as a lion is indicated by the act of roaring which is connected to Devadatta,
so too is the action indicated by the oblation.

Therefore, the expiation applies when [the fire] is entirely emaciated. Soma says: When the fire has baked the potsherds to their proper degree and the sprinkling of water and so forth have reached the required measure, then even from a slight burning, the production of the cooked result fit for consumption occurs.

But when cooking and so forth are not of such a nature, then in some cases there is inedibility due to the burning of many parts, and in other cases there is inedibility of one portion due to the total burning of that single object; thus, since in all instances partial burning is invariably concomitant with a cooking process resulting in inedibility, it is impossible to speak of a partial burning distinct from that [inevitable process] as being the cause.

And thus, in that case, while the middle, the front, and the rear portions are completely burnt, the portion from this side is cooked and fit for consumption. Even there, since only the specific places for the cuttings (*avadāna*) of the middle, front, and rear remain, and these lack the nature of sacrificial oblation (*havis*) themselves—given that the sacrificial oblation consists of the *puroḍāśa* cake itself, which still exists—one should offer by making two cuttings from whatever part remains intact. Nor should it be argued that, because the oblation itself would be absent if everything were burnt, the statement "when that [offering] is completed" would be untenable.

Because the word *tadviḥ* (that sacrifice) refers to the sacrifice itself through the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that whose sacrificial offering is the *puroḍāśa*," and because a sacrifice possesses the designation of a "completion" (*saṃsthā*), even in the case of the destruction of all [offerings], the completion of the sacrifice characterized by that *dvirājya* is possible on the basis of the scriptural statement, "That whose sacrificial offerings are all [destroyed]. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
Vi— "In the case of *kṣāma*, the sacrifice [is completed] with two [offerings]; or, in the case of total burning, as before, with two."

Because the burning of a portion is constant, there would be a repeated performance [of the rite] whenever any burning occurs. The Bhaṭṭas [hold]: "When both *puroḍāśa* cakes of one [sacrificer] are burnt, Varuṇa seizes him; when that sacrifice is concluded, then he should offer that very same oblation. In this scripturally prescribed expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the burning of the entire *puroḍāśa* is indeed the occasion (*nimitta*).
This is because, when the oblation is cooked by fire, the burning of a single part is unavoidable.
Nor can the burning of only a portion [of the oblation] be the occasion for the rite, because it is impossible to determine precisely what that portion is.

Nor can it be argued that since the scripture states, "It concludes with that," one understands from the remaining oblation that the sacrifice continues, and thus only the burning of a single part is the occasion; for we observe everywhere that such expressions are used only when the performance is complete, and therefore, by implication (*lakṣaṇā*), it must be understood here as well that the occasion is the completion of the performance itself.
Consequently, this expiation in the form of a renewed performance applies only when the entire oblation is burnt.

"Whatever sacrificial offering (*havis*) may be burnt, one should offer another at that very time"—from this statement of Āpastamba, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the burning of the whole [offering].

Furthermore, because Āpastamba prescribes a re-performance (*punarprayoga*) "if one should not be able [to complete the rite] from the portions cut off" (*avadāna*), an expiation is untenable in the case of the burning of a portion insufficient for the cutting of portions; for such a partial burning is already accounted for by that rule.

Therefore, even though the burning of a single portion can be determined, the possibility of an expiation in that case arises from the very Vedic text (*śruti*) which is the source of this [Āpastamba] rule.

In the case of such a burning of the sacrificial ground, however, according to the principle of the destruction of the substratum (*prāktananāśādhikaraṇanyāya*), the completion of the ritual procedure is achieved merely by means of clarified butter (*ājya*) or by what remains after the burning.

Likewise, in the event of the total failure (*sarvakṣāma*) of the offering, the completion of the procedure should be understood as being effected either by clarified butter or by the production of another sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
Maṇḍana states: "In this case of total failure, there is an injunction for the performance [to be done] with clarified butter."
Śaṅkara says: "It is for the sake of all the moments (kṣaṇas).
When Kṣāmavatī and the others occur within the middle of the ritual sequence (tantra), there is a displacement (utkarṣa)."

"One should not offer another oblation; one should sacrifice on the full moon day itself when it has dawned"—by this [text], the prohibition of another sacrifice between the *anvādhāna* (preliminary rite) and the principal sacrifice applies to all [sacrifices] because there is no distinction.
This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin replies]: for it is not proper to commence another ritual action while the previous ritual action has already been set in motion.
Therefore, it is not the case that the permanent (*nitya*) or optional (*kāmya*) rite is what is attained here;

rather, it is specifically the occasional (*naimittika*) rite, because this prohibition applies by extension (*prasaṅga*) to it, as it occurs upon the presence of another specific occasion (*nimitta*).

• A sky-flower:
"That which does not have the nature of coming into being, or that which has the state of being eternal,
cannot be something produced (i.e., cannot be the object of the act of making), just like a sky-flower or space."

For indeed, only that which is already in the process of being produced, or whose production is possible, when employed by another agent, is determined as being the object of the action, and not anything else.
And thus, no one is ever observed to be making a sky-flower or the ether (ākāśa). Vākyapadīya 2.1.11, p. 377.
• Regarding "sky-flower" (*khapuṣpa*):

since no connection is perceived from the word *khapuṣpa* alone when it is not in a compound, one must admit that the connection with the sky-flower is delimited by the compound. Furthermore, the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is what is expressed by the compound.

Furthermore, since the conjunction of the sky with a flower is not perceived through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the analytical compound (*vigraha*) "there is a flower of the sky" is untenable; and since no compound is perceived in the sense of the sentence "there is no flower of the sky," the primary meaning (*mukhya-artha*) of the word *khapuṣpa* is simply the non-existence of a sky-flower (Su.

p. 505). [Objection: But surely, because flowers in the sky and the like lack qualities invariably concomitant with their own referents, there would follow the impossibility of figurative usage (*gauṇa-prayoga*).
[Reply: No.
"Since the nature of a sky-flower is superimposed [upon it], how can that [self] be a non-entity?

Regarding the usage such as "the Ātman stands in the place of a sky-flower" or "a sky-flower is your established doctrine," which among these is the sky-flower that is determined as something other than [the self] and thus superimposed?
Therefore, one must admit that the very essence of a sky-flower itself is of the nature of a superimposition.

Nor is there any perception in the world of this [term] as being secondary (gauṇa), because it possesses a primary referent; and because it is the first cognition [of its object], the form of "sky-flower" and so forth does not lose its primary status. ... For no cognition of a real nature arises regarding a sky-flower and the like.
Furthermore, when there is the apprehension of a form that is a different entity [from the object], no connection with a sky-flower or the like is apprehended.
Vākyapadīya 1.4.123–1, p. 359.
*The Maxim of the Sky-Flower*.
It is stated in the *Pīyūṣadhārā* (Sāhasrī 561) that the observation of an increase in lunar days (*tithi*) within a fortnight is equivalent to the logic of a "sky-flower" (*khapuṣpa*).
This is the investigation of the sky-flower.

In such cases as "the sky-flower is the established tenet," because things like sky-flowers have never been previously experienced, one is unable to define them as being "like this"; thus, since there is the possibility of superimposition upon the tenet and so forth, the status of being figurative (gauṇatva) does not arise.

Now, even though a "sky-flower" (*khapuṣpa*) is not established as a collective entity (*samudāyatva*) therein, because the word *khapuṣpa* is etymological (*yaugika*), one may take recourse to the well-known [meaning] of "flower in the sky" (*viśvakalita*). Having accepted that the flower—which is well-known to reside in its own substratum—is superimposed upon a creeper (*latā*) and so forth through the relation of being the locus of such superimposition, and having thereby accepted it as the referent of the compound *khapuṣpa*, it is said that the word *khapuṣpa* is figurative (*gauṇa*) in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) due to that superimposition. If this were the case, then since the word *khapuṣpa* would function with a meaning consisting of a superimposed relation, the word *khapuṣpa* would result in being figurative only with respect to the creeper and the flower which serve as the substrata for that [superimposition].
Nor is this an unintended consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*); for that [instrumentality] is not perceived as being figurative (*gauṇa*).

For this very reason, even the definition of "object" (*artha*)—consisting in being the locus of superimposition and being the instrument—is not applicable to the creeper and the flower, because even that possesses the status of being a locus of superimposition, and thus its figurative nature is established by virtue of its having a real substrate (*sārthāśraya*).
(Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa, *Vyutpattivāda*, 1.4.123, p. 374).

By superimposing the relationship with the sky upon the flower and so forth, and thereby accepting the referent of the term *khapuṣpa* (sky-flower) as something superimposed, and because its qualities—such as non-existence—are established in the final doctrine (*siddhānta*), there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "The sky-flower is your final doctrine" regarding the definition of the secondary (*gauṇa*).
(Mahābhāṣyadīpikā 1.4.123, p. 377).

(Now, an objection is raised: "In cases where a proponent employs the expression 'The sky-flower is your established doctrine' (*khapuṣpaṃ bhavasiddhāntaḥ*) for the purpose of demonstrating the absolute non-existence of the opponent's tenet, since sky-flowers and the like lack any connection with the qualities of a primary referent due to their absolute non-existence, one must admit that their being figurative (*gauṇatva*) consists solely in having a superimposed meaning. [Response: How then can words such as "sky-flower" be figurative in expressions like "The sky-flower is your established doctrine"?
For they have no primary denotation (*mukhyam abhidheyam*), by virtue of which they could be figurative through similarity (*sādṛśya*). It is said in reply:
(For one who maintains that [words] have superimposed meanings indeed accepts figurative usage because of the superimposition of a primary meaning onto something else.

Thus, since it is possible to superimpose non-existent things such as sky-flowers onto something else, he states that this same objection applies even to that view: If these [non-existent things] have no denotable object, how then can there be a superimposition from elsewhere?
For that which does not exist in its own nature cannot be superimposed upon another.

(Objection: Because it is not the ultimate [reality], he says—) Therefore, that very form must be accepted as superimposed (*āropita*). Consequently, since even that which is superimposed possesses primacy (*mukhyatva*), the analysis of a sky-flower [applies] to the carving [of a pillar] at the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*).

It is appropriate that in other cases [the term] is used figuratively. For primacy is not established by being non-superimposed; rather, it is established by the employment of a word without regard for either [of two possible referents].
And the sense is that this is possible even for that which is superimposed.

Furthermore, if the proponent of the "superimposed meaning" (āropitārthatva) does not accept figurative usage (*gauṇatva*) by taking the superimposition of the primary meaning onto another object in order to avoid the counter-argument previously stated, but instead accepts it by taking the superimposed meaning itself, then he states the fault: "In your view, however, the word 'sky-flower' would be figurative only with respect to a sky-flower [itself], because it expresses a superimposed thing.
If it is argued, "Let it be so," we say no, because that would contradict all worldly convention.
Therefore, superimposition is not the definition of figurative usage.
However, there is a similarity in terms of their own referents.
Even regarding things such as "sky-flowers" (*khapuṣpa*), worldly people employ figurative usage precisely with the intention of expressing a primary similarity.

For example, the transformation of space into the nature of a flower, or of the parts situated on the head of a hare into horns, is utterly unknown and lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).

"Likewise, the established conclusion regarding existence (*bhavasiddhānta*)"—by this passage [the author] refutes the objection: "Since it is space alone that serves as the counter-correlate of similarity (*sādṛśyapratiyogitva*), and not space in its own right (*svarūpeṇa*) as the counter-correlate of similarity, but rather as a modification (*vikāra*) of flowers and the like; and since even that which is near [to being a modification], such as a flower, exists in its own right (*svarūpeṇa sattvāt*), how can that which is absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsataḥ*) function as the determiner of similarity? Thus, the doubt is dispelled.

Śā. Soma. 1.4.12, p. 85: Since the word *khapuṣpa* (sky-flower) has as its meaning the nature of a conjunction between "sky" and "flower," it would follow that the sky-flower itself is the secondary (gauṇa) referent.
Consequently, by virtue of being the object of a secondary verbal function (*gauṇa-śabda-vṛtti*), it would be the superimposed (*āropya*) sky-flower itself that would have to be considered secondary.

What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? They should be performed in order to favor the injunction.
This being the case, we say that regarding the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*), there is no carving, nor the pouring of earth (*paryūha*) and so forth.

There would be a refutation of others' views; for it is such [an object] that is enjoined to perform the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Indeed, when the function of the sacrificial post is assigned to that which has become a threshing-floor fence (*khalevālī*), the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled.
Once the purpose of the scripture has been accomplished, one need not strive for another quality;
moreover, the carving and so forth are for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*),
and there is no further requirement for the post here.
For the *ayūpa* (non-post) must be employed for the function of the sacrificial post;
therefore, acts such as carving and so forth should not be performed.
This is also because of the prohibition.
Commentary: For this reason as well, they should not be made.
A contradiction would arise if they were made, [namely] that of the carpenter with the *khalevālī*.
That piece of wood which has been set up in the threshing floor to ward off [animals] is the *khalevālī*.
It should be taken up with exactly such [a piece].
If carving were performed [on it], it would perish, and a different interval would arise; whereas the prevention [of this] has already occurred in the threshing-floor.
Approval (*joṣaṇa*), however, occurs only at the time of the *bhṛgu* [rite].
That [term] *joṣita* is used in another sense;
for it is the "acceptance" (*joṣaṇa*) of trees that is meant, not of a modification.
Furthermore, "cutting down" (*uccūyaṇa*) is simply impossible in the case of something that has grown high (*ucchritāyāḥ*).

Therefore, [one might argue that] carving and so forth should not be performed. Soma [responds]: "Even when using a pre-existing *khalevālī* (a threshing-post), carving and so forth must be performed because they are possible"—this is the connection [of the objection]. As for the meaning of the *sūtra*, however, it is the prohibition of others, such as cutting and so forth.
Vi— "In the case of the *khalevālī*, there should be the selection, cutting, carving, and raising;
or rather, they should not exist, because [the rule] applies by extension (*codaka*), and because otherwise there would be both futility and contradiction."
"Because of futility and contradiction, acts such as *joṣaṇā* (smoothing) should not be performed.

[The Bhaṭṭa replies: This is the answer for one who maintains that even though cutting is discontinued because the *khalevālī* (threshing-floor post) is taken exactly as it is found, acts such as carving (*takṣaṇa*) do not cease;
furthermore, carving and the like are omitted due to the absence of purpose.

For, if their purpose is indeed seen to be smoothing and so forth, then since that [smoothing] exists as being already accomplished by the very act of using the threshing-floor post (*khalevāraṇa*), it is established through *prasaṅga* (incidental application); thus, there is no need for the separate performance of carving and other such acts.

However, if—on the other hand—it has been established that the purpose of the rites to be performed at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is to produce the transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*) nature of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and since in the present case the prescription of wood used for the *khalevāraṇa* necessitates the sublation of properties such as cutting and so forth, the status of being a sacrificial post cannot be achieved due to the absence of the requisite totality of factors (*sāmagrī*).

In the case of the *khalevālī* (the threshing-floor post), the tethering of the animal is indeed something unprecedented; therefore, there is all the more reason for the absence of ritual elements such as carving and those to be performed during the period of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
For this very reason, there is also no sharpening (*aṇaśrīkaraṇa*).

As for the burying (*nilayana*) and raising (*ucchrayaṇa*), although the essential form of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is absent when these are not performed at the time of initiation, they are nonetheless unnecessary because their purpose is accomplished through incidental application (*prasaṅga*), since the *sādyaska* sacrifice is prescribed to be performed at the very spot where the *khalevālī* stands.

Maṇḍana: "In this case, there should be no planing and so forth. Śaṅkara: "When the purpose is absent, as in the case of the *khalevālī* (the hitching post for the oxen), [the ritual acts] such as selecting the wood (*joṣaṇa*) need not be performed."
The performance of the consecratory rites, such as the pouring around (paryūha), takes place at the threshing-floor post (khalevālī).

Now, [one might argue that] the status of being a *saṃskāra* (consecration) would apply even in the case of non-existence. The Bhāṣya states: There is doubt regarding the *khalevālī* (the threshing-floor post) itself: should the ritual acts performed on the ground with the staff of Maitrāvaruṇa—such as sprinkling with water, smearing with ghee, and anointing—be performed, or not? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? They should not be performed.

It has been stated that there must be a prohibition of others. Just as the exclusion of cattle occurs in a threshing floor, exactly such [an animal] should be employed for the purpose of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). It is not a sacrificial post.
And the consecrations (saṃskāras) obtained through the extended application (codaka) are for the purpose of the sacrificial post (yūpa), as they are prescribed in relation to it.
This being the prima facie view, we reply:

in the absence of the purpose—that is, in the absence of the function—if there is no function for the threshing-floor post (khalevālī) by means of those consecrations, then the sacrificial post alone would be the occasion for them; they would not apply to the threshing-floor post.
In this case, however, there is an equal action with the [sacrificial] grounds, and by means of the water and the wooden post (*khalevālī*), firmness must be achieved through powerful attention.
For that [firmness] would indeed become loose if it were merely by means of a threshing-floor post (*khalevārana*).
And thus, the term *khalevālī* is not applicable.
Therefore, they must be performed.
Even the application of collyrium, which is non-injurious and obtained through the force of the injunction, when performed, would lead to an additional excellence rather than a defect;
therefore, for this reason as well, it must be performed.
The connection [of this section] is established by the statement that acts such as the carving of the *soma* and the sprinkling (*paryūhaṇa*) do not apply to the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*).

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: "In the absence of a purpose, there would be a cessation [of the rite] regarding the threshing-floor post, because one would have to resort to its being for the sake of an unseen consecration (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*) like that of a sacrificial post; however, here there is no absence of a purpose.
Viśvarūpa states: "Acts such as the sprinkling and the anointing would either not take place or they would, just as in the previous case."
It would not exist; however, because it does not contradict what is seen and what is merely unseen, it must exist.

Those acts whose purpose is visible—such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and others like final sprinkling (*pariṣecana*)—are indeed to be performed on the *khalevālī* (the threshing-post used as a sacrificial post). This is because they are not to be performed at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), and thus they do not serve the purpose of producing the [wooden] sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Furthermore, since there is no loss of purpose (*arthalopa*) regarding the material of the post itself, their performance is desired on the *khalevālī* by virtue of being prompted by the tethering of the animal, which is the means for accomplishing the animal sacrifice.
In this same way, sprinkling and other such acts should be understood to apply to the final sprinkling as well.
Maṇḍana says: "Anointing and so forth should take place upon it."
Śaṅkara: "In this context, it would be for the sake of the direct meaning.

Here, in the case of the *khalevālī* (the threshing-post), there is no restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the natural *khadira*-wood [of the sacrificial post], nor is there a restrictive rule that the rice grains used in the *citraidha* sacrifice must be produced from either *vrīhi* or *yava*."
"In the case of a conflict, there should be an omission of the original qualities because of that specific statement, and because of the connection with the ritual action.
Commentary: Regarding the *sādyaskra* sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "The threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) becomes the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

In this regard, a doubt arises: is the *khalevālī* to be made of *khadira* wood as obtained by the general rule, or is it not so obtained, such that the *khalevālī* may be made of *khadira*, *bilva*, or other woods?
Similarly, regarding the Citrā sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "Curd, honey, ghee, milk, parched grain, water, and rice—these mixed together constitute the offering to Prajāpati.

In this case as well, there is a doubt: are rice grains obtained by the word *vrīhi* (rice), such that rice grains must be used; or are they not so obtained, such that rice grains from any source, whether large or small, may be taken?
What, then, is the prima facie view? Just as a threshing-floor post made of *khadira* wood is to be used [as the sacrificial post], so rice grains produced from rice plants must be used.
By the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), *khadira* wood and *vrīhi* rice would be obtained;
thus, there will be favor shown to the *codaka*.
Once these have been obtained, the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) is enjoined: "That which is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) must be made into a threshing-floor post."
For it is possible to make a threshing-post (*khalevālī*) into a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), but a threshing-post can never become a sacrificial post by any means whatsoever.
Indeed, a sacrificial post is made from *khadira* wood and other such timbers through consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as cutting and so forth; it is not made from others.
In that context, the statement "it becomes a sacrificial post" would mean that it performs the function of a sacrificial post; thus, the word would involve figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Even in the case of rice, the grains are already obtained through the water;
once they have become that [rice), their state as flour is indicated, and then the connection with the deity is established.
Therefore, the *khadira* wood and so forth must be brought to the state of being a threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*).
And the rice grains are to be reduced to the state of husked rice.
This being the case, we reply:
in the event of this contradiction, there shall be the omission of the original (archetypal) quality.
How is there a contradiction? Because of that statement.
It is the state of being a sacrificial post (*yūpatā*) that is enjoined for the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*), not the state of being a threshing-floor post for the sacrificial post.
This being so, because of its connection with the immediately preceding verb *bhavati*, it constitutes a direct syntactical sentence (*pratyakṣaṃ vākyam*).
Otherwise, [the connection] would be indirect and thus remote.
The word *khalevālī* denotes that which functions in the prevention [of cattle] in a threshing floor (*khala*).
And such a thing is enjoined for the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) by the statement: "That which is a *khalevālī*, that is the sacrificial post."
And it is possible to employ [the term] for the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
As for the claim that the word *yūpa* is intended to indicate its function by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), even such indication is preferable over mediation;
for indication is direct, whereas a syntactical connection (*vākya*) involving mediation is remote.

Therefore, the threshing-floor post (khalevālī) should be employed for the function of a sacrificial post (yūpa) of the same species as the tree from which it was made. The general injunction (codaka) is not able to restrict it to a specific [other] species;
otherwise, the direct Vedic revelation (pratyakṣa-śruti) would be sublated by that injunction.

"Therefore, there is a restrictive rule regarding the *khadira* wood and so forth. [Durga says: "'The state of being a threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) is not enjoined for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), because [in that case] there would be a direct sentence due to its connection with the immediately preceding verb *bhavati*;
otherwise, by connection with a remote [verb], it would be an indirect [sentence]'—this refutation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is incorrect."
How so? This sequence is a property of the word; with respect to the meaning, the word is subordinate, and with respect to the word, the sequence is subordinate.
Therefore, only that meaning which is the denoted object of the word should be grasped (because it is primary).
And the sequence should be disregarded, as it is a property of the word (being subordinate to the meaning).
Therefore, the refutation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) as stated [previously] is incorrect; it is explained otherwise [as follows]:
If, by means of a reference to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the state of being a *khalevālī* (a threshing-post) were enjoined, the injunction would result in an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*).
However, if the function of the sacrificial post is enjoined for the *khalevālī*, its purpose is indeed visible: namely, the prevention of the cattle from wandering away.
Therefore, since [the Siddhānta] has a perceptible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatvāt*), the sentence remains exactly as it was heard (*yathāśrutam eva*) through an immediate connection;

the Siddhānta does not result from the postulation of an immediate [connection] that was not originally there. If so, how is this passage of the Bhāṣya to be understood? The answer is: as a supplementary addition (*upacayatvena*).

(What is meant is this: And there is another merit (obtained in the Siddhānta), namely, that [the term *khalevālī*] has a connection with the immediately preceding verb *bhavati*. Soma—here, one who knows the *adhikaraṇa* (topic) has a doubt as to whether the archetypal [requirements], such as being made of *khadira* wood and so forth, apply or not.

Is the formulation of the statement: "That which is a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) must be made into a threshing-post (*khalevālī*)," or is its meaning: "That which is a threshing-post is a sacrificial post"? This is the doubt.

As in the previous case, here too the connection [of the topic] is established by the statement that there is no sublation of the injunction (*codaka*). As for the meaning of the Sūtra: when there is a conflict and doubt arises, there should be the cessation of the archetypal quality (*prākṛtaguṇa*), such as being made of *khadira* wood, because of the specific scriptural statement regarding the *khalevālī*—namely, the statement that it serves as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)—and because of the word *khalevālī* [applied to the threshing-floor beam]. (Mīmāṃsākośa 193; Khalevālī-śabda 1538).
Regarding the rice-grains at the *khalevālī*: the archetypal... [text fragment].

Because of the statement regarding its being made of *gāgīya* wood, and because of the connection with ritual acts such as tying [the animal] by means of that substance—the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) and so forth—it follows:
"Is the *khalevālī* and the rice [to be made of] *khadira* wood or not?
It is indeed *khadira*, because it is designated for the purpose of functioning as the primary [substance] for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)."

In the case of threshing and so forth, even when performed with large grains, it must be done because of the direct scriptural statement; let it be understood as being characterized by the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Since there is no connection with the deity through the oblation (*havis*), there is no extended application (*atideśana*) here.
Therefore, the quality of being made of *khadira* wood cannot be restricted to these two [the sacrificial post and the threshing-floor fence].

In the *Bhāṭṭasādhyaka*, it is heard in scripture: "The threshing-floor fence (*khalevālī*) becomes the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). In that case, there arises the inquiry: does the *khadira* nature, obtained through extension (*atideśa*), cease to apply or not? Similarly, regarding the *Citra-iṣṭi*: "Curd, honey, ghee, milk, parched grain, water, and rice—these mixed together are for Prajāpati. Here, the inquiry is whether or not the application of *vrīhi* rice to the rice-grains ceases. Regarding the first example, the threshing-floor fence is not enjoined as being established in its current state to perform the function of the sacrificial post, because that would entail a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the function by the word "post" (*yūpa*).

However, with reference to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the state of being a threshing-post (*khalevālītva*)—which consists of the act of warding off [cattle] from the threshing floor—is enjoined as a preparatory refinement (*saṃskāraka*).

Nor is there any fault in accepting a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) because it would otherwise result in an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), for according to the principle of the *Niṣādasthapati* section, such a figurative interpretation is not a defect.

Therefore, having prepared the sacrificial post out of *khadira* wood itself, as prescribed by the archetype (*prakṛti*), one must bring about its state as a threshing-post precisely within the course of the ritual performance.

Or, let it be that there is indeed an injunction for the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) itself with reference to the function of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*); even so, since the quality of being made of *khadira* wood is obtained through "transference of position" (*sthānāpatti*) along with the other properties, that very *khalevālī* which was previously made of *khadira* must be taken. Likewise, in the case of the rice grains, there is a restriction to *vrīhi* and other specific grains by virtue of the extended application (*codaka*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: first of all, there is no injunction of the *khalevālī*-ness with reference to the sacrificial post; for if the word *khalevālī* itself were to provide the object of the injunction (*uddeśya*), then there would be a violation of the principle of "single thrust" (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*).

If, however, the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) were used, then—since there can be no mutual non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between two nominative case endings—the word *khalevālī* would necessarily involve secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This would be required both to convey the meaning of the verbal cognition "one should effect the sacrificial post by means of being a threshing-floor-enclosure" (*khalevālītvena yūpaṃ bhāvayet*), and to establish that "being a threshing-floor-enclosure" (*khalevālītva*) is the qualifier within the word *khalevālī*. Nor can it be argued that such indication does not apply here, as in the case of "the staff-bearer recites the *praisha* formulas" (*daṇḍī praipān vāha*); for in that instance, although the person qualified by the staff is understood as the agent in the verbal cognition, the injunction is properly restricted to the staff alone through the principle of distinguishing between what is already established and what is not (*prāptāprāpta-viveka*).

In the present case, however, since it is impossible for the *khalevālī* (the threshing-floor post) to be connected as the substance itself within a single productive operation (*bhāvanā*) directed toward the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), one must necessarily assert that the state of being a *khalevālī* is connected to the *bhāvanā*.

And since that [connection] cannot be established without the predominance of the qualifier, there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), just as in the case of the word "eaten" (*khādita*) and so forth. This is the conclusion.
From the group [of archetypes],
the properties such as being made of *khadira* wood are extended [to the modifications].

Because the properties of being made of *khadira* wood, such as for the *sruva* ladle and so forth, would not otherwise apply to the modification (*vikṛti*) in the absence of an extension (*atideśa*), and because of the fear that this would result in a redundancy (*dviruktatva*), the status of being for the sake of the modification was not established for the *khadira*-ness and other such properties.

However, since the *āhavanīya* fire and other such fires are already established by direct injunction (*upadeśa*) for the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)—such as the *nakṣatreṣṭi*—even when they serve that purpose, there is no occasion for their being mentioned twice [in the context of the primary sacrifice]. Consequently, the logic of the *khadira* tree (which applies when a specific material is prescribed) does not apply here. Just as the act of cutting (*cheda*), which produces the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), serves the purpose of the primary sacrifice because the post itself serves the primary sacrifice, there is no reason whatsoever for the act of establishing the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) to serve the purpose of the primary sacrifice. *Sūtra* 3.7, p. 42: Even if a *khadira* tree is available and possesses the capacity for the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as carving, it must still be taken only if it possesses the functional capacity for the primary task of tying the animal (*niyojana*). (*Kevalāṅgavākya*)

If, due to the unavailability of *khadira* wood, an animal has been tied to a post made of *kadara* wood, then even if *khadira* is subsequently obtained, it should not be taken up, because the purpose has already been fulfilled.

Bhāṣya 6.3.17.36. If, due to the unavailability of *khadira*, a substitute (*pratinidhi*) such as *kadara* has been consecrated (*saṃskṛta*), and *khadira* is later obtained, then operations such as carving must be performed on that [newly obtained *khadira*]; for even though it was a substitute, it remains a substitute once consecrated.
Vi. 6.3.17. There is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the sacrificial post materials such as *khadira* and others, because they serve a single purpose.

Māna: 12|3|14|10–15. In the *vājapeya* and other modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), regarding the optional original (*prākṛta*) materials such as the *khadira* wood and others, when one of them is mentioned again, this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*).
Ga. The letter *ga*, the letter *ka*.

Although there exists the property of being produced by the proximity of distinct sounds due to the difference in the manifesting sounds (*vyañjaka-dhvani*) for each phoneme, this view [is held] regarding the cognition that "this is the letter *ga*" or "this is the letter *pha*," and so forth.

Su. Pṛ. 706: Since the letters beginning with *ga* possess the properties of being a letter (*varṇatva*), sound (*śabdatva*), and quality (*guṇatva*), and since distinctions such as rapidity (*druta*) and so forth are merely extrinsic conditions (*paropādhi*), the oneness of the letter *ga* and others is established; thus, the universal *gatva* alone is not something imagined. Vā. 2.2.12, p. 471: The maxim of churning the sky (*gaganaromanthana-nyāya*) applies to the undertaking of a futile effort toward an impossible object.
The chewing [of food] by animals after it has been swallowed is called *romantha*.
(Sāhasrī 666). The maxim of the sky-lotus (*gaganāravindanyāya*) operates as an illustration of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
"Just as a lotus in the sky does not exist at all, so too [is this case].

This is the *sāhasrī* (715). The maxim: "When many rivers have entered the Gaṅgā, they are included by the mention of the Gaṅgā. (This maxim takes the form of an illustration for the maxim: "That which falls within the middle of something is included by the mention of that thing.")

(ke. *Bhūtiḥ*, p. 298. In expressions such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the connection with another word is possible even without secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). *Sukhabodhinī*, p. 793. In some cases there is persistence (*anuvṛtti*), like the current of the Gaṅgā;
(just as the flow of the Gaṅgā moistens all the ground situated along its path, so too [the word persists]).
*Maṇi*, p. 71. [The term *gaṇa*] is used in proximity to *gajaghaṭā*. For example: "the herd of elephants blinded by rut" (*madāndhasindhuraghaṭā*); and likewise:

"Wherever this cloud-blue herd of elephants moves, there the Rākṣasa should go; let this force of radiant horses be maintained by the Rākṣasa. (Note: *gaṅgāghakaṃ* appears to be a scribal error for *gajaghaṭā*.)
"Thinking, 'Let him lead away the army of the Rākṣasa lords,' he remained here in the city out of affection for the battle; thus there stood a thousand Rākṣasas.
(From the *Mudrārākṣasa* Nāṭaka, Act 2).
Sāhastrī. 208. The maxim of the elephant eating the wood-apple (*kapittha*).

Just as it is well known that a wood-apple (*kapittha*) fruit eaten by an elephant comes out from its stomach only as a pulp (*bhrāma*), and even while being that pulp, it appears as if washed because it is devoid of marrow; likewise, just as it does not fall within the scope of logic to ask how the marrow and other internal parts emerge with such bliss from the mouths of those who are free from desire, so too, even though Fortune (*lakṣmī*) has departed, she is not perceived at all. As it is said: "When she has gone, she is not perceived at all, like a wood-apple eaten by an elephant" (Sāhasrī 269). This is the maxim of the flow of gadulikā.
Just as when one of a herd of ewes falls into a well, then all of them fall there even though they are being held back, so it is in the present case as well.
(The reading *gadulikā* also exists;
Sāhasrī 21. ꠵. Only a herd (*gaṇa*) is capable of assisting in the movement by means of the properties of a collective.)
Bhāṣya 8.1.10.17: "Accretion from the group [occurs] because it is not the archetype.
It is understood that in the *śatokthya* and other such rites, as well as in the *śata-atirātra* and others, the ten days belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) proceed;
and those [ten days] have the *ukthya* as their concluding form (*saṃsthā*), with two *agniṣṭomas*.

When it is said, "The Śatōkthya [is to be performed]," the addition of Ukthya-stotras must be made in the Agniṣṭoma, and in the Śatātirātra, they must be added during all the night-rounds (rātriparyāya). Regarding the inquiry as to whether this addition of stotras follows the pattern of the Dvādaśāha or that of the Jyotiṣṭoma, the author states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): from the group, namely the Dvādaśāha, the stotras are added...
In the sections on the *gaṇa* of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), there is a collection of chapters concerning the *gaṇapati*.
This is because the multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*) have the twelve-day sacrifice as their archetype (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, the increase [of stotras] is from the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*),
or rather, from the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*), because those [stotras] are common to both.

The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that in the groups beginning with the hundred *ukthya* sacrifices, the increase of the *āgamana* stotras should be performed from the twelve-day sacrifice which serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*).
The accumulation of the *stotra*s should not be performed according to the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), but rather according to the one-day rite (*ekāha*);

for those [elements] belonging to the twelve-day rite are equal to the modified days (*vaikṛta-ahaḥ*). Those [twelve-day rites] also require a specific sacrificial conclusion (*saṃsthā*), and these [modified rites] do as well.
For one beggar does not beg from another beggar.
Since the *saṃsthā-stotras* are not specifically prescribed for the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), they must be taken from where they are prescribed;

and since those are prescribed in the *jyotiṣṭoma*-type *ukthya* and *atirātra*, it is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the accumulation of the *stotras* must be performed from that very one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*).
In this regard, accumulation is being considered; now, diminution is being considered. What [is it]?
Among the *gaṇas*. Here, the word *gaṇa* denotes the groups of days (*ahargaṇa*) beginning with the *dvirātra* and ending with the *saṃvatsara*.

In those groups of days (*gaṇa*) and multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*), the model (*vidhyanta*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) proceeds. This is because there is no interruption in the application [of the ritual procedure], as seen in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with the *dvādaśāha*" and "one should sacrifice with the *dvirātra*.
Furthermore, the word "day" (*ahaḥ*) denotes a full day-and-night (*ahorātra*).
The word "night" is likewise [indicative]; this is a linguistic mark (*śabdagata-liṅga*). There is also a semantic mark (*arthagata*) to be understood.

Thus, starting from the passage, "By two [days] [the calf] has hair, by two [days] flesh," it shows that the twelve-day nature and the ritual procedure (*dharma*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) apply to the Gavām Ayana.

Therefore, the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is the archetype (*prakṛti*) for multi-day sacrificial sessions (*ahargaṇa*). Why? Because in an injunction for a session, that which has the characteristic of constant repetition (*sadāvṛtti*) is understood [to be the archetype]. For instance, in the Janakasatra, it is heard in scripture: "There are four days consisting of the *trivṛt* stoma."

In this regard, there arises a doubt: is this prescribed practice intended for the first repetition of that which occurs in the *pṛṣṭha-ṣaḍaha* (the six-day period of *pṛṣṭha* chants), because it has been stated as being *trivṛt* (ninefold)? Or rather, is the *trivṛt-stoma* nature enjoined when the four days in sequence within the *dvādaśāha* (twelve-day sacrifice) are obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction)?
Regarding this, he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*):
"The injunction is for the group of four days."
When such an injunction regarding the group (gaṇacodanā) exists, the repetition of that day which possesses the characteristic mark should be understood.
In the present case, the term "trivṛt" refers to the threefold nature of the first day of the six-day period (ṣaḍaha).
Therefore, this fourfold repetition is understood to belong to that very day alone.

Just as in the case of the Āgneya [offering], where—due to the identity of the deity and the commonality [of the term] such as "to Agni Pāvaka" or "to Agni Śuci"—there is a repetition of the Āgneya ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*), so it is here.
Or rather, they are distinct days because they form a collection, as indicated by the application of the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the injunction.

Regarding the Janakasattra, the arrangement of the days (*ahaḥklṛpti*) is recited in the Satyāṣāḍhīya [Kalpasūtra] (17.8.24) as: "Its four days are threefold (*trivṛt*), beginning with the Agniṣṭoma; then the Viśvajit, the Mahāvrata [stotra], and the Atirātra. Thus, there are seven days: the Agniṣṭoma is the first day; then the four threefold days make five; the Viśvajit is the sixth; and the Atirātra is the seventh, wherein the Mahāvrata stotra occurs. Among these, this group of four days is what is referred to here.

The number "four" resides in distinctness; it occurs only when there is a plurality of days. Furthermore, there exist various days belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), which proceed by means of an injunction for a sacrificial session (*sattra*).
It is possible to enjoin the state of being "threefold" (*trivṛt*) with reference to those [days]. However, it is not logical to enjoin the number four with reference to many threefold days.

Therefore, because it is a composite whole, due to the indication of the procedure, and because of the injunction regarding its generative nature, the four days of the Janaka-satra should be distinct twelve-day periods.
And in those [periods], the state of being "trivṛt" (ninefold) is prescribed; this is the distinction.
Such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The word "or" (*vā*) serves to exclude the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Likewise, there is the observation of another scriptural passage (*anyārthadarśana*):

regarding the Janakasatrātra, where it is stated, "There are four *trivṛt* days; they are distinct twelve-day periods, not of the nature of the first repetitions found in the *pṛṣṭha-ṣaḍaha*," there occurs the observation of another passage stating, "The four *trivṛt* days have the *agniṣṭoma* as their opening."
The Agniṣṭoma is indeed the mouth; however, the four subsequent days have the Agniṣṭoma as their opening.
From this observation of another purpose, it is known that those four days belong to the Dvādaśāha sacrifice.
For them, however, the rule of having the Trivṛt as the final [stotra] is prescribed.

This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). [Now] the chapter on *gaṇa*. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *gaṇa* denotes a group, number, a multitude, a fierce person, an army, and a division."

Just as the word *gaṇapati* finds its application in two senses— either as "the lord (*pati*) of a group (*gaṇa*) consisting of a multitude of Rudra's attendants (*anucara*), each of whom is distinct, or as the lord of a single collective entity (*samudāya*) that has arisen from those very same distinct individuals"— so too is it in the present case regarding the meanings of words such as *gandharva*. Thus, the word *gaṇapati* fulfills its purpose within the scope of these two meanings.

The impulsive [act] (*sāhasī*). 1. [Rituals] such as the *gaṇayāga* have been observed to possess multiple procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) [and thus are not devoid of worldly procedural requirements].

Bhāṣya 7.4.2.12. In the science of calculation (*gaṇitaśāstra*), when an equal division is impossible, a division based on logical justification (*upapatti*) is stated by either assuming [an integer] or subtracting one. Saṃkarṣa 2.3.4. When [the ritual] has passed, it is like the *asthiyajña* (bone-sacrifice).

When the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice has been performed and the sacrificer has passed away, the remaining rites are to be carried out like the *asthiyajña* (bone-sacrifice); having become a friend, the Teacher says this.

[The view is] that it should be performed for the sake of the rite, beginning with the *audumbarī* pillar, the *śukra* cup, and the *ādāra* offering, but nothing else—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). [Question: For those who have attained prosperity? Or for others?
"The three who have attained prosperity (*gataśrī*) are the learned Brahmin, the village headman, and the Kṣatriya," so says the Śruti.
"Aurva, Gautama, and Bhāradvāja," so says the author of the Kalpasūtra. "The wife of one who has attained prosperity [should kindle] the Āhavanīya fire."
"Those who have attained prosperity are those whose prosperity has departed. (Vi.

1|4|8). "The *jyotiṣmatī* [bricks] are not to be maintained for one whose prosperity has departed at the time of the *dhārya-agredāna*. (1|4|8). "The Āhavanīya fire is to be maintained by one whose prosperity has departed."
And this is for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). When that has been extinguished, however, the mental oblation (*manasvī-homa*) is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
In this village, every day such items as sweeping around the fire, sprinkling water around it, and strewing grass around it must be performed.
Ke. 1.4.8. *gataśriyaḥ* (this is the genitive case): the Āhavanīya fire must be maintained perpetually. Vi. 1.2.4.10.

For those whose prosperity has departed (*gataśriyām*), at the time of performing the ritual, there is only the rekindling (*prāduṣkaraṇa*) of the Āhavanīya fire, not its repeated installation (*punarādheya*).
Saṃkarṣa. 3.2.6. "The world follows what has already gone before; it is not a world that perceives ultimate reality"—this is the maxim (*nyāya*).
For instance, a certain Brahmin heard from someone that in a particular village there was a donor who gave a silver *maṇḍala* to every Brahmin.
Upon hearing this, that greedy Brahmin, desiring to go there, dug a hole in the ground along the path, placed a jeweled *maṇḍala* within it, set two lumps of dough upon it, and went there.

And when he had departed, every person who arrived there, seeing those two lumps of clay and conceiving the idea that they were sacred fords (*tīrtha*), fashioned two lumps of earth there and established them.

Thus, when the time had come, by the power of fate, he obtained a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) from a wealthy man. Later, desiring to take back the vessel he himself had held, he saw two balls of rice given to him by people in the world. Confused and not knowing the place where he had deposited his own water-pot, his mind overwhelmed with grief, he recited this verse: "The world follows what comes before it; it is not a world that perceives ultimate truth.
By the giving of two balls of rice, my copper vessel has vanished."
Thus it is said.

Furthermore: "Seeing one person perform a censurable act, another also performs it; people follow like those who walk in the footsteps of one who has gone before. Such is the world; it is not the ultimate reality."
Thus [it is said].

This is the principle of "uniformity of movement" (*gatisāmānyāt*). The citation of passages from multiple Vedic branches is for the purpose of establishing that they have their own specific meanings without contradiction, by means of the principle of "uniformity of movement."

*Upadeśasāhasrī*. Prose 6: Rāmatīrtha. Regarding the *Brahmasūtra* (1.1.10): "Because of the uniformity of the course" (*gatisāmānyāt*). "Course" (*gati*) means comprehension (*avagati*) or ascertainment (*niścaya*).
For the comprehension that the conscious [Self] is the cause is indeed identical in all the Vedānta texts; such is the meaning of the *sūtra*.

Because, according to the principle of the uniformity of approach (*gatisāmānyanyāya*), all Upaniṣads are established as having Brahman as their essential nature (Śrīkaṇṭha Bhāṣya 1.4.28). According to the principle of the uniformity of approach, it is established that the fruit of all meditations is the attainment of Brahman (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.18).
Therefore, by the principle of the uniformity of approach, it should be understood that the *Puruṣasūkta* of twenty-six verses has Paraśiva alone as its subject matter.
1|1|27 Brahma Sūtra: Refutation of universals such as *gatva* and *auttva*.
The "Sphoṭavāda" is to be found in the chapter of the *Śāstradīpikā* titled *Cintā*. *Ke.* [is] the act of speaking; *gaditṛ* [is] one who speaks; *pāṭha* [is] the act of reciting.

Mā. 2|1|3|42: The term *gadita* applies to that which is not composed in verse (*apādabandha*). For that which is not bound by metrical feet is called prose (*gadya*). 2|1|3|44: The maxim of the city of the Gandharvas (*gandharvanagaranyāya*).
A "city of Gandharvas" (gandharvanagara) is like a city of the Gandharvas.

Just as in the sky there is perceived and seen the form of a particular arrangement of clouds—consisting of blue, yellow, and other colors and shapes in the form of royal cities, complete with banners, flags, arches, and the rays of the sun’s light—and yet, upon approaching it, it is not found; in the same way, the world should be known as non-existent. And it is said in the *Tattvaviveka*: "When a rainbow of many colors has vanished, what remains all around is called a halo (*pariveṣa*)."
"Likewise the falling of the sun, likewise lightning, and likewise the variegated city of the Gandharvas," and so forth.
*Sāhasī* 443. "The [cities] called Gandharva-cities are named 'Ranti'."
These and others are *yajus* mantras.
Who are they? They are the Gandharvas and so forth, who possess long lifespans such as a thousand years or even a year.
However, they do not have the qualification for the *āhavanīya* fire.
A specific indicator: 1543. In the Garga-trirātra sacrifice, indeed, there is an exclusive indicator.
Vākyapadīya 3.4.1.3, p. 919: There are three types of indicators (*gamakaviśeṣa*): the sense organ (*indriya*), the inferential mark (*liṅga*), and the designator (*abhidhāyaka*).
That which makes an object known through its mere presence when in contact with it is the sense organ.
That which, being known as the pervaded (*vyāpya*), makes the pervader (*vyāpaka*) known is the inferential mark.
That which causes understanding precisely by virtue of its being a signifier (gamaka) is the denoter (abhidhāyaka).

Ratnākara, in the *Saṃbandhakṣepavāda* (Chapter 31): "The word *gami* [when] joined with *kṣī* signifies sexual intercourse. See *Sukhabodhinī*, p. 133. [This concerns] the relationship between the signified (*gamya*) and the signifier (*gamaka*).
It should be considered whether the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) between cause and effect alone was intended by the author of the *Bhāṣya*;
however,

that [view] is incorrect, because the relationship of the signified and the signifier is well-established even for properties such as impermanence and being produced (*kṛtakatva*), which do not stand in a causal relation to one another.

Furthermore, even between cause and effect, the cause is not an indicator in the same way as the effect, because of the high frequency of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). (Vārttika 2.2.1126, p. 544). When a relationship of the indicated and the indicator exists, the word *liṅga* (logical mark) is employed. (Vārttika 1.3.78, p. 249). And that which is being understood cannot be conceived as false.
Bhāṣya 1.4.3.4, p. 334: "Even that which is being understood [as the meaning] possesses the status of being expressed by words (śābdatva) when it is endowed with the intended purport (tātparya).
Sūtra-pañcikā, p. 573: "Because no qualification is observed for a meaning that is merely being understood.
As the venerable authors of the Vārttika have said: "No qualification whatsoever is ever seen for a meaning that is being understood."
"Or [it may be expressed] by other words or by a case-ending, as in the expression 'this smoke is burning'" (Ṛjuvimalā, p. 70).

It is argued that there is no connection with a specific [quality] for that which is already understood; therefore, because such a connection is observed, there must be a direct denotation (abhidhāna) of it. This too has been refuted on the grounds that even otherwise [i.e., without such a connection], such usage is seen in the sections concerning the primacy of the *ākṛti* (form/class) and so forth.

Or rather, as stated at 3|4|1|3, page 940: "The connection with the act of stealing (*moṣa*) belongs only to those who are understood [to be thieves], as in the expression, 'The horsemen have plundered the city.
At 3|4|1|3, page 940: In the case of 'Let the Gargas be fined a hundred,' the sentence is completed with respect to the collective whole.
At Bhāṣya 3|1|6|12, page 697: In the *Gargatrirātra* sacrifice, there is the placing of the *ājyadohana* vessel upon the ordinary fire."
In a case of doubt, it should be the worldly fire, because it serves all purposes.
The Commentary states: Regarding the *ājyadoha* chants in the Garga-trirātra sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture, "They praise while placing the fire nearby.
Herein lies the doubt: is the fire to be placed nearby the worldly one, or the Vedic one?
What is established? That it is Vedic.
Why? Because the fire is produced for the purpose of all rites with the words, "Whatever rites I shall perform, [I shall do] for Vaiśvānara, loudly.
Therefore, it is to be placed down according to the Vedic method.

This being the case, it is replied: in a matter of doubt, the worldly [practice] should prevail, because it serves all purposes. In this matter of doubt—namely, whether it is worldly or Vedic—the worldly should prevail.
Why? Because it serves all purposes.
The worldly fire serves all purposes; no specific task for it has been prescribed.
Therefore, whatever is to be accomplished by fire—whether visible or invisible—is not contradictory when it is employed.
Therefore, it should be worldly;
it is not Vedic, because its purpose has been specified.
The Commentary states: Now, as for what was said—that since the Vedic [mantra] has arisen for the sake of all ritual acts, it should therefore be applied [to this one as well].
To this we reply: the Vedic substance of fire is not produced by the scripture;
rather, its function is specified by the scripture, beginning with the injunction, "One offers oblations in the Āhavanīya fire."
If it were intended for all purposes, the specific instruction would be meaningless.
Therefore, a common-world fire should be placed nearby.
Furthermore, the quality of being "for all purposes" will apply to water when it is employed according to one's own desire in various tasks.
Thus, he explains that being for all purposes is contradictory in both ways;

likewise, because their origin is equal. The Commentary states: "Now, why are the fires of the *chelyā* not deposited? To this it is replied: the origin of the other *chelyā* fires is also [the same]."
It does not mean "all purposes.
Why? Because of their equality; these too are equal to the others.
For these as well, the function has been specified: "Seated previously, he establishes the hearths (dhiṣṇya)."

"Therefore, they should not be placed [as subsidiaries]," says the Ṭupṭīkā: "The Āhavanīya and other fires are intended for optional rites (*kāmya*). Once their purpose has been fulfilled, they become free of expectancy; there is no authority for them to serve as subsidiary elements (*śeṣa*) elsewhere."

The *chelyā* ladles also have arrived for the purpose of sprinkling (*vyāghāraṇa*); therefore, being satisfied by that alone, they are not to be employed elsewhere. Once the sprinkling has been performed and the ritual act concluded, [the fire] becomes worldly (*laukika*). Thus, since it is possible to perform the placing down (*upanidhāna*) through incidental application (*prasaṅga*), any effort made to bring another [fire] would be improper.
Furthermore, the scripture [states]: "Because it denotes only the *barhis* grass, it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*)."

In the *Gargatrirātra* (15.4.4), regarding the ownership of those born as slaves (*garbhadāsa*) and others, there arises the occasion for refuting the status of [the words] "soma," "clothing" (*vāsaḥ*), and so forth as being Sanskrit; furthermore, because the status of the word "aśiḥ" as Sanskrit is also refuted, there is a logical connection [to this topic].
As for the meaning of the Sūtra: when there is a doubt as to whether [a word] is worldly (*laukika*) or Vedic (*vaidika*), it should be considered worldly.

Why? Because it serves all purposes, whereas the Vedic [mantra] does not, since its requirements are satisfied by the specification of the purpose through the indication of the function of the oblation (*homa*) and so forth.
Here, the *guṇasūtra* "not the Vedic, because of the specification of the purpose" has also been written as a single unit [with the preceding].

(That it was not printed that way by the publishers is another matter—Ke.). Vi.: "Whether Vedic or worldly, it should be used without distinction, because of the connection with the consecrated [fire]."
The first [point]: the preparation for the *homa* is worldly (*laukika*) because it serves the purpose of producing the substance (*jāty-arthatvena*).
In the *Bhāṭṭa* school: regarding the *ājyadoha* Sāmans in the *Gargatrirātra*, it is heard in scripture: "One should praise after placing the fire nearby" (*agnim upanidhāya stuvīta*).

In this regard, there arises the inquiry whether the fire is Vedic (*vaidika*) or worldly (*laukika*). Although in the twelfth book (12.2.1.1–7) the suitability of the *āhavanīya* and other fires for worldly purposes is refuted, nevertheless, by the general statement—"by those [fires] with which his sacrifice can be performed"—it is understood that they serve the purpose of all Vedic rites; therefore, it is indeed Vedic.

This being the prima facie view, since there is no evidence that specific injunctions such as "he offers in the Āhavanīya fire" are intended merely as indicative references (upalakṣaṇa), and since the statement "by whom he is authorized" remains meaningful even if it refers only to the offerings and so forth, one must take ordinary clouds. For, even when the specific placement [of the fire] is not performed, the injunction—"He whose consecrated fire spills over is indeed deprived of power and vigor"—cannot imply the removal of the fire from its seat; therefore, only ordinary clouds are to be taken.
For this very reason, even the *śiṣyāmī* [grains] are not included, because their purpose is merely for supporting the fire (*vyādhāraṇa*).

If, however, it were argued that after the supporting, they alone are to be taken because there is no distinction from worldly [grains] and because they are present at hand, then let it be so. Maṇḍana says: "In the *stotra*, the *taso* is indeed worldly fire."
Śaṅkara says: "O Mother, this is a worldly [praise] in the hymn.
In the Garga-trirātra, the second day has the Vāmadevya-pṛṣṭha;
there, even though the Bṛhat-sāman is absent, it is preceded by the Śukra because of its non-contingent (anaimittika) prescription.

This indicates futility;
