(Bhāṭṭa 5.1.16). Wearing the washed garment of a washerman who has been impregnated [by a woman] is improper conduct among both the Northerners (*udīcya*) and the Southerners (*dākṣiṇātya*).
The remaining people use the clothes of a washerman after sprinkling them with drops of water;
Vārttika 13.3.17, p. 204. "Womb" (*garbha*) is a quality of women; by the expression "they become wombs," he indicates the feminine gender;
Bhāṣya 8.1.6.17. A slave from the womb (*garbhadāsa*).
The purpose of the action belongs solely to the master; the ox is purchased with the thought, "It will carry" (*vakṣyati*, from the root *vah* in the *luṭ* future).
But surely, even for a slave born in the house, the master would obtain some benefit by means of an agreement?
We say: no.

Ah! Even while speaking of his own consciousness, he falls into the state of being a subordinate quality; for, by being inseparable [from it], he benefits either the master of a slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*) or the ox.
Bhāṣya 3.1.12.
For he is established as such by ownership from the very moment of his birth.

An ox is [employed] for the purpose of carrying, but the owner is not understood as being for that purpose. Nor does one's activity toward a born slave (garbhadāsa) and so forth proceed from the intention to benefit him; rather, it is prompted by the accomplishment of one's own purpose.
Or, it is like the service of a slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*).
For in that case, there are two efforts inherent in two distinct conscious beings.
Among these, the effort of the master proceeds toward the benefit of the slave born in the house for the sake of his own interest.
Even a slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*) proceeds toward his own security (*yogakṣema*) only by means of a mental disposition that is attentive to the interests of his master.
*Kaṇikā*, p. 94. Slaves born in the house and those who are pure [by birth] can be given away in the gift of all one's possessions (*sarvasvadāna*), because they are one’s own property.

*Kevala-tantra* 6.7.5. In the case of the master of a slave born in the house and others, the status of being a "remainder" (*śeṣatva*)—which is actually non-existent—is to be understood as a figurative designation (*upacarita*) based on the possibility of their being beneficial.
Or: Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 3.4.14.2, page 905:

"In the eighth year from conception, one should perform the initiation (dīkṣā) for the Gavāmayana sacrifice; one should perform the initiation (upanayana) of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception."
"The Kṣatriya [is purified] by the initiation of the embryo, but the Vaiśya by the twelfth [year] from the embryo" (Manu).
This is a textual rule (*vācanikī vyavasthā*) based on the sacrament of the embryo (*garbhasaṃskāra*).
Bālaṃbhaṭṭī, p. 19. The maxim of the sandals on the neck (*galepādukānyāya*).

Just as when someone has come to a house under the pretext of seeking food and sits down, and having been recognized as a thief, is told repeatedly by the owner "Go away!"—yet when he does not consent to leave of his own accord due to stubbornness, he is then forcibly expelled after being bound at the neck with a sandal and beaten; so it is in the present case as well. (Sāhasī 384). Regarding the phrase *galaveṇikābandhaṃ ca*, some authorities remember it as referring to the *nivīta* (the sacred thread draped over the shoulder), while others [remember] it as the binding of a girdle (*parikara*).
In that regard, the binding of the neck-turban (*galaveṇikābandha*) does not apply except in the case of combat;
however, the binding of the sash (*parikarabandha*) is applicable in all activities because it produces freedom from distraction.

(Vārttika 3.4.14.2) By the principle of the long rays of light issuing forth from cows and horses, the intellect (*buddhi*), which has issued forth through the ears and other senses, always blazes forth in its true nature.
Upadeśasāhasrī, Verse 15.21, Rāmatīrtha. Cattle and other such [sacrifices];
the *ekāha* sacrifices which are modifications of the Soma sacrifice;
these must be performed only after the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), not before.

Bhāṣya 5.4.126: There is a deliberation as to whether the sacrifices beginning with the *go* sacrifice occur after or before the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. While the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that they occur before, it is stated [in reply]: there is no scriptural statement that would enjoin the time of the *soma* sacrifice as being prior to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

From what, then, [is it obtained]? It is obtained through the sense of the matter (*arthaprāpta*). And the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) does not cause that which is already obtained through the sense to be brought about.
Now, if it be argued: "The time for the *soma* sacrifice follows immediately after the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), because of a scriptural injunction."
It is not possible;
for that which is not opposed by its nature cannot be a modification.
For it must be either something to be descended upon by the original form (*prakṛti*) or by the modification (*vikṛti*).

In that case, if the archetype (prakṛti) is not described [as having a specific accessory], there is no acquisition of the modification (vikṛti) at all. And if the capacity is already occupied by the archetype, there is no room for the others by virtue of that very capacity.
Therefore, it is established that the Gavya and other sacrifices come after the Darśapūrṇamāsa.

Vārttika 5.4.126: It is understood that for cattle (*gavādi*)—that is, animals—that have been touched by a *caṇḍāla* or similar person, purification occurs through bathing and washing, because there is no rule [to the contrary]. Vārttika 13.3.13, p. 182. Since there is no prohibition regarding cattle and the like when they are offered as a gift (*praṇīta*), the fault known as "hell" (*naraka*) does not apply. Sūtra, p. 1491. The word *apaśu* ("non-animal") is established by means of the remainder [of the category] beginning with cattle, as in the statement: "Others are indeed non-animals compared to cows and horses."
VI. 1.4.16 (Mīmāṃsākośa 194): Purchases whose means are cows and so forth must be accepted as being distinct in their essential nature.

VI. 3.1.6: In the performance of optional rites involving cows and Soma, the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is not the regulator; rather, the specific desire (*kāma*) itself is the regulator. Bhāṣya 5.3.12–16: The purchase is the motivator for bringing the cow, not the ritual action regarding the footprints (*padakarma*).
VI.4.1.10. The initiation for the Gavāmayana takes place four days before the full moon of the month of Mādhava, and not that of Caitra.
There is no restriction regarding the full moon because there is no specific distinction [stated].
Commentary: Regarding the Gavāmayana, it is heard in the scripture: "They should undergo initiation four days before the full moon."

In this regard, there is a doubt as to which full moon day it refers to. What is the prima facie view? That there is no restriction regarding the full moon day. Why? Because there is no specification.
"There is no distinction here whatsoever, because it is simply devotion, as is seen in the world.
Commentary: This is not so.
For the term "one day" (ekāha) applies figuratively to other eighth days;
this one, however, is primary, as it occurs in the middle [of the month].
And between the primary and the secondary, the understanding rests upon the primary.

Therefore, it is the full moon day of Māgha alone [that is intended]. And because of the inclusion [of other days] in the event of a transgression regarding the initiation (*dīkṣā*). The Commentary states: "They should undergo initiation on the *ekāhyā*; this *ekāhyā* is indeed the wife of the year; or rather, until the full moon day."

Having prescribed the initiation (*dīkṣā*), [the text] shows the eligibility for the midday full moon (*mādhyā paurṇamāsī*) by stating: "The purchase (*kraya*) of them is accomplished on the *ekāhī* day; therefore, they do not fail (*chambaṭ-kurvanti*) the *ekāhī* through that [purchase]. Thus, by taking up the *ekāhī*—which had fallen away from the initiation—through the purchase (the reading *krayeṇānugrahan* is the correct one in the Citralakārīya), it demonstrates the eligibility for the midday full moon.

And when this eighth day of the midday [fortnight] is being sacrificed to, there occurs the mantra: "The night which people greet with joy, like a cow approaching, she who is the wife of the year—may she be auspicious."
"To Aṣṭakā, in the spirituous liquor, svāhā!"—
this indicates that the aforementioned eighth day of the month occurs on a single-day (ekāha) occasion. Furthermore...
"It is performed. Thus, it is obtained here by the general rule (codaka); therefore, it should be sung in three verses.
This being the case, we reply:
it is indeed prior, and it belongs both to its own [verse] and to the *pragātha*;
this application pertains to each pair of verses.
In this way, the chanting will be performed on its own [proper] verse.
On which [verse] is it its own? On the *pragātha*.
How is the *pragātha* its own? For, having introduced the *brahmasāman* in the context of the *gavāmayana*, it is prescribed; therefore, the *pragātha* is the own [verse] of the *brahmasāman*.
And because of the statement using the word "pragātha," it is called its own *pragātha*;
also because of the indication of the characteristic and the excess.
For there is indeed the observation of a characteristic mark.
"In five months, the Bārhata Pragāthas are completed. This applies to the method of *pragāthana* (interlacing verses), not to the chanting of triplets (*tṛca-gāna*).
Why? Because those *pragāthas* amount to one hundred and four.
In that context, there are two *pragāthas* for Bṛhat and Rathantara in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
There are also two *pragāthas* for the *Indra-sūkta* and the *Āleya* in that very same place.
The *pragātha* named *Indra-kratu* occurs on the northern wing (*uttara-pakṣas*).
These are the ninety-nine *pragāthas* [recited] during the *pṛṣṭhya* [six-day period] of the *śiṃgava* *āyana*.
In the Gavāmayana,
during the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans] are to be performed one by one on each respective day.
The *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] has two *sāmans* simultaneously, as in the case of the *ekāha* sacrifice.
Commentary: This is prescribed in the tradition: “The *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) has the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* as its *sāmans*.
Regarding this, there is a point of doubt: should both *sāmans* be performed on each day, or should the *rathantara* be used on some days and the *bṛhat* on others?

Whence arises this doubt? Whether these two *sāmans* are combined or whether they are separate, the expression "the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) of the *pṛṣṭhya* sacrifice has the *Bṛhat* and *Rathaṃtara* as its *sāmans*" remains applicable.

In this regard, there is this deliberation: Is this a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing a *dvandva*, meaning "that which has the *Bṛhat* and *Rathaṃtara* as its two *sāmans*," or is it a multi-word *bahuvrīhi*, meaning "the *Bṛhat* belongs to it" and "the *Rathaṃtara* belongs to it"?
If it is a *bahuvrīhi* containing a *dvandva*, then the two *sāmans* are combined every day; if it is a multi-word *bahuvrīhi*, then they are separate.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That it applies to the whole [compound]. Consequently, this is described as a *bahuvrīhi* containing a *dvandva*.

Why? Because of the immediate sequence of the words *bṛhat* and *rathantara*, because the view of *vṛtti* (compound formation) has been adopted, and because in the case of *vṛtti*, the compound is obligatory.
Furthermore, because the *dvandva* expresses its own primary meaning, there is both conformity with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and internal proximity (*antaraṅgatā*).
Otherwise, both of these would be sublated.
Therefore, the *bahuvrīhi* contains within it a *dvandva*.
If this were so, both *sāmans* would exist together every day. Why? Because of the presence of the *dvandva* compound denoting mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).
Where there is the *rathaṃtara*, there is the *bṛhat* along with it.
This simultaneous injunction is that which constitutes mutual conjunction;
therefore, [the rite] is performed in its entirety every day,
as in the case of a single-day sacrifice.

For example: "One who has been long ill should perform both [the Bṛhat and Rathantara]; one who is about to sleep should perform both; even one who has performed the Apaciti sacrifice should perform the Bṛhat and Rathantara on a single-day rite.

Regarding this, [Durga asks]: Is this a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing a *dvaṃdva*, or is it qualified by multiple words? [This is the doubt. In that regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:
The word *bṛhat*, once uttered, requires a listener; so too does the word *rathaṃtara*.

Because these two are uttered in immediate succession, first there arises a relationship between them characterized by their proximity (i.e., a *dvandva* compound), and only afterwards [a relationship] with the word *aśva*.
By the phrase "because the position of the *vṛtti* has been adopted" in the Bhāṣya, the word *vṛtti* refers to a compound (*samāsa*).

Because it involves a relationship with the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*), the *dvandva* compound occurs first (as it is *bahiraṅga*), and only afterwards does the relationship with the meaning of the other word take place.
Now, one might object that by the rule *vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 2.1.11), the compound would be optional (not obligatory) in this context.

In that case, when a sentence (*vākya*) is adopted, there is only a connection with the meaning of the other word, and not the intermediate *dvandva* (the mutual conjunction known as *itaretarayoga* which is the cause for the *dvandva* formation).
When a compound (*samāsa*) is adopted, then an intermediate *dvandva* is obtained.

Regarding the dilemma—whether a sentence (*vākya*) or a compound should be resorted to—the author of the *Bhāṣya*, by stating "And because a compound is obligatory under the view of syntactic integration (*vṛttipakṣa*)," demonstrates that in such cases a compound is necessarily employed. This is done to dispel the doubt that one might resort only to the sentence due to the force of the *codaka* (the injunction), which would otherwise result in each [element] being a separate means of accomplishment.

How [is there] eternality? The answer is: Kātyāyana stated thus: “Regarding dvandva and tatpuruṣa compounds, when the final member is present, it must be stated that the compound is obligatory” (this is a *vārttika* on Pāṇini 2.1.51 concerning a final member expressing a secondary derivative meaning).
He provides an example: for a *dvandva*, [the form is] *vākyatvapriyaḥ*; for a *tatpuruṣa*, [the forms are] *pañcagavadhanaḥ* and *daśagavadhanaḥ*.
Thus.

If [the compound] were formed first as a whole, then [the suffix] *aprayoga* (non-application of the final compound-suffix) would result (meaning that even non-application might sometimes occur). Therefore, because the compound is obligatory, the intermediate compound (*dvaṃdva*) of the two prior members (those between which a *dvaṃdva* is possible) is necessarily established. Alternatively, since it is prescribed without being compounded, there is no prohibition regarding its division.
Commentary: It is not the case that [the term] *aharha* refers to two [separate] days.
On some days there is the *rathaṃtara*, and on others the *bṛhat*; the two *sāmans* are not enjoined for the whole [period].
Why? Because if the word *bṛhadrathaṃtarasāmā* were applicable to both sides, it would be logical that the *sāmans* are distinct.

Why? Because in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *pṛṣḍha* stotra is accomplished by means of a single *sāman*, and it must likewise be accomplished by means of a single one in the ectype (*vikṛti*), as permitted by the extended injunction (*codaka*).
This being the case, both the occasion for the application (*vṛtti-nimitta*) and the occasion based on the *rathaṃtara* will be fully realized.

However, if the combination of the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* accomplishes the *pṛṣḍha* such that neither the *bṛhat* nor the *rathaṃtara* individually is the means of accomplishment, then that [specific] occasion would not be established.
In that case, there would be an obstruction of the water.
Not only would that [specific] motive not be established, but neither the *bṛhat-pṛṣṭha* nor the *rathaṃtara-pṛṣṭha* would be established.
There would thus be an inconsistency; it would indeed be a different performance altogether.

Furthermore, when it is figuratively designated as "the entire *pṛṣṭha*," it is characterized by such statements as "the *bṛhat* becomes the *pṛṣṭha*" and "the *rathaṃtara* becomes the *pṛṣṭha*"; this is a mark [indicating] that the term denotes the collection [of the two].
Moreover, in the *gavāmayana* sacrifice, during the *pṛṣṭhya* [six-day period]...
In the Gavāmayana sacrifice, when the *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha] requires a connection with the word "sāman" for its covering, it would not be connected with the word "rathantara.
Furthermore, the proximity of the word "rathantara" to the word "sāman" is equal [to that of other terms].
Moreover, in the view that [the compound] is a *vṛtti*, there is even more clearly a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) between the members of the *dvandva*.
Nor is it the case that, according to the *vṛtti* view, a compound is necessarily obligatory;
for the Blessed Pāṇini has stated that such a compound is optional (*vibhāṣā*).
Furthermore, the hearing of the word "sāman" indicates that it serves as a characteristic mark for both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara.
Therefore, both sāmans should be present together.
And this has already been stated: even when the sāman is divided, the term "Bṛhat-Rathantara-sāman" remains uncontradicted.

Just as when it is said, "Devadatta is to be fed with *vrata* and *talla* for a month," [it may be understood that] he is fed with ghee for half a month and with oil for half a month—the word is thus applicable even in this way. However, in the case of a single day (*ekāha*), because there is only one [day], a division is impossible; therefore, the whole [period] applies: "One who is suffering from chronic illness should perform both. Soma says: In the previous case, although the act of looking was not subject to injunction because its purpose was already established, here, since the combination (*samuccaya*) was not previously established, it is stated to be a specific injunction (*viśeṣavidhi*). This is the connection (*saṃgati*).

In this context, regarding the *sāman* consisting of the *Bṛhat* and *Rathaṃtara*, there is indeed a fixed rule: the *Rathaṃtara* is used in the first, third, and fifth [days], while the *Bṛhat* is used in the second, fourth, and sixth.

As stated in the Sūtra: "When the *Bṛhat* and *Rathaṃtara* Pṛṣṭha-lauds are prescribed simultaneously, because they serve as the cause for the *Saṃsava*, *Gosava*, and other rites, both *sāmans* would belong to a single [day]."

Furthermore, it should not be argued that "in a *dvandva-garbha* (compound-within-a-compound) *bahuvrīhi*, there is an acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable of *bṛhadrathantara*, whereas in a multi-word *bahuvrīhi*, the vowel *ā* of the word *bṛhat* is acute by virtue of the original accent of the preceding member; thus, because of this difference in accent, only that compound which possesses the accent established by traditional recitation (*adhyayana*) should be accepted—this is the required deliberation.

For in many places within the Veda, a transposition of accents is observed, and since it is impossible to determine meaning based on accent alone, the determination of meaning must be stated to proceed through reasoning (*nyāya*) itself.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to infer numerous *adhikaraṇas* (sections) proceeding through various types of compound formations for the preceding and following positions (*pūrvottarapakṣa*). For example:
"In the *Gavāmayana*, during the six-day period of the *pṛṣṭhya*, two [sāmans] are performed each day; should the *Bṛhat* and *Rathaṃtara* both occur, or should one or the other be excluded?"
The suffix *āy* occurs after a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing a *dvandva*; furthermore, *sama*, *hasu*, and others [follow this rule].
For those that are mutually independent, the final member of the list [of *udaka* and so forth] shall apply.
Bhaṭṭa: In the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* is traditionally taught as being joined with the six *sāmans* known as *rathaṃtara*, *bṛhat*, *vairāja*, *śākvara*, and *raivata*.
In the *gavāmayana*, it is heard in scripture: "The *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* should be performed with the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* *sāmans*.
By this, the exclusion of the *vairūpa* and the others is beyond dispute.

In considering whether that which effects the exclusion is the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* combined together, or each one individually: since this [compound] is a *bahuvrīhi* containing a *dvandva*, and because the *dvandva* implies a mutual association between the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*, there is the cognition of their combination on each individual day—just as in the case of the *Saṃsava* sacrifice and others; therefore, it is the combination alone that effects the exclusion. Furthermore, because the two [notes] qualified by the combination are enjoined by the compound as specific objects of the injunction, there is no multiplicity of things enjoined (*vidheyanekatā*), no multiplicity of things intended (*uddeśyatānekatā*), nor any violation of the principle of "single impulse" (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*).

Nor should it be argued that even though this [compound] is possible as a pure three-word *bahuvrīhi*, there is no requirement for the extension (*atideśa*) [of the *dvandva* rule], because—given the adherence to the fact that each day is a means of accomplishment for only one [deity] individually—the two [deities] together cannot be understood as the performers.
This is because, by the statement of Kātyāyana, "In a three-word *bahuvrīhi*, the *dvandva* must necessarily be expressed in the final member," a *dvandva* is mandatory here.

Nor can it be said that there is a difference in this case when a *dvandva* is absent versus when a *dvandva* is formed—as in the case of *vākyatvapriya*, where the formation of the *dvandva* results in a different form.
In that case, since the status of being a compound-final member is established, the form *vākyatvacam* is achieved by not treating it as caused by that [compound-final suffix].
Otherwise, if a *dvandva* were formed, the undesirable form *vākyatvapriya* would result.

In this regard, the rule prescribing *dvandva* compounds is intended to specify that the term applies only to a person joined with the suffix *-dvat*, and not to anyone else, because its purpose is to state a required predicate.

However, it should not be argued that in the present case, since there is no purpose for applying the rule for *dvandva* compounds in either way due to the specific nature of the form, it is appropriate to consider this [the opponent's position] as mere foolishness. For even in the present case, under the view of a pure *bahuvrīhi*, the initial member would incur its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), whereas if a *dvandva* were formed, the final syllable would incur the acute accent (*antodātta*); thus, the specific accent itself serves as the purpose.
Therefore, because the *dvandva* is necessary, and because of the inclusion of both members through that [compound], only the two joined together possess the capacity to exclude [the individual].

This being the position reached, [we reply]: since the coexistence (*sāhitya*) inherent in a *dvandva* compound is compatible even with the *dvandva* alternative, there is no basis for assuming that it is defined by the *pṛṣṭhatotra* (the *stotra* performed behind) which is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), because that [coexistence] is independent of it. Therefore, there is no conjunction (*samuccaya*) of both in each individual day.

Furthermore, one does not first form a *dvandva* and subsequently a *bahuvrīhi*; for if that were the case, it would result in a *dvipada-bahuvrīhi*, and the term "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) would be inapplicable, as the word "subsequent member" is a technical term used in grammar.
If, therefore, the *bahuvrīhi* is formed first, then immediately thereafter the *dvandva* would be prescribed with the subsequent word as its cause, and not otherwise.
For this very reason, Pārthasārathi’s prior rejection of the *dvandva* [in that position] is set aside.
Consequently, having first formed the three-word *bahuvrīhi*, the rule for the *dvandva* is subsequently applied to achieve the desired result.

Therefore, since in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound there is no mutual connection between the meanings of the subordinate members (*upapada*), and because the connection between the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* is understood only subsequently, and since this subsequent conjunction is possible even in relation to the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) rather than a single day, there can be no simultaneous performance (*samuccaya*) of the two on one day.

For this very reason, in accordance with the general rule of extension (*atideśa*), the sequence is established as "the *rathaṃtara* on the first [day] and the *bṛhat* on the second"; thus, even the sequence understood from the *dvandva* compound must be explained as being based solely on the proximity of the items.
Maṇḍana: "There is no state of being two *sāmans* every day.
Śaṅkara: "The statement regarding the *sāmans* is made by dividing them within the *pṛṣṭhya* [six-day period].
In the *Gavām ayana*, at the end of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, there is the performance of either eating food on the road (*adhvaśana*) or offering oblations into the fire (*hutāśana*).

Regarding the *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha], when it has concluded and the *saṃsthiti* [ceremonial conclusion] has occurred, it should take place on the third day from that point, following immediately thereafter as in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Commentary: In a certain specific ritual, it is heard in scripture: "The *pṛṣṭhya* ṣaḍaha begins with the *tryaṃśiśara*.
Regarding the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), there is the statement: "When the *pṛṣṭhya* ṣaḍaha has concluded, at midday, either clarified butter [is offered]."

This matter of eating honey and eating ghee, which is obtained through the general injunction (*codaka*), gives rise to a doubt: should it be performed at the end of the *tryanika* (three-day period), or at the end of the *ṣaḍaha* (six-day period)? What is the prima facie view? On this point, the Sūtra itself states: "The consumption of the essence (*rasabhojana*) should be performed when the *pṛṣṭhya* [period] has returned and the *ṣaḍaha* has concluded on the final day of the *tryanika*.
Why? Because of its position at the end."

In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the consumption of the *rasa* occurs within an interval of three parts; if one were to act here as in the archetype and likewise perform it within an interval of three parts, one would follow the injunction (*codaka*). But if, on the other hand, one were to perform it immediately after another [act], one would sublate the injunction.
For sequence is indeed endlessness.
And it has been established that this [specificity] is the cause for the connection;
furthermore, this has been observed in the case of one who has eaten rice accompanied by meat along with a third portion [of other food].
Therefore, it is performed immediately after the third portion.
Or rather, it would be at the beginning, because of its connection with the *kuta* period.

The Commentary states: "It is not the case that the consumption of *rasa* occurs immediately after the three-part [period]. What then? It should take place at the end of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*)."

Why? Because it is said, "when the six-day period has concluded" (*saṃsthite ṣaḍahe*), not "when the three-day period has concluded" (*saṃsthite tryaṃśiśe*). This refers to the termination characterized by the six-day period, not that characterized by the three-day period.
And the six-day period is completed over six days, not on a single three-day period day.

As for what was said— that because the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) of the three-year period is observed there, here too, by that same immediate sequence, there ought to be eating [only] according to the original rule (*prakṛtivat*)—
this is not correctly stated. For in that case, the three-year period had indeed concluded as a matter of fact.
Why? Because on that day, in that twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) has concluded.
Here too, where it concludes, there the eating will take place.

Therefore, the connection of the eating is with that which is characterized by the conclusion of the six-day period—as in "when the six-day period is completed"—and not with that which is characterized by the conclusion of the three-day period.
As for the claim that sequence is the cause of a specific connection, it is true that it is a cause; however, it is not so when it is contradicted by a stronger means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
In this case, however, it has been stated that [the performance] is enjoined by the sentence (*vākya*) at the conclusion of the six-day period.
Therefore, since a specific connection is established by the sentence, mere proximity (*ānantarya*) alone is not the cause.
Therefore, it might be argued that the eating should occur at the end of the six-day period.

But the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: "For its procedure is understood to extend to the end of twelve days by virtue of the ritual context; or else, from the direct statement (*vākya*), it belongs to the six-day period, and its status as an auxiliary to the three-eyed [deity] follows from the sequence."
Therefore, at the end of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), there should be a meal of *rasa* (juice).

The connection [of this discussion] arises from the following objection: even though the previously established optional alternatives obtained through the force of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) are set aside here, there is no setting aside of the sequence known from that context.
In the Sūtra, "eating *rasa*" means eating honey or eating clarified butter (*ghṛta*) when the performance is being carried out in reverse order.
[The opponent asks: "In the commencement of the Tryaṃśi sacrifice, does the eating of honey (madhubhojana) take place at its end, or rather at the end of the six-day period?
It should be at the end of the six-day period because of proximity; however, according to the direct statement (vākya), it is the latter [at the end of the Tryaṃśi]."
In the archetype, the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice is prescribed as a six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) consisting of the *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, *saptadaśa*, *ekaviṃśa*, and *tryaṃśiśa* stomas.
In the *gavāmayana* sacrifice, when that [six-day period] is performed in reverse order during the fortnight (*pakṣas*), the *tryaṃśiśa* becomes the first.
Furthermore, it is prescribed in the archetype: "When the six-day period has concluded, one should eat honey or ghee."

And here, because the injunction for the meditation on eating at the [proper] time (*madhvaśana-bhāvanā*) is qualified by the alternative (*vikalpa*), there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Although this [meditation] was performed at the end of the *tryaṃśiśa* in the archetype (*prakṛti*), here it must be performed specifically at the end of the *trivṛt*. This is because, in the archetype, since the *tryaṃśiśa* itself constitutes the end of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), its being the "end" is established by the force of the context (*ārthika*); for the phrase "when the six-day rite is completed" (*saṃsthite ṣaḍahe*) has already distinguished that the end of the six-day rite is the point of completion. Indeed, this [meditation] is not a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *tryaṃśiśa* based on the order of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sadeśya*), such that it would necessarily apply at the end of that in the modified rite (*vikṛti*); rather, according to the principle of the *vaimṛdha* offering, it is a subordinate part of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*) based on the direct statement (*vākya*).

Because the *anuṣṭhāna* (performance) is set aside by the direct statement (*vākya*) regarding the *sādeya* (the *sadyaskr̥t* sacrifice), for this very reason, even the *saṃsthā* (conclusion) need not be suspected [of being the occasion]. Since the *saṃsthā*, which consists of cessation, is of no utility, it cannot be the object of the injunction (*anudeya*).

Therefore, the *saṃsthā* either serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the past time denoted by the suffix *-ka*, or it functions solely as a causal condition (*nimitta*), just as in the expression "when [a son] is born again."

And therefore, by the principle of *ivarātin* (the "one who eats first"), since the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*)—though already connected as a qualifier of the cause—is present, it is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to that [six-day period] alone, just like the *vaimṛdha* sacrifice, rather than being a subsidiary to the entire twelve-day period through the assumption of another word.

As for what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—that it is a subsidiary to the twelve-day period because of the context (*prakaraṇa*)—that refers to the first day of the *gavāmayana* when it is performed in a condensed form (*samūḍha*). In the *gavāmayana*, [it occurs] in the condensed form.
That [position] was disregarded because it leads to an undesirable consequence (*āpatti*).

Furthermore, as for his statement that it is a *dvādaśāha* sacrifice because it produces satisfaction for the neutral participant (*madhyastha*) to the extent that it is perceived to assist in the performance of the subsequent ritual items—that too was disregarded, because if that were the case, it would follow that one must know only those specific items that constitute such a "gap" (*chidra*).
In every respect, in the *gavām ayana*, the consumption of honey occurs only after the *trivṛt* [stoma].
Maṇḍana: "At the end of the six-day period, there should be eating. Śaṅkara: "At the end of the six-day period, there is the eating of honey.

In the Gavām Ayana, the first day is the Prāyaṇīya; and in the Dvādaśāha, the first day is also the Prāyaṇīya. Since there is no relationship of archetype (prakṛti) and ectype (vikṛti) between these two, there is no extension of ritual properties (dharmātideśa).
VI. 7|312. In the Gavāmayana sacrifice, at the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra, the procedure (vidhvant) is that prescribed for the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Ṭup. 7|4|1319. On the day called Mahāvrata within the Gavāmayana, it is said: "The panis sing along (upagāyanti).
In that case, there is no sublation of the original (prākṛta) singers by the singers who sing along with the Upaniṣads.
This is a supplementary song (*upagāna*) for the *dundubhi* songs. (Vi.

10.4.16). Regarding the three *svarasāman* days in the *gavāmayana*, their specific characteristics (*dharma*) are extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to the two final *svarasāman* days within the eight-night sacrifice (*aṣṭarātra*).

(7.3.10). In the *gavāmayana*, when the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* is repeated with an intervening period of a different six-day rite (*vijātīya-ṣaḍaha*), there is also a repetition of the eating of honey and other such observances.
Commentary: In the Gavāmayana sacrifice, it is heard: "There are four Abhiplava six-day periods; the Pṛṣṭhya six-day period is the second, that is the third, that is the fourth, that is the fifth.
In this context, the rule extended by the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) is obtained: "When the Pṛṣṭhya six-day period has concluded, one should eat honey or ghee.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: does the consumption of the liquid food repeat every month, or should it be performed only once at the very end?
What, then, is logical? According to the stated reasoning, it is "simultaneously" (sakṛt).
For he ceases from the activity belonging to the six-day period only at the very end, not before.
Even after having performed the six-day period earlier, he indeed proceeds again toward the six-day period.
Furthermore, that six-day period does not remain established [as a separate unit] if one proceeds toward that very purpose again;
however, at the very end, one does not proceed again.
Therefore, the conclusion reached is that one should perform it at the very end.
This being the case, we reply:
there must be repetition when there is an intervention due to the difference in time;
that is, there should be a repetition of the consumption of the essence, not a single performance.
Why? Because the occasion does not recur.
The completion of the six-day period is the occasion;
and that six-day period recurs again.
When that [six-day period] recurs, the *saṃsthā* (concluding rite) recurs; it recurs when extended.
As for what was said—that he indeed ceases after the six-day period at the very end and not before, and even having performed it, he again exerts effort for its sake—it is replied here:
although he begins it again, nevertheless, having completed it, he begins it once more.
Furthermore, it concludes [the cycle] in a manner different from the repetition of the six-day period;
for in that case, there is a repetition of the *pṛṣṭhya* without interruption,
whereas here it is separated by four *abhiplava* periods.
Therefore, because it is interrupted by subsequent actions, the operation belonging to the *pṛṣṭhya* [stotra] is understood to have reached its conclusion; this is the distinction grasped.
And while that [operation] has not reached its conclusion, another action cannot be performed.
Furthermore, there are two ways in which an action ends: either by reaching a state of indifference (*audāsīnya*) or by being interrupted by another action, as has already been stated.
Therefore, the *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha] recurs every month with an interval;
as it recurs, the meal occasioned by the completion of the rite (*saṃsthā*) also recurs.
Hence, it recurs every month.

Śā—Where, as in the Gavāmayana and other rites, there is a repetition of the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha which has been interrupted by the Abhīlva and others, there, due to the recurrence of the *nimitta* (the cause, namely the completion of the sacrifice), there is a recurrence of the *naimittika* (the effect, namely the eating of honey and so forth).

Soma—The connection [of this section] is as an exception (*apavāda*) to what preceded. Vi—“Is the eating of honey at the end of the whole [sacrifice], or monthly, or at the end of each Pṛṣṭhya? At the end of the whole, it is as before; but not so, because the completed [Pṛṣṭhyas] are distinct.”

Bhāṣya: Where, as in the Gavāmayana and other rites, the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha is prescribed to begin with the commencement of the six-day period, there—even after the first six days—because another activity is performed and the activity directed toward that [six-day period] has ceased, there is a repetition of the eating of honey. Here, since the Abhilava-ṣaḍaha is also a modification of the twelve-day (Dvādaśāha) six-day period, the statement regarding the intervention by that [period] even there in the case of the eating of honey should be considered as intended to exclude it. Maṇḍana: "Its repetition occurs every month."
Śaṅkara: "But [this applies] for repeated performance.

In the Gavāmayana, the Vaiśvānara Jyotiṣṭoma becomes the Prāyaṇīya day. (Bhāṣya 7.3.125). In the Gavāmayana, the Samūḍha-dvādaśāha-anīkā is obtained through the force of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction).

The repetition of the three divisions (*tryanīka*) and so forth must be performed. And that [repetition] belongs to the various days (*nānānāman*) endowed with specific initial [elements] arranged in sequence, which are obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction). When they are performed in that very manner, the repetition is obtained again and again by the *codaka* in the same way; thus, the repetition is "like a swung staff" (*daṇḍakalitavat*). This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). However, it must be performed so as to fill the interval between the *prāyaṇīya* and the *udayanīya* [sacrifices].
And that [purification] must be performed precisely according to the purification of its own place;
having divided the intermediate space into nine parts,
[it is applied] to the Gavāmayana and other such rites.

The conclusion accepted by the Bhāṣya is that the performance should be carried out in this sequence: the precedence of the Aindravāyava cup in the days belonging to the first third, the precedence of the Śukra cup in those belonging to the second third, and the precedence of the Āgrayaṇa cup in those belonging to the third third, and so on again. The conclusion following the Vārtika is that one should divide the first [set of days] into nine parts and assign one form of precedence to each part, as each part consists of twenty equal units; this is known as "increase according to position" (sthānaviddhaddhi).

In the case of the *jyotiḥ* and other days within the *gavāmayana*, when there is a doubt as to whether the *dvādaśāha* (twelve-day sacrifice) rules should apply—on the grounds that the *codaka* (extended injunction) prevails over the name, since the *dvādaśāha* rules would be obtained through the *codaka*—or whether the *ekāha* (one-day sacrifice) rules should apply on the grounds that the name prevails; [the following is argued]: because each individual day lacks the capacity to be a means to the result and thus does not require its own specific rules like the name suggests, and because the application of the name is possible even for the transfer of additional non-conflicting rules, and because of the two indicative marks (*liṅga*)—namely, the presence of the *daśāha* (ten-day) defects and the similarity in the performance of the *ekavihāra* (single session)—the *codaka* is favored and the *dvādaśāha* rules are applied. However, although the collective nature of the days as means to the result is understood from the sentence stating the fruit, their status as means is understood individually due to their distinctness, which makes the requirement for rules logical. Furthermore, names are more powerful than the *codaka* because they are directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), whereas the *codaka* is inferential (*ānumānika*); because the name pertains to the specific enjoined rules rather than the general category of "sacrifice" (*yāgatva*); and because it does not depend on multiple indicative marks. Since the names such as *jyotis* denote the sacrifice itself, they cannot transfer additional rules. Therefore, the conclusion is that the rules of the *ekāha* type of *jyotis* and others are transferred; this is established in the section on "Similarity" (7.4.3).

In the Gavāmayana and similar rites, during the performance of the *pṛṣṭha-ṣaḍaha*, the consumption of honey occurs only once at the end of the entire six-day period, not at the conclusion of each individual six-day period.
And regarding repetition, there is the repetition of that [act], because of the repeated performance of the ritual action.
The Commentary states: "It is heard in scripture: 'They undergo the Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha in rotation.
In that context, this is obtained through the *codaka* (extended application rule): 'When the Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha has concluded, one should cause [the sacrificer] to consume honey or ghee.'"

In this regard, there arises a doubt: should the eating be repeated with each repetition of the six-day period, or should it be performed only once at the conclusion of the six-day period? What is the prima facie view? The eating should be repeated when the six-day period is repeated. Why? Because of the repeated performance of the ritual action.
For that ritual act is subject to repetition;

by its repetition, whatever is connected to it would also repeat, just as the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns connected to the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*) are repeated, so too the meal connected to the six-day rite would be repeated.
Or rather, it should occur at the end, because its time has already been fixed.
Commentary: It is not the case that what was stated—"eating also would recur by the repetition of the six-day period"—is correct.
What then? It should be performed only once at the end of the six-day period. Why? Because its time has already been fixed.
For the time for eating has indeed been established by the rule "when the six-day period has concluded" (*saṃsthite ṣaḍahe*).
"Conclusion" (*saṃsthāna*) means termination, the cessation of the activity belonging to the six-day period.
One who is performing the six-day period, however, is not said to have ceased from activity merely because that activity belongs to the six-day period.
Furthermore, the six-day period does not conclude while the agent has not ceased [the performance].
For "conclusion" (saṃsthā) with respect to an action consists either in indifference toward it or in performing another activity after the previous rite.
However, one who is performing the six-day period again does not fall into indifference, nor does he perform another activity; rather, he performs a repetition of that very same rite.
Therefore, it is not concluded.
And since there is no formal conclusion (*saṃsthā*) when it is not concluded, the consumption (*prāśana*)—which is not explicitly prescribed—is not performed.
As for what was stated, "Just as other six-day rite properties such as the *stotra* and *śastra* are repeated, so too should the consumption be repeated," this is not correct.
For those [acts] are connected with the days; since there is a repetition of them in connection with the days, it is logical that there is a repetition of the hymns and so forth.
Indeed, they are not enjoined in relation to the days by way of a connection with their conclusion (*avasāna*).
But here, the reason has been stated: the injunction for eating is by way of a connection with its conclusion.
Therefore, the repetition of the feeding is not appropriate.
Furthermore, if this feeding were to last for six days, then it would recur by virtue of the repetition of the principal rite;
but this is not the case.

Why? Because there is an absence of any cause for it being an auxiliary (*aṅga*), such as [established] context (*prakaraṇa*), syntactic connection (*vākya-saṃyoga*), or the observation of a direct benefit (*pratyakṣopakāra*). Among these, we do not perceive any reason here.
To begin with, the context pertains to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), not the six-day sacrifice (*ṣaḍaha*).

Furthermore, the syntactical connection in the phrase "when the six-day sacrifice is concluded" (*saṃsthite ṣaḍahe*) indicates that the eating occurs upon the conclusion of the six-day sacrifice. And the six-day sacrifice is said to be "concluded" only if no further subsidiary part of it remains.
Furthermore, honey-eating and curd-milk eating do not directly assist the six-day period.
Why? Because they are performed after it has concluded.

Granted that one may perform the act of satiation to whatever extent and in whatever manner is necessary, it should assist in producing the capacity for those rituals that follow; however, this does not apply to what has already passed, namely the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*).

As for the reasons such as sequence (*krama*) and so forth, even they become causes for a specific connection only by depending on a connection with another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), not independently.
Therefore, the act of eating is enjoined for the persons at a time characterized by the six-day period; consequently, the eating is not to be repeated.
Regarding the chanting in the Gavāmayana and other rites (1555), [the text] mentions the *raurava-ogha-jā* [sāmans].

However, the refutation in the Bhāṣya that the *rasabhojana* (the eating of meat) is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) should not be taken too seriously as it is merely a hyperbolic statement (*atiśayokti*).
As for *Soma*, the connection [of this section] arises from relying on the previously mentioned omission of the six-day period.

Regarding those cases established by the Sūtra: "They proceed to the *pṛṣṭhya* when it has been turned back"—where there is a repetition of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), there should be a repetition of the eating of honey (*madhvaśana*), because the ritual action is performed again.
Objection: Should one repeat the practice in the case of the repeated six-day period, or not?
The first [position] holds that it should be repeated, like the *stotra*, *śastra*, and so forth. Response: Not so; for that is prescribed as being completed [once].

Bhaṭṭa: In cases such as "They perform the six-day rite repeatedly," where the repetition of the six-day rite is heard to occur in immediate succession, the eating of honey occurs only at the very end; for the completion (*saṃsthā*) of the six-day rite consists in the cessation of the activity directed toward the six-day rite, and because that [completion] exists only at the very end. Therefore, on each individual day, the rite is not performed precisely because the occasion (*nimitta*) for it is absent.

For in this case, neither the completion of the performance nor merely the time subsequent to it constitutes the meaning of the term *saṃsthā* (conclusion), such that the eating of honey would have to be repeated because it exists at the end of every six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*). Rather, the word *saṃsthā* denotes the finality of the activity, as is evident from its usage in expressions like "the battle has concluded" (*yuddhaṃ saṃsthitam*). And when the six-day period is to be performed, the finality of the activity directed toward that purpose cannot possibly occur at the end of each individual day.
Therefore, at the end of every *ṣaḍaha*, there is only a single consumption of honey. Maṇḍana [states]: "But there is no repetition of the eating.
Śaṅkara [states]: "That [eating] occurs once more at the end of the *ṣaḍaha*."
That is the consumption of honey.
Words such as "cow" and "horse" denote a genus (*jāti*).
Words such as "reciter" (*pāṭhaka*), however, have their application based on action (*kriyā*).
VI. 7.3.11. *Gavīdhukāḥ*: wild wheat (*āraṇyagodhūma*).

(In the Koṅkaṇa region, it is the name of a particular kind of grass known as *kaśeḍa* or *kaśāda*. "Indeed, *jartila* seeds and *gavīdhukā* are not [proper] oblations" (VI. 10.8.4). By the term *gavya*, we mean the *Gavām Ayana* sacrifice, because of its connection with cattle, as in the text: "The cows, indeed, performed this sacrificial session."
There is an extension of its properties to the *satras* (sacrificial sessions) in such cases as "the Ādityānām-ayana," and so forth;
and [this applies] to the *gavya* [sacrifice] and those beginning with it. Bhāṣya 8.1.19.

Regarding the term *gavya*: from the word *go* (cow), in connection with a sacrificial session (*satra*), there are three [meanings]. First, because of the connection with cows—as in the statement, "The cows indeed performed this sacrificial session"—it refers to the *Gavāmayana* sacrificial session due to its connection with cattle.

Regarding the phrase "in those beginning with that": "that" refers to the *gavya* sacrificial session; those for which that is the beginning are "those beginning with that," such as the *Ādityānām-ayana* and other sacrificial sessions.
The *bahuvrīhi* compound is one where the meaning is not recognized from its constituent parts (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).

In the case of sacrificial sessions (*satra*) such as the *ādityānām ayana* and others that begin with the word "that" (*tadādi*), there should be the procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *gavya*, that is, the *gavāmayana*, because of the commonality of being a year-long rite (*saṃvatsara*).

This is shown by the statement, "The *panayas* sing along," which indicates a characteristic (*dharma*) of the *māhāvrata* [rite] within the year-long session, and by the statement, "The priests (*ṛtvij*) sing along," which applies to the year-long session.
And therefore, the Gavāmayana is the archetype of the year-long sacrificial sessions (*saṃvatsarasattra*).
*Gāna* is one thing, and *udgāna* is another; for the singing (*gāna*) is distinct, while the chanting (*udgāna*) is distinct.
"Singing" (*gāna*) refers merely to vocal performance, whether worldly or Vedic.
The second section of the *Sāman* is well known as the denotation of the root *gā* (to sing) in its unprecedented sense.

Bhāṣya 3.5.8.26: singing, responsive singing (*upagāna*), the responsive singing of the wives with lute-like instruments (*kāṇḍavīṇābhiḥ*), drum-singing (*dundubhigāna*), bodily singing (*śārīragāna*), and stringed singing (*tantrīgāna*).

VI. 10|4|16. Here they perform the singing from the *udgātr* [the Udgātṛ priest]. The assistance to that is called *upagāna*; the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) perform it with the sound "ho" and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) with the sound "o". There are also specific musical instruments called *kāṇḍavīṇā*.

The Panayas sing along; indeed, they perform the drum-song at the Mahāvrata by beating drums. The "bodily song" is the singing performed by singers using the parts of the body, such as the throat and so forth.
Thus, many types of chanting (*gāna*) have been demonstrated.
In the *ekatrika* rite, the chanting is performed on a single verse (*ṛc*) repeated thirty times in the *dhruva* [stotra] (Mīmāṃsā 10.5.13.10–11).
In the *mādhyandina-pavamāna-stotra* of the *ekatrika* rite, the chanting is performed on the entire first triplet of verses (*tṛca*).

In the chanting, the *iyāvā* and *svāgnīgava* [are used]. 1556: The *gāyatrī* verse, serving as the *puro'nuvākyā*, is to be chanted upon the three-verse hymn (*tṛca*) beginning with "svādiṣṭhayā madiṣṭhayā," which is composed in the *gāyatra* [meter] by means of the expansion of the *bṛhatī-vihāra-paṅkti* meters.

3|3|12|9. The visible fruit of singing is the manifestation of the specific form of the *ṛc* syllables through particular tones.

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: in every respect, during the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, the Gāyatrīs must be produced by not omitting any syllables from the ordinary Triṣṭubhs and Jagatīs; furthermore, the word "Gāyatrī" refers to the numerical count [of syllables]. The sūtra refutes this with the word "or" (*vā*): "Or the word for a substance may be used figuratively because it applies to all cases.
In the Bṛhaspatisava, the statement "This day consists of Gāyatrīs" indicates that the word "Gāyatrī" denotes the number [of syllables]. The word "or" sets aside the prima facie position.

This word *gāyatrī* does not denote a number; rather, it is a distinct substance-word (*dravyaśabda*) derived from a quality (*guṇa*), namely the number twenty-four. It must be the designator of a Vedic verse (*ṛgdravya*) consisting of twenty-four syllables, because its scope is not universal [with respect to numbers]. Its object is not the number twenty-four itself, nor is it the property of having that number.
For no one would say, "The Gāyatrī is our body," when they ought to say, "The twenty-fourfold [metre] is our body.
Because it does not encompass all objects, this word "Gāyatrī" is not a numeral.
Thus says the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin).
And the application [of the term] is like "cowness.
In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the word *gāyatrī* denotes the substance of the *ṛc*, he states another reason:
the application of the word *gāyatrī* to the substance of the *ṛc*—that is, its relationship as a denoter—is like "cowness" (*gotva*).

The word *go* is derived from the verbal root *gam* (to go); although it is based on the cause of going, it nevertheless applies directly as a definition when denoting a general substance (*sāmānya-dravya*). It is just like that.
The analysis of the compound is "possessing *gotva*," similar to [the analysis] "of *gotva*.
And because number also possesses the nature of being a word (*śabdavat*).
In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he states another reason:

there exists a word that denotes the number twenty-four, and this [number] has no other meaning than that expressed by the word *gāyatrī*. Therefore, the word *gāyatrī* denotes specifically the substance of the *ṛc* verse as qualified by a particular meter.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: that which possesses sound is "sound-possessing" (*śabdavatī*), namely number; the state of being that is "sound-possessingness" (*śabdavattva*); [the reason is] "because of that. Furthermore, because the other [alternative] is not heard [in scripture], he states another reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Because there is no scriptural mention of "the other"—that is, a distinct *ṛg* substance different from the number mentioned in the preceding sūtra—and because a word distinct from the word "gāyatrī" is heard [in its place], and because some designation (*saṃjñāśabda*) is necessary for that [substance] as well for the sake of conventional usage, the word "gāyatrī" is meaningful.
However, in the case of a number, it would be purposeless.
Therefore, the word "gāyatrī" denotes the substance of the *ṛc*.
Alternatively, in the archetype (prakṛti), namely the Agniṣṭoma, Gāyatrī verses are employed; however, more Gāyatrīs than those are required for the Bṛhaspatisava.

But since there is no mention of any other collection of Ṛks and there is an absence of an injunctive scriptural statement (*vidhi*), when the question arises as to which ones should be taken, the conclusion is that they must be taken from the Ṛgveda alone. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to collect further supporting reasons.
Because it cannot be applied to another substance, it would be characterized by the omission of the *dukthya* [stotra].
Regarding the production of a *gāyatrī* from the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* meters in the *bṛhaspatisava* sacrifice through the non-omission of syllables, the example of the *agniṣṭoma* was cited;
the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) refutes that.

Since the term *agniṣṭoma* cannot be applied to any other substance and thus lacks a [direct] application, it is not possible for the status of an *agniṣṭoma* to exist in the *Śatāgniṣṭoma* sacrifice without the omission of the *ukthya* days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*). Therefore, it is logical that the word *agniṣṭoma* denotes the ritual action of the sacrificial hymns as qualified by the omission of the *ukthya* chants—that is, distinguished by the omission of the *ukthya* stotras.
On the other hand, the word *gāyatrī* is well-known as denoting the substance of the *ṛc* verse;
therefore, the attainment of the *gāyatrī* state occurs through the omission of syllables.
And because they lack the characteristic of being branches (*aśākhallakṣaṇatvāt*).
Regarding the attainment of the status of an *agniṣṭoma* through the omission of the *ukthya-stotra*s of the twelve-day rites within the *śatāgniṣṭoma*, he states another reason:

because the *ukthya-stotra*s in the *śatāgniṣṭoma* lack the characteristic of being branches—that is, because they lack the characteristic of being branches due to their non-scriptural (non-Vedic) nature—there is no contradiction with the rule for the *agniṣṭoma*.

In the case of Bṛhaspati’s [Soma sacrifice], however, the Gāyatrīs are indeed those defined by the scriptural characteristic, namely, "The Gāyatrī is this day. Therefore, there can be no sublation by the Triṣṭubhs and Jagatīs which are based on inference, because the Triṣṭubh and Jagatī meters do not possess that scriptural characteristic.
Since they are names derived from their origin, they may apply figuratively to those [verses] that exist separately.

Regarding what was stated in the sūtra, "That [word] is used as if it were eternal, even though [the things denoted] exist separately," the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) speaks in order to refute that claim that the word *gāyatrī* is observed to denote a numerical measure. He says: The word *gāyatrī* is a name given at the very time of the origin of a ṛc verse characterized by a specific meter; thus, it is a name based on its origin (*utpatti-nāmadheya*). Because it is such a name based on origin, the word *gāyatrī* may be used figuratively—that is, through a secondary or metaphorical application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*)—for the purpose of praise when referring to *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* verses which exist separately from the *gāyatrī*.
For the purpose of praising the Gāyatrī and other meters, it is said: "Indeed, two Gāyatrīs are one Jagatī.
Therefore, the word *gāyatrī* does not denote a number.
If it is argued that it is a statement [of fact], [we reply: no.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) raises the objection that, because of the scriptural statement, the word *gāyatrī* must be expressive of a number;
for there is the statement: "He makes three *anuṣṭubh*s into four *gāyatrī*s."
In an injunction (*vidhi*), the primary meaning of a word is not [to be disregarded].
It is impossible to perform three *anuṣṭubh*s and four *gāyatrī*s;
however, it is possible within the count of sixty-five [syllables] in those three *anuṣṭubh*s to have four sets of twenty-four [syllables].
If it is argued that, therefore, the word *gāyatrī* refers to that number [of syllables],
it is said in response by the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) as follows: "Only so far as has been stated."
It is exactly as stated:

"He makes four *gāyatrīs*. Here, in this single instance, the word *gāyatrī* has the sense of a number, but not elsewhere, because its status as a designator of a number is observed only in some specific cases.
In some manuscripts, the sūtra itself reads only: "As far as it is stated, so far only does it have the sense of a number in one place, and not elsewhere, because it is not seen anywhere else."
Regarding the word *ka*, there is the sūtra: "The meaning of number applies only in one instance [of the word] *yāvadartha*, and not elsewhere, because it is not seen [so used] anywhere.
Regarding the word *bahu*, however, the sūtra is simply: "As stated" (*yāvadukta*).

In the Bhāṣya, however, a distinction is made: the subtle point is that "as stated" (*yāvadukta*) means the meaning of number applies only here in this one instance and not elsewhere because it is not seen [so used], while the remainder is merely an explanation (*vyākhyā*).

Therefore, we consider that following this [interpretation] constitutes a reasonable state of exposition, rather than an unjust one. Even in the *Vivaraṇakārikā*, the sūtra was formulated as merely "yāvaduktam" (as much as has been stated).
Furthermore, there would be an option regarding the unprecedented [matter] only if there were an injunction of number.

If, in the passage "On the Bṛhaspatisava day, this day consists of a Gāyatrī," the word *gāyatrī* were to enjoin a number, then there would be an option between this Gāyatrī verse—"O you who offer oblations, worship; bring [the gods]; choose the carrier of the oblation"—and any other [verse] containing twenty-four syllables, because of the direct scriptural statement of the original form (*prakṛtiśruti*) in the archetypal Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. But such an option is improper when a valid alternative exists. Therefore, the word *gāyatrī* does not denote a number.
If it is argued that [the word *gāyatrī*] refers to the quality of being a *ṛc*, the proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*) states:

"In the case of the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, where it is said, 'On this day, the Gāyatrī occurs,' if the word *gāyatrī* is accepted as denoting a number, an option (*vikalpa*) would result regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses at the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. To this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) replies: "In that instance, because the performance possesses the quality of being a *ṛc*, there will be no option."
In that context, the *sāmidhenī* verses are prescribed as *ṛc*s.
Therefore, in that case, the concluding (*paridhāna*) is performed with the *gāyatrī* verse beginning "ājuhotā duvasyata.
Those *sāmidhenī* verses which have the quality of being *ṛc*s are called "those characterized by the quality of *ṛc*" (*ṛguṇāḥ*).
The state of those [verses] is "the quality of being Ṛks";
therefore, it should be as in the previous case. The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) says:

If, because the *ṛc*s are subordinate qualities (*guṇa*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses in the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, no option regarding the *ṛc*s arises, then the previous model applies: that which possesses the previous [model] is the "one possessing the previous" (*pūrvavān*).

The Bṛhaspatisava is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma; in that "one possessing the previous," there would likewise be the quality of being subordinate to the *ṛc*s, just as in the *sāmidhenī*s of the Darśa and other sacrifices.
Thus, in the Bṛhaspatisava, the word "Gāyatrī" in the statement "On this day it is Gāyatra" must indeed denote the *ṛc*.
Because the performance of the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice is subordinate to the Ṛgveda, just like the performance of the Darśa and other sacrifices;
therefore, there is no production of the Gāyatrī by means of omitting syllables from the Triṣṭubh and Jagatī meters.
Furthermore, the penetration of qualities occurs everywhere.
The proponent says: In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one concludes the *sāmidhenī* verses with the *gāyatrī* verse beginning, "ājuhotā duvasyata.
In that case, the introduction of the quality—the introduction or placement of the number twenty-four—occurs throughout the entire verse "ājuhotā," and not in its parts.
By that [rule], both the quality of being *ṛc*s and the number are maintained.
However, in the case of the *bṛhaspatisava*, the number is applied to the constituent parts of those very *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* verses which are obtained through the *codaka*;
therein, the quality of being *ṛc*s is not maintained.
But if the archetypal *gāyatrī* meters were to be adopted, both [the original and the modified] would be favored; therefore, there should be the introduction of the archetypal *gāyatrīs*.
Alternatively, the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) raises an objection:
"And the penetration of qualities occurs everywhere."
But why are you so insistent on the number being restricted to syllables alone?
Let the number twenty-four be taken as applying to the days, or the cups, or other objects,
since there is a general scriptural statement that "this day consists of the Gāyatrī."
Therefore, the inclusion of the number twenty-four as a quality would apply everywhere, even to the cups (grahas) and so forth.
If it is argued that the term "completed" (niṣpanna) is intended as a qualification,
the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) says:
In the passage, "This day belongs to Bṛhaspati; it is a Gāyatrī," although the word *gāyatrī* denotes a number, it is nevertheless well-known as referring specifically to the number of syllables.
And since the established meaning must be accepted, the word *gāyatrī* cannot be used to denote the number of cups (*graha*) or goblets (*camasa*).
Therefore, the word *gāyatrī* expresses only the number of syllables contained within a *ṛc*.
Therefore, there is no application in all cases. In the case of *gāyatrī* verses, [the rule applies] to the original ones from the *gārhapatya* fire to the *āhavanīya* fire.
If it is argued that because the word expresses a number, there is no arrival of the original *gāyatrīs*,
then the same would apply here as well.
The proponent says:

Just as the word *gāyatrī* is well-known to refer specifically to the number of syllables—as in the statement, "In the Bṛhaspatisava, this day is a Gāyatra"—so too should it be here; for it is well-known in this very context and not elsewhere, such as in the twenty-four-syllable *gāyatrī* meter.
Or, if there were no distinction, the rule would apply by connection with the archetype (*prakṛti*), and thus it would be well-known even with respect to the syllables themselves.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is as follows: although the word "gāyatrī" is well-known to refer to *ṛc* verses—as in the statement, "In the Bṛhaspatisava, this day consists of Gāyatrī verses"—nevertheless, by the force of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), the original Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī meters are brought forward.
In that case, the Gāyatrīs must be produced by omitting syllables from the Triṣṭubhs and Jagatīs.
This being so, both the original (prākṛta) and the modified (vaikṛta) injunctions will be upheld.
In response to this doubt, the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) says:

Even in the absence of a specific distinction—that is, in the absence of a subject for the term *gāyatrī* and thus an absence of doubt regarding it—if there were a restriction because it is introduced by the archetype (*prakṛti*), because it is regulated by the archetype, because it is enjoined, and because it is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), then even the word *śara*, which is well-known to mean "reeds," would have to be interpreted as meaning "kuśa grass" in the sense of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) in the passage, "The sacrificial grass consists of *śara*.
And that is undesirable.

"If it is argued that usage [of the term] has been observed"—thus the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) raises an objection: "Is it not the case that even for something other than the *gāyatrī* verse, the use of the word *gāyatrī* is observed, as in the statement: 'Those two *gāyatrīs* together with one [more] constitute a *jagatī*'? "
If this is argued,
then the same applies to the arrows as well.

To the doubt raised by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*)— that the word *gāyatrī* is seen to be used even for that which is not a *gāyatrī*— the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*) replies:

If the application of the word *gāyatrī* is observed to refer to the number twenty-four based on its syllables, then likewise, the application of the word *śara*, which is well-known to mean "reeds," is also observed to refer to *kuśa* grass;
for a forest of *kuśa* grass is also called a "forest of *śara*.
This is the answer by way of a counter-objection (*prativandyuttara*).
"If it is by way of metaphor," the proponent says: "The word 'śara' is used metaphorically for *kuśa* grass."
This usage is figurative;
because of its long stalks and broad leaves, this is a statement based on similarity.
Therefore, the word "śara" is not a valid example.
If this is argued, then it is likewise in the other case;
thus says the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin).
Likewise, just as in the case of the word "arrow," there would be a figurative application of the word *gāyatrī* even to the *jagatī*;
and none of this is logical,
because since the meaning is not fully exhausted, [the application] would have to occur only with respect to a portion of those [metres].
The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), concluding the section and refuting the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), indicates the established conclusion by implication:

in the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, those Triṣṭubh and Jagatī verses that are obtained through the extended application (codaka) do not have their meaning completed when a portion of them—consisting of twenty-four syllables—is cut off;
furthermore, the employment of a mantra is for the purpose of expressing its meaning.
In that case, the application of the mantra would indeed be meaningless.
Thus, because the meaning is not fully realized in a single part, the term *gāyatrī* could not be applied to a single part of those *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* verses consisting of twenty-four syllables.

Therefore, when it is stated regarding the Bṛhaspatisava, "On this day, there is a *gāyatra* [sāman]," the importation (*āgama*) of the very *utpatti-gāyatrīs* from the *Daśatayas* must be performed in order to fulfill the required number of *gāyatrīs*.
However, *gāyatrīs* are not to be produced by omitting syllables from *triṣṭubhs* and *jagatīs*.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that by the instruction "it is *gāyatra*," the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) for *triṣṭubhs* and *jagatīs* is set aside.
[In this case], there are two *gāyatrīs* following, and the first is an *anuṣṭubh*; when those have been carefully prepared as *anuṣṭubhs*, they are the *dyāvācāgnīvasāgnīgarnī*.

Bhāṣya 12.6.25–28, Section 3: The term *gāyatrī* refers to the insertion of the *sāmans* that are being introduced into the *bṛhat* and *triṣṭubh* [verses], specifically in the *mādhyandina-pavamāna* and *ārbhava-pavamāna* of sacrifices characterized by increased *stomas*, but not in other *tucas*. Sūtra 5.3.13–14 states that the word *gāyatrī* denotes the substance of the *ṛk*.
But where there is an injunction such as, "He makes three *anuṣṭubh*s and four *gāyatrī*s," there the word *gāyatrī* refers to the number. 23. The *Gārhapatya*:

At the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), having heated the two fire-drills (*araṇī*) on the day sacred to Brahmā and having churned [the fire], the *Gārhapatya* alone—the entire churned fire—is to be established, but not all the fires.
Saṃkarṣa 3.2.1:
The Gārhapatya is the western fire at the *iṣṭi*.

Furthermore, in the Jyotiṣṭoma, within the middle of the great altar (*mahāvedi*) and inside the hall with the beams facing east (*prācīnavaṃśaśālā*), the Āhavanīya also becomes the Gārhapatya; its name is "Śālāmukhīya."
The ancient Gārhapatya fire of the Prācīnavaṃśa hall is named Prājahita. [Vi. 12.1.5-6] He draws out the blazing Āhavanīya fire from the Gārhapatya alone. [1561] ...of the word *girā*.

In this context, by the statement within the section on the *agnihotra*, the origin of the *āhavanīya* fire from the *gārhapatya* is indicated (*saṃkarṣa*. 3.1.7). At the time of the formal establishment (*ādheya*), the *āhavanīya* is to be established from the *gārhapatya* alone, and not from a common (*laukika*) source (3.2.2). Likewise, the establishment of the *dakṣiṇāgni* is from the *gārhapatya* alone, and not from a common source located in the southern direction.
3|2|4: The production of the Āhavanīya fire from the Gārhapatya itself for each ritual act, and not from the two kindling woods (araṇīs).
3|2|7: Regarding the stone-nature of the Gārhapatya, this will be established under the sūtra "In the case of substances, when there is a connection with an action" (Pūrvapakṣa, 6|1|1).
Vārttika 3|2|2|3, p. 752. The name "Prājahita" is an ancient designation for the Gārhapatya.

Bhāṣya 12.1.6.12: "The constant kindling of the Gārhapatya fire, or the method of constantly maintaining the two fire-sticks (araṇis), [is the means]. Saṃkarṣa 3.1.6: "'He offers the Patnīsaṃyāja oblations in the Gārhapatya'; here, the Gārhapatya is prescribed following a specific oblation. Vi. 10.8.8: "'Cooking is prescribed in the Gārhapatya; that same [fire] exists when it is employed, and there would be 'prasanga' (incidental application) when it is not employed. (This is what is stated).

The same principle applies here as well (regarding the cooking of the *agnihotra* at the *Kuṇḍapāyinām ayana*). [Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.2.1.6–13]: "He cooks the sacrificial oblations on the *gārhapatya* fire"—thus there is the employment of the *gārhapatya* in ritual acts.
[Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.1.3.12]: The *gārhapatya*-principle.

This is precisely the principle of Indra [the principle that a term denotes its primary meaning when it is not contradicted by other factors]. Bhāṣya 3.2.14.14: The word *gārhapatya* is based on consecration (*saṃskāra*); it denotes fire that has been consecrated.
Vi. 7.1.12: In the case of the *gārhapatya* and other fires, there is the performance of worldly rites.
The section concerning the sacrificial fires (*vihārādhikaraṇa*).

Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 12.1.11–7. Based on the reasoning that the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires do not serve as the substrates for the primary rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, [it is concluded that] both the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires are to be looked upon [as distinct]. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 780).
When the *āhavanīya* fire has fallen and only a remnant remains, it becomes the *gārhapatya*.
Bhāṣya 12.1.15. Without these—the *gārhapatya*, *āhavanīya*, *āhāryapacana*, and so forth—these rituals (*agnihotra*, *darśapūrṇamāsa*, etc. are not accomplished.

2.3.14. In the worship of the *gārhapatya*, the mantra "the non-abiding one, the gatherer" must be employed because of its explicit statement (*vacana*), and not for the worship of Indra on the basis of its indicative power (*liṅga*).

Bhāṣya 3.2.13–14: Words such as *gāvī*, *goṇī*, and *gopolatikā* are corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*) of the word *go*; they are not authoritative. Bhāṣya 1.3.8.24–29: Through words such as *gāvī*, the object possessing a dewlap and so forth is understood, for [the meaning] is consistent with the word *gāvī* as it relates to the word *go*.

Bhāṣya 1.3.8.28: From the perception of *gāvī* (i.e., from hearing the word *gāvī*), there is the recollection of the word *go*, and from that, the object possessing a dewlap and so forth is understood.

1|3|8|29. Regarding the phrase *girāgirā*: in the injunction "One should not say *girā-girā*" and "Having substituted *irā*, one should sing," when the word *irā* is prescribed following the prohibition of the word *girā*, there would follow the permanent cessation of that which was prohibited.
This is stated [as an objection].

Because it has not been previously obtained, the *irā* word is enjoined; once that [new] word is enjoined, the *girā* word—though already established by the text—is set aside, and that setting aside is confirmed by the prohibition "not with *girā*. (Vi.
1.4.2). Having prohibited the *girā* word, the *irā* word is enjoined; in that case, the function of the *irā* word is the same as that of the *girā* word, for the reason is identical.

The word *girā* is prescribed in the sacred text; from that, it is understood that the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is to be accomplished by means of the Sāman, and it is also understood that it is to be accomplished by means of the word *irā*. These two words have the same meaning; one is for the purpose of praise, and the other is likewise. Therefore, there should be an option between the word *irā* and the word *girā*.

(Dup—[In the second chapter, beginning with the rule *asāmapradeśe* (12.1.32), he will set forth the confusion regarding the Sāman; for now, he considers its preliminary introduction. With reference to the *yajñāyajñīya*, [the Bhāṣya states] "having made it *aira*, one should sing" (*airaṃ kṛtvā udgāyet*). This much is from the Bhāṣya itself. Herein lies the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*):
"Having made it *aira*, one should sing"—by the word *irā*, only the production (*utpatti*) of the Sāman is effected, not its application (*viniyoga*).
