Although the verse can be construed by taking the word *irā* to mean "the offspring of *irā*," nevertheless, the reading "the production is merely by means of the word *irā*" (or the sentence containing *irā*) appears more appropriate, as it is consistent with the preceding and following text.

For here there is no substitution of the word *irā* for the word *girā*; rather, it is stated here that the word *irā* takes the place of the word *girā*. Furthermore, after the [substitution] has taken effect, the subsidiary status (*aṅgatā*) of the *yajñāyajñīya* chant—which is still expectant of a purpose—is enjoined by the performance-injunction (*prayogavacana*) stating "one should praise with the *yajñāyajñīya*. The subsidiary status of the word *girā* is likewise [enjoined] by that very same performance-injunction of the *yajñāyajñīya*.
Therefore, because both possess equal authority, there is an option (*vikalpa*).

Alternatively, although the word *irā* is enjoined by this sentence (*airaṃ kṛtvā*) as an auxiliary to the hymn (and not by any other means of knowledge), nevertheless, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) cannot bring about what has not yet been produced; thus, its production must be expected from the sense of the context.
By the injunction "one should praise with the *yajñāyajñīya*," the status of the word *girā* as a means of praise is established. Its production is already established through the [Vedic] recitation.
Therefore, in one case (*irāpada*), the origin (*utpatti*) is to be expected, while in the other case (*girāpada*), the application (*viniyoga*) is to be expected.
Consequently, because both are deficient in one of these two factors, there is a remoteness of the cognition (*pratyayaviprakarṣa*) in both instances.
And this remoteness constitutes an option (*vikalpa*).
And because of the instruction regarding the Sāman.
The Commentary says: Here it is objected that there is no equality between these two.
In the word *girā*, only the *sāman* is mentioned, and no injunction of performance is prescribed;
however, in the word *irā*, the injunction of performance is prescribed. In that case:
Why? Because of the instruction regarding the *sāman*.
For the *sāman* is indeed instructed [as follows]: "They praise with the *yajñāyajñīya*.
And the *yajñāyajñīya* is like the *girā*-verse.
When that [sāman] is being taught, even a single word becomes taught.
Therefore, it is an option (*vikalpa*).
Or rather, it is a restriction (*niyama*) due to a specific scriptural statement; otherwise, it would be like the observation of the *sāman*.
The Commentary: Or there should be a restriction regarding the word *irā*. Why? Because of a specific scriptural statement (*śruti-viśeṣāt*).
By a specific scriptural statement, the word *irā* is taught [in the injunction]: "Having made this," whereas the word *girā* is taught as a general rule.
How, then, can the performance of the *sāman* be enjoined? There is merely the recitation of the word *irā*; there is no injunction for its performance.
However, since the *sāman* cannot otherwise be accomplished, the performance of the word *girā* is inferred through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*).

The substitution of the word *irā* must be performed by virtue of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) itself. Since the *sāman* is thus established by that, there is no need for presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) regarding the word *girā*.
Now, what is the scope of that which was taught in a general sense? To this it is replied:
The other [element] is the appearance of the *sāman*; it would be so. The appearance of the *sāman* enters into the modified forms (*vikṛti*), and the other [element] is also a modified form.
"It deserves to be adhered to.

Regarding what was stated—that by the phrase "the *aira* is the *kṛtodreya*" origination (*utpatti*) [of the *aira*] is effected alone, whereas by the injunction regarding the performance of the *yajñāyajñīya* its status as a means for the Vedic revelation (*śruti-sādhanatva*) is established—in that case, if it were heard thus: "The *aira* comes into being," then there would be origination.
In this case, however, the status of *irā* as the means is enjoined by the Vedic text itself through the expression "having made it *irā*, one should not turn back from *irā*.
But regarding the *yajñāyajñīya* chant, the status of the word *girā* as the means is enjoined through the principle of *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise inexplicability).
And that *anyathānupapatti* is expressed by the directly perceived word *irā*.
As for the claim that even from the word *irā* there is an expectation of arising from its meaning, it is said in reply:
by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), a specific instance of the word *irā* is enjoined in the hymn (*stotra*);
its arising from the meaning [of the word] follows from that.

It is argued that while the word has no function there [in the case of the *irāpada*], here [in the case of the *girāpada*], a specific ritual effect must be enjoined by the word itself. In that regard, there exists no established word [within the *girāpada*] that could enjoin a specific ritual effect. For such a word is neither heard [in the text] nor can it be inferred, since the hymn of praise (*stotra*) is already satisfied by the directly heard *irāpada* alone.
Therefore, there is a restrictive rule regarding the word *irā*.

[The opponent argues: "The other word, *girā*, possesses the appearance of a *sāman*"; thus, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) does not correspond to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*).
How so? Starting from the injunction, "One should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses," it is heard in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices that, "One should recite fifteen."

In that context (by virtue of the subject matter), the application of the *sāman* is sublated by the side-verse (*pārśvadaśya*) which has an established connection. However, in certain modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), such as the *Paśumitravindā* and others, the application of the *sāman* is enjoined again.
By that [substitution], what is obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) is set aside as it is replaced by the *pratyāmnāta* (the directly prescribed substitute).

Furthermore, the word *girā* does not appear in any *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice), such that the word *irā* would have to exclude it. Moreover, the word *irā*, having its utility already established, is obtained in the *vikṛti* by means of the *codaka*.
Furthermore, the word *irā* is obtained neither by direct injunction (*upadeśa*) nor by extended application (*atideśa*).
Therefore, the sūtra and the commentary [asserting] that "in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), it is indeed the word *irā*" are simply untenable.
It is said:
Just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *sāman* seen there is set aside by the *pāśvadaśya*, so too is the word *girā* set aside by the word *irā*; this much constitutes the illustration.
In those modified rites (*vikṛti*) for which there is authoritative evidence, it will apply.
And let there not be even a trace of it due to the absence of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*).
Alternatively, even without being a means for praise, the word *girā* occurs in certain modified rituals (*vikṛti*) by virtue of other authoritative evidence;
for instance, it is heard [in the scripture]: "He sings the *yajñāyajñīya* at the tail."
In that case, the word *irā* itself, joined with the word *pada*, should be employed exactly as it is [prescribed].
For where the *yajñayajñīya* chant is performed by means of the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*, there the word *girā* is set aside by the word *irā*, which has its function already established.
This is because its instruction occurs in the archetype (*prakṛti*) only in that specific context, and thus it does not apply elsewhere.

Śabara: Now, prior to the rule "In the case of the Sāmans, there is modification in the place of the Sāman" (12.1.9), he considers the preliminary discussion regarding the *ūha* (adaptation) that is about to be introduced. For those Sāmans, which are chanted upon certain syllables, are adapted to other syllables.
In this context, in order to state the attainment [of the *irāpada*] through the principle of "substitution" (*sthānāpatti*) for the *girāpada*, the author first considers that very substitution.

Just as there is the attainment of the *meṣa* (ram) for the *agniṣṭut* formula, so too, when the *irāpada* is attained in place of the *girāpada*, the *girāpada* undergoes substitution; therefore, since that will be established in the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*), the principle of substitution is examined here for its utility.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: In the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the *irāpada*—which is different from the *girāpada* prescribed in the text—is a permanent modification (*vikāra*) of the *girāpada*, because it is enjoined by an explicit scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavacana*).
"It is its sublater.
Vi— "There would be an option between *irā* and *gīrā*, especially in the latter case.
[Objection: No, it should not be so, because *irā* was prescribed previously by Brāhmaṇa."
There arises a doubt as to whether there should be an option between *irā* and *girā*, or whether it should be *irā* alone.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the first alternative holds due to the absence of any specific distinction. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that one should sing "āyīrā yīrā," and not "gāyīrā yīrā."
Bhāṭṭa: Following the discussion on the modification of mantras (*mantroha*), an introductory section (*upodghāta*) is commenced in order to examine the *sāman* chants.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, within the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the Agniṣṭoma stotra, it is heard: "One should not say *girā-girā*; one should chant the *ira* [verse] as *udreya*. In that regard, it will be stated that there is a modification (*ūha*) of the word *irā* in place of the chanting of the word *girā*.
And that [substitution] cannot occur without the substitution of *irāpada* in the place of *girāpada*; this too will be explained later.
In this regard, it is considered whether this substitution of place (*sthānāpatti*) is fixed or unfixed.

In this context, although there is no injunction in the passage "airaṃ kṛtvodgeyam" (having made it *aira*, one should sing) that prescribes the subsequent singing characterized by the *irāpada* as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) to the *stotra* and so forth—because there is no evidence for its being a different chant (*gāna*) in relation to the *yajñāyajñīya* which is a constituent part of the *agniṣṭoma* *stotra*—and because the prohibitory statement "not with *girā*, not with *girā*" would otherwise be an unintelligible restatement (*anuvāda*).

For this very reason, there is no injunction of the *irā* word with reference to the singing (*gāna*). If that were the case, although the *irā* word would be an auxiliary to the singing by way of being a *stobha* syllable, there would be no basis for the prohibition to be a restatement (*anuvāda*), because there is no evidence for the sublation of the *girā* word—which serves as its refinement. Therefore, as a restatement of a prohibition, the *irā* word alone is enjoined as a quality in the form of an *utkara*, taking over the function of the *girā* word. The phrase "udyem" (or similar), however, is a restatement of the singing already established as a means of refining that [word].
And it is possible for the word *irā* to perform the function of the word *girā*, because it expresses that same meaning.

For just as the word *iṣkartāram* (Ṛgveda 10.140.5) was explained by the author of the Mahābhāṣya through the elision of the letter *n* as having the sense of *niṣkartāram*—as seen in the examples of Vedic vowel elision under Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.1.9 (*sanyaloḥ*), which states: "In the case of *iṣkartāram adharasya* and *niṣkartāram asya* [the *n* is dropped]"]—so too, the explanation of the word *irā* as having the sense of the word *girā* through the elision of the letter *g* is not untenable.

Consequently, although by means of direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*) there is the production of the word *irā* and its status as a constituent of the hymn (*stotra*), whereas the word *girā* has its production through recitation and its status as a constituent of the hymn through sequence—or rather, its status as a constituent of the hymn is implied by the impossibility of the permanence of the *sāman* in the injunction "one should praise with the *yajñāyajñīya*" since the *sāman* functions as a constituent of the hymn only by way of manifesting the syllables of the *ṛc*, and thus the establishment of those *ṛc*-syllables is also accomplished—nevertheless, in either case, the word *girā* remains weak, even though it is common to other such words.

Nevertheless, since the *irāpada* being enjoined depends upon the accomplishment of the function of the *girāpada* (which it supersedes), there is a permanent sublation (*bādha*) of the *girāpada* by way of the specific nature of what is depended upon (*upajīvya*). However, this is not so; rather, as in the case of the rule "he does not perform those two *payas* [offerings]," there is merely an option (*vikalpa*).

This being the prima facie view, we reply: first of all, it is not heard in the scripture that it is "the function of the *girāpada*" that is [being superseded]; rather, it is the *girāpada* itself—referred to in the restatement of the prohibition—that is to be substituted for the *girāpada*.
By force [of the context], there is merely the status of being a *girā* word and a sentence.

And by that, just as the capacity of the *girā* word to produce that effect is postulated—because that effect requires a means and because the *girā* word requires an effect—likewise, by that very force, there is also the prevention of the postulation of a means for the *agniṣṭomīya* sacrifice for the *girā* word.

For this very reason, it is not by the fact that the effect is the objective (*uddeśyatā*), but rather by the fact that the *girā* word denotes a quality of a different class which serves as a means for the *agniṣṭomīya* sacrifice.

The conventional usage of the term "capable of performing that function" (tatkāryakṣamatva) is merely the contingency of the *girā* word itself, in the absence of a prohibition or a restatement of a rule.

For this very reason, even the recitation of the *girā* word is meaningful in cases such as the *Cayana* sacrifice, where it is enjoined: "One sings the *Yajñāyajñīya* [Sāman] on the tail. In that context, the *Yajñāyajñīya* Sāman serves its purpose solely by generating the manifestation of the syllables of the *ṛc* verse named "tail," which pertains to a perceptible object. Since there is no injunction for the *girā* word in that specific instance, the application of the *girā* word—which is not otherwise prescribed—is meaningful.

Therefore, it is established that by the force of the restatement of a prohibition (*niṣedhānuvāda*), the *girā* word and the like do not serve as the applicator (*viniyojaka*) for the *girā* word within the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice; consequently, since the *girā* word is specifically enjoined by the direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*) "The *aira* [verse] is to be sung," its status as part of that specific sentence and its assumption of its function are indeed certain.

As for the statement made in the *Tantraratna* and the *Śākhadīpikā* regarding the summary verse (*uddāna*) that this is a rule concerning the *irāpada*, that has been disregarded; for if it were a rule concerning the *stoma*, then since the singing would be different, it would be impossible for the *girāpada*—which functions as the expression of the qualities to be combined with the singing—to constitute the sentence. Furthermore, if the singing were extended to the subsequent [verse] as well, there would be the undesirable consequence of extending the *stoma* which is a subordinate part of that [singing], just as there is an extension of the singing itself.

As for the claim made by some that the *girā* word is enjoined because it is not known to belong to the *stoma*, and that—since it is possible for the *pūtīka* plants, which are prepared by the *abhibhava* rite, to serve as the means for the sacrifice just like [the soma]—there is a re-enjoining of some *gāna* (chanting) due to its rapid application, intended to prevent the connection of that *gāna* with the *girā* word: that too is disregarded, because even if the *gāna* were excluded, there would be no resulting exclusion of the *girā* word; and since, even if this [prohibition] were connected to the *gāna* of the context, one would have to resort to a mere restatement of a prohibition to exclude the *gāna* of the *girā* word alone, and thus both [the *girā* word and the *gāna*] would be excluded by that very [restatement], rendering the injunction of the *gāna* redundant.

Therefore, the truth is this: its function is solely to enjoin the word *irā*; the phrase *udgītham* is a restatement (anuvāda) of what is already established by the context (*sthāna*). Maṇḍana [Miśra] states: "The word *irā* is to be employed as a restrictive rule.
Śaṅkara [Bhagavatpāda] states: "In the case of *girā*, the first [syllable] is indeed the word *irā*."
26. *Irāpada*: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the Yajñāyajñīya [sāman].
According to Bhāṣya 9.2.139, when the *irāpada* takes the place of the *girāpada*, the singing (*gāna*) must be performed using the *irāpada* in the Jyotiṣṭoma at the Yajñāyajñīya.
"Because there is no singing [of the word], the instruction regarding the final syllable must be understood as referring to the word as it actually exists.

The Bhāṣya states: Regarding the *yajñāyajñīya* chant in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, they prescribe: "One should not say *girā-girā*; if one were to say *girā-girā*, the Udgātṛ would thereby destroy himself; having substituted *ira*, one should sing.
Thus, it is established that in the Jyotiṣṭoma, the word *irā* must be used in place of the word *girā*.

Now this is doubtful: should the word *irā* be chanted, or should it be unchanted? What is the prima facie view? Since another word [other than *girā*] is heard, we say that the word *irā* should be performed unchanted. Why? Because there is no chanting [of it].
For that which is not sung is not taught;
indeed, whatever is taught as being of a certain nature must be employed as being of that very nature.
But is it not the case that it is not said to be "not sung"? This designation is made by means of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).
By this, some particularity of accent is indicated.
To this it is replied:
although there is indeed a particularity of accent, other modifications of song, such as *āībhāva* and so forth, are not indicated.

The secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is produced from the unmodified form; therefore, that unmodified form should be employed. Now, it might be argued that the mention of "having become that" (*tadbhūta*) is not intended to be significant.
It is said:
the reason for not intending [to express something] must be stated;
however, when there is an intention to express it, the very mention [of it] is the reason.
Therefore, it should be employed without chanting. [Objection: The chanting of the word *girā* would not apply to the word *irā*.
Why? Because the syllables are refined by the chanting.

Song (*gīti*) is that which embellishes the syllables of the word *girā*; it embellishes those very syllables and is employed with those same syllables, not with the syllables of the word *irā*, because song is characterized by the specific nature of the syllables of the word *girā*.
Therefore, the word *irā* must be employed exactly as it is [in the original text].
But surely, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) has been applied in the sense of modification to form the word *airam*?
Furthermore, the modification of syllables consists precisely of the melody;

therefore, the singing is taught by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix itself. (It is replied: In this case, the secondary derivative suffix has not been applied in the sense of a modification; rather, it is used in its own primary sense (*svārtha*).
As far as it is stated, "having made *irā* [the object], one should drink," so far it is *airam*.

And if the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) were produced from the word after it has been chanted (*pragīta*), then, having applied the rule "the palatal [vowel] becomes long, or the first vowel [becomes long]," there would be the substitution of *āyī* for the letter *i*. ("When the palatal becomes *āyī*...")

By the rule *vṛddham* in the *Chandaḥsūtra*, which means that in the state of singing (*gītidaśā*), that palatal sound (*tālavya*) which has become "increased" (*vṛddha*) by having three morae (*trimātrātmakatva*) becomes *āyī*;
in that case, according to Pāṇini 4.2.120, *vṛddhācchaḥ*, the suffix *cha* (which becomes *īya*) is applied. Thus, the form would be *āyīrīya*.
But this is not heard [in the scripture].
Therefore, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in "airam" has its own meaning as its referent;
or else, the suffix would apply to that which occupies the place [of the original], which would result in a change of the word-form.
Commentary: The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position.
Whether it is the melody of that word in whose place the word *irā* is employed, or the melody belonging to that original word itself—that [melody] should belong to the word *irā*.
Why? Because the primary factor is the change of the word.
For this sentence has as its primary meaning the substitution of one word for another; namely, that in place of the word *girā*, the word *irā* occurs.
It does not mean that it should be employed unchanted, for the mode of expression is indeed different.
When a specific [substitution] for the word *irā* is being prescribed, there is another [instance of the] word *irā*.
For it is heard in scripture: "Having made a modification of the word *irā*, one should utter this.

In that case, by this method the word *irā* is prescribed; one should not state a modification of the word *irā* other than through the *pragāṇa* (chanting), nor [a modification] of the word *girā*—this is what is expressed by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
In this case, the modification of the word *irā* in the song is not determined by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix;

rather, it is the secondary derivative itself that subsequently expresses the modification. Thus, it is merely restated. That which is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), namely the word *irā*, is what is being enjoined.
Therefore, this statement concerns the difference between words, not the non-connection with the melody (*gīti*).
For the melody is indicated by way of its general application.
Ḍuṣyaṃta says: "The melody should be performed at the word *girā* (the meaning is: that melody which is [prescribed] for the word *girā* should be performed at the word *irā*)."
Why? Because the melody is indeed employed for the sake of the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the hymn (*stotra*), not for the sake of the phonetic form of the syllables.
Therefore, even in the absence of the word *girā*, the melody persists.
And that [melody] remains expectant [of the text to be sung].
Even the suffix *irāpada*, when being applied, is expectant with respect to the song (*gīti*);
therefore, there is a connection between the two.
But is this not a *vikāra-taddhita* suffix, rather than one used in its own sense (*svārthika*), since [otherwise] the consequence would be meaninglessness?
If it is argued that, therefore, the melody itself is enjoined by the word [gīti],
that is true;
however, four possible modes of interpretation present themselves here.

(1) When this *taddhita* suffix occurs in the modification of the *irāpada* chant, the *irāpada* is restated and [the modification] is enjoined; (2) or else, having restated the *irāpada*, the chant (*gīti*) is enjoined;
(3) or else, both [the chant and the *irāpada*] are enjoined [in the sense that "the *irāpada* must be sung"];
(4) or else, the pure *irāpada* [itself] is enjoined.
He refutes the first position: In that regard, the singing of the word *irā* is not well-known in either common usage or the Veda;
and because it is not well-known, it cannot be the object of a restatement (*anuvāda*).
(He refutes the second position: Even the word *irā*, precisely because it is not well-known, cannot be the object of a restatement.
Furthermore, if the *gīti* (melodic chanting) were enjoined by taking the word *irā* as its basis, the displacement of the word *girā* would not follow.
Syllables are not displaced by a melody, because their functions are not identical.
In that case, the restatement of the prohibition of the word *girā* would not be applicable.
In that case, a prohibition must be stated for each individual instance of the word *girā*. If that were stated, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
Furthermore, if the word *girā* were prohibited, the syllables would apply to its place without restriction; it would not necessarily be the word *girā* itself.
(He refutes the third view: Now, if both [the word *irā*] and the act of singing were enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Therefore, in the word "aira," it is the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself that is enjoined. And that which is being enjoined—whether it be the singing of the word *girā* or [the word *irā* itself]—obtains [the status of the original] through the principle of functional displacement (*kāryāpatti*).
And because of the connection with singing. The Commentary states: There is a connection with singing; the phrase "udgītham airā vā dākṣāsā" shows the singing of the *irā* syllable.
If it is argued that this is a statement [of the author], the Commentary says: "If you view it thus, then this is merely an observation regarding the singing.
This is not so.
The statement will be "This is Udrea or Āirā or Dākṣāsā.
No, because that is not the primary factor.
The Commentary says: This is not so.
For this sentence has that as its primary subject. What is its primary subject? It has the word *irā* as its primary subject, because of its explicit mention.
It was stated that it does not have the melody (*gīti*) as its primary subject, because there is no such mention.
Likewise, there is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the word *irā*, not concerning the song:
"I bestow *irā* upon the sacrificer.
And this explanatory passage refers to the word, not to the song.
Therefore, it should be employed as sung.
What is the purpose of this deliberation? There is no distinction here [in the case of the word *pra*].
However, there is a purpose for this term in another context: "One should not say *pra*, one should say *praprī*."
If it is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), then either *prapadam* or *praprīpadam* should be stated;

if it is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), then only *praprīpadam* should be stated. Ḍup—(Although this Vārttika is printed immediately after [the discussion on] *anvaya* in the Ānandāśrama edition at Sūtra 55, in reality, this belongs to Sūtra 58.)

Since the purpose beginning with "prapa-praprī" has already been established in the commentary on Sūtra 58, it follows that the *prayojana-vārttika* must also be written in that very place. Therefore, it should be understood that this [purpose] is written precisely under Sūtra 58.
"If it is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), either *prapadyam* or *pramīpadam* should be employed;
if it is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), only *prapīdam* should be employed" (this is a certain variant reading of the Bhāṣya). This is not the purpose of the immediately preceding section.
He states the alternative regarding the application of the word, [noting] that it does not apply to the *pragāṇa*.

Therefore, this is the purpose of the preceding section: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), either *prapadya* or *prapīda* [is used] for the verse beginning with "āmnātād antya," whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), only *prapīda* is used.
(This was) written here through oversight.

The purpose of the phrase "because it is not sung" (*apragāṇāt*) is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the *irā* word is to be used unchanted, whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it should be used chanted.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "There is no distinction here; the purpose lies in something else similar to that," this is the purpose of the sūtra (57–58) beginning with "If it is argued that this is a scriptural injunction" (*vacanam iti cet*).
Because of the scriptural injunction concerning the *irā* word, or by virtue of its occupying the same position (*sthānāpattyā*), the *irā* word must in every respect be employed chanted.
However, regarding *prapīda*, there is no scriptural authority for chanting.
What then? It follows from logical reasoning (*nyāya*).

In that case, if chanting were obtained by explicit statement (*vacana*) in the instance of the word *irā*, then because there is an absence of such a statement for *prapīda* and the others, they would not be chanted.

Therefore, there would be no lack of chanting for the *prapīda* and other such elements. However, because the sentence is primarily concerned with the difference between words, there would be chanting.
Since it has been established that "the other word is restricted," a doubt arises as to whether that [other word] should be employed unchanted (*apragīta*) or chanted (*pragīta*).

(And thus, since the opportunity has arisen, there is an investigation; this is the "connection by occasion" [avasarasaṃgati]. In that regard: "It would not be a means of knowledge, because of the injunction for that which is not sung; if the *vṛddhi* suffix were produced from what is sung, the consequence would be [the application of] the *āyīrya* suffix."
The Chāndogya-sūtra states that there are seven notes (*svaras*) characterized as *kṛṣṭha*, *prathama*, *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *caturtha*, *mandra*, and *atisvārya*.
Among these, the *kṛṣṭha*, *prathama*, *dvitīya*, and *tṛtīya* are "elevating" (*utkṣepinaḥ*), to be characterized by qualities such as upward movement (*utkṣepa*) and harshness (*āruṇya*).
The *caturtha*, *mandra*, and *atisvārya* notes are "descending" (*avakṣepinaḥ*), because they possess the nature of descending through downward release (*anvavasarga*) and other such qualities.
The middle note (*madhyama-svara*) resides within the interval delimited by the third [note] as the raised (*utkṣepa*) and the lowered (*avakṣepa*).

Thus, from the middle note named "third," the second is raised; from the second, the first is more raised; and the *kṛṣṭha* is most raised. In this same way, the gradation of intensity should also be understood for the lowered notes.
And for this reason, since the second name, *utkṣipta*, is acute (*udātta*), it results in the acute nature of that which has been raised (*utkṣipta*).
Likewise, it has been stated by the commentators on the *kṛṣṭha* sūtra that *kṛṣṭha*, *vṛddhi*, and *pluta* are synonymous designations for phonemes consisting of three morae (*trimātra*).

And thus, since the first vowel of the word *irā* is palatal (*tālavya*) and possesses the previously stated characteristics, it undergoes prolation (*pluta*) and becomes augmented (*vṛddha*). Because the rule "the vowels [in the *udgītha*] are like those in the source" (*yonivat svarāḥ*) extends [the properties of the source] to the *udgītha*, the first vowel of the word *irā* is also the first vowel [of the source]. Consequently, when the augmentation characterized by prolation occurs, another statement—"that which is palatal and augmented becomes *āyī*"—effects the change to *āyī*. Since the word *āyī* is augmented according to Pāṇini 1.1.73 ("the augment is that which is augmented in the Ṛgveda verses, beginning with the first vowel"), the suffix *cha* is applied by Pāṇini 4.2.114 ("*cha* after an augmented [word]"). Then, by the rule Pāṇini 7.1.2 (*āyīnīyau ca chandasi*), the substitution of *ai* for *āy* takes place, resulting in the undesirable form *āyīrīyam*.

In reality, however, the objection that the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) from a pre-existing chant would result in the suffix *ayi* being applied in its own primary sense (*svārthika*) is the proper point of refutation here. (Soma. Therefore, there is no chanting; for this [new word] is prescribed as the substitute for the word *girā*.
One should obtain that which is sung as the *irāpada* of that [verse].
Therefore, it should be employed in a chanted manner.
17. Vi—The *irāpada* may not be sung, or it may be sung; this is the omission of chanting.

It is not *geya* (to be sung), because it is sung in the place of that which is being sung. Even though the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *vimuktādimyo'ṇ* (Pāṇini 5.1.61), the word becomes *airaṃ sāma* because the term *sāman* is carried over from the rule *matau chaḥ sūtranāmnor-bahulam* (Pāṇini 5.1.69). And the quality of being a *sāman* consists in its similarity to song (*gīti*).

However, when the suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of "its modification" (*tasya vikāraḥ*, Pāṇini 4.3.124), then in the analysis *irāyā vikāraḥ* ("a modification of *irā*"), the aforementioned mode of singing is obtained.
Therefore, it must be sung. Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the doubt as to whether that *irā* word should be used unchanted or not—because of the hearing of "aira" as unchanted, it is unchanted.

For if this secondary derivative (*taddhita*) were in its own primary sense, then from the understanding of the meaning "having made it *irā*," the injunction of the *irā* word alone would be quite clear.

This secondary derivative (*taddhita*) does not arise from the state of being sung (*pragīta*), for if it were so, the vowel *i* would be palatal (*tālavya*), and since it would become long during the state of being sung, the *Chandoga-sūtra*—"that which is palatal and long (*vṛddha*) becomes *āyī*"—prescribes *āyī* with the meaning that whatever is three-mora (*trimātra*) and long and palatal during the state of being sung becomes *āyī*. Consequently, because it begins with *ā*, the suffix *cha* would be produced during the state of being sung by Pāṇini’s rule "from a long [base], *cha*," resulting in the form *āyīrīyam*.
Furthermore, if it were a secondary derivative in its own sense (*svārtha-taddhita*), it would result in redundancy; therefore, it must have the sense of a modification (*vikāra*).

If it is argued that this secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is applied precisely after producing the word *giri*, and that the modification (*vikāra*) pertains only to the property (*dharma*) consisting of the chanting (*pragāṇa*) of the word *irā*, even if that were so, there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*vidhigaurava*) in accepting the property of chanting as a qualified injunction. Alternatively, it is more appropriate to treat the secondary derivative as a restatement (*anuvāda*) by accepting that its referent is the property of denoting the word *giri* in a non-chanted form.

Nor is the reference "it should be sung" (*udeyam*) untenable as a restatement (*anuvāda*), even though only the *irā* word is prescribed for the occasion of the transgression (*āpada*), because that reference is justified by accepting the following meaning: "having made [the *girā*] into *irā*, it should be sung with other syllables. Nor does the transgression follow from the fact that the *girā* word is what is expressed, even if singing is not established through any other means; for there is no evidence that the *irā* word takes over the function of the *girā* word simply because the *irā* word lacks the nature of the sound of the Agniṣṭoma hymn. Furthermore, since the *irā* word lacks the status of being a means to that [Agniṣṭoma] through its connection to it, there is no possibility of its application via that [function].
For this very reason, even the chants in the *Ūhagrantha*—such as "āīrā-āīrā cā dākṣāsā"—are indeed not authoritative.

Nor can it be argued that because this [work] is rooted in *śruti*, the *nyāya* (logical principle) itself lacks authority; for by virtue of its designation as an *Ūhagrantha*, it is rooted in reasoning (*tarka*) and thus lacks a basis in *śruti*.
Consequently, in cases where there is no contradiction with existing [scriptural evidence], this [Ūhagrantha] is simply not authoritative.

As for the claim that this recitation of the *gīti* (chanting) is Vedic because it appears in texts concerning death and so forth—that should be disregarded, since it is found in the *ūha* (adapted) texts of the Vaidikas. This being the position reached, [the reply is: True; the injunction pertains to the actual form of the word *irā*, not to the chanting (*pragāṇa*). Nevertheless, since even the absence of chanting is denoted [by the term], the attainment of the chanting through the path of ritual action is not contradicted.

For instance, although the word *irā* has no direct utility toward the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the hymn (*stotra*), nevertheless, because the function consisting of the expression of qualities is identical for both the words *girā* and *irā*, such acquisition of ritual properties (*dharma*) is appropriate.

Although ritual duties (*dharma*) have as their purpose the expression of qualities (*guṇābhidhāna*), nevertheless, because this very *apūrva* produced by the expression of qualities is utilized for both the *agniṣṭoma-stotra* and the piling of the altar (*cayana*), and because it is accepted—following the logic of the restriction of subsidiaries in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* that the subsidiary elements such as chanting (*gīti*) are prompted by the intermediate *apūrva* produced by the expression of qualities which serves as the function of the *girā* word; therefore, it is entirely appropriate that those duties should apply to the *irā* word, which takes over the function of the *girā* word that has become a means to the *apūrva* of the piling, and which generates the function that serves as a means to the *apūrva* of the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*.

Or, let us set aside the objection that there is no "assumption of the function" (*kāryāpatti*) because we do not accept a difference in the intermediate effects; nevertheless, there is still an "assumption of the position" (*tāsthānāpatti*) for this *irāpada* on the grounds that it sublates the word *girā*.

Consequently, once the *irāpada* is understood from the context to belong to the stotra, there is nothing to prevent the transfer of its properties (*dharmāti-deśa*) to the *girāpada*, which presents itself as a sublater through its possession of the properties of being a song-form (*gītirūpa*).

Furthermore, it is necessary that the song (*gīti*) be characterized by the *girāpada*, which serves as the means for producing the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the fire-altar construction (*cayana*).

In reality, just as the *yajñayajñīya* [sāman] is employed in the piling of the fire-altar (*cayanam*) by the injunction "one sings the *yajñayajñīya*," so too is it employed in the *agniṣṭoma* chant by the injunction "one should praise with the intention of sacrifice."

Therefore, while one might assume that the application of the *girā* word to the chanting is for the purpose of its own substrate—that is, by way of assuming its application to the piling (*cayana*) through its connection with the piling of the *girā* word contained therein—there is rather the assumption that its true nature is to serve as the bearer of the *girā* word which is a constituent part of the *agniṣṭoma* hymn; thus, its application to the hymn (*stotra*) also follows from the very instruction [of the text]. Consequently, there is no transfer (*atideśa*) of the chanting of the *girā* word to the *irā* word based on that [instruction] alone.

Even though one might suspect that the *irāpada* undergoes substitution (*sthānāpatti*) for the *girāpada* in the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*—since the *girāpada* is also employed in the *ārcika* before and after [the *sāman*], and because both share the commonality of not being recited in the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*—nevertheless, due to the difference in their intermediate functions (*avāntarakāryabheda*), or even if there were no difference, because the unchanted *girāpada* is read in the *ārcika*, and because the chanting of the *girāpada* is utilized only in the *cayana* (altar-building) and so forth by means of the *girāpada* itself and thus has no utility in the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*, the application of the *irāpada* in that context occurs not through substitution (*atideśa*) or modification (*ūha*), but rather through direct instruction (*upadeśa*) itself, as indicated by the word "after" (*upari*).

The reality, however, is that in the passage "airaṃ kulaudreyaṃ," the syllables of the word *irā* are not being enjoined, because they exist even in the recitation associated with the word *girā*; rather, since it is a restatement of a prohibition (*niṣedhānuvāda*), the result of the injunction is merely the exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the letter *ga*. Consequently, in the song "gāirāgātrā cā dākṣāsā," although the quality of being a property of the syllables of *irā* actually resides in the occurrence of the word *girā*, just as if the letter *ga* were present, there is no impairment of its residing in its own substratum; thus, there is neither an independent instruction (*upadeśa*) of the song of *girā* in the place of *irā*, nor an extension (*atideśa*), nor a modification (*ūha*).

However, in cases such as "one should not say *pra*, one should say *prī*," where the vowel *i* is prescribed by subverting the vowel *a*, there is an independent instruction (*svatantropadeśa*) according to the method previously stated;
in every respect, the word *irā* is indeed sung (*pragīta*). Maṇḍana: "That word *irā* should be accompanied by singing."
21. Śaṅkara: "There should be chanting upon the word *irā*. 27. The maxim: "A mouse having built up a mountain, it was then dug out.
This applies where, even after performing an action that is difficult to accomplish despite great effort, only a trivial result is obtained.

And so it is said in the *Pañcatantra*: "By scratching with the tips of its own claws, a lion may obtain either a heap of stone fragments, or a fall from a mountain precipice, or perhaps become a mouse. (Sāhasī 131)
Gīti: Internal.
Gīti is that which manifests the specific sounds produced by internal effort among the means of singing.
That [sāman] is denoted by the word "sāman.
Bhāṣya 9.2.7.29. Song (gīti) consists of the combination of the essence of the notes beginning with ṣaḍja.
Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 855. Song is employed for the sake of the transcendental result (apūrva) of the hymn (stotra), not for the sake of the specific nature of the syllables.

Ḍu. 9|1|2|1855: By means of singing (*gīti*), the phonemes (*varṇa*) are not produced anew, because their function is not identical [to that of ordinary speech]. 9|1|2|155: By means of singing, the phonemes are modified (*saṃskriyante*).
9|1|2|154: The word *sāman* denotes a *gīti* characterized by its specific *ṛk*, *stoma*, accent (*svara*), duration (*kāla*), and repetition (*abhyāsa*).

Bhāṣya 9.2.17.35: In the context of song (*gīta*), the *sāman* possesses a perfected form by virtue of being a collection of the sweet tones beginning with *ṣaḍja*. Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 861: In songs, the *ṛc* verses, which consist of the *sāman*, are not the primary element; rather, they are subordinate. Bhāṣya 9.2.1.1 (First Section): The designation *sāman* applies to the songs.
Now, regarding the definition of *sāman*:

at this point, by way of a digression, since there is a stronger [authority], the offering of a substance (*dravyadāna*) does not undergo sublation, option, or combination with that [other rite]; therefore, according to the rule "and because of the accessory" (*guṇaśca*), one should postulate a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).

Nor should it be argued that even so there would be no distinction based on the accessory (*guṇa*), because in the section "In the case of connection with a prior [action], it is an injunction of an accessory" (PMS 2.2.12), it will be stated that an accessory also serves as a differentiator of actions. For [the sūtra] states:
"Or rather, in the case of connection with an injunction of an accessory, [there is no difference in action], because the two sentences are equal. (Ku. 2.2.12). Oṃ.
In the Vaiśvadeva section of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the scripture records: "He pours curds into hot milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas; [and] the *vājina* for the Vājins.

Regarding the inquiry here—whether this is an injunction of the *vājina* as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) within the ritual characterized by the *āmikṣā*, or whether a separate ritual characterized by the *vājina* is being enjoined—the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
"And a subordinate element, like a name (*saṃjñā*), is a differentiator of rituals."
When there is a connection with something unprecedented—that is, a connection with a previously unestablished designation of a deity—even a subordinate factor differentiates the ritual action.
This is because the two sentences are equal;
both sentences are independently injunctive regarding the connection and non-connection with the unprecedented, respectively, without depending on one another.

In the sentence concerning the *āmikṣā*, the specific deities' status as the recipients of the offering (*devatātva*) is established by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*); in the sentence concerning the *vājina*, it is established by the dative case ending.
In one case, there is syntactic unity with the *āmikṣā*, while in the other, it is with the *vājina*.
Therefore, the specific deities' status as the recipients of the offering belongs to the sentence concerning the *āmikṣā*, not to the sentence concerning the *vājina*.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that "vājibhyo vājinam" constitutes a separate ritual action. [Ke.
Oṃ] Because the two sentences are equal in their connection with the teaching of a subordinate quality (guṇa).
In the Vaiśvadeva section of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, they recite: "He pours curds into the heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas; [and] the *vājina* for the Vājins."

In this regard, a doubt arises: is the *vājina* (curd-mixture) an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) for the sacrifice characterized by the quality of "having been gazed upon" (*aikṣāguṇaka*), or is it a separate sacrifice characterized by the *vājina* accessory? Having previously established the distinction between actions based on their names (*saṃjñā*), it must now be explained that the distinction is based on both accessories (*guṇa*) and context (*prakaraṇa*). However, because it is the more fundamental factor, the distinction between actions based specifically on the accessory is presented here. In this matter, the intention of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows.
From the understanding expressed in "vājibhyo vājinam" (the whey for the Vājins), the connection of the deity denoted by the word "Vājin" with the whey is perceived;
for [if it were otherwise], the deity would be none other than the "nākasads. Yet that [deity] is not well-known as such, because the deity is none other than the "nākasads."
Nor should it be argued that the horse also possesses the status of a deity, as in the case of [the injunction] "one sacrifices kapiñjala birds for the sake of spring";
for this very reason, that was accepted there.
Here, however, by means of the power of the constituent parts (*avayava-śakti*), it is the Viśvedevas themselves who are connected with the *vājina* offering.
For instance, *vāja* is food, and *āikṣā* is also indeed food.

And in the immediately following sentence, because those very [substances] possess the quality of being *āikṣā*, it is stated that "there is *āikṣā*. Thus, in the sacrifice—which is inferred from the preceding sentence and has the Viśvedevas as its deity—the name *vājinaḥ* alone is enjoined.
As it has been said: "By means of the *vāja*, which is food, taught immediately [afterward], they are called *vājinaḥ*."
"All the gods are understood [as the recipients], and that sacrificial offering (*vājina*) is the ritual act here" (Vārttika, p. 532).

Nor should it be argued that because the sacrifice is already occupied by the quality of *āmikṣā* prescribed at its origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), and thus lacks further expectancy, there can be no connection with the quality of *vājina* mentioned in another sentence.

Even though the quality [of the material] is already enjoined by the originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), one may speak of it through an isolated restatement (*anuvāda*) because another quality is being introduced.

Now, an objection is raised: in the case of "He buys Soma with a reddish, yellow-eyed, one-year-old cow" (*aruṇayā piṅgākṣyaikahāyinyā somaṃ krīṇāti*), since the isolated act of buying is denoted by the verbal root *krī* (to buy), it is appropriate to enjoin the cloth and other items in passages such as "He buys with cloth," because there too the isolated act of buying is restated by the word *krī*.
However, in the present case, since the word *yaj* (to sacrifice) is absent in both sentences, how can there be an isolated denotation of the sacrifice?

Similarly, in the case of "vājibhyo vājinam" (the whey for the Vājins), since the relationship between the object of action—the substance—and the recipient of the action—the deity—cannot exist without a sacrificial act, the postulation of a sacrifice is necessary. Because the word *vāji* refers to a specific deity associated with the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture), and because the connection between substance and deity is established through that very *āmikṣā*, the word *vāji* is postulated by the force of the heard implication (*śrutārthāpatti*) as the indicator of that [sacrifice].
This much is the distinction: in the former sentence, since no other sacrifice is under discussion (*aprakṛtatvāt*), a sacrifice qualified by both substance and deity is enjoined.

In the case of the *vājina* statement, however, since the deity is already established prior to this [statement], the mere sacrifice is enjoined by means of the inferred root *yaj* (to sacrifice), which has been extracted [from the compound].

Nevertheless, even though there is a similarity in the extraction of the word, this is the distinction here: because they serve different purposes, there is indeed a combination (*samuccaya*) of substances with the purchase; but here, because they are both subordinate (*upakārya*), there is only an option (*vikalpa*) between the *aikṣa* and the *vājina*.
Nor should it be argued that there is a combination despite the simultaneity, as in the case of "they appease with the scrapings of the *vāruṇī* and with the husks."

Even among things that have the same effect, there may be mutual dependence and a distinction through their inclusion in a single sentence; let there be a "conjunction" (*samuccaya*) for those factors combined as *kārakas*. However, in this case, according to the stated reasoning, since the injunction in the *vaiśvadeva* sentence prescribes a sacrifice qualified by both material and deity, whereas the *vājina* sentence does not prescribe the *vājina* alone by way of restating that [sacrifice], a difference of sentences (*vākya-bheda*) is established. Once this is established, between the *nīvāra* and *yava*, which are prescribed by separate sentences and serve the same purpose, there can only be an option (*vikalpa*). As for the mention of "conjunction" in the *Vārttika*, it is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhavāda*).
It must be considered as follows:
Is it not the case that the connection of a substance with a sacrifice is mediated by a deity?
In that regard, the connection of the *aikṣā* (the stalk of sugar-cane) with the deity is established through the direct denotation of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).
But by the statement regarding the *vājina*,
how can there be an option between two conflicting injunctions?
Do not say so.
For he thinks as follows:
this would indeed be the case if the connection with *ikṣu* were understood through the word *vaiśvadeva*.
What then? Because it is characterized by the co-utterance (*sambhinyāhāra*) with *ikṣu*, this is established from the sentence itself.

If, once a general connection with the substance is understood from the word *vaiśvadeva*, only the specific detail is then cognized from the word *āikṣā*, then—in the same way that a general substance to be offered is understood from the dative case in *vājibhyaḥ* and the specific detail is understood from the word *vājina*—there would be no distinction whatsoever regarding what is conveyed by the sentence.

Nor should it be argued that, according to the principle "if the word *vidhi* were a mantra, there would be [a separate] existence" (*10.4.1.23*), the deity for the *vājina* is introduced by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the *vājina*;
for the word *vājina* serves merely as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the deities associated with the *āikṣā*.
And because the deity belonging to the *aikṣāgāmīya* sacrifice is denoted by the term "Viśvedevas," [the milk] designated as having the Viśvedevas as its deity is the *vājina*.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be a difference of ritual action (*karmabheda*) even when the deity is the same— as in the case of "the curd for Indra on the new moon day"— because in that instance,
a difference between the sacrifices involving the substances of curd and milk is appropriate, since the connection with Indra is understood through two independent sentences.

But here, because the word *vājī* (possessing *vāja*) establishes a connection with the Viśvedevas who are already connected to the preceding *aikṣāsa*, there is a difference of ritual action (*karmabheda*).
Therefore, it follows that the injunction is merely for the quality of *vājina* (curd-milk) within the very sacrifice prescribed by the preceding sentence.
This being the position reached, it is replied as follows:
This would be so if the injunction of the quality *vājina* were possible within a ritual act already occupied by the *āmikṣā*, which is established by a Vedic originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*).

For instance, first of all, the prescription of *vājina* as a conjunction with the previous ritual act is not possible; for it has been stated that even when two things are mentioned in separate sentences, there can be no conjunction of their respective effects. Nor can it be by way of option, because an option is impossible between two injunctions of unequal status (*viṣamaśiṣṭatva*).

For the connection of the *vaiśvadeva* [offering] with the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) is based on direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), whereas the connection with the *vājina* (whey) arises from syntactical context (*vākya*).

Now, it was argued that the connection with the *āmikṣā* is also based on syntactical context; this would indeed be so if, by the pronoun "the Viśvedevas" (*viśve devāḥ*) as the deity, only a mere substance were denoted.
Because the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) has a specific substance as its object, it is understood through the hearing of that derivative.
Thus, the qualification for the gods is their connection with the *āmikṣā*.
As it has been said: "Indeed, the deity is not expressed by secondary derivatives merely in relation to a substance."
The deity belongs to the specific entity denoted by the word "horse" (aśva);
the secondary suffix (taddhita) indeed expresses the deity as connected with that [entity].
Due to the proximity of the word "āikṣā," there is the attribution of that [deity] to that very [entity].
Thus (Vārttika, pp. 533–534).

In the expression "to the Vājins" (*vājibhyaḥ*), neither the nominal stem nor the case ending denotes the oblation or the deity; nor is there any change in the deity of that very [oblation]. Rather, because of its co-occurrence with the word *vājina*, it is understood solely through the sentence (*vākya*).

As it has been said: "The oblation is not expressed by the nominal stem, nor by the case-ending, nor by itself; and its connection with a deity is understood only from the sentence" (Vākyapadīya, p. 535).

[Objection: But surely, in the case of the statement, "They dispose of the scrapings with the whey and the husks," although there is a scriptural connection between the whey (*āmikṣā*) and Varuṇa, we observe that the scrapings and husks are connected to Varuṇa in another manner as well; likewise, even if there is no such [scriptural] connection, there will be a connection between the *vājina* and the *vājins*.
[Reply: Not so.

Even in that case, a connection between the scrapings and husks and the deity must necessarily be postulated, because there is no reason to abandon the deity who is already present [in proximity]. Therefore, [the connection] was not accepted in that way.
In this case, however, there is a disparity because the matter is established simply by the injunction of a different ritual action (*karmāntara*).

Furthermore, since that which is already occupied by the curd (*āmikṣā*) enjoined at the time of origin cannot have a connection with the whey (*vājina*) also enjoined at the time of origin, how could there be an option (*vikalpa*)?
This, then, is what must be stated here.

What, then, is this type of contradiction known as "obstruction by a quality enjoined at the origin" (*utpattiśiṣṭaguṇāvarodha*)? To this it is replied: this is indeed a contradiction regarding the application (*pratipatti*).
For once the expectation of a word has been satisfied, there is no further requirement for another [quality].

And when a ritual action is obstructed by a quality specified at its origin, there is no longer any expectation for other qualities that perform the same function; thus, it is not [an obstruction] by something else enjoined at the origin.

But where there is a difference in function (*kāryabheda*), even when another substance is prescribed by the originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), there is indeed a connection with substances prescribed by a subsequent injunction (*utpannaśiṣṭa*).

Therefore, even though the purchase is already occupied by what is prescribed by the originative injunction, since there is a possibility of expectancy due to the difference in function, the combination (*samuccaya*) of the cloth and other items prescribed by the subsequent injunction is entirely appropriate; thus, there is a disparity [between this case and others].
Furthermore, by the maxim "conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) sets aside etymological meaning (*yoga*)," the word *vājinaḥ* denotes the Aśvamedha sacrifice, and not the Viśvedevas.

Furthermore, divinity does not belong solely to those who dwell in heaven (*nākasad*); rather, whatever is enjoined as the intended recipient of a particular oblation (*havis*) is the deity of that oblation. Thus, just as in the cases of *śārdūla*, *vasanta*, and so forth, it is not contradictory for the horse (*aśva*) also to possess the status of a deity.

Or, let the word *vājina* be etymological (*yaugika*); even so, how could there be a connection with a deity? For in the *Āmikṣā* sacrifice, they [the Maruts] have the status of deities by their very nature, whereas in the *Vājina* offering, they are such through their connection with *vāja* (strength/food) by virtue of being mentioned in the mind.
Consequently, there is indeed a difference in deity, just as between Indra and Mahendra.
Since there is no disregard for the Vājapeya sacrifice and because of the abundance of causes [for its application], indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) itself constitutes a fault.

Therefore, it is established that since the ritual action is already occupied by the curd (*āmikṣā*) which is enjoined as the originative material in the Vedic text, the [new] action characterized by the deity Vāja and the substance *vājina*—which would otherwise find no entry—is construed as a distinct ritual altogether.
As it has been said: "Because it is occupied by another accessory (*guṇa*), it is impossible within the previous ritual."

(Vākyapadīya, p. 532) A quality (*guṇa*) intended as a scriptural injunction is a differentiator because it is unfit for connection with a prior action and [requires] connection with a new action. As it is stated in the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*: "A quality cannot be connected with a prior action;
or rather, it effects a connection with a new action—therefore, it is a differentiator."
Thus [it is said].
