This is explained as follows: "For it is not the mere substance that is designated as the deity by the secondary suffix (*taddhita*);
rather, the deity belongs to that specific [entity] which is the denotation of the word *asya*."

For the phrase "the Viśvedevas are its deity" does not denote a general substance by means of the pronoun; what then? It denotes a specific [substance] present at hand, for that alone is capable of being employed in linguistic usage, not an unqualified substance in general.

Therefore, the meaning conveyed by the nominal stem—that specific substance which is apprehended through other means of knowledge—is declared by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) to be its deity. This is what is stated.

And so, when the cognition of a specific substance—qualified by a deity whose relationship is internally implied—is brought about by a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix that is independent of any other word, and once this has occurred, one seeks to identify "what indeed is this specific [substance] for which the deity was expressed by the *taddhita*?"—it is then presented as "this" through direct perception (*āmiṣvāda*).
In that case, if the relationship has already been expressed prior to the qualified cognition itself, then it does not become something merely indicated (*lakṣyamāṇa*).

Furthermore, even though a connection is understood to exist in the interval between a base and a suffix precisely because they possess their own respective meanings due to their contiguity, nevertheless, in this case, because of the unity of the word, that which is understood as stronger than what is obtained through the proximity of two words is called "directly heard" (śrauta).
Consequently, there are these two connections:
one is the connection between the substance and the deity, and the other is the relationship of qualifier and qualified.

In this regard, the distinction is that the former [the word *vaiśvadevī*] is based on direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), while the latter [the word *āmiṣvā*] is characterized by syntactical connection (*vākya*).

Consequently, the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the words *vaiśvadevī* and *āmiṣvā* here does not occur through their meanings—as in the case of "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*)—but rather, this secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) expresses the *āmiṣvā* as being connected with the deity; the application of the term "Viśve Devāḥ" (All-Gods) to it occurs solely due to its proximity to the word *āmiṣvā*.

In this case, a single meaning is not expressed by the word ending in a *taddhita* suffix, and another [meaning] is subsequently expressed by the *upapada*; nor is there a relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two, because that which is denoted by the *taddhita*-ending is perceived first.
What then? Here, the *taddhita*-ending merely brings about the cognition of something that has not been employed or denoted; the *upapada* merely provides the objective domain for it.
Therefore, by the force of the proximity of the word *āmiṣvā*, the word *vaiśvadevī* itself denotes her.
Nor can there be a subsequent application (*anuvādakatva*) of the word *āmiṣvāpada*, because without it, the referent of that which ends in a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) would not be understood.
Nor can it be the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), because the referent of the word ending in a secondary suffix is not independently established.
For the meaning of a sentence is not cognized without first grasping two independent word-meanings.
Therefore, because it functions merely by bringing forward the denotative meanings, there is no remoteness of meaning caused by the nominal suffix (*taddhita*) through the word *āmiṣvāpada*.
Thus it has been said: "The meaning of the subordinate element is denoted by its own name through direct audition (*śruti*) itself."
"In that case, the three [terms]—the upapada, the pronoun, and the secondary derivative (taddhita)—form a single syntactical unit by means of that very derivative suffix.
(That is, "of the three," namely the upapada, the pronoun, and the taddhita.
Therefore, that which is indeed the *āmikṣā* will enter into a relationship with the deity; being thus expressed, it is designated by the word *vaiśvadevī*.
Therefore, in this case, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words themselves, not between their referents.

But in the other case (*vājine*), it is understood from the sentence that "the sacrificial oblation is neither [connected] by the nominal stem nor by the case-ending in its own right, nor is there a connection of this [oblation] with a deity."

Regarding the word *vājibhyaḥ*, neither by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), nor by the case-ending (*vibhakti*), nor by both together, is any one of the properties—such as the generality of substance (*dravyasāmānya*) or its particularity (*viśeṣatva*)—denoted. What then? It has been stated that by the nominal stems, only this much is expressed: "the recipient" (*saṃpradāna*).

In that case, no connection with a substance is contained within the word in any way; therefore, it must necessarily be conveyed by the sentence alone, through proximity to the word *vājina*. Furthermore: "Just as here, even the meaning of the word is traditionally held to be contained within the secondary derivative (*taddhita*)."

The meaning of the dative case is not prescribed here by the rule "that which belongs to it" (*sā'sya devatā*, Pāṇini 4.2.24). According to that rule, a *taddhita* suffix denoting a deity is prescribed for the referent of the word "its" (*asya*), but the dative case is not prescribed in such a way as "that is its recipient" (*tat saṃpradānam asya*) so that the referent of the word "its" would also be included [in the formation]. Rather, only the recipient itself is stated as the denotation; and thus it is understood.
However, that [word], being otherwise inexplicable, merely presents a general expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding the object to be given.

And by this much alone, it does not become something denotable (*abhidheyatva*), for that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the meanings of all sentences are nothing other than word-meanings.
What is accomplished by expectancy is simply this: that when another word is uttered, a connection arises.
If there were no further expectancy, that [connection] would also exist;

therefore, although it has been stated that the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) is the meaning of the dative case, nevertheless, the connection with the substance (*dravya*) occurs only through syntactical connection (*vākya*).
And since our dispute concerns that point, the connection with the *vājina* is weaker.
Furthermore: "The meaning of *śruti* is proximity (*saṃnikṛṣṭatva*), while the meaning of *vākya* is remoteness (*viprakṛṣṭatā*).
Therefore, every variety of the remote type is explained here.
(In the first half [of this verse], the meanings of the words *śruti* and *vākya* in the *Bhāṣya* refer to proximity and remoteness, respectively.)

By the second half [of the verse], however, the eightfold classification of proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*) and remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) is promised; for while every form of connection characterized by proximity possesses the status of being directly stated in scripture (*śrautatva*), the connection with the *vājina* [offering] possesses the status of being derived from syntactical context (*vākyīyatva*) due to its remoteness.

(Regarding the first method—namely, that in the case of *āmikṣā*, there is a general designation of another deity, but not for the *vājina*—it says: For example, even if the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix does not express the status of being a deity for a specific substance, it nevertheless expresses it for the general category; whereas by means of the dative ending, even the general category is not expressed—this is the distinction.
As for the claim that the general category is not incompatible with the *vājina*, that is incorrect.
For in the word *vaiśvadevī*, by virtue of the feminine suffix (*ṅīp*) and the fact that it is a single compound, some neuter entity in proximity is indicated.
Furthermore, since the horse has neither femininity nor proximity [to the offering], [the injunction] would be without a substratum.

(He states the second mode, which consists of the conceptualization of the act of giving: Moreover, there is no syntactic connection in the statement "one should prepare the *vājina* for the *vājins*"; therefore, when that [connection] is required, one must necessarily assume the supplying of acts such as giving.

The statement of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā-vacana*) is not subject to objection, because even in the case of the *āmikṣā* sentence, it is understood by supplying [the verb] from the performance-injunction (*prayoga-vacana*).

However, in the case of "vājibhyo vājinam" (curdled milk for the Vājins), it is impossible to understand the connection without supplying the verb "gives" (*dadāti*), as is the case with "vaiśvadevī āmikṣā" (the curdled milk for the Viśvedevas).
Why? Because in all sentences, the connection of nouns is established in only two ways.

We perceive grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "vājibhyaḥ" either through coordination or by means of a genitive case. However, we do not perceive such coreferentiality with "vājibhyaḥ" through coordination or a genitive.
Furthermore, the case-ending of the agent (*kāraka-bhakti*) in "vājibhyaḥ" cannot be connected with anything other than a verbal root, and no such verbal root is present here.
In that case, there is one remoteness due to the assumption of an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), and another due to the difficulty of connecting three words.
If it is argued that in the other case as well there is the assumption of a sacrifice (*yajati*), we say no; for that [sacrifice] is only inferable after the relationship has been established.
Indeed, once the relationship "the *āmikṣā* belongs to Viśvedevas" is established, the sacrifice is inferred; the cognition of the relationship does not depend upon the sacrifice.

In your view, however, because the transfer of ownership to another is possible, that [transfer] will occur for the sake of establishing a relationship with the purpose; and from the very beginning, the term *dadāti* (he gives) is used to establish the status of the sentence as having both substance and deity. This is the distinction.

Once *dadāti* is postulated, there is a connection with it first, because of the mutual relationship between the two factors (*kāraka*s); thereafter, because they share a single purpose, there is a mutual restriction. Thus, there is remoteness.
But in the case of the *āmikṣā*, since there is no *taddhita* suffix, there is proximity.

(He states the third mode, characterized by grammatical coordination [sāmānādhikaraṇya] and lack of grammatical coordination [vaidhikaraṇya]: Even though there is a direct relationship between the horse (*vāji*) and the whey (*ājina*), there is remoteness due to their lack of grammatical coordination. However, in the case of "vaiśvadevī āmikṣā," there is proximity because of grammatical coordination.
And so he will say (in the commentary on 3.1.6.12): "For words with the same case-ending are more powerful; distinct case-endings are weak."

(He states the fourth type, which consists of the definition based on scriptural authority: Furthermore, "The dative case ending would express merely the status of being a recipient for the *vājina* [curd-milk]; however, the deity is indicated [only] with respect to the substance, the *vājina*. For it is not traditionally taught that the dative case arises to denote a deity in the same way as a *taddhita* suffix does."
Where, then? In the case of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
Nor does the status of being a deity belong exclusively to the recipient; otherwise, in the sentence "he gives gold to Ātreya," Ātreya would have to be the deity.
Furthermore, if the deity were the recipient, there would be no distinction at all between sacrifice (*yāga*) and giving (*dāna*).
Furthermore, that which is occupied with receiving becomes the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
And it is not possible for a deity to be a receiver.
Therefore, that which precedes its status as a recipient—the dedication to that deity—must necessarily be indicated by the dative case.

Alternatively, [the remoteness] consists in the sovereignty that arises subsequent to the connection with the transfer of ownership to another, because the nature of a deity (*devatātva*) is established through identity (*tādātmya*).

Even if it is accepted that a deity is simply a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) characterized by the absence of rejection, nevertheless, due to the deviation from the general definition and the necessity of a specific definition, there is remoteness.

(Because it is doubtful, he states the fifth type, which is a doubtful definition: Furthermore, "there is remoteness due to doubt regarding whether it takes the form of the dative or the ablative case."
"But because there is no doubt regarding the *taddhita* suffix, the intellect is not distracted.

While the word *vājibhyaḥ* might initially suggest [the dative] due to the similarity of its form, as long as the status of being a fifth case (*pañcamī*) is set aside and its status as a fourth case (*caturthī*) is established, there is a distinct mental effort involved.
[Objection: "But even in the case of a *taddhita*, this is equal, since there is doubt regarding the meaning of multiple word-elements."
This is an unequal comparison. I have proposed a doubt regarding the word, whereas you have proposed a doubt regarding the meaning.
In any case, however, its status as a secondary derivative (taddhita) is beyond doubt.
Furthermore, the meaning is determined to be of the nature of a deity because of its suitability and the impossibility of any other [meaning].

Even when the word has been determined among you, there remains a remoteness [of application] for this very [word], because the meaning of the dative case is not explicitly stated and because there is doubt regarding the technical definition of the subordinate factor (*upapada-kāraka*).
Therefore, since the doubt regarding the meaning is equal in both cases, it does not reside in the single Vedic word alone.
"But because of the ambiguity regarding the word, it is urged [as a fault] due to its being uncommon.
(Thus he states the sixth type, characterized by being "prescribed by another" [ityayupañcādiṣṭa]): Furthermore, "it is connected with the ritual action prescribed by the *āmikṣā* [offering];
therefore, from another sentence..."
But with the *supraśna* [verse], one should address the horse.

And just as that which is taught at the time of origination (*utpattiśiṣṭa*) possesses greater force, and it is not possible to extract the mere action (*kriyā*) alone to enjoin another quality (*guṇa*), so it has been stated in the *Citrā* section and the *Vaiśvadeva* section.
Furthermore, the *Vaiśvadeva* section requires the context (*prakaraṇa*), whereas the other [sentence] regarding the *vājina* requires only the sacrifice (*yāga*).
Why? Because the connection between a substance and a deity requires only the sacrifice.
It would be [understood] as belonging to the *āmikṣā* sacrifice alone because of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

For since the *vājina* is not connected with the "possessors of vigor" (*vājibhiḥ*) without a sacrifice, someone expects a sacrifice; in that case, it is assumed that even this [vājina] is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice itself because of that context. Consequently, although the Viśvedevas are enjoined for the *āmikṣā* sacrifice by means of the sentence (*vākya*) itself, nevertheless, because they are enjoined independently of anything else, the *āmikṣā* possesses greater force than the *vājina*, which is enjoined by a sentence that depends upon the context—this is the distinction.

Furthermore, when there is a connection with a sacrifice independent of the context (*prakaraṇa*), since no other [sacrifices] are perceived here, it is a new sacrifice that becomes the correlate; thus there is a distinction.

And it has been stated regarding the *Āgneya* and other [offerings] (1.4.6–9) that for such [terms], whose human activity is not explicitly mentioned, there is no dependence on another sentence as long as a sacrifice has not been inferred.
[He states the seventh mode, characterized by conventional and etymological meaning: "And the Viśvedevas are connected with the milk-offering by means of convention alone."
However, the connection with the *vājina* would pertain to its constituent parts;
for by the well-known meaning of the parts, the Viśvedevas are indicated by the term "vājinaḥ.

Since this [connection] occurs by combining the meanings of the parts and postulating a relationship—just like the meaning of a sentence—it is weaker than the conventional meaning of the whole, which is obtained through the direct application of the Vedic word itself. Thus, the connection of the *vājina* is even weaker.
"Furthermore, the word *vājina* is naturally well-established in its primary sense [as 'possessing strength'] from its very origin;
it applies to the Viśvedevas only through effort, without any [other] purpose.

Deityhood belongs only to that which is expressed by the word itself—whether it be appropriate or inappropriate—and thus it is not based on a genus (*jāti*), such that this word *vājina* would have to be forcibly led elsewhere."

Therefore, the word *vājinaḥ*, while expressing the deityhood of the whey (*ājya*), is applied to the Viśvedevas based on a weak etymological derivation (*avayava-prasiddhi*) without any functional necessity; thus, there is remoteness (*viprakarṣa*).

Even though the etymological meaning exists, the determination of the context (*prakṛta-niścaya*) arises only through the difficulty of [interpreting] *vājina* as "that which possesses food" (*vājinī*) or "another deity," such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and so forth.
For all [deities] beginning with Agni are understood to be "possessors of food" (vājinaḥ) by means of "foods" such as the *puroḍāśa* cake;

in that regard, there is first the difficulty that the word "food" (*anna*) is employed only in reference to the *āmikṣā* curd-mixture, and not to the *puroḍāśa* and other offerings. Furthermore, if only the *āmikṣā* were taken [as the referent], then the portion belonging to the Vaiśvadeva would have to be understood as referring exclusively to that *āmikṣā*. Thus there is a second difficulty.

Consequently, while the scriptural mention (*śruti*) functions elsewhere by its own inherent force (*svarasa*), it must be restricted to a specific instance by the context (*prakaraṇa*); however, there is no basis for such restriction here, because the deity is mentioned merely as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāvena*). Furthermore, if the act were something to be accomplished (*satkāryatva*), then—as in the case of "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*)—there might be an inclusion of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements through an indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*). But that is not the case here, since the purpose is established even without that sequence. Or rather, let the consecration (*saṃskāra*) be a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the whey (*vājina*) itself, not of the deity.
Furthermore, if the contextually relevant [deities] were to be grasped, there would be uncertainty because Agni and others are present [therein].
Now, if it is argued that they are included because they are subsumed within the Viśvedevas, that is incorrect, because such a universal inclusion lacks authoritative proof.
If it is argued that the inclusion of all [deities] follows from the scriptural use of the plural number, we say no.
If it is argued that this is because its purpose is fulfilled by those three alone, and that there is no cognition of restriction regarding the three, we say no;
for the cause of restriction exists, as stated in the rule: "Or rather, the primary [is taken] because of the injunction previously mentioned" (1.2.8.12).
Therefore, there is no authority for including the Viśvedevas.

Furthermore, a deity requires a substance with which to be connected; and since that deity is presented here as already possessing a substance by being designated through the word *vājina*, it is conveyed as being free from further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*) and thus cannot admit a connection with another substance.
(He concludes the seventh method: Therefore, there is a disparity in their strength.
Furthermore: "By the Vedic revelation itself, the deities are established as the inherent participants (samavāyin) in their respective rites;
in that context, the mention of the Viśvedevas would be difficult to obtain through the word *vājinaḥ*.

For if the Viśvedevas alone were accepted as the deities even for the *vājina* offering, then the mention of the Viśvedevas must necessarily be pronounced in the places where the *nigama* formulas occur.

Furthermore, that [injunction] cannot be obtained here because it is not explicitly uttered in the word *vidhi*. In that case, it would have to be obtained through such effort: the word *vājinaḥ* conveys something, and that, by means of its form (*rūpa*), indicates the word *viśvedevāḥ*; then, that [group of deities] is enjoined as being designated by the term *vājinaḥ*. Thus, there are difficulties. Moreover, since there is no distinction in the indication of the word by its meaning, all [groups] such as "all the gods" (*sarve devāḥ*) or "the gods without exception" (*niḥśeṣā devāḥ*) would apply; therefore, the word *viśvedeva* is difficult to obtain.

Furthermore, when another word is uttered, those [deities] do not attain the status of deities; as it will be stated [in the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra]: "The existence [of deity-status] occurs when the word of the injunction is the mantra" (10.4.1.21–23).
Since it is only by means of the word *vājina* that the person is impelled here by the scripture, the deity-status of the *vājina* must be accomplished through its utterance alone.
Consequently, although the *vājina* here is indeed for the sake of the Viśvedevas—

When expressed by the word [Mahendra], it becomes a deity; in other cases, it is so by means of the word *viśvadeva*. Nevertheless, according to the principle of Mahendra (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 2.1.5.13), because of the difference in application (*viniyoga*), there is a clear distinction between deities; thus, this further connection between substance and deity is recognized.

Furthermore, it is not possible to enjoin multiple subsidiary qualities (*guṇa*) when a ritual action (*karman*) has already been established. Therefore, this is logically consistent with the statement: "In a connection where qualities are primary, [the action] is differentiated."
"But when the word [expressing] an action lacks a specific quality, a quality is understood therein.

The Commentary states: Now, as for what was described—namely, that when it is said, "One performs the Agnihotra," statements such as "One offers with curd" are injunctions of qualities—it is replied to this:

It is appropriate that there be an injunction of a quality therein, because in that case there is no inclusion of any unmentioned quality; rather, there is an inclusion of the sacrifice which is already under discussion (*prakṛta*).
Therefore, this is not a descriptive etymology.
Śabara says: "Because of their connection with the *vāja* (sacrificial food) in the *abhikṣā* offering, the Viśvedevas are indeed the *vājinas*.
Since they are the subject under discussion, and since the word *vājinaḥ* is etymological (*yaugika*)."

"Therefore, since both are equal, there is either an option (*vikalpa*) or a combination (*samuccaya*) regarding the very same prior ritual action. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the following is established: "The curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) is stronger because it is enjoined at the time of origin (*utpatti*); the whey (*vājina*) is [enjoined] after the rite has originated, based on a syntactical statement (*vākya*). Therefore, that [latter] is considered weaker."
Therefore, since the word *āmikṣā* does not find a place within the previous ritual action, there is a distinction of the ritual action (*karmabheda*) due to the quality (*guṇa*) of *vājina*.

Soma—[The connection is as follows: immediately after the discussion on names (*saṃjñā*), it is appropriate to explain the quality itself, because it shares the common characteristic of being a differentiator from the proximate ritual action.

As for the meaning of the sūtra: when there is a connection with something new (*apūrva*), provided that inclusion within the previous ritual action is possible, even a quality (*guṇa*) is a differentiator.

The sense is this: because both sentences are equal in that they involve the introduction of a prior action (*pūrvakarmaniveśa*), and because they are independent of one another, it might be thought that one sentence could introduce a prior action by depending on the other, but such is not the case here. Vi [ṭhaka]: "In the statement *vājibhyo vājinam*, there may be either an accessory (*guṇa*) or a distinct action (*karmāntara*). Regarding the accessory, since the deities have already been mentioned, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) or an option (*vikalpa*)."
Because it is prescribed as a remnant of the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture), the *vājina* (whey) is stronger in that context;
thus, as a subordinate element (*guṇa*), it cannot enter into the existing ritual but must postulate a different ritual dedicated to Vājin.
Therefore, because the form—characterized by the combination of substance and deity—is distinct, it constitutes a separate ritual action.
"And that [cognition] becomes a realization," as will be stated.
(Mīmāṃsākośa 199)

Bhaṭṭa: In the case of "vaiśvadevyāmikṣā" (the curd-mixture belongs to the Viśvedevas), once a sacrifice qualified by both substance and deity has been enjoined, the subsequent statement "vājibhyo vājinam" (the whey belongs to the Vājins) does not enjoin a mere accessory (*guṇa*). This is because enjoining multiple accessories while restating an already established ritual act would result in the fault of *vākyabheda* (splitting the sentence).

Nor should it be argued that, based on the etymology "those for whom there exists *yāja* (sacrificial food) in the form of *āmikṣā*," the injunction of *vājina* alone—either as a cumulative addition or as an alternative—should apply with reference to the Viśvedevas or the sacrifice qualified by them.
Because the word *vājina* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*), it is impossible for it to be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Viśvedevas;

furthermore, when a substance prescribed at the origin of the rite (*utpattiśiṣṭa-dravya*) already occupies the place, it is impossible for another substance to be introduced there. By this reasoning, the following undesirable conclusion is also refuted: that the word *vājina*, by virtue of its connection with the *vājina* produced as a byproduct of the *āmikṣā*, is accepted as the name of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice, and that there is an injunction of the deity Vāja with reference to that [sacrifice].
Because when there is an obstruction by a deity prescribed at the time of origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), it is impossible for another deity to be introduced.

Furthermore, the connection of the *āmikṣā* with the deity is established by direct word-hearing (*pada-śruti*), whereas that of the *vājina* is by syntactical connection (*vākya*); thus, the latter is weaker.

For the scholar understands that the *taddhita* suffix has its power (*śakti*) in a specific substance qualified by deityhood, and the word *āmikṣā* serves as the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*).
The potency (śakti) is distinct with respect to the substance, such as the *ābhikṣā* oblation, and with respect to the deityhood; however, the relation is that of being the qualifier (*nirūpakatva*).
Alternatively, the potency resides in the deityhood alone, while with respect to the substance there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*). [This applies to] a particular substance...

The Principle of Qualities (guṇanyāya): 1586. Regarding the category of quality (guṇapadārtha), according to the traditional rule (smṛti) stating, "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together, and between those two, the meaning of the suffix is primary," the efficient force (bhāvanā) is primary due to its being the meaning of the suffix. Consequently, by way of a restatement (anuvāda) of the pure efficient force enjoined in the fruit-sentence (phalavākya), all root-meanings are enjoined simultaneously by sentences concerning Soma and other materials—whose internal sequence is not yet established—and therefore the principle of qualities does not apply here. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 701–702).

This is because, according to the principle of the subordinate element (*guṇanyāya*), another root-meaning cannot be introduced into the productive energy (*bhāvanā*) while it is already colored by one root-meaning (p.

In the case of "Aindravāyavam," since there is a difference in the substance denoted by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) and a difference in the deity denoted by the base (*prakṛti*), it is well-established either by the principle of "different words" (*śabdāntaranyāya*) or by the principle of the "subordinate element."

An objection is raised: "Since there is no room for the meaning of another verbal root when the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is already colored by the meaning of one root, the distinction between efficient forces is established precisely through the principle of subordinate elements (*guṇanyāya*); therefore, because the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is possible, a doubt regarding the distinction or non-distinction of the efficient force is not appropriate. Anticipating this, [the author] says: Su. p. 700.

Furthermore, the statement "he buys with ten" is not itself an indicator of the intent to restrict [the number of cows], because that statement can also be explained as being intended to enjoin a collection of purchases; thus, it is unfit to set aside the distinction established by the principle of the subordinate element (*guṇanyāya*). Bhaṭṭa 3.1.6. Now, one might object: "In the *Jyotiṣṭoma* injunction as well, since a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) colored by the sacrifice is perceived, and since it is impossible for it to be colored by another verbal root-meaning, there is no transgression of the principle of the subordinate element. Anticipating this doubt:
Su. Pṛ. 701:

In the sentence stating the result (*phalavākya*), if a pure efficient force (*śuddhabhāvanā*) were enjoined with heaven as its objective, and if it were accepted that the sentences concerning *soma* and other materials function as injunctions of qualities (*guṇa*) by way of restating that [efficient force], then—because all [the material sentences] would be directly connected [to the principal action]—the principle of the "quality" (*guṇanyāya*) would not apply [as it does in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)].
Page 138:

Since it is understood that the fruit-statement (*phalavākya*) enjoins a pure productive operation (*śuddhabhāvanā*), the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*) in the *soma*-statement and others would have to be construed with each [subsequent word], resulting in the injunction of an object qualified by *soma* and so forth as its instrument. Furthermore, because all [the substances] are taught after the rite has already been established (*utpannaśiṣṭatva*), the principle of subordinate qualities (*guṇanyāya*) does not apply; thus, due to the absence of any means of proof for differentiation, the unity of the productive operation is established (as stated in the prima facie view).

Nor should it be argued that, although it is possible for a single *grahaṇa* (act of drawing) to possess multiple deities, there can be no introduction of another deity because the deity enjoined at the time of origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) would be obstructed;

for this is not a case governed by the principle of subordinate qualities (*guṇa-nyāya*), since there is no evidence for a single purpose (*eka-kāryatva*) when the connection with the deity in the *grahaṇa* serves an invisible transcendental end (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

In the section on qualities (guṇādhikaraṇa), the relative strength and weakness of the original injunction (utpatti-śiṣṭa) and the subsequent injunction (utpanna-śiṣṭa) are established. (Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, Tantravārttika 2.4.1.12).

In the section on qualities (*guṇādhikaraṇa*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) will be set forth as follows: "Now, just as in the case of the statement *'vājibhyo vājinam'* (curdled milk for the Vājins), the word *vājin* contained within its own sentence indicates the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*); since the *vājina* being enjoined has no requirement for the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is an absence of conflict caused by that. Consequently, even though the sacrifice is already occupied by the curd-mixture enjoined at its origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), because the sacrifice—by virtue of the requirement for another substance being enjoined—arouses a further expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), the inclusion of the *vājina* in that very same sacrifice is logically possible. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 477).

For it will be stated in the *Guṇādhikaraṇa* (Jaimini Sūtra 2.2.2) that a quality (*guṇa*) enjoined at the stage of production (*utpannaśiṣṭa*), when it finds no place in either the word or the sacrifice already established by a quality enjoined at the stage of origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), differentiates the ritual action (*karman*). [Objection: But surely, since it is impossible to enjoin the *vājina*—which is a quality enjoined at the stage of production—into a sacrifice whose scope is already delimited by the *āmikṣā* enjoined at the stage of origin, its differentiating power will be stated in the *Guṇādhikaraṇa*. [Response: No; for in that context, the relative strength (*balābala*) will be discussed as being determined by the *taddhita* suffix and the dative case (*caturthī*), and not by the fact of being enjoined at the stage of production versus the stage of origin.
Su. pṛ. 473:

Because it was established in the *Guṇādhikaraṇa* (PMS 1.4.9–13) that the state of possessing a specific devotion characterized by proximity is the meaning expressed by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

Because of the subordination [of the animal] to the previous ritual action, even by the principle of the "dependence on qualities" (*guṇāśrayapūrvasaṃyoga*), the sentence concerning the *paryagnikṛta* ("encircled with fire")—namely, "They release the *pātnīvata* after it has been encircled with fire"—is intended solely as an injunction for a different sacrifice; this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In the prima facie view of the section on qualities (*guṇādhikaraṇa*), those gods who have *vāja*—food known as *āmiṣa*—as their share are the *vājins*; by accepting that [the term refers to] the Viśvedevas with the words "To them, the *vājina*," the suspicion regarding the superior force of what is enjoined at the time of origin (*utpattiśiṣṭaprābalya*) is dispelled.

And in the Siddhānta, by establishing that the word *vājina* has a conventional (rūḍha) meaning, the very absence of any means of recognition (*pratyabhijñāpaka*) is demonstrated. (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Bhāṣya 1.4.1.13).

This is the logic of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the section on qualities (*guṇādhikaraṇa*): "The *vājina*s [are so called] because of the mere whey (*vājina*) taught immediately thereafter."
"All the gods" (*viśve devāḥ*) are understood [as the deity], and that [offering] is indeed the *vājina* (curd-mixture).

Nor should it be argued that, according to the logic of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the section on subordinate qualities (*guṇādhikaraṇa*), there is the possibility of enjoining another deity even for one whose [injunction] is already established;

for although the curd (*āmikṣā*)—which is "that which belongs to the Viśvedevas"—could potentially have its substance mentioned in its own sentence, it is more appropriate that it pertains solely to the sacrifice mentioned in its own sentence, since it is impossible to assume that it pertains to two distinct types of divisions when such a distinction is not possible.
249: The established logical principle (*siddhāntanyāya*) regarding the locus of qualities (*guṇādhikaraṇa*, 2|2|12–13):

What is the category of *guṇa*? It is that which rests upon multiple substances (*anekadravyāśrita*), such as conjunction, disjunction, duality, and so forth, which consist of number and rest upon multiple substances; as well as color (*rūpa*) and the like, which are restricted to being substitutes for a single quality (*ekaguṇapratinidhiniyama*). This is the rule regarding substances that have become qualities (*guṇabhūtadravyavidhi*).
Substantive (dravyāśrita).

The refutation concerning the locus of qualities:

In the Agnihotra sacrifice, "He offers with curd" is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). However, when the word for the rite does not [itself] denote a quality, a quality would be understood therein.
Commentary: Alternatively, this is a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).
Actions such as "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) are established with the desire to avoid [the fault of] optionality (*vikalpa*).
However, that very same action is understood from the word "offers" (*juhoti*); it is not a different action.

Therefore, it is established that in that very case, the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is to be inferred from the statement itself. Or rather: "But when the word denoting the action is not accompanied by a quality" is a counter-example sūtra. For, "where a quality is enjoined that is not already restricted by another [injunction]..."

In that case, since the injunction of qualities is possible, the action is not divided. Because each [quality] is presented individually—such as *soma* and so on—and because all [qualities] arise simultaneously, whichever one is first [perceived], by the logic of the previous [section], another [action] is impossible when that [quality] is delimited; thus, from the conclusion that there is a different action (*karmāntaratva*), the connection [of the topic] is established.
The purpose [of the discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), all the actions qualified by curd and the other [substances] must be performed.
In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, since there is a single purpose, the performance consists of an option (*vikalpa*) between substances such as curd and so forth.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra—(in the sense of the counter-example Sūtra to the preceding section)—it means that in the case of the rite produced by the statement "He offers the Agnihotra," which is devoid of a specific accessory, a prescription of an accessory is possible through sentences concerning curd and the like; it is not possible, however, in the case of the sentence concerning the *abhikṣā* offering, which is already heard with an accessory.

This section is meaningful because, in the section on the *Ādhāra* and *Agnihotra*, it was stated that when a sentence containing an accessory occurs in proximity to a primary action, it serves to prescribe that accessory. Thus, this present section has its purpose.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that the statement made in the *Ādhārāgnihotra* section has no scope where there is only a single qualified (*saguṇa*) passage in proximity to a qualityless (*nirguṇa*) one; for in the present case, since there are many qualified passages, all of them would result in an option (*vikalpa*) regarding a single rite. Therefore, because [the *ādhāra* principle] serves to refute the suspicion that these are distinct rites (*karmāntara*), it is not redundant.

In the presence of the Nirguṇa [texts], it must be stated that even though many qualified (saguṇa) statements are heard, they serve only to enjoin attributes; otherwise, it would be impossible to refute the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the introductory and *agnihotra* passages, which holds that they are mere restatements (*anuvāda*) of a collective whole. As Viśvarūpa states: "In the case of the curd-oblation, there is either a different rite or an attribute; but the other is as before.
Because the *agnihotra* is devoid of attributes, the curd and so forth are properly understood as attributes."

Bhaṭṭa: However, where there is no hearing of an accessory (*guṇa*) in the original injunction of production—as in "He offers the Agnihotra"—there, by way of referring back to that [original act], all accessories such as "He offers with curd" and "He offers with milk" are enjoined as alternatives.
This is because, according to the maxim of the pigeons on a threshing floor (*khalekapotanyāya*), they all apply simultaneously, and thus there is no single delimitation [of one over the others].
This is merely a counter-example.
Maṇḍana: "In the injunctions 'one offers with curd' and 'one offers with milk,' there is no difference in the oblation.
Śaṅkara: "But in the case of the Agnihotra, it is not so;
there is a difference in the ritual action."

There is a contradiction when the subordinate and the principal, the injunction and the restatement, and the subject and the predicate occur simultaneously in one and the same place. The purpose of names [of sacrifices] is their connection with qualities and results (*guṇaphalopabandha*). Maṇi, p. 7. When a sentence is intent upon establishing a relationship between a quality and its fruit, it does not constitute a separate ritual action (karmāntara).
For the sequence of things is subordinate to them.
And that which assists something while it is being brought about is subordinate to it;
and that in the presence of which a thing does not even come into existence is subordinate to it.
Without that [latter], there is no deficiency.

There is no evidence whatsoever to suggest that simply because something is seen to be subordinate in one context, its primacy must also be understood as being expressed [by the word] in another;
for the states of being subordinate or primary are inherent according to the specific usage of the word.

The principle of the transposition of the primary and the subordinate based on a distinction of qualities; the principle of the differentiation of ritual acts based on a distinction of qualities (2.2.2).
This is stated in the Māṣa commentary on the section concerning repetition (Abhyāsādhikaraṇa), Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 809:

When there is a conflict between a subordinate and a primary element, because the purpose is for that [primary], the Vedic connection is determined by the primary;
the fire-consecration (ādhāna) belongs to the Yajurveda.
In that context, the Sāmans are enjoined by the rules: "He sings the Vāravantīya" and "He sings the Yajñāyajñīya.
These must be chanted loudly because the Sāmans belong to the Sāmaveda, and the tone of the Sāmaveda is loud, according to the rule: "The Sāman is chanted loudly."

Thus, when the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been reached as stated in the aphorism, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "The subordinate" (*guṇaḥ*). When there is a conflict between the subordinate and the principal (*mukhya*), which are both employed by the Veda as injunctions, the connection with the Veda follows the principal; that is, the natural force of the Vedic determination must be accepted.
This is because the subordinates exist for the sake of the principal.

Therefore, according to the path following the Bhāṣya, the low tone (*upāṃśu*) associated with the Yajurveda is the one that prescribes the fire-laying (*ādhāna*); thus, the *vāravantīya* and other *sāman*s are to be performed for the purpose of the fire-laying. According to the Vārtika, however, the subordinate element (*guṇa*) is the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), while the primary element is the applicatory injunction (*viniyogavidhi*).

In the event of a conflict between these two, since the *vāravantīya* and other *sāmans* are recited in the *Sāmaveda*, they constitute an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*); whereas in the *Yajurveda*, the statement "he sings the *vāravantīya*" and so forth constitutes an applicatory injunction (*viniyogavidhi*).

Therefore, the connection with a Veda and the determination of the Veda—specifically the connection with its specific accentuation—must be accepted according to the primary applicatory Veda, because the originative injunction exists for the sake of that applicatory injunction.
Thus,
in both cases, the *sāmans* of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) are to be sung in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
Who [says this]?
When there is a conflict between a subordinate and a primary element, the connection with the Veda is determined by the primary, because [the subordinate] exists for the sake of that [primary].

When there is a conflict between the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) rites prescribed in different Vedic branches, a doubt arises as to whether one should override the property (*dharma*) obtained for the principal by following its own Vedic branch—thereby obstructing the property based on the subsidiary’s own form—or whether one should follow the property based on the subsidiary’s own form in accordance with the property of the principal’s door. Since the performance of both subsidiary and principal is for the sake of the purpose of the principal’s door, it is logical to override the property based on the subsidiary’s own form in accordance with the property of the principal’s door; thus, the connection with the *prayogaveda* (the Veda of performance) is established through the principal’s door. This is the explanation of the Sūtra.

Su. Pṛ. 1107. It was explained under the rule *guṇamukhyavyatikrame* that subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) receive the designation of the primary Veda to which they belong. Vā. 3.7.23–50, Pṛ. 1109. Commentary: "He who, knowing thus, establishes the sacred fires"—this [injunction] belongs to the Yajurveda.
In that context, the Sāman singers recite: "He who, knowing thus, sings the Vāravantīya," "He who, knowing thus, sings the Yajñāyajñīya," and "He who, knowing thus, sings the Vāmadevya.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the singing of the Sāmans at the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) to be done loudly (*uccais*), or in a low voice (*upāṃśu*)? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it should be done loudly.
Why? Because that which is performed with the Sāmaveda is the Vāravantīya and so forth;
therefore, these sāmans should be sung with the *cāra* (the *ai* sound).
This being the position reached, we reply:

Whether one should set aside the primary in accordance with the subordinate, or the subordinate in accordance with the primary—it is logical that the subordinate should be set aside; the meaning is that the primary must be favored.
Why? Because the subordinate exists for the sake of the primary.
One engages in the performance of the subordinate with the thought: "How may the primary be endowed with its qualities through the performance of the subordinate?"

If, through the operation of a quality (*guṇa*), there were a loss of the primary [quality], then by the operation of that quality, the result would indeed not come to fruition. Now, if one thinks, "I shall make the principal endowed with a quality," and proceeds toward a quality, he causes the quality of that quality to fall away; its own purpose is not lost.
He does not proceed to make a quality endowed with a quality.
Furthermore, the singing of the *sāman* is a subordinate element (*guṇa*), and that subordinate quality—namely, the loudness prescribed by the *Sāmaveda*—sets aside the primary quality [of silence].
Therefore, the *sāmans* should be sung in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).

Or rather: now, where a primary rite belonging to one Veda has an auxiliary (*aṅga*) belonging to another Veda, there arises the doubt as to which Vedic property of the auxiliary should be performed. Since the properties designated by verbal expression are essentially dependent on their locus, the property of whichever [Veda] it is recited in should belong to that [Veda].
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"In a subordinate element, a property [is determined] by its own form; in another case, [it is determined] through the principal element.
Wherever this may be, there the sublation of the subordinate property is to be understood."
When it is necessary to transgress one of two duties, the duty that is subordinate must be transgressed;
for in this way, the primary duty remains unimpaired,
and that [preservation] is the very purpose of the subordinate element as well.

For he also proceeds for that very purpose. This is the principle of the transgression of the subordinate and the primary (guṇamukhyavyatikrama-nyāya). The principle of the transgression of the subordinate and the primary.

If, however, one were to render the principal act defective for the sake of conforming to its own subsidiary elements (*ātmīyadharma*), then his very engagement in the rite would be lost. Even if a subsidiary element remains defective once the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the principal has become endowed with its qualities, there is no fault therein, because the quality of the subsidiary is of no consequence in that context. Therefore, since the *Ādhāna* (fire-consecration) belongs to the Yajurveda, the *sāmans* occurring within it must be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśutva*).
[Objection: Is it not the case that this rule of *upāṃśutva* (low-voiced recitation) applies only to that much which is enjoined by the Yajurveda? It would not apply to the singing of Sāmans.
Furthermore, only the principal acts and the other subsidiary acts (*aṅga*) are Yājurvedika; therefore, for those alone there is *upāṃśutva*.
[Response: This is not so.
For it will be stated: "But the subsidiaries are taught along with the principal because they constitute its procedure" (11.1.2.16);
likewise, "because in the case of diversity, there is an injunction of the objects such as the *akṣatras* and so forth" (11.1.2.16).

Therefore, since they are encompassed by the injunction for the performance of the principal, even in other cases where the subsidiaries have been lost, the injunction applies only where the principal exists.
In this case, since it belongs to the Yajurveda by virtue of being an integral part [of the ritual], it must necessarily be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).

If that is so, then the low-voiced nature of the Sāman chants themselves—due to their belonging to the Yajurveda—is not a matter of conflict between the properties of a subordinate (*guṇa*) and a principal (*pradhāna*) element;
rather, because they reside within the subordinate parts, that low-voiced quality is equivalent to being loud (*uccais*).
It cannot be said that this [quality] exists there as belonging to the principal [element];
nor, when that which possesses it is sublated, is the property of the principal thereby sublated;
for in that case, the principal would not have been performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
Now, by some means,
[one might argue that] the principle of the subordination of the subordinate to the principal (*guṇamukhyavyatikramanyāya*) applies here.

Since this has already been established by the previously mentioned all-pervasive *upāṃśu* rule, the present statement is merely a restatement (*nityānuvāda*) intended to praise the reality of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites.

Regarding the *agnīṣomīya*, however, there is a reinstatement of the original (*prākṛta*) accents—beginning with "the *ājyabhāgas* are in a low tone" (*mandrāḥ*) and so forth—precisely through the division of the *savana*s.

Alternatively, the division of the *savana*s consists in dividing the entire performance, including its subsidiaries, into three parts and accomplishing the utterance in low, middle, and high tones respectively.
By this, the specific modes of pronunciation for the *anubandhyā*, the *utpadyodavasānīyā*, and others are also explained.

Even though the *satyākāla-savanīya* and other such offerings would likewise [initially] be subject to this same accentuation, because they are included within the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), their accents are exactly according to that specific pressing.

If it is argued that—since the words "pressing" (*savana*) denote parts of the Soma sacrifice—their accentuation should follow that of the whole, just like the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other subsidiaries, we say: no.
Because the use [of the mantra] at that specific time is heard merely through the indication of the locative case;
for if the genitive were used instead of the ablative "from the pressings" (*savanebhyaḥ*),

But in the seventh [case], whatever mantra is employed as having that [substance] as its substrate,
for all of that, there is the sequence of qualities beginning with *mandra*,
due to the transposition of primary and subordinate elements and the omission of subordinate elements.
Its weakness lies precisely in its being a matter of mental construction (*kalpyatva*).
Otherwise, even the *hotṛ* and other such priests who are constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma would have to be performers of the *acyuta* [recitation],

Therefore, it should be considered as follows: in cases where there is an origin (*utpatti*) in one Veda and an application (*viniyoga*) in another Veda—as in the case of the *Vāravantīya* and others—when the question arises as to which accent should be used, the accent based on the origin is stronger because the origin occurs prior [to the application] and thus lacks any contradiction.
Consequently, it is heard in scripture: "It is performed with the *ṛk*, that is, by means of the *Ṛgveda*" (*ṛcā kriyate upāyātte*), meaning "it is performed loudly (*uccais*) with the *ṛk*."

This being the position reached, [the author] says: Since the mere recitation of the mantra does not lead to an understanding of its purpose, and since its application is not yet understood, it has no requirement for a specific accent; rather, the connection with the accent occurs only after the *viniyoga* (application) has taken place. This is because the word "is performed" (*kriyate*) is understood to mean "is employed" (*prayujyate*), and since employment is dependent upon application (*viniyoga*), it is the application itself that first presents itself immediately prior [to performance]. Therefore, in the absence of a subverting factor, the accent based on the *viniyoga* must be observed.

Anticipating the objection that the designations such as *Ṛgveda* and so forth would also fail to apply to the subordinate elements (*guṇa*) through their connection with the primary ones (*pradhāna*), thereby rendering the principle of "the conflict between the subordinate and the primary" (PMS 3.1.2.9) devoid of scope, he states the difference: since there is no contradiction in those [designations] also being applied to the primary elements, and because of the designation by the word *veda* in the sense of "that which is used" (*prayoga-vācin*), it is understood that properties such as loudness (*uccais-tva*) pertain to the *veda* as a whole in its practical application (*prayoga*). (Regarding the section on the establishment of that): *Ku.* 1.4.2.139, p. 113. The maxim of the omission of qualities (*guṇalopanyāya*).
The maxim of the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle.
In the Pavamāna sacrifices performed at the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna), there is indeed an offering even with the Agnihotra-ladle. [The principle is:
"When a subordinate element is omitted, the primary act remains.

‘In the case of *pavamāna* and when there is the elision of a quality (*guṇa*),
[the suffix] is applied after words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*).’
The *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle is a subordinate element (*guṇa*), while the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is the primary act (*pradhāna*).
Thus, even when the subordinate element is omitted, the primary act must indeed be performed. Therefore, the pouring out must be performed in the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices.
By means of another vessel.

Why? Because although the quality of being "as heard" (yathāśrutatva) in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) lacks the status of being a constant quality of an injunction (*vidhi*), the explanatory passage nonetheless possesses the quality of serving the purpose of the constant quality of the injunction. Thus, by the maxim "when a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is omitted, the primary action (*mukhya*) should take place," one might suspect that—just as the act of ascending is performed by means of the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) due to the injunction being understood from the explanatory passage—the specific distinction created by the prior and subsequent utterances [of the mantra] would apply here as well. However, since the application of the meaning of the injunction occurs before the determination of the meaning of the explanatory passage, and because [the explanatory passage] is not the primary factor, it does not fall within the scope of the maxim regarding the omission of a subordinate element. In the case of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), even in the absence of the *prasra* (flowing milk) when performing according to one's capacity, the throwing away of the branch (*śākhā-praharaṇa*) takes place by the principle of "the omission of a subordinate element" (*guṇalope ca*). However, where the performance of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) and so forth is solely for the purpose of curing a disease in either the husband or the wife, there—despite the other partner lacking the status of a wife—the principle of "the omission of a subordinate element" applies. Thus, although the act of looking at the clarified butter (*jyāvekṣya*) may be performed by another person in place of the one who would normally hire a substitute (*parikraya*), there is no authority for such an assumption in all cases.

9|1| 10|133, p. 1675. Regarding the rule *guṇavacanānām* and others, the meaning of the word *guṇavacana* (quality-expressing) is that which has as its primary function the employment of a word expressing the locus (*āśraya*), gender, number, or other such properties, and whose referent is characterized by being a qualifier (*viśeṣaka*) of its own denoted object (*svaśakyārtha*). It is a single word whose connection with the individual instance (*vyakti*) is inseparable. In this context, if one intended to include merely those things that are "capable" (*yogya*) [of being qualifiers], then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of applying feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* even in cases like *ajāyāḥ śuklaḥ* ("the white of the goat"), because even though that [word *śukla*] does not function as a secondary indicator (*lakṣaka*) at that time, it still possesses "capability" (*yogyatva*), just like the word *araṇya* [in *araṇyakhaṇḍa*].
Therefore, to exclude that [possibility], there is another qualifier.

For this very reason, in cases such as "there is no gender residing in the substratum," the rule "white and other qualities are masculine when [the quality itself is] not a substance" (Amara-kośa 1.6.17) prescribes the masculine gender solely for the sake of grammatical correctness.
Furthermore, even in expressions like "there is form" (*rūpam asti*), the first [qualifier] applies because the substance is connected [to the verb] as the mode (*prakāra*).

And therefore, since the suffixes *ṭā*, *tṛ*, and so forth are possible even in the absence of a specific individual (*vyakti-lakṣaṇā*), the word *aruṇā* is intended to convey the connection of the quality (*guṇa*) with the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*). (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Bhāṣya, 3.1.612, p. [number]).
Regarding words expressing qualities:
167–168. Words expressing qualities take their gender and number from the substratum [of the quality].

In the Mahābhāṣya, the rule *aviśeṣaṇānāṃ jātyākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.52) has been rejected as it stands; instead, it is explained with the intention that the word *viśeṣaṇa* refers to *guṇa* (quality), meaning that "the gender and number of words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) follow the substrate [of the quality]. Consequently, the gender [of the word] in the expression *triḥprathamāmānave* is justified by its dependence on the substrate.

Although grammarians maintain that the application of gender and number from the substrate occurs only at the stage of denoting [the substrate] as qualified by a quality, and not at the stage of denoting the quality alone, nevertheless—since words denoting qualities are adjectives—the denotation of a substance qualified by a quality can, even without an explicit [stated] number, result in the application of gender and number through syntactic coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with another word expressing the substantive object; thus, this sūtra would be merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*) regarding the refinement of the sentence.

Therefore, in order to establish that this sūtra functions as a prescriptive rule (*vidhāyaka*), one must state that its intended meaning (*tātparya*) is also that the gender and number [of the word] are determined by the substratum (*āśraya*), which serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), even during the stage of denoting a mere quality (*guṇa*).
[Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa says: "Under the view that word formation (*pada-saṃskāra*) occurs first, this is based on an explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*). ]
But when there is syntactic refinement (*vākya-saṃskāra*), then this is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*);
for even though the particular substratum has already been qualified by its specific attributes in the preceding sequence, gender and number are established as residing in that [substratum] itself.
Furthermore, the status of being a quality-word (*guṇavacanatā*) is observed in cases such as *aruṇā* (red).

The singular number is used for words such as *udvid* (Bṛhatī, p. 124). Furthermore, for grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*) refers to the substance (*dravya*), because [for them] the quality exists as dependent upon the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*).
For grammarians do not enumerate qualities in the same manner as the Vaiśeṣikas do.
Rather, the designation of "quality" and "qualified" is made with respect to the manifestation [of a thing] from ignorance (*ajñāna*).
Vārttika 3.1.612, p. 685. There is a mutual connection among sentences concerning qualities.

Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1487. "Qualitative discourse" (*guṇavāda*) is explanatory discourse (*arthavāda*); when there is a contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), "in case of contradiction, it should be qualitative discourse."
