They are not to be given. (p.
31). "The functions of the qualities":
"the denotation of its own primary meaning while abandoning it," "conjunction," and "metaphorical attribution."
Likewise, a derivative meaning (vṛtti) accompanied by an affix is a conventional usage of a whole (samudāya-prasiddhi).
A sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) has little conventional usage; thus, it is rarely employed.
Furthermore, figurative indication (guṇalakṣaṇā) is established as being distinct from the eight types of [primary] denotation.
Similarity is the ninth.
These nine secondary positions (gauṇapakṣa) are to be understood together with those set forth in the *Tatsiddhi-sūtra* (Vākyapadīya 3.1.1, p.

(1) *Jahatsvārthābhidhāyitva* (the state of denoting while abandoning its own primary meaning): "Abandoning its own meaning" (*jahatsvārtha*) refers to the state of denoting while abandoning [the primary sense]. In the case of figurative usage (*gauṇatva*), the cause is the operation [of the word] upon qualities such as tawny color (*paiṅgalya*) by abandoning its own meaning, namely the primary object such as fire (*adhyādi*). (2) *Saṃghāta* (conglomeration): A conglomeration of a universal (*jāti*) such as fire and a quality (*guṇa*) such as tawny color—which is not directly expressible by words like "fire" and so on—is the cause of figurative usage because it serves as the basis for the application of the word to a mere quality devoid of a universal.
(3) Metaphorical construction (*parikalpanā*):

The cause of metaphorical usage (*gauṇatva*) is the conceptualization of words such as "fire" (*agni*) and so forth with respect to things such as a young Brahmin (*māṇavaka*), by means of a word expressing a quality (*guṇaśabda*) such as "fire" and so forth. (4) A compound (*vṛtti*) accompanied by a prefix (*sopapadā*).

The cause of secondary usage (*gauṇatva*) is the dependence on the material cause, which is a subordinate quality known as "tawny-ness" (*paiṅgalya*), in the case of words such as *agni* when accompanied by an attendant term such as *māṇavaka*.
(5) This is [an instance of] conventional usage based on the whole (*samudāyaprasiddhi*).

The well-known application (*prasiddhi*) of a word such as "fire-boy" (*agnimāṇavaka*) toward qualities like tawny color (*paiṅgalya*) by way of its component meaning—namely, in the form of the quality of tawny color—is the cause of its figurative nature (*gauṇatva*). This is because the word "fire" (*agni*), which constitutes a part of the whole compound, functions toward the tawny color as if it possessed the quality of being a constituent part of that whole. (6) Regarding the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*): the fact that tawny color and so forth constitute the sentence-meaning of "fire-boy" and similar expressions is the cause of the figurative nature of the word "fire" with respect to tawny color, because this word possesses the quality of being a constituent part of that sentence.

(7) Limited renown (*alpaprasiddhitva*): The fact that words such as "fire" (*agni*) have limited Vedic renown (*śrautaprasiddhi*) with respect to qualities such as tawny color (*paiṅgalya*) is a cause for their being secondary (*gauṇatva*), based on the ground of dependence upon a subordinate factor known as ignorance (*ajña*).
(8) Limited usage (*alpaprayogitā*).

That in which words such as "fire" (*agni*) are used by speakers with little frequency—referring to qualities such as tawny color (*paiṅgalya*) and so forth—is called "infrequently used" (*alpaprayogin*); its state (*bhāva*), namely infrequency of use (*alpaprayogitā*) or lack of common renown (*alpaprasiddhatva*), is the cause of being secondary (*gauṇatva*). Having set aside these positions regarding the causes of being secondary, the *Bhāṣya* establishes that the word "fire" is secondary when applied to one possessing the quality of fire, such as a boy (*māṇavaka*), because it functions through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the quality of fire—such as tawny color—by means of the universal "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) residing in the word "fire. This is established as the cause of being secondary in the form of the denotable object of a secondary word, since it serves as the ground for the application of the word "fire" to that which possesses the quality of fire. (Sūtra-pṛ. 1083). [Objection: "If it is argued that the word 'quality' (*guṇa*) is likewise [secondary]."

In the *nirvāpa* mantra of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is recited: "I offer what is pleasing to Agni. Regarding this word *agni*, there arises an inquiry: is it not enjoined in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), and does it not denote something inherent to the ritual action (*karmasamaveta*)? Or rather, must it be modified (*ūhya*) so that it denotes something inherent to the ritual action? In considering this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) states: in the sense of the word *juṣṭa* (pleasing), Agni is subordinate to the act of pleasing (*joṣaṇa*).
The word "fire" (agni) denotes that [substance].
It is a quality-word (guṇaśabda).
As such, this quality-word—like words such as "white" (saci) and others—expresses something inherent in the action; therefore, it should not be modified in the modified ritual (vikṛti).

For instance, by the statement "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" (*agnaye juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*), the offering of that which is already pleasing is expressed; however, in this case, there is no offering of something already pleasing,
because that which is to be offered must be something not yet pleasing— that is, something not yet consecrated.
That [offering] will indeed be approved as a pouring out (nirvāpa);
therefore, it expresses a collective sense.
The word "pouring out" is employed in the sense of "its utterance," having an equivalent meaning.
If this is argued, or alternatively:
regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in the scripture: "Thou art grain; prosper the gods; [thou art] the strength of the rice-grains."
In this regard, concerning the inquiry as to whether the word *dhānya* denotes that which is inherent (*samaveta*) or not, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

"The word *dhānya* is intended here as a term denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*), because it is a quality in the act of pleasing the gods. Thus, this word *dhānya*, being a term for a quality, does not denote that which is inherent."

If it is argued that the word "guṇa" (quality) means "tathā" (so/likewise), then because it denotes a quality, the *nandra* and other such [substitutions] should not be applied in the *Śākyāyanas* sacrifice and similar rites.

If it is argued: "The word 'grain' (dhānya) applies to those [seeds] that still possess their husks, but not to the rice-grains from which the husks have been removed; thus, it should be understood that the term does not denote what is currently present [in the ritual]. If this is your position:
No, because of inherence.
In the offering-mantra of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, "I offer what is pleasing to Agni," the word "Agni" does not denote something that is not inherent, because of inherence—
that is, because of the connection and relation with the Agni who has been enjoined by the ritual injunction through the performance of the rite.
Nor is the offering of what has been "pleased" (juṣṭa) enjoined by this sentence; rather, it is the act of making [the oblation] "pleased" through the offering that is enjoined.
The meaning of the word "juṣṭam" is "that which is agreeable" (abhirucita).

In the phrase "rucyatārthān prīṇamānaḥ" (pleasing those who find pleasure), the fourth case ending is used because Agni is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Furthermore, since Agni’s desire for the material substance that will become the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) exists even prior to its pouring out (*nirvāpa*), there is no inconsistency in using the suffix *ṛt* in its sense of a completed action (*bhūtārtha*).
Thus says the *Kutūhala*.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the word *agni* denotes what is actually present (*samaveta-vacana*) and must be modified in a modified ritual (*vikṛti*), such as the Auryā. Alternatively, as for the statement that in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the word *dhānya* in the mantra "Thou art grain (*dhānya*), prosper the gods" does not denote what is actually present because it refers to rice (*taṇḍula*)—that is not correct; [in this case, too, it should be modified].
Even for the word *dhānya* (grain), which denotes rice (*brīhi*), there is an inherence (*samavāya*) in the rice grains because they are its products;

just as when it is said, "Śāli rice is being eaten" in reference to *kodrava* seeds, it is not the husked grain that is eaten. Therefore, the word *dhānya* denotes that which is inherent [in the product].

In the sacrifice of the Śākyas, the mantra "This is meatless; satisfy the gods" is to be recited. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Why? Because it is the locus of a subordinate element (*guṇa*); that is, because it is the section concerning the remainder of subordinate elements (*guṇaśeṣādhikaraṇa*), the section concerning the counter-examples of subordinate elements (*guṇapratyudāharaṇādhikaraṇa*), or the principle of the contradiction of subordinate elements (*guṇavirodhanyāya*). As the Sūtra states: "But when the word denotes the primary action (*karmaśabda*) and not a subordinate element, a subordinate element is understood therein" (2.1.10.24).
Nor can the primary be subordinated to the qualities by means of figurative speech;
nor does the primary exist as something subject to the control of the qualities.
Bhāṣya 1.1.14.
Even according to the sequence of qualities (*guṇa*), when no other course is possible,
the predominance of the primary [quality] is established by the logic of qualification and so forth, as seen in the case of the *kalpa* and others.
Furthermore, the repetition of performance is observed for the sake of attaining a perfection of qualities that has no other means of attainment.

Su. Pṛ. 702: A primary entity (padārtha) need not be modified for the sake of a subordinate quality (guṇa). Bhāṣya 1.1.17: For the sake of a subordinate quality, the principal (pradhāna) should not be repeated.

Or rather: "It is not proper to abandon the principal on account of the subordinate" (vā. 3.1.15); this is the principle of the section concerning the conflict between a substance and its refinement (*dravyasaṃskāravirodha-adhikaraṇa*). [End of] Parāśara.
56.2: Because the primary element cannot be modified according to a subordinate quality;
this is the principle of the *indrapīta* section.
Furthermore, it has been stated in the *vaiśvadeva* section that it is not possible to extract the mere action and enjoin another quality.
Or [as stated in] Pāṇini 2.1.123 (p. 537): through the production of another quality (*guṇāntara*), the sacrificer becomes fit for the acquisition of the fruit.
In that regard, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) produce another quality, because of the absence of [any other] quality [prior to them].

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: although in the act of threshing (*avaghāta*) it is possible for the word *haviṣkṛt* to possess a secondary sense (*gauṇatā*) characterized by its connection with the quality of being the cause for the preparation of the oblation (*havis*), nevertheless, because there is an absence of the characteristics of invocation, address, the vocative case, or an injunction, and because—despite the possibility of a secondary capacity for the word *haviṣkṛt* itself—the two words consisting of the vocative and the verb (*āhvaya*) lack even a secondary capacity; furthermore, since the scriptural statement (*vacana*) pertains to the entire mantra and is incapable of enjoining an application without the capacity of the entire mantra, the application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra is not possible. This is the meaning of the Sūtra.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: Even though the word *haviṣkṛt* lacks the capacity to indicate the act of threshing (*avaghāta*), it must nevertheless apply [to that act] because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the word *ehi* ("come"). Furthermore, since the calling of the wife (*patnyāhvāna*) is not known [from the context], and because when both the gender (*liṅga*) and the expressed meaning (*vācya*) can be accommodated, there would be the consequence of subverting the sentence (*vākya*), one cannot accept either of these two positions. Thus, it is not logical for the gender alone to indicate the act of threshing; this is the sense of the Sūtra (Su. p. 1095). [Objection: "Because it denotes a subordinate quality (*guṇābhidhāna*), the mantra beginning with *mandra* should be a single mantra, since those two [the qualities and the action] are connected to a single purpose."

In the *makṣānuvāka* of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is heard [in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.2.12]: "May Vāk, the non-dull, the overcomer, the banner of sacrifices, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma; O Agni, you who possess the auspicious covering of the Vasus and who know the mind; of the morning pressing, which has the Gāyatrī meter, of that which is drunk by Indra, which is honey-sweet, and which is invited—being invited, I partake. In this regard, the portion ending with "may [Vāk] be satisfied" (*tṛpyatu*) is one mantra, and the portion beginning with "O Agni, you who possess the auspicious covering of the Vasus" (*vasubhadra-cchadasaḥ*) and ending with "I partake" (*bhakṣayāmi*) is another.
Therefore, due to the difference in meaning, there is a division of sentences (*vākya-bheda*).

Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been reached that the two [mantras] should be employed separately according to their respective purposes, the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
"The mantra beginning with *mandra* and ending with *bhakṣya* should be a single mantra.

This is because it expresses a quality; that is, since it expresses a qualifying attribute in the form of the speaker's satisfaction—extending from the word *prāpteḥ* to the end of the word *tṛpyatu*—it attains the status of a single syntactical unit (*vākya*) within the act of eating.
Because of the connection of a single purpose between those two sentences ending in "tṛpyatu" and "bhakṣayāmi," the qualified meaning is established;
therefore, because they denote a quality, [this is] the section concerning the denotation of qualities (guṇābhidhādhikaraṇa) regarding mantras and so forth.
The mantra beginning with "makṣyāya" is a single mantra, not two;
all of it must be employed for the act of eating.
Why? Because the mantra is a single unit due to its expression of a single quality.

Even if one were to assume that the consumption of Soma has the purpose of purifying the consumer as a secondary effect (*ānuṣaṅgika*), since the purification of the consumer lacks the status of a fruit—just like heaven—it cannot be fit for manifestation (*prakāśana*) for the sake of providing encouragement (*utsāhana*). Furthermore, because there is no mention of such a fruit, and because the injunction "I consume" (*ahaṃ bhakṣayāmi*) is not subject to doubt due to its being prohibited by the extent of the scriptural text (*yāvacchruti*), it is not possible for it to be fit for manifestation. Since the power of denotation (*abhidhāna-sāmarthya*) functions as an applicatory factor (*viniyojaka*) only when a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would otherwise result in meaninglessness, and since the power to form a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) exists through compatibility with that [denotation], the mantra is applied to the consumption by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). As for the two parts of the mantra ending in *tṛpyatu* and *vasubhadraṇa*, because they are connected to a single fruit—the act of consumption—and because the root *tṛp* (to satisfy) is understood as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) to the act of consuming, the entire mantra is considered a single mantra; such is the meaning of the Sūtra.
Su. pṛ. 114:
It is precisely the collection of qualities [that constitutes the teacher], because of the acts of approaching the guru and so forth.
Earth and the other substances are merely an aggregate of qualities (guṇasamudāya) and nothing more than that— this is the view of the Cārvākas.
And this is because, in the case of earth and the others, the destruction of the prior form and the production of a subsequent one through baking and so forth are established by experience.
Maṇi, p. 22:
Terms denoting qualities in general do not override the *codaka* (the extended application of archetypal rules).
In the injunction, "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," the word "white" refers specifically to the white goat obtained through the *codaka*, and not to any white animal whatsoever.
"The knower of qualities delights with those who possess qualities"—this is the maxim.
Its meaning is clear.
It is rash [to say] that what is being multiplied is not seen; for this is directly perceived—that which is being multiplied is repeated again and again.
Bhāṣya 1.3.27.
This rule regarding the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the rectum is shown in the case of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice during the *upayāja* offerings.

Bhāṣya 12.4.48: In a group of animals, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the rectums which serve as the means for the *upayāja* offerings; this is to be understood as the "principle of the combination of the rectums in the *upayāja*" (12.4.48). The disposal of the rectal section is the *upayāja* oblation in the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice.
Smṛti texts such as "The teacher is to be honored" are authoritative regarding dharma. Bhā. 1|3|11-2:
Regarding the scriptural injunction that "the teacher is to be honored and saluted," the qualification for this applies to one who has been initiated (upanīta), not to one who has not been initiated.
Tri. 6|2|6: [The teacher] is to be followed, honored, and saluted.

Although this has a visible purpose, because it is prescribed by rule, it produces an unseen merit (*nyāyāpūrva*), and because it is contingent upon a specific occasion (*nimitta*), its repetition must be performed as a contingent duty (*naimittika*); however, following and so forth should not be done merely at will, once or repeatedly.
As for the teachers of the Prabhākara school, they accept that all cognitions have the threefold nature (*tripuṭī*) as their object.

And the Tripuṭī consists of the objects of knowledge, the self, and the means of knowledge (Maṇi., p. 18). Through following the teacher, one becomes pleased; the teacher, being satisfied, will explain [the truths] and will speak of the principles found in other treatises as well.

Bhāṣya 1.3.12, p. 165: Since acts such as approaching the teacher (*gurūṅgamana*) are performed even by those who have already acquired knowledge, they cannot have a purely visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Therefore, because their necessity would otherwise be inexplicable, and because one must avoid the mental remorse (*pratyaya*) caused by non-performance, and since that [remorse] has no other source of authority, its basis in the Veda is established.
Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 126: Because approaching the teacher and so forth are occasional duties (*naimittika*), there is remorse for their non-performance, but not for their performance.
And a visible result is observed, such as "the teacher, being pleased, will teach [me]."

Vā. 1.3.12, p. 166: The duties such as approaching the teacher (*gurūpasaṅgama*) and so forth are to be performed after the time of initiation (*upanayana*). Regarding the qualification (*adhikāra*) for performing Smārta and other rites belonging solely to one who has been initiated, this should be consulted in the *Bindu*.

When there is a repetition of the occasion for acts such as saluting the teacher (*guru*), there should be a repetition [of the act]. This would be the case when these acts are undertaken according to established custom (*ācāra*), because they serve a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*).

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: "The teacher is to be saluted and honored; those of advanced age are to be met and honored. Regarding this, there is a doubt: must that which has been prescribed be performed every time the teacher or those of advanced age arrive? Or is the requirement fulfilled by performing it only once?
Regarding the rule "it should be so when they are taken according to custom, because it serves the purpose of the person," this is the instruction on the locus of the discussion.

In that regard, whatever was the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) there, that is the prima facie view here; whatever was the final conclusion (*uttara-pakṣa*) there, that is the final conclusion here.

"Having performed it once, one has accomplished the purpose"; this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). "Because it is contingent upon a specific occasion (*nimitta*), there must be repeated performance"; this is the final view (*uttarapakṣa*).

O gentle one—since these acts are contingent, the avoidance of the obstacle is the primary fruit of going to the teacher and so forth, while the teacher's satisfaction is merely a secondary (*ānuṣaṅgika*) result.

Therefore, the Teachers have stated (Āhnika 1.3.12, p. 166): "Since acts such as approaching the teacher are occasional (*naimittika*), the obligation (*pratyaya*) arises when they are not performed, but not when they are performed.
And this is observed: [the thought] 'The teacher, being pleased, will teach [me]' and so forth is accomplished.
Furthermore, from the restrictive rule (*niyama*), there is the prior establishment of the purpose of completing what has been undertaken."

And it should be noted that in the *Nyāyasudhā*, it is explained that the word "is produced" (*niṣpadyate*) indicates its status as a secondary result (*ānuṣaṅgikatva*). Bi—Regarding whether there is freedom of choice (*yāthākāmya*) in [acts such as] approaching the Guru's wife and so forth: [the opponent says] it would exist because they are causes of pleasure; [the author replies] the last [alternative] is brought forward [as the conclusion].

Bhaṭṭa: Since we observe that in the authoritative instances of established practice (*ācāra*), such as following a teacher and so forth, the practice itself is repeated, it follows that in the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) which is its source, the act of following the teacher and so on is characterized by being contingent upon a specific occasion (*nimitta*). Therefore, there must be repetition for every occasion. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this contingency, as the practice is not merely performed out of a desire for some desired result; for even if it were for the sake of pleasing the teacher, there would be no proof for its being contingent, since the teacher’s pleasure could be achieved through other means. Furthermore, because the practice is performed after the study [of the Vedas] has been completed, its performance is mandatory; thus, by virtue of being a fixed obligation, it is understood to be contingent upon a specific occasion.

As for what was stated in the *Tantraratna*— that the status of being a cause is understood through the scripture itself by means of the seventh case-ending, the suffix *śatṛ*, and so forth, in the phrase "of approaching the teacher" (*gurūpasaṅgamanādeḥ*)—
that refers to the *Gṛhamedhīya* [rite]; for in the *Gṛhamedhīya*, the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are prescribed.
VI. 10.7.9. The ritual named Gṛhamedhīya is indeed a distinct action (karmāntara) and not a modification (vikṛti).
Regarding the statement "he performs the two Ājyabhāgas," that is a unique (apūrva) offering of clarified butter (ājya).
Ke. 10.1.9. The scriptural mention of the Ājyabhāgas is for the purpose of indicating the unique nature (apūrvatva) of the Gṛhamedhīya.

Su. Pṛ. 939. In the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice, the two *ājyabhāga* offerings must be performed because they are prescribed as something not previously established (*apūrvavidhāna*). Furthermore, because of the injunctions "He makes an oblation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" and "He invokes the *iḍā*," the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *akṣa* (the eating of the remains) must also be performed. Thus, only that which is explicitly stated should be done. Vi. 10.1.10: "In the Gṛhamedhīya, he performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings."
In this regard, there are three positions: the first is that this is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings which have been obtained through extension (*atideśa*).

The second is that, in order to avoid meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), since the two *ājyabhāgas* are prescribed in both [the archetype and the ectype], they are here conceived as bringing about prosperity (*abhyudaya*); thus, because it follows the nature of the archetype, there is an injunction through both instruction and direction, stating "it should be performed in this manner.

The third is that, since prescribing them by both would result in an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and because we observe a praise stating "he offers the two *ājyabhāgas* for the sake of sacrifice," it is equal to the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice under discussion.

The fourth [view] is that, because there is no syntactic unity with the injunction regarding the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, and because it is connected to the purpose of praising those [two], the phrase "for the sake of sacrifice" (*yajatyai*) is understood as a praise of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings; furthermore, since this repeated mention is not intended for anything else, it serves to enjoin the performance of the *ājyabhāga* duties as a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*).

The fifth [view] is that, because it would result in the word *ājyabhāga* being used in the sense of indicating its constituent duties (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), and because there is no possibility of enjoining a separate ritual act, the two *ājyabhāgas* are already established in the *prajāpati-vrata* and other rites through extended application (*atideśa*); therefore, the repeated mention of the *ājyabhāgas* is for the purpose of excluding others (*anyapari-saṃkhyā*).

The sixth [view] holds that because the application of the injunction (*codaka*) occurs first, and because a restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*) is untenable as a result—since the three defects (*tridoṣa*) cannot be avoided—even when [the subsidiaries] are taught, they follow this very direction. The seventh [view] holds that since all constituent elements (*padārtha*) are obtained simultaneously through the extension (*atideśa*) of the assistance provided by the *alaṇḍa*-performance, the position of excluding them was refuted in the third book at [Sūtra] 3.6.18, "But because of the purpose of the injunction and the primary action, there is no exclusion from the archetype"; therefore, the extension is restricted solely to the two *ājyabhāga* offerings.

Since extension (*atideśa*) has as its object specific items within the category of ritual acts, it is unfit for subsumption (*upasaṃhāra*) under the principle that "a general rule which is unclear is restricted by a specific one. Having thus rejected the seventh position, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) will be stated in the tenth book (10.1.12–33): because the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice lacks the requirement for archetypal *ājyabhāga* offerings—since their assistance is already established—the absence of extension means this scriptural statement is intended to indicate the unique character (*apūrvatva*) of the Gṛhamedhīya.

Su. P. 106. Regarding the fifth position—that the re-enunciation of the *ājyabhāga* offerings in the *gṛhamedhīya* rite serves as a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*)—the demonstration of its purpose is that the mention of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering likewise excludes other disposal rites (*pratipatti*) of the same class that would otherwise apply to the remnants.
There should be a prohibition against consuming the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, because the reason [for its consumption] is the same.
The Commentary states: There is the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice.
Regarding it, it has been established that the *gṛhamedhīya* is an original (*apūrva*) rite.

In this regard, they recite: "He sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Here a doubt arises: does the word *sviṣṭakṛt* exclude these other subsidiary acts and the consumption [of the remnant], or not? It is argued: since the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice is an unprecedented (*apūrva*) rite, there are no subsidiary acts or consumptions of remnants at all.
To this it is replied:
the case of the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice is considered as a hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvācintya*). The purpose of the preceding section is now being examined.
If it were an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), then the sacrifices would be exclusively specified by the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, and no others.
This also serves as a purpose:
whether the consumption of the remnants is exclusively specified by way of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, or not.
What is established? When the *sviṣṭakṛt* is heard, there would be an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the portions to be consumed.
Why? Because the reason is the same.
For the reason for the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the consumption [of the portions] is indeed equal.

Both [the injunctions] are for the purpose of the remaining consecrations (*śeṣasaṃskāra*). In that case, because of the specific statement, this particular consecration of the remainder occurs and no other; thus, the consumptions (*bhakṣas*) would be prohibited.
Or rather, there is no prohibition, because it is observed here that this [consecration] should take place.

The Commentary states: Just as upon hearing the injunction for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the absence of other subsidiary rites (*śeṣakārya*) is observed, and thus it is said that there are no subsidiary portions to be consumed (*bhakṣa*), so too, from the observation of consumption, it is understood that such portions do exist. And between observation and non-observation, observation is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
What is that indication? It is: "He invokes the *iḍā*.
For invocation is the act of causing [the deity] to perform;
that occurs when there is eating, not when there is no eating.
Therefore, there is a prohibition;
or rather, it is a prohibition, because we observe that it is preceded by a positive injunction.
The Commentary: "Or rather, it is a prohibition."
For when the cause is identical, that which is based on perception sublates that which is inferential.
Now, as for the observation that was mentioned, it will pertain to eating preceded by a ritual injunction.
For thus it is recorded in scripture: "He cuts off the *iḍā* portion, but he does not invite [the gods]; he eats the *iḍā*. This is the observation regarding that.
The purpose of the *kṛtvācintā* need not be stated,
for that purpose belongs to the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*).
Furthermore, the purpose of a purpose is not mentioned.
Whatever is the purpose, that is its purpose;
and that is the preceding section.
In the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice, as much as is stated [is required], namely the two Gṛhamedhīya Ājyabhāgas.
The connection [of this section] is established by its conclusion with the statement of the purpose of the *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) regarding the Soma.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: when the *sviṣṭakṛt* [offering] is heard [in the context], there should be a cessation of eating, because both [the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *prāśitra*, etc. are of the same class insofar as they serve the purpose of the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remnants.
Vi— "In that very case (namely, the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice), if it is an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), does the *prāśitra* and so forth exist or not?"
There is the perception of "it exists," but it is not so; by that statement, it does not exist here.

In the *Bhāṭṭa* school, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) has been explained by unifying it with the ninth section. Maṇḍana states: "The *iṣṭakṛt* offering does not perform the function of a remnant (*śeṣakṛtti*) when there is a preceding [rite] (*sapūrve*)," [meaning that for the *Gṛhamedhīya*, there is an absence of being a new, independent rite (*apūrvatva*)].
Śaṅkara says: "The *sviṣṭakṛt* performs the remaining rites.
The *sviṣṭakṛt* is that which supersedes the remaining rites.
In the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, only what is explicitly stated should be performed.
Even more than that, it would be as has been stated.
The Commentary says: *Gṛhamedhīya* is the example here.
In that case, the requirement (*upadeya*) has been fully understood; since it is satisfied by the two *ājyabhāga* offerings alone, it does not take [the requirements] from other sacrifices.
That too is stated:
Why is it that this creation does not grasp all other cognitions? This being the case, it is replied:
even from that, only as much as has been stated [is grasped].
Thus, having been stated in this way, it does not take up other subsidiaries.
If no distinction were perceived, one would not take them up;
however, a distinction is indeed perceived here because the two Ājyabhāga offerings are prescribed by direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Therefore, in all those cases where there is an explicit statement, a distinction is understood once again;
thus, it should be as much as has been stated,
such as "he cuts off portions for Agni" and "he invokes the iḍā."

Soma: Regarding the statement that what is heard again as a constituent part of the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*) brings about an unprecedented result (*apūrvatā*), there arises a connection [to the present discussion] because of the specific inquiry as to whether this applies to each individual part or to all of them.
The meaning of the Sūtra is: "Even beyond the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, everything stated—such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and so forth—should be performed.
Vi: "In that case, no other constituent part should be performed, or rather, it should be performed, because there is no dependence on others."
It is not a ritual act (kārya), for the Sviṣṭakṛt and other such acts are ritual acts by virtue of being enjoined.
In the Bhaṭṭa school, however, this section has been explained in the ninth section itself, and thus it should be viewed in that very manner.
Maṇḍana: "Therefore, it should be joined with as many subsidiaries as are stated. Śaṃkara: "In that case as well, there should be only what is stated."
In the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice, even though there is a displacement of the *sāmidhenī* verses, there is no sublation of the invocation (*āvāhana*).
Because of the prohibition of *sāmidhenī* verses in the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice—namely, "one does not recite the *sāmidhenīs*"—the invocation (*āvāhana*) should also not be performed.

This is because, in the Kauṣītaki [Brāhmaṇa], following the rules for invocation, there is a reference to the *sāmidhenīs*: "Now, as for why one mutters the *sāmidhenīs* afterwards, the *sāmidhenīs* are indeed a thunderbolt" (2.3). Since this occurs within that intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), it is understood that the invocation is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to those *sāmidhenīs*.

This being the position reached, since the two [rites] serve different purposes, there is no evidence for their mutual relationship as principal and subordinate (*aṅga*) according to the maxim "and because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another" (*guṇānāṃ ca parārthatvāt*). Since it is possible to explain [the subsequent mention] even as a restatement (*anuvāda*) following the injunction regarding the *pavitra*, there is no sublation of the *āvāhana* (invocation) by virtue of the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*). This is the *Gṛhamedhīya-ājyabhāga-nyāya*. (Sūtra 4.4.7).
The principle of the *ājyabhāga* offerings; the principle of the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice; the principle of the injunction regarding the *ājyabhāga* offerings in the *gṛhamedhīya*.
The Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice possesses the status of an independent rite (apūrva) because of the repeated mention of the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga).
Because the original injunction is taken up in the modified sacrifice, the restatement would be purposeless.
The Bhāṣya states: In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, it is heard: "For the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhins, [one prepares] the evening porridge with the milk of all [the cows].
Therein they recite: "He offers the two Ājyabhāga oblations."

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is this merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings already obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), or do both the *codaka* and this [text] enjoin a single ritual act? Or is it a partial inclusion based on the sense of the matter? Or is it the originative injunction (*utpatti*) of two additional distinct rituals? Or is it for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*)? Or does the *codaka* extend the application of everything else except the two *ājyabhāgas*? Or are only the two *ājyabhāgas* obtained through the *codaka*, while the *codaka* itself does not exist at all because the *gṛhamedhīya* is an unprecedented (*apūrva*) rite? (These are the eight positions.)

What is established? In this modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), when the two original butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) have already been obtained and are about to be understood, their being heard again would not be for any other purpose; it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). Having become very firm in this view, the Teacher taught: "The mind should not be troubled by the suspicion of another meaning; it is known that this is merely a restatement—let something else be considered.
Why? Because that [restatement] is understood, while nothing else is perceived.

Just as in the world there are those who merely repeat what has been said, saying, "Let those Brahmins who are in this house be brought— Devadatta, Yajñadatta, Viṣṇumitra," so too is this [the *gṛhamedhīyājyabhāga*].
Regarding the *ājyabhāga* of the *gṛhamedhīya*:
alternatively, there may be a threefold designation as in the case of the *āgneya*;
thus, this [term] is used in connection with "for the sake of the sacrifice."
It is said:
No, not from the sentence—the commentary states—(he states the second position: for if indeed...
When a matter has already been established by another sentence, there is nothing further for the explanatory passage (arthavāda) to do;
its capacity would be understood only as that of restating what has already been said,
yet it does have a purpose.
Therefore, this [text] is intended solely for the injunction of another sacrifice;
consequently, it could have no other purpose.
However, if there were something else also to be performed by him...
This is not a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda).
But surely there is no other sacrifice named "ājyabhāga";
since there is such capacity [in the word], how is it that there is no connection with a different meaning?
It exists. It is said:
it will have the characteristics of the *ājyabhāga* offerings.
Nor is there a mention of a single purpose together with both the quality and the capacity by means of this *codaka* (injunctive text),
as in the case of "he offers the two butter-portions with the *apvyamantra*."
It is said:
for the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice is indeed like the archetype (prakṛti); what [is the consequence]?
It will be [regarded as] established.
Therefore, the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are taken up by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
He asks: why is this burden [of interpretation] resorted to?
For if the two *ājyabhāgas* were not directly perceived as being included, the *codaka* alone would be able to take them up.
Since the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) is already included by means of the explicit statement (*pratyakṣa-vacana*), what is the purpose of the prolixity (*gaurava*)?
It is said in reply:
there is no beneficial purpose whatsoever for this prolixity.
But that which is performed out of respect is not as if it were not performed;
yet there is a fault in the act of respect.
Even when such a fault exists, the prompter does not take the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāgau).
Just as one who goes to a village by way of a detour incurs the fault of the detour, yet his arrival does not fail to take place;
therefore, because [the other offerings] are not mentioned, there is the mention of the two *ājyabhāga* portions.
*Ṭup*: In the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, the two *ājyabhāga* portions are obtained directly, whereas the other [offerings] are obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal extension).

But surely the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are also obtained [by extension] through the *codaka*? True; however, their acquisition is immediate through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), whereas that by the *codaka* is delayed.
Therefore, the *codaka* brings about everything else except for the *ājyabhāga* offerings.
And in this way, there will also be no other action [and thus] no "exclusive specification" (parisaṃkhyā) involving the three defects.
No, because it is equal.
The Commentary says: This is not so.

For if the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) were to look toward each individual archetypal (*prākṛta*) constituent element separately, then—having already taken up the two *ājyabhāga* offerings—it would not look toward them again, but would instead take up other elements.
However, it does not look toward the constituent elements individually;
rather, it looks toward the archetypal *apūrva* (the transcendental result), thinking: "Whatever was accomplished by that [archetype], let that be accomplished by this [modified sacrifice]."

When that [the Agnihotra] is being looked for, the state of having *ājyabhāga* offerings is also required. In that case, it follows that "a scriptural injunction becomes purposeless when its purpose has already been fulfilled.
Therefore, because they are equal to other auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), the two *ājyabhāga* offerings of the Agnihotra are not included by the extended application (*codaka*).

Ṭup—If the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) were to depend upon the scriptural injunctions (*śāstra*) or the constituent elements (*padārtha*), then it would not bring about the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāgau*), because [those are] directly perceived [as belonging to the archetype]. But this is not the case. Rather, the modified sacrifice depends upon the *prakāra* (the mode, i.e., the ritual framework established by logic).
And that [mode] is one [and not many]; there is evidence for the dependence on the *prakāra*, but not for the dependence on the scriptural injunctions.
(He states the proximity: It is accomplished by means of the offering to Sūrya.
How? By way of similarity.

(First of all,) the cognition arises regarding the offering to Agni (not regarding the individual constituent items); and by means of the offering to Agni, the modes (inherent within it) are presented, those [being]...
The modification (*vikṛti*) adopts [the details];
and those [varieties] are required, while the scriptures and the constituent elements (*padārtha*) are unrequired and remote.
(By the word "and," it is also implied that they are unsuitable.)
Therefore, the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) brings forward the entire set of constituent parts (*aṅga-jāta*).
It would be so if they were grasped in that manner.
The Commentary says: (He states the seventh position—) Now, if it should be argued that only the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are grasped by the *codaka*.
The Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice is [performed] according to its original nature (prakṛti). How so? Because it says, "He offers the two Ājyabhāga oblations in this manner.

Just as, due to the supplementary statement in the *Adhvarakalpa* and other texts that "there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses," the seventeen-fold number applies to those sacrifices and not to other *iṣṭis*.

Just as when one says, "Bring a śiṃśapā tree; bring its horn," no other tree is brought, but the śiṃśapā alone is understood by the word "tree," so too here it should be seen that the two Ājyabhāga offerings alone are grasped by the extended application (codaka).
This being the case, we reply:
it would be so in the grasping of that [specific] thing.
If there were no grasping [of the archetype], then that grasping would be equivalent.
In the case of the injunction (*codaka*), there would be a non-grasping of other auxiliary elements because they depend upon distinct constituent objects (*padārtha*).
However, this is not tenable if one relies upon the archetypal *apūrva*.

Ṭup—(Although the subsequent portion of the text is printed in the Ānandāśrama edition immediately after the sūtra "na tulyatvāt," nevertheless, since the *Tantraratna* reads the sūtra as "tathā tadgrahaṇe" and explains the subsequent portion accordingly, we shall insert that Ṭup-text at this very point in accordance with the *Tantraratna*.
[In this regard, let there be no such doubt: the requirement for the *ājyabhāga* portions is already established by the general rule of extension (*codaka*), so they need not be enjoined again.]
"But it will serve for the purpose of restriction (upasaṃhāra). [To this] the reply is: "There is no restriction because of the attainment of the whole.
Now, one might object: "Is it not possible for even a general rule to be restricted by a specific one?"
If that is the case, then the injunction is purposeless;

the sense is that since the *ājyabhāga* offerings are established by direct perception, their restriction [to specific vessels] is not appropriate. However, it should demonstrate novelty (*apūrvatā*), because the act of taking [the portions] would otherwise be rendered meaningless.

The Commentary: (He states this position, which constitutes the established conclusion—) In that case, then, the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice is *apūrva* (an original rite not previously established). Why? Because the mention [of the Ājyabhāgas] would otherwise be purposeless.
In this way, the mention "he performs the two Ājyabhāga offerings" will have its purpose fulfilled.

If it were already established by the previous rule (*pūrvavat*), however, [the injunction] would be redundant; for the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, being rendered independent by the two directly perceived *ājyabhāga* offerings, does not require other subsidiary elements through the extended application (*codaka*).

But in that modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) where some new subsidiary element has been mentioned, it takes up the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries only as a last resort, in order to form a single syntactical unit with that [new element].
Why? Because there is an expectancy regarding the manner [of performance], namely, "In what manner should one act? and "What should one do?

And in the archetype (prakṛti), the manner known as "being possessed of subsidiaries" (aṅgavattā) exists; furthermore, it is perceived through the injunctive statement of performance (prayogavacana). However, in the ectype (vikṛti), being possessed of subsidiaries is not already established.

Once it has been conceptualized, it becomes something desired; however, it is not logical for a relationship with what is to be conceptualized to be established based on a scriptural statement (*upaśruti*) regarding that which has already been conceptualized.
Therefore, in that case as well, the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) are grasped by means of the extended application (*codaka*).

Furthermore, lest the injunction of the modified (vaikṛta) subsidiaries be rendered meaningless when the archetypal (prākṛta) ones are already being employed, their status as subsidiaries is postulated, and they are thus included by the performance-injunction (prayoga-vacana) which encompasses all subsidiaries.
[The Ṭupṭīkā states: "One should bring about the result.
By what means? By the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice."
To the question "How? [the answer is: he takes the two *ājyabhāga* offerings [by virtue of the context].
And those two are seen in the archetype (*prakṛti*) as having their assistance already established;
therefore, he takes them.

"Upamitaprāptam" means that its attainment is by way of a comparison (*lakṣaṇā*) based on a similarity; the simple meaning is that the attainment is through the means of comparison (*upamāna-pramāṇaka*). As long as the nature of the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice does not come into being, the Gṛhamedhīya is not connected with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings perceived [in the archetype].
(He states the meaning of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "In which modification...": Whatever accessory (*aṅga*) is new (*apūrva*), that does not have a fixed benefit (*klṛptopakāra*).
Furthermore, because its assistance has not been established, it is unable to satisfy the requirement for the "how" (*kathambhāvākāṅkṣā*).
In that case, some *prakṛti* (archetype) necessarily required [to fulfill it] must be sought; and by that requirement, the [expectation] is satisfied through the *codaka* (extended injunction).
Śā— In that case, since the two Ājyabhāga offerings are obtained from the archetype by means of the *codaka* (extended injunction),
and because there is no other quality [to be enjoined], let it be accepted as a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Furthermore, because it would result in meaninglessness, this [interpretation] is not convincing;
therefore, what is seen here is that both [the agent and the object] are enjoined.

The established conclusion, however, is: "Therefore, it should be exactly as before; for the Gṛhamedhīya rite has no requirement for archetypal subsidiaries, and thus it does not necessitate the application of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer)."
Thus [it is said].

Soma [says]: Even though there is a share of the clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) for the *pratiprasthātṛ*, it is stated that in the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, there is no mention of the other auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) beyond the *ājyabhāgas*; this constitutes the connection as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*).

As for the meaning of the sūtra: since the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) adopts the procedure of the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the repeated scriptural statement (*punaḥśruti*) would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
In the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, however, the phrase "from the *ājyabhāga*s" is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

This is because, whether by virtue of the injunction through the *codaka* (archetypal transfer) or otherwise, even though it serves to establish a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), there is no lack of proximity (*asaṃnidhi*) since [the elements] are present through the application of the *atideśa*.

However, according to the method stated in the section concerning a different context (*prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇaka*), even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) there is no absence of proximity (*asaṃnidhi*).
Therefore, the fifth [view] is that the repetition of the mention of the *ājyabhāga* is for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*).

But is this exclusion an exclusion of the remainder—meaning that in other modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) there is no *ājyabhāga* at all—or is it an exclusion of the remainder consisting of the *prayāja*s and so forth, other than the *ājyabhāga*? It cannot be either way, because both alternatives would result in the occurrence of the three defects (*tridoṣa*).
Nor is it another [type of restrictive injunction], because of the non-existence of other modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) and their non-appearance.

Since there can be no removal of the *codaka* (the rule of extension) due to the impossibility of reciting the *gṛhamedhīya* *ājyabhāga* procedure in other modified sacrifices—which would result in their being satisfied by that alone—it follows that a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) is logically untenable. Furthermore, if it were a restrictive injunction of what is already obtained, then since that which is established by scripture cannot be set aside by anything else, it would lead to the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*), as in the case of the statement, "One does not perform those two at the animal sacrifice."

Furthermore, even if the assistance [of the subsidiaries] were already established, it would be impossible for the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice to achieve self-sufficiency (*nairākāṅkṣya*) through the mere *ājyabhāga* offerings; consequently, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), which effectively takes the form of a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) by way of indicating its *apūrva* (novelty) through the annulment of the extended injunction (*codaka*), would also be untenable.
For it is not the case that, according to the principle of the *ājyabhāga* in the *gṛhamedhīya*, there is any heaviness (*gaurava*) [of assumption] based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Because of this, [it is stated in] Soma 9.4.13: "The [sacrificial portion] for Tvaṣṭṛ accompanied by the Patnīvats.
By means of the restatement of the preceding rite in the injunction, "He offers the Patnīvata [portion] after it has been moved around," only an accessory (guṇa) is being enjoined.

Nor is there an absence of an injunction (*vidheya*), because the very substratum (*adhikaraṇa*)—which is the meaning of the suffix *pratyaya*—is the object of the injunction; and since that [substratum] is the original (*prākṛta*) one itself, it is the object of the injunction by virtue of its prior application through extension (*atideśa*), according to the logic of the "house" (*gṛha-nyāya*).

(Bhāṭṭa 2.3.8). In the case of the texts, "One should sacrifice the *tvāṣṭra-pātnīvata* animal," and "They release the *pātnīvata* after it has been cooked around (*paryagnikṛta*)," let there be either an injunction for the mere act of cooking around (*paryagnikaraṇa*) alone, or an injunction for the entire collection of its subsidiary parts, which—by means of making known its novelty (*apūrvatā*) according to the logic of the "house"—has as its result the exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of other subsidiary elements.

Kī. 2|3|8|9, p. 56: Nor does it follow that, because the benefit has already been established [by the archetype], the repetition [of the injunction] results—according to the principle of the *gṛha* (house) [inclusion]—in an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of internal elements; for here too, since the status of being a *puñjīya* (to be reached) is obtained through the extension (*atideśa*), it is impossible for it to sublate that very extension. Furthermore, in cases such as the *dvirātra* sacrifice, there exists the presence of indicative marks (*liṅga*) for the injunction of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) as obtained through extension.
The maxim of cow’s milk (*gokṣīranyāya*): 1612 Just as cow’s milk is [pure], so too even instruction given by a wicked person must certainly be abandoned.
Summary: Oṃ, the analogy of cow’s milk.
Just as even a cow’s milk remains in its raw state until it is boiled, so it is in this case.

"Because even for a dharma such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), if it were possible [to perform] by its own nature according to the analogy of cow's milk, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it being an adharma. (Vi.
1314, Varṇaka 2).
There is a sublation (*bādha*) of the mere number twelve hundred of cows—which are occasional (*naimittika*) and so forth—by the gift of a cow.

Even in a case where the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) is absolutely non-existent because the master (*svāmin*) is not distinct from the lineage (*gotra*), it should be understood that this [status] is used figuratively (*upacarita*), since the possibility of providing assistance (*upakārakatva*) exists there as well.
Vārttika 3.4.12, p. 905.
Oṃ, regarding Gotravayantī: "In whom indeed does the confusion between a *go* (cow) and a *gavaya* not arise? It is known correctly through milking: 'This is a cow; it is not a *gavaya*.'"
Thus [ends] the *Sāhasrī*, verse 652.
The lineage (*gotra*).

In the case of the *audumbara* Soma-cup, which serves as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the *ṛtapeya* (Soma sacrifice)— as indicated by the injunction "it is to be given to the beloved Brahmin of the same lineage"—
even its status as a substratum (*āśraya*) for the cup is found to be restricted to its own specific purpose and cannot be extended elsewhere.
The principle of the previous section applies there even in the case of that which is without cause.
This being the position reached, it is said in reply:
"But the occasional (naimittika) applies to the archetype (prakṛti), subverting the permanent (nitya). Three reasons for this have been explained previously and are thus accepted."
Its connection is distinguished by being unobstructed due to the absence of [prior] conjunction;
this is because there is the inclusion of a performance qualified by an agent once again.
And because it is directly for the sake of the human goal, whereas [the other] goes toward its substratum elsewhere;
thus, its superiority being established, its application remains fixed in the archetype (prakṛti).

"But it is not correct to say that there is a contradiction between the state of having the same object and the states of being for the sake of the agent and for the sake of the person; for there is no contradiction between those two, as they have different domains."
And for this reason, because it serves a human purpose, the act of carrying [the Soma] separately does not apply;
for the prior sacrificial rite is accomplished by means of the cup alone.
Just as that [act] does not accomplish its own purpose because it belongs to another,
so too the sacrifice performed for the sake of another is not a means for accomplishing his [the patron's] purpose.
Nor can it have both meanings simultaneously, because that would entail the fallacy of sentence-splitting (vākyabheda).
In the case of the injunction regarding the fetching [of water], there is indeed no syntactical unity with respect to the result;
for the means of fetching is indeed different. Therefore, the *godohana* vessel does not constitute a separate topic (*adhikaraṇa*).

[the locative case] is obligatory in a single word (*kapade*), obligatory in the formation of verbal roots (*dhātusargeyoḥ*), and obligatory in a compound (*samāse*); however, in a sentence (*vākye*), it depends upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
In this context, the separate mention of *samāhāra* (compound) follows the logic of the *Gobhilīya*; for its inclusion is already established by the very term "in a single word" (*ekapade*).
*Śabdakaustubha*: "aiuṇ.

*Oṃ*, Devadatta possesses cows.
"Without a qualifying word, the arising of a specific cognition is not desired."
Furthermore, in this context, "cows" are the qualifier; there is no connection whatsoever [between the word and the cows].
For Devadatta is intended to be delimited by the cows, and these [cows] are indeed already expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
As for the claim that "that which is not connected is not delimited," it is true that it is not delimited;
however, by that very fact, the cognition of a connection (the apprehension of the relation) with those [cows] is obtained through implication (*arthāt*).

In any case, once it has been expressed by the word *gomat* that "the object is qualified by cows," as to how those indefinite cows qualify that [object], this is the function of the cows themselves and not of the word.
For it is said: "Cows do not denote a specific object as something situated on the earth;
in that case, how could it be claimed that the earth is also denoted?
Indeed, that without which an object cannot attain its own existence need not necessarily be denoted; rather, only that without which a qualified cognition is not produced [need be denoted]."
By means of these [words] such as "cow" and "milk," neither the cognition of that [owner] is produced, nor even the connection [between them].
Furthermore: "The consideration of the relationship consists merely in the activity of the speaker;
for he does not intend to speak of one possessing cows [as being] unconnected with cows."
"...Furthermore, since the properties of things (*vastudharma*) do not intend to convey what is unrelated [to them], that is their own operation, not that of the word. Therefore,
whatever they are able to qualify as it actually exists, they qualify it as existing in that very state."

And that [word] attains the state of being a qualifier in relation to its connection; thus, for this purpose, it is connected [as follows]: "Endowed with the state of being a qualifier and joined with its own qualifiers, the word *gomat* will denote [the object] as 'this is distinguished by a cow' (*goviśiṣṭaḥ*)."
Therefore, for this reason as well, the relationship is inexpressible. Vārttika 3.1.6.12, pp. 675–76. 卐 The maxim of cow-dung and milk-porridge (gomayapāyasanyāya).
The inference that "cow dung is milk-porridge because it is a product of a cow, like curd" is sublated by perception;
it is just like that.
Summary:

卐 The maxim of the scorpion from cow dung (gomayavṛścikanyāyaḥ): It is observed that scorpions and other such creatures, which possess consciousness, arise from cows and other things well-known to be insentient; therefore, an absolute similarity between the material cause (upādāna) and its effect (upādeya) is not required.
Consequently, [there is no contradiction] regarding the world and Brahman being sentient—
Even though there is a difference in terms of being conscious (*cetanatva*), the relationship of material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) would still exist.
This has been explained in detail in Śaṅkara’s *Bhāṣya* on [Sūtra] 2.1.16.

Gomahi | The state of being secondary (gauṇatva) | And [the rule] regarding the secondary and the primary (gauṇamukhyayośca).
The section concerning the secondary and primary [meanings].
There is a secondary function [of words] which is employed.
And this does not entail the consequence [of the term] being primary in its literal sense, because [the meaning] is superimposed.
However, where that very same meaning is not superimposed, there it is primary; thus there is no fault. So it stands in that case.

Page 367, line 1412123. Regarding *gauṇatva* (secondary usage): the three [definitions]—namely, functioning by abandoning a well-known meaning to function through an unknown quality (*tadguṇa*) of that object; functioning as a part of a word denoting a whole (*samudāya*); and functioning with a superimposed meaning—are not appropriate. Rather, the definition of secondary usage (*gauṇavṛtti*) is functioning based on the cause of connection with a quality (*guṇayoga*). Su. pp. 492–93. *Gauṇatva* is a defect of the sentence (*vākyadoṣa*).

Some [hold that] the secondary nature (*gauṇatva*) of the sentence-meaning is perceived with respect to a single word by virtue of its being a subordinate part (*guṇa*) of the sentence; thus, some say there is "secondary status" (*gauṇatā*). [Sphuṭākṣarā, p. 1081: Secondary nature is the state of being perceived through connection with the qualities (*guṇa*) of the expressed meaning. [p. 1082: The secondary nature of that which is understood through the sense is caused by the arrival at those qualities (*guṇāgamana-hetuka*).
"Since the qualities of another do not exist elsewhere, [the designation] necessarily arises from those qualities; such is the definition of figurative usage (*gauṇatva*).
Vākyapadīya 3.2.1, p. 746. When that [designation] refers to a whole (*samudāya*), the figurative nature of the part (*avayava*) is established.

Some maintain that from the word *guṇa* (secondary/quality), there is understood the state of being both a part and a whole of two words, which constitutes "secondary application" (*gauṇatā*). (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1081). The fault of secondary application (*gauṇatva-doṣa*) occurs when one assumes a greater number of items than are actually present. For example, in the injunctions "He lays down the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks" and "He lays down the *prāṇabhṛt*-bricks," the term *sṛṣṭi* refers only to those mantras containing the word *sṛṣṭi*. Thus, while the fewer [mantras] are primary, if one were to include even more mantras—such as those containing the word *sudhīpa*—by means of secondary application (*gauṇyā*), it would result in the fault of secondary application due to the assumption of a greater number.
And that [secondary application] is accepted out of necessity.
Bāla. pṛ. 3. When one resorts to the primary for the sake of a secondary derivative meaning, then it follows that "the application belongs to the primary alone.
Bhāṣya 3.2.1, p. 751. And there is a comprehension of the function for both the secondary and the primary.
(Paribhāṣā 15) | That which is based on a quality (*guṇa*) is secondary (*gauṇa*). For example, the word *go* [applied] to a *vāhīka* because of qualities such as dullness (*jāḍya*).
Even the name and so forth of that which is not well-known is understood only through the superimposition of its qualities.
Because it is the primary [cause], it is like the root; "primary" (mukhya) means "first. When a word is employed in a secondary sense, it functions by superimposing the primary meaning upon it.
And thus, since being figurative (*gauṇa*) or indicative (*lākṣaṇika*) is not established here as being figurative, the substitution of *traya* occurs in forms such as *priyayavanām* and so on;
for although the meaning of the word *tri* functions as an adjective to another [word] there, it lacks the aforementioned quality of being figurative.

Furthermore, this rule does not apply to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself; rather, it applies only to the operation of a word (*padakārya*) where a specific form (*viśiṣṭarūpa*) is employed that brings about a particular meaning.
For instance, in forms such as *śāśvariḥ*—meaning "one who resembles a father-in-law"—the phrase "employed" (*upātta*) and so forth is stated in order to establish the substitution of *iṇ* for *at*.

In the case of "The two boys are Agni and Soma," even though the word *īṣoma* refers to those resembling the well-known pair of deities, the suffixes *aitasvat* and *tva* still occur because they are internal (*antaraṅga*).

It is stated that [the rule] does not apply when there is a *dvandva* compound of two words whose meanings are both primary (*mukhya*) and secondary/indicative (*lākṣaṇika*), or when the meaning is "one who has those names," because in the first case there is a secondary/indicative nature (*gauṇa-lākṣaṇikatva*), and in the other case there is a lack of established usage (*aprasiddhatva*).

For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *agneḥ stotramomāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.14), which serves to exclude the stronger [application] by means of the maxim of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇa-mukhya-nyāya*) regarding the sentence "The two boys are Agni and Soma," becomes consistent. Furthermore, in the *Bhāṣya* on [Pāṇini] 6.5.9.35, it is stated: "In the case of the primary and the secondary, the operation is understood to apply to the primary."
