| The section concerning the secondary and primary [meanings].
The principle of the *barhis* grass.

In the section on the secondary and primary [meanings] (Bhāṣya 3.2.1.1–2), for the purpose of establishing the investigation into the application of mantras to both secondary and primary subjects, the nature of secondary function (*gauṇavṛtti*) and that which is not denoted by it will be set forth.
However, here the definition of function based on the connection with qualities (*guṇayoganimittavṛttitva*) is established; thus, the distinction from that [previous section] should be understood.

In the *Gauṇamukhyādhikaraṇa* (Sūtra 3.2.1–4), it is established that among mantras to be applied by means of indicative power (*liṅga*), the primary function is the denotation of the primary [meaning]. (Sūtra 3.2.1–4, p. 73). This is because, in the *Gauṇamukhyādhikaraṇa*, the secondary mode of operation (*gauṇī vṛtti*)—which is characterized by indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the connection with qualities (*guṇa*) perceived in what is being denoted—is determined to be subordinate to the objective to be accomplished.

The distinction between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*) is established for the sake of determining the specific meaning for the listeners. Vākyapadīya 1.4.23, p. 358. Regarding the application of the scriptural text (*śruti*) common to both the secondary and the primary, the investigation into the delimiters of the subordinate (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*) is to be seen in the *Bhāṣya* on the section "teṣām athādhikaraṇam" (3.1.4).
Ke.: The secondary (*gauṇī*) is another method.

Some maintain that because the power (*śakti*) for the primary form [of the word] is impossible, there is instead a figurative (*gauṇī*) presentation. However, in that case, since the cognition (*citti*) serves as the cause for presentation, it is untenable for the presentation itself to be the cause. On the other hand, when Devadatta is understood as possessing an action similar in nature to the meaning "one who is struck by a lion," then it will be called figurative.

*Maṇi*, p. 75: The secondary function (*gauṇī*) is sublated by the indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*), because the indicative function requires only a relationship with the primary meaning (*śakyasaṃbandha*), whereas the secondary function requires an additional requirement of similarity (*sādṛśya*) to that relationship. *Bālabodhinī*, p. 141: The secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*).
Now, what is this so-called "secondary" [function]? The secondary function is a relationship with the primary meaning based on similarity (*sādṛśyarūpa-śakyasaṃbandha*).
Therefore, the Naiyāyikas maintain that [the secondary meaning] is included within the definition [of denotation].
Some define "secondary" (*gauṇa*) as a function based on the connection with qualities that are themselves being characterized (i.e., indicated).

Regarding the example "Devadatta is a lion," they say that there is here another function, distinct from the primary one, which is caused by the connection with qualities such as ferocity that are indicated by the word "lion."

Secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*): In passages such as "The secondary function [involves] indication based on possessive meaning" (*gauṇyā matvarthalakṣaṇa*), the word *yajamāna* (sacrificer) is used in a secondary sense with respect to the *prastara* (grass-bundle), due to its connection with the quality of having the form of the sacrifice.
Therefore, the secondary function is distinct from indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And they will establish the signs for that, such as *tasiddha* and so forth; this is the general direction. (*Maṇi*, pp. 76–78). The secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*).

Since [the arguments] such as "functioning through metaphorical application" (*upapādīnavṛttitva*)—which are characteristics of figurative usage (*gauṇavṛtti*)—would result in the invalidation of the authority of the Vedas, they are not refuted here; rather, they will be refuted in the section concerning the primary and secondary meanings (*gauṇamukhyādhikaraṇa*). (Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 503). Regarding "figurative usage" (*gauṇī vṛtti*): it should be explained as follows: that which functions based on a connection with qualities (*guṇayoga*) is "figurative" (*gauṇa*). That is to say, it is "figurative" because its application (*pravṛtti*) is caused by a connection (*yoga*), which is the purpose or motive (*prayojana*) for its application, consisting in the presence of many qualities of the primary referent in another object.

Page 503. Secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*): that which abandons its own primary meaning (*jahatsvārthā*). Vārttika 3.2.1. Page 790. Secondary function: “But secondary status is desired when there is a connection with a quality being indicated (*lakṣyamāṇaguṇayoga*)”; 1.4.12.23. Page 354. Secondary function: well-known among words.

In that regard, there are six [grounds] for the figurative application (guṇacchitti) [of a word]. As it has been said: "The figurative function (gauṇī vṛtti) of words is everywhere established through these six: accomplishment (tatsiddhi), genus (jāti), similarity (sārūpya), praise (praśaṃsā), mark (liṅga), and delusion (bhrami)."
Thus [it is said].
Its establishment is seen in such passages as "The sacrificer is the prastara," where *prastara* refers to a specific handful of *darbha* grass.
The accomplishment of that ritual action is *tatsiddhi*.

The *prastara* (grass-bundle) also accomplishes the ritual action through the pouring of the oblation (*juhū*), while the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is well known as the accomplisher of the ritual action.
Thus, the accomplishment of that [action] is a common quality shared by both the *prastara* and the sacrificer.
Therefore, the use of the word *yajamāna* (sacrificer) for the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is figurative (*gauṇa*).
Regarding *jāti*, which means birth: in passages such as "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed of Agni," [it is explained that] Agni was born from Prajāpati, and the Brāhmaṇa likewise.
Thus, the birth from a single source is a common quality between fire and the Brāhmaṇa;
by virtue of that, the term *āgneya* (related to fire) is used in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the Brāhmaṇa.
Similarity (*sārūpya*) is seen in such cases as "The sacrificial post is the sun" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*).
The form of these two is the same; they are "similar in form" (*sarūpa*). Their state of being so is "similarity of form" (*sārūpya*).
The sun is radiant, and the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is also radiant because it has been smeared with clarified butter and turmeric.
Thus, by virtue of this similarity through radiance, the word "sun" is employed in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the sacrificial post.
Regarding the praise: "Other animals are indeed non-animals (*apaśavaḥ*), while cows and horses are [true] animals.

By the rule *sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.122), there is the preservation of the original stem form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Having called other animals "non-animals" and thus censured them, one then praises cows and horses by declaring them to be "animals."

And thus, animals are praised; cattle and horses are also praised. Therefore, the quality of being "praiseworthy" (praśastatva) is common to both animals in general and to cattle and horses specifically. Consequently, in this context, praise is the reason for the figurative usage (*gauṇaprayoga*), as in the passage:
"He places the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks."
*Bhūmā* means abundance or multiplicity as a quality.
There are seventeen mantras for the creation and dissolution [of the phonemes].
Among them, in the four mantras—the first, the fourteenth, the sixteenth, and the last—there is the emergence of creation; in the remaining thirteen, the verbal root *sṛj* (to create) occurs.
And by the rule *sṛṣṭibandena*, bricks located on the foundation (*āśraya*) are stated to be of the nature of mantras composed of the verbal root *sṛj* (to create):
"The mantra used for placing [the bricks] is considered to apply to both the bricks and the mortar" (Pāṇini 4.1.126).

The meaning of Pāṇini’s sūtra is as follows: after a word ending in the suffix *matup* that is syntactically related as a nominative, the suffix *yat* may be applied in the sense of the genitive case "of these," provided that this first-related term is a mantra used as a means of placing [bricks], and provided that "of these" (*āsām*) refers to a sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), and those [referred to] are bricks (*iṣṭakā*).
Furthermore, there shall be elision (*luk*) of the suffix *matup*.
This is the meaning of the sūtra.
And likewise, there is the elision (*lūk*) of the possessive suffix *matup* following the word *sṛṣṭi*, as well as the Vedic elision of the *yat* suffix.
Although not all the mantras here contain the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*), nevertheless, there is an abundance of those containing the verbal root *sṛj*.
Consequently, all seventeen mantras come to be designated by the term "creation," because of the plurality of those joined with the root *sṛj*.
And thus, multiplicity itself is the determining factor here, even in the case of the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) occurring in mantras that do not describe creation;
this is the indicative mark (*liṅga*), as seen in such passages as "he lays down the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks," where the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks are laid down with exactly that many mantras.
In this context, those bricks for which the *cinmantras* contain the word "prāṇa" (breath) are called *prāṇabhṛts*; these constitute the second and third decades.
The other forty-seven mantras are not like that.
Nevertheless, the fifty bricks to be laid down by means of those mantras are designated by the term *prāṇabhṛt*.
There is no plurality here of mantras containing the word "prāṇa";
nevertheless, that characteristic mark indeed exists within them.
Thus, all these mantras, which are the substrates for that [characteristic], are called "Prāṇabhṛts" (the Life-sustainers).
And thus, in this context, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone is the quality (*guṇa*).
Regarding the use of the term "breath-bearer" (*prāṇabhṛt*) for the fifty [deities],
all six qualities that serve as the basis for figurative application (*gauṇavṛtti*) have been mentioned here.

Secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*): that which is characterized by being based on the connection with qualities (*guṇa*) indicated by its own primary denotation will be established in the section concerning the secondary and primary [meanings] (1.2.1). Su. p. 492. The secondary [function] is sublated by direct statement (*śruti*, i.e., primary denotation).

*Bāla.*, p. 141: By the secondary function (*gauṇī*), the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) is set aside. *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, p. 145: Regarding the passage "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice with the *dyeta*," there arises an inquiry as to whether the word *dyeta* indicates a sacrifice possessing the *dyeta* through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), or whether the word *dyeta* itself denotes the sacrifice by being applied to it through a quality consisting of the form of the *nipa* bird. In this investigation, by the secondary function (*gauṇī*)—the possessive... [text fragment ends].
The sublation of the secondary sense (gauṇī) by the primary indicative sense (lakṣaṇā)—that is, the sublation of the excessive "cow-ness" (gaurātiśayya)—is accepted.
Thus, the meaning of the sentence is: "One should effect the destruction of the enemy by means of the sacrifice initiated by [the word] 'dyū'."
"Who indeed could contradict that meaning which the Veda supports, whether by means of secondary sense (gauna), indication (lakṣaṇā), or even by the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa)?"
(As stated in the Vārttika on page 223: “Whether it be figurative (*gauṇa*) or indicative (*lākṣaṇika*), or again by means of a syntactical split [of the sentence]”).

If there were support from the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the *Rājasūya* injunction, then—by the consensus of the Āryas—the meaning of the word *rājan* occurring in that sentence would have to be taken as "protector" alone, disregarding the heaviness of the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) according to the method of the sentence and the resulting necessity of resorting to a figurative sense (*gauṇavṛtti*), in accordance with the maxim: “By way of figurative or indicative function... (*gauṇyā lakṣaṇayā*).

*Parimala* (on *Brahmasūtra* 3.2.1.28): By stating that "for figurative [expressions], the basis for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) consists in the connection with a quality being indicated," it is suggested that even a word that does not directly denote a quality expresses its own primary meaning first, and then expresses the quality through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

(*Sūtrabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, p. 498). Among the various types of figurative functions (*gauṇī-vṛtti*), that which is based on the presence of both the quality (*bhūma*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) sublates other figurative functions. This is because, as in the case of the previous [type] involving metaphorical indication of possessive sense (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*), the primary meaning is still connected to the sentence-meaning; whereas in the latter [type], that [connection] is absent.

Likewise, even in the case of a conflict between *bhūmi* (the ground of application) and *liṅga* (indicative mark), the latter is sublated by the former; for in the former case, many possible syntactic meanings can be integrated, whereas in the latter case, that is not possible. Bāla. p. 142. Regarding all secondary functions (*gauṇavṛtti*), or rather, the definition and cause of those secondary functions which are distinct from *lakṣaṇā* (indication), it is stated in the *Tasiddhipeṭikā*. Vā. 1.4.12.23, p. 354. As for the "cause of secondary function," Akṣapāda and others have mentioned various other factors besides [those such as] genus (*jāti*) and so forth, namely: association (*sahacaraṇa*), location (*sthāna*), and so on. Vā. 1.4.12.23, p. 354.

This is according to the sūtra: "The application of a word to something other than its primary meaning occurs due to association, location, purpose, activity, measure, support, proximity, connection, instrumentality, and sovereignty—as in the cases of 'Brāhmaṇas,' 'platforms,' 'mat,' 'king,' 'barley meal,' 'sandalwood,' 'Ganges,' 'cloth,' 'food,' and 'person'" (Pāṇini 2.1.60). (1) For example, through association (*sahacaraṇa*), the word *yajñiya* ("fit for sacrifice") is applied to Brāhmaṇas; [the term "usage" (*prayoga*) is to be supplied in every instance].

(2) "The beds cry out"—here the word *mañca* ("bed") refers to the persons [on the beds] by virtue of their location (*sthāna*). (3) "He cuts the mat"—here the word *kaṭa* ("mat") refers to the straw and so forth used for its purpose (*tādarthya*). (4) "This king is Yama"—here the word *yama* refers to the king by virtue of his conduct (*ācāra*). (5) "An *āḍhaka* is here"—here the word *āḍhaka* refers to the barley meal (*saktu*) by virtue of measure (*māna*, i.e., *parimāṇa*). (6) "He anoints with an equal amount"—here the word *tulā* refers to the sandalwood by virtue of weight (*dhāraṇa*). (7) "A hamlet on the Ganges."

Thus, they say: (8) the use of the word *gaṅgā* for the bank is due to proximity (*sāmīpyāt*); (9) the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word *nīla* with respect to the cloth is due to connection (*yogāt*, i.e., relation), as in "the blue cloth" (*nīlaḥ śāṭakaḥ*); (10) the coreferentiality of the word *anna* with respect to strength is due to being the means (*sādhanāt*, i.e., the state of being a means), as in "food is strength" (*annam balam*); and the use of the word *puruṣa* in coreferentiality with respect to the family is due to lordship (*ādhipatyāt*), as in "this man is the family" (*ayaṃ puruṣaḥ kulam*).
They raise this objection: since other grounds for figurative usage (*gauṇavṛtti*) have also been mentioned, even this group of six does not encompass all figurative usage.

Su. Pṛ. 494. Regarding the distinction between the causes of secondary application (*gauṇavṛtti*) and the state of functioning without abandoning one's own primary meaning, these have been explained in the *Tasiddhi* (Vākyapadīya 3.2.1, p. 486). Vā. 3.2.1, p. 486. [Regarding] the definition of secondary application:

since the definition of secondary application as "functioning based on the connection with qualities that are being indicated" is untenable, it must be accepted that the definition of secondary application is "functioning through those qualities" (*tadguṇavṛttitva*) by virtue of occurring within well-known sentences.

For if the word *siṃha* (lion) were to denote its own primary meaning, it would be capable of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Devadatta; since the conceptualization [of the word] is caused by the presence of those qualities [in Devadatta], that [quality] exists in Devadatta as well. Thus, coreferentiality can be established just as in the case of "Devadatta is a bull" (*gauraḥ*). (Sūtra-pṛ. 498). Regarding the definition of figurative function (*gauṇavṛtti*), it is the occurrence of a word denoting a whole in one part of it. However, that is not possible here because it would result in the contingency of the word's meaning being non-eternal, due to its dependence on a specific referent distinct from the whole. Furthermore, it cannot be the case that this leads to a lack of authoritativeness (*aprāmāṇya*).
Su. Pṛ. 499: An extensive discussion regarding figurative application (gauṇavṛtti) is made in the Vārttika on the *Tatsiddhi* [sūtra]. Ke.:
The *Dharmaśāstra-sūtra* of Gautama and Gobhila is adopted exclusively by the Chāndogas. Vā. 1.3.15, p. 244: *Gaurava* is a subordinate genus inherent in the specific qualities of humans.
Su. pṛ. 1410: Complexity (*gaurava*).

The definition of complexity is [the presence of] multiple alternatives (*vikalpa*) due to the consequence of assuming multiple words for a single meaning or the assumption of multiple meanings for a single word.
Alternatively, complexity is the state of having multiple alternatives due to the consequence of the necessity of postulating many distinct conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*).

p. 852: In the injunction of another sacrifice, there is complexity (*gaurava*) because it would involve enjoining multiple unestablished specific details. p. 860: There is no beneficial purpose whatsoever in complexity; however, what has been accomplished by means of complexity is not rendered undone.
However, there is a fault regarding the honorific (*gaurava*).
For example, when someone goes to a village by way of a detour, they incur the fault of taking a detour, yet it does not mean that the act of going to the village does not take place.
Bhāṣya 10.7.130. On account of an excess of respect, people address this Devadatta in an assembly of kings and others using terms such as "Ācārya" or "Upādhyāya."

Regarding the first type [of roots]: for instance, although *magh* (to give) and others have meanings distinct from [the general sense of] "becoming the master of the world," they are considered transitive (*sakarmaka*) because, by virtue of the property consisting in their expressing an activity residing solely in Caitra, they require an object (*karma-sākāṅkṣatva*).

Because it expresses an activity that has ceased (*puṣyaniṣṭa-vyāpāra*), it does not require an object (*karmanākāṅkṣatva*); therefore, it is intransitive (*akarmaka*). *Rahasya*, p. 51. The *ṣoḍaśī-graha* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

*Bhāṣya* 10.5.9.34–41. The *ṣoḍaśī-graha* is to be postponed (*utkarṣa*) in the *jyotiṣṭoma* along with the *stotra*; this postponement is for the sake of conforming to the primary time (*mukhya-kāla*), which consists in its occurring after the *ukthya*.

VI. 5.1.18. The cups (*graha*) [are]: *Aṃśu*, *Adābhya*, *Antyāgra*, *Ājyapa*, *Āditya*, *Āśvina*, *Upāṃśu*, *Aindra*, *Aindravāyava*, *Dadhigraha*, *Dhruva*, *Manthin*, three *Marutvatīya*s, *Maitrāvaruṇa*, and *Śukra*—these in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
The *Arka* [cup] is at the *Viṣuvat*. The *Bārhaspatya* [cup] is at the *Bṛhaspatisava*.
The *mahimānaḥ* [cups] are in the Aśvamedha;
the *surāgrahas* and *somagrahas* are in the Vājapeya. Thus it is said.
Regarding the cups (grahas) in the section on ritual procedure: the first is the Upāṃśu;
the second is the Antaryāma;
the third is the Aindravāyava; and the fourth is the Maitrāvaruṇa.

(vi. 10.5.15), the *śukra*, the *manthin*, the *āgrayaṇa*, the *ukthya*, the *dhruva*, and the *āśvina* as the tenth—these ten cups (*graha*) are the remnants of the seasons. (vi. 5.1.16). In the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice, the cups for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra are prescribed.
Bhāṣya 3.5.14: Even when the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) of the *graha* is being enjoined, it is accepted that there is an intention to refer to it as the deity of the *daśāpavitra* as well.

Vārttika 3.5.17, p. 718: "Having either taken up the *graha* or having lifted the *camasa*, he begins the *stotra*"; thus, the *stotra* follows the taking of the *graha*. Vi. 10.5.12: The statement "having either taken up the *graha*" is for the purpose of enjoining merely an optional time for the preparation of the *stotra*, which arises from the word *stotra*.
Saṃkarṣa 3.1.16: "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*).

Here, *graha* is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and singularity is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*). What follows from this being so? This follows: for the case-ending expresses its own meaning, which resides in the meaning of the nominal stem, by direct denotation (*śruti*) itself.

This being the case, what follows? The cleansing would not be connected [with the cups]. For that which is connected by direct statement (śruti) is connected by the sentence (vākya); and that which is connected by another [direct statement] cannot be severed from that connection by the sentence to be connected with something else.
However, the wiping (*saṃmārga*) is connected with singularity; if it were not performed as qualified by singularity, nothing would be altered.
(3.1.17, p. 723) "He wipes the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*).
For this is not an injunction of the substance's singularity.
To what, then, does it apply? It is the injunction for the connection between the substance and the cleansing.
In this way, through direct statement (*śruti*), there is an injunction of two word-meanings; otherwise, another word-meaning would be enjoined by syntactical connection (*vākya*).
And syntactical connection operates only when a direct statement is possible, not when a direct statement is already present.
3|1|17, p. 724: "He cleanses the cup. The cleansing is a subordinate element (*guṇa*) with respect to the cup;
the cup is the primary element (*pradhāna*) and the object of reference (*uddeśya*). Vi. 3|1|17:

"If the Soma sacrifice has the *Rathantara* as its *sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu; if it has the *Bṛhat* as its *sāman*, [those] for Śukra; if it has the *Jagat* as its *sāman*, [those] for Āgrayaṇa."
That [day] in which the *sāman* produced on the *jagatī* meter occurs is the *jagatsāman*;
that is the *viṣuvant*.

Bhāṣya 10.5.18. There is a combination of the *indravāyu* and other cups, as prescribed by the two cups taught in the *Aśvamedha*—namely, the golden and silver ones—as well as those extended by analogy.

however, the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the *iṣṭi*, and so forth are merely auxiliary (*aṅga*).
Ke.: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the first performance of the *graha* vessels—such as those for Indra-Vāyu, Mitra-Varuṇa, and others—is [the primary act].
The same applies to the *kāmayoga* (the connection with a desired result). Bhāṣya 10.5.18.62–66: The mental cup (*mānasa-graha*) is a subsidiary part of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
