And [the rule] prior to the Aindravāyava cup.

(10.5.10–72). In a modification such as the Bṛhaspatisava, there is a combination of the cups that are directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*), such as the Aindravāyava and others, with those cups that are indicated by general injunction (*ādideśika*).
This combination is to be seen in the *Samuccayacintā*.
10|4|12|3-. When there is a change in the deities of the cups (*graha*), there should be no modification (*avikāra*) of the *stotra* and *śastra*, because they are ritual acts (*karman*).
Regarding the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) called *agniṣṭut*, it is heard in scripture: "The cups belong to Agni.

In that case, even though there is a change in the deities of the cups—meaning they have deities other than those of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—there is no modification (*ūha*) of the *stotra* and *śastra* because they are ritual acts, that is, because they are primary acts (*pradhāna-karman*); this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Alternatively, he states the purpose of the section on *stotra* and *śastra* (sūtras 2.1.13–), namely: "But [the *stotra* and *śastra*] are purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*). If the *stotra* and *śastra* are purificatory acts, the result is modification (*ūha*) according to the respective deity; however, if the final conclusion is that they are principal acts (*pradhānakarma*), the result is the absence of modification (*avikāra*).
The literal meaning has already been stated.
Regarding the acceptance of the cups for the dual-deity offerings (*dvidevatya*), the *hotṛ* mantras are those with which the *adhvaryu* hands them over.

For the cups other than the *dhruva*, after placing a layer of clay beneath them, one should pour [the liquid] upon that clay for the sake of those [deities] whose [offerings] are for the *maghā* [constellation],
and for the purpose of the *maghā* [sacrifice].
Regarding the placement [of the vessels]: however, the placement of the *dhruva* vessel occurs after the *anupopta* [rite].

Vi. 3.6.1. For those cups (*graha*) for which the scriptural injunction is taught as being directly connected, serving as the applicatory rule (*viniyojaka*) for their status as subsidiaries to the sacrifice, there is no repetition at each pressing (*savana*); rather, their performance takes place only once. Bhāṭṭa. 5.3.6. That the cups occurring in other pressings possess the same ritual procedure (*samānavidhitva*) as those belonging to the morning pressing will be explained in the sixth-pāda topic (3.6.9–30).
Su. p. 1167: The arrangement of the planets (such as the Sun, the Moon, and others) in terms of their favorable or unfavorable positions is the subject matter of Jyotiḥśāstra.

p. 120: Optional rites involving the planets are [stated as follows]: "One who desires that his progeny may be well-ordered according to seniority should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu; one desiring firm standing should draw the cups beginning with the Śukra cup; one seeking cattle should draw the cups beginning with the Manthin cup" (Vi. 10.5.18).
Even when there is a displacement of the placing (*sādana*) in the sequence of the cups (*graha*), there is no displacement of the offering (*pradāna*).
And the offering is like the placing.

Commentary: This is recorded in the tradition: "One suffering from indigestion should take the cups beginning with the Āśvina; one practicing sorcery [should take] those beginning with the Śukra; one being practiced against [should take] those beginning with the Manthin."
In that regard, it has been stated that when the drawing (*grahaṇa*) is postponed, the placing (*sādana*) is also postponed.
Now, this is being deliberated: when the cup (*graha*) is postponed, is the offering (*pradāna*) also postponed, or not? What is the prima facie view? That it is postponed.
Why? Because it is existent. For both the taking up and the giving away are existent; indeed, that which is given away is what is taken up.
For it speaks thus regarding a visible purpose;
otherwise, that which occurs after the placing [of the vessel] would be for an invisible purpose,
yet this is not for an invisible purpose.
Therefore, at whichever time the offering is performed, the taking up [of the vessel] must be done then;
for if this is so, then because of the connection that wherever there is taking up, there the offering may also take place, it is like the act of placing [the vessel].
Just as when the drawing [of the cup] is postponed, the placing [of it] is postponed, so too is the offering.
Or rather, it is not so; because the offering is the primary act and the placing is subordinate, the placing is not postponed in that manner.
Commentary: This is not the case—that the offering is postponed.
For that is the primary element;
it does not serve as an auxiliary to the grasping.
Therefore, it is not drawn back [to a later point].
As for what was said regarding "like the placing [of the Soma]," the placing is indeed the remainder;
therefore, it is drawn forward. It is stated that, just as with the placing of the Soma, there is also a drawing forward of the offering; this constitutes the connection.
The word "is drawn back" (*pratikṛṣyate*) is to be supplied from the Sūtra. Mi. Ko.
204 vi—Is there a drawing back of the offering (*pradāna*), or not? It should be like the placing down (*sādana*).
However, because the offering (*pradāna*) is the primary element, its displacement (*apakarṣa*) here is not appropriate;
it is not proper to displace the principal (*śeṣin*) in accordance with the subordinate elements (*śeṣa*).
Bhāṭṭa: But there is no displacement of the offering at all, due to a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇābhāvāt*).

Furthermore, there is no evidence that the sequence beginning with the drawing [of the cup] and ending with the offering constitutes a single ritual act (*ekapadārtha*), as is the case for the sequence beginning with the *chātra* and ending with the offering; rather, it is interrupted by several distinct acts.
Therefore, it should be performed in its own proper place.
Maṇḍana states: "But the offering is not to be brought forward."
23. Śaṅkara says: "In that case, there is certainly no [separate] offering. 24. The distinction regarding the *graha* (cup) is prescribed for the Jyotiṣṭoma alone;
for by the two words "if it has the *Rayaṃtara* as its *sāman*" and "if it has the *Bṛhat* as its *sāman*," it is the Jyotiṣṭoma itself that is thus designated.

In the *Grahādhikaraṇa* (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.4.1–10), it was established that the singularity expressed by the case ending is intended to be significant, whereas the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is not;

furthermore, as stated in Vārttika 6.1.3.6, even if a qualifier is heard in connection with something being referred to (*anūyamāna*), it does not function as a restrictive attribute— this was also proven in the *Grahādhikaraṇa*.
3|4|1|13, p. 943: It has been established in the *Grahādhikaraṇa* that it is not possible to intend to express a qualification of that which has already been indicated.

*Ratna.* 6|1|3: Although the phrase "the sacrificer, being clever, should perform the offering with five cuttings" (*pañcāvatī vapā kāryā*)—by means of this [phrase]—expresses a connection with the substance and the act of giving, and is stated in connection with a singular number and gender; nevertheless, having referred back to that [substance], fifteen-foldness (*pañcadaśya*) is enjoined.

And if the gender of that which is being restated were intended to be significant, and it were further qualified by the omentum (*vapā*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) according to the principle of the section on the cups (*grahādhikaraṇa*, 3.1.7). Therefore, the number five is enjoined for the nominal base (*pratipadika*) of the portioning-off (*avadāna*).

*Dupū* 10|7|20|73. According to the principle stated in the *Grahādhikaraṇa-vārtika*: "Even if it were dependent on the scripture (*śāstratantratva*), even so there would be a multiplicity of those [acts]," the suffix, though uttered only once, possesses the capacity to enjoin multiple functions conveyed by a single word; nevertheless, through a single operation, its possession of multiple capacities necessitates a single [application of] that operation. (The reading in the *Vārtika* is: "Even if it were dependent on the scripture, the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) would apply to each cup" — *pṛ.* 705). *Su.* p. 419.

And [the fire] is for the purpose of grasping, because it is desired as something already established; and because of the purpose of maintenance, as stated in the sūtra (12.1.10.19): "In the Soma sacrifice, at the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites, the *anvādhāna* (adding fuel) need not be performed, because its purpose is maintenance.
And furthermore, it is for that purpose.
The section on the primary dharma (pradharmādhikaraṇa) concerning the singular number [of the agent] establishes that it is itself the object of injunction;
page 1012, regarding the singular number.

Even if the injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*) does not extend as far as the qualification of the substance, and thus number is intended to be enjoined through *arthāpatti*—characterized by the impossibility of establishing the performance of an action qualified by its own qualifiers—nevertheless, singularity is a qualifier of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

On page 1012, in the section concerning singularity (*ahaiktva-adhikaraṇa*), the distinction between the scopes of the two principles—the principle of individual pervasion (*pratyeka-vyāpti-parisamāpti*) and the principle of completion within the collective sentence (*samudāya-vākya-parisamāpti*)—has been stated.

The former [word] applies when there is primacy (*prādhānya*), while the latter applies when there is subsidiarity (*guṇatva*), as in "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*) and "He purchases [the Soma] with a one-year-old red cow" (*aruṇayā ekahāyanyā krīṇāti*). This is stated in the *Kaustubha* on the section concerning the singularity of the vessel (*āghāraikatvādhikaraṇa*), at *Cāla.* p. 165: multiplicity in the productive capacity [of the word] arises because of the qualification by the plurality of the receptacles, as in "He places the materials in the receptacles" (*āyataneṣu saṃbhārān nidadhāti*). In the case of "One desiring sense-power should sacrifice" (*aindriyakāmasya juhuyāt*), there is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) because, even regarding singularity and so forth, there is the injunction of a factor (*kāraka*) qualified by curd (as in "one should sacrifice with an animal" [*paśunā yajeta*]).
And how this is so will become clear in the section concerning the sublation of oneness (*aiktvabādhādhikaraṇa*). It is said:
"Regarding the cognition [of this], there is no contradiction whatsoever for anyone."
However, even though [the truth] is already recognized, this investigation into injunction and non-injunction is undertaken;
first of all, unity in this case is undoubtedly established,
and that this is a sign of apprehension is likewise beyond doubt.

In this context, however, it has been stated that there are three kinds of Vedic revelation (*śruti*): first, that which denotes all meanings; second, that which is subordinate to application (*viniyojaka*); and third, the injunctive (*vidhātrī*), upon which the performance of ritual action depends. Furthermore, both the verbal root (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) possess the capacity to denote their respective meanings.
The word and the case endings of the grammatical factors (kārakas) serve as the means of application (viniyojaka).

However, the optative (liṅ), the subjunctive (leṭ), the gerundive suffixes (tavya), and the fifth verbal mood (pañcamalakāra) possess the capacity for injunction (vidhi). In that regard, at the time of performance, the person is dependent upon the authority of the injunction.
For wherever it proceeds in such a manner, it proceeds equally whether [the word] is expressed or unexpressed, or enjoined or unenjoined.
But where one is not enjoined by an injunction, the person does not proceed even when [the action] is expressed or enjoined;
for that person [does not act] toward the performance [of the action] based on either of those two [between the expressive and the enjoining words].
The scripture itself declares that one who is capable should perform the *prahanyā* [striking] repeatedly.

Now, this being the case, what follows? It will not be connected with the *saṃmārga* (the act of wiping). For that which is being wiped is connected by the direct statement (*śruti*); and that which is connected by a direct statement cannot be severed from it by the syntactical connection (*vākya*) and connected with something else.

If the act of cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) were not performed as qualified by singularity while being undifferentiated by it, it would have no effect whatsoever. It is not that the cleansing and so forth are not qualified by singularity; rather, it is enjoined for the cup (*graha*) and other items alone. Therefore, why should it not be performed for the second and third [cups] as well?
Or—(the author begins the final conclusion)—this action, which is characterized by its own kind, is restricted to the singular.
That which is prescribed as a subordinate factor is understood to serve every purpose.
(This is the *grahādhikaraṇa-siddhānta-nyāya*).
Here, first of all, in the passage "Because it is heard as a separate injunction, it should have the same properties as these" (*2.4.1.10*), the reading is "sadharmaḥ.
In this context, there are two readings: "sadharmā" (masculine) and "sadharmam" (neuter), both ending in the suffix *ani* and thus being indefinite pronouns.

(The reading "sa dharmaḥ" in the Ānandāśrama edition is indeed incorrect. Thus, from the use of the accusative case and because of the presence of a purpose, it is understood that the cups (*graha*) are the primary objects and the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) is subordinate. Even so, since the state of being a cup (*grahatva*) is unfit for cleansing, they remain as things to be refined (*saṃskārya*).
Because they are directly connected [to the action], the cup is resorted to as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
This is the meaning understood from the injunction:
that which is the function of the cup becomes endowed with its quality through the act of wiping.
If it were not designated for that very purpose, its function would remain defective.

Therefore, all [the cups] must be cleansed. However, if the cup were enjoined as a subordinate element (guṇa) by virtue of being subordinate to the act of cleansing—which itself is subordinate to the sacrifice—then, since the purpose would be accomplished by one alone, another would not be taken. For in that case, no deficiency would be observed even if other cups were not taken, because the purpose of the scriptural injunction would have been fulfilled.

But in the view that [the *śāstra*] is primary, since there would be a different *śāstra* for each primary element, it would follow that even when a single [element] is being performed, the status of the *śāstra* pertaining to all of them would apply. Furthermore: "Even if the cleansing were to take place because it is the end of the *śāstra*, nevertheless, by not performing it, the knowledge pertaining to that [cleansing] is sublated."
But when cognition has not been obstructed, if another [cognition] is likewise not produced,
then an offense (pratyavāya) results there due to the non-performance of what was enjoined.

(He concludes the established doctrine: "Therefore, because of the non-sacrificing, because of the connection with what precedes, and because of the specific context, there is cognition of all [the mantras].

Anticipating the objection, "But surely the singular number is heard [in the text]," and seeing no reason for that to be unintended, he says: "The claim is not made that everything merely heard in the text must be performed."
For in that case, both the application and the injunction must be understood, whether they are explicitly stated or not.
For that which is prescribed and applied is accepted even if it is not explicitly heard;
however, even if it is heard, it would not be accepted if it is disregarded by those two.

In this regard (as found in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*), when there arises a consideration within a single sentence as to which among the many meanings established by the hearing of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is embraced by injunction (*vidhi*) and application (*viniyoga*), and which is excluded— since all [meanings] are seen to be present through different modes of verbal expression—
it is deliberated upon which one is enjoined and applied, and which is not.
For when the investigation of the meaning of a sentence is undertaken, the Mīmāṃsakas obstruct common worldly perspectives with the dust of their verbal formulations.
What indeed is enjoined here by the fifth lakāra (the leṭ), which has the form of the present tense and is characterized by the recollection of the meaning of the optative?
Mere cultivation (bhāvanā) is never enjoined;
rather, it is enjoined as something qualified by the nature of what is to be performed.
Is that [action] qualified by the mere meaning of the verbal root through its relation [to it],
or rather by its world-established form consisting in being capable of performance?
What is the use of the substance of the vessel, or what is the use of its relation as belonging to it?
The term *daśāpavitra*, however, is intended to signify all things [required for the rite].
Because it has the same meaning, it is not examined separately along with the others.
And what is the purpose here of defining the planets and so forth by means of a formal injunction?
Regarding the two [terms] *saṃmārga* and *graha*, is there an option (*vikalpa*) or a conjunction (*samuccaya*)?
Or rather, the connection here is with the qualified efficient force (bhāvanā) within the aggregate.
Alternatively, one of the two is distinguished by the other;
thus, by means of that [distinction], the meditation itself is enjoined as being characterized by the three.

Among the triad of the cup (*graha*), its oneness (*tadekatva*), and the cleansing (*saṃmārga*), there first arises the alternative (*vikalpa*): between the cup and the cleansing, does the cup alone qualify the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), or does the cleansing alone? Likewise, is it a conjunction (*samuccaya*)—that is, either the cup or the cleansing—or is it a relationship between the cup and the cleansing, or rather [a relationship] with the aggregate (*samudāya*)?
Alternatively, the act of cleansing is qualified by the cup, or the cup is qualified by the act of cleansing.
Thus, an investigation into the eightfold relationship must be performed.
In this manner, there is an examination of the eightfold relations between the cup and the cleansing.
[The author] extends [the analysis] to the sweeping and the oneness: "Having thus analyzed the sweeping and the oneness, [the same applies] to the eight cups.
[He] extends [it] to the cup and the oneness: "Having analyzed in this way, that very same [analysis] applies again to the cup and the oneness.
(The two sets of eight are to be analyzed.)

Likewise, is it the cup (*graha*) itself as qualified by cleansing (*saṃmārga*) that qualifies the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), or is it singularity alone? Such is the method of the *prakarṣapraśna* (the successive inquiry).

The first set of eight alternatives (*aṣṭapakṣī*) consists of the form of *niyoga* (injunction) and its variations: "Is it the cleansing itself qualified by the cup? or "Is it oneness itself? and so forth; the second [set] consists of the form "Is it the cup itself qualified by oneness? or "Is it the cleansing itself? and so forth; the third [set] consists of the form "Is it oneness itself qualified by the cup? or "Is it the cleansing itself? and so forth; the fourth [set] consists of the form "Is it the cleansing itself qualified by oneness? or "Is it the cup itself? and so forth; the fifth [set] consists of the form "Is it the cup itself qualified by the cleansing? or "Is it oneness itself? and so forth; the sixth [set] consists of the form "Is it oneness itself qualified by the cleansing? or "Is it the cup itself? and so forth.

Thus, after the three sets of eight-fold positions (*aṣṭapakṣī*) previously mentioned, six other sets of eight-fold positions are to be examined. As it is said: "Having thus established the relationship of qualifier and qualified between two [of the first set], there is a similar examination of one [term] together with the third."

(One must distinguish whether the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) applies to the collection of the cups and their unity, or to each [cup] individually; likewise, it is said that their status as the "to-be-taken" (*upādeyatva*) and the "subject of reference" (*uddeśyatva*) must also be investigated: "In this regard, do they possess the status of being 'to-be-taken' or the status of being 'the subject of reference' with respect to the cleansing, either in combination or individually?"

(Regarding which view there is collective application, or which view involves a requirement for each individual: "In that regard, when the action is primary, there is a conjunction of the substance and the number;
having performed it all at once in such a manner, the agent becomes successful."
Just as when there is a unity of the object, the cleansing is taught as being performed upon each individual instance,
so too, in that case, the two [the substance and the action] are completed within each respective sentence of action.

Since both the status of being the subject of reference (*uddeśyatva*) and the status of being the thing to be enjoined (*upādeyatva*), like their respective qualifiers, cannot be established without investigation, one must first examine the nature of the subject of reference. Is it (1) the cup alone that is the subject of reference with respect to the cleansing; or (2) the singularity alone; or (3) either the cup or the singularity; or (4) both the cup and the singularity; or (5) the relationship between the cup and the singularity; or (6) the aggregate; or (7) the cup qualified by singularity; or (8) the singularity qualified by the cup? Having thus investigated these eight specific alternatives, he says: "In that case as well, is the cleansing enjoined for the cup alone?"
Is it [the negation] of unity alone, or rather, by way of an alternative, of both as well?
Is it enjoined with respect to two things that are already appropriate, or with respect to the relationship and the collection?
Or is it enjoined for the cup itself as qualified by singularity? Or is it enjoined with respect to the number as qualified by the cup?

(Regarding its status as something to be accepted, he says that this same set of eight positions must be examined: "Is it understood that [the number] belongs to each individual object of apprehension? Does it belong to the grasping alone? Does it belong to the unity alone? Or does it belong to both alternatively?"
Is it [the injunction] of both together, or rather of both by way of option?
Is it of both together, or of the relationship and the collection? Or is it enjoined for the cup alone as qualified by oneness?
Or rather, is it the number one, qualified by the cup (*graha*), that pertains to the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*)?
When such a doubt has been raised by these modes of expression,
the opponent considers that the number is the predicate to be enjoined as something to be adopted.
In whatever manner it is grasped in the seizing [of objects] or prescribed in the path of purification, it will bring that very state about.
Just as when something is being designated, the prescription of place and time occurs by means of the action,
so too would it be for the state of being a cup and for oneness.
Whatever verbal formulation he may compose as a rule,
the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) will refute each and every one of them by means of a division of the sentence.
Because of its predominance, it will not be something to be taken up from Prahasta;
likewise, because of being under his control, it is not possible to take up unity.
Since the application of the sweeping rule depends on its being directed toward the cup (graha),
its power will be exhausted by that alone, and thus it will not enjoin oneness.
To that extent, it is not possible to enjoin the act of grasping, because there is no further scriptural statement;
for if it were so, there would have to be two injunctions for the grasping.
For when a permanent connection between the cup and the number is being established,
and an additional matter— the connection between the cup and the cleansing— is enjoined.
The great [section] must also be repeated in order to establish two relationships;
for those two are not established by a single injunction.
For two relations can be perceived either simultaneously or successively;
how could a single cognition perceive them both at once?
Even though both the connection with number and the connection with purification are obtained [by repetition],
that which is heard only once may obtain them both when authorized by two [injunctions].
When the recitation has been exhausted after performing the cleansing (saṃmārjana) of the vessel,
then another recitation must be performed for the purpose of establishing oneness.
Furthermore, the cognition that arises when [the Veda] is being recited again, standing outside of its completion,
would result in being a means of valid knowledge because it is produced by a person.
If singularity were not accepted, it would be impossible to enjoin [the sacrifice] in all its various forms through distinct modes of verbal expression.
If, by some means, there were a scriptural injunction for this,
one would have to abandon the status of being the agent in the case of being bitten by a planet or the like.
In that case, since the action is primary, the injunction of the qualifiers would necessarily follow by force of the injunction of the qualified whole;
thus, it would be a case of a secondary injunction (vidhyantara) arising from the sense (ārtha).
If, however, the predominance of the action is obtained through the act of disregarding [the agent],
then it follows from the acceptance that everything stands in a relationship of being both subordinate and principal.
Therefore, we shall understand that one should perform the cultivation of purification (*saṃmārgabhāvanā*) by means of that oneness which is based upon the cup (*graha*).

Once the relationship of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*) has ceased with respect to the cultivation, there subsequently arises a relationship of qualifier and qualified, according to the principle of the "red [cow] and the one-year-old female [cow]" (*aruṇaikahāyanī*);
this very [relationship] is conveyed by the word.

Alternatively, when it is determined that singularity is incapable of being subsisted as a subordinate element for the sake of the act of taking (*graha*), then its cultivation (*bhāvanā*) within the sentence is not prevented from occurring. For when it is even more strongly inclined toward "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), thinking: "Since this is being grasped by the injunction (*vidhi*) for the sake of cultivation, it will subsequently delimit me even as I am being restricted; otherwise, if I were not grasped by the injunction and were thus neglected, I would not belong to the cultivation," [the singularity is accepted]. Or rather, let this [singularity] be for the sake of the act of taking itself.
The manner in which that status of being an object of apprehension (*grahārthatva*) is established will now be demonstrated.

In this regard, if the cup (*graha*) were to enter into the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) merely by its own form, then oneness—being subsequently apprehended—would not belong to the productive operation; rather, it would belong to the form of the cup itself.
Therefore, it attains its own identity either preceded by oneness or simultaneously with it, precisely because it is expressed by a separate word.
Why? "For a qualified injunction in its entirety does not [apply] when the qualifier has not been activated;
that [injunction], being qualified, enters into its intended meaning (tātparya) as something qualified."
The cognition designated as "meditation" grasps the oneness that has been heard;
it does not grasp that [oneness] as qualified by the qualifiers already grasped.

And this being the case, when it has entered into the process of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and is touched by that procedure (*vidhi*), the determination of the substance and its quality having been reached, the status of being a "cup" (*graha*) arises for it.
Now, if it is argued that because the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is more powerful, its connection with the substance is asserted, that would be utterly contradictory;
for the substance denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would, by virtue of being expressed within the same word, become subordinate to the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*).
But here, because of the employment of a common case-ending,
oneness is understood more rapidly as a qualifier of the *kāraka*;
and the *kāraka* is that which is conveyed by the case-ending and constitutes a single part of the manifestation of the action (*bhāvanā*) whose prior and subsequent stages have become manifest.
Thus it has been said:
because it is the meaning of the suffix, this alone is the primary element;
and every relationship pertains to the primary element.
Therefore, both the singularity of the *graha* and its being the instrument (*kāraka*) are cast into the *bhāvanā* by the very hearing of the case-ending (*vibhakti-śruti*), and thus it is enjoined;
for that [enjoining] occurs through a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhāna*).
For he will say: "It is obtained through the presence of the word; for when that [word] is introduced, that [meaning] is seen, just as there is knowledge of it in the case of others" (4.1.5.16).

Just as that which is prescribed for the *daśāpavitra* is not performed with anything else, and the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) prescribed [for it] is not performed as threshing (*avaghāta*), and that prescribed for a cup (*graha*) is not performed for what is not a cup, so too, what is prescribed for one is not to be performed for many.
And for all these cases, there is mutual restriction according to the principle of the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*).

(He concludes the prima facie view: Therefore, just as in the case of the proponent who adopts a position (*pakṣa*), the number of that which is being pointed out (*uddiśyamāna*) is also intended to be significant.

(In the Bhāṣya, the mention of) "masculinity" (*puṃstva*) was cited by way of illustration; however, gender (*liṅga*) is not treated here [as a separate issue], because, due to the same underlying logic, it has already been practically examined along with the discussion of number. This is done so that there may be no redundancy with the rule: "On account of the specification of a particular gender, [the masculine form is used]—so says Aiśāyana" (Pāṇini 6.1.136). Or rather, all [gender markers] serve as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), for a specific characteristic is indeed a defining characteristic.

Commentary: This is not so, as it was stated—that these items are to be performed upon the cups (*graha*) and other objects when they are singular. Rather, the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*) applies to all the cups; the fire-altars (*agni*) are for all [the offerings]; the third-day oblations (*apacyaya*) are for all; and the act of carrying fire around (*paryagni*) is to be performed for every sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Why? Because, having indicated the substance by means of the genus (*jāti*) "cup," the cleansing and other rites are enjoined.

And the characteristic is common to all substances. In that regard, no distinction is perceived as to which [substance] possesses the property of being wiped and which does not. Because of the comprehension of the general rule and the non-comprehension of any specific distinction, [the property applies] to all substances.
The same applies to the fire-offerings of the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).
But surely, the singular number is heard in the text; that [number] qualifies the object.
This is not so.
For the singularity being heard [in the word "one"] would express singularity regarding the cups and so forth, but it would not prohibit a second or others.
That [word] is the denoter of singularity; it is not a prohibitor of a second or others.
Therefore, since a second and so forth are not prohibited, why should the cleansing and other acts—which are obtained through the general statement—not be performed?

In this regard, it might be argued: since the singular number is heard here, what else could it do regarding the single substance that is already established, as well as regarding the second and subsequent substances, other than by way of exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*)?
For if the singular number did not exclude the second and subsequent substances, it would be entirely meaningless;
yet, it is capable of excluding the second and subsequent substances.
Just as the statement "he takes up the horse's halter" excludes the donkey's halter, so too here [in the case of] "thou art the substance.

This is not so. In that case, there is a relationship between the mantra and the act of naming; the statement "with the words 'imāmagṛbhṇan,' he takes up the horse's halter" is intended to enjoin that specific connection, rather than enjoining "he takes it up with this mantra," because the use of the mantra for the act of taking is already established by its inherent indicative power (*liṅga*). Therefore, exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) is appropriate there.
Furthermore, in this case: the singular number that is heard in reference to the substance, even though it is heard, cannot function as an exclusion because it is not being enjoined.
It is just as if someone, having pointed out some rice, were to say: "If anyone—a dog or a cat—should eat this, he is to be driven away."

In that case, if eating were enjoined as the condition (*nimitta*) and not the connection with a dog or a cat, then even a crow arriving would be excluded; for even though a dog or a cat is mentioned, the connection with a dog or a cat is not enjoined as the condition.
Likewise here, since the connection with oneness is not enjoined, even though oneness is heard [in the text], only the cup (*graha*) is to be wiped.
Furthermore, there is no word here that enjoins a connection between the substance and oneness.
But is it not the case that "he cleanses" (*saṃmārṣṭi*) is an injunctive word?
Indeed, this [word] is not an injunction for the connection with the singularity of the substance;
rather, it is an injunction for the connection between the substance and the cleansing.
Having heard this, [the number] is enjoined as a qualification of its own word; otherwise, it would be enjoined by syntactical connection (*vākya*) with reference to another word.
And when both [direct hearing and syntactical connection] are equally possible, direct hearing (*śruti*) prevails, not syntactical connection.
Therefore, the singularity, which is not being enjoined as a specific qualification, cannot serve to exclude the second and so forth.
This being the case, the sweeping and other such acts performed on a second [vessel] and so forth would neither be unenjoined nor prohibited.
For just as that [act] is understood to be enjoined for one [vessel], so too it is for a second and others.
Furthermore, there is this additional defect: that singularity would not be restricted to the substance within the scope of the sweeping and other such acts.
For that substance in which the singularity is restricted by the act of cleansing and so forth does not function as a qualifier.

Here, the cleansing and so forth are indeed enjoined; it is not prescribed as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the substance, for it is impossible to enjoin something and simultaneously utter it as a defining characteristic.
Indeed, only that which has a well-known relationship can serve as a defining characteristic.
Nor is such a thing as this, which is not enjoined,
capable of being understood through verbal testimony when its relationship [to the action] is already well-known;
yet, acts such as the cleansing (saṃmārjana) are indeed enjoined.
Therefore, it is not a qualifier.
If it is not a qualifier, one cannot maintain that singularity is restricted to the substance.
Now, if singularity is stated in relation to the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*), there too there are two possible courses: either singularity is primary, or the cleansing is primary.
And both of these [alternatives] are untenable.
First of all, the sweeping cannot be performed upon a single entity;
nor does that which is performed upon a substance benefit the singularity in any manner whatsoever.
Furthermore, there is no purpose served by assisting the oneness, for it is not heard in the scripture as being subordinate.
If it is argued that oneness is subordinate with respect to the cleansing, that too is not the case.
Why? Because it is incorporeal.
For that [act] does not bring about the purification (*saṃmārjana*).
Even if an immaterial action brings about the means (*sādhana*) as prescribed, nevertheless this cannot be the case.
For here the cup (*graha*) is not for the sake of the purification; rather, it is the purification and the cup that are mentioned here, for that [purification] possesses a purpose.
The act of cleansing has a purpose that must be postulated.
If the cup were to benefit the cleansing, then—since it would be benefiting that which benefits [the sacrifice]—it would become a subordinate factor of the cleansing; however, this is not the case.
Therefore, there is no connection between oneness and the cleansing.

But surely, although the cups (*graha*) and so forth are the primary elements, they are nonetheless to be accomplished through the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*); therefore, that [cleansing] is their means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and being thus qualified, it will assist them.

Just as the properties of the *praṇītā* water assist in the cooking when [that water] is for the sake of curd and milk, and the properties of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) assist in the binding when they are for the sake of encircling; therefore, this is not a valid solution.
To this it is replied:

We do not say that those things which establish a different purpose are unable to provide assistance; rather, what we mean is this: when a primary element such as the cup (*graha*) is mentioned as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), then the number "one" has no connection with the cup, nor with the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*), and so forth.

Why? Because in this context, whenever something is stated as a defining characteristic, there is a corroboration (*saṃvāda*) therein, but it is not enjoined for the sake of producing a specific cognition.
For what purpose, then, is it stated? It is because something else is prescribed for it.
Having characterized the cup (*graha*) and so forth, its cleansing (*saṃmārga*) and other rites are then prescribed.

If, however, another connection with singularity were prescribed either for the substance or for the cleansing and so forth, the sentence would be split due to the prescription of two distinct connections.
Now, it might be argued that after characterizing the cups and so forth, their connection with oneness is enjoined, but not their connection with the act of cleansing and so forth;
and thus, the study of the cleansing and other rites would have to be accepted as a mere error, which is not the case.
Therefore, the singular number is not connected with either of the two [the cups or the cleansing].

This oneness of the cup (graha) does not provide any assistance either to the cup itself or to the wiping (saṃmārjana); thus, being merely a restatement of what already exists, it is not intended to accomplish anything at all. Therefore, the wiping and other rites must be performed for all the cups and so forth. Why? Because [the singular number] is merely a restatement.
Because there is no distinction in their connection [to the action], yet there is a distinction in the context.
If singularity were not intended to be expressed, why then is the singular number used? [He himself asks: "Surely, when plurality is intended to be expressed, the plural number ought to be used.
It is replied:
We do not deliberate on whether the singular number should be uttered or should not be uttered.
Rather, when it is being uttered, what is to be understood?
Is it that the cleansing and so forth apply to only one, or to all? And that it applies to all has been established.
Furthermore, the case ending does not have expression alone as its sole purpose; rather, it also serves to indicate the relationship with a *kāraka*.
When singularity is not intended to be expressed, the utterance of this [ending] will serve the purpose of indicating the *kāraka* relationship.
Therefore, it is not meaningless.

Furthermore, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is the "cup" (*graha*), while singularity is the meaning of the case ending (*vibhakti*). What follows from this being so? This follows: for the function of the case ending pertains to that which is contained within the meaning of the nominal stem.
Thus, it serves to indicate the cup.
Regarding the apprehension [of the Veda]: even the intention to speak will be accomplished for him by means of that [apprehension].
Therefore, the mere fact of having heard [the words] is not the cause for the apprehension of an injunction.
Therefore, this [oneness] is not comparable to [qualities] such as whiteness, nor is it comparable to other qualifiers; rather,
this oneness would be a qualifier of either the substance or the action,
by which one might appropriate it through the cultivation of meditative absorption.

In this regard, the qualification of the substance (*dravyaviśeṣaṇa*) is first refuted. For that [qualification] must occur either by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) or by way of the exclusion of multiplicity (*anekatva-nirākaraṇa*).
Among these, regarding the position of its own essential nature, the fruit of the qualification is indeed possible even when all [substances] are being mixed together.
How so? For he who cleanses many [cups] also cleanses one.

Therefore, since the act of cleansing is established by the mention of the cup itself and is not prohibited by the singular number, why should this cleansing not be performed for the second cup and the others?

In this regard, it might be argued that although the act of cleansing applies to one or many cups based on the nominal stem alone, the explicit hearing of the singular number—which cannot function as a mere descriptive praise (*guṇārthavāda*)—must serve as a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*).

This is not so. Why? Because: "Where something is obtained through a general rule and is heard again in a specific context, there it serves as a restrictive enumeration (parisaṃkhyā); but here, there is no such repetition."
And that is manifold;
it is the Great Logic, the Great Logic.
Oneness must be accepted as the [intended] meaning;
however, we shall refute that further below.

But if it were a qualifier of the pure substance, then the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) would be connected only with the cup (*graha*), not with the number, and the number would also be connected only with the cup, not with the efficient force.

In that case, since the qualified injunction results only in the implication of the qualification of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) itself, it is not possible for it to imply another object. Furthermore, the productive operation does not grasp that cup as qualified by [the number] "one," because it is interposed by its own form; that is to say, since the number is a qualification of the cup, it is separated from the productive operation by the very form of the cup which qualifies the productive operation. Thus, the productive operation does not perceive that number at all.

Nor can oneness be a qualifier of the specific instance of the *bhāvanā* (the ellipsis being: "of the cup, which is the qualificand with respect to the *bhāvanā*"), lest there again be merely a specific instance of the *bhāvanā*.
For the *bhāvanā* cannot qualify a cup that is itself unqualified by oneness.
Therefore, since the fundamental injunction has no further expectancy (*anākāṅkṣatvāt*), it is not possible for [oneness] to function as a qualifier of the substance.

Even if an injunction (*vidhi*) were admitted under such circumstances, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), because that [injunction] would be untenable without a connection to a return [to the original subject].

Furthermore, even if [the injunction] were admitted, unity (*ekatva*) should not be respected as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), because the injunction establishes the connection with unity for the cup (*graha*) as an independent entity. As stated in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* (3.1.6–12, p. 689): "The purchase (*kraya*) being enjoined does not qualify the substance that is connected with a quality; for a qualifier must be something already well-known."
And it is stated in the Vārttika itself (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1027): "Furthermore, the act of purchasing (*kraya*) is not well-known as something to be enjoined.
Therefore, for that reason, there is no inclusion of that which serves as a qualifier of the substance.

Now, even if this oneness is enjoined as a constituent part of the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it cannot be established either as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) or as a primary factor (*pradhāna*).
In that regard, its status as a primary factor is first untenable, because it is impossible to effect a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that which is formless (*amūrta*).
Nor is its refinement a refinement of a substance (*dravya*), because it is distinct from the substance.
Alternatively, this [number] might be enjoined as the oneness of the cup (*graha*); however, since that [oneness] is already established by itself, there would be no purpose in enjoining it again.
Furthermore, at the time of performance, the cup is recognized precisely as it was previously seen; thus, the cognition based on oneness would not arise.
In this same manner, the absence of a subordinate quality (*guṇābhāva*) must also be refuted.

If it is asked how redness (*āruṇya*) is a quality (*guṇa*), he says in response: "Even though it is a quality, it is accepted as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) because it delimits the substance used for purchase; however, a quality that does not contribute to a fruitful action is not accepted here as a subsidiary. (Because it delimits the substance—the one-year-old cow—used for the act of purchase, redness, although a quality, is accepted as a subsidiary of the purchase.)

The meaning is that, because [the subordinate] is connected with the principal (*akṣatvāt*) even toward a constituent part (*samāṃga*) that is fruitless, it is not logical for unity to possess the status of being a constituent part (*samāṃgārhatā*) by virtue of delimiting that [principal].
For even a quality (*guṇa*), if it relies on what is not a constituent part (*anaṅga*), would itself become non-constituent (*anaṅga*).
[This refers to the Bhāṣya passage: "But even though it is the principal... (*nanu pradhānabhūtam api*).
That which is the inherent capacity of a substance to bring about [an action] at the outset will, by means of that [substance], assist the unity of the constituent part.

Furthermore, even though the cup (*graha*) is the primary element, it undergoes the state of being delimited by the subordinate qualities of the action through the properties of the subordinate substance.
For a subordinate element does not assist by depending on another subordinate element; rather, it assists by depending on that which is beneficial. This we shall establish everywhere.
"But the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) will arise through the sequence of means of knowledge such as direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth.

However, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) argues that even when a thing is presented with multiple meanings, because the injunctive word lacks the capacity [to convey them all], one must either accept a mediated meaning, a secondary quality (*guṇa*), or another alternative; thus he speaks of abandoning the singular number.

(He objects to the commentary which rejects the intentionality [of the number] on the grounds that singularity is a qualifier of the action: "But this cannot be the case, for it is not possible that [the singular number] be unintended."
How so? "The lack of intention to express [the gender] would be appropriate when the substance is the qualifier;
however, the relation of being a constituent part (*samāṅgatva*) has been refuted in both ways.

As for what was stated—that because it is incorporeal (*amūrtatva*), it cannot be consecrated—that applies equally to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as well, since the universal (*jāti*) is corporeal.
Furthermore, if its refinement (saṃskāra) occurs by way of the individual (vyakti), that is the same in the case of number as well.
If it is produced when made upon the individual, how could it belong to the genus? The same applies to oneness (ekatva).
Likewise, if the genus has the purpose of characterizing the substance, so too does oneness.

Now, if it is argued that the refinement (*saṃskāra*) applies directly to the universal (*jāti*) itself by relying on its corporeality and its distinctness from the substance, that too is no different for [the property of] unity.
As for the statement that "an action performed upon a substance does not affect the number," that too is no different for the universal in your own position.

Now, if it is argued that the term *graha* denotes the individual [act of grasping] and thus the objection is avoided, then the principle of the section on "Substance" (*dravyādhikaraṇa*) would have to be accepted; for there is no experience of anything distinct from the *grahas* situated within the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice across various places and times. Furthermore, if the word were applied only to those [individuals] already perceived, the term *graha* could not be used at all.

Therefore, some universal (*sāmānya*) must necessarily be resorted to as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). And since that [universal] cannot exist apart from the word *graha*, it itself—by virtue of being the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)—must logically be the primary denotation.

Nor can the word "cup" (graha) denote a form by designating a specific part [of a vessel], because it is distinct as having a certain additional component. Furthermore, there exists no other universal called "cup-ness" (grahatva) that is excluded from other substances and yet persists through those various [vessels]; therefore, the great principle [of the Vaiśeṣika] holds.
The great logic is this: that very point must be stated.

As for the argument that "since the [graha] being made is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, it is understood through the determination of its belonging to that [sacrifice] as having a single object, and thus the restatement (*punaḥśruti*) has little fruit," to that we reply: "If the action were indeed connected even by way of oneness (*ekatva*)."
Therefore, it might be argued that this distinction [of the singular number] would be fruitless for this consecration (*saṃskṛti*).

However, this very thing is the distinction because of its connection with singularity: that which is performed upon one [individual] is not otherwise; for otherwise, there would be a consecration of the cup (*graha*) in general.

Thus, since the restriction between the substance and the quality is established, the word "red" (*aruṇā*) has a distinct purpose in its connection with singularity; hence, its status as a consecration is logically justified.

However, the establishment of [the quality] as a subordinate factor (*guṇatva-pratiṣṭhāna*) has been demonstrated by the Commentator himself, just like the case of the excellent dharma (*praṇītā-dharma*).
This assumption—that a quality itself must be assisted by another quality because it is dependent—is based on weak reasoning.
Why? Because: "Those things which are directly incapable of connection reside in that which is connected to the action."
"Qualities do not accomplish an action when they are unconnected.

Qualities being applied to things that are unconnected would not delimit the action; therefore, they resort to a substratum connected with the action. However, there is no distinction between the substance and the qualities in this regard.
Thus it is taught.

Just as the means of action (*kriyāsādhana*) requires consideration such as "of what number shall this [means] be?", so too the primary factor (*pradhāna*) requires consideration such as "by what number [means of action] shall I be assisted? And this much is the cause for their relationship. Furthermore: "That which makes the assistance rendered by a subordinate factor its own, will indeed receive that factor with even greater intensity, provided it is itself to be refined."
"For an action must assist the principal even by means of a subordinate factor.

And this [action], being situated in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), could not produce any substance for the Tathāgata who is thus being assisted. This is a great favor, namely, that which is called "taking recourse" to the principal.

Furthermore, it will be stated in [Sūtra] 1.3.6 that even those purificatory rites of the sacrificer—which fall under the category of being enjoyers—possess the status of being auxiliary to the sacrifice, because they serve as the means for the sacrificer’s reception of the fruit, which exceeds the mere purchase that is subordinate to the sacrifice.
That same principle applies here; thus, there is no contradiction in their being auxiliaries by virtue of depending on the primary act.

As for what was said regarding the incapacity of the injunction when these [auxiliaries] are established, that remains equally true even in the case of the animals and other items that are directly enjoined.

For even in that case, since there is no distinction of substance, deity, or sacrifice within the sentence, if another connection with gender and number were enjoined either in the action or in the substance, it could be said that the sentence would be split (vākya-bheda).

However, if there is no split of the sentence because of an injunction of a qualified whole (viśiṣṭa-vidhāna), then that [connection], although being a part of the whole, remains unqualified because it was not previously established.

In this case, only this much distinction remains: that the *graha* (cup) is being referred to (*uddiśyamāna*), while the *paśu* (animal) is being enjoined (*upādīyamāna*). Yet, nothing is established by this alone; otherwise, the distinction between what is intended and what is not intended would be established even by the mere difference in the relationship between the animal and the cup. Furthermore, in this very same sentence, even though the subsidiary parts are enjoined with reference to the cup, the intentionality (*vivakṣā*) of the *daśāpavitra*, its singularity, and so forth is accepted, and yet there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); the same will hold true for the status of the *graha* as well.

As for one who would assert a distinction based on the employment of another word, for him there is some distinction everywhere; thus, there can be neither an example nor a simile, because there is no scope for those cases where the same logic applies. Furthermore: "How could that which is intended as a desired quality residing in another word be unintended when it is presented by a synonymous term?"

(The objector summarizes the lack of distinction regarding the desire to express a qualification of both the subject and the predicate: Therefore, even the singularity of the cup (*graha*) is intended to be expressed. For there is indeed a contact with the injunction (*vidhi*) even for the cup which is being indicated as the subject; otherwise, if the subsidiary act were performed even without the cup, the purpose of the scripture would be fulfilled.
If it is argued that the cup is not enjoined because it is already established by another rule (*prāpta*), that is incorrect, because it is not established in relation to the subsidiary act itself.

Now, regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma: if it is argued that [the injunction] is not an original prescription (*apūrva-vidhi*) because it is already established in common worldly practice even for the *pathin* and other such things;
or if it is argued that this [cup] is prescribed as something not previously established in the sacrifice, then that is no different for the cup (*graha*) itself.

Or, if it is argued that the prescription of the cup is stated because the constituent part (*samāṅga*) falls outside the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, then that is no different for the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*) as well, since it too is included within common worldly practice.
For it is possible to say "the animal which" just as one says "the cup which";

because [the animal] is being pointed out (uddiśyamāna). That objection regarding the non-injunction of the cup here is incorrect, due to the absolute difference between what is enjoined and what is restated, and between what is pointed out and what is taken up.
For it is established that even for a location and so forth that is being pointed out, there is invariably an injunction.
Furthermore, although the taking (*ālambha*) is already established as something to be adopted, it is enjoined because it has not yet been [otherwise] obtained.

Therefore, since the injunction implies the prescription of a specific aggregate, there is a contact with the injunction regarding both the "cup-ness" (*grahatva*) and the "oneness" (*ekatva*). Consequently, there is a relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) based on the sense [of the injunction]: oneness is subordinate because it serves no purpose, while the cup is principal because it possesses a purpose.
Moreover, "the enjoining and non-enjoining of an injunction are logical, but they do not occur within the utterance of a single word."

Furthermore, a division of the word is not logical; [the rule] "the suffix follows the base" (*prakṛtipratyayau*) applies when both are uttered simultaneously within a single word. In such a case, it is enjoined with respect to knowledge that there is a singular number, not that there is oneness—this would be contradictory. Nor is the case-ending a separate word, because it is never used independently and lacks a fixed sequence of preceding or following elements.

If it is argued that a word (*pada*) is so called because it possesses the capacity to convey meaning (*gamakatva*), this is not the case, for such a definition would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of smoke and other such things.

Furthermore, since multiple meanings are understood even from a single suffix, such as a verbal suffix (*ākhyātādipratyaya*), it must be accepted that a suffix also possesses the status of a word (*padatva*).
(In the Ānandāśrama edition, it is printed as: "by means of a single suffix, such as a verbal suffix, one meaning [is conveyed]").
We, however, have reversed [the interpretation] in accordance with the meaning of the sentence;
it should be divided as "na eko 'rthaḥ pratyaye" (there is not one meaning in the suffix).
Furthermore, the word *pada* is a worldly term; wherever it is employed by common usage and wherever it is remembered by the grammarians (*sūtrakāra*), it cannot be removed from that [usage].
And there is the traditional rule (smṛti): "That which ends in a nominal suffix (suP) or a verbal suffix (tiṄ) is a word" (Pāṇini 1.4.14).
It is precisely in this sense that the term *pada* is employed. Therefore, a word (*pada*) is a collection of both base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*), not merely a constituent part.

However, even if one were to admit this, if it is desired here that the objecthood (*karmatva*) expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*) be intended to be significant, then its number (*saṃkhyā*) cannot be intended to be significant as well, because it is likewise expressed by that same [case-ending]. When there is no intention to signify [the number], the principle is resorted to that a word [expressing what is not intended] is equivalent to what is not heard at all.

"As long as even a word that has been heard is imagined to be unheard, who could then remove its expressed meaning from the sentence-meaning? Therefore, in this case, if the case-ending is abandoned due to the abandonment of number, then the status of being an object (*karmatva*) would also necessarily follow as being abandoned; consequently, the fact that the *graha* (cup) is the object of a purificatory rite (*saṃskārya*) would be lost.

If it is argued that [the vessel] is to be consecrated because it serves a purpose, [we reply that this is not so], because there can be no connection with an action in the absence of a case-ending denoting a factor of action (*kāraka*). For the word *graha* by itself, lacking a case-ending, cannot logically be connected with the verb *saṃmārṣṭi*. Therefore, its status as the object (*karman*) must necessarily be intended.

And for this reason, since there is no abandonment of any part when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is used as a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the intention to express number (*saṃkhyāvivakṣā*) is difficult to avoid; thus, it is impossible [to achieve the desired result] by any means. For instance: "The *sarvādi* group [is taught] because singularity is not intended to be expressed in all of them; nor is there a distinction for anyone [in the case of the *prahā* suffixes] because the action of abandoning is not intended to be expressed."

Indeed, in a single word— whether in its base (prakṛti) or its suffix (pratyaya)— the conceptualization of being audible and inaudible is not tenable due to contradiction, like existence and non-existence. Likewise,
there can be no simultaneous [perception] of objects denoted by audible words in that manner.

"The grasping of what is already grasped is illogical, like [the case of] half a hen being cooked for food while half is kept for breeding; the meaning is that just as this is neither logical nor possible, so it is here.
However, the intention to express [the object] as a subordinate factor (guṇabhūta) is precluded by the contradiction with the accusative case."

For when the *saṃmārga* (cleansing) is enjoined with reference to the singularity of the cup (*graha*), since there is no mutual relationship between the two things being referred to, the sentence is completed for each individually; thus, there is one [instance of] sentence-split (*vākya-bheda*).

However, because the objects to be taken up (*upādeya*) are distinct, and because the purpose is the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) qualified by all [attributes], there is unity of sentence (*ekavākyatva*) on account of their having a single effect through their status as injunctions.
In this very view, because the primary action exercises control, the mutual restriction of the qualifiers is established.
The phrase "the state of those being terrified again," and so forth, should be applied as before.
Furthermore, it is logical that the plural number in the word "tṛṇāni" (grasses) is not intended to be significant.
The same applies in cases such as "He offers when [the ladle] is broken" (*bhinne juhoti*).

If, first of all, the states of being broken and being one were said to be the conditions for the ritual act through options, alternatives, or combinations, then—since each would be restricted by its own sentence—there would be no mutual connection between them.

Alternatively, if being one were presented as something to be adopted (*upādeya*), and being broken were also presented as something to be adopted, then even though there is no contradiction between being subordinate (*guṇatva*) and being primary (*pradhānatva*), there remains a contradiction of the same kind as before.
If there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), then the form of multiplicity—consisting of what is to be adopted and what is not to be adopted—is not intended to be expressed.
And truth would be intended to be expressed through expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
Furthermore, that expectancy arises with respect to those things being adopted, not with respect to those being referred to as the subject of the proposition (*uddiśyamāna*).

For when [a term] is being pointed out, there is no requirement for number because it depends merely on the connection with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), since its referent is already known through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, it is determined that the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) and so forth apply to such things as the *graha* vessels as they have been ascertained by other means of knowledge.
In all defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), because they serve merely the purpose of cognition, they are not auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) to the actual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*).

Likewise, in the case of the statement, "Bring that one who is seen wearing white garments," [the fault of] syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) should be understood to apply even in the *dravyakhaṇḍa* by the principle of the *ahanyāya* (PMS 6.2.31) and the principle of the *yāvajjīvādhikaraṇa* (PMS 2.4.1), because the occasioning factor (*nimitta*) would entail two distinct results.
And just as by two distinct conditions there is no projection of a single result, so it is clearly explained in the *Kaustubha*.

For this very reason, in cases involving a condition (*nimitta*) and its result, or a condition and a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because there is no disruption of the unity of action (*ekakarmakatva*).
Nor does such a split occur when there is a multiplicity of objects to be designated, such as time, place, and so forth.

Just as in this case, that which is accompanied by its fruit and so forth cannot be the object of a single cognition, so it is clearly explained in the *Kaustubha*. Therefore, if there is an intention to include that accompaniment, a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) is indeed unavoidable; this has been discussed in detail elsewhere.

Now, one might argue: "Even so, there is no intention to emphasize singularity and the like as the occasioning factor (*nimitta*), because it is logical for [singularity] to possess a result as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) within the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of the cleansing."

Nor should it be argued that, because the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) characterizes [the object] as an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the case of oneness and so forth, and because predominance is expressed in respect to the cup (*graha*), there would result a change in form and a contradiction in having two simultaneous functions.

This is because the second case-ending has the power to denote mere "objecthood" (*karmatva*) common to both the desired and the undesired; thus, even when a specific distinction is obtained from another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the connection of both [the cup and the juice] is possible through a uniform nature.

Even so, it cannot be argued that singularity is impossible as a means (*dvāra*) for the purification and other rites through the cups (*graha*), which are their constituent parts (*aṅga*), because—even if there is a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the subordinate status [of the purification], it is possible for the cup to serve as the means just like heaven in the mantra "agnim," merely by virtue of proximity.

Therefore, if it is claimed that singularity is intended to be expressed, we reply: no, because it is improper to accept a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of instrumentality in the suffix in accordance with the singular number, which has become a subordinate factor; for this would involve the contradiction of two simultaneous functions (*yugapad-vṛtti-dvaya-virodha*) and the fault of inconsistency (*vairūpya*).
Therefore, since that [singular number] is disregarded, it is merely a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) according to the principle of the section on the "rope" (*pāśādhikaraṇanyāya*, 1.3.4).

Nor does the aforementioned fault follow from the mere denotation of the objecthood (*karmatva*) common to both desired and undesired [objects]; for if that were the case, the syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result due to the collapse of the status of having either one or two objects. Consequently, when a secondary indication is resorted to for the sake of establishing the subordinate status [of the action], the aforementioned fault arises; thus, the singular number—being for the purpose of indicating plurality—is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) and is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).

And this being so, the fact that the number "eight years" and so forth is intended to be significant in such injunctions as "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age" has been established in the Kaustubha itself.
Maṇḍana [states]: "The identity of the cup is not intended. Śaṅkara [states]: "There is no intention to signify the identity of the cup."

The principle of the sweeping away of the planets (*grahasaṃmārjananyāya*).

The principle of the combination of cups (*grahasamuccayanyāya*):

The Commentary states: In the Bṛhaspatisava it is heard, "He takes the Bārhaspatya cup";
and at the Viśuvat, "He takes the Arka cup.

For there is indeed for them a connection with the taking [of the cups] by means of their natural characteristic.
This being the case, we reply:
in every instance, the taking [of the cups] ought to be additional.
"There is no exclusion of the archetypal [elements].
Why? Because both are established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The extended application (*codaka*) is a means of valid cognition, and direct scriptural audition (*pratyakṣa-śravaṇa*) is also one."

If it is argued that the word *graha* (cup) possesses its original gender, this is not so. If both the collection of cups and the accessory (*guṇa*) were being enjoined, then the original cups themselves would be modified by the accessory.
Alternatively, if a non-cup is enjoined in connection with the cup, then because it performs the function of the cup, it would exclude the original one.
"Just as the threshing-post is the sacrificial stake.
However, this other word "graha" denotes the act of seizing.
One takes up the cup named Arka; one takes up the cups named Mahimānau.

Therefore, the word "cup" (graha) is not an indicator of eating.
For there is either an option (*vikalpa*) or a sublation (*bādha*) between things that serve a single purpose.
Yet, these [subsidiary acts] do not share a single purpose with the modified forms (*vaikṛta*).
[Objection: But surely all of them are for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice; therefore, they indeed have a single purpose.

these are the causes for the sacrifice in combination; not each one individually, independently, is the means of accomplishment.

How then? The injunction of application (*prayogavacana*) is the grasper of these; and it grasps those that are proximate. Nor...
The Principle of the Collection of All (Aha-samuccaya-nyāya): 1645. The Principle of the Collection of All states that there is a distinction in proximity;
therefore, it is the collector of all [elements], both archetypal (prākṛta) and modified (vaikṛta).
As in the archetype.

the division [of the substance], the visible purpose, the purification, and the dedication to the deity [are likewise established].
Because the effect is not perceived, it is not known that the former becomes the effect of the latter.

Furthermore, because of the inclusion of the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance), there is a conjunction; it is not only with the Maitrāvaruṇa and others, but also with those studied in the section on the *apakaraṇa*.
Thus, even in the case of a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there ought to be a conjunction.
He says: "But surely, in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, a quality is prescribed by mixing [the vessels], namely, 'with gold and silver'?
To this it is replied:
Those two are not ordinary cups;
for it is stated [in the sūtra], "And the name [is applied] because of its connection with the origin," that the term is differentiated in the context of the cup-rite.

In that case, the statement "he takes the Bārhaspatya [cup]" would be for the purpose of enjoining a deity. It is replied:
when the cup (*graha*) is being enjoined, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is more consistent; whereas if it were for the deity, it would be a syntactical connection (*vākya*).
And direct Vedic statement (śruti) is more authoritative than syntactical connection (vākya).
It says: "As in the case of the Āgneya [offering]."

Just as in the Agniṣṭut sacrifice, there is an injunction regarding the deity in the statement, "The cups belong to Agni," so too it occurs even with a word ending in the singular number, because that [singular number] is not intended to be significant.
