To this, it is replied:
This has already been stated: that [the injunction] cannot be based on *śruti* alone.

For instance, having heard the sentence "The cups belong to Agni" (*āgneyā grahā bhavanti*), one does not find there the [direct] statement "He takes the cup belonging to Agni" (*āgneyaṃ grahaṃ gṛhṇāti*).
In that case, since the state of being dedicated to Agni (āgneyatva) is enjoined by the sentence through the interruption of the direct Vedic text (śruti), it is indeed appropriate.
Therefore, Bārhaspatya maintains that the original *anu* cup is combined [with the new one];

just as in the archetype one takes the *anu* and one takes the *adābhya*, where they are combined with those not belonging to the archetype, so too here the modified (*vaikṛta*) cups should be combined.
Ṭup: First, let us determine this with respect to the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Sentences such as "He draws the cup for Indra and Vāyu" (*aindravāyavaṃ gṛhṇāti*) and "He draws the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa" (*maitrāvaruṇaṃ gṛhṇāti*) are heard in the archetype, as are [injunctions] such as "One should sacrifice with the cup for Indra and Vāyu" (*aindravāyavena yajeta*) and "One should sacrifice with the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa" (*maitrāvaruṇena yajeta*).

If it were heard in this manner [as direct injunctions], then there would be an option (*vikalpa*) between the *lādirādi* [groups] and others; but what is the case? [The author] states that the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) expresses the deity, as in "Indra and Vāyu are its deities."
And since that substance (dravya) is grasped by the accusative case, it is the primary element. Furthermore, the act of "grasping" (gṛhṇāti) is the separation of the substance;
and that act of grasping has a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārtha).
The mention of a deity here serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

This statement was made with the intention that even if one were to assume a visible purpose for the act of grasping (*gṛhṇāti*), since that visible purpose consists precisely in the connection with a deity, it is possible to assert their combination (*samuccaya*).

From the perspective of ultimate truth, however, it is only that which has been perceived [by the senses] that is grasped. As it has been said: "Even when a substance is not [previously] grasped, if it is present at the time of the injunction, it is possible to dedicate it to a deity; therefore, the injunction serves a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*)."
(Vākyapadīya, p. 520) And here too, the Commentator has stated: "The mention of the deity has a visible purpose, namely, the act of distribution" (Bhāṣya, p. 1113). [Ratna:
This is because the deity is not enjoined elsewhere (i.e., in another sentence).

Therefore, because it is not so enjoined (*acoditatvāt*), this same principle applies to the second and subsequent extractions as well—namely, that "the connection with a deity serves an invisible purpose" (*adṛṣṭārtho devatāsaṃyogaḥ*). And since it serves an invisible purpose, there is no evidence that "this Aindravāyava cup performs the function of the Maitrāvaruṇa cup" (which would allow for an option based on syntactic unity).

Therefore, because they produce distinct invisible results through their connection with different deities, these extractions are distinct; that is to say, they must be performed separately and are thus to be combined (*samuccayante*).
In this context, the sacrifice requires a deity, as no deity is mentioned within its own specific designation.

Furthermore, since deities—as expressed through secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*)—cannot exist without a sacrifice, they require a sacrifice. A connection between these two (the sacrifice and the deity) occurs through proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), not through syntactical connection (*vākya*).
And that proximity is common to all the cups (*graha*); therefore, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of both the cups and the deities.
Such is the nature of the case:
the sacrifice is the primary element because it is enjoined for the sake of the fruit;
all the sentences concerning the deities are for its sake, since there is no difference in their proximity.
Therefore, the sacrifice itself is indeed the primary element;
it is repeated by implication.
However, in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*), the [actions] such as "he draws the cup for Indra-Vāyu" are obtained through the extended application (*codaka*) and are thus present.

The other [texts] as well—such as those of Bṛhaspati and others—are indeed included by virtue of their being mentioned in the scriptural tradition (*āmnāna*). Therefore, the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavacana*) grasps all of them simultaneously, because there is no difference in their proximity (*saṃnidhāna*). [Objection]: But in the case of the cups obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal transfer), Bṛhaspati is prescribed as the deity; therefore, since there is no separate extraction (*mādāntara*) there, that case is not an illustration.
[Reply]: It is said in response:
The injunction regarding the deity is not possible, because the word *bārhaspatya* denotes a substance (*dravyavacana*).
It prompts [the understanding] that the staff is subordinate to it, because the person [the sacrificer] is already established [as the primary referent].
It is the same here as well.

How so? (The respondent’s answer: Bṛhaspati, being subordinate (*upasarjana*), is enjoined as the connection between the substance and the deity, which is already obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer). (The opponent says: This cannot be enjoined for the sake of something subordinate, because it lacks the status of a substance (*adravyatvāt*). How is there a lack of capacity? (He answers: In that case [the analysis would be] "Bṛhaspati is the deity of this."

When, in a syntactical construction, there is this relation "this has a deity," and the word *asya* is uttered as a qualifier of the deity, then its utterance is for the sake of another (i.e., for the sake of qualifying the deity), not for its own sake;
it is not for the purpose of an injunction.

When, however, there is a connection between *bṛhaspati* and *asya* (that is, the word *asya* is connected with the word *bṛhaspati*), then its utterance is for its own sake—that is, to enjoin [the offering] as qualified by Bṛhaspati—and not for the sake of another (i.e., for the sake of a qualifier). And when uttered once, an utterance exists that serves both its own purpose and the purpose of another. This is what was previously called "incompetence" (*tadasāmarthyam*).
But when, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the word *asya* is not uttered as a qualifier of the deity, then the word *asya* is indeed primary (and not a qualifier).
For in that case, not only is the word *bṛhaspati-pada* for that purpose, but even the word *devatā* (the deity-indicating term) is for that purpose.
Therefore, the substance qualified by both [qualifiers] together is enjoined (namely, "one should prepare a substance having Bṛhaspati as its deity"), and it is not a subordinate element.
Consequently, it is *bārhaspatya*.
The act of taking [the substance] (grahaṇa) occurs in the case of one desiring a village;
therefore, that which remains after the taking is the means of accomplishment.

The Commentary states: This is recorded in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "One should draw the cups beginning with the *āśvina* for one suffering from illness (*āmayāvin*); one should draw those beginning with the *śukra* for one who has recovered from illness; one should draw those beginning with the *manthin* for one who is being cured.

"Having drawn the Aindravāyava cup, one should set it down; then one should set down that [cup] for whatever desire they might draw it. This shows the postponement (*pratikarṣa*) of the means as well.
The connection [of this section] arises from its departure from the previous case regarding Soma.

No, it is not so; for it is supplementary to the act of grasping, and that is a different matter due to incapacity.

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the *dhārāgrahaṇa* (the drawing of the stream), the established rule (*nityakalpti*) is as follows: having drawn each preceding cup and set it down on the mound (*khara*), one draws each subsequent cup; and when all have been drawn and set down, they are offered in sequence at later times. However, in the case of a desire-based rite (*kāmya*), even when the drawing of the *śukra* and other cups is postponed, it is not merely the act of drawing that is postponed, but rather the means (*sādhana*) itself. This is because the setting down of the preceding cups is an auxiliary (*upakāraka*) to the drawing of the subsequent one; therefore, in the absence of that setting down, the drawing of the subsequent cup—which lacks its supporting basis (*āśrayabhūta*)—would be impossible.

Furthermore, regarding the rule for the performance (*sādhana-niyama*), even if this [act of] taking up is accompanied by the subsequent act of taking up, its meaning is already established as being subordinate to the act of taking up; therefore, if it were performed at the end of the *sattra* sacrifice, it would result in the sublation of that [established order].
Since the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) sublates the sequence of the text (*pāṭhakrama*), there is a "drawing back" (*pratikarṣa*).

However, in reality, because of the scriptural statement following the act of taking up—namely, "having taken up, he sets it down"—and because there is no sequence of the text [contrary to this], there is no obstacle whatsoever to the drawing back.

This is the principle regarding the word "all" (sarva).
The principle of the *hāriyojana* [cup];
the principle of the word "all" (*sarva*) as it occurs in reference to the *hāriyojana*;
[and] in reality, there is no consumption [of the soma] because it is not so prescribed.

The Grāvastut priest should not consume [the Soma]. Why? Because they do not prescribe a consumption for him.
Thinking that the Hāriyojana cup pertains specifically to the Camasins, the author of the Sūtra says this; for thus it is recorded in the sacred tradition: "There is a consumption."
Or rather—it has been concluded through the attainment of the general principle (*samālābha*).
Now, he follows the explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*) itself.

In this regard, there arises a doubt: does this statement—"As each cup-bearer drinks from his own cup, then all indeed desire a share of this Hāriyojana cup"—apply to the entire subject matter by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*) and thereby establish the act of drinking even for those not explicitly mentioned; or, because it is restricted to the cup-bearers (*camasin*) specifically mentioned in its own sentence, does it not? With that very intention, he says: "It does not exist."
Or rather, [the portion] belongs to the Hāriyojana cup, because it is connected with all [the deities].

for thus they have handed down the tradition.
"As they consume the other goblets according to their respective vessels,

therefore, the Grāvastut priest should also consume the Hāriyojana cup,

*Soma* 10.6.11: The word *ca* does not denote an alternative (*paryāya-vacana*) for conjunction (*samuccaya*).

*Dvapu* 10.3.14/156: The word *ca* should be understood as standing in place of the word *tu*, as in the expression "nothing here belongs to you. (In the context of [Jaimini Sūtra] 3.4.30: *acoditaṃ ca karmabhedāt*).
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 3|4|11|30, page 164: the word *ca* (and) serves to include the word *tat* (that), just as in the phrase "whatever occurs here. [And as in:
"The penetration of the qualities (*guṇāveśa*) occurs everywhere" (the meaning being that the penetration of the qualities indeed occurs everywhere).
Bhāṣya 8|3|6|28.
The word *ca* expresses a different meaning through direct hearing (*śruti*) of that which follows it, not through syntactical connection (*vākya*).
For if it were by way of syntactical connection, it would convey this same meaning even when uttered before [the word it qualifies].
The word *ca* is used in the sense of "and" (*cit*).
The word "and" (*ca*), while expressing a conjunction, expresses it as a subordinate element;
the word "and" [is not primary]. 1654: The analogy of the eye and the lamp.
It refers to itself as the primary element.
Therefore, that for which the word "and" (ca) is subordinate is connected with both the action and the quality.
This is established because the effect is understood to reside in the primary element.
In *Ṭup-ṭīkā* 10.3.14.56, the word "ca" (and) expresses conjunction (*samuccaya*), yet not as the primary element.

The word "conjunction" (*samuccaya*), however, expresses conjunction as the primary element. The particle "ca," by contrast, expresses conjunction as a subordinate attribute of the grammatical factor (*kāraka*).
The word *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), but it is not the indicator of the conjunction itself;
rather, it adopts the conjunction for the purpose of qualifying the subsequent word.
For if the conjunction were connected with the action and qualities already indicated, [it would be redundant].
Just as one says, "The collection (*samuccaya*) is beautiful" or "The collection is substantial," so too one might say "the *ca* [particle] is beautiful" or "the *ca* [particle] is substantial.

Furthermore, just as the genitive case occurs here for the two things being collected—as in "the collection of *dhava* and *sadir* trees"—so too one would expect the dual number to occur, as in "the *dhava* and the *khadira*"; yet it does not occur.
Therefore, the word *ca* indicates the collection itself.
Bhāṣya 10.3.14.56: The word *ca* functions as an indicator (*dyotaka*).
Ḍupū 10.3.14.56: By virtue of being a particle (*nipāta*), the word *ca* is non-expressive (*avācaka*) [since particles are indicators].

Soma 6.1.13: Although the word *ca* does not assume the status of a full word (*pada*), nevertheless, due to the lack of a fixed rule for its usage and because it does not denote [an object] on its own, it is employed only after [another word].
For two horses yoked in front do not convey the intended meaning.
*Ratnaprabhā* 10.3.14.56. The word "ca" (and) expresses mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), and that is its meaning.

The *cakraka* (vicious circle) principle: when mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) itself is repeated, it becomes a *cakraka*. And that consists in the nature of being dependent upon what is itself dependent.
For this [self] as well, there is a threefold nature of being self-supported.

卐 The Principle of the Hub of a Wheel (cakranābhinyāya).

In the *Mokṣadharma*, within the dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya (*Mahābhārata* 12.308–309; commentary on verse 11), it is stated: "The unmanifest (*avyakta*), the unevolved (*abhya*), the created (*ākṛta*), *māyā*, the variegated (*śabala*), and the space of the heart (*hārdākāśa*)—these are synonyms denoting the causal Brahman, which consists of the three *guṇas*.
This is known from the usage seen in the expression: 'resting like the nave in a wheel'."
In that context, the object which is inferior, situated within the superior like the nave of a wheel, stands otherwise.
Being asked by you, "What is the Unmanifest? What is the Supreme Brahman? And what is beyond that?", [the answer is] "I am that," O rash one. 76.1.
The Principle of the Whirling Wheel (cakrabhramaṇanyāya):

Just as when the potter's activity—the cause of the wheel's whirling—has ceased, the whirling continues due to the momentum alone even after that error has subsided, so it is in the present case as well. (Even when ignorance is destroyed, there is liberation while living.)
(Compendium) The Bold One. 277. 卐 The Maxim of the Cakravākī and Cakravāka Birds:

It is heard that this pair of water-fowl, being united during the day, sport as they please on the riverbank; at the time of sunset, one of them flies up, goes to the opposite bank, and calls out. Then the other, following suit, flies to the opposite bank; while standing there, he descends [to meet] the one who has arrived; then, standing on the far side, having gone from this shore to the other, he returns. In this manner, they continue until the end of the night.

"During the day they meet again, and at night they are separated"— in this way, when there is an intention to express a specific subject matter, [the text] descends [to this conclusion]. [The statement], "These two Ājyabhāga offerings are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice," is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding the results of the two Ājyabhāgas, but it is not an injunction of results for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Bhāṣya 4.3.12–3: It is understood from observation itself that form is perceived by the eye.
1.1.2.12, p. 16: Even though the eye requires light, form is its object (*artha*;
i.e., its *viṣaya*).
Vārttika 3.2.1.4, p. 747: Even though the generality of impermanence is not apprehended by the eye, its capacity to grasp color-form (*rūpa*) is not contradicted.

Vārttika 3.4.4.13, p. 140: Since the eye possesses the quality of being a grasper through a relationship characterized by fitness (*yogyatā*), it is logical that even that which occupies the same location as the color-form grasped by the eye is not apprehended due to a lack of such fitness.
Sūtra-pañjikā, p. 772: The refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the eyes [in the context of initiation] is not prompted by the fruit [of the ritual].
Bhāṣya 4.3.11–3:
Even for the eye and other [senses], their innate capacity to perceive form is not at all obstructed even when they are covered.
Bṛhatī 194: There is no modification (*ūha*) of words such as "eye" and so forth—which denote substances in a state of conjunction—when they are applied to groups of animals and the like.

Bhāṣya 1.3.10–28: Words such as "eye" (*cakṣus*) do not denote the physical eyeball (*golaka*), but rather denote the capacity for perceiving form (*rūpa-darśana-sāmarthya*), light (*tejas*), subtle matter (*mātra*), and so forth.
Vivaraṇa 1.3.10: The sense organ of sight (*cakṣur-indriya*) consists of rays of light (*tejorashmi-rūpa*). Caturakhatta 1656: The section concerning the fourfold portion (*caturgṛhīta*).
It is performed at home; one offers four spoonfuls (*caturavatta*). The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) or the *sannāyya* is not for the purpose of the oblation itself.

Since the eight-pot-sherd cakes (*aṣṭākapāla*) and others constitute the oblation, when the portioning (*avadāna*) is undertaken according to the rule "he portions twice from the oblation," the act of spreading under (*upastaraṇa*) and pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*)—which are included for the sake of consecrating that portion—is understood through another injunction, and thus the four-fold portion (*caturavatta*) is accomplished. (Bhāṣya 10.8.13.4)

Or [it may be taken] from the principal substance. (Vārttika 4|4|6|9, p. 340). Furthermore, where the fourfold cutting is not accomplished by means of the mantra from the principal substance, there it must be cut four times from the principal substance.
In this case, the fourfold cutting is to be performed upon that [substance]; it does not mean that the state of being fourfold-cut is achieved by taking [bits] here and there. (Bhāṣya 10|8|13|4).
When the purpose is not clarified by a fourfold urging, the rule "twice of the oblation" (*dvir haviṣaḥ*) prescribes a mere number, not an oblation qualified by duality;
thus says the teacher Tuṣṭīṭa. Ke. 5.2.3–4.

In the case of the statement regarding the *caturgṛhīta* (fourfold portion), if one holds the position that the injunction for the oblation (*homa*) is made by restating the *caturgṛhīta*, then even though both [portions] are the subject matter of the two *dvāvadāna* (twofold portions) statements, it is established that the fourth [portion]— in each of the four— is for the sake of the *anuyāja* offerings, while the other is for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings.

Bhāṭṭa 4.1.10: In the fourth chapter, the state of the injunction (*vidhi*) in its form as performance (*prayoga*) has been described. Kaṇikā, p. 412: In the fourth chapter, the section concerning the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the non-instigator (*aprayojaka*) has occurred; therein it must proceed. Bhāṣya 5.1.11–12.
The commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) stated that in the fourth chapter, the definition of the instigator (prayojaka) and the instigated (prayojya) was treated; however, that is incorrect.

Why? Because the author of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) proposed the inquiry into what is for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvartha) and what is for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha); it is precisely that which must be concluded.
It is said:
even the instigator of an instigator is included under the proposition "equality or inequality in the matter" (4.1.8.121).
For when two [factors] are present, even if only one is subordinate (*upasarjanībhūta*), the other is indeed characterized.
Alternatively, one should conclude by stating "the instigator and the non-instigator," because there is a distinction in their definitions based on their unique characteristics (*asādhāraṇya*).
Otherwise, the term *dvādaśāha* (in the third [section], eighth [chapter], and fourth [section], four [verses]) would constitute a single definition.

As long as the remnant is not deposited [according to the *Tantraratna*], there is no occasioning of the substance; rather, it would be the act of sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) that constitutes the occasion. Consequently, in the Vājapeya sacrifice, another vessel would be absolutely necessary to hold the remnant of the *prayāja* for the purpose of sprinkling the *prājāpatya* cups.
In that case, the status of being a disposal (*pratipatti*) is established for the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings with respect to the object to be disposed of.

Now, it may be argued that here "disposal" is indeed employed in the sense of "retention," because otherwise a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) would result, and because that [retention] cannot be performed by anyone else.
For this very reason, in a *sattra* sacrifice, there is the production of common vessels.

It is for this purpose: if, when those [vessels] have been employed, there should be an occasion for negligence on the part of that sacrificer such that the prescribed disposal (*pratipatti*) of the vessels during the *paridhānīya* rite (or others) were omitted, then a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) would result.
If the disposal were not the motive for the retention [of the vessels], then, disregarding the omission of disposal, the use of the vessels by anyone at all might occur.
Therefore, the statement that the remnant of the *prayāja* must be disposed of would be meaningless.

This has been rightly stated by the learned; however, in this case, since the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *prayāja* remnant is accomplished by its sprinkling over the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal for the sacrifice (*ṛtu-paśu*), its retention is not purposeful.
But for the sacrificial oblations (*havir*), the primary [action] is the fourth [offering].

According to Pāṇini 1.4.40, *pratyābhyāṃ śruvaḥ pūrvasya kartā*, when the verbal root *śru* is used in conjunction with the prefixes *prati* or *ā*, the agent of the preceding action [of requesting] is designated as the *saṃpradāna*. For example: *devadattāya gām āśāste pratiśṛṇoti vā* ("He hopes for or promises a cow to Devadatta").
This is because the solicitor is pervaded by the meaning of the verbal roots such as *pratiśravaṇa* (promising).

Regarding the rule *anupratigṛṇaśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.41), when the root *gṛṇāti* is preceded by the prefixes *anu* and *prati* in a co-occurring utterance, the agent of the preceding action—such as the reciter (*śaṃsan*)—is designated as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). As in the example: *adhvaryur hotre 'nugṛṇāti pratigṛṇāti* (the Adhvaryu priest encourages the Hotṛ; the meaning is that the Hotṛ recites and the Adhvaryu provides encouragement). This is because [the agent] is pervaded by the encouragement (*protsāhana*) which is the objective of the verbal root's denotation.
And thus, the dative case is used in its primary sense.

"However, in cases where the object of the verbal root (*dhātvartha-karma*) is being pervaded (*vyāpyamāna*) and no other [object] is possible, there the case-ending of the *upapada* (governing word) applies because it connects with the meaning of the *upapada*—characterized by 'being for that purpose' (*tādarthya*) and so on—and thereby connects with the principal action. This is seen in examples such as *muktaye hariṃ bhajati* ('He worships Hari for the sake of liberation') and *bhaktir jñānāya kalpate* ('Devotion conduces to knowledge').

Here, because the action of 'worshipping' (*bhajanādi*) connects directly as a *kāraka* (participant in an action) through its connection with the implied action of 'attaining' (*prāpti*), and because [the *upapada*] functions metaphorically (*lakṣaṇika*) merely to indicate the state of being an end to be accomplished (*sādhyatva-mātra*), so say the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇāḥ*)."

Others, however, maintain that here the dative case does not function as an *upapada*-case (a case governed by a verbal derivative), but rather functions specifically as a *kāraka*-case characterized by the state of being an object (*sādhyatva*).

For this very reason, they assert that in such instances as "The New and Full Moon sacrifices [are performed] for all desires," the connection with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is accepted as being through the state of being an object.
Others, on the other hand, maintain that even there—in the phrase "all desires"—the dative indeed functions as an *upapada*-case.
Therefore, in cases such as "He establishes the fire" (*agnim ādhatte*), the fact that the accusative case is a "case of the co-occurring word" (*upapada-vibhakti*) must simply be disregarded.

Similarly, in "The lightning is tawny for the wind" (*vātāya kapilā vidyut*), there is a case of the co-occurring word through its connection with an inferred act of cognition; and in "He goes for the sake of fruits" (*phalebhyo yāti*), there is a case of the co-occurring word through its connection with an act of fetching inferred from the suffix *tumun* (the infinitive). In "He goes for the sacrifice" (*yāgāya yāti*), according to Pāṇini 2.3.15–16, there is the status of being a case of the co-occurring word through its connection with an inferred act such as seeing.
In the sense of "a vehicle to be accomplished by sacrifice" (*yāgasādhyaṃ yānam*), however, as before, it is simply a case of a kāraka-case ending.
In the expression "arghya for Janardana" (*janardanāyārghyam*), it is likewise a case of an upapada-case ending, though in another view it is a kāraka-case ending.

The dative case prescribed by Pāṇini 2.3.16—"and [the dative] in connection with *namaḥ*, *svasti*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *alam*, and *vaṣat*"—when used in connection with the word *namaḥ* and others, is an upapada-case ending.
For example, in “*namo haraye*” and “*svayaṃbhuve namaskṛtya*,” the meaning is “in order to propitiate Hari.
However, in the case of “*nārāyaṇaṃ namaskṛtya*,” the dative case is used.

From such applications as these, it follows that the nature of a deity (*devatātva*)—which consists in being connected with the oblation being offered and in having the purpose of manifesting the *sūkta*—is twofold and must be understood as such. This is because, within the section on deities, following the grammatical rule *sā'sya devatā* (Pāṇini 4.2.24), various suffixes such as *ḍhak* and others are prescribed by rules like *agnerḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.133).

In the rule "sā'sya devatā" (that which is its deity), although the two types of *sūkta* (hymns) and *havis* (oblations) are understood as qualifiers because they are mentioned in the locative case, in the aforementioned usages they are perceived through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as being qualified by the referents of words such as "Agni.
This is because that [rule] merely conveys the status of being a deity for those [referents] like Agni which are not otherwise specified.

Consequently, once it is established that the *taddhita* suffix denotes either a *sūkta* or an oblation qualified by Agni and so forth, who are themselves qualified by the status of being a deity, the power (*śakti*) of the suffix resides in the status of being a deity itself, according to the maxim of "not grasping the qualifier unless the qualificand is grasped" (*nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇanyāya*).

Thus, even in cases such as "agnaye svāhā," since the fire (*agni*) is perceived as a qualifier in the act of relinquishing the oblation denoted by the word *svāhā*, and because there is no other possible relation, its status as a qualifier is solely by way of being a deity (*devatātvena*); therefore, the dative case has its primary expressive power (*śakti*) in that sense.
The ancient teachers (*jīrṇāḥ*) maintain that the same applies to the wording of the mantra.
On this point, the venerable ancestors (*pitṛcaraṇāḥ*) [state as follows]:

This Vārttika does not intend to teach that the instrumental case-ending (tṛtīyā) has the power to denote deityhood; rather, while providing a definition for other designators of deity, it refers to the fact that the instrumental case-ending, the words of a mantra, and so forth, indicate deityhood through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
This is because of the statement: "But the indirect [method] is weak.
For instance, the word *devatā* (deity), as well as words ending in taddhita suffixes, the instrumental case, and the accusative case, are the designators of deityhood.

In that regard, since in expressions such as “Agni is the deity” or “Vāta is the deity,” there is a manifestation (*bhāna*) of Agni and others as having the mode of being deities (*devatātva-prakāraka*), the denotative power (*śakti*) resides in both forms of deityhood.
The resulting cognition is: “Agni is the one revealed by the hymn (*sūkta*), or he is related to the relinquishment of the substance (*dravya-tyāga*).

However, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is weaker than this, because it presents the oblation (*havis*) as being located in Agni and others through the conceptualization of relinquishment and so forth.

The dative case (*caturthī*), however, which denotes the status of a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) characterized by being the intended object of the substance being relinquished, is even weaker than that [the genitive], because it indicates the state of being a receiver through a partial metaphorical indication (*ekadeśalakṣaṇā*) involving the exclusion of the act of relinquishment.

Furthermore, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) in expressions such as *viṣṇuṃ yajati* ("he sacrifices to Viṣṇu") is weaker, because it denotes merely the status of being the intended object (*uddeśyatvamātra*) while being metaphorically indicative of the qualified whole.

The status of being a deity (*devatātva*)— which must be postulated because the knowledge of the connection between the mantra and its ritual action is untenable, and which is further postulated because the knowledge of the connection between the mantra and the *dharma* that reveals the mantra is untenable— is extremely weak [as a basis for the meaning of the dative]. Therefore,
they say that the primary power (*śakti*) of the dative case lies only in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradānatva*),
and not in the sense of being a deity.
Regarding this, some maintain that in a sentence containing a *taddhita* suffix and so forth, there is an original (*apūrva*) injunction of the deity.

Others say that, just as by the injunction of the sacrifice the generic substance is implied, so too the generic deity is implied; therefore, it is an injunction of restriction (*niyamavidhi*), whose purpose is to restrict the deity to specific ones such as Indra.
Through the derivation expressed by the *taddhita* suffixes, the dative case endings, and so on, the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) is established for the meaning of its own base (*prakṛti*).

For this very reason, by means of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) following the nominal stem *indrādi*, a single deityhood residing in both nominal stem meanings—namely Indra and Agni—is established as subsisting in the clarified butter (*ājya*).
Likewise, by means of the secondary derivative following the word *mahendra*, deityhood belongs to Mahendra alone; thus, in that case, Indra does not possess deityhood.

Furthermore, being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) consists in possessing a mental apprehension (*dhī*) whose content is the expression of one's own [intention] at a time immediately preceding the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*).

Therefore, since the deity is connected to the preparatory ritual (*prayoga*), the establishment of the Vedic term is understood even through its connection to both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. Further details should be noted in the *Matvākṛtakusumāñjali*.
*Maṇi*, p.
[x]: According to the rule *caturthī saṃpradāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.13), the dative case is used in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) when it is construed with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).
This is defined in the rule *karmaṇā yam abhipraiti sa saṃpradānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.32).
The meaning of the sūtra is that the recipient toward whom one gives by means of the agent of the act of giving is the *saṃpradāna* (recipient).
From the force of the etymological definition—that "it is given to him" (*saṃpradīyate asmai*)—the acquisition of the act of giving is understood.

Accordingly, the authors of the *Nyāyasudhā* and others maintain that the state of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) consists in being the intended object of the substance being relinquished, while simultaneously possessing the nature of acceptance.
Their intention is as follows:
acceptance (*pratigraha*) is that which causes the loss of the fitness for disposal according to one's will;
in the expression "he gives a cow to a Brahmin," the application of this definition is clear.
And the connection of the cow with the Brahmin is one in which [the Brahmin] accepts the status of being the intended recipient (*uddeśyatva*).

In this context, "status of being the intended recipient" means the state of being the object (*viṣayatva*) produced by the utterance of a word ending in the dative case at the time of relinquishment.
Nor is there a lack of evidence for this; for the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) itself serves as the proof.
Having pronounced the name and lineage, one who is endowed with perfect faith should speak, having announced the place, time, and so forth: "I give this unto you."
One should not even mention the cessation of one's own sense of ownership with the thought "this is mine";
thus endowed with faith, one should perform acts such as giving and fire-offerings.

This is also because of the statement of Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha cited by Hemādri: "On the eastern petal, [one should worship] the deities beginning with Indra. For this very reason, since acceptance (*pratigraha*) is forbidden there in the ninth chapter, [the deity] must be accepted as such.
Therefore, the state of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) of the substance being relinquished exists in both the entity in the form of Indra and so forth, and in the word [denoting them].

Alternatively, deityhood (*devatātva*)—defined as being the object of the utterance of a word ending in the dative case at the time of relinquishment—is denoted by the *taddhita* suffix, according to the usage of the elders.

And in cases such as "He offers to Prajāpati" (*prajāpataye juhoti*), there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding such deityhood; thus, the author states in the *Ākara* that this [deityhood] is weaker than that [deityhood expressed by the dative case].

And since acceptance from the seller and others also lacks that [quality of being the primary object], it is included by the first part [of the definition]; thus, the latter part is for the sake of exclusion. Even there, all such things as renunciation are obtainable elsewhere;
only the state of being the intended recipient (*uddeśyatva*) and acceptance are [uniquely] expressed by the dative case.

Thus, through a high degree of indirect succession (*paramparā-sambandha*) and through a coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) constituted by the objective state (*viṣayatā*), there is an application of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) mediated by the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
And so, wherever the instrumental case (*caturthī*) is employed in accordance with such a definition, it is always within the scope of that definition.
This is precisely the intention of the author of the *Kāśikāvṛtti* as well.

According to the Vaiyākaraṇas, however: that which is intended as the goal by virtue of being the recipient of a result produced from the possibility of a connection with the object of a particular action is the *saṃpradāna* (recipient) of that action. In the example "He gives a cow to the Brahmin" (*viprāya gāṃ dadāti*), there is a relationship consisting of ownership initiated by the substance—the cow—which is the object (*karman*) of the act of giving; the result produced by that [relationship] is pleasure and so forth. Since the Brahmin is the intended goal in the form of being the possessor of that [result], he is the *saṃpradāna* of the act of giving; such is the application of the definition.

The intention is that even when wealth is given to Brahmins with the aim of [attaining] heaven for one's father, although the father becomes a partaker of the fruit in the form of heaven and so forth, the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) is not used because the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is intended [as the primary object]. Thus, since both [the use of the fourth case and its absence] are justified, the rule (*sūtra*) would be redundant. Furthermore, the usage "he goes to the village" (*grāmāya gacchati*) is justified on the grounds that the village is the locus of the well-being (*svāsthya*) produced by the act of going.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of the application [of the rule] even in the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*) for *adya* and so forth; for it is established in the Bhāṣya that [the rule] is not rejected with respect to those portions.

For the author of the Bhāṣya does not consider *adya* and the others to fall within the scope of an exception by their own form, because otherwise, in the case of "he goes to *adya*" (*adyaṃ gacchati*), there would be the unwanted consequence of the mandatory application of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*).

Moreover, since both the path and the woman are already reached by virtue of being the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), there would be a restriction of the accusative case in the expressions "he goes along the path" (*panthānaṃ gacchati*) and "he approaches the woman" (*striyaṃ gacchati*). To demonstrate this, [the author] says: "It must be stated that the accusative and dative cases occur when the object (*karman*) has not yet been reached. The author of the Vārttika also accepts this very point. Therefore, it is established that in such instances, the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) according to the Vārttika consists precisely in being the locus of that fruit of the action which does not delimit the meaning of the verbal root.
Thus, by the grammatical rule *ruccarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.33),
the fourth case (*caturthī*) is employed in instances such as *ruce caturdaśarātram*.
The meaning of that [suffix] is "that which went" or "that which goes. And in the present context, that suffix is *ghañ*.

Nor is its purpose already covered by the rule "the dative case is used in the sense of 'for the sake of that' (*tādarthye caturthī*)," because, unlike the infinitive suffix *tumun*, the dative does not establish the state of being for the sake of something else; rather, since there is no reason to bypass the nominative—given that the nominative would otherwise apply by default—the rule prescribing the dative is meaningful.

Furthermore, the suffix *ghañ* cannot be applied solely to the abstract state (*bhāva*), because it would follow that the dative case could be used in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*).

This is because the meaning of the rule "and those expressing an action" (*bhāvavacanāśca*) is that the suffix *ghañ* would be superseded by the suffix *tumun*, which is specifically prescribed for an action performed for the sake of another action; consequently, the dative in the sense of "for the sake of that" would not apply to what ends in *ghañ*.

Therefore, since the suffixes such as *ghañ* are also prescribed in the sense of "for the sake of that," the rule prescribing the dative in the sense of the nominative (as an agent) becomes meaningful when [the suffix] is applied for that purpose.

Thus, by the rule of the grammar (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.3.16), "And [the fourth case ending occurs] in connection with *namas*, *svasti*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *alam*, and *vaṣat*," the fourth case is employed in expressions such as *haraye namaḥ* ("salutation to Hari"), in the sense that the fourth case occurs when these words are joined [with another].

The meaning of the fourth case is the state of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*). And its relation to the verbal meaning is the possession of existence as qualified by the intention directed toward itself.

The status of the case ending as an "upapada-vibhakti" (case ending of a subordinate word) is established because the subordinate word functions as a constituent of the semantic relation and because it serves to indicate the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).

Nor can its purpose be considered redundant on the grounds that it is already covered by the dative case expressing "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*), as in the example "curds for the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇāya dadhi*); for it possesses its own utility in that it precludes the genitive case when used in conjunction with the word *namaḥ*, and it precludes other dative endings when used in conjunction with words whose meaning is "bowing" (*namana*).

However, when *namas* has the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then, because the verbal root functions as a marker for the intentionality that includes the relation [of the object], the accusative case expressing the object—as in "he pays homage to the gods" (*devān namaskaroti*)—is not untenable, since it is a kāraka-case ending. [Examples include:

"well-being to the subjects" (*prajābhyaḥ svasti*), "svāhā to Agni" (*agnaye svāhā*), "svadhā to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ svadhā*), and "Hari is enough for the Daityas" (*daityebhyo harir alam*). In the phrase "enough for the Daityas," the word *alam* has the sense of "paryādi" (i.e., the group of words beginning with *pari*, such as *alam*, *kṣama*, etc.).
And this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of words such as *prabhu*, *samartha*, and *śakta*, because of the usage "he has power over that" (*tasmai prabhavati*).
However, there is no exclusion of the genitive case here;
therefore, there is no contradiction with the expression "the lord of the world" (*prabhur bhuvanasya*, Māgha 1.49).
[The word] *varṣadantyāya* [is used].
The particle *ca* serves to prohibit the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

Similarly, by the rule *manyakarmaṇyanādare vibhāṣāprāṇiṣu* (Pāṇini 1.4.94), which means that when contempt in the form of disregard is intended toward the object of the verb *man* (to think/esteem), provided it is not a living being, the fourth case may optionally be employed; thus, in the example *na tvāṃ tṛṇāya vā manye*, there is an optional fourth case.
In this context, the state of being an object (*karmatva*) is the meaning of the dative case.
Furthermore, here the word "grass" (*tṛṇa*) stands for something similar to grass.
Thus, the meaning is that [the cognition] has as its object something similar to grass; that is to say, it is a cognition having that as its object.
In the knowledge that your actions are like a blade of grass, the distinction between actions—which are here comparable to a blade of grass—is ultimately resolved within you.
And in that context, when there is an intention to express disregard, the resulting meaning is: "I do not consider even you to be equal to a blade of grass. This is the established sense.
Therefore, when there is no intention to express the sense of "having done so many times," the use of the dative case does not apply.
Here, because the word *manye* is employed, the dative case is not used after *manye*.
Therefore, the usage should be "tvāṃ tṛṇaṃ manye" (I consider you a blade of grass).
In this context, having removed the restriction "in the case of inanimate objects," it should be stated: "in the case of a boat, a crow, food, a parrot, a jackal, and a calf.
Consequently, even though these are inanimate objects, there is no dative case in examples such as "na tvāṃ nāvam ahaṃ vā manye" (I do not consider you a boat).
Furthermore, even in the case of sentient beings, the dative case indeed occurs in expressions such as *na tvāṃ śune manye* ("I do not consider you a dog").

Nor does it follow that the dative would consequently apply to the word *yuṣmad* (you) as well, because the object of the verb *man* is indistinct [in both cases]; for the rule "the dative is used when there is disregard" (*anādare*) is intended as a qualification of the object, and thus the injunction of the dative applies specifically to an object that expresses disregard, thereby preventing its over-extension.
Thus, it is established that all dative endings are connected with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).
[The view of] Māṭhara [is as follows]. (Page 101–112).
The dative case in the mantra-text is sublated.

In the passage, "That which he offers in the evening to Agni and to Prajāpati," the dative case serves to establish that Agni alone is the deity; it does not establish that Agni—as qualified by the manifestation [of the deityhood] through the mantra-text—is the deity.

Regarding the doubt that, according to the maxim "in the dative case, the deity is predominant," the action itself must necessarily possess superiority over all things because it is the cause of nourishing all beings;
[this is addressed in] *Śrīkara*, 3.2.37. *Tras.* (Exposition).

Fasting on the fourth day and so forth is the constant practice for all maidens. (Vārttika 1|3|15, p. 205). When the fourth [day] is indicated by a nominal suffix (*taddhita*), the status of being a deity for the gods is established by the word itself; when it is indicated by a sentence, it is established by hearing [the statement].

"The connection with the deity is intended there either by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix, or by the instrumental case, or by the wording of the mantra; and among these, each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding. (Vārttika)

In the full moon sacrifice (Paurṇamāsī), fourteen oblations are offered, and thirteen in the new moon sacrifice (Amāvāsyā). This refers specifically to the transformation of the *vaṣaṭ*-oblation offered in the Āhavanīya fire.

There are fifteen [offerings] in the full moon sacrifice: five *prajāpati* offerings, two *ājyabhāga* portions, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, three *anūyāja* offerings, and the principal oblation (*pradhānāhuti*).
In the new moon sacrifice, there are thirteen: the *saumya* offering together with the *anūyāja*s, two principal oblations, and the remainder is the same as above.
"By fourteen [verses] he sows. In the *Cayana* rite, when the ground has been ploughed, one sows both cultivated (*grāmya*) and wild (*āraṇya*) seeds with fourteen [verses].
*Saṃkalpa* 2.1.15.

"Those desiring stability should perform the fourteen-night rite. This is a sacrificial session (*sattra*); here, there is an extension (*atideśa*) from the twelve-day rite which has become a sacrificial session.

Regarding the fourteen-night rite (caturdaśarātra): the fourth preparation is for the purpose of consumption, because—just as in the case of the fruit of fasting on the fourteenth day and so forth—the fruit of the Agnihotra and other rites also arises from the latent impressions (vāsanā) of previous births; thus, desire is impossible for those who [possess such impressions].
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

Soma 6.12 states that the fourth making (*caturthīkaraṇa*) belongs to the *āgneya-puroḍāśa* alone in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), as it says: "He performs the fourth making for the *āgneya*."

VI. 3.1.16: The fourth division (*caturthākaraṇa*) occurs only in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, specifically for the sake of distributing the *āmeya-puroḍāśa* among the many officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). The assignment, such as "This is for the Brahman," is for the purpose of ensuring that the portions are not intermixed. However, in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* beans, there is no distribution of these portions among the priests at all; furthermore, the assignment [of the portion] to the Brahman alone is not even necessary, and thus those two [acts] do not take place.
X. 2.7: The fourth division in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is performed with the hand.
And the mantras are such as "This for the Brahman," "This for the Adhvaryu," and so forth.

In the Vaiśvadeva *caru* sacrifice, when performed optionally for the purpose of destroying enemies, the fourth portion (*caturthākaraṇa*) is taken with a clearly visible *śamyā*; and the mantra is "I take this portion for the Brahman," "I take this portion for the Adhvaryu," and so on. (Jaiminīya Sūtra 10.1.12, Section 3, the Fourth Portion).

"He divides the *puroḍāśa* into four parts," "He makes the *āgneya* into four parts"—this is the concluding statement. The division into four parts is for the purpose of consumption (*bhakṣa*). Since consumption is heard [in the text], it is associated with the taking [of the portion]; [the division] is for the sake of purchase (*parikraya*).

The Commentary (Bhāṣya): Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "This is for the Brahman priest, this is for the Hotṛ priest, this is for the Adhvaryu priest, this is for the Āgnīdhra priest. In this regard, there is a doubt: is this division of the portions for the purpose of hiring (parikraya), or for the purpose of consumption (bhakṣa)? What is the prima facie view? The division is for the purpose of hiring.
Why? Because of the hearing of the word "eating.
It is not heard that "it should be eaten.
Whatever fault there is in the abandonment of what is explicitly stated, that same fault exists in the postulation of what is not stated.
Food is given to the laborer;
therefore, this is a form of purchase (parikraya).
Alternatively—in the case of the fourfold division of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), the scriptural direction "This for the Brahman," and so forth, is heard.
And how is it that this [gift] becomes a "padyā" for Brahmā and the others if it were not given to them? Therefore, the giving is prescribed.

Now, is that [gift] enjoined for the purpose of hiring (*parikraya*) so as to allow for the priests' disposal of it as they wish, or is it for the purpose of the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the remainder after it has been consumed?
He says: it is for the purpose of hiring.
For here, unlike the case of "The sacrificer and his wife eat the *iḍā*," neither the predominance of the substance nor the act of eating is heard [as the primary injunction].

Therefore, since substances are subsidiary to the ritual action and are given to those engaged in the ritual, even in the absence of an explicit scriptural statement regarding purchase (*parikraya*), they serve the purpose of purchase—just like the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—because they are associated with that [purchase]. Furthermore, because they are connected to that [purchase].

The Commentary states: "This indeed is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Just as the conclusion of the rite is characterized by the sacrificial fee, we consider this [gift] to be for the purpose of hiring (*parikraya*).
The Vārttika says: "'This indeed is the sacrificial fee for the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
For the sacrificial fee is that which confers entitlement upon the officiating priests."
And this is the nature of the purchase:
it is for the purpose of consumption, because of the equality regarding the substance.
Commentary: The division [of the substance] is indeed for the purpose of consumption.

Why? Because of the absence of giving. How so? For it is possible for one who has power to give, not for one who lacks power. Why is there no power? Because the sacrificer, in brief, [says] "this is for the deity."

Furthermore, the learned do not conduct themselves as if they were dealing with a deity through mere mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) alone; rather, they act as if dealing with [the deity] as if it were their own self.
Therefore, it is impossible for [the argument] that follows the practice of the learned to prevail.
Consequently, there is no purchase (*parikraya*).
Now, as for what was said— that "one should not eat what is not heard"— that there is as much fault in the abandonment of what is heard as there is in the postulation of what is unheard—
it is replied: there is a connection with the portions of Brahmā and the others, by means of such expressions as "this is for Brahmā."
In that case, the portions would benefit Brahmā and the others, or Brahmā and the others would benefit the portions.

It is not observed that Brahmā and the others provide any visible benefit to the portions; however, it is possible for some kind of visible benefit to be produced by the portions when they are being consumed as benefactors of Brahmā and the others.
Therefore, the division is for the purpose of consumption.
If it is asked, "What, then, is the harm? [the answer is: there arises the capacity for those who have been satisfied to bring the remainder of the ritual action to completion.

Or rather—he says this to refute the interpretation of others regarding this division: "It has been stated that 'the portions beginning with the Brahman priest do not benefit any substance whatsoever,' but that is because a substance is observed to be required at that specific moment."

(Regarding this, it appears that the *Paddhati* belonging to the Ānandāśrama edition is understood to contain the following commentary: "It does not state that [the act] has the purpose of merely purifying the agent because it is seen," and so forth.
However, we propose the reading *dṛṣṭamityuktaṃ vadati* for the Vārttika, instead of the reading *dṛṣṭamityuktaṃ vadati* [as found in some manuscripts].)

For this very reason, the logical reason (hetu) employed in the passage beginning with "of the substance-moment" (*dravyakṣaṇasya*) is consistent; however, in the reading of the *ṭippaṇī*, that reason would be inconsistent.
Furthermore, by the statement "but [it is] for a portion [of them], being benefactors of Brahmā and others," the necessity of the ritual preparation (*parikriyā*) is even more clearly established.
And it is certainly not the case that they are benefited merely by eating.
For assistance is established even through the seizing (*grahaṇa*), leading (*nayana*), and so forth.
Furthermore, he will state that the consumption (*bhakṣa*) is for the purpose of consecrating the substance (*dravya-saṃskāra*) in all cases (at *Mīmāṃsāsūtra* 12.1.15, sūtras 31–32;
specifically at sūtra 32, where it is said: "Because there is no other way," this consumption of the remnant is not for the sake of livelihood, for it is not sufficient for that purpose).
This has the purpose of consecration (*saṃskāra*), because it serves as a consecration for what has been consumed; thus [it is called] *bhakṣaṇa* (eating/consumption),
since the designation is established by means of such [etymological] factors.
For the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the person are accomplished by means of vows.
(He states the meaning of the Bhāṣya according to his own view: Therefore, it should be stated as follows:

It is true that there is the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the portions; nevertheless, when the requirement for the purpose of this [disposal]—which is to be performed in the present context—is considered, since a visible result exists, one assumes a purificatory rite in the form of capacity for the performers, on the grounds that the invisible result is weaker than the visible one.
And the refinement of the agent consists in the act called "consuming" (bhakṣaṇa) for that which is most internal.
Furthermore, as long as the consumption is not performed after having taken and brought [the substance], there is no benefit because it has not been utilized;
therefore, one must necessarily proceed even to great lengths until the process culminates in consumption.

In this regard, because there is no reason to bypass the first [portion] and because it must necessarily be completed by consuming from the beginning according to its fitness (*yogyatā*), it is understood that one should benefit [the ritual] by consuming the *brahma* portion and so forth.
Furthermore, since the remainder also requires disposal (*kṣapaṇa*), its consumption itself is determined to be the appropriate disposal.
From the assignment (*vyādeśa*), the praise of the gift [is derived].
Commentary: As for the statement that "this is a praise of the sacrificial fees" (*dakṣiṇā*), it will serve to preclude that [praise] because of the commonality of the injunction according to logic.
Or rather, the reference "of the Brahman" and so forth will occur in view of the assistance rendered during the morning ritual;
therefore, it is established that this instruction is for the purpose of consumption.
Śabara: "Since the eating [of the remnant] is not explicitly heard [in the text], its being for that purpose is not understood. [Objection:
Its being for that purpose arises from the fact that it is mentioned in close proximity.
[Reply: It is not so."
For a master may be hired by the gift of wealth, but not one's own self. Ownership belongs to someone else, since the sacrificial offering is given to the deity;
Soma is the purpose [of the rite].

They bring [the portions] for the sake of the sacrificial session (*satra*); no modification should be made if it is for the sake of the sacrifice itself, but it should be made if it is for the sake of consumption (*pratipatti*).
As for the statement, "This is for the Brahman"—is it for the purpose of purchase or for the purpose of consumption?
Since it is for the purpose of consumption, let them employ it as they wish.
Since the entire [cake] has been assigned to the deity, there is no ownership [on the part of the priests].
Therefore, the consumption of the remnant is appropriate only for the purpose of its disposal (*pratipatti*).

In the Bhaṭṭa school, regarding the cake dedicated to Agni (*āgneya-puroḍāśa*) which has been divided into four parts, a scriptural injunction in the form of a distribution is heard, established by the wording of mantras such as "This for Brahman," "This for Hotṛ," and so forth. This is determined through reasoning (*nyāya*).

In considering whether this [gift]—being for the purpose of a ritual service (*parikriyā*) in the form of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—is for the sake of consecrating the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), or whether, being for the purpose of disposal (*pratipatti*) in the form of consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*), it is for the sake of consecrating the remnants (*śeṣa*): since no consumption is heard of in the text, and because the mention of "of the Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*) and so forth would otherwise be strained, it follows—as in the case of the Vāsiṣṭhas—that ownership has been transferred to the Brahman and others. Since that ownership is untenable without a gift, and since even on your own view the assumption of acceptance is possible in the case of the *puroḍāśa* cake as if it were already offered to the deity, it is concluded that here, just as with the *soma-camasa*, a rule for the giving of a fee is inferred for the purpose of consecrating the officiating priests.
For this very reason, the indicative mark (liṅga) found in the text, "This indeed is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the New and Full Moon sacrifices," is also consistent.
Therefore, [the cake] is for the purpose of hiring [a priest].
This being the prima facie view, [we reply]: since the entire sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) has been offered to Agni, the sacrificer is no longer its owner and is thus unable to hire others with it.
Therefore, in your view, there would be the assumption of multiple factors, namely: re-acceptance, giving, and respect.
However, since "acceptance" follows from hearing of the "renunciation," there is no fault even in assuming acceptance.
Consequently, it is better to regard the act itself as the agency of eating, by way of the general relation denoted by the verbal root.

Having postulated a purpose consisting of the cognition of the remaining requirements, the act of eating itself—performed by agents such as Brahmā—is enjoined by means of an injunction based on the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*).

Furthermore, satisfaction (*ānati*) must necessarily be included as being useful for this eating; it is not, however, like a house or gold, useful for another action, because it is unsuitable for that.

Therefore, it is the necessary eating itself that is postulated as the factor effecting the connection, and not another action, due to the complexity [of assuming] actions such as offering (*samarpaṇa*).
Therefore, the dedication of the connection with Brahman itself constitutes the disposal of the remainder.
Having taken it by that means, either personally or through another, the consumption must be accomplished;
the division into four parts is for the purpose of consumption, as in the case of the four handfuls of grass.
Even this [objection] is refuted;
for when the cognition of the necessary eating itself is established through reasoning, it is more cumbersome (gaurava) to postulate another action.
As for the scriptural mention of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), it is a mere explanatory praise (arthavāda), because it serves as a means to a secondary purpose.
Maṇḍana: "The division [of the cake] would not be for the purpose of preparation. Śaṅkara: "In the fourfold division, there is eating.

Just as the fourfold division does not apply to the offering to Indra because it has mixed deities, so too it is not mentioned for the clarified butter of the Upāṃśuyāja because it has mixed deities."
Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 5.4.6.21: The division into four parts is the ritual act to be performed with the remnants.
Vārttika:
The section concerning the division into four parts.

This is the principle of the *āgneya-caturdhākaraṇa-adhikaraṇa* (Bhāṣya 3.1.15.26–27), the principle of the section on the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*). Even when the repetition [of the offering] is made to Indra, the consumption [of the remnant] is accompanied by the mantra, specifically with the words "drunk by Indra" (*indrasya pītasya*).

Although the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) has a collective application (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), the drinking (*pāna*)—or rather, the acceptance denoted by the word *pīta*—exists as an individual application; thus, it can be designated by a single term. Since the relinquishment pertains to the aggregate of both what has been offered (*huta*) and what has not been offered (*ahuta*), it does not pertain solely to that portion which is to be consumed. Therefore, the word *pīta* does not figuratively denote [the whole] through the exclusion of the rest. Consequently, since it is not subject to the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*), its consumption should also be accompanied by the mantra. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin replies]:
according to the principle of the section on the fourfold division (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 3.1.18), because Indra and Agni possess a collective status as the deity (*devatātva*).

Kau. 3|2|18|139 (40). By the logic of the "fourfold division" (*caturdhākaraṇa*), just as in the case of the recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses for the purpose of kindling and illuminating the fire, it is stated that even though the optional (*kāmya*) recitation of the *sāmidhenīs* is a distinct ritual act, its performance within the main sacrifice depends upon the primary injunction due to the force of the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*). Su. p. 1058.

And in the case of an offering to two deities (*dvidevatya*), by the logic of the section on the fourfold division, since Pūṣan alone lacks the status of being the deity [of that specific portion], the grinding (*peṣaṇa*) occurs only where Pūṣan is the sole deity.
Bhaṭṭa. 3|1|15.
The principle of the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇanyāya*).
This is precisely the principle of the fourfold division of the offering to Agni (*āgneyacaturdhākaraṇanyāya*).

Śabarabhāṣya 3.1.15.26–27. In the injunction for the fourfold division, the term *āgneya* does not include an offering dedicated to two deities, but refers only to that which is dedicated to a single deity, Agni.

Bhāṭṭa 5.1.3: According to the determination of the four [theories] and two [others], there is a simultaneous performance (anusamaya); in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, that much constitutes a single ritual act (padārtha). Vārttika 3.1.15.26–27.
The piling (cayana) can be performed in four nights.
Bhāṣya 10.5:
Gold weighing twenty-four mānas is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the introductory (prāyaṇīyā) sacrifice of the Śyenīya.
Bhāṣya 8.1.1.16:
The connection [of the suffixes] is fourfold, twofold, and threefold.

Just as when a certain sick man, having heard from someone that much wealth in the form of cattle, gold, and so forth was to be given to the four gods, said, "I know there are four [gods]," but when saying "the sacrifice (makha) is to be given," he obtained that instead and lost the former; likewise, it should be understood that one who knows only this much—that Brahman is the inner self (pratyagātman) whose nature is being, consciousness, and bliss—and desiring to give that for its sake, whether out of devotion or through the conceit of being a knower of reality, does not attain that [Brahman] and becomes an object of ridicule.
(Sāhasī. 78. The Principle of the Fourfold Manifestation).
There are four arrays (*vyūhas*), which is to say, four divisions.
As stated in the *Pāñcarātra* doctrine, they are designated by the terms "hearing" (*śruti*) and "vision" (*dṛś*) as having their basis in the forms of Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.

Furthermore, in the *Bahvṛca Upaniṣad*, they are designated by the terms "hearing" (*śruti*) and "array" (*ūha*) as having their basis in the body-form, the meter (*chandas*), the person of the Puruṣa, the person of the Veda, and the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*).

In the Sāṃkhya and Pātañjala systems of philosophy, four categories (*vyūha*) are to be expounded: abandonment (*hāna*), the cause of what is to be abandoned (*heyatva-hetu*), and the means of abandonment (*hānopāya*).

Among these, the threefold suffering is that which is to be abandoned; its absolute cessation is abandonment; the non-discrimination (*aviveka*) between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is the cause of what is to be abandoned by way of their conjunction; and discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is the means of abandonment.
In the science of medicine (*cikitsāśāstra*), however, four categories are declared as the fourfold division: disease, health, the etiology (cause), and the remedy.

Likewise, in other scriptures as well, the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*) should be understood according to the possibility; such is the application of this principle. [Śābarabhāṣya 4.1.2] "One should touch the full moon sacrifice with the *caturhotṛ* formula."
"With the *pañcahotṛ* [formula] on the new moon day;
with the *caturhotṛ* [formula], Pṛthivī is the *hotṛ* for the *caturhotṛ* [offerings], and Agnihotrā is the *hotṛ* for the *pañcahotṛ* [offerings]" (Vi.

3.14). "One should touch [the offering] on the full moon day with the *caturhotṛ* [formula], and on the new moon day with the *pañcahotṛ* [formula]"—this restrictive injunction (*vyavasthāvidhi*) must be performed.

"The *camasādhvaryus* [should offer] the cups, because of the designation.

This is the sūtra for the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position in the discussion concerning the knowledge of the duties of the *camasādhvaryus*: regarding those who are the *camasādhvaryus* in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, should they themselves offer the cups, or should others offer the cups?
The *camasādhvaryus* should offer the cups—the Soma-cups—because of their designation, that is, because of the etymological name "cup-attendants" (*camasādhvaryu*).

If their ritual duty did not consist of the offering of the cups accompanied by the oblation, the designation *camasādhvaryu* would be meaningless for them. Therefore, they should offer the oblations.

In this context, because of the designation *camasādhvaryū* (cup-attendants), it is understood that they are employed in all the functions pertaining to the cups (*camasa*). Furthermore, since the accusative case in the word *camasān* can be justified as denoting mere activity (*vyāpāra*), the meaning of the Sūtra is established by supplying a verb, such as: "The cup-attendants should cause the cups to perform their activity. By that same logic, the Adhvaryus [are also included].
Thus he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
By the word "or" (vā), he refutes the prima facie view:

That is the *nyāya* (logical principle) which applies to it; that ritual act of oblation (*homakarma*) is "possessing that *nyāya*," and its state is "the condition of possessing that *nyāya*" (*tannyāyatvam*); [the conclusion follows] from that. Nyāya: Here, the word *nyāya* is derived from the root *nī* with the prefix *adhi*, meaning "that which is led toward" or "attained. It is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Thus, in this context, the word *nyāya* refers to the ritual action (*karman*).

Why? Because of designation by them: "the cup-attendants of the middle-performers," "the cup-attendants of the Hotṛs.
The genitive case occurs when there is a relation of connection.
They are designated by their priestly functions (*ṛtvig*);
they are the masters of those [functions], not the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
And it has been asserted by us that these others are preceded by the sacrificer.
The sacrificer should not choose the *camasādhvaryus* for himself; rather, they should be chosen by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

Bhāṭṭa: "One should choose them"—in this statement regarding the choosing, there is multiplicity, just as there is in the case of the singular.
If it is argued that this is not so because of the lack of parity here, we reply: no, for multiplicity is established by the direct scriptural hearing (*śruti*) of the plural.
Therefore, those who are the *camasādhvaryus* are many, due to the hearing of the plural number in the sentence concerning their appointment.

Although in those cases there is no intention to express plurality because the word functions as a qualifier of the subject (*uddeśya-viśeṣaṇa*), nevertheless—just as in the case of "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*)—the specific qualification is established at the stage of determining the application (*viniyoga-kalpanā-daśā*) due to the impossibility of applying the logic of a purificatory injunction (*saṃskāra-vidhi*).

Following this same line of reasoning, one should understand that in such instances as "He chooses the domestic priest" (*purohitaṃ vṛṇīte*) and "He chooses two Adhvaryus" (*adhvaryū vṛṇīte*), singularity is intended to be expressed.

In reality, however, even though there is application in each respective context, the specific qualification is established by the scriptural mention of plurality or singularity in passages such as "The cup-bearers (*camasādhvaryavaḥ*) follow the cups" and "The Adhvaryus divide [the sacrificial cake] in front."

Maṇḍana: "They are many, because of the scriptural mention of plurality. Śaṅkara: "Even though there is a mention of plurality, they are not distinct individuals; for according to the principle of the *camasādhvaryu* priests, the unity of the *adhvaryu* priest who is being appointed is intended."

The nature of the principle regarding the plurality of the *camasādhvaryu* priests is as follows: In the injunction "He chooses the *camasādhvaryus*," since the connection of the *camasādhvaryus* with the status of agent was not previously established, and because the mere act of choosing them for their own sake would be illogical, they are brought forward as being for the sake of the ritual (*kṛtvartha*) in order to constitute the office of *camasādhvaryu*. By this very sentence, through the origination (*utpatti*) of the *camasādhvaryu* quality, the plurality heard in the origination is intended to be significant because it resides in that which is to be enjoined (*upādeya*).
