The *caru* would be a modification of the *havis*, because of its connection with sacrifice. In the text, “One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* to Sūrya,” the *caru* is mentioned.

In considering whether it is a modification of the potsherds (*kapāla*) or a modification of the oblation (*havis*), and even if it were a modification of the oblation, whether it is a modification of the cooking vessel (*syālī*) or a modification of the cooked rice (*odana*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
the *caru* should be a modification of the oblation, not a modification of the potsherds.

Because of its connection with the sacrifice, as indicated by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in the word "sauryam," it is understood that the *caru* is for the purpose of the sacrifice; therefore, the *caru* is the oblation.
And because it is based on the apprehension of what is well-known:
in the injunction "one should offer a *caru* to Sūrya," the word *caru* would denote a cooking pot (*sthālī*), since it is of such a nature that its meaning is apprehended through common usage.
Indeed, the word *caru* is seen to be employed for a cooking pot from the Himalayas as far as Kumārī.
Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that "caru" refers to a cooking vessel (syālī). However, it is rather cooked rice (odana), because of its connection with that which is to be eaten;
as in the injunction, "One should offer a caru to Sūrya," the caru must be cooked rice, not a vessel.
Because of its connection with that which is fit to be eaten;
for the learned perform sacrifices to the deities using substances that are fit to be eaten,
and a cooking pot is not fit to be eaten.
The word "or" (vā) is for the purpose of excluding the alternative of the cooking-pot (syālī).
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that what is called *caru* is boiled rice (*odana*).
It is not [the pot], because that would be purposeless.
In the injunction “One should offer a *caru* to Sūrya,” the word *caru* does not denote boiled rice (*odana*).
It is well known to refer to a vessel;
otherwise, it would follow that it [the *caru*] is itself a substance.
Furthermore, it is not logical for two meanings to be accepted for a single word;
for if that were so, by the consequence of [the word] being a substance (*dravyatva*), the *caru* would simply be the cooking pot.
This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
"Or it is a modification of the *kapāla* (potsherd), because of the purpose and logical consistency.

Regarding the doubt as to whether, in the injunction "One should offer a *caru* to Sūrya," the *caru* is a modification of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) or a modification of the *kapāla*, it must be a modification of the *kapāla*.
This is because of the purpose and logical consistency.
Even though it is not something to be offered, because the pot (*sthālī*) is edible, the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) "for the Sun" (*sauryam*) is possible;
furthermore, since it is logical to conceive of a sacrifice based on what is cooked in the pot being the offering material (*pradeya-havis*),
therefore the *caru* is a modification of the potsherds (*kapāla-vikāra*), and the meaning of the word *caru* is the cooking-pot (*sthālī*).
Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Regarding the distinction between the subordinate and the principal:

in the injunction, "One should offer a *caru* to Sūrya," the word *caru*—by virtue of being prescribed as the substance to be offered—sets aside the principal *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake) which would otherwise have been obtained through the extended application of the archetypal rule (*codaka*).

If, however, the potsherds were enjoined as subordinate elements for the purpose of baking the *puroḍāśa*, they would be set aside. Since there exists a distinction between the subordinate and the primary—namely, that in the case of *prasaṅga* (incidental application), it is the subordinate that should be set aside, not the primary—it is logical that by the word *caru*, the cooking vessel (*sthālī*) is enjoined for the purpose of baking.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the meaning of the word *caru* is the cooking vessel, which is a modification of the potsherds.
Because, despite the hearing of that word, there is the status of being an oblation for another substance.
Even when that word "caru" is heard—that is, upon its being uttered—only another substance is seen to have the status of an oblation (*havis*).
For example, having prescribed, "One should offer a *caru* in ghee for Prajāpati, consisting of a hundred *kṛṣṇala* [berries]," it is further stated, "He should eat four *kṛṣṇalas* at each interval."
In this case, although the word *caru* is heard, it is well known that the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) consists specifically of *kṛṣṇala* seeds.
Likewise, in the present instance as well— in the injunction "One should offer a *caru* to Sūrya"— the *caru* would be a cooking pot (*syāli*),
and the oblation would be what is placed within that pot.
Therefore, the meaning of the word *caru* must be the cooking pot (*syālī*), and that [pot] is a modification of a sacrificial pan (*kapāla*).
This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

In the statement, "One desiring a village should offer a *caru* of *praiyajña* grains cooked in the milk of spotted cows," the meaning of the word *caru* is the cooking pot; thus, the *priyajña* is the oblation (*havis*) and the oblation is something else, and that which is called *caru* would be prepared in the cooking pot.
This indicative mark (liṅga) is seen in the case of the oblation (havis). Likewise, it would also apply here in the passage, "One should offer a caru-oblation to Sūrya.
Therefore, the meaning of the word *caru* must be a cooking vessel (*syālī*).
And that [caru] is a modification of a potsherd;
or rather, it is cooked rice (odana) because it is what is employed [in the ritual].
In the injunction "One should offer a caru to Sūrya," the caru must be cooked rice itself, not a cooking vessel.

The word "vā" (or) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Regarding the term *caru*, it is a modification of the sacrificial oblation (*haviḥ*) known as *caru*. This is the section on the *caru* (*caru-adhikaraṇam*).

Because it is employed from boiled rice (*odana*) as far as the Himalayas and even among young girls; because it is a clear, established metaphor for that which has not been winnowed; therefore, the word *caru* refers to boiled rice.
The modification concerns the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), not the modification of the potsherds (*kapāla*);
nor, in this context, does the word *caru* refer to a cooking vessel (*syālī*).
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
And because of the designation as something unprecedented:

"The gods placed the *puroḍāśa* in this world, and the *caru* in that world. Thus, there is a designation of the *caru*—the boiled rice—as something unprecedented. It is said that while the *puroḍāśa* brings prosperity in this world, the *caru* brings prosperity even in the next world; therefore, the *caru* is declared to be superior.
That which takes the place of the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake) must be *odana* (boiled rice) itself, not a cooking pot.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that what is called *caru* is indeed *odana*, a modification of the sacrificial oblation (*havirvikāra*).
And there is also the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*):

having prescribed, "The *prāyaṇīya* oblation is a rice-porridge for Aditi; the *udayanīya* [oblation] is for Aditi," and then stating, "Aditi with the *odana*," there is likewise this observation of an indicative mark that what is called 'rice-porridge' (*caru*) is indeed *odana*.

Therefore, the *saurya* rice-porridge (*caru*) is a modification of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), namely boiled rice (*odana*), and not a modification of the potsherds (*kapāla*); nor is the *caru* here a cooking vessel (*syālī*).
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Who [holds this view]?

In the case of the *caru* oblation, these many ritual acts (*dharmas*) are to be understood: placing the pot on the fire, sprinkling water over it, removing the embers with the mantra "Bring [the gods] to the place of sacrifice," placing the pot on the fire with the ladle using the mantra "Thou art firm," pouring ordinary water into it and adding the rice grains with the mantra "The ritual duties are thine," carrying fire around it, giving the command "O Agni, slay the Rākṣasas," pouring clarified butter over it with the mantra "May it swell," taking it off the fire with the mantra "When cooked, he bathes," and pouring butter over it again with the mantra "Moist, he goes forth," and so on.

The sublated [elements], however, are: the consecrated waters (*praṇītāḥ*), the grinding (*peṣaṇam*), placing the embers upon the cooking pot (*sthālī*), the muttering of mantras during the joining of the potsherds (*kapālayogajapaḥ*), the pouring together (*saṃvāpaḥ*), the kneading (*saṃyavanam*), the forming of the lump (*piṇḍīkaraṇam*), the spreading out (*prayaṇam*), the making of the crust (*tvakkaraṇam*), placing the embers over the oblation (*havir-aṅgārabhasāyāropaḥ*), the pouring of water (*āpyāninayanam*), the preparing of the seat (*sadanakaraṇam*), and the removal from the embers (*masāyāduddharaḥ*). The removal (*nyuddharaṇam*) is included because it serves the same purpose as the original. Also included are [mantras] such as "He who is your self" (*yasta ātmā*) and "Below each joint" (*adhastāt pratyajñam*). In all these cases, the loss of purpose (*arthalopaḥ*) is to be understood through reflection.

At the piling of the fire-altar, there is a sacrificial porridge of wild rice for the purpose of placing the bricks.
The meaning of that [word] is connected with the word whose own meaning is already established, because of its connection with the Vedic text.
Commentary: There is the Agni sacrifice. In that context, after stating, "There is a sacrificial pap made of wild rice (naivāra)," they recite, "That he places this sacrificial pap."

In this regard, a doubt arises: is the *caru* intended for the purpose of sacrifice, such that what remains after performing the sacrifice is to be used for the laying down [of bricks], or is it intended solely for the purpose of the laying down itself?
We say it is for the purpose of sacrifice;
for the well-known function of the *caru* is sacrifice, not the laying down.
It is said:

although it is well known that the *caru* (gruel) is for the purpose of sacrifice, nevertheless, because of the absence of a connection with a statement regarding a deity and because of the absence of a connection with the word *yajati* (he sacrifices), it is understood that it is not for the purpose of sacrifice.
To this, it is replied:

In the supplementary portion of that very passage, it is heard: "The wild rice (nīvāra) is indeed the food of Bṛhaspati. Therefore, by means of this proximate statement regarding deityhood, there will be syntactic unity; thus, Bṛhaspati’s status as the deity is for the purpose of the placing (upadhāna).
Consequently, the conclusion reached is that the caru is for the sake of a sacrifice.
This being the position, we reply:

It is enjoined by means of a word expressing its own meaning (svārtha) conjoined with a word expressing the action (kārya); therefore, it must serve that very purpose, namely for the sake of the placing (upadhāna). Furthermore, its syntactical unity (ekavākyatva) with the act of placing is direct (pratyakṣa), whereas its connection with the mention of the deity is only inferable (anumeya).
For the statement "He places the *caru*" is a direct (perceptual) injunction,
whereas "He places the *bārhaspatya*" is inferential;
therefore, the entire *caru* is to be placed.
And consequently, if it were employed in some other sacrifice, that which was intended for one place would become performed elsewhere.
As for the statement, "The wild rice (nīvāra) belongs to Bṛhaspati," that is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
Furthermore, as for what was said—that the well-known status of the cooked rice (caru) as being for the purpose of sacrifice is contradicted by the mention of its established nature—it is not so.

Therefore, it is established that [the formula] is for the purpose of placing [the vessel]. Or rather: previously, [the formula was used] at each taking of the animal victim; but this [formula], however, is for the purpose of the pouring out [of the grain] by way of the sacrificial porridge (caru).
The undertaking here is because the term "deity" (*devatā*) is predominant within this context.
In that regard, the status of the *caru*, *puroḍāśa*, and other offerings as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice is innate (*autpattika*).
And in every respect, the relinquishment of one's own ownership (*ātmīyatva*) of these must be performed.
And because of the use of the accusative case in the injunction "He places the *caru*," the act of placing (*upadhāna*) is a disposal (*pratipatti*).
Furthermore, a disposal is not appropriate for that which has no other use elsewhere.
Thus, by virtue of its suitability, it is established that the *caru* serves as a means for the sacrifice.
Furthermore, if what is heard as a supplement to the statement of Bṛhaspati were not connected with the injunctive portion, it would be utterly meaningless.

Therefore, the conclusion reached is that one should prepare an oblation of cooked rice (caru) for Bṛhaspati modeled after the Āgneya sacrifice, and having prepared it, the rice should be placed [upon the fire] without performing the other subsequent rites.
This being the position reached, [the author states: "In this situation..."
We reply:
"The *cara* and other such elements are not established as inherently incapable [of performing a function].
Their application is understood precisely according to how they are obtained."

For when there is a need for a purpose regarding the mere act of placing [the vessel], the direct injunction is seen in the form, "He places this *caru*," which indicates it as having a desired result by being an auxiliary to the sacrifice, namely, "That he places this *caru*.
Furthermore, once the *caru* has its requirement satisfied, it could not have a connection with another function even through a directly stated one, much less through an unstated sacrifice.
Nor can this be a disposal (*pratipatti*), because its utility is not perceived at the outset.

Furthermore, even in the case of a purposeful ritual act (*arthakarman*), there is primacy with respect to the placement (*upadhāna*); therefore, it does not bring about an unrefined location. Thus, there is no distinction in the use of the accusative case.

"And the connection of this sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the deity is threefold and inferential, because of the absence of *taddhita* suffixes and the like found in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning *nīvāra* grain."
Being connected with *nīvāra* rice, it is inferred that this pertains to the *caru* offering of Bṛhaspati;
likewise, the remainder of the sentence must be interpreted so as not to require a connection with a deity for the injunctive portion (*vidhyuddeśa*).

Otherwise, the status of being a deity would have to be postulated in some way through the use of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), the dative case, or the wording of a mantra, and so forth.
Furthermore, the labor involved in inferring [the deity] through sacrifices and the like remains as it was;
therefore, it is more appropriate to employ [the mantra] solely for the purpose of mental concentration (*upadhāna*).

And for those [passages] where there is an auditory mention of a deity in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)—such as "it belongs to Bṛhaspati" (*bārhaspatyo bhavati*)—which functions as the locus for the rule regarding the *caru* offering, even for them, since the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*) for the initial placing [of the bricks] is already established, the deity cannot be enjoined because there is no further expectancy. Consequently, in accordance with the statement of an existing fact (*vartamānāpadeśa*), we understand that this [mention of the deity] is merely cited for the sake of praise, exactly as we observe the state of belonging to Bṛhaspati (*bārhaspatyatva*) to exist in the present. Furthermore, the meaning of this Taittirīya statement, "this is indeed the food of Bṛhaspati," which is the conclusion of the scripture, is determined to be the very same as that of the statement "it belongs to Bṛhaspati."
Therefore, this [term *caru*] also does not denote an act of sacrifice (*yajimat*), until its status as being used according to its literal meaning is established.
As for the connection [of this section]: it arises from an objection based on the dissimilarity with the previous case.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: the *caru* is connected with the word "purpose" (*artha*), which is a word denoting an effect (*kārya*) and is associated with the term "upadhāti"; thus, it is not for the purpose of a sacrifice, because of its direct connection with the Vedic text (*śruti*).

And its status as being for the purpose of placing [the bricks] should be understood with the intention that even the *caru* (gruel), which has the purpose of consecrating the placement, serves as an instrumental means (*sādhana*) by implication. As stated in the *Citrādhikaraṇa*: "The *caru* is made of wild rice; he places the *caru*. Is this a sacrifice or a placement? It is a sacrifice, because the deity has been mentioned as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*)."
Having performed the sacrifice,
the section concerning the vessel for the *caru* [stating] the word *caru*.
Since the remainder is not to be expected when certainty [of the purpose] exists, how could there be a sacrifice?
Rather, it remains as merely a placing, exactly as stated, within the *caru*.
Bhāṭṭa: It is heard in the *Agni* [section]: "He places the sacrificial pap (*caru*); for nivāra grains are indeed the food of Bṛhaspati.

Here, how could the food of the sacrificer be the food of Bṛhaspati unless Bṛhaspati were the deity? Thus, by implication, Bṛhaspati is understood to be the deity; furthermore, because the Taittirīya recension contains the supplementary statement containing a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) word, namely, "It belongs to Bṛhaspati (*bārhaspatya*)," this is indeed an injunction of a sacrifice inferred through the relationship between the substance and the deity.

And since that [oblation] consists of medicinal substances, when the disposal (*pratipatti*) such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering would apply from the perspective of the *āgneya* and other [deities], the act of placing (*upadhāna*) is enjoined as a disposal by the statement, "He places the *caru*.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), although there is the hearing of a *taddhita* suffix in the Taittirīya recension, nevertheless, due to the absence of an injunction and because it would result in breaking the syntactical unity with another injunction, this is not a *taddhita* suffix denoting a deity.

By the statement "he places the *caru*," since the injunction for placing (*upadhāna*) is intended as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *caru* that produces the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and because there is no requirement for a deity, one cannot postulate an injunction regarding a deity even if such an injunction were inferred from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
For this very reason, an injunction is postulated for the *nīvāra* grain itself, which serves as the required material substance (*prakṛtidravya*) for the *caru*.

Consequently, since the praise "the *nīvāra* belongs to Bṛhaspati" found in the Brāhmaṇa is thus logically consistent, it is established that the phrase "of Bṛhaspati" does not, by means of postulating a deity, establish a sacrifice.
Maṇḍana: "In the placing of the *caru* oblation, there is no sacrifice (*yajati*). Śaṅkara: "It would be the same even in the placing of the *caru* oblation;
thus, there is an absence of sacrifice."
The section concerning the *caru* vessel as an accessory (*carupadhānādhikaraṇa*).

Since the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning Bṛhaspati cannot possibly have another purpose, and since the necessity of postulating a deity mentioned in the *arthavāda* entails the validity of postulating a sacrifice, the principle [of the *muktaka*] would apply. (This is the body of the *nyāya*). Ko. 2.3.7.18.
Beauty (*carutva*) consists in having a nature characterized by unstable forms.
Here, the portion of rice (*bhakta*) is "unstable" according to its own logic;
the *maṇḍaka* (scum) is "inside" according to its own logic.
"And from *sūpa*, *śākhā*, etc., [the suffix is applied] when *taṇḍula* follows. (Bhāṭṭadīpikā 1.3.14).

The ritual properties (*dharma*) of the *caru* (offering to Bṛhaspati) come first because it is situated in the middle; after that, the ritual properties of the *ājya* (clarified butter) of the Sārasvata [offering].

In the *Adhvarakalpa*, the Bārhaspatya cake is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the Agni offering which occurs first, and the Sārasvata clarified butter is a modification of the Upāṃśuyāja offering which occurs later. (Vi. 5.1.10). This is the principle of the *caru-padhāna-adhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the placing of the *caru*). (Saṃkarṣa. 1.3.21).

The logical principle (*nyāya*), however, is as follows: "Even though the action of dividing [the sacrificial cake] occurs after the series of actions beginning with the sowing of the rice and ending with its kneading into a dough, because it remains part of the archetypal rite (*prakṛta*), the mantras for that subsidiary act proceed at that very time and not at the time of offering, since the subsidiaries must follow the primary.

Where a single lump is prescribed for many sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the mantra for dividing must be employed precisely at the time of offering. This is because at the time of offering, the division of the oblation (*havis*) is necessary; thus, according to the logic of the section on *caru* and *puroḍāśa* (*Saṃkarṣa* 1.3.12), the division-mantra should be used at the moment of offering. (*Saṃkarṣa* 1.3.24).
Some maintain that the status of the *caru*, *puroḍāśa*, and other such items as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice is based solely on scriptural injunction (*autpattika*).
[They argue: "The nature of the *caru* and other items does not inherently establish them for this purpose;
rather, their application (*viniyoga*) is understood precisely as it is established by scripture."
Or rather: Vārttika 2.3.7.18. When there is the presence of two heaps consisting of *caru* and *puroḍāśa*, the designation of the deities must be performed by combining them.
In those very cases where there is no intermingling (*vyatiṣa*), there should be no mention of the deities, because there is no determination [of them] among those other [deities].
However, in the case of intermingled [deities], since a contradiction with the sequence would arise, it follows that—

given the absence of any authority for subverting what is obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer)— one must indeed perform the mention of the deities by way of conjunction, in the manner of "this [belongs] to such-and-such and also to such-and-such."
In the absence of that [distinction], since the doubt would arise as to which heap should be divided— and because such an uncertainty would obstruct the performance of the ritual sequence (Saṃkarṣa.
two heaps must be made when the sacrificial materials consist of both *caru* and *puroḍāśa*, for the purpose of threshing and other preparatory rites of the oblations.
Where rice-porridges (*caru*) and sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are intermingled, there, for the sake of maintaining the sequence, they should be divided one by one.

This being the prima facie view, [the conclusion is]: since there is no deviation from the sequence when the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is common, two heaps alone should be made simultaneously—one for all the porridges and one for all the sacrificial cakes.
(Saṃkarṣa 1.3.22)
The word *caru* denotes a medicinal herb (or sacrificial food).
Bhāṣya 8.1.9.18: The word *caru* is also used for a lump of flour, as in "a flour-caru is prepared.
1.3.14.38: They apply the word *caru* figuratively to well-cooked boiled rice (*odana*).
For in the Piṣṭapaśu sacrifice, the flour-mixture (*piṣṭaka*) would indeed be like the omentum (*vapā*).

From the Himalayas to the land of the Kumārīs, all common people, having added some letter such as *ga* or *va* at the end according to the conventions of their own regional dialects, employ the word *caru*— as in *caruī*, *caru*, or *carvī*— to refer to a small vessel made of copper or other materials used as a receptacle for cooking.
Thus, *caru* is a cooking-pot (*sthālī*).

Nevertheless, in such injunctions as "one should offer a *caru* to Sūrya," the word *caru* is to be understood as referring to clearly cooked rice consisting of husked grains that have not yet been winnowed. (Vi.

In the sacrifice to Sūrya, there is a sublation of the original oblation by the boiled rice denoted by the word *caru*. [The sūtra states: "The *caru* would be a modification of the oblation, because of its connection [with the deity].
The Bhāṣya says: "The *caru* is heard [in the scripture]."
"One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer a caru-oblation to Sūrya.

It has been established that this offering to Sūrya is a modification (vikāra) of the offering to Agni. Regarding this, it is said: "Within a single chapter, [the application] is restricted; for the qualification is as before."
In this regard, the Sāṃkhya view is as follows: Is the *caru* a modification of the *kapāla* (potsherds), or a modification of the *havis* (sacrificial oblation)?
When it is a modification of the *havis*, is the *havis* prepared in a cooking-pot (*sthālī*), or is it rice (*odana*)?
What, then, is the prima facie position? It should be a modification of the *havis*.
Why? Because of its connection with the *iḍā* offering.
For that [offering] is prescribed for the *caru*; and by means of the *odana* (boiled rice) denoted by the word *caru*, the two [portions] are [connected].

Furthermore, since there is no evidence for accepting a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix in the sense of a general relationship, the pot and the oblation are enjoined as being like the *kṛṣṇala* grain.
Consequently, it would either be the original oblation itself, or,
because rice porridge (*odana*) here is suitable for the injunction of an oblation, it would be a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

In that case as well, because the word *caru*—by virtue of its established usage among ritualists (*yājñika*)—does not have a fixed etymological meaning, and because it has been established in the third book (*adhyāya*) that it denotes boiled rice (*odana*) used as the material for the sacrificial staff (*daṇḍa-prakṛti*), it replaces the cooking pot (*sthālī*). Therefore, since the cooking of the rice would otherwise be impossible, the pot is obtained by implication; and because it thus takes the place of the potsherds (*kapāla*), the ritual duties pertaining to the potsherds—such as placing them down (*āsādana*) and offering (*pradāna*)—need not be performed upon it. Furthermore, since the *caru* is cooked within the vessel, the *praṇītā* waters and their associated duties certainly apply to it as well.

In this way, grinding (peṣaṇa) is also set aside for the sake of the *caru*, because the *caru* is accomplished even without it, since its production occurs independently of the *puroḍāśa*. The same applies to the placing of the potsherds (*upadhāna*) and other properties of the potsherds.

In reality, however, in the injunction "the placing of the potsherd" (*kapālasyopadhātā*), the potsherd is intended [as the object] just as the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is; furthermore, the status of being the locus for cooking the oblation resides in the cooking-pot (*sthālī*).

Regarding the bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices: the bringing forward of the fire in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices occurs only during the two middle seasonal festivals (*parvan*).
The bringing forward [of the fire] in the first and last [festivals] is excluded because of the prohibition of the *uttaravedi* (high altar).
The Commentary states: "It is heard in the scripture, 'They lead forth two.
In this regard, there is a doubt as to which two. When no specific rule has been established, it is said in reply:"
The carrying forward of the fires occurs at the first and the last [sacrifices].
Why? Because of the prohibition of the *uttaravedi* (high altar).
In that context, the *uttaravedi* is prohibited: "They do not prepare the *uttaravedi* for the Vaiśvadeva, nor for the Śunāsīrīya."

In this ritual procedure (praṇayana), the placing of the fires on the northern altar (uttaravedi) is prescribed; therefore, wherever there is a carrying forward of the fire, there the northern altar is obtained. And since it is thus obtained, there follows a prohibition [of its use].
And this [fire] belongs to the first and the last;
therefore, its leading forward is performed for those two.
Or rather, it belongs to the middle two, because of the explanatory passage concerning the act of going.
Commentary: Or rather, the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) takes place on the two middle *parvan*s. Why? Because of the explanatory statement regarding movement (*gatyarthavāda*).
This is to be understood through the explanatory statement regarding movement: "Therefore, he goes by means of these two," which speaks of the carrying forward.
And these two sections are inferred [to be praised as such] in the passage: "The *guṇapradhāta* and the *sākamedha* are indeed the thighs of the sacrifice.
For the thigh is a means of locomotion;
thus, the connection for this praise is understood.
The Varuṇapraghāsas and the Sākamedhas are the two thighs of the sacrifice. They lead forward the fires for these two;
therefore, the sacrifice reaches its completion through these two alone.
For by means of being carried forward (*praṇayana*), those two become powerful, because they have become constituent parts (*aṅga*).
This is the purpose of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in that context. There is a prohibition regarding the altar of the Uttaravedi based on a general statement (*anārabhyavāda*).
Commentary: Now, regarding what was stated—"because of the prohibition of the *uttaravedi* (high altar)"—we reply as follows.
Without reference to any specific section (*parvan*) among the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the *uttaravedi* is prescribed [by the rule] "they pile it up here" (*upātra vapanti*).
This prohibition refers to that general injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*).
Objection: Since the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings are already established by the subsidiary injunctions, this statement "of these very [offerings] here" would merely be a restatement of them.
Response: This is not so; because of the context, it refers to the Cāturmāsya sacrifices as a whole.
If this were a statement concerning the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, then in that prohibition, one would have mentioned all three seasonal festivals (parvan).
If it should be argued that let it be a statement concerning two festivals, we reply:
there is no context for two festivals, nor is there a context for the Varuṇapraghāsas.
In the context of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, there would be no mention of two seasonal festivals (parvan) in the prohibition;
therefore, this is indeed a statement concerning the Cāturmāsya sacrifices as a whole.
[Objection: Even so, it is understood from the explanatory passage (arthavāda) that the carrying forward of the fires (praṇayana) occurs in the middle two months.
For what purpose is there a further hearing of the *praṇayana* (carrying forward) which has already been established?
No specific purpose has been stated here.
In the absence of another purpose, it serves solely for the sake of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*).
In that regard, defects have been stated.
Therefore, this hearing is solely for the sake of qualities.
But surely, there is no quality whatsoever?
It is said:
A quality is heard in the injunction for placing the fire on the *uttaravedi*;
therefore, there is a restatement for that purpose.

Ḍupa:—(Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya has explained two sections: the eighth by means of the four sūtras beginning with *atra saumikam*, and the ninth by means of the three sūtras beginning with *prathamottamayoḥ*.
However, having examined that, the author of the Vārttika has explained all seven sūtras as constituting a single section.

This is the Vārttika: "If the original mode of fetching [the water] is established, then the hearing of these words is for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*)," and so forth—these sūtras are mutually disconnected.

How so? When there is an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*)—namely, "they lead forward the fire for the two middle [pressings] alone"—then, because of the absence of leading forward for the other two, there is an absence of the *āhavanīya* fire; and due to the absence of the *āhavanīya*, there is an absence of sacrifice. Furthermore, the leading forward of the fire does not belong to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices as a mere property (*dharma*), such that when an exclusive specification of the property alone is made, the leading forward would be performed for the other two in a purely non-ritualistic manner.
Nor is it possible for it to be an injunction of a quality (*guṇadharma*).

How so? Where, within that very same sentence, having mentioned the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), a quality is enjoined—as in "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) or "The sacrificial grass consists of *śara* grass" (*śaramayaṃ barhirbhavati*)—there an injunction of a quality occurs.
But here, nothing whatsoever is enjoined regarding the act of leading forward (*praṇayana*).

If it is argued that there is a rule for the *uttaravedi* altar, we say no; because the *uttaravedi* is heard mentioned in a separate sentence from the sentence concerning its bringing forward (*praṇayana*).
Furthermore, an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is inappropriate here [as a rule], for an explanatory passage occurs only where something is being enjoined.

The *praṇayana* (carrying forward of the fire) is prescribed for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; however, since it is not so prescribed here, what is the purpose of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)? (In this very context, because of the introduction to the refutation of the *arthavāda*, he bypasses the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) sūtra of the immediately preceding section—"of the first and the last"—and refutes its concluding (*siddhānta*) sūtra: "Or rather, [it applies] to the middle two, because of the explanatory passage regarding the movement. This too is untenable. Why? Because the *praṇayana* is heard again in the context of the *varuṇapraghāsa* and *ākamedha* sacrifices, it is indeed appropriate as an explanatory passage through syntactic unity with the injunction of the *praṇayana*.
And regarding that [prescriptive] position (*vidhipakṣa*), the fault has already been stated [in the section on *parisaṃkhyā*].

Likewise, this sūtra—"The carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of the first and last [fires] is [required] because of the prohibition of the *uttaravedi*"—is also not applicable when the original (*prākṛta*) carrying forward remains in force.
For the meaning of this sūtra is as follows: [regarding] the carrying forward of the fire...
Regarding the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the carrying forward of the fire (agnipraṇayana) is obtained;
therefore, wherever there is the carrying forward of the fire, there is the fire, and in that very place the high altar (uttaravedi) is obtained.
Or rather, [the fire] is preparatory;

therefore, where it is prohibited in the context of the Vaiśvadeva and Śunāsīrīya sacrifices, there the fire is enjoined (for, a prohibition presupposes a prior application; thus, its application to those two is inferred). And in that very case, the carrying forth [of the fire] (*praṇayana*) is also inferred.
For fire does not exist without the act of leading forward (*praṇayana*).

By this indicative mark (*liṅga*)—the prohibition of the *uttaravedi*—it is determined (through a series of inferences) that the leading forward occurs at the first and last [sacrifices]. However, this sūtra is incoherent.
How is it incorrect?— If the original procedure (*praṇayana*) were established, there would be no room for doubt,
and the restrictive rule (*niyamapakṣa*) would be followed.
Therefore, the sūtra "of the first and the last" would be irrelevant as a subsequent statement.
He states that this [position] itself is untenable: "Because the *uttaravedi* is not applicable.
Regarding the position that "it occurs in the first and last [pressings]" based on the prohibition of the *uttaravedi*, there is no basis for its root.

Furthermore, as for the sūtra stating, "Or rather, in the middle two, because of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the movement," the refutation has already been stated in the context of criticizing that *arthavāda*.
He recalls that very point: "Because the *praṇayana* (carrying forward of the fire) has not been prescribed, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is not applicable.

(Thus, demonstrating that the Sūtra—"The prohibition of the *auttaravedika* [is] a non-contextual statement (*anārabhyavāda*)"—is also inconsistent, he shows the meaning of the Sūtra by explaining the Bhāṣya: "But surely, since they are already obtained through the qualifying statements of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, this statement 'they sow here' would refer to those very sacrifices" (this is the Bhāṣya).

What is the meaning of this? (He shows it here: Regarding the statement "they strew [the altar] here" (*upātra vapanti*), since the *uttaravedi* (northern altar) is obtained for the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices alone due to the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), [the Bhāṣya]—having raised the objection that the attainment of the *uttaravedi* involves an ablative case (*pañcamī*) used with the elision of a verbal suffix (*lyablope*)—states [the following] as a refutation of that objection: "In that case, if there were a prohibition, all three sections would have been mentioned. This explains the impossibility of the prohibition regarding the first and last [sections].

(Thus he explains the *Bhāṣya* on refutation: If, within the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices (of all three sessions), the prohibition regarding the *uttaravedi* were to be performed because of their equality (the logical connection being that since it applies to the others by default, a prohibition must be made of what has been obtained through the force of the context), this would not be a restatement for the sake of praise (*tiyānuvāda*) (as that would result in pointlessness). Where a prohibition functions as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)—as in the case of the prohibition against using the word *girā* (where the meaning of the Vedic text is actually *irā*)—there the prohibition constitutes a restatement for the sake of praise.
But this is not the case here.

Therefore, because it is heard as not being commenced [independently], the *uttaravedi* altar— which is obtained without distinction for the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices— is excluded from the first and the last [of those sacrifices].
Thus, the Sūtras do not fit within the context of the ordinary (*prākṛta*) carrying forward of the fire;
therefore, it is explained otherwise.

For here there are two positions: [regarding the statement] "they carry it forward for both"—does it refer to the carrying forward belonging to the Darśa sacrifice, or is a new, extraordinary (*apūrva*) carrying forward, characterized by the properties of carrying forward, being enjoined?

In this context, having first set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "this [fire-installation] is indeed for the *dārśika* [sacrifice]," it is negated by the word "but" (*tu*) in the statement: "But the bringing forward [of the fire] belongs to the *saumika* [sacrifice]"— the reading in the *Tantraratna* being thus,
whereas in the *Ṛjuvimalā* commentary on this very point,
the reading is "But the bringing forward belongs to the *saumika*."
In this way, the word "but" (*tu*) becomes meaningful in the phrase "the carrying forward, however" (*praṇayanaṃ tu*).
This is precisely the explanation of the commentary on the sūtra: "And the prohibition of the *uttaravedi* is likewise.
And [the sūtra] "Or rather, it is the archetypal [one], because it lacks a specific name" (*prākṛtaṃ vā'nāmatvāt*) is the sūtra of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The meaning of this is: an unprecedented (*apūrva*) carrying forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), not preceded by the original model (*aprakṛtipūrva*), is prescribed for the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices. Specifically, in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, the carrying forward of the fire belonging to the Soma sacrifice (*saumika-praṇayana*)—from which the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) has been excluded—is enjoined for the first and last [of the four seasonal sacrifices].
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"The term 'he leads forward' (praṇayati) is not a designation for that which pertains to the Soma sacrifice;
and if it were a restatement of the archetypal [rite], the scriptural statement would be purposeless."
Therefore, this act of "leading forth" (*praṇayati*) is not part of the original model sacrifice (*prakṛta*), but belongs to the Soma sacrifice;
it must be stated that it is a new (*apūrva*) leading forth of the fire, because it is performed on a specific day.
[The word] "Soma" indicates its connection with the obtained subsidiary elements (*prāptāṅga*).
Vi— "Because of the occurrence [of the rule] between the first and last intermediate joints;
by the force of the root *ru*, it would occur between the middle joints of the first and last [sections].
This is because of the prohibition resulting from a secondary application (*prasañja*) and a counter-application (*pratisañja*)."
(This has been stated according to the Bhāṣya;
however, according to the Vārttika: "Because it is not a name [of the sacrifice] and because it would be redundant, the carrying forward of the water is neither Soma-related nor archetypal.
That carrying forward is a new element for which another hall is prepared."
The statement from another recensional branch (*śākhā*) says, "They carry the fire forward from the *āhavanīya*. Therefore, the statement here—"they carry it forward for two"—is as follows.

Regarding the second section (*adhikaraṇa*), according to the opinion of the *Bhāṣya*, there arises the inquiry whether this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) concerning the first and last fires, or the middle two; [the conclusion is] that it concerns the middle two, because in that case, the *uttaravedi* altar is obtained there.
Because it would otherwise result in the impossibility of [the rule] extending up to those limits for the first and last [sacrifices], this prohibition must indeed pertain to the first and last.
Consequently, since the *uttaravedi* (northern altar) applies only there, this prohibition also applies only there; thus, for those two, the *uttaravedi* is optional.

Because the statement, "He goes with two," and "Verily, these two belong to him—the Varuṇapraghāsas and the Sākamedhas"—is for the purpose of the *praṇayana* (carrying forward of the fire), and because that [usage] would be improper [if applied elsewhere], this restatement refers only to the middle [sacrifices], due to the restrictive application of the *uttaravedi*.

Thus, since there is no possibility of obtaining the *uttaravedi* (northern altar) in the first and last [parvans], the prohibition of it therein is a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*). And its application is expressed by the passage beginning with "They strew [the grass] here" (*upātra vapanti*). This constitutes the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) for the Varuṇapraghāsa. For in the absence of this, since the *uttaravedi* read within that intermediate context would necessarily be an auxiliary only to that [specific rite], the prohibition would be a permanent restatement only for the other three parvans, not for two.

Therefore, since both [the intermediate and the great] contexts apply to all auxiliary parts by virtue of the force of the constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) of the two, the restriction of the *uttaravedi* altar to the middle two [days] by the statement "they lead forward [the fire] on two days" is appropriate. Nor should it be argued that even so, because the intermediate context is set aside by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the first and last days, the production and application of the *uttaravedi* would be established as pertaining only to the middle days, rendering the statement "they lead forward on two days" redundant.

For by the statement "He places the fire on the *uttaravedi*," the *uttaravedi* is not enjoined as a restatement of the act of placing (*nidhāna*), because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is it enjoined as a restatement of the placing of the fire, because that would result in the fire being restricted to a specific location. Nor is it enjoined with reference to the fire in general, because that would result in the *uttaravedi* being required even for the *gārhapatya* and other fires.

However, because it operates prior to the application of extended injunction (*atideśa*), the prescription of the archetype qualified by the *uttaravedi* altar is enjoined by means of another location, having the *uttaravedi* alone as its result.

Consequently, in the absence of an original (archetypal) injunction for the carrying forward of the fire (*praṇayana*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of that [altar] occurring even during the placing of the fire for heating the potsherds (*kapāla*), just as in the case of the placing of the fire for the *praṇītā* water. But when the original injunction for *praṇayana* exists, since that very injunction—which is more immediate—requires a location, the place for the *uttaravedi* is prescribed first according to the rule of extended injunction; therefore, there is no occurrence of the *uttaravedi* during the placing of the fire for the purpose of heating and so forth.

For this very reason, even though the injunction for carrying [the fire] exists as a direct teaching (*aupadeśika*) for one case, the application of the *uttaravedi* altar would follow for the other two cases because the carrying of the fire exists there only by extension (*ātideśika*).
This is rejected;

Therefore, even according to the view of the Bhāṣyakāra, there is no room for the criticism stated by the Vārtikakāra. The justification for the Vārtikakāra’s position, however, is as follows: the first sixty-three sūtras constitute a single adhikaraṇa. Furthermore, even in the *Sākamedha* sacrifice, according to the *Kalpasūtras* of Baudhāyana and others, because one must assume an injunction that prescribes [the carrying] immediately after the [initial] *praṇayana*—since it has the same meaning as this [text]—it is understood that it prescribes [the carrying] immediately after the *praṇayana*. Consequently, since the sentence "They carry [the fire] for both" (*dvayoḥ praṇayanti*) is likewise determined to prescribe [the carrying] immediately after the *praṇayana* with the *Āhavanīya* as its point of departure, it is untenable for it to be a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*) of the original (*prākṛta*) *praṇayana*. Therefore, a new (*apūrva*) [carrying] with the *Āhavanīya* as its point of departure is enjoined immediately after the original *praṇayana*.

However, because of the specific injunctions—"A Brāhmaṇa in spring, a Rājanya in summer, a Vaiśya in autumn"—this [general rule] must, in that case, serve to prescribe the times for the Brāhmaṇas and others based on their respective status.
And thus, there is a distinction: for the Brāhmaṇas and others, the time [for study] is fixed, but for the Śūdra, it is not fixed.
Therefore, the Śūdra also has the qualification [to study]. If it is argued that this is not so because of a deficiency [in his status], [we reply: no.
The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) raises an objection:

since the *bārhadira* and other *sāmans*, the *payaḥ* and other vows, and the commencement with *adya* and so forth belong to the Brāhmaṇas and others, and the Śūdra is devoid of these, his ritual action would be deficient (*vaiguṇya*).
If the proponent should say that because of this deficiency—due to the occurrence of such a defect—the Śūdra’s performance of the rite is not possible; [this is the objection].
No, because it is optional. The proponent refutes the doubt raised by the opponent:
"The defect of deficiency does not apply."
Because it is something desired, the Śūdra will desire it. A particular *brahmasāman* named *abhīvarta* has been taught without reference to any specific context;
that the Śūdra will desire.
Regarding the statement, "One should establish the fires with four omens," the Śūdra will desire this fire-establishment (*ādhāna*) which has no fixed sequence.
Furthermore, since the vow for a Śūdra has already been declared as "curd (*mastu*) is for the Śūdra," he will desire that as well.
And thus, there would be no deficiency;
and because the presence of excellence is possible, he too has the qualification for ritual action,
since the refinement [of the body] is primary in that regard.
On that very point, the proponent states another reason.
The letter *śa* has the sense of adding another reason.

Since the vow (*vrata*) is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person, it is subordinate to him; because the person is the primary factor, there is no deficiency even in the absence of the consumption of the vow-food.
For milk and other such substances possess the status of being *dharma* (religious duty) specifically for the purpose of generating capacity (*sāmarthya*).
However, a person who possesses the necessary capacity even without consuming the ritual fast-food (*vrata*) performs the sacrifice independently of that requirement;
therefore, there is no deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) even in the absence of the fast-food.
Therefore, there is no contradiction even in the Śūdra’s entitlement to perform ritual acts.
(Mīmāṃsākośa 213) Because of the distinction of the four castes; [and] regarding the black antelope horn in the *cātvāla* pit. (1698)
Alternatively, it is understood from the Vedic injunction that [Vedic rites] are for those other than Śūdras.
The word "api" (even/also) serves to refute the prima facie view.

Regarding the term "apaśūdrāṇām" (of those other than Śūdras): since in the section on initiation (*upanayana*) the Veda specifies only those castes beginning with Ādityas as being [eligible], it is understood that Vedic ritual action belongs only to those other than Śūdras, and not to Śūdras.

After the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), there is the study of the Vedas; after that, the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas; and following that, Vedic ritual action (*vaidika-karma*) is to be performed.
Since for Śūdras there is no initiation at all, how could they perform Vedic ritual action?
In the section concerning initiation, it is stated: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring, a Kṣatriya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn"; thus, only the three [higher] castes are specified.
"If it is argued that [the Śūdra may study] because of his desire for the qualities [of the ritual]," the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says:

"Let there be no initiation ceremony for the Śūdra; nevertheless, when even a Śūdra desires the Vedic study which is a quality of the ritual action, then, because of his desire for those qualities—that is, his desire for study—he will study by himself. Through that, he will possess the capacity for the ritual action."
"What is the use of the initiation ceremony?
Since its purpose is the acquisition of virtues, one should not suspect an absence of Vedic study.
If the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) should say this:
"Because the sacrament has that as its purpose, the mention of the person (*puruṣa*) occurs in relation to knowledge (*vidyā*). The proponent (*siddhāntin*) says:

Since the sacrament in the form of initiation (*upanayana*) has that as its purpose—namely, the purpose of Vedic study—the scriptural mention of persons such as Brāhmaṇas in passages like "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa [should initiate]" is established as being merely a causal condition (*nimitta*) for the acquisition of knowledge.
It is performed by the preceptor through the act of initiation;
and one becomes a preceptor by means of teaching the Veda.
Therefore, for the study of the Veda, the [obligations] heard in the scriptures regarding persons apply to the Brāhmaṇa.

But for a Śūdra, the study of the Veda has not been prescribed. Therefore, because he is uninitiated and thus lacks knowledge of the Veda, the Śūdra is incapable and is not entitled to perform ritual acts.
[Objection: But what about the mention of "learning" (vidyā)?

"A Śūdra will impart knowledge; he will study even that which has not been [formally] taught," so says the *Bhāṣya*. "Because of the imparting of knowledge (*vidyā-nirdeśāt*), there is an option [to study]," so says the *Subodhinī*.

Regarding the statement that because there is no formal instruction for the study of the Veda (*vidyāyā vedādhyayanasya anirdeśāt*)—that is, an absence of instruction regarding it as a duty—a Śūdra, having acquired the Veda through other means such as examining manuscripts, will perform the ritual acts, and there will be no deficiency (*vaiguṇya*); this is the view of the *Kutūhala*.

If the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) should argue that, in the same way, even a Śūdra possesses the qualification for ritual action because he can possess knowledge, the proponent might say: "Since it is not sanctioned by the Veda, there would be an absence of qualification for ritual action. To this objection raised by the proponent—that a Śūdra, having acquired knowledge through means such as examining books and so forth, will perform the rituals—the proponent (siddhāntin) replies:
One who possesses knowledge is a *vaidya* (learned person);
a *śūdra*, however, is not a *vaidya*.
For it is prohibited that a *śūdra* should study, according to the injunction: "A *śūdra* must not study."
Even if knowledge is acquired through the study of books and similar means, no fruit will result; rather, a fault arises.
Therefore, according to the scriptures, a Śūdra is indeed unlearned (avaidya). Due to this lack of learning, there would be an absence of eligibility for ritual action (karman).
Therefore, the Śūdra has no entitlement [to Vedic study].
Likewise, there is an observation of another point [in the scriptures] to this effect.
The phrase "and likewise" (tathā ca) means: "In this regard, there is no study for the Śūdra."
In this regard, there is the observation of indicative marks (liṅga) bearing a different meaning:
"The Śūdra is indeed a cremation ground; therefore, one should not study in the vicinity of a Śūdra"; "Upon hearing the Veda, there shall be the filling of the ears with molten lead";
and "Upon its utterance, the tongue shall be cut off; upon its retention, the body shall be split asunder."
From this observation of indicative marks, the absence of knowledge for the Śūdra is clear. Because of his lack of knowledge, the Śūdra has no entitlement to the Agnihotra and other rites;
such is the established conclusion (siddhānta).

In the passages "one should beg alms from the four castes," "one should beg alms with [the word] 'bhavat' at the beginning," and "one should beg alms among Brāhmaṇas," the rule is restricted by the concluding statement; it is not a general injunction for those who have not received permission. (Bālambhaṭṭī, p. 17). The Rathakāra, who is distinct from the four castes, has the entitlement to perform the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) ceremony.
Bhāṣya 6.1.214:

Just as in the case of wealth belonging to the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), there is a distribution of the hearing [of the word] part by part (in the case of the *sṛkvāka* [lip-corner] and *sudhā* [mortar]).

For example, in common worldly usage, when it is said, "Wealth is to be given to those of the four castes," it is well known that for the wealth designated as "the knowledge of the four Vedas," a fourth part belongs to each knower of a single Veda; thus, there is a connection with the parts.
Or [it is said]:

"Looking at the *cātvāla* pit, they chant with the *krauñca-sāman* during the *mahāvrata*. (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa). "He throws the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit"—this is an injunction for a secondary act (*guṇakarma*) in the form of a disposal (*pratipatti*), which serves a visible purpose.
(The *kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā* is the horn of a black antelope;
Bāla. p. 13). "He throws the *kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā* into the *cātvāla* pit"—this is the comprehension of the subject matter as enjoined by the number and other factors [of the injunction]. (p. 24).
This is a *pratipatti-karman* (disposal rite) performed subsequent to the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*).

• In the Dvādaśāha sacrifice, on the final day, the throwing away of the black antelope horn at the Cātvāla pit occurs because of its connection with the desire to perform the subsequent [rites] after the giving of the sacrificial fees. 1699. Because of the connection with the desire to perform [the rites].
[This is] the subsequent [point].
And the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*) functions starting from the time of the first consecration (*dīkṣā*).
Bhāṣya 1.1.3.14.13–14. Furthermore, the throwing away of the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit is not the primary motive (*prayojaka*) for its use.
The lunar year (*cāndramasa-saṃvatsara*) consists of three hundred and fifty-four days (*Bhāṣya* 6.1.12–18).
In the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, only lunar months (*cāndra-māsa*) are to be taken, not solar (*sāvana*) ones (*Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa* 3.1.18).
The *Cāndrāyaṇa* is a specific penance (*prāyaścitta*) to be completed within a month.
In that regard, an increase or decrease is made in the number of mouthfuls of food;
from that [system], there arise the *pipīlikāmadhya*, the *yavamadhya*, the *municāndrāyaṇa*, and so forth.
Furthermore, he refutes the view of the Cārvāka, who maintains that the self is nothing more than the body.
This is to be seen in the discussion on *āmravāda* (Vārttika 2.1.2.15, pp.
401–02). Some proponents of the Cārvāka school maintain that there is no such thing as a genus (*jāti*) at all.
