22) [This is] the Cārvāka doctrine. Alternatively, one may resort to the view of the Great Teacher (*Suguru*): we perceive that these three Vedas are merely conventional usage (*vyavahāra-mātra*).
"It is maintained by the wise as a restraint for the sake of accomplishing the worldly course of life.
"By [this] view, the straightforward ones subsist," so it is said in the *Bṛhatī*, p. 208.

"This is merely for the sake of worldly convention; it is devoid of any unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭa-prayojana*). Though proclaimed in the three Vedas, well-restrained, and well-employed, we see that it is hypocritical in nature and must be maintained.
As they say: "The *agnihotra* sacrifice, the three Vedas, the triple staff, and smearing oneself with ashes—Bṛhaspati says these are the livelihood of those bereft of intelligence and manliness."
Thus [ends the section].
This is the *cālanī-nyāya* (the logic of the winnowing-basket).
Just as a winnowing-basket discards the essence and retains only the chaff, so it is in the present case as well.

Furthermore, just as all grains and the like fall through the holes of a winnowing fan (*cālanī*), so too, where it is possible for all the things to be excluded—whether they be the objects of definition (*lakṣya*) and so forth, or those that are pervaded (*vyāpya*)—activity [of the definition] occurs therein.

For example, when the definition of "pervader" (*vyāpaka*) involves the absence whose counter-positive is the probandum (*sādhya*), since the absence of the mountain-fire exists in the locus of the kitchen-fire, and since the absence whose counter-positive is fire exists in each respective locus, there would be an absence of fire for all fires according to the definition of a pervader. Thus, [the definition fails].

[The altar] is one thousand [square feet]. 327. Regarding the statement "And because of the connection with the desire to perform" (*cikīrṣayā ca saṃyogāt*), Bhaṭṭasomeśvara has stated in the section on *cikīrṣayā ca saṃyogāt* (3.7.13) that the phrase "I shall be able to perform it" (*iti śakṣyāmahe kartuṃ*) is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the injunction regarding the measurement of the great Soma-altar (*saumikamahāvedi*) as being thirty-six steps; it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in the form of an injunction concerning location. (Kauṣītaki-bhāṣya 2.1.5.12, p. 84; Bālakṛṣṇa, p. 57). [The altar is] one thousand [square feet], and because of the connection with the desire to perform.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the altar (vedi) is prescribed as follows: "Thirty-six steps long, twenty-four steps wide, thirty steps deep; we shall be able to perform [the rite] to this extent.
The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that this altar is intended solely for the sake of the principal (pradhāna) rite, not for the sake of the subsidiary rites (aṅga).
Regarding this, there is the following sūtra:

The word "of the principal" (*pradhānasya*) is carried over from the preceding sūtra. The word "great altar" (*mahāvedi*), however, is supplied according to the subject matter of the relevant passage.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the great altar should belong to the principal [sacrifice] alone.

Why? Because of its connection with the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*). According to the rule *samānakartṛkeṣu tumun* (Pāṇini 3.3.158), which states that the suffix *tumun* occurs after a verbal root when there is a word expressing a desire (*icchā*) having the same agent (*ekakartṛka*) as an attendant word (*upapada*), the word "to do" (*kartum*)—ending in the suffix *tumun* prescribed for desire—expresses the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*). This is understood from the sentence "In this much [space], we shall be able to perform it. Furthermore, since only the primary element is desired to be performed because it is the means to the result, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the altar (*vedi*) is for the sake of the primary element.
In the previous sūtra, the reason "because of the connection with the fruit" was stated; here, the word *ca* (and) serves the purpose of providing an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
For if that were so, there would be a desire to perform everything because of the scriptural mention of the fruit.
Rejecting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) established by the [previous] sūtra with the word *tu* (but), he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The scriptural statement regarding the result, namely, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," applies when the primary rite is performed together with its subsidiaries.

The meaning is that the result is heard as being directly [attained] from this [composite act], not from the primary alone. Therefore, because the result belongs to the whole including the subsidiaries, the desire to perform (*cikīrṣā*) pertains to all—the subsidiaries as well as the primary. Thus, the desire to perform, or the wish to do, expressed by the sentence "I shall be able to do it," would apply to all of them.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the great altar (*mahāvedi*) serves the purpose of both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the principal rite (*pradhāna*). Regarding this, the *Sudhā* commentary states: because the subsidiary, which was previously mentioned in connection with the principal rite and is presented here as its correlative (*pratiyogin*), is referred to by the word "that" (*tat*), the third-case (*tṛtīyā*) hearing in the phrase "by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma" (*jyotiṣṭomena*) establishes the Jyotiṣṭoma as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Because the fruit-contemplation (*phalabhāvanā*) of Thomas [the primary sacrifice] and the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of what is mentioned elsewhere possess a relative means-status, and because the means-status known as *ātithya* (hospitality) is of a minor form and thus dependent upon a lower-order desire for results, there is a scriptural declaration of a fruit (*phalaśruti*) with respect to the subsidiary (*aṅga*) in relation to the principal (*pradhāna*). Therefore, even though the subsidiary is directly connected to the fruit, since it is connected to the fruit by way of the injunction of that connection, the desire to perform (*cikīrṣā*) is possible for every principal and subsidiary. Consequently, because the connection with the desire to perform exists even in the case of the subsidiaries—which is the reason for excluding them [from the fruit]—it does not serve as a differentiator.

In this context, since the measure of the connection with the desire to act (*cikīrṣā-saṃyoga*) is equal, and because the altar (*vedi*) possesses authority as something intended to be performed by its own [text], the word *tu* (but) serves to refute the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it pertains solely to the primary rite—[a view] reached through mere indicative marks (*liṅga-mātra*). Thus, it is introduced as the reasoning for the principal final conclusion (*mukhya-siddhānta-yukti*). Page 317, line 8. Ke. x: The Chapter on the Desire to Act (*Cikīrṣādhyāya*).
The altar of the Soma sacrifice serves the purpose of both the subsidiary and the principal rites;
and there is a desire to perform it because of its connection [with the sacrifice].
The Bhāṣya states: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "Thirty-six steps toward the east, twenty-four toward the north, thirty toward the rear—at this much space am I able."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is this [injunctive] Vedic statement for the sake of both the subsidiary and the principal acts, or is it for the sake of the principal act alone? What, then, is the prima facie position? It is that, because of its connection with the desire to perform (*cikīrṣā*), it is for the sake of the principal act. What is this "desire to perform"? It is the thought, "I am capable. This [statement] is heard as being for the purpose of that which is desired to be performed, namely, "I am able to do this."

And it is the primary element that he intends to perform, not the subsidiaries; for the primary element possesses the fruit, whereas the subsidiaries do not. He asks: "If the subsidiaries are not intended to be performed, why are they performed?"
It is said:
unintended actions are performed.
Even though those [actions] are not intended to be done, nevertheless, by means of those unintended [actions], other things are intended to be done.
"Its own [suffixes] are applied"—this refers to that which one intends to perform; its Veda is for that purpose. Therefore, it is for the sake of the primary object.
Let it remain for now as an unsettled point.
Or rather—by the aforementioned reasoning, the sacrificial altar (*saumikī vedī*) is understood to be intended solely for the primary rite.
It is designated in this way precisely with reference to that which one intends to perform, thinking, "I am able to do so much upon this [altar]."

That which is intended to be performed is like the fruit [of the action], not the injunctions; for, while they are not themselves what is intended to be performed, they are employed as the means for accomplishing that which is intended to be performed. While this point has not yet been fully concluded, he introduces another line of inquiry.
"But when that [subordinate] is connected, the scriptural mention of the fruit would apply; thus there would be a desire to perform everything.
Commentary: This is the reply to what was established previously.
As for what was stated—that the primary act is what is intended to be performed, not the subsidiaries, and therefore the fruit belongs to the primary—regarding that:
When that [action] is joined [with the result],
there is a declaration of the fruit;
the fruit is heard directly.
Therefore, that which is intended to be done directly [must be performed].
Although the ignorant [actions] are not what is intended to be done, nevertheless they must be performed on the altar;
otherwise, it would not be as if they were performed directly on the altar.

Or rather—since the altar (*vedi*) consists of a specific location, its connection with place and time is determined by its being the object of the performance of both the primary and auxiliary rites; thus, it serves all purposes.

As for the connection with the desire to perform (*cikīrṣā-saṃyoga*), that too is understood to have that [performance] as its object, because the attainment of the fruit depends upon the performance. Therefore, since it is determined to be something to be brought about by the primary rite along with its auxiliaries, it must also serve the purpose of the auxiliaries.
This being the case, [the altar] must be performed in the modifications (*vikāra*) of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice and others, such as the *nirūḍhapaśu* and so forth.

Soma: Just as the primary acts alone possess fruitfulness, and therefore acts such as shaving (*vapana*), which are useful for the accomplishment of that fruit, serve the purpose of the primary acts alone; likewise, for that very reason, since it is the primary act alone that is intended to be performed (*cikīrṣita*), the altar (*vedi*) connected with it also serves the purpose of that alone—this is the connection (*saṃgati*) because of this counter-argument (*pratyavasthāna*). Vi: The Soma-altar (*saumikī vedī*) has the primary act as its purpose, by means of the primary [act].

Because it is the primary object intended to be performed, and because its performance does not occur on the altar [of the mind], yet because it is the cause of the full perfection of the primary rite, that which is intended to be performed is an auxiliary to it;
therefore, like the primary rite itself, it is beneficial even to those ignorant of the altar.
Bhaṭṭa: Having established an altar (*vedi*) measuring thirty-six steps and so forth, it is heard in scripture: "I am able to perform [the sacrifice] upon this much.

Although that altar, by virtue of its location, would apply to both the subsidiaries and the principal rite, nevertheless, because of the aforementioned statement regarding the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the sacrificial fire (*agni*), it serves the purpose of the principal rite alone.

For by the suffix *tumun* in the word "to do" (*kartum*), which expresses desire, there is the cognition that the object is intended to be performed; and since it is the primary act alone that is intended to be performed, and because subsidiary acts—even those not themselves intended to be performed—are carried out solely for the sake of the primary act that is intended to be performed, the altar (*vedi*) is for the purpose of the primary act alone.

[It is said in reply: Although the altar has as its object that which is intended to be performed, nevertheless, because the officiant intends the attainment of the fruit for the entire ritual together with its subsidiaries, it belongs to both the subsidiary and the primary.
In reality, however, because it is a location, its status as being for the sake of both the subsidiary and the primary is established through the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself.
This statement, "I am capable in this much," is merely an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise).

For this very reason, by accepting that the expression "I am capable" serves only to indicate the activity of the agent, its application to both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary rite (*pradhāna*) is also rejected.

Therefore, the altar (*vedi*) serves all purposes; and since its measurement is established in the archetypal rites (*prakṛti*) such as the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice through the taking up of the oblation materials (*havirādāna*), its extension (*atideśa*) to the modified rites (*vikṛti*) is thereby established.

As for what will be stated—that there is an extension (*prasaṅga*) of the twelve-fold natural altar—that is done by considering it as being merely for the purpose of the performers' activity, as a hypothetical deliberation (*kṛtvācintā*). According to the chapter on the desire to perform (*cikīrṣādhyāya*), the section on the *cityā* altar states: "The Soma-altar is for the sake of the ritual together with its subsidiaries."
Śaṅkara: Like Maṇḍana.

[Objection: By the third chapter on "Desire to Act" (3.1.17–9), since [substances] such as curd would have as their object the performance of both the primary and auxiliary rites, there arises the contingency that they serve all purposes.
Vārttika 3.1.19.

The term *citi* refers to the construction of an altar (*vedi*) of various shapes, such as those of birds and so forth, on a plot of land that has been ploughed with a plow; this is the *cit* (altar).
Furthermore, each individual layer (*stara*) therein constitutes the "Principle of the Variegated Substratum" (*citrādhikaraṇa*), which is the "Principle of the Variegated Limbs" (*citrāṅganyāya*).
This sixth [verse] is for the purpose of establishing [the number];
and with reference to those [verses] along with the *purīṣa*, there will be a praise by way of the number twelve.
This is because of the contradiction between the number six and the number twelve belonging to one and the same thing.
Even when the inference is unequal, there occurs a sequential enumeration as if it were equal, such as: "The gods, humans, and ancestors—they were from another [place].
Śā—In that case, the ordinal suffix would not apply because it is not the completion of the number six;
for this [number] could complete it only when joined with the five, and not by itself.
It is not so; for the word "yat" (which) clearly expresses the causality of non-abiding. The completion of the number six would occur with reference to the act of denotation.

Soma: This is a case of extended application (*atideśika*) of connection. The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: the fire-altar consisting of six layers (*ṣaṭ-citika agni*) should be permanent (*nitya*), just like the previous one, or like the *dadhi-graha* offering;

or rather, "just like the previous one" means that the state of having five layers (*pañca-cititva*) applies, such that the sixth layer (*ṣaṣṭhī citiḥ*) should also be permanent, just like the five layers.
Vi— "The sixth [fire] is either eternal or produced by consciousness; it is the last because it depends on five.
Because it depends on the substratum, the last is produced by a cause."

Bhaṭṭa: In that very context, the sixth layer (*ṣaṣṭhī citiḥ*) mentioned in the scripture—namely, "He who, having piled the fire-altar, has not established it; there are five previous layers, and then he piles the sixth layer"—is indeed contingent (*naimittikī*), because the non-establishment is the occasion (*nimitta*) for it, by virtue of the force of the relative pronoun (*yat-śabda*) through the resolution of the existence of the introductory statement.
As for the fact that in the conclusion the suffix in *ṣaṣṭhīm* serves to complete the number six, that depends upon the expression itself and not upon the actual performance.
It means that while five layers were intended previously, now the sixth is also intended.

Therefore, following the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicaya*), when the occasion of instability (*apratiṣṭhā*) arises, only one *citi* (piling) is to be performed; it is enjoined either as a subordinate part of the piling through a variation in the ritual application, or for the sake of the fruit of stability.
Maṇḍana says: "The fire-altar consisting of six *citikas* is not indeed permanent. Śaṃkara says: "The sixth *citi* is occasional (*naimittikī*)."
In passages such as "cittaṃ ca cittiśca," there is no transformation [of the case ending] into the dative (caturthī).
"Citaṃ ca cittiśca ākṛtaṃ ca ākṛtiśca" and so forth are the *jyā* mantras.
"Iha śrutiḥ svāhā, iha vibhūtiḥ svāhā" and so forth are the *śrutimantra*s.
Among these, those ending in the nominative case must be transformed into the dative case at the time of practical application for the purpose of offering (*homa*).

"Food is offered to the gods either with the utterance of *svāhā* or with the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*. According to this Vedic scripture (*śruti*), just as the word *svāhā* is to be supplied where it is not explicitly mentioned, so too the dative case-ending must be supplied—even though it is not mentioned—by the traditional law (*smṛti*) stating "namas, svasti, svāhā [take the dative]. For this very reason, in another recensional tradition (*śākhā*), the reading is "to *citta* [in the dative], *svāhā*," and so forth. This being the position reached, we reply: although a word not heard in the text might be supplied—as in the case of [the verb] "cuts"—if the possibility of [the required number] five exists, the abandonment of the case-ending actually heard in the text would result in a violation of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) itself. Thus, the dative ending must remain as it is.
In the case of the rule "bahulam chandasi" (in Vedic usage there is diversity), the application is exactly as in the case of the Sāmans.

For this very reason, the sūtra "dhṛtihomena prayujyamāno'mu tathāṣṭasu caturthīm" (when employed with the Dhṛti-homa, [the word] 'amu' likewise [takes the dative] in the eight [verses], and the fourth [is used]) is a definition of the meaning established by the logic of this particular section. (Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa 2.4.21).

There is no conjunction of the mantras from other recensional branches, such as "To the piled [altar], svāhā! To the piling, svāhā! and so forth, with those beginning with "And to the piled [altar], svāhā! and so forth.

Since the mantras belonging to different Vedic branches (śākhās) differ in their word order due to differences in case endings and the absence of the particle *ca*, they constitute distinct mantras. Because the form of a mantra—like that of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) or the *āhavanīya* fire—is non-worldly (*alaukika*), there should be a combination (*samuccaya*) of those mantras whose purpose is transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhānta is as follows]: although the mantras consist of non-worldly words, because they are enjoined by the rule "one should sacrifice with the *jyā*" as the instrument for the oblation, they serve a perceptible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) and, having a single function, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between them. (Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa 2.4.22).

In the passage, "May the mind purify you; may the Lord of Speech purify you; may the god Savitṛ purify you with an unbroken filter by means of the rays of the sun, the Vasu," the phrase beginning with "with an unbroken filter" (acchidreṇa) and so forth must be construed with each of the two instances of "may he purify" (punātu).
Bhā. Rā. [states]: "The milking of the cows by Agopa is wonderful"—this is a genitive case used in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*), a *viniyoktrī* (injunctional) *śruti*.
(One whose cowherd has been separated from him is unable to milk the cows because the cows are difficult to milk; therefore, it is a wonder that he should be in such a state.

Citra is the king here; he alone rules over all others who follow Sarasvatī. Like Parjanya with his rain, may he bestow a thousandfold gifts.

Just as a woman depicted in a painting, though visible, is unable to produce the fruit of embracing a handsome man and so forth, even so, actions— whether prescribed or prohibited— that are performed by one who knows reality through the absence of egoism, are incapable of initiating another body born of their own fruit. Therefore,
this is the logic of the "painting fire" (citrānalanyāya) from the Citrā-adhikaraṇa [of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtras].
They say the meaning is that a sentient being is not joined with the fruit of its own performed karma.
[This is] the principle of the variegated fire (citrānalanyāya). 289. Ή The Principle of the Variegated Fire.
Just as fire depicted in a painting does not burn, so too saṃsāra, when encountered by one who is liberated while living, does not cause him suffering.

The analogy of the variegated cloth (*citrapaṭanyāya*). As it is stated in the *Citradīpa* chapter of the *Pañcadaśī*: "Just as a fourfold state is seen in a variegated cloth, so too should that fourfold state be understood in the Supreme Self."
Just as a cloth is washed, rubbed, marked, and dyed, so too are the inner controller (antaryāmī), the thread-self (sūtrātmā), and the cosmic self (virāḍātmā) perceived.
Here, "washed" refers to being pure by nature; "rubbed" refers to being polished by the removal of impurities.
"It should be marked with the shape of a musk-deer and colored by the filling of pigments.
Thus [it is described].
Sādṛśī. 285.
The full moon day of Citrā. "The full moon day of Citrā is indeed the mouth of the year. (Vi. 6.5.10)

The statement "one should sacrifice with the *citrayā*" refers to the *Citrā* sacrifice, because the word *citrā*, through its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb *yajati*, serves as the name of the sacrifice.
Its "variegated" nature (*citratva*) is due to the variety of the sacrificial offerings (*havis*).
In this regard, the full textual reading in the detailed exposition is: "Curd, honey, ghee, water, parched grain, and rice; that mixture belongs to Prajāpati."
The reading in the *Śāstradīpikā* is: "curd, honey, ghee, milk, parched grain, water, and rice.
In the *Bhāṭṭa-kaustubha*, however, it is: "curd, honey, milk, ghee, water, parched grain, and rice" (1.4.13, p.
[This is the] reading:

"One should sacrifice with the Citrā," "The Bahiṣpavamāna is threefold," "The Ājya-stotras are fifteenfold," "The Pṛṣṭha-stotras are seventeenfold. Thus, the words *citrā*, *pavamāna*, *ājya*, and *pṛṣṭha* are names of rituals (karmanāmadheya).
Bhāṣya 1.4.13.
"One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā.
In this case, the fruit of cattle is attained in this life when there is no obstruction; however, when there is an obstruction, it is attained in the next life.
The section on the Citrā sacrifice;
the section on the *ājya* (clarified butter) of the Citrā;
the principle of the Citrā.
The principle of the *citrā-indra* [sacrifice]: the word *citrayā* and others are names of sacrifices (*yāga-nāmadheya*).
In that case where there is an instruction regarding a quality (*guṇopadeśa*), the connection is primarily [with the action].

The commentary provides the following examples: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citri*"; "The *bahiṣpavamāna* chant is threefold (*trivṛt*); "The *ājya* chants are fifteenfold (*pañcadaśan*); and "The *pṛṣṭha* chants are seventeenfold (*saptadaśan*).
(*Citri* is the name of a particular sacrifice.)
The *bahispavamāna* is a specific stotra (hymn) in the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

There are those [stotras] characterized by the fifteen-fold chant (*pañcadaśa-stomaka*), and likewise those characterized by the seventeen-fold chant (*saptadaśa-stomaka*). Now, there arises the doubt: are the words *citra*, *pavamāna*, *ājya*, and *pṛṣṭha* injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)?

Because of their established usage, because they possess meaning, and because they denote specific activities, these terms have qualities as their object. Furthermore, these are not well-known in the sense of ritual action, nor are they merely derivative (yaugika) terms.
For these are words denoting genus (*jātiśabda*),
while *citrā* is a word denoting quality (*guṇaśabda*). Furthermore, the phrase "one should sacrifice with the *citrayā*" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the sacrifice.
Because [the sacrifice] is already known, there is no injunction for the sacrifice;

when a result is postulated for a subordinate element (guṇa), the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is not intended [as the primary object]. This is likewise the case in the statements, "The ājya offerings exist" and "The pṛṣṭha chants exist."
Even if one were to assume that these are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), there would still be no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, they are indeed injunctions of qualities; such is the position reached.
This being the position reached, we reply:

When there is a doubt as to whether it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) or a name (*nāmadheya*), and another quality is taught, its connection is with the principal action; thus, it is to be designated as the name of the action.
For if it were an injunction of a quality, the sentence would be split.

[In the case of the *citrayā yajeta*], since a male animal is already established, one could not enjoin by a single sentence that "animals" are the sacrifice, "animals" are the fruit, and "variegated color" (*citra*) is the quality.
The quality *citra* (variegated), being enjoined, would be enjoined with reference to the female animal, but not with reference to the *agnīṣomīya* [bull];
and it would be enjoined with reference to the *pañcaka* [fivefold sacrifice], but that too is not in the *agnīṣomīya*.
Likewise, in the statement "the *ājya* [chants] are fifteen," the number fifteen applies to the *ājya* chants.
Furthermore, the *ājya* hymns are not prescribed for the *stotras*,

nor is there any other prescriptive statement. Therefore, this [statement] would have to prescribe the *ājya* hymns, and [subsequently] prescribe the number fifteen (*pañcadaśatā*) for those already prescribed.
And it is understood that there is a connection between the number fifteen and the *ājya* chants;
furthermore, a connection with the hymns (*stotra*) for the *ājya* chants is intended,
as is a connection with the number fifteen.
It is impossible for two distinct matters to be enjoined by a single sentence.
However, if it is the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*), this contradiction does not arise;
in that case, only the connection with the number is being enjoined.
Furthermore, by the word "ājyāni stotrāṇi" (the Ājya hymns), a quality is enjoined through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) alone.
Therefore, these are the names of rituals that have been enjoined in other sentences such as "they praise with the Ājyas" and "they praise with the Pṛṣṭhas.
As for the claim that the name of the rituals is not well-known, [it is not so].
[The term] is established through its constituent parts.
They are called *ājyāni* because of their arrival at the race (*ājigamana*).
How is there an arrival at the race? From the statement in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "When they went toward the race (*yadājimīyuḥ*)."
Therefore, this [is called] *ājya* because of its name;
the *pṛṣṭhas* because of their resonant sound;
and the *bahiṣpavamāna* because of the absence of mantras for the *stoma* and because it is connected to the exterior (that is, because it is connected to a location outside the *saumika-vedi*).
"Curd, honey, milk, ghee, parched grain, rice, and water—these mixed together constitute the *prājāpatya* [offering]. Because it consists of various substances, it is called *citrā*.
Therefore, such terms are names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*).
Now, why are clarified butters (*ājya*) qualified by the number fifteen enjoined in the ritual acts of the *stotra*? Because there is no word that denotes them as being thus qualified.

But will this pair of verses not be expressive of the specific [offerings], namely "the fifteen butter-portions," and thus enjoin that [pair] in these stotras? This is not so; even this pair of verses is not injunctive.
Here, one is injunctive and the other is merely referential.
If both were prescriptive, there would be no mutual relationship between them. If neither were prescriptive, the connection with the *stotra* would not be enjoined.
Furthermore, in this case, a single word cannot simultaneously be a reference (*uddeśaka*) toward a qualifier and a prescriber (*vidhāyaka*) toward the *stotra*.
Because of the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*).
Therefore, this [is the topic] for us:

now, an investigation into genus-words (*jātiśabda*) and quality-words (*guṇaśabda*) that are conventionally established in the world among those who are not yogins, such as "rice" (*vrīhi*) and so forth.

For it is not possible for what is well-known through perception to be overridden by conformity with an inferential instrumentality; thus, there was no lack of proof in the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Now, one might object: since these are originative statements (*utpattivākya*), such as "They praise with the *ājya* [chants]," "They praise with the *pṛṣṭha* [chants]," and "They praise with the *bahiṣpavamāna*," these should have been cited as examples.
For it has been said: "At the time of origin, whether it be a name or a quality, that which is determined..."
That very [origin] becomes capable of being cited when it is known through common usage;

however, that origin was not cited by the author of the Sūtras because he relied upon the statement regarding qualities, namely, "in which qualities are to be enjoined. Why was that relied upon by him? Because a specific result follows whenever [the origin] is established in any particular instance.
Alternatively, syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is the reason for rejecting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*);
this is what was illustrated there by the phrase "it is possible.

(He offers another resolution according to his own view: Or rather, since the word *ājya* and so forth in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) is directly present in both positions, there is no reason to determine even one of them; thus, because it depends on something established elsewhere, it is not cited as an example.
Furthermore, because it is heard [in scripture], the name *Citrā* is first understood not to be the name of a hymn (*stotra*).

For it is also heard [in the text]: "They praise with those which are the *ājya*s. In that case, what indeed are these names, and how are they denoted by them? This must be determined even in conjunction with the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*).

Indication (*lak� clarified butter* and so forth, because they are substances, are not grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*), which seeks only the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consisting of the specific details of what is to be done. (He refutes this: There is no such reproach here, because action itself exists in the form of being (*sattva*).
Furthermore, because the place of the principal [rite] belongs to the ignorant [performers], the *ājya* and other [chants] must occur in proximity to the *stotra*.
Therefore, just as in the case of "they praise after placing the fire nearby," where the fire assists by its mere presence, so it is here as well; thus, there is no fault.
Consequently, this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
To this it is replied:
"The connection is according to the principal [element]"—this is the word from the Sūtra.
For the prescription of multiple objects is only possible when there is a prescription of a principal action.
In this case, however, a quality is enjoined with reference to an action that has already been restated;
and there is no mutual relationship between qualities.

In that situation, if one quality were enjoined while there is no requirement for another quality, yet one were to assume the operation of multiple scriptural injunctions, there would result a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), as the suffix would have to be applied repeatedly.

And it has been said: "The mental cultivation (bhāvanā), having established even a single object from among many objects, grasps a qualifier that is connected through the injunction of a specific [attribute]."

Furthermore, even though [the word] is expressed as a single unit, because there are multiple injunctive powers in a case such as the *citrādhikaraṇa* (Jaiminisūtra 1.4.8–9)— due to the distinctness of "variegated" (*citram*) and so forth— and because the instrument (*karaṇa*) residing in the animal is already established and thus not intended to be enjoined, it is impossible to enjoin a factor (*kāraka*) qualified by both [the quality and the genus].

And therefore, because the injunction of "femininity" is incompatible with the context—given that the contextually prescribed male animal for the Agni-Soma sacrifice is enjoined by the statement "The goat [is] for Agni-Soma"—this cannot be an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).

Consequently, since the word *citrā* indicates the sacrifices under discussion as having variegated materials, it is a name (*nāmadheya*). It is with this intention that the feminine suffix is employed.
The same applies to the words *ājya* and so forth.

Since a qualified [action] has not been produced because [the terms] are not compounded, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if one were to enjoin both a substance and the number one as qualities while restating the already established stotra.

Nor should it be argued that the injunction for the stotra qualified by the substance occurs in the very originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), and therefore let there be an injunction of the number alone.

Since it is impossible for *dhṛti* and the others to function as instruments (*karaṇa*) in a hymn (*stotra*), a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is untenable; furthermore, if the suffix *-ti* in words such as "fifteen-fold" (*pañcadaśāni*) were intended as an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), it would be illogical because that suffix denotes the nature of a hymn characterized by a specific number.
Therefore, in both sentences, the words *ājya* and so forth are names (*nāmadheya*) of the hymns.
By means of these words, there is a reference (*anuvāda*) to the hymns, while in every case within the sentences enjoining qualities, there is only the injunction of the number.
And in the sentence concerning the origin of the *ājya* [stotras], it follows from the plural number, assisted by the indicative power (*gamaka*), that there are four stotras designated by that term.
The same would apply to the sentence concerning the *pṛṣṭha* stotras.
However, those to be performed are fixed at four.

In the case of the first two substances, both [options] apply; however, for the other two, namely the *naudhasa* and *dyata*, there is an injunction of an option (*vikalpa*) by means of a specific statement.
As for the refutation of those remaining [positions] here and the criticisms of other views, these are detailed in the *Kaustubha* under Sūtra 2.4.3.
Maṇḍana states: "The word *citrā* is likewise [to be understood]."
Likewise, it is like the word *udbhid*.
Śaṅkara states: "Even in the case of a variegated place, there is the status of being a name.

For even when the locus of the variegation (*citra*) is delimited by its variegated nature, it is impossible to raise the objection regarding the fault of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indirect indication of the sense of "possessing") in the injunction that [the action] has as its object a substance qualified by that [quality].

In the *Citrā-adhikaraṇa*, Pārthasārathi states (Kau. 1.4.16, p. 220): "If there were a compound [such as] ‘pañcadaśyāni’, then there would be no split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). In the same *Citrā-adhikaraṇa* (Kau. 2.1.16, p. 198), he says: "The defects such as metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*) arise from imagining additions or omissions in a directly heard (*śrūyamāṇa*) sentence; however, these do not apply to that which is inferred (*anumita*)."
Thus, in the hypothetical sentence cited, it is stated that there is no syntactical split (vākya-bheda) even when the plurality of the subject (*uddeśya*) is intended to be expressed;
see Bālakrīḍā, p. 122.

Nor should it be argued that plurality is indeed present in that case, since the author of the Vārttika cited the sentence "They praise with the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]" as an originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*) in the *Citrā-adhikaraṇa*.
*Soma* 7.3.1: To avoid redundancy, it was stated in the *Kaustubha* under the *Citrā-adhikaraṇa* that the *ṛk*, *sāman*, and others possess their own functional efficacy (*svakāryakāritva*).

The followers of Akṣapāda (the Naiyāyikas), who accept that sacrifices such as the Citrā yield results only in this life, respond to the objection—“Why then do none of the other fruits of ritual acts become the result?”—by attributing it to a deficiency in the performance of the rite (*karmavaiguṇya*). According to their view, one would have to admit that for those who have not performed the necessary actions in this world, the fruit arises from inherent nature (*svabhāva*). As it is said: “Those who, asserting that there is an absence of fruit due to a deficiency in all [past] actions, maintain that [the result] follows immediately [from nature], are proponents of inherent nature (*svābhāvikavādinaḥ*).
(However, the doctrine of inherent nature is not at all tenable.)

Bālapriyā, p. 7. In the Citrā sacrifice, there are oblations with mantras such as "agne gobhinne" intended solely for nourishment.
Having prescribed, "One should offer these various *iṣṭi* oblations," the scripture states, "These indeed are the deities who are the lords of prosperity (*puṣṭi-pati*).
In this regard, since there is no restrictive rule, those [mantras] containing signs of prosperity (*puṣṭi-liṅga*) should be employed.

(The discussion [of this] is in the section beginning with "In the case of the *salekhālī*, of the archetypal [rite]" [Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 10.2.13–17].

(In this context, regarding the statement "because it is perceived while existing without blinking," there is the following: "But the relationship between a word and its object is innate; from that [relationship], knowledge [of the object arises]. )
The meaning of this portion of the Sūtra is summarized here according to the view of the commentator (*vṛttikāra*).
Since the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) for the Citrā-vāda is presented as a digression within this very section, the name "Citrā-vāda" has been applied to it in numerous texts.
By the very force of the context, both the critique of the Citrā sacrifice (*citrākṣepa*) and its refutation (*parihāra*) are already included herein.
Commentary: Now, let it be granted that perception and the other means of knowledge are indeed valid;
however, verbal testimony (śabda) is not a valid means of knowledge.
Why? Because "it apprehends what is present without the closing of the eyes" (*animiṣaṃ vidyamānopalambhanatvāt*).
Sound is signless and immeasurable.
For that which is not perceived despite being an object of perception does not exist, such as the horn of a hare;
yet the sense faculties of animals and other beings are indeed objects of perception.
Furthermore, animals are not obtained immediately after the *paśukāmeṣṭi* (meaning, after the *citreṣṭi*). Therefore, the sacrifice does not have cattle as its fruit;
and the fruit must arise at the time of the performance of the ritual action.
For at whatever time there is crushing, at that very time the result of the crushing is easily obtained.
If it is argued that "it will yield fruit at another time," we say no;
for we understand that the desired fruit is [to be obtained] at another time.
Why? Because when it existed, it did not give its fruit; and when the fruit is said to be produced, it no longer exists.
How can that which has ceased exist give [the fruit]? Furthermore, another cause of the fruit is perceived through direct perception.

Furthermore, when a visible cause exists, it is not possible to postulate an unseen one due to a lack of evidence. Likewise, because the Veda has a visible purpose, we consider that even heaven and such are not its fruit.
Moreover, there is something here that is even contrary to what is desired.

Having prescribed the piling of the sacrificial vessels (in other sacrifices), [the scripture] points to the perceptible body itself— saying, "This very sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes to the heavenly world"— and not to the Self; for that [body] is indeed perceived as departing to the heavenly world.
Nor does one say "this goes" by the force of an injunction;
for a verbal authority of such a kind contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just as, for example, the statements: "gourds sink in water" or "stones float."
Because of this commonality, there would also be a lack of confidence even in injunctions such as the Agnihotra;
therefore, the object that is the dharma is not characterized by injunction.
(This is the prima facie position.)

(He states the established conclusion: "But the relation of a word with its meaning is innate; the knowledge thereof [is the means of knowing Dharma]. The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
This is indeed a novel assertion.
The relationship between a word and its meaning;

that is, the knowledge of that meaning characterized by the Agnihotra and other such rites, which is not apprehended through perception and the other means of knowledge. And thus it is said: "Right cognition is characterized by the Vedic injunction (codanā)."
For if the word were of human origin, the falsity of the cognition produced by it could be established, because in that case there would be a subsequent cognition [contradicting it].
But when the word itself speaks, how can it be false?
For at that time, we do not seek to obtain understanding from any other person.
It is said that [the word] "speaks," "makes one understand," or "becomes the cause for one who is understanding.
And when the word is the cause, one understands by oneself.
How could one, being thus deceived, say, "This is not so"?
Nor does its injunction produce a conceptual cognition such as "Is it *svāhā* or not?
Nor does a contrary cognition arise later in time, in another place, in another state, or in another person, thinking "This is false.

Even the inferential cognition that might arise—having observed a subversion of this cognition elsewhere and concluding that it will likewise be subverted here—is itself sublated by this perceptual cognition which is being experienced.
Therefore, Dharma is characterized solely by Vedic injunction (*codanā*).
[This is because] it is an accomplished entity (*siddha*), and since there can be no dispute regarding an accomplished entity that depends upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The author of the Bhāṣya reveals by the words "nor does it go" that even that independence, though it might be thought possible, does not exist.
Is the relationship of the word independent of other means of knowledge? It is innate (*autpattika*).
(With this passage, he begins to resolve the objection raised previously.)

For if the relationship between a word and its meaning—the relation of denoter and denoted—were dependent upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), then in sentences such as "The Citrā sacrifice [is to be performed]," the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth would express a state of being an action (*kāryatā*) by defining it as a means to a result experienced through another means of valid cognition; thus, their lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) would indeed follow.
However, when the capacity to denote is innate (*autpattika*), inherent (*svābhāvika*), and independent (*nirapekṣa*), authority is logical because the object is determined autonomously.
But surely, in common worldly usage, they say that everything depends upon another means of valid cognition?
Truthfulness pertains to linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), but not to denotation (*abhidhāna*).
Just as even in the world denotation is indeed innate (*autpattika*), so too shall we explain this in the section on the refutation of the objection regarding the relation [between word and meaning].

(In linguistic usage, characterized by the employment of words, there is dependence [on other means], because in the world people employ words after having cognized the object through another means of knowledge; however, there is no dependence in denotation itself, since the meaning is denoted directly by the word).

Moreover, dependence on other means of knowledge does not constitute a defect in the Veda within the context of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), because it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). For a person indeed depends upon the cognition of other means of knowledge in order to employ a word;
however, in the absence of such [human agency], there is no such dependence.
If the relationship were of human origin, there would be dependence.
However, when [the author] will later state that it is not of human origin, then its independence will be established.

Now, as for what was said—that "the word is without cause" (Bhāṣya, pp. 58–60)—why is this being raised? This has already been answered by the statement regarding the innate nature (*autpattikatva*) of the relationship. Or rather, of what else could an answer be understood through its innate nature?
Why is it not simply that [the injunction] does not apply again to another?

For it has been shown that, precisely because it is a perception of what is already present (*vidyamānopalambhana*), there is no other object [of cognition]—as in the case of "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citri* [sacrifice].
Since it is a perception of what is already present, the relationship of means and end between the sacrifice and the cattle is indeed established through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, it was previously demonstrated that the object (*viṣaya*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such terms is precisely the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*), preceded by the relationship between the goal and the means, which is accessible through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it is not some other object.
Consequently, its refutation has already been provided by means of its innate nature (*autpattikatva*). Why, then, is something else being presented, even though it has not yet been refuted?
True; this very [objection] has been stated as a rebuttal to the view that the relationship is innate (*autpattika*).
However, even if the relationship were innate, the exclusion of other objects appears to be as if it were not.
To distinguish between these two, this [sūtra] is further presented.

That quality of being human-made (pauruṣeyatva) which, given the existence of a human-made relationship [between word and meaning], would forcibly result in the Veda being dependent on other means of knowledge—this has been refuted by the statement regarding the "inborn" (autpattika) relationship.

Furthermore, the suspicion that a word might have as its object a domain already within the scope of another means of knowledge, based on the observation of independence in worldly usage, is here dispelled.
When the relationship is innate (*autpattika*), the distinction is that the word has an independent object-domain;
this appears as if it were not yet stated.
To clarify that distinction, this objection will be raised once again.
"Because the fruit is seen at the time of the action, and because the action is absent at another time" (Bhāṣya, p. 58).
Now, what is the purpose of this?

Since there is no other object [for it], and since it would be dependent [on something else] by virtue of being the object of another means of knowledge, its lack of authority in the absence of that [other object] has already been shown (in the critique of the Citrā sacrifice).
Here too, why is that very same thing being proposed again? It appears to be [the following]: this is it.
For when there is the relation "this [is] by means of this," provided that it is not an object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is an injunction (*niyoga*).
And in that case, since [the object] is not perceived, its lack of authority is quite evident;
this has already been stated previously.
Furthermore, when this [perceptual] object is possible, the fulfillment of the mandate cannot arise from the mandate alone.
Thus it can be inferred.
(The connection is as follows: "This [point], though not explicitly stated, is expressed by this commentary.

Even though the fruit is not established immediately after the ritual act, and yet there is no ritual act at a later time, nevertheless, the fruit will arise at a later time precisely because of the *niyoga* (the authoritative injunction); this is what is resolved by this introductory commentary.)

Because, in this matter, it is impossible for there to be the possibility of being an object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, it cannot be postulated that [the goal] is established through the mandate (*niyoga*) alone, since at that time the mandate itself lacks the status of a means of valid cognition.
For how could a mandate—which is of the nature of a Vedic form known through another means of valid cognition—be an object of verbal knowledge that depends upon yet another means of valid cognition?

Therefore, because the fruit is seen immediately after the action, and because the action no longer exists at a later time, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the sacrifice being the cause of the animal-sacrifice's fruit. Consequently, since the clear authority is perceived through the *Cintāmaṇi* [of the Nyāya school], the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is more powerful than the revealed scripture (*śruti*).

It is understood that one performs a sacrifice named "Agni. Alternatively, because the word "Agni" occurs in grammatical apposition with the root "to pile" (*cinoti*) as a restatement (*anuvāda*), and because [otherwise] it would be untenable, it is determined from the sentence that one piles the fire-altar which is known by the name "Agni. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 146).
This is the maxim: "Having obtained a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), one takes up glass.
This maxim finds its application where people abandon inquiry into the distinction between the words of Brahman and instead take delight in something else.
Sahalī. 388.

Oṃ. At the moment of the oblation (*iṣmakṣaṇe*), protection is performed preceded by the sound "juhupuṣa" (in the Bhāṣya it is "juhupākāra," and in the Bhāṣṭe it is "juhupuṣākāra"). Having made such a sound, one should likewise perform the consumption of the remnants (*śeṣabhakṣaṇa*) in the manner of the *śatakṛṣṇala* rite. (Vi.

10.2.3). Oṃ. By the worldly maxim that the upward movement of a conscious being who is devoid of effort is dependent on something subsequent to consciousness, those who move [the souls]—the conductors (*gantāraḥ*)—of those devoid of effort must be non-conscious, such as the *arciḥ* and others.
Śrīkara. 4|2|4 vas.
Oṃ. It is accepted that the entire world is presided over by consciousness (cetanā). Su. pṛ. 108; [these are] denoted by the word "consciousness" (cetanā).

In the *Citi-saṃśāna*, the term *cetanā* denotes the consciousness characterized by perfect knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). Therefore, those who are denoted by the word *cetana* are by their very nature [wise] and not of dull intellect. (p.
138) Oṃ! The *Ṛgveda* and other [Vedas] are permeated by consciousness (*caitanya*).

"Likewise, whatever bodies there are, whether they be given by the Ṛgveda or otherwise distinct from one another, they too are always permeated by consciousness as objects of experience for the selves.
(Vākyapadīya 3.1.7.3, p. 703)
Oṃ, consciousness is the forest of knowledge.

Oṃ, however, in the case of the salutation to shrines (*caityavandana*) and so forth, there is a refuge [in the Buddha] because they are of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), [referring to the one who prescribes them].
Straightforward. Page 23: Oṃ, the Caitraratha Dvirātra sacrifice;
therein, the subsequent day is an Atirātra.
Oṃ! The *codaka* is weaker than the direct instruction because it is to be inferred.
The *codaka* (the impeller) is capable of bringing about qualities.
Mīmāṃsā 10.3.1.8. The *codaka* is of two kinds: the verbal impeller (*śabdacodaka*) and the objective impeller (*arthacodaka*).

In this regard, that which impels toward the meaning (arthacodaka) is stronger than that which impels toward the word (śabdacodaka). For it is for the sake of conveying the meaning that the impulsion toward the word operates; it does not function independently, due to the fear of postulating a separate [meaning].
The challenger [is defeated] when his activity is pervaded by the counter-argument;
and because of the direct scriptural statement, the mind is refuted.
Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 10.6.1.63.

The injunction (*codaka*) is stronger with respect to the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), because even though the order indicated by the injunction of performance exists, the order of the principal (*mukhyakrama*) is more capable of being assumed as its nature; and since an assumption must have a basis, the requirement for the injunction of performance is satisfied by the order obtained through the sequence of the original text (*pāṭhakrama*), which results in the cessation of further expectancy. Therefore, the order established by the sequence of the original text—whether it be the first-order indicative (*ādideśika*) or the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)—is indeed more powerful.
(Bhāṭṭa 5.1.10)

The *codaka* (the rule of transfer) conforms to the meaning of the mantra, not to the syllables of the mantra; for those [syllables] are subservient to the meaning, and do not have their own form as the primary concern. Bhāṣya 9.3.16: The *codaka* does not enjoin an auxiliary that has lost its purpose in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
The *codaka* (the rule of extension) extends only those items that follow the established sequence.
[Vi. 5.1.10] The *codaka* is stronger than the *samākhyā* (name/designation).

Bhāṣya 3.1.2.15: "And the *codaka* does not cause something to be brought about merely by implication. 5.2.1.8: "Furthermore, when it is possible, the injunction of application (*prayogavacana*) is not to be respected in preference to the *codaka*; for the *codaka* is more powerful."
For that [injunction] is the producer and the obtainer of the constituent elements (dharmas).

The statement of the application (prayoga-vacana) is the collector of the subsidiaries (prasaṅga). That [application] is weaker because it occurs at a later time, due to the remoteness of its purpose.
9|4|15: By means of the *codaka* (the rule of extension), that which has become an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is taken up.
3|6|17: When, by means of the *codaka*, the remnant of a particular *apūrva* (transcendental result) is presented, there is consumption (*bhakṣa*) for one who performs that ritual act;
for in this way, it becomes a benefactor to that [result].
10.7.123: An auxiliary element is obtained for the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by means of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), provided that it exists in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*).
It is the purpose (*artha*) that is extended to the modified sacrifice by the *codaka*, not the denotative word (*śabda*).
This we shall explain.
[This is] the second section (varṇaka) of [the commentary on] sūtra 9.1.13.19.
It is established that, because the injunction for the *anarambhaṇīyā* sacrifice is weaker than the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), it does not apply [to the *iṣṭi*].
This is from Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 3.6.14.
The distinction of rituals based on the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) has been stated in the section concerning number (*saṃkhyā*), as in the case of the seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati.

The introduction of a distinction of rituals in the absence of a *codaka* occurs in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, according to the rule: "They release those [animals] after they have been circumambulated by fire (*paryagnikṛtān*)."
Bāla, p. 86.

The principle that "the word denoting a name is stronger than the *codaka* (the general rule of transfer)" is established in the section beginning with "And [it is] the *Agnihotra*" (12.1.6.13) and is indicated therein. Ke.:
It was stated in the section "Or rather, not so, because of the expression of the sentence" (7.4.15) that "the word denoting a name is stronger than the *codaka*."
Bhāṣya 12.1.15:

The injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) is weaker than the extended application (*codaka*), because its status as an auxiliary is established by the *codaka*, whereas the status as an auxiliary is established by the injunctive teaching of the modified sacrifice (*pratyāmnāyopadeśavidhi*).
Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1186.

Because the direct statement (*codaka*) possesses the authority of explicit instruction (*upadeśa*), it is stronger than both indicative mark (*liṅga*) and sequence (*krama*), as otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of meaninglessness.
Direct statement is more powerful than the *codaka*.

The direct Vedic text (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) states that [the animal] is to be sacrificed by its characteristics (*lakṣaṇena*); the extended application (*codaka*) states that it is to be sacrificed by its name (*abhidhānena*). Bhāṣya 10.4.12, Section 3.
In the absence of the *codaka*, there is a new injunction (*codanā*) which constitutes a fresh commencement (*punarārambha*).
In the absence of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), there is an absence of the *prājāpatyā* sacrifice.
Bāla. pṛ. 87.

According to the sequence understood through the *codaka*, there is a displacement [of the ritual] ending with that; this is the principle of "displacement of what is connected to that" (*tadādyapakarṣanyāya*).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the Agniṣomīya and Savanīya offerings, the sequence of the preceding and succeeding ritual acts (*padārtha*) is precisely what determines the rule of "ending with that" (*tadantatva*) and so forth.
(Soma.

5.1.12). Because they depend upon the *codaka* (the extended application of rules), the direct statement (*śruti*), the purpose (*artha*), the textual order (*pāṭha*), and the section (*kāṇḍa*) possess greater strength; whereas because they depend upon the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*), the primary act (*mukhya*) and the order of procedure (*pravṛtti-krama*) are weaker.
Dvaidhasūtra 5.1.20.18:

For the one-day duration obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) is set aside by the statement, "He who [performs] with an *iṣṭi*, with an animal sacrifice...

"Whatever duty has been obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) and whose performance can be accomplished by a direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), let that be performed by that [direct statement].
Mānava Śrautasūtra 10.1.2.18 (68).
Because they are obtained through the *codaka*, the ritual details (*dharma*) of the Bārhaspatya sacrifice come first; after that, those of the Sārasvata."
In the *Adhvarakalpa*:
the operation of the *codaka*.
One should effect [the sacrifice].
What? The variety of animal sacrifices. By what means? By the puroḍāśa sacrifice.
By the word "how" (*katham*), the procedure (*vyāpāra*) of the sacrifice is [intended].
And that [procedure], through the definition of comparison (*upamitalakṣaṇā*), expects similarity with whatever procedure belongs to the *agnīṣomīya* [sacrifice] (which is part of the *paurṇamāsa*).

In that context, the specific restriction of the procedure belonging to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice—which is established by the definition of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*)—is its "origin" (*utpatti*), as it were.
And that which constitutes the establishment of a connection between that function and another [element] is *prāpti* (meaning *viniyoga*, or application).
Both of these are functions of the *codaka* (the general rule of transfer).
(Duhkha 12.1.13)

By "codanā," we mean the *apūrva* (the unseen force); [as stated in the Bhāṣya: "Codanā, moreover, is the commencement" (2.1.2.5). Exhortation (*codanā*):

Therefore, in this treatise, it is the sentence that impels action which is set forth."

In the doubt as to whether an injunction is indeed a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding *dharma* or not—the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) being that since a word is observed to be authoritative everywhere only in dependence upon another more fundamental means of knowledge, and since there is an absence of any other foundational means of knowledge for a word consisting of an injunction, that [injunction] is also non-authoritative, and thus *dharma* remains unestablished.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because verbal testimony (*śabda*) possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) independent of other means of knowledge, Dharma has *codanā* (Vedic injunction) alone as its authority.

Oṃ. "Furthermore, the commencement [of the inquiry] is due to *codanā*."
To explain how the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is understood, he says:
"The injunction (*codanā*). This refers to the misconception regarding the *apūrva*. It is stated that because the injunction of an action is for the sake of a result, the *apūrva* is implied.
The word "exists" is to be supplied.
The term "apūrva" exists.
The word "punaḥ" has the sense of "since" or "because"; thus says the *Kutūhala*.
Since the undertaking of an action is taught for the sake of a result,
the injunction would be purposeless in the absence of the *apūrva*.
Therefore, the existence of the *apūrva* is established because the injunction of the action cannot otherwise be justified as producing a result.
The *apūrva* inheres in the self.
Because of the existence of the *apūrva*, the performance of a substitute is carried out when the prescribed substance or quality is unavailable.
And this *apūrva* is either a subtle potency (*śakti*) produced by the ritual act or simply the subtle fruit itself.

Regarding the phrase "codanā punarārambhaḥ": some commentators have explained this sūtra for the purpose of defining the nature of *codanā* by stating that *ārambha* means that which is commenced—that is, having produced the suffix *-an* from the root *ā-rabh*, it is that which commences or sets something in motion; thus, *codanā* is a sentence that impels action. However, this explanation has been rejected because it is irrelevant, as it does not consist of the words necessary for the means of understanding the *apūrva* under discussion. Furthermore, if this sūtra were intended merely to define the nature of *codanā*, it would logically have to be placed immediately after the sūtra on *codanā* (2.1.2). Thus, it has been stated [that this interpretation is incorrect].

By the Bhāṣya statement, "The undertaking (ārambha) is taught," the meaning of the word *ārambha* is obtained as being "injunction" (*codanā*). This is because, based on the grammatical rule from the Dhātupāṭha (Curādi-gaṇa sūtra) stating that "from a verbal root expressing the production of a result, the suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of 'one performs that' or 'one describes that'," when the suffix *ṇic* is applied to the word *ārambha* in the sense of "one describes the undertaking," and then the suffix *ac* is applied, the word *ārambha* is explained as "one describes the undertaking, which is the production of a result. Thus, the meaning of the word *ārambha* is established as "injunction. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 613). "Injunction, moreover, is the undertaking."

Furthermore, the objection that "the nature of being an effect is simply the state of being an instigation (codanā), as is well understood in the world," has been refuted. This is because there is a restatement [of the point]: "The nature of being an effect is simply the state of being an instigation. Thus, that [objection] is rejected.

Since it is possible for that which possesses both forms [desire and injunction] to be an object of action (*kārya*), even that which was stated by others—that in the world, the comprehension of an action (*kārya*) in accordance with all systems is the cause of engagement—is merely an assertion based on superimposition; for that too is simply an action consisting of a physical act (such as cooking) prompted by another purpose.
If, in the Veda as well, the comprehension of such an action is measured to be the cause of engagement, then that is indeed accepted.

Nor should it be argued: "Whatever is produced immediately after something else must be that which is accomplished by an effort directed toward the former, as in the case of eating, which results from an effort undertaken with the aim of satiety.
However, the fruit is not produced immediately after the sacrifice;
therefore, the sacrifice is not something to be accomplished by an effort directed toward the fruit."

For the volitional effort (*kṛti*) initiated at the moment of aiming at the target culminates merely in the drawing and releasing of the bowstring; the piercing of the target is not accomplished immediately thereafter.
What then? It is accomplished only after a long succession of impressions (*saṃskāra*) known as momentum (*vega*).

Consequently, since it is observed in the world that an effect can have a mediated means even when the means is not proximate, there is no logical inconsistency in defining "effect-ness" (*kāryatva*) as having a mediated means.

Now, if it is argued that even in that case, only the group of actions separated [from the result] by the piercing of the target possesses the status of being the "effect" (*kārya*), then is this because [the piercing] is the object of desire (*uddeśyatva*) or because it is a means to the action (*kṛtyupāyatva*)? It cannot be because of its being the object of desire, since the piercing of the target itself is what constitutes the object of desire.
Nor can it be because it is a direct means to the action, for an action is completed by the mere production of the verbal root-meaning (*ākhyāta-kriyā*).

Therefore, just as the piercing of the target—though its means are separated by intermediate operations—is accepted as the "effect," so too let the sacrifice be accepted as such; what is the use of postulating an "unseen potency" (*apūrva*) as the effect?
Therefore, there is a lack of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) regarding the nature of the effect called *apūrva*, which is distinct from the fruit (*phala*).

Or, let it be that the *apūrva* itself is the effect; even so, how can it be denoted by the word of injunction (*vidhiśabda*)? To explain: the denotative power (*śakti*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) must be postulated for an effect in the form of being an immediate means to what is desired, based on the otherwise inexplicable nature of its co-occurrence with the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*).
This being the case, since it is the object of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the assumption of its being "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) is indeed impossible.
As for what was stated— that the assumption of the *upasthā* [mantra] arises from presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), whereas for the sake of a new means of knowledge (*apūrva-pramāṇa*),
it must indeed be expressed by the word *liṅ*, just as the assumption of the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) occurs at the beginning of an injunction— that is incorrect.

For in the case of words such as those expressing injunctions (*vidhi*), since heaven is understood previously as being common to all [desirous persons], its presence is established; thus, it is logical that the word *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven), which denotes it, is postulated through the presumption of the heard meaning (*śrutārthāpatti*) as being implied by the injunctive word.

Here, however, because the unprecedented task (*apūrvakārya*) is not presented from any other source and is itself unprecedented, its presentation must be stated to occur solely through the means of valid cognition (*arthāpatti*).
It is truly a source of ridicule to claim that a means of valid cognition presents it, and yet there is no means of valid cognition for it.

In that regard, if presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) were the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the *apūrva*, then the optative suffix (*liṅ*) would lack authority because it would merely be a restatement (*anuvādaka*). For the status of presumptive testimony cannot apply when the *apūrva*—the unique causal effect—is not present, since the relationship between signifier and signified has not been ascertained in connection with the optative suffix and other such markers.
Nor is there [any such relationship] through the word...
Even though it is an injunction, because no fruit is mentioned in the injunction, [it is not a primary injunction].

"Whether it pertains to engagement or withdrawal, that cognition which arises upon hearing a word—this is the general definition of *codanā* residing in the heart. (Ślokavārttika 1.1.2, verses 210–211). [Objection: "Even if *codanā* conveys an object that is to be accomplished (*kārya*), nevertheless, a human-authored *codanā* would result; because the independence of speech is observed [only in the Veda], and because [human speech] depends on other means of knowledge, it would fall into the state of being invalid. [If this is argued, we reply: No."
If an injunction (codanā) conveys a task (kārya) as its object, then it is not of human origin;
for men employ speech in order to communicate what is already known through other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
and a task is not something that can be cognized by other means of valid cognition.
Therefore, that which establishes it is not of human origin;
hence, even though it is unperceived, its independence is postulated by the force of the cognition of the effect.
In the case of the veneration of caityas and the like, however, there is a human-based recollection.
Therefore, the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is independent [of other means of knowledge].

According to the principle stated in *Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 23—namely, "Or [it is] an injunction of subsidiary elements" (*codanā vā guṇānām*, 2.1.36)—the establishment of a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*) on account of a subsidiary element is also possible, because it is characterized by the presentation of multiple meanings (as in cases such as: "If the Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara-sāman...").

Pṛ. 889: By the statement, "Or rather, there is a simultaneous injunction of the subordinate elements because of the scriptural text," [it is shown that] through the Viṣṇu-passages (such as "another [is the deity] in the forms of Viṣṇu, etc."), even in the case of the injunction for sacrifice, there would result the injunction of a separate ritual act by means of the intermediate passage. First of all, another cause for apprehension cannot be inferred, because it is certain that nothing exists apart from the assemblage of the enumerated means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, instruction can arise even from delusion;
and in the absence of delusion, it can likewise arise even from the Veda.

Therefore, because it does not depend on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is not contingent upon that [other means]; rather, its capacity to convey meaning is intrinsic, and its contact with the object is self-evident. (Ṛjuvimalā, p. 24)
“Because no fruit is heard of in the injunction, only the ritual act would be enjoined; for that which is not expressed by the word is not understood.

(JS 4.3.5.10) Furthermore, it is heard in scripture: “Therefore, one performs [the sacrifice] for the ancestors on the previous day,” and also: “He who undertakes the *satra* should sacrifice with the *Viśvajit*, a three-night rite, having all *pṛṣṭha* chants, all *stomas*, and the giving away of all his possessions as the sacrificial fee (*sarvavedasa-dakṣiṇa*).”

Regarding this ritual for the ancestors (*pitṛkarma*) or the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, a doubt arises as to whether it is a fruitless action consisting merely of the act itself, or whether it is fruitful. The author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): In this injunction—that is, in the prescriptive statement—because no fruit is heard, meaning because a result is not mentioned, the action is enjoined as being merely an act devoid of fruit.
For a fruit that is "non-verbal"—that is, not communicated by the word—is neither perceived nor can it be understood [as part of the injunction].

Therefore, because no fruit is heard [stated], the *pitṛyajña* and the *viśvajit* are enjoined as being without fruit; for they are enjoined precisely by virtue of their being connected with the act of giving. Indeed, the words of those things that possess meaning are understood through their meaningfulness; for there is no connection between things that lack meaning even when they are in immediate proximity. Therefore, that [connection] is merely a part of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).
The word "api vā" (or rather) is used to refute the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
That action is not fruitless;

for in that action there is an injunction regarding the result, as understood from the verbal expression of its necessity—such as "one should perform" or "one should sacrifice"—which conveys that it must be done.
On account of the force of the scriptural injunction (*āmnāna*).
"Injunction" (*āmnāna*) refers to that which is enjoined—that is, the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) conjoined with a mandate.
From the force of the injunction, meaning from the force of the productive activity associated with the mandate, the impulsion toward the fruit (*phalacodanā*) is understood.
But is it not the case that there is no word here denoting the fruit?
True;

however, because the meanings heard in common worldly usage must be meaningful and logically consistent, statements—even those separated by a distance—are understood as connected through processes such as textual supply (*adhyāhāra*).
Otherwise, however, those words which are semantically incapable of conveying a meaning regarding a word-meaning lack a connection—even if there is immediate proximity—and thus no relation arises.

In the expression “The king’s man is Devadatta’s wife,” although there is immediate proximity between the word *bhāryā* (wife) and the word *rājaḥ* (king), there is no connection whatsoever between them. Therefore, even if it is situated at a distance, a word that conveys the result should be understood as a *śruti-ekadeśa*, that is, a portion of the heard sentence (*śruta-vākya*).

In terms of semantic meaning (*arthataḥ*), a connection can be understood even for that which is spatially distant; however, even if it is semantically beneficial, a connection cannot be understood for that which is not connected.

In the present case, in expressions such as "he performs [the rite] on the previous day for the ancestors," when there is a connection with the word for the result (*phala*) situated at a distance, the fruitfulness of the action is established, just as in the case of a sentence-meaning that possesses a subordinate element (*guṇārtha*).
12. The Siddhāntin himself says:
the word *ca* (and) is for the purpose of dispelling doubt;
it is merely inserted in place of the word *tu* (but).
The meaning of the sentence becomes possessed of its purpose through a quality (*guṇa*).

Just as in the sentence “A boar for King Indra,” the meaning becomes complete when a verb is found within the sentence itself, so too this present sentence would become meaningful, purposeful, and complete by finding a word for the result (*phala*) elsewhere, through that quality consisting of the result.
And thus, the meaning of the sentence would be rendered complete.

Therefore, the ancestral rite (*pitṛkarma*) and the Viśvajit rite are indeed enjoined as being fruitful.
