"Because of the unity of the injunction, due to the connection [of all parts] with the Rājasūya, the subsidiary rites (aṅgas) are performed as a single performance (tantra), since their place and time are not specified.

(Jaiminisūtra 11.4.19). In the investigation of whether there is a single performance (tantrabhāva) or a separate performance (bheda) regarding the subsidiary rites in the Rājasūya—wherein there are thirty principal acts whose place and time are not explicitly stated—the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) states:

"Because of the unity of the injunction, by virtue of being enjoined by the word 'Rājasūya' in the singular number, and because of the connection, that is, because all [the acts] are connected toward the accomplishment of the result, in the Rājasūya, there should be a single performance for those thirty principal acts and others whose place and time are not stated."

Or rather, [the subsidiaries] are connected with each individual sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), because they are subsidiary elements just like the desired result; for it is through the accomplishment of that [result] within the aggregate that there is a single designation by a single word due to its unity.
The subsidiaries do not function as a common ritual complex (*tantra*), but rather separately, because of their connection with the agent in relation to each individual sacrificial fee.

Due to the difference in the sacrificial fees, there is a difference in the connection with the agent; from that, there is a difference in the performance (*prayoga*); and from the difference in performance, there is a difference in the subsidiaries.
It is like the *iṣṭi* sacrifice.
Just as the various rites belonging to the time of the *paurṇamāsa* are performed separately due to the difference in time, so it is here.
Therefore, there is no single common procedure (*tantra*).
As for the argument beginning with "because the injunction is one" (*codanaikatvāt*), he says in response:
For because that [injunction] is accomplished through the attainment of a single result, there is a collective whole.
Therefore, due to that unity—that is, the unity of the result—there is the designation by a single word.
By means of the singular-ended word "by one *rājasūya*," there would be an instruction for all the principal rites.
The term "like the *iṣṭi*" is also connected here;
just as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, despite the difference in performance, there is a single collective whole because the fruit is one, so it is here.
Therefore, it is not dependent on the context.
The word "or" (vā) is for the purpose of refuting the previously mentioned lack of dependence on the context.
And likewise, there is the observation of another meaning.

8|1|16|1. We have stated in the *Codanā-sūtra* that the knowledge of *dharma* has its source in *codanā* (Vedic injunction).
Regarding the true nature of *codanā*:

since a recitation by a single person could not be established as being free from error, one must accept that its authoritative status is determined solely through an uninterrupted tradition (*pāraṃparya*), because it is impossible for there to be certainty regarding the true nature of *codanā* otherwise.
And because it is beginningless, there is no occurrence of the fault of infinite regress.

(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 123). That which is characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is taught as something to be performed (*kartavyatā*); and that which is taught as something to be performed is not for the sake of [any external] purpose.
For it is precisely from the comprehension of what ought to be done that the cessation of harm occurs.
*Rju*, p. 28. "Dharma is that which is characterized by Vedic injunction" (1.1.2). By this sūtra, both the essential nature of dharma and its means of valid cognition are stated.
In this regard, the Veda is the authority for Dharma in general;
and specifically, the subject matter—the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), the ritual formulas (*mantras*), and the names (*nāmadheyas*)—is the authority.
(Maṇi., p. 7. *Codanā*.)

This is the aphorism [defining] *dharma* as the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely: "The injunction (*codanā*) is the [means of knowing] this. As it has been said: "An injunction (*codanā*), an instruction (*upadeśa*), and a rule (*vidhi*) do not denote something already accomplished. Furthermore, this [aphorism] is intended to state the general nature of *dharma* by way of its definition.
If this meaning is intended by the statement as well, it is expressed even by a single sūtra.
In that case, one formulation (*vacanavyakti*) is verbal and the other is based on the sense.

Therein, having designated "that which is dharma," [the statement] "it is characterized by injunction (*codanā*), i.e., it has injunction as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)"—this is the formulation based on the means of valid cognition.

Having stated "that which is characterized by an injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, [the author] says "that is *dharma*"; this is the explicit statement of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). In that context, since being characterized by an injunction (*codanā-pramāṇakatva*) is the definition of *dharma*, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because even a prohibition is characterized by an injunction—being an object of impulsion (*pravartanā*) in the case of what is to be enjoined, and an object of dissuasion (*nivartanā*) in the case of what is to be prohibited. To prevent this, the word "beneficial" (*artha*) is a qualification [implying] the absence of being a means to what is harmful (*anartha-sādhanatva*).
As for the phrase "the attainment of prosperity through both sacrifice and non-sacrifice," this is the meaning in the Bhāṣya.

For its fruit is indeed injury (*hiṃsā*). In that regard, the conclusion [of the argument] rests upon the latter formulation (*vacanavyakti*); however, according to the Teacher (*ācārya*), two restrictive rules (*niyama*) are intended.

"One view is that regarding that which is *dharma*, the *codanā* alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is for the purpose of excluding perception, inference, tradition, and so forth.

Another view is that regarding that which is *dharma*, the *codanā* is indeed the means of valid cognition; this is for the purpose of refuting the claim of those who deny the Veda (the *nāstikas*) regarding its authority.
Such is the meaning of the *Codanā-sūtra*.
Bāla., pp. 4–5. *Codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ* (1.1.2). When there arises the inquiry as to what "dharma" is, the definition of dharma is stated.
*Codanā* means an injunction that impels one toward action; that is to say, it refers to an injunctive statement (*vidhivākya*).

That which is indicated—that is, known—by an injunction (*codanā*) is "defined by injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*). It is an "object" (*artha*) in the sense that it is an object desired by a person as a result.
Thus, the definition of Dharma is: being useful for the human goal while being appropriate to an injunction.

If only the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) were employed, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to eating and similar acts; if only the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) were employed, there would be over-extension to malevolent rites such as the *śyena* sacrifice, which is an indirect cause of undesirable results. Both terms are used to exclude these two cases. Thus, since the definition of Dharma exists, Mīmāṃsā must be undertaken for the sake of knowing it; this is the meaning of the introductory section (*adhikaraṇa*).
[The sūtra begins with] *codanā*.

Nor should it be argued that because this Sūtra establishes a restrictive rule (*niyamakaraṇa*) stating that "the Vedic word in the form of an injunction (*codanā*) is authoritative with respect to Dharma," and because one accepts the authority of the first [of the three] starting from the third, there follows the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding its definition. For in that context, the word *codanā*—based on the natural sense of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika, namely, "An injunction (*codanā*) is a sentence that impels toward action" (Bhāṣya) and "Injunction (*codanā*), instruction (*upadeśa*), and prescription (*vidhi*) are synonyms for what is not already established" (Ślokavārttika, p. 211)—denotes only a prescriptive statement (*vidhi*). Thus, such a restrictive rule is established within that Sūtra.

For this very reason, we shall explain in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa* (at page 1) that this Sūtra is not intended to propose the general subject matter of the entire second chapter (*adhyāya*), but rather only to propose the general subject matter of the non-origination (*anutpatti*) rule established in its first quarter (*pāda*).
(However, it is somewhat less than elsewhere, and nothing more than that.)
By that [statement], a restriction (*niyama*) of exactly this kind is established: "Dharma alone has the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) as its authority.

And although a restriction is also made in the form "The injunction alone is the authority," nevertheless, it should be understood as intending to mean "That alone is the authority by virtue of its predominance.
It does not, by this much, constitute a denial of the authority of other [means of knowledge] as well.

The interpretation of the words in the Sūtra is as follows: "The meaning of the Veda, characterized by *codanā*, is of the nature of what is to be accomplished (*kārya-rūpa*); it is not characterized by the senses and so forth, nor is it the relation between action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka-saṃsarga*) and the like.

The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position. In that regard, first concerning the former [view]: since there is no compound in the means of establishing the *gāyatrī* metre as being "dependent" (*sāpekṣa*), the status of being a *gāyatrī* metre would be untenable; therefore, only that mantra in which the *gāyatrī* alone is employed is denoted by the word [“gāyatrī”], and no other.
Or rather, it applies to all [mantras] because of the existence of a single metre.
The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): Or rather, the mantra [should be so called] in all cases.
Why? Because of the absence of a single *chandas*.
There is no Soma at all that possesses a single *chandas*.
Therefore, this [term] is a qualification of the *chandas* according to how this [Soma] actually exists.
Therefore, the mantra should apply to the *soma* sacrifice that possesses multiple meters.

This being the position reached by the word "or" (*vā*), it is replied: "Wherever a qualifying attribute may be applicable independently, there the dependent [attribute] is not excluded; but this is not the case wherever such [an independent application] does not exist."
This was also stated in the fourth section:
"If there were no deity consisting solely of Indra in this context, then even that which has a dependent deity would [be included] as it is.

Therefore, because of the existence here of a deity consisting solely of Indra, the quality of being "drunk by Indra" (indrapīta) is excluded from that which has a dependent deity; however, there is nothing whatsoever that possesses the quality of having the Gāyatrī meter exclusively.
Because among the three Vedas, there is necessarily the presence of other meters in certain common portions;
therefore, just as the quality of having the *ṛyantara* melody occurs only in verses of various meters, so too does the quality of having the *gāyatrī* meter [occur only in such contexts].
For this very reason, this [rule] will not apply to those that are eternally dependent, according to the principle that "that which is dependent [on another] is incapable [of independent function]."
Therefore, it is established that a mantra may consist of various meters (*nānācchandas*).

Regarding the *Sudhā*: because a compound involving mutual dependence (*sāpekṣasamāsa*)—as mentioned in the preceding section—is inappropriate here, the internal connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*) of this section lies in its serving as a clarification of the meaning.
Regarding the *Soma*: the meaning of the aphorism (*sūtra*) is that, just like the deity (*devatā*), the meter (*chandas*) would also [be determined] by association with another.

Viśvarūpa says: "In the case of the *aindrāgna* [hymn], it would belong either to one who possesses only the *gāyatrī* meter, or to another who possesses other meters as well; for such is the statement regarding the mantra.
A *bahuvrīhi* compound is common to both cases, but there is no instance where there is only a single meter."
This deliberation (*kṛtvācintā*) was made precisely because of the diversity of opinions;
it was stated that even for the sake of *savarṇa*, the word "toki" is the opening [of the discussion].
Therefore, in all ritual gifts (*sarvadāna*), the mantra recitation remains exactly as it stands.
Bhāṭṭa: In that very mantra, it is heard: "of the Gāyatrī metre.
Likewise, in this prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), this [term] is indeed a qualifier of the Soma.

Therefore, the meaning of the statement applies only where there is an offering to Indra accompanied by the Gāyatrī metre—such as in the Bṛhaspatisava and others, where it is heard: "this day becomes characterized by the Gāyatrī metre"—but it does not apply to the Jyotiṣṭoma, because there is no offering consisting solely of the Gāyatrī metre.

Nor is there an absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the general connection [of the mantra with the sacrifice]; for since the Indra-deity-mantra of the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) does not exist in the world [outside the Vedic context], the application [of the mantra] to the Bṛhaspati-savana is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: even in the Bṛhaspati-savana, another *ṛc* verse belonging to the pressing is recited; furthermore, the statement "this is a Gāyatra [hymn]" (*gāyatram etat*) can be explained by its predominance (*bhūmnā*). Since there is an absence of exclusively Gāyatrī-meter verses either in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*), and since a compound is justified here due to the constant requirement [of the meter], the mantra's placement is indeed within the archetype.

In reality, however, because each *gāyatrī* verse is an independent means, there is no violation of the compound even when other *ṛc* verses are present. Maṇḍana states: "There is also a *makṣa*-mantra in another meter.
Śaṅkara states: "A mantra consisting of various meters."

"One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Soma.

But both [the animal and its dedication] are enjoined as a single complex act.
In this context, by the first [sentence] (*ārṣeyaṃ vṛṇīte*), the act of choosing (*varaṇa*) is enjoined;
by the other [sentences] (*ekaṃ vṛṇīte*, *dvau vṛṇīte*, *trīn vṛṇīte*), the number three is enjoined for the choosing through a statement that praises the specific numbers of its parts.
There is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) because there is a difference in purpose, since they are expressed as distinct entities due to the difference in their objects.
Commentary: Or there is a restriction.
For when there is identity of meaning between the words "animal" (paśu) and "goat" (chāga), the word "animal" expresses the general class, while "goat" and others express specific instances.

How so? Because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). For example: "the animal is a goat" (*paśuś chāgaḥ*), "the animal is a he-goat" (*paśuś chagaḥ*), "the animal is a ram" (*paśur meṣaḥ*), "the animal is that" (*paśuḥ saḥ*).
This being the case, the wording of the mantra is not contradicted by the word "animal."
Therefore, even a goat is declared to be the animal to be sacrificed.

When the wording of the mantra is taken into account, it is understood that this word "animal" (paśu) was uttered with the intention of referring specifically to a goat, and not to other particulars (such as sheep and so forth).
Thus, the equipment for a goat is prescribed for this sacrifice.
Regarding the mention [of the animal], the word *paśu* (animal) refers to a goat;
this is the *chāgā-chāganyāya*. 1732. The application of the *chāgapaśunyāya*:
"Is the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice any kind of animal, or specifically a goat?"—thus it is enjoined.
Without distinction, anyone might [be used], but the goat [is required] because of the specification in the mantra.

Bhaṭṭa: In such injunctions as "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma," the word *paśu* (animal) does not denote a universal (*sāmānya*). For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a universal "animality" (*paśutva*), because it cannot serve as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for either effecthood or causality.
Nor does it consist in possessing a tail and so forth, because since that [quality] is not present in all [animals], it lacks the status of a universal (*sāmānya*).

Therefore, the word "animal" (*paśu*) denotes the individual (*vyakti*). Consequently, since all individuals—such as horses and others—are included by this [term], there is no doubt [regarding its application].
Therefore, unlike an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the mantra “of the goat’s omentum” does not possess the power to determine [the specific animal].

Even if the word *chāga* were to denote the class [of goats] in general, nevertheless, because the mantra constitutes a distinct sentence, the injunction—existing independently of it—is concluded as having universal application; thus, it does not express that specific reality [of the goat].

This being the case, even if the mantra were prescriptive, there might be a relationship of qualifier and qualified—as in the cases of “he chooses a lineage” or “he chooses three”—but this is not so here.

Therefore, regarding the mantra, the word *chāga* (goat) refers to all sacrificial animals (*paśu*), either by virtue of its connection to the state of being a "cut animal" (*chinna-paśutva*) or because it denotes a specific age. Alternatively, this mantra may apply specifically to the goat. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: since the word *chāga* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of a "goat" (*aja*), its etymological derivation (*yaugikatva*) is untenable; furthermore, because it is prescribed as masculine, it is appropriate to accept its conventional meaning rather than an etymological one. Thus, it does not possess an etymological character.

Or, even if [the word *paśu*] denotes a specific stage of age, just like words such as "red" (*śoṇa*), it is appropriate to include horses and other animals because that particular age is what is expressed;

furthermore, since there is no contradiction in including goats within the category of "beast" (*paśu*), it is illogical to assume that the mantra is merely optional (applicable only to some cases), and thus only the goat is to be taken.

Even if the word *paśu* were to denote an individual instance (*vyakti*), nevertheless, since all instances cannot be grasped simultaneously, the mantra would have no scope if only one instance were grasped; therefore, there is no obstacle whatsoever to taking the goat as the sole instance.

In reality, however, this [term] denotes a universal (*sāmānya*). And although that [universal] consists of such things as "masculinity" and so forth, nevertheless, since it is possible to speak of a commonality (*anugata*) existing in all instances delimited by "substanceness" (*vastutva*), there is no contradiction. In fact, even when the tail and other parts are not perceived, the cognition of "cowness" (*paśutva*) still occurs; thus, "cowness" is indeed a genus (*jāti*), and its status as a denoter of a universal remains unimpaired. Therefore, the determination based on the mantra is entirely appropriate.

Furthermore, even though the words *paśu* (animal) and *chāga* (goat) are distinct sentences, their relationship as qualifier and qualified does not contradict the unity of the sentence (*vākyaikavākyatā*).

And all of this should be understood as a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintā*), assuming that the statement from another recensional text, "The goat is for Agni and Soma" (*ajo 'gnīṣomīyaḥ*), does not exist.
Thus it is established that only one who possesses a goat has the qualification [to perform the sacrifice].
Maṇḍana: "The goat mentioned by the consecrated one (dīkṣita) should be the sacrificial animal (paśu); it is prescribed for the consecrated one. Śaṅkara: "The mantra is that which governs the goat."
This is the principle [stated] in *chāgo vā mantravarṇāt* (6.8.10–11):
regarding the injunction, "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma," no specific species of animal is mentioned in the revealed text (*śruti*).
In that case, a specific species must necessarily be selected.

If it were taken without restriction, then although the injunction would not be contradicted, that which is prescribed as a constant requirement for the *mantra* and the *āmnāna* would become merely optional. Therefore, this injunction, being mandatory, is interpreted as referring to a specific genus (*jāti*) by considering the wording of the *mantra*; this is according to the principle of the goat (*chāga-nyāya*). [Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 10.8.10.20]

Because the *Ṛsu-saudhanvana* is fit to be superseded by the *Sāvitra* [offering], the specific caste of the *rathakāra* (chariot-maker) is included in the rule "during the rains, the *rathakāra*" according to the principle "or the goat, because of the wording of the mantra" (*Chāgo vā mantravarṇāt*).
And in this case, the principle "or the goat, because of the wording of the mantra" does not apply.
How so? In that regard, the mantra should be employed as far as the apūrva (unseen potency) of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice extends.
Since in the injunction "One should immolate the animal for Agni and Soma," no specific species of animal is heard [stated], a specific species must necessarily be selected there. (Dupa.

According to the logic of the goat-sacrifice (*chāgapaśunyāya*), words such as *Sat* and others, as well as words such as *Nārāyaṇa*, have Śiva alone as their ultimate referent, based on the Vedic scripture: "All indeed is Rudra" (*sarvo vai rudraḥ*).

This is the logic of the goat-sacrifice. As stated in the *Śrīkarabhāṣya* (1.1.2): "Just as through the logic of the goat-sacrifice, the identity between the general and the particular is established."

11|12 Brahmasūtra: Nor should it be said that a statement concerning the *nirguṇa* (devoid of qualities) undergoes a restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) to specific qualities through the logic of the "goat-sacrifice" (*chāgapaśunyāya*), as in the cases of "devoid of the three qualities" (*traiguṇyavarjitam*) or "without qualities and so forth" (*vinā hyairguṇādibhiḥ*). This is because, since the repetition "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) is understood as a negation of everything under discussion, it is impossible to state that only a few specific [qualities] remain. Advaita 2|4|388-389 Pa.: Even though the principle of the "Anointed [Clarified Butter]" (*aktādhikaraṇa*) has been established, there arises a further doubt: that a general term which has not yet reached its final conclusion must be restricted to a specific scriptural reference, whereas once it has reached its conclusion, it need not be restricted. It is against this doubt that the logic of the "goat-sacrifice" is introduced.

And it is observed that because the injunction "He offers the Agnihotra" is already complete, it cannot—without implying an indefinite substance and deity—be subject to the prescription of a substance and deity found in other sentences such as "He offers with milk" and "If [the offering] is for Agni and Prajāpati, he offers in the evening.

Even in that case, since it is accepted that the requirement for a specific [application] of the injunction through performance results in the determination of the specific [details] such as the mantras and so forth;

in the Chāndogya, the causes of chanting—such as the modification of syllables and so on—are distinct according to the differences between the Talavakāra and other branches of scripture. And these are to be treated as options (*vikalpa*) in practice, not as things to be combined (*samuccaya*).

The world is beginningless; and if its means of proof, such as dharma and so forth, do not exist at all, then [the world] is beginningless.
No creator whatsoever creates anything without means;

Furthermore, from the devouring of living beings, saliva flows from his mouth.
Because of the absence of those [ordinary] forms of compassion, no such pity arises in him;
yet, impelled by compassion, he would emit only that which is auspicious.
Furthermore, a creation characterized by impurity and so forth is not possible through [the Lord's] mere will to maintain existence;
for if he were dependent upon means such as "self" and "belonging to self," what indeed would be difficult for him to achieve?
Moreover, for one who thus depends on external factors, his sovereignty is obstructed.

And for Him who created the world, what is there that cannot be accomplished? Even a fool does not act without a purpose. If His activity were thus [without purpose], what would become of His consciousness?
If one were engaged in play, the sense of having accomplished one's purpose would be frustrated;
and in the state of constant activity, suffering would become even greater.
(Thus, play is not possible.)
Even his desire for withdrawal [is] the world-differentiation,
which is beginningless; and as for the scriptural mention of a fruit for this [knowledge of the Self], which has the world as its locus, that too is for the sake of another.
This must indeed be a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*); there is no other fruit such as heaven [distinct] from heaven itself.
And if liberation were conceived as consisting in the enjoyment of pleasures, it would simply be heaven in another form, and that too is subject to decay.
For nothing whatsoever is understood to be imperishable in the manner of a cause;
therefore, one is liberated solely through the exhaustion of karma due to the absence of its cause.
Indeed, there is no cause for the permanence of liberation other than that which consists of non-existence.

And for those who have realized the true nature of the self, no fruit of existence is desired. In that regard, for those who have realized the true nature of the self, because of their enjoyment [of the fruits] of prior actions, a body is not produced again due to the absence of subsequent accumulation.
The body does not function for the sake of experiencing [results] produced by karma;
in the absence of that [karma], no cause remains there. One who seeks liberation does not engage in either optional or prohibited actions.
One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to avoid transgression;
however, the fruit that is sought after, even if known, will not accrue to one who lacks desire for it.
[The Self] abides within oneself.

Or rather—previously, it was deliberated whether the context (*prakaraṇa*) is contradicted by the majority [of other factors] or not;
now, it is deliberated in relation to indicative mark (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*).

In that regard, one must formulate the alternative positions (*pakṣas*) exactly as in the previously concluded section (3.4.2): namely, what would be the purpose of the bathing at sacred fords (*tīrthasnāna*) prescribed in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, and of the recitation of mantras prescribed in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa on account of yawning?

Because they are even more substantial, they are introduced here in the immediately preceding section: namely, the duty pertaining to man in general, the duty pertaining to the man connected with the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), and the duty pertaining to the ritual (*ṛtu*).
These very same categories continue to apply here as well.
In this regard, since the previous section established that [the duty] must be performed on the basis of the *prakaraṇa*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is now adopted.

"Just as the number twelve is set aside by the *ahīna* sacrifice according to the specific context, so too are both *dharma*s— namely, the sacred site (*tīrthasthāna*) and the recitation of mantras (*mantrocāra*)— set aside by the person."
Bathing, for its part, is understood as a human goal because it serves the purpose of removing impurities; it is simply fitness itself.
The section concerning the *jambhyamāna* [is] the section concerning the *jambhyamāna*.
Because the portion consisting of the fruit is not something that can be enjoined. Therefore, it should be construed exactly as stated.
Furthermore, by the rule "In the case of substances, preparatory acts, and rituals," its status as an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) will be explained.
And [the sūtra] stating, "But the fruit [accrues] when there is its application," will explain that [the action] has that [fruit] as its purpose when it is connected with the word "kāma" (desire).

He says: "We accept that it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person"; by uttering the word "refinement," the Commentator accepts that it is a duty of the person associated with the sacrifice (*ṛtu-yukta-puruṣa-dharma*).
For a refinement is not intended to be independent, since it possesses a fruit [only through being subordinate].
Regarding the statement "only for one performing the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," this [is not the case];

for in the section concerning the *jajñyamāna* (the sacrificer being born), there is no [such requirement] because the fruit in the form of drinking and holding [the soma] is already established within its own sentence, and thus that [fruit] is absent [in the other case]. This is the *Janakasattranyāya*. 1742.

Even if this were an *arthavāda* (explanatory passage), nevertheless, in view of the requirement for a result for the sacrifice understood from the context, it is more appropriate to assume another word signifying a result for this very [act] presented by its own sentence.
Therefore, it is a duty (*dharma*) pertaining solely to the person.

This being the position reached, we reply: first of all, no result is established, because the present tense indication in the word "he bears" (*dhatte*) is sublated by the non-perception of what is otherwise possible.

Therefore, having accepted its connection solely for the purpose of praise (*stuti*), one must either postulate another word such as *kāma* (desire) to supply the expectation for a result, or else, by assuming that this very [word] has a future sense, one must conceive it as being directed toward a result; and then, somehow, its status as something to be attained by the agent currently performing the action must be asserted.

If that were the case, one would have to assume a result, its production, and the fact that [the action] is preceded by the mental projection (*adhyāhāra*) of that result; therefore, rather than such an assumption, it is more appropriate—given the requirements of the context and because it is needed by the sacrifice—to assume merely the production of a fitness for the acquisition of the fruit of the sacrifice as already established. Thus, this is indeed a duty of the person associated with the sacrifice (*kratuyuk-puruṣadharma*). Furthermore, because it brings about the fitness for the acquisition of the fruit, it belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*); this is the practical application (*prayojana*). Maṇḍana: "The qualified person (*adhikārī*) under discussion is one who is being born."

Śaṅkara [says]: "Being born thus from the sacrifice... 11. By this, even the Mīmāṃsakas—who, like the Naiyāyikas, maintain that the agent is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) in the case of the agent and the instrument, and that the present middle participle suffix (*śānac*) signifies the locus of the agent being born—are refuted.
[This is stated] in the *Śabdacintāmaṇi*.

By the principle of the section concerning the one being born (*jajñyamānādhikaraṇanyāya*), it is established that [the red turban, etc. is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the person engaged in the sacrifice.

(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 320). By the principle of the section concerning the one being born, since even the red turban and so forth are understood to be purificatory rites—just like shaving and the like—[they are not independent acts].
(p. 310, l. 59). [They are] qualities of the person engaged in the sacrifice, according to the principle of the section concerning the one being born (*jajñyamānanyāya*).

Su. Pṛ. 1389: The statement of the mantra recited at the time of being born (*jajñyamāna*) is an occasional (*naimittika*) injunction; since it serves the purpose of avoiding a fault, it is a subsidiary injunction (*kratvartha*) pertaining to the qualification for the rite. Bāla. Pṛ. 14: The recitation of the mantra at the time of being born is restricted solely to the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). (And the mantra is: "In me, skill and... etc.)
Ratna. 6|5|122. The maxim of lac and wood (*jatukāṣṭhanyāya*).

Just as lac and wood, being conjoined, can be separated from one another through a specific effort—such that the wood is separated from the lac, or the lac from the wood—in the same way, where two things are actually distinct but appear non-distinct due to some [superimposition], their separation is again effected by a different effort; such is the application of this principle.

As it is stated in the tenth chapter of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, in the section on the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paranomasia): "In this regard, some say that only the case of complete commingling (*saṃbhedaka*) is the province of verbal *śleṣa*."

"In which [case], because two words are uttered with a detailed expansion such as the distinction between the acute (*udātta*) accent and so forth, there is a remainder [of one] in both words according to the analogy of lac and wood. (Sāṃkṣepaśārīraka 6.8). Janakasattram.
Among the householders, I have never seen [this] in the Śatarātra sacrifices.

And that [sacrifice] is a modification (*vikāra*) because it is included within the days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), as stated in *Soma* 8.3.2: "In the Janakasaptarātra, there are four *triṣṭubh* days, with the *agniṣṭoma* as the principal. Among those, the first day has the character of an *agniṣṭoma*.
The remaining three [sacrifices] are modifications of the *agniṣṭoma*.
The specific characteristic common to all four is that they consist of the *trivṛt* stoma.

In the first four days, the ritual details (*dharma*) of the four days belonging to the *pṛṣṭha-ṣaḍaha* of the twelve-day sacrifice—namely the *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, *daśada*, and *ekaviṃśa* stomas—are to be extended [by analogy], with the exception of the *pañcadaśatva* and other such qualities.
The characteristics of the *gaṇa* (group) [apply] to the whole, but not to the first day among the subsequent three. Vi.
8.3.2. The principle of the Janaka-sattra:
in the Janaka-samarātra, there is a sequential extension (*atideśa*) of the seven-day rites belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
In the case of an injunction for a group (*gaṇacodanā*), there is a repetition of that which possesses the characteristic mark;
this very point is understood.
The Commentary states: It is heard in the *Janakasaptarātra* sacrifice that "there are four days consisting of the *trivṛt* stoma."
Likewise, it is heard elsewhere: "There are nine days consisting of the *trivṛt*.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is it the repetition of the first day of the *pārthika* (*pṛṣṭha-ṣaḍaha*), or is it the injunction for the Soma-offerings of the various twelve-day periods?
What is the prima facie view? When there is an injunction for a group, that which possesses the indicative mark is understood to be repeated, as in the case of the *Āgneya*.

In this very same injunction regarding the *gaṇa*, since the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the first day of the terrestrial group is the state of being threefold (*trivṛttva*), its repetition is understood in that very way, due to the commonality of the injunction (*codanā-sāmānyāt*), as in the case of the *Āgneya*.

Likewise, because of the identity of the deity—as in "to Agni Pāvaka" and "to Agni Śuci"—there is a repetition of the concluding portion (*vidhanta-abhyāsa*) of the *Āgneya* due to the commonality of the injunction; so it is here as well.

Or rather, the various days of the twelve-day sacrifice should proceed; not the first individual day. Why? Because it is a composite whole (saṃghāta). Commentary: Or rather, the various days belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice should proceed, and not the first individual day.
Why? Because it is a composite whole.
It is precisely in the sense of a collective whole (*saṃghāta*) that it is said, "four three-day periods in a day";
for the number "four," which resides in distinct entities, applies to the days by way of their distinctness.
And there, in that sacrificial session lasting several nights, there are four sets of twelve-day rites that proceed by way of injunction on various days.
It is possible to enjoin the state of being "threefold" (trivṛt) with reference to those;
however, it is not the case that the number four is enjoined with reference to many threefold days.

The Ṭup-ṭīkā states: They exist. Therein, by means of the injunction for the *gaṇa*—namely, "one should sacrifice with the *Janakasaptarātra*"—four days belonging to the *Dvādaśāha* have been introduced (*upāditāni*).

Having referred to those [days] by the statement "the four days are *trivṛt*," it is possible to enjoin their *trivṛt* nature; thus, the *trivṛt* nature is enjoined (this is the reading in the Ṛjuvimalā on the Ṭup-ṭīkā).

This [commentary] is incorrect. (Why? It is said: "One should sacrifice at the Janakasatrarātra"—this is an injunction for performance (*prayogacodanā*) (because a fruit is heard), and performance depends upon origination (*utpatti*), since [the agent] is already occupied elsewhere. [The reading in the Raṅna is: "But the injunction for performance depends upon origination.
The reading in the Ānandāśrama edition is: "It does not abandon origination."

The word *ahaḥ* denotes a specific sacrifice (namely, the Soma sacrifice); this [word], being heard in the expression "four days" (*catvāri ahāni*), leads one to infer even that specific [Soma] sacrifice which is not explicitly mentioned.
For this qualification is not possible without the [Soma] sacrifice, just as the qualification "the slayer of Vṛtra" (*vṛtrahan*) leads one to infer Indra. Thus is this case as well.
In that context, since the plural number is used, when an indefinite plurality would otherwise apply, the number "four" is restricted.
For these [days], the state of being *trivṛt* and the state of being *agniṣṭoma* are enjoined.

Therein, by the statement "there are four *trivṛt* days" (which are primarily *agniṣṭomas*), the [ritual] acts already established are referred to (*anūdya*) and then enjoined with respect to the result in the form: "One should sacrifice with the Janaka-Ṣaṭsata-night rite."
(But it is not by this mere incitement that there is an injunction of a quality.

How, then, does he state the view of the *adhikaraṇa*?—) In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), by the mark (*liṅga*) of being "threefold" (*trivṛt*), there is the displacement (*vidhvanta*) of the first day [of the *pārthika* sacrifice]—that is, the fourth [day].
In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the quality is the aggregate (*saṃghāta*) of the principal sacrifices.

By virtue of that quality [namely, *saṃghātatva*, or "the state of being a composite"] belonging to it, the property of the various twelve-day rites (*dvādaśāhika*) is extended by analogy, due to the commonality of being a composite.
However, the quality of being threefold (*trivṛttva*) resides in the subordinate parts [because it is the measure of the stotriya verses];
therefore, it is weaker because it is extrinsic [compared to the mark of the composite, which is intrinsic].
Thus, the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) is to be described in this manner (and not as in the *Bhāṣya*).
For if it were described as the *Bhāṣyakāra* has explained, many faults would arise.

How could it be said that, having restated "four," the state of being "threefold" (*trivṛttva*) is enjoined? Moreover, there are not four [days] in the *sattra-ahargaṇa*, because those four which might be restated are not themselves being enjoined.

We speak having granted [the opponent's position] for the sake of argument: let there be four [sacrifices], even then, because "having the Agniṣṭoma as the primary" would be a second quality to be enjoined, the sentence would suffer from syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), since multiple qualities are being enjoined with respect to an action already established [by another injunction].
Therefore, it is established that this alone is the original injunction (*utpatticodanā*).

The *Tantraratna* states: Where the injunction consists solely of a quality, there the state of being first, second, and so forth, being a dependent designation (*sāpekṣapratīka*), is weaker than the state of being threefold (*trivṛttva*), which is independent (*anapekṣa*) and thus more powerful.

Therefore, in the Janaka-Ṣaḍrātra sacrifice, the first four days, due to the commonality of being *trivṛt*, follow the nature of the first [day] of the Pārthika [sacrifice]. Consequently, there is the performance of the four *pṛṣṭha* chants and so forth. And thus, this sacrifice is appropriately characterized as having the *agniṣṭoma* as its primary [stotra], because the first day is an *agniṣṭoma*.

In this context, although there is the application of four [elements], because of the contradiction with the scripturally stated *trivṛt* nature, fifteen-foldness (*pañcadaśatva*) and so forth do not apply; rather, it should be understood that the *vidhvanta* occurs as something distinct from those.
The eight *samarātras* are the Soma-family groups; among them, the eighth is the Janaka-sattrarātra.
Its connection follows from the previous increase.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: regarding the injunction of a hundred [stomas] such as "four threefold [stomas]," the repetition of that which possesses the characteristic mark of the threefold stoma and so forth is understood, just like the Āgneya; for example, the concluding portion of the earlier Bārhaspatya belongs to the Āgneya. Thus: "Is this the first day of the twelve-day sacrifice characterized by the threefold stoma, or is it another [day] based on the sequence of the days? It is the former, because of its possession of the threefold stoma. It would be another [day] according to the connection with the days.
In the *Janakasaptarātra* sacrifice, there are four days consisting of the *Trivṛt* stoma;
this is the principle of the *Janakasaptarātra*. [The rule applies] because the recitation (*japa*), the similar benediction (*tulyāśīḥ*), and the designation (*abhidhāna*) are common to all.

Nor should it be argued that, because there is a lack of evidence for the threefold nature in the other four [stomas], the injunction of the characteristic of being an *agniṣṭoma* is necessarily restricted to the *āgneyī* alone;

for there is no reason to bypass the first [option], and since the three others have their stoma prescribed by another injunction, the threefold nature is obtained in all four through the *āgneyī* alone.
This is the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya.

In reality, however, if one were to enjoin the quality of being threefold with reference to the number four, it would result in the injunction of the triad applying to the four *stomas* dedicated to Agni among the days that possess *sāman*; if it were enjoined with reference to the days alone, it would apply everywhere; and if it were enjoined with reference to the days qualified by the number four, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, this is precisely the injunction of the quality of being a *kratvartha* (subserving the sacrifice) characterized by the triad as distinct from the number [four]. Furthermore, there is an injunction for the three [days] by means of another injunction, and for all of them, the mere connection with the fruit is established by the sentence stating the result.

Thus, since the status of being a *gaṇa* (group) for all four is understood from the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), and because that [status] resides in the originative injunction, the state of being three (*tritva*) is also present; yet, even though they are equal in this regard, the state of being three is weaker than the state of being a *gaṇa* because it subsists in the subsidiary *stotras*, whereas the *gaṇa*-status subsists in the primary [rite]. Regarding the term *japa*: the nature of being a *japa* consists in being enjoined by a *japati*-injunction, and not in being performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). For if it were the latter, then the *yājyā* verse which is a subsidiary of the *upāṃśuyāja* would also incur the status of being a *japa*, which would lead to an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*).

Nor is it the case that its status as having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) is due to a desire to express a meaning; for when a visible purpose is absent, it is logical to assume an unseen purpose, since there is no evidence for a desire to express a meaning. For this very reason, the *Pāṇinīya Śikṣā* (5.2) states: "A mantra deficient in accent or phoneme, if wrongly employed, does not convey that meaning," thereby showing that the manifestation of meaning occurs in recitation (*japa*) and the like when accompanied by the correct accents.

For this very reason, even though they are enjoined by injunctions for recitation (*japaticodanā*), it does not follow that they have exclusively an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), since it is also possible for them to function as instruments (*karaṇa*) or as mantras (*mantra*).
Praise (*stuti*), however, is an expression whose primary intent is a quality; although it may have an unseen purpose, it is useful for the ritual action by way of generating faith and so forth.
Expression (*abhidhāna*) is the act of making known a quality as qualified by other qualities.
And even if there is some overlap (*sāṅkarya*) among these, it is not a fault, because each serves its respective purpose; this is the eightfold meaning here.

Among them, those such as *japa* (muttering) which reveal what is for the sake of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), have an option (*vikalpa*) precisely because they are *karaṇa-mantras*. However, those whose purpose is to reveal what is inherent in that which is not to be performed—though they are revealers—they must be combined (*samuccaya*) precisely for the sake of generating greater faith, since they are useful for the ritual by way of generating faith and so forth. But those whose purpose is to reveal what is inherent in that which is for the sake of the unseen, their combination is like that of the *praiṣa* and other such mantras.

Nor can there be a suspicion of optionality (*vikalpa*) based on the application of designations such as "single recitation" (*ekajapa*) and so forth, or because they lead to a single result; for in the case of recitations with visible purposes (*dṛṣṭārtha*), a difference in results is necessary, making it untenable to assume that all recitations have the same single result.
Maṇḍana [states]: "There is a combination (*samuccaya*) of recitations and the like.
Śaṃkara [states]: "And that [combination] applies to recitations, blessings, and so forth."
That is the collection [of rules].
Regarding the mantras for recitation (*japa*) and so forth, there is a fixed order established by the traditional transmission (*samāmnāya*) of the mantras;
this is to be seen in the section concerning the spoken word (*bhāṣāstra*).
Bhāṣya 1.4.18–20–22: "Recitation and so forth are not connected with ritual acts.

As for what was stated in the twelfth [book] regarding recitation and so forth having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), that was intended to mean that the expression of the meaning accomplished by a mantra has an unseen purpose.

Or, let it be that recitation and so forth have as their sole purpose the mere utterance of those things inherent in the ritual act; nevertheless, while it is possible for even *karaṇa-mantras* (instrumental mantras) and others—which express meanings inherent in the ritual act—to be employed through a visible means (*dṛṣṭavidhayā*), it is not proper to assume that they serve the purpose of utterance for an unseen result.
"Taking away.
[Examples include]: "One should offer the Jaya oblations with that ritual act for which one desires [victory]," "He offers the Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations," and "He offers the Abhyātāna oblations."

In this regard, are these [the *kṛcchra* and other penances] subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to all actions, such as those that produce evil results (*kuṣṭha*, etc.), or are they subsidiary to Vedic rites, such as the *agnihotra*?
Their status as subsidiary is established because they involve the accumulation of specific actions and because a fruit is heard [in the scriptures].
What, then, is the prima facie position? They are subsidiary to all actions, because no specific distinction is stated.

Or rather—here, since the remaining parts of the ritual acts have been determined by the two sentences, [the opponent] considers that the connection with their specific details occurs at the end of the scriptural statement regarding those details.

Although the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) perceives there the connection of the oblations with the *āhavanīya* fire, because of the predominance of the oblations, he thinks that the attainment of the *āhavanīya* occurs through that part; and since even agriculture, service, and so forth possess the specific quality of being means for attaining prosperity (*ṛddhi*), he considers that the phrase "by whatever rite one desires prosperity" is intended as an illustration. Thus, thinking this, he says: "The *jaya*-oblations are subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to all rites. Therefore, desiring prosperity even through service and the like, one should offer the *jaya*-oblations in the *āhavanīya* fire.

Nor are these [rites] non-instrumental for the Āhavanīya fire, because the Āhavanīya is prescribed with reference to the mere act of offering (homa). Therefore, while they may indeed not apply to one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni), they must be performed by one who has maintained the fires (āhitāgni), even when he performs ordinary worldly acts characterized by the [four] social classes (varṇa). In this way, the inherent force of the independent injunction (anāramyavāda) will not be frustrated.

Furthermore, these [rites] such as plowing (*karṣaṇa*) and so forth would not be directly connected to the ritual acts (*karma*) as their primary referents (*prakṛtyartha*); or, at most, they might be excluded from the modified rites (*vikṛti*) for fear of redundancy. However, in the case of *kuṣmāṇḍa* and other such rites, there is no suspicion of redundancy whatsoever; thus, it is more appropriate that they are simply not mentioned [in this context]. As for the oblations (*homa*), they should be restricted [to the *āhavanīya* fire], because of their connection with the *āhavanīya*. The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: "And this is not the case—that [these rites] such as plowing and so forth are subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of all ritual acts."
These are oblations; therefore, they should be restricted [to the Āhavanīya fire].
In the case of oblations, there is a connection with the Āhavanīya, as it is said: "When one offers in the Āhavanīya, by that means this Agni becomes pleased.
Therefore, for whomsoever there is an Āhavanīya, these [oblations] are its subsidiary parts.
Furthermore, activities such as plowing do not pertain to the Āhavanīya fire;
nor does the Gārhapatya fire exist for them, from which the Āhavanīya could be carried forward (praṇīta). Therefore, the Jaya and other offerings do not belong to plowing and similar acts.
Or rather—these oblations would remain restricted to Vedic rites alone; they would not apply everywhere.
Why? Because "the co-location of the subsidiary and the primary is always required.
And these [oblations] could not have the same location as the *kuṣmāṇḍa* and other such [non-Vedic] acts.
For ploughing is performed on the ground, as is service in the royal court;
furthermore, since the Jaya and other offerings are of the nature of *homa*, they must exclusively be performed in the *āhavanīya* fire, as no other specific locus has been prescribed for them.
In that case, if there were no scriptural injunction to the contrary, the separation of the subsidiaries from the principal act (*aṅga-pradhāna-vaideśya*) would result in a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*).
There is indeed a case of irregularity regarding the object, wherein [the materials] become defective;
and when that exists, the substitution of a different location is not permitted by presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*).
Nor does an action performed with what has been permitted by the scripture yield its fruit.

Therefore, since permission is granted even to those who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) and those who are ignorant, solely for the sake of attaining the possession of qualities (*saguṇa-saṃpad*), these [rites] do not apply;
likewise for other ritual acts as well.
But does it not say that the field itself is the *āhavanīya* fire, and that one will offer oblations after having brought [the fire] there?
No; nevertheless, this is because the difference in location between the *vilekhana* (digging) and the *homa* (offering) is avoided.
For in that case, mere proximity is permitted, not identity of location.
Indeed, it is not possible to place the *āhavanīya* fire into each individual fissure in order to perform the offering.
Nor, however, does [the fire] come to occupy the same location [as the offering materials] by that much alone.
Furthermore, the statement "but there are oblations" (*homāstu*) is an explanatory reason (*hetūpadeśa*);
because these are oblations, therefore they should remain distinct.

"And the remainder [is for the Vedic] because of the traditional designation. The Commentary: For this reason also we see that they are subsidiary to the Vedic; why? Because of the traditional designation (*samākhyāna*).
Because of the designation.
For since the *jayas* and other rites are recited in the Veda designated as "pertaining to the Adhvaryu" (*ādhvaryava*), they are to be performed by the Adhvaryu.
If they were performed by one who is not the Adhvaryu—such as in the case of plowing and other activities where the Adhvaryu is absent—they would contradict that designation.
Therefore, they are subsidiary to the Vedic [rituals].
Or rather— for this reason as well, the *jaya* and other [rites] are subsidiary only to the Vedic [rituals],
because there is conformity with the traditional designation (*samākhyā*).
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other such sacrifices, the Adhvaryu exists;
being subordinate members of that [sacrifice], these [rites] attain the status of having him as their performer.

However, because the Kuṣmāṇḍas lack the status of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and because there is no mention of a separate selection (*varaṇa*) for the Jaya and other rites, and because they are *apūrva* (novel), they do not obtain application through the extended injunction (*codaka*).
And if the Adhvaryu exists for that very purpose, then a difference of agents would also result;
for the Adhvaryu does not perform [the duties] in the midst of agriculture.

Therefore, by virtue of the designation (samākhyā), that which is the supplementary portion of the sentence—whether it be that which is to be performed by the Adhvaryu, or the Adhvaryu himself who is the subordinate agent—is thus assisted; in this way, the systematic determination (vyavasthā) is established.
Śabara: In the preceding section, the discussion of *anārabhyavāda* (independent injunctions) was introduced as a consequence of the inquiry into the human goals (*puruṣārtha*) to be accomplished.

Therefore, since it has been established by the sentence itself that the *jaya* and other such rites—which are studied independently (*anārabhyadhīta*)—belong to the category of ritual acts (*karman*), a specific detail regarding them is now heard:
"In that case, because there is no distinction, they are understood to serve the purpose of all ritual acts."

Therefore, even by means of a *kuṣmāṇḍa* [oblation] or the like, one should offer there; thus, because of the absence of deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) even in that case, the *jaya* and other offerings would serve all purposes. This is not so, because a deficiency arises from the fact that they are located outside the primary ritual (*pradhāna*).
Soma says: Regarding the statement, "That which they conquered is the victory of the *jayas*," the *jayas* are the oblations performed with mantras such as "The mind (*citta*) and...

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: that which is understood from the context to be a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to a specific rite, by virtue of the [general] statement, becomes a subsidiary to all rites because there is no distinction [specifying otherwise].
Viśvarūpa says: "In the case of the *jaya*-oblation, its application to every purpose is determined by the specific rite through which one desires success."
Or rather, they belong to Vedic rites alone, because [the rule] applies to all without restriction;
for while the *homa* should take place in the *āhavanīya* fire, that [fire] does not exist in the case of black antelope skins and the like.
Therefore, even though they are mentioned in a non-Vedic context, those *jayā* offerings belong only to Vedic rites.
13. Bhāṭṭa: It has been taught that there is no commencement [of the Jaya offerings] with the words, "In whatever rite this [failure] occurs, one should offer the Jaya oblations.
The meaning is that one who desires to obtain success—that is, an abundance of the fruit of the rite—through that rite [should perform them].
Therefore, for the sake of the fruit as it stands, the rites are performed even without the Jaya offerings and the rest.

[The term] *karmaṇyāḥ* [refers to] those rites such as the *jaya` offerings performed out of a desire for an abundance of results. Since the nature of the rite (*karmatva*) is already included within the result itself, it does not stand in need of them in the same way that the *juhū* ladle does.
Nor is it possible for worldly actions such as agriculture or eating—which have visible purposes—to take up the *jaya` offerings and others which have invisible purposes.

Just as in the cases of "one should perform agricultural work under the asterism Rohiṇī" and "prior to the agricultural work, one should offer an oblation to Heaven and Earth at the boundary of the field," the inclusion of this [offering] is justified for the sake of completing the rite without obstacles or for the sake of increasing the fruit;

nor does it follow that the Jaya-homas and others are not ancillaries to agriculture simply because they are accomplished by means of the Āhavanīya fire and thus do not exist during the dark fortnight (Kṛṣṇapakṣa), since it is logical that the Jaya-homas themselves, being of the nature of *homa*, necessitate the bringing forward (*praṇayana*) of the Āhavanīya fire.

Nor is it the case that [the subsidiary] lacks the status of an auxiliary (*anaṅgatva*) because of the impossibility of its being in the same location as the primary (*pradhāna-sādeśya*); for even if that [exact co-location] is impossible, the subsidiary is still established by the principle of "conflict between the quality of the subsidiary and the primary" (*aṅga-guṇa-virodha-nyāya*).
This is because co-location is possible by bringing the fire to the site of the ploughing.

In reality, however, since there is no injunction [for the fire] as something intended for the site of the ploughing, there is no performance-injunction (*prayoga-vidhi*); thus, there is simply no authoritative basis for the subsidiary and the primary to occupy the same location.

Or let it be so; nevertheless, since that [injunction] lacks the status of a means of knowledge such as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the like, it is impossible for it to restrict the scope of the sentence. Therefore, rites such as *jayā* and others must indeed pertain to all actions, both worldly and Vedic, in common.

This being the position reached: since the fire [of the *āhavanīya*] exists for the sake of Vedic rites and its dependence on the *praṇayana* (carrying forward) rite is based on that [Vedic context], whereas for the sake of other (non-Vedic) rites there would be the fabrication of a connection to that [fire], it is—due to such factors as complexity (*gaurava*) and inconsistency (*vaigunya*)—just as the scriptural injunctions regarding desires (*kāmaśruti*) have as their scope only those who have established the fires (*āhitāgni*), so too, by the injunction of the *jaya* and other offerings, for the sake of its own parsimony, these are prescribed as being for the sake of rites possessing the fire alone; therefore, they do not pertain to other rites. Maṇḍana: "The *jaya* and others belong to Vedic oblations. Śaṃkara: "The *jaya* and others are merely auxiliary to the ritual action (*karmāṅga*)."

Just as the postulation of a result occurs in worldly (laukika) rites by way of the *jayādi* [mantras] but not in Vedic ones, so too, even though it is prescribed, the act of carrying the fire (*tatpraṇayana*) and so forth is prompted in that case where fire is present, but not elsewhere; thus there is a disparity (*vairūpya*). Indeed, the scriptural injunction regarding desire (*kāmaśruti*) itself permits its own restriction in accordance with the requirements of the injunction and its sublation (*vidhibādhava*). Therefore, only those words associated with rites involving fire are the objects of reference (*uddeśya*). And even that is not by way of being a subordinate element (*śeṣitā*), but rather solely by way of being a condition (*nimittatā*).

10.8.4]. The section concerning *jartila* and *gavīdhuka*.
The *jartilayavāgū* (gruel of wild sesame) is to be understood as follows:

"One should offer oblations with *jartila* gruel, or one should offer oblations with *gavīdhuka* gruel; one does not harm domestic animals, nor does one harm wild animals. Furthermore, there is the statement: "Indeed, *jartila* and *gavīdhuka* are not valid oblations (*anāhuti*); one should offer the *agnihotra* with milk. From this injunction (*vidhi*) and from the inference of a prohibition based on the censure (*nindā*) that they are "not valid oblations," both an injunction and a prohibition are established.
This being the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is:

"If one does not postulate another [meaning], it would be a restatement of what is already established (*prākṛtārthavāda*), because of its pointlessness and because of the capacity of the other. However, the statement "But the prohibition is for the sake of instruction" is to be applied as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the preceding section.

If one were not to assume another injunction—provided that no direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*) is present here—then, as in the case of the sentence regarding the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, there would be an injunction by the first part and a prohibition by the second. However, in this case, since another injunction, "One should offer the *agnihotra* with milk," is already established, this [statement] must be an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) subordinate to it. Otherwise, in the absence of syntactical unity with a prohibition, its character as a censure (*nindā*) could not be determined; and since the mention of its being "not an offering" (*anāhuti*) would then be impossible to interpret as implying a prohibition, it would result in meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*).

Even if a prohibition were somehow imagined, since it would be like the prohibition of taking the *ṣoḍaśin* cup and would thus serve the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*), and since that option is established here by the injunction of other substances such as milk, its [the imagined prohibition's] purposelessness (*ānarthakya*) cannot be avoided.
Having raised the objection as to how the censure of gruel (*yavāgū*) can be equal to the censure of milk, it is stated: "and because of the force of the other."

The meaning is that, although *jartila* (wild sesame) and *gavīdhuka* (a type of wild grain) are praised because they do not involve the slaughter of domestic or wild animals, they are nonetheless inferior to the use of milk; therefore, by implication, milk is "more excellent" (*praśastataram*) when construed with the subsequent injunction regarding milk.

Thus, since it is possible for them to form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), even the optative suffix (*liṅga*) in the word "one should sacrifice" (*juhuyāt*)—which would otherwise lead to the acceptance of multiple unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*) and distinct ritual acts—is established as being for the purpose of praise (*stuti*).
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, pp. 61–62). [This establishes that the prohibition of *jartila* rice-gruel is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the injunction for the milk-oblation.]
Bhāṣya 10.8.4.7: "Or [the text mentions] wild sesame gruel.
This is a prohibition of wild sesame gruel and the like in the Agnihotra, serving as an explanatory praise (arthavāda) for the injunction regarding the offering of milk.

For if it did not establish another [prohibition], it would be an explanatory praise for what is already established, since it would otherwise be purposeless and because of its capacity to relate to something else.

The Commentary states: This is handed down in the Agnihotra ritual: "One should offer either a gruel of wild sesamum (*ajartila*) or a gruel of *gavīdhuka* seeds; one does not harm domestic animals nor wild animals. However, they also say: "Wild sesamum and *gavīdhuka* are indeed not a valid oblation; one should perform the Agnihotra with milk."

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the injunction "He offers with a gruel of jartila seeds or with a gruel of gavīdhuka seeds," and the statement "Jartila seeds and gavīdhuka seeds are indeed no oblation" a prohibition; or rather, are both of these explanatory passages (arthavādas), while "He performs the Agnihotra with milk" is the injunction?
What is the prima facie position? "With a gruel of jartila seeds" is an injunction, because the word of injunction is directly perceived.
Likewise, "It is no oblation" is also a directly perceived prohibition.
The other injunction, "One offers the Agnihotra with milk," is likewise directly perceived. This being the case, there is an option:
one may offer either with a gruel of wild sesame (*jartila*) or with a gruel of *gavidhuka* seeds, or one may not offer with those two, but rather offer with milk.
And in this case, a preclusive negation (*paryudāsa*) is not possible;

for the word "not" (*na*) has no capacity [to negate] either the *jartila* grain gruel or the *gavīdhuka* grain gruel, because it is compounded with the word "oblation" (*āhuti*). Or, even if such a capacity were assumed, there would be no syntactic connection at all in the expression: "He offers with *ajartila* grain gruel, [that is,] he offers with *jartila* grain gruel."
Furthermore, in the case of a prohibition by exclusion (paryudāsa), the injunction would become purposeless,
because that [which is excluded] has already been established.
Moreover, if milk were being enjoined, the exclusion would be rendered meaningless.
Because wild sesame and *gavīdhuka* seeds have not been previously obtained [as prescribed],
there is therefore an option (*vikalpa*).
This being the position reached, we reply:
This alternative would be a negation if it did not imply another injunction. In that case,

the statement regarding *jartila* and *gavīdhuka* seeds for the *agnihotra*, as well as the statement that [other offerings] are not oblations, would serve the purpose of an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) for the injunction "one offers the *agnihotra* with milk," because otherwise they would be purposeless.
For in that case, the prohibition would be meaningless.
When one offers with milk, then, as it is not according to the rule, the *jartila* and *gavīdhuka* seeds would constitute a non-oblation (*anāhuti*).
But how can that which is offered in a sacrifice be a non-oblation?

Through the force of another [text], namely by the injunction "one offers the Agnihotra with milk," the capacity for both the injunction regarding *jartila* and *gavidhuka* seeds and the prohibition [of them] arises.

Therefore, all this constitutes a single sentence. How so? It is connected directly with the words of censure: "One should offer with *jartila* gruel or with *gavidhuka* gruel; indeed, *jartila* and *gavidhuka* are not offerings."
And also: "Day.

Just as in the case where it is said, "Poison must never be eaten," the sentence is fixed for the purpose of connecting with the prohibition of the performance of eating poison, and not for the purpose of its performance—so too should it be understood here.
Ṭup— [In this regard, there are partial differences in the readings among my own manuscript of the Ṭup-ṭīkā, the printed edition from Ānandāśrama, and the manuscript following the Tantraratna.

[The printed edition adds: "If this were so..."; the manuscript further adds: "One should offer with the gruel of wild sesame; therefore, the injunction of wild sesame would be purposeless."]

Now, if it were argued that "an offering not consisting of an oblation (*anāhuti*) must be performed," and so forth—the remaining portion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is the same for all three cases—then the conclusion (*siddhānta*), being essentially one due to the absence of difference, is presented as a single unit by filling in the lacuna: It is said: This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) praising the milk-oblation (*payohoma*). How so? He says: "By the statement 'the *jartila* and *vāra* seeds are non-offerings' (*anāhutitvaṃ jartilavā*), you (the proponent of the prima facie view) intend a prohibition through the term 'non-offering. But that option is obtained precisely by the injunction 'one should offer with milk,' even without a prohibitory statement."
Therefore, a prohibition is not tenable.

However, all of this is tenable only as a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the injunction "one should offer with milk," just as [the statement] "Devadatta is handsome" [is supplementary to an injunction regarding Devadatta].
"Regarding the statement 'he is learned' and 'even though he is distinguished by such qualities, compared to Yajñadatta he is unlearned and not excellent':
therein, the praise and blame directed at Devadatta are not uttered for the sake of Devadatta (that is, not intended to enjoin or prohibit Devadatta), but rather for the sake of Yajñadatta."
Even so, the censure and praise are for the purpose of enjoining milk;
as Bhaṭṭabhāskara states: "Soma—jartila means black sesame (kārale); gavedhuka means grass-grains."
*Jartila*s are wild sesame seeds; *gavedhukā*s are wild wheat.
So say some [others hold that] wild wheat must be bamboo-seeds (*veṇuyava*), because other types of wild wheat are not found.
However, even in this case, *veṇuyava* (wild barley) is prescribed separately.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: if nothing else were being enjoined, then the *nañ* heard here would indeed have the sense of a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). But since it is a corroboration (*anvayavyatireka*) of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it serves as a restatement of that injunction; for the option (*vikalpa*) regarding *jartila* and so forth is already established by that very injunction. Thus, because a prohibition would be redundant for the sake of an option, and because it is incapable of enjoining another substance, it has a single purpose through praise (*stuti*).

Bhaṭṭa: In the Agnihotra, it is heard in scripture: "With wild sesame" (*ajartila*), as in the Bhāṣya.

In this regard, there arises the consideration: is the prohibition "it is not an oblation" (*anāhuti*) directed toward *jartila* (sesame growing wild) and *ādhika* (wild rice) which were enjoined by the first two sentences, or does this entire passage constitute a single injunction for the milk-oblation (*payohoma*)? Upon reflection, because the hearing of distinct verbal roots (*ākhyāta-bheda*) indicates that the sentences are separate, and because there is no evidence to assume they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) through the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of praise, and because the clear hearing of injunctions in the first two sentences necessitates that the *jartila-yavāgū* and *ādhika-yavāgū* must be enjoined, and because the phrase "it is not an oblation" is understood as a prohibition of those very things being censured, these two [substances] are both enjoined and prohibited; therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
But there is another injunction regarding milk alone.

This being the case, even if the first [injunction] were an injunction of *jartila* (wild sesame) and *ākhyaka* (wild rice), nevertheless, because of the censure "it is not an oblation," it is not to be understood as an independent prohibition.
For its result—namely, the option—is already established by the injunction of milk itself, according to the logic of the *vrīhi-yava* (rice and barley) rule.

Therefore, the censure stating "it is not an oblation" (anāhutiḥ) serves solely to establish the injunction regarding milk, according to the maxim of "censuring one thing to praise another" (nāhi-nindā-nyāya).
In reality, even the injunction regarding *jartila* (wild sesame) and *ākhu-kaṇā* (rat's droppings) is intended only for the praise of milk by means of censuring animal products;
it is not intended as an injunction for those substances themselves.
Regarding milk, even though both [the *jartila-yavāgu* and *jala-taraṅga*] are praiseworthy,
they follow the maxim of the *jartila-yavāgu* (1751) and the maxim of the water-wave; since these two are actually censurable in comparison to milk, the praise is that milk alone is more excellent.
Moreover, even though an injunction is heard, it is not prescriptive because its injunctive power is obstructed by the word *vā*.
Indeed, this word *vā* does not enjoin an option (*vikalpa*), as that is established through reasoning alone;
rather, it has the purpose of enjoining something else, just as in the expression: "One might even eat poison, but one should not eat the food of others."
Therefore, this entire passage, characterized as praise, forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction regarding milk and serves the purpose of praise.
In this way, syntactical unity is also achieved. As Maṇḍana says: "Praise is a sentence distinct from [the injunction]."

The Rash One. 925. The Analogy of the Water Wave:

Just as the qualities of water, such as sweetness, clarity, and coolness, when a wave arises on the surface of the water due to the force of the wind, reach that wave—which is a transformation (*vivarta*) of the water—and reside in it; and subsequently, after the wave has subsided, they likewise follow into the foam—which is a transformation of the wave—and reside in it.

Even though there exists the conventional distinction between water, waves, and foam, since water and the others have no essential nature apart from their sweetness, substantiality, and coolness, they consist essentially of sweetness and substance; for each subsequent differentiated form is a manifestation (*vivarta*) of its preceding substrate.
By this principle, it is demonstrated that each subsequent effect is non-different from its preceding substrate.
