The Principle of Immersion in Water.
This is a specific type of divine ordeal (*divya*) in legal procedure.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states: "Protect me with truth, O Varuṇa"—this is the formula for the invocation.
Having grasped the thigh of one standing in shallow water, he should enter the deep water.

*Mitākṣarā*: With this mantra, "O Varuṇa, protect me with truth," one should consecrate and empower water (*ka* = *udaka*). Then, having grasped the ankles of a person standing in water reaching up to the ankles—water that reaches the level of the navel—the person to be purified shall enter the water and submerge himself.
This is to be done after the worship of Varuṇa has been performed.
To the question of what should be done next, [Yājñavalkya] says: "At the same moment this [vessel] is released, a swift man shall bring it back."
If, after he has departed, one should see him with his body submerged [in water], one shall attain purification.

Before submerging, while three arrows have been discharged, one swift man goes to the place where the middle arrow falls, retrieves it, and stands there in the same manner. Another swift man stands at the base of the archway at the spot from which the arrows were released.

While the two [contestants] remain thus positioned, at the third clap of the hands, the one to be tested (*śodhya*) sinks down; at that very same moment, the arrow-catcher standing at the base of the archway also moves much more swiftly to the spot where the middle arrow falls. When he has reached it, if the catcher does not see the person who had gone into the water, then the one to be tested is declared pure.
This is the principle of the "falling of a drop of water" (*jalabindunipātananyāya*).
Just as a jar is gradually filled by the falling of drops of water, so too does the accumulation of knowledge, merit, and wealth occur step by step; such is the application of this principle.
And it has been said: "A jar is gradually filled by the falling of drops of water;
that is the cause for the acquisition of all branches of knowledge, as well as of merit and wealth."
Thus [it is said].
This is rashness. 642.
The maxim of churning water.
Just as the churning of water is futile and does not yield butter, so too is that [effort] of the reckless one. This is the "water-and-pearl" maxim (298).

"Even this [small gift], though possessing the excellence of place, time, recipient, and faith, attains greatness through the analogy of water becoming a pearl; thus it is said 'from the poor' (*dīnāt*)," as stated in the commentary on *Maṇibhāṣya-anuvyākhyāna*, Anu-bhāga 12, Chapter 9, Verse 9.

(Sāhasī, p. 763). (Water from the *svātī* constellation alone becomes a pearl. This natural distinction has been clearly explained in the *Jijñāsādhikaraṇa* according to various examples such as the *amarakīṭaka* insect, mercury, water, and pearls.
Śrīkara (on BS 2.1.18):
The analogy of the leech (*jalūkā-nyāya*).
For even though it is attached to the breast, it does not take the milk but takes only the blood; so too is the wicked man.
Summary:

There is also another analogy, that of the leech (*jalūkā*), as stated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*: “Just as a grass-leech (*tṛṇajalāyukā*)—a small insect on grass—having reached the end of a blade of grass, having moved from one [blade] to another, draws itself together [and moves to another blade]; even so this Self, having cast off this body, having moved from one to another (having taken up another body through latent impressions), draws itself together.
This is the analogy of the waking state.
Because it is more appropriate that there be *tantratva* (common performance) when ten [rites] fall together.

By this, even though there is similarity (*sājātya*) between the daily (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites such as the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*), there is indeed *tantratva* since no distinction is perceived; however, there is no subsumption (*prasaṅga*) of the daily by the optional, for there is no evidence [for such a claim].
Since it is authoritative that when the desire exists, that very [desire] is the motivator (*prayojaka*) even for the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), there is no evidence for postulating its absence.

Otherwise, since one could equally argue for the opposite—that by assuming each optional rite (*kāmya*) to be a cause for the production of its own specific fruit, the obligatory rite (*nitya*) might produce its result through that same logic—it would lead to an inconsistency. Therefore, when there is a difference between the two types of acts, the common saying that "the obligatory is accomplished through the optional by way of incidental application" (*prasaṅga*) refers specifically to cases where an optional act such as the *godohana* vessel accomplishes the purpose of the obligatory rite.
Or, let it be granted that incidental application (*prasaṅga*) occurs even in the case of a single act performed with multiple purposes.
Nevertheless, there might be some contingency due to the distinctness (*vaijātya*) of the *ahaha* [sound].
For this very reason, it is said: "Having threatened [to strike], one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance;
for actually striking, the *atikṛcchra*; and for drawing blood, the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra*" (wherein there is a metrical break in the third quarter).
In this context, however, the reading in the *Smṛti* is: "For a Brāhmaṇa, this staff is a *kṛcchra*; for a [Kṣatriya], a *atikṛcchra*;
and for a [Vaiśya] upon contact, a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*.
Regarding the statement "the wives [are led] by the tail," it is said that when performing a modified rite (*vikṛti*), it is prescribed even though it has already been stated.
"Or rather, it is an injunction, because it is something not previously established.
Commentary: Or rather, the tail (jāghanī) is enjoined as a subordinate element (guṇa) of the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.
Why? Because it is something not previously established (apūrvatvāt).
The tail (jāghanī) has not been previously established as a subordinate element of the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.
In this context, the Patnīsaṃyājas themselves are enjoined by their own specific terms, whereas their connection with the tail is not yet enjoined.
And wherever a connection is being enjoined, there is the injunction of one of the two related entities; the connection itself follows as a necessary consequence.
Alternatively, there is the injunction of a relationship, wherein the two related entities are inseparable.
Where both are presented as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there the relationship is enjoined by its own specific term.
But where only one is a defining characteristic, there, having characterized one, the other is enjoined.
And here, the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are indicated by way of a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
How is this understood? Because every sacrifice involves a connection with the wives (*patnī*), yet only a certain one is marked out as that for which the wives serve as the means of accomplishment.

Now, why is it not the case that the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are enjoined by taking the tail (*jāghanī*) as the characteristic mark? It is because the wives cannot be enjoined as belonging to this new, previously unestablished sacrifice.
If, however, the *jāghanī* (the tail) were being characterized while a sacrifice accompanied by a wife (*sapatnīka*) were being enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
But here, there already exists an enjoined sacrifice accompanied by a wife which is to be characterized by the mention of the wife;
therefore, having characterized the sacrifice, the *jāghanī* is enjoined.
As for the claim that the injunction regarding the tail (*jāghanī*) is made by means of a sentence (*vākya*), while the injunction regarding the sacrifice is made by direct statement (*śruti*),
it has already been stated here that an injunction of the sacrifice is not possible in this case, because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, it is an injunction of the tail.
If this were so, then in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the *patnīsaṃyāja* would be deficient without the *jāghanī*;
therefore, there must be an upward displacement (*utkarṣa*). Or rather—there is no upward displacement of this injunction.
Why? "The tail (jāghanī), being indicated as the object of reference, would be the cause for the displacement of the ritual act;
however, here it is taken up as a subordinate element (aṅga), whereas in the sacrifices it is something entirely different."
It has been stated that in every such sentence, the application [of the injunction] proceeds to the subordinate element (*guṇa*) because it is the object of the injunction.

Furthermore, the *patnīsaṃyāja* sacrifices, having been enjoined immediately prior, remain present in the mind and thus cannot be the objects of a new injunction here. Nor is it appropriate to apply the *patnīsaṃyāja* and so forth belonging to the animal sacrifice at this point, because there is no cognition of them [in this context].
Nor is the *jāghanī* (the tail) non-adoptable because it is like time (*kāla*) and so forth—which would necessitate drawing this injunction [of the *jāghanī*] into the context;
for, as Jaimini argues, it is something to be employed (*saṃkārya*).
[To this we reply: No, because there is no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for overriding the quality conveyed by the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*).

Even if the injunction were to operate with reference to the tail (*jāghanī*) once its purpose had already been fulfilled, it might still—perhaps like the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings—be interpreted as having a third-case sense (*jāghanyā*) where a second case (*jāghanīm*) is actually intended.
However, in this case, the tail is being enjoined as something previously unestablished (*apūrva*).
Therefore, it does not deserve to be displaced [to another context].

Nor can these *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings withstand displacement on the grounds that they possess a *prakaraṇa* (context), because the *vākya* (syntactical connection) is stronger. If this is argued, it is not so; for even a *vākya* such as this is weaker than the *prakaraṇa* because it depends upon what is already established.
For if this were the very originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) of the *patnīsaṃyājas*, then they would indeed be separated from the *prakaraṇa*.

However, since these [subsidiary acts] arise from separate sentences, they can be grasped by the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices in the same amount of time that it takes for them to be subsumed under this [single] sentence by way of their arrangement.
Furthermore, the fact that the tail (jāghanī) possesses a fruit is not known, such that it could satisfy the requirement for a purpose on the part of these [acts].

Therefore, as long as one considers "for what purpose [are they]?"—until then, they have been rendered subsidiary by the "how" (kathambhāva) requirement generated by the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices which possess a fruit.
Nor is there here an injunction for a previously unknown sacrifice (*apūrvayāga*), because it is not heard as being merely a sacrifice (*yajimātra*).
For this is indeed the hearing of the *patnīsaṃyāja* sacrifices.
In that case, if an action were enjoined with reference to the tail (*jāghanī*), then the wives would be enjoined.

Consequently, because multiple things would be enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by dissimilarity (*vai rūpya*), according to the principle: "When a single word has multiple meanings, it is like [the case of] another's purpose. Furthermore, the presence of various few objects cannot be resolved by means of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*). Therefore, having indicated the sacrifice as qualified, the substance is enjoined.
[Objection: But even so, because of the restatement of a qualified [subject], the sentence would be split all the more.
[Response: This is not a fault, because the word "wife" (*patnī*), being obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*), is not the restrictive factor (*atantra*).

Just as in the case of the general expression "he offers toward the village," a specific *prayāja* is understood due to the context (*adhikāra*), so too by the mere statement "that which they perform as the *saṃyājana*," the *patnīsaṃyājas* authorized by that context will be recognized.
Therefore, there is displacement (*utkarṣa*).
If it is argued that this is a single unified application (*ekādeśa*):

Commentary: Now, that which was stated—that because the tail (*jāghanī*) is a single part, it will not motivate the animal sacrifice, and therefore there must be a displacement (*utkarṣa*)—must be refuted. Or rather, regarding what was said—"The single part is not a motivator because of its connection with something already existing in the Vedic text"—to that it is replied: (Even though the meaning of the term *itthetaddravya* in the fourth section is "that sacrifice of which a single part is the substance," nevertheless, it is accepted here as being denotative of the word *jāghanī*; this is indicated in the *Sudhā*).
In the *Tantraratna*, however, the term "ekādaśadravya" (the eleven substances) is accepted as neuter in the fourth section because it functions as a specific object of action (*karman*).
It is not so in the archetype (*prakṛti*) until the completion of the ritual according to the scripture.
The *Bhāṣya* states: "In the archetype, namely the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the tail (*jāghanī*) is not mentioned by the scripture."
Thus, the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are to be performed with the tail that has arisen from the animal sacrifice; in this way,
the tail is enjoined without any further qualification.
It occurs in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*),
being brought in as the *vrīhī* (rice) and so forth;
therefore, there is an upward displacement (*utkarṣa*).
From this commentary, the reading of the sūtra "na prakṛtau aśāstraniṣpatteḥ" is established.
The negative particle (*nañ*) found in the commentary is an explanation of the *nañ* contained within the compound *aśāstraniṣpatteḥ*.
However, the *nañ* found in the sūtra itself serves to negate the "science" (*śāstra*) mentioned in the preceding sūtra concerning the suffix *-cedi*.

Or rather— that [word] indeed becomes non-efficient (aprayojaka) whose meaning is not understood without reference to the subject matter at hand, as in the case of "He cuts off for the Sviṣṭakṛt from the northern portion.
However, the word *jāghanī* (the tail), like the words *hṛdaya* (heart) and so forth, denotes a specific form (*ākṛti*).
And that [sacrifice] can be undertaken even without the acquisition of an animal, or by means of the life of an animal employed by another;
for as it is said, "Or the form [may be used], because all beings are included," so it can be performed by undertaking it in whatever way is appropriate through any means whatsoever.
Nor is this [form] not current in the world as a constituent part.
For meat-sellers sell animals as if they were directly before their eyes;
in that case, it is possible to obtain the tail by purchase or other means.
Furthermore, this [tail] need not be taken from a goat alone, because the scripture mentions it merely as a part of the hindquarters (*jaghanāvayava*).

Even in the case of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, the procurement of the heart and other parts from the world is indeed possible; nevertheless, because their specific genus and the manner of their production are established only through their distinctness and by means of the *saṃsparśana* (touching), there is no mention of purchase or begging.
But here, the production is not brought about in that manner by the scripture. Furthermore, the inclusion of the "archetype" (*prakṛti*) extends up to the attainment of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

Therefore, it is established that the tail (*jāghanī*) is to be used as an alternative to the clarified butter (*ājya*) as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *dāśīpūrṇamāsa* and the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Śābarabhāṣya—(The Siddhānta: For the tail is understood from its own [textual] indication by the instrumental case-ending (*jāghanyā*) as a subordinate factor;
furthermore, the requirement for a substance is established by the context of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Therefore, the tail (jāghanī) is enjoined here as a subordinate element (guṇa) for them;
nor does it possess a dependent function like that of the subsequent portions (uttarārdha).
Consequently, the tail finds its place only within the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Regarding *soma*: since its meaning has already been stated, there is no [further] connection.

And in the Sūtra, the word *ca* (and) implies a displacement (*utkarṣa*). As it is said: "They perform the *saṃyājana* with the tail-bone (*jāghanī*); this [is done] at the animal sacrifice (*paśu*)."
That [use] is appropriate for the animal sacrifice because of the connection with the tail (jāghanī).
For that portion called the tail is indeed connected with the New Moon sacrifice (darśa).
It should not be postponed, nor should it be combined [with another], because it is an instrument [denoted] by the third case-ending.

Bhāṣya: In the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings within the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "They cause the wives to sacrifice with the tail (*jāghanī*)."

In this regard, there arises a deliberation: does this sentence enjoin the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with reference to the tail (*jāghanī*) of the animal sacrificed to Agni and Soma—thereby resulting in the displacement of this injunction from its original context—or is the tail enjoined as the substance for the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings? Upon consideration, since the word *jāghanī* (tail), like the word *uttarārdha* (upper half), denotes a part-substance, the tail is already employed for another purpose. Consequently, because it is understood to have a specific utility, it is recognized as the object of reference (*uddeśya*), similar to the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings. Thus, accepting that the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) implies the sense of the accusative (*dvitīyā*), it is concluded that the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings themselves are enjoined with reference to that tail.
Thus, there is the parsimony of accepting the second type of injunction; otherwise, the third type of injunction would result.

And so, because the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the syntactical connection (*vākya*), the Patnīsaṃyājas would merely follow [the main sacrifice]. Consequently, even in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the statement "They perform the Patnīsaṃyājas with clarified butter" would become devoid of scope. Therefore, since the context is not sublated, and since that [context] indicates subsidiarity to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices through being a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), it is untenable for this statement to enjoin subsidiarity to the Agnīṣomīya animal sacrifice as a direct auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*).

Nor can it be argued that because the tail (*jāghanī*) could exist even in the world as part of an animal used for purposes other than sacrifice, how could there be an understanding of its connection to the sacrifice—given its lack of connection to a ritual performed by Agni? For, through another scriptural statement heard within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Agniṣomīya, namely, "They perform the Patnīsaṃyājas with the tail," which prescribes the Patnīsaṃyājas with reference to the tail that serves as a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the rite under discussion, the connection to the sacrifice is established; thus, just as in the case of the statement "He takes the limb," the acquisition of the connection to the ritual is logically possible even for one who has not studied this [text] in an Aryan manner.

As for the claim made by some that—since the connection of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with the animal sacrifice is understood from the context (*deśa*) alone—the contextual statement must, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), enjoin an intermediate purpose for them: that is disregarded. For even if the connection of the *patnīsaṃyāja*s with the animal sacrifice is understood through extension (*atideśa*), there is no evidence for the presentation of the tail-tendon (*jāghanī*) belonging to that sacrifice in a statement not studied by the Āryas, provided there is no indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). Furthermore, since there is no possibility of a separate context (*prakaraṇāntara*) when [the rite] is established through extension, it is impossible for it to be a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*). Thus, [the opponent's position] is rejected.
Therefore, since the syntactical connection (*vākya*) overrides the context (*prakaraṇa*), this injunction is displaced and applied to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.
This being the prima facie view, the *jāghanī-nyāya* [applies]. [This concludes] the *jāteṣṭi* and the *jātakarman*.

Although the word *jāghanī* denotes a part of an animal, it lacks a correlative relationship like words such as "the latter" (*uttara*) or "the first" (*ādi*). Therefore, since it is possible to enjoin the use of the *jāghanī* established in common worldly usage—just like clarified butter (*ājya*)—for the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, there is no justification for accepting an indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the instrumental case-ending.

Furthermore, since the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are obtained through extension (*atideśa*) and are remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), their status as immediate auxiliaries (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) could be secured by the very sentence situated within the context of the animal sacrifice; thus, the sentence situated within the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) would otherwise result in being purposeless.
Therefore, the injunction regarding the tail (jāghanī) is made precisely with reference to the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings themselves.

Nor should it be argued that, since the Patnīs are also enjoined by way of restating an already established rite—and since they are obtained as deities even in the Āneya offering—there would result a syntactical split (vākyabheda) due to the specification of a particular location;
for, by virtue of the intermediate context (avāntaraprakaraṇa), there is no syntactical split because the injunction is made with reference to a specific rite.
Therefore, there is no displacement (*utkarṣa*) of this [passage] from its context.
As for the sentence situated within the *agnīṣomīya* context, it will be explained that it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) regarding what has been obtained through option.

Nor is it the case that, because a restriction is possible there only with respect to the *ajāghanī* (tail) used in the sacrifice, there is a lack of authority for taking the one produced as a by-product (*anuniṣpanna*) of the animal-sacrifice; for it will be stated in that very place that since there is no other disposal (*pratipatti*), there is no authority for abandoning that which is already present.
Maṇḍana: "The tail (jāghanī) is to be employed in the sacrifice.
Śaṅkara: "There is no displacement (utkarṣaṇa) of the tail at all. This is the principle of the combination of the tail (jāghanī-samuccaya-nyāya).
In the case of a modification (*vikṛti*), there is an option regarding that which is merely extended by analogy (*atideśa*), as for example:

"They perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with the tail (*jāghanī*), or with clarified butter (*ājya*). This is prescribed [in the archetype]. However, it is heard again in the context of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*): "They perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with the tail. This does not serve to establish that the *patnīsaṃyājas* have the tail as their sole purpose, because that would result in the performance of a non-archetypal function (*aprākṛtakārya*). Rather, it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the tail, which is already obtained as an optional alternative from the archetype.
And in that context, because it is to be taken as a means (*upāya*), the status of being a "tail" (*jāghanīkatva*) is intended [to be specified].

There, when a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*) is to be consecrated, there is a repetition of the consecration; thus, according to the principle of the combination of tails (*jāghanī-samuccaya-nyāya*), since the procedure applies, any tail whatsoever may be taken—this is the option (*vikalpa*).
And this has been stated in the twelfth book, in the section beginning: "But the modification of the substance, like the previous case, would be a primary act... (12.4.16.10).

(This may be the name of the *nyāya* following the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), but the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is indeed an alternative option. Bāla. p. 162. "He takes [it] with the *jāta-nyāya*," meaning after the churning of the fire.
Regarding *saṃkalpa* (4|3|6): "The *Jāteṣṭi* follows the kindling of the fire.
The *Jāteṣṭi* is to be performed after the execution of the *Jātakarman*.
"But the connection with the fruit would not apply to that which is not enjoined, because it has already come into existence in its entirety. (4.3.16) [Section 2] Commentary: Or rather, it is thus.
"One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: is it at the very moment of birth, or after the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) has been performed?
[The answer is: at the very moment of birth.
For when the occasion has arrived, that which is contingent upon it must come to pass.
This being the case, we say:
"When the birth-rite (jātakarman) has been performed."
Why? Because of the inherent capacity [of the text].
For it is only when the *jātakarman* (birth rite) has been performed that the consumption [of the sacrificial remains] is prescribed for him.
If the *iṣṭi* were performed prior to the *jātakarman*, the time for the consumption would be displaced, and in that case, he would not yet possess a body capable of sustaining life.
"But for those who are ignorant, the connection with injury is for the sake of a specific occasion.
The Commentary says: Now, as for what was stated—that when there is a conjunction [of conditions], there must necessarily be a contingent effect—it is replied:
The connection with the affliction of the ignorant is for the purpose of indicating the occasion (*nimitta*).
"Affliction" refers to the birth of a son; that which has already occurred is the occasion. Its timing is not a constituent factor (*aṅga*) [of the rite].
And that causal factor does not disappear even when the birth-rite (jātakarman) has been performed.
In the other alternative, the time [for the rite] would lapse;
moreover, there would be a figurative interpretation (lakṣaṇā) in this alternative.
Therefore, [it is said] "when the *jātakarman* has been performed.

Soma: The connection [of this verse] arises from the determination of that for whose sake it was stated that the fruit resides in the son. Vi: "Immediately after birth, or when the *jātakarman* has been performed, the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) [is to be offered]."
Therefore, another occasion for the rite [of initiation] is the subsequent event;
for it is seen that after the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) has been completed, there is bathing and the first feeding.
Thus, let the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) take place before the boy's death, or after it.
Māṭṭa: Or rather, it is thus.

This *iṣṭi* must be performed immediately after the birth of a son; for since the seventh day is understood to be the occasion (*nimitta*) for the birth, another occasion and its corresponding rite (*naimittika*) are appropriate [only when that specific occasion has arrived].

Nor is the statement in the *Tantrasāra*—that here the seventh day is prescribed as a time subsequent to the birth—correct, because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) in the word "in a son" (*putre*) would otherwise be untenable.
Therefore, in the expression "when [the son] is not divided" (*abhinne*), the locative case is used solely with reference to the occasion (*nimitta*).
And because of its dependency, there is a desire to express both [the father and the son], according to the principle of the *havirdhānī* [which requires two poles].

Even if the mere birth of a son were the occasion, nevertheless, by obtaining a distinct occasion, the occasional rite (*naimittika*) must be performed immediately, even in terms of the time for purification (*śauca*).

Nor does the absence of bathing and drinking result in the contradiction of the son’s death; for even though the consumption of sacrificial food (dakṣiṇānna) following the Vaiśvānara sacrifice—which is preceded by the honey-consecration (madhuprāśana) and is fit for the birth-rite (jātakarma)—occurs at a later time, the Jāteṣṭi sacrifice is performed out of natural inclination (rāgataḥ). Since it is possible for some form of consumption to occur after the Jātakarma and the Jāteṣṭi, there is no occurrence of death [due to lack of sustenance].
Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (vinigamanāviraha) because the rite of birth (jātakarma) is also necessarily required immediately after birth;
for only that which is enjoined by direct Vedic revelation (pratyakṣa-śruti) possesses the power of determination.

This being the position reached, [we reply]: since the Jātakarma is ordained to occur prior to the cutting of the umbilical cord, and since the act of eating is prohibited when the cord is not yet cut, if the sacrifice (iṣṭi) were performed immediately after birth, death would result due to the violation of the primary element (śeṣivirodha). Therefore, the performance must be postponed (utkarṣa).

Nor can the prohibition found in the Smṛti be restricted to those who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) merely by following the literal sense of the word "occasion" (*nimitta*); for in a case where an occasion has actually occurred, the rite corresponding to that occasion must necessarily be performed.
This being the position reached, we reply:
it is indeed enjoined as part of the birth-rite (*jātakarman*).
He who asserts that "immediacy following birth" (*jātānantaratā*) is the cause has established a term denoting a universal as a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for a particular.
An interval immediately following birth cannot be conceived,
for it is indeed momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
Therefore he says: "Time should pass.
Even within ten days, it is not performed because the impurity (aśauca) has not yet subsided.
Therefore, it should be performed on the full moon or the new moon day occurring after the ten-day period.
The injunction "He offers when [the vessel] is broken" is performed immediately;

for the sequence based on a specific occasion (naimittika-pāṭhakrama) enters by subverting the other sequence of recitation (pāṭhakrama). As stated in the Śāstra: "When another occasion arises, it takes precedence over that which possesses a conflict with its purpose."
It is superior; however, due to the absence of that [superiority], it does not deserve further elevation.
Even without one who knows the rules of purification, it must indeed be performed on account of a specific occasion (*nimitta*).
For it will be stated in the alternative view (*pakṣa*) that "it may even be done in a single part."
It is said:
First, that [application] which was obtained by the natural force of the cause has been set aside;
first, the inclusion of the subsidiaries is precluded by the contradiction with the purpose.

To avoid deficiency, [the rite] should be performed at the time of the full moon and so forth, while waiting for the period of purification (*śauca*) to arrive. [The word] *soma*—[is used here] because the objection is raised by way of a contrast with the previous case. "Upon the arrival of the period of purification" means that [the rite is performed] when the impurity has ceased due to touching the vessels (*bhāṇḍa*).
Vi— "It should take place either immediately after the *jātakarman* or once the period of impurity (*āśauca*) has passed;
because of the proximity of the occasion, it is for the performer that the subsequent [act] is seen to be purposeful.
This is contained within the second section (*varṇaka*) of the *Bhāṭṭa* school.

Maṇḍana: "It should be performed on a pure [lunar] festival day. Śaṅkara: "Or it may take its own time even during a period of impurity. The Jāteṣṭi sacrifice, because it pertains to the son, is prompted by two fruits.
The section concerning the connection with the fruit (phalasaṃyogādhikaraṇa).
Bhāṣya 4.3.16.38–39. The *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice is prescribed by the rule: "When a son is born, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara.
Vi. 4.3.12. Regarding the *jāteṣṭi*: it is to be performed after the *jātakarman* (birth-rite), and not at the time immediately following birth, prior to the *jātakarman*.
The fruit of the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice is [the attainment of heaven] (1760). Regarding the principle of the *jāteṣṭi* (Vi.
4.3.18), even there, the *jāteṣṭi* must be performed after the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*).
(4.3.19) The fruit of the *jāteṣṭi* belongs to the son alone, and not to the father who is the performer.
From the statement, "He upon whose birth one performs the sacrifice becomes purified," the fruit resides in the son, while the ritual procedure belongs to the father. This is the *jāteṣṭi-nyāya*.
The section on Vaiśvānara;
the principle of the Vaiśvānara passage;
in the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, there is an offering on eight potsherds and an offering on twelve potsherds.

This is not an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), because it is understood from the preceding [text] that it is part of the established tradition (*samāmnāya*) due to its inherent capacity. The Commentary states:
"It is heard in scripture: 'One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born.'"

In this regard, alternative options for the sacrificial potsherds (*kapāla*) are heard in the scripture, such as: "That which is on eight potsherds purifies through the *gāyatrī* [meter] itself, through spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)," and so forth.
Regarding these, a doubt arises: are these injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*), or are they merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)?
On this point, we maintain that they are indeed injunctions of accessory qualities.

How so? For those who speak of things previously known, such as the meaning of "son," do not intend to enjoin them. Thus, the power of this statement lies in its recitation (*samāmnāya*), namely, that it brings to mind what was not previously known. What is that? It is the capacity for injunction (*vidhāna*).
In this way, that which is not yet enjoined will be enjoined; otherwise, being mere explanatory passages (arthavādas),
they would be purposeless.
Furthermore, the twelve potsherds cannot be regarded as a mere remnant;
for the praise of eight potsherds is direct (pratyakṣa), whereas that of twelve is indirect (parokṣa). And where there is no direct [evidence], the indirect may be accepted.
Therefore, they are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*).
Or rather—now it is being deliberated whether they are indeed injunctions of accessory qualities, or whether there is only an injunction of an accessory quality;

or else, because the state of having eight potsherds (*aṣṭakapālatva*) stands in grammatical apposition with *vaiśvānara*, the term "twelve-potsherd" (*dvādaśakapāla*) functions as a name (*nāmadheya*), while [the other] is an injunction of an accessory quality.
Since the original sacrifice is established by means such as common renown (*prasiddhi*) and because it lacks perceptibility, [the point] must be justified;
even there, having set aside [objections], it will be concluded that it is already established by means of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

(He refutes that [position] by first presenting it, in order to state the reason why the Commentator [Śabarasvāmin] provides an explanation with the elision of the vowel *a*, thereby abandoning the interpretation of the sūtra as composed without such an elision by other commentators: "In that case, there is meaningfulness through the rule of *pūrvavat* (as before), because it is determined that these are names of previously unknown rites, according to the principle: 'That which is new at its origin [is a name].
Therefore, if it is argued that these are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*), such as 'the eight-pot-sherd cake' (*aṣṭakapālaḥ*), that is incorrect."
For its status as a name is not established merely by being unprecedented (*apūrvatva*).

Indeed, because it is unprecedented—just as it is not an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) due to the lack of recognition of a worldly referent—it is all the more well-established that it denotes a Vedic ritual action; yet it would not follow that it cannot also be a name.

Moreover, it has been stated that the status of being a name (*nāmadheyatā*) occurs everywhere when there is an existing worldly object, through such means as *sambhava* (possibility) and *vihāra* (usage).

Therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra is exactly as stated in the Bhāṣya: "When there is the expression of a name for an object already known, these [criteria] would apply here because [the object] was not previously established, just like the options regarding the Vedic character."

For if the eightfold [offering] and so forth were obtained from some source in the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, then its status as a name or its being an explanatory passage (arthavāda) might occur by way of agreement;
however, there is no such obtainment, because only the number twelve is prescribed.
For instance: "Even though, in its essential nature, this very [sacrifice] is included within the great forms (mahāsaṃsthā)."
Because they do not serve as delimiters, the first two [words] are not qualifiers of the action.
Number is not pervaded by mere existence. What then? It is by the delimitation of that which is to be numbered.
And when the potsherds are delimited as being twelve, the eight and so forth do not possess the quality of being delimiters; thus, they are non-existent [in that context].

Even if existence is somehow admitted, it would still be merely this much: "there are eight," but not "consisting of eight potsherds" (*aṣṭakapāla*). For this is a *taddhita* derivative formed with the suffix *aṇ*, which is prescribed by Pāṇini 4.2.16: "In the sense of being prepared (*saṃskṛta*), the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word ending in the locative case, provided that what is prepared consists of edible foods (*bhakṣāḥ*). (In this context, the word *tatra* from the previous rule is understood as continuing. Thus, the term *aṣṭakapālaḥ* signifies something prepared upon eight potsherds.

[The term *aṣṭakapālaḥ* refers to] a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) prepared on eight potsherds (*kapāla*). By this, in the sense of "prepared upon eight potsherds," the word *aṣṭakapāla* is established through the elision of the *aṇ* suffix prescribed after the nominal stem *kapāla* following a numeral (as in *aṣṭan-*), according to the rule *dvigor lug-anapatye* (Pāṇini 4.1.88)—which states that when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) beginning with a vowel (other than those denoting descent) follows a *dvigu* compound, there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix.
This is a compound formed on account of the meaning of a secondary suffix (*taddhitārtha-nimittaka-samāsa*).

(Regarding the rule "taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca," since a compound consisting of a directional term and a numeral occurs when there is co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with respect to the meaning of a *taddhita* suffix, it is argued that the status of being a sanctifier (*saṃskāraka*) is merely an adventitious condition (*upādhi*). Consequently, because it is impossible to delimit the eight sanctifying factors—which are themselves delimited as twelve—by the number eight, the term *aṣṭakapāla* would be untenable. Furthermore, those two (the *taddhita* derivative and the compound) occur only when there is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*).
And semantic competency exists only when there is independence from anything else.
Because it is dependent [on another], the eight-pot-sherd cake does not possess the status of being twelve-fold; thus, the twelve-fold cake cannot be designated by the term "eight-pot-sherd.
Consequently, since there is no mention of its own essential form, the purpose of praise would become something entirely different from what was intended.
Furthermore, the eight-pot-sherd cake and so forth are not distinct from the state of being twelve-fold.
The application of the ritual action is possible because it possesses the nature of a number (*saṃkhyātva*).

And although the state of being twelve is praised by means of the praise of the state of being eight, this is not a praise of the eight-potsherd [cake] by means of the twelve-potsherd [cake], because there is an absolute difference between the qualifier and the qualified.
Furthermore, this very state of being twelve has its own specific praise: "In him, indeed, is the whole world."
Therefore, these [injunctions] are indeed injunctions of subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhi*), as they are considered alternatives to the number twelve.

And since all this constitutes a single originative statement (*utpattivākya*)—because the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is enjoined with various alternative numbers—there is no distinction in their relative strength.
("Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a Vaiśvānara cake on twelve potsherds.")
When it is on eight potsherds, he purifies him with the Gāyatrī and with spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa).
When it is on nine potsherds, he bestows brilliance upon him with the Triṣṭubh. When it is on ten potsherds, he bestows the enjoyment of food upon him with the Virāj.

"When it is on eleven potsherds, he bestows *indriya* (vital power) upon him by means of the *triṣṭubh*; when it is on twelve potsherds, he bestows cattle upon him by means of the *jagatī*. He for whom, once born, one performs this sacrifice, becomes indeed purified, radiant, an eater [of food], possessed of *indriya*, and rich in cattle"—this is the single originative statement (*utpattivākya*). Therefore, because "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) depends upon the suitability of what was previously mentioned, the term *vaiśvadeva* is derived from the *parvan* (section).
For that capacity indeed exists within this recited collection (samāmnāya), and the refutation stated there does not apply here.
Therefore, it is for the purpose of enjoining [the action].

However, if it were for the purpose of enjoining a quality (guṇa), then those qualities would be useless in the performance [of the rite], because they possess no purposeful efficacy with respect to that [action].

Commentary: It is not the case that these are injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*). While being for the purpose of enjoining an accessory, these [texts] enjoin a number for the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) upon the potsherds;
they are not able to enjoin the performance of the sacrifice itself.

For the state of being on twelve potsherds belongs to the sacrifice by virtue of the direct statement (*vākya*), whereas the state of being on eight potsherds and so forth belongs to it by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Therefore, those [latter qualities] will not apply to the sacrifice.

Moreover, since the qualities such as "eightfold-ness" are syntactically connected with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) within a single sentence, they will not belong to the sacrifice because they set aside the context.
Furthermore, they would be meaningless if connected with the sacrifice, because there is no fruit in connection with the *puroḍāśa* cake.
However, as explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), the praise of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice becomes appropriate.
Therefore, they are *arthavādas*.

Or rather: "Whether it be the sacrifice—both the primary and the non-primary—or likewise the substance, or even the substance possessing a quality, in no way is [the substance] enjoined in this manner."

In the present context, since there is an ascent to the number twelve, the *aṣṭakā* and other offerings are not enjoined; nor can they be brought over from a distant location, as there is no word for such an appropriation.

Furthermore, it is not possible for this to be a separate ritual action characterized by qualities such as "solely," because there is no direct hearing of a sacrifice associated with a specific material and deity.

By this, the injunction regarding the number [of cakes] for the *puroḍāśa* is also refuted in three ways (refuted in three ways as to whether it is an injunction of a quality related to the archetype sacrifice, related to a distant sacrifice, or related to an entirely new sacrifice). Likewise, the injunction of the *aṣṭakapāla* and other *puroḍāśas* is also refuted in three ways. [In that regard, he states the lack of connection with the archetype sacrifice: For the sacrifice delimited by the twelve-pot-sherd *puroḍāśa* does not take up another *puroḍāśa*.

(Regarding the lack of connection when [the action] is remote: Nor, when the action has not been restated by its own word, can the injunction of the *puroḍāśa*—which is not the subject under discussion—be of any use in establishing a connection with the means of attaining a fruit. Furthermore, because it consists of the performance of another [action], the substance cannot be enjoined [as an independent act].
For this very reason, as in the case of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice and others, a fruit is not to be inferred through the "assumption of a result" (*ādyahāra*).

(He states the possibility of an injunction regarding a novel sacrifice: "Nor is the word *vaiśvānara* here restated for the sake of a sacrifice, because it is joined with a different case-ending; furthermore, this [word] would not be purposeless [if it were not so]."
(He explains the verse by way of the subsequent word: This might be the case;

however, from the term *vaiśvānara*, there is no establishment of a separate sacrifice, because it is a prescription for the connection between a substance—such as the eight potsherds—and a deity. That [separate sacrifice] does not exist.
Because the second case endings are supplied by ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) to those [words] ending in the nominative.

Nor is there a change of case endings (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*), since other [case endings] would also be applicable. For if the prescription of "eightfold" were meaningless without ellipsis and change of case, why would it not be done? Since it is justified as being for the purpose of praise (*stutyarthatva*), it is not meaningless.

And in that case, there is no fault even if the designation of the case-ending is altered due to the restatement (*anuvāda*). (He concludes that even in this way, the injunction of the *puroḍāśa* cake is not possible: Therefore, there is no injunction of the *puroḍāśa*.

Furthermore, on the twelve-potsherd [cake], the *puroḍāśas* consisting of eight potsherds and so forth do not exist as distinct entities by their own nature, because only the specific distinction of the eight potsherds and so forth is observed.
And it has been stated that those [elements], such as the eightfold oblation (*aṣṭakā*) and so forth, are enjoined neither in the sacrifice nor in the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

Nor is it possible for you [to claim] that the injunctions regarding the eightfold oblation and others form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the twelve-pot-sherd cake, because there is an absence of a unified purpose due to the various distinct purposes of the diverse injunctions. Furthermore, there exists no mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) among these diverse elements when they are separated.
And if it were a single sentence, then, because of the injunction of a single *bhāvanā* qualified by all [the factors], there would be no option (*vikalpa*).

Furthermore, since the offerings to the Aṣṭakas and so forth are subordinate (*guṇa*), it is not possible for them to be performed separately through the completion of the sentence for each one individually.
Nor is it possible for them to be combined, because that would entail the disappearance of all [individual] numbers due to the production of a different number.
However, there is no addition of a different number nor a conjunction [of numbers] in the case of the "twelve," because the "eight" is included within it;
and such is the case for those [texts],
as stated in the Mīmāṃsākośa (221).
Regarding the *jāteṣṭi* principle (sūtra 17.6.2):
since [the result] is already established by the injunction of the twelve-fold [offering], there would be the consequence of these being mere restatements (*anuvāda*).
Therefore, you must necessarily accept that independent injunctions are established by these distinct sentences.

Consequently, the number twelve is established by the original injunction (*utpattivākya*), whereas the others are established by different sentences; being weaker than the context (*prakaraṇa*), they do not connect [with the primary rite].
Thus, the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, because it is already occupied by more powerful qualities, does not admit the number eight and so forth.
Furthermore, even the number eight and the rest cannot be tolerated at all.
(The word *soḍha* [is explained as follows]: it is established in the sense of the agent; *saṃde*: in the sense of the agent; *siddha*: established).
Since those [other deities] also form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyabhūta*) with the *puroḍāśa*, they do not at all obtain [the status of being deities] for the Vaiśvānara sacrifice.
Therefore, how could they exist without subverting that [status]?
And likewise, [if they were] connected only with the *puroḍāśa* offering, they would be purposeless in that performance;
"for there is no meaningfulness (*arthavattā*) toward that *puroḍāśa*.

(Having thus explained the Sūtra by way of commenting on the Bhāṣya, he explains it differently according to his own reasoning: How then are these not its qualities? To this he says—the Sūtra: "For there is no meaningfulness toward that sacrifice in relation to another [substance]."
That remainder is not tenable.
The Commentary states: "What has been said must be refuted.
Thus ends the aphorism with the introductory remark (*ābhāṣā*).
(The Vārttika, however, is to be seen in the subsequent sūtra:
"Because there is no distinction, they would not be suitable for the purpose of injunction or for the purpose of praise.

The Bhāṣya: But when it is understood that [the passages concerning] the eight potsherds and so forth are meaningless with respect to their stated purpose, then, by way of indirect indication (lakṣaṇā), the praise of the twelve potsherds will serve the purpose of promoting the Vaiśvānara sacrifice.
For within the number twelve, there exist undifferentiated specific numbers such as eight and so forth.

Therefore, it is logical that the praise of its parts serves as a glorification of the twelve-pot-sherd [offering], just as one might say, "The nave of this wheel is beautiful," or "The elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry of this army are excellent. Thus, the praise is logically established.

If it is argued that there must be a causal basis, the Bhāṣya says: "If you view these as mere explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), why does the *brahmavarcasa* (spiritual luster) and so forth not arise from the eightfold oblation (*aṣṭakapāla*) and the rest? For one desiring *brahmavarcasa*, there is the eightfold oblation;
likewise for the subsequent ones, according to one's desire."
Why should it be so? Even if the *puroḍāśa* is treated as having its qualities enjoined (*guṇavidhāna*), there will be no pointlessness (*ānarthakya*).
Nor will the praise of the twelve-potsherd cake (*dvādaśakapāla*) have to be assumed through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, these shall be injunctions for the sake of specific desires (*kāma*).
Although the two words *cet* and *iti* were not read by the author of the Bhāṣya, they were included by the author of the Vārttika because they are seen in other recensions.
[The sūtra reads: "If it be argued that the remainder of that is not possible, [we reply] no, because of the teaching of non-separation; [the others] would be for the purpose of praise.

(Even though the word *nañ* is not read anywhere in the subsequent sentence here, nevertheless, according to the sense, it is appropriate to read the sūtra as containing *nañ*: *iti cet, nāvibhāgāt*).
Since the number eight and so forth are already prescribed by rule, there would be no purpose for praising them;
therefore, the number twelve is praised as being beyond conventional usage.

(Although in the *Ānandabhairavī* commentary, the first half of this verse is printed as an explanation of the *tacchedasūtra*, and the second half as the beginning of the explanation of the *avibhāgasūtra*, nevertheless, according to the view of the *Vārttika*, since it constitutes a single sūtra, the present verse must also be accepted as being indivisible;
thus, we have done so.
That which is enjoined is precisely what should be praised.
And here, the number twelve is that which is to be enjoined.
Therefore, in whatever way possible, that very [number] must be praised.
(He explains the word *avibhāga* from the Sūtra as having the sense of proximity: And because of their proximity, it may be inferred that the eighteen [verses] constitute a part of that [twelve].

And by means of praising a single part, the whole becomes praised. By this it is meant: "This twelve-potsherd [offering] is so highly distinguished that when it is performed, even the eight-potsherd and others become possible;

and since those qualities such as the number eight and so forth are praiseworthy for the attainment of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) and other goals, therefore this [twelve-potsherd offering] is praiseworthy."

As for the claim that this is another praise of the very same number twelve, there is no fault in this; it follows the *jāteṣṭi* logic. [Sūtra 1764: "One whose son is born" refers to the time [of the rite]; [Sūtra 1765: "One whose hair is black" refers to the age. If it is argued that the section concerning caste (*jātyadhikaraṇa*) is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), it is replied: [as follows].
"First of all, being taught by a sentence that establishes [the rite] is not tenable;
for in that case, the sentence would be split because of the difference in the purposes of all these [subsidiaries]."
Nor is it the case that all [of these] are established by originative injunctions;
for a twelve-potherd cake does not constitute a specific sacrificial oblation.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"If these qualities were for the sake of the fruit, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda) due to their distinctness;
however, because of the identity between the opening and the conclusion, there is a single syntactical unity (ekavākyatā)."
Therefore, this is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
12. Soma—the connection is through the similarity of the suffixes in words such as *vaiśvadeva*.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: words such as *vaiśvadeva* are "possessing a prior [basis]" (*pūrvavantaḥ*), meaning they refer to what has already been established previously; indeed, they do not serve to enjoin a new accessory (*guṇa*), for their capacity would lie in that general sense of the eight-pot-sherd offering (*aṣṭakapāla*) and so forth.
Vi— "That which is heard immediately after the Vaiśvānara sacrifice on twelve potsherds,
such as [the offering] on eight potsherds and so forth— is it a subordinate quality (guṇa), a name (nāmadheya), or a praise (stuti)?"
Because it is included within [the primary rite], the name "Aṣṭādaśa" (Eighteen) and so forth would apply here, just as in the case of the Agnihotra;
for if it were not [included] as one substance among other substances, then that [name] would serve the purpose of qualifying the accessory with respect to the fruit.
The unity of the sentence is clearly stated through the concluding summary; however, when there is an injunction of various qualities, praise is intended for the sake of that purpose.

The teacher’s view is stated as follows: "If it is argued that [the Veda] is not an authority because it is devoid of qualities, lacks a name, is mindless, lacks internal consistency, and is incomplete—[we reply] no, for it is not so, since its author is the Lord."

12. Bhāṭṭa: Having enjoined a sacrifice by the text, "Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara," there follows the passage: "In that it is on twelve potsherds, he purifies him with the splendor of the Gāyatrī," and so forth. After mentioning cakes on eight, nine, ten, eleven, and twelve potsherds, it is heard: "Upon whose birth one performs this offering, he indeed becomes purified, radiant, an eater of food, possessed of sensory power, and wealthy in cattle."

In that regard, since the number twelve is already established by the [term] *aṣṭatva* (eightfold nature) and so forth, and since the *aṣṭakapāla* (cake on eight potsherds) is already established, one view is that "Vaiśvānara" is merely the name of the sacrifice (*yāga-nāmadheya*).

Alternatively, although these [qualities] are established by their own nature, because they are not yet established as delimiters (*paricchedaka*), they are indeed injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*).
Thus, either the number eight or the substance *aṣṭakapāla* is enjoined in the preceding sentence.

Furthermore, since the status of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) is perceived through the unity of the opening and the conclusion, the twelve-potherd cake (*dvādaśapāla*) is not something enjoined as part of the original production (*utpattiśiṣṭa*).
Alternatively, let there be a plurality of sentences;
even so, its injunction is established by the very statement: "That which is on twelve potsherds."
The second position is that in the Vaiśvānara passage, the mention of "heat" (*tapas*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).

The third position is that, with a view toward results such as spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), qualities such as the eight-pot-sherd offering (*aṣṭākapāla*) are enjoined as being based upon the sacrifice under discussion.

However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), since it is improper to split a single sentence when its unity is possible, this entire scriptural statement pertains to the very sacrifice under discussion.

Since even a single *kapāla* [of the] eight-*kapāla* offering is a means for achieving each individual result, what doubt could there be regarding the twelve-*kapāla* offering—which possesses all its constituent parts—being the cause of all results? This is the meaning of the scriptural injunction (*yāga-śruti*).
