By the logic of the word "fire-oblation" (*agnihoma*) having the power of denoting a class (*jātiśaktyanyāya*), even though it expresses a number, it refers to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice by the logic of the individual (*vyaktinyāya*), because its nature is connected to itself. (The Logic of the Power of Denoting a Class: The Section on Form/Configuration).

Kau. 2|3|102, p. 68: "The purpose of genus (*jāti*) and number (*saṅkhyā*) is to indicate the individual (*vyakti*), because it is impossible for a genus to be a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) in relation to an individual.
Su. p. 1522: *Jātisādhana* (from the *Jātinirṇaya* section of the *Prakaraṇapañjikā*): "Scholars dispute in many ways regarding the nature of the genus (*jāti*)."
This [definition] of theirs is stated according to the opinion of Prabhākara.
Some declare that "universal" (jāti) is merely a manifestation of conceptual construction (vikalpa).
Others, however, maintain that although the universal exists, it is non-different from its substrata.
Others, however, say that the object of inference is distinct;
others still maintain that it is both distinct and non-distinct.
And thus, it is observed that for some people, the linguistic usage of "universal" (jāti) occurs even when it is not cognized.
To refute that [view], this [work] is commenced:
"The universal (*jāti*), which is distinct from its substratum and is the object of perceptual cognition,
is held by the teacher Prabhākara to be apprehended through the recollection of a previous form."

But surely, the substratum itself is the substance, while the universal (*jāti*) is non-existent—so say the followers of Yoga. For instance, it is not accepted that a universal resides in atoms, nor even in the fourfold [elements], nor in the sixty [categories] beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), because these are composed of parts. This is because a universal must be capable of producing a cognition of a recurring form (*anuvṛttākāra*). When a universal is postulated as non-different among things that are different, there arises therein a cognition characterized by the appearance of a recurring form.
Furthermore, even that cognition which perceives atoms is held by the Mīmāṃsakas to have as its cause a quality characterized by dimension (*parimāṇa*).

Even "earthness" and the like are the basis for the cognition of earth and so forth, because they are defined merely as the inherence (*samavāya*) of specific common qualities such as number and the rest.
Nor can a universal (*jāti*) inhere in gross substances, precisely because those [gross substances] are difficult to comprehend [in their ultimate nature].
Indeed, the production of a gross substance is not tenable;
for it is impossible for it to originate another gross substance through a sequence beginning with atoms (*aṇu*) and so forth.
Nor is it distinct from each individual substance, since it does not inhere in each individual substance.
Nor can it be inherent in a single substance, because multiplicity is impossible without the presence of multiple [entities].
By this very same reasoning, the possibility of a triad (tryaṇuka)—which is to be originated by three dyads (dvyaṇuka) and possesses the quality of magnitude—is refuted.
Thus, the talk of origination by one's own minute parts is cast far away.
Furthermore, it must be considered whether the whole exists in its parts either in its entirety or through a relation of inherence.
First, we do not perceive it as existing in its entirety, because that [entirety] is not apprehended in each individual part.
Moreover, if there were trembling or coloring in each individual part, it would follow that the entire whole would be perceived as trembling or colored.
Likewise, in the case of another part [of the whole], there would be an absence of trembling and coloring, yet an attachment to that absence of trembling and coloring;
and the whole would both tremble and not tremble, and both be colored and not be colored, due to these particular contradictory states.
This is the proof by means of a genus (*jāti*).

One might object that this would refute the proof of [the category of] genus (*jāti*); however, there is no fault, for even in the absence of multiple entities exceeding the number one, there is still a single substratum accompanied by a second [entity] as the locus of conjunction.

Now, it may be argued that when those two substances have arisen, the conceptualization of conjunction appears, but there is no distinct quality (*guṇa*) called "conjunction" existing apart from them.

That is not so; for when a substance is perceived, it is recognized, yet another state of those two [the parts and the whole] is seen to occur only occasionally. Thus, the establishment of their difference is indeed accomplished.
Recognition has been established in the *Mīmāṃsājīvarakṣā*.

Therefore, it is logical that the parts themselves—assisted by the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) characterized as the common quality of conjunction—are the inherent causes (samavāyikāraṇa) of the whole.
The objection that was raised regarding the mode of existence (*vṛtti*) of the whole (*avayavin*) is also untenable when the whole is perceived.
The whole exists pervasively across its parts; it does not exist fully in each part, as if it were a genus (*jāti*).

Furthermore, even in another part, what special power (*mahiman*) does that whole possess such that it is conceived as being one while simultaneously permeating many parts? Even if the whole does not reside [fully] in each individual part, there is no fault in this, because the atoms that are the producers are the substratum only when accompanied by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), since they are the substratum precisely by virtue of being producers.
[This arises] from the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

For this very reason, there is no fault in [the argument that] conjunction has a substrate accompanied by a second [factor]; nor is the perception of the whole dependent upon the perception of all its parts, because it is distinct from them.

Nor, on this account, is it logical to maintain that the perception [of the whole] must extend to the point of grasping even a single part. This is because the postulation of a cause is in accordance with the effect; for a cause is postulated for the sake of establishing the effect, not for the destruction of the effect.

Therefore, it is accepted on the basis of direct perception that the apprehension of the whole occurs only upon the apprehension of as many parts as there are; the cognition of that [whole] is dependent solely upon those parts.
Even though they are distinct, the necessity of their simultaneous apprehension follows from that very fact, due to the relationship between the end (upeya) and the means (upāya).
The whole is the end, while the parts constitute the means.
Regarding the parts:
it can indeed be asserted that each of them is perceptible individually, even when the whole (*avayavin*) possessing those other parts is also apprehended.

For its status as a distinct entity is determined through the presence and absence of the other parts; and even while being understood, the whole certainly functions as a distinct object of cognition.
For it is the whole (*avayavin*) alone that comes to the heart as a single entity, whereas its parts are more numerous and more minute.

And this whole, because it possesses magnitude (*mahattva*) and color (*rūpa*), is perceptible to the eye; or [if it possesses touch], it is perceptible by touch. Whether it be earthen, watery, or fiery, it is perceived in this manner. However, an aerial whole, due to its magnitude and possession of touch, is perceived solely by touch.
The dyad (*hy-aṇuka*), however, although composed of four elements (*cātu-bhautika*), is indeed perceptible because it possesses magnitude (*mahattva*).

Magnitude arises from the absence of those causes of magnitude, namely: the plurality of constituent parts (*avayava-bahutva*), magnitude itself, and a specific accumulation (*pracaya-viśeṣa*). This is the proof for its genus (*jāti-sādhana*).
Furthermore, because even great substances such as the ether (*ākāśa*) are devoid of color and touch, they do not fall within the range of perception; enough of this excessive detail.

Now, one might object: since a whole (*avayavin*) is dependent upon all its parts, how can there be contact with the whole when there is no sensory contact with those parts that are concealed? Nor is it tenable to establish that an external sense organ can produce cognition without being in contact [with its object], for that would result in the undesirable consequence that even the parts themselves would be substances with which the sense organ is not in contact.

This has already been answered: since the whole (avayavin) is distinct [from its parts], even when there is conjunction with another part, the sense-object contact of the whole—such as a cloth—is indeed established through the cognition of that conjunction. Thus, by this line of reasoning, it is established that the substance which is the substratum is distinct from the configuration (ākṛti). Now, as for the claim that no substance is perceived apart from color and so forth—is this not a form of theft in plain sight? For a large whole is indeed perceived as distinct from color and the rest.
For this very reason, even when its own color is eclipsed by the proximity of a hibiscus flower, the crystal substance is still recognized.
How indeed could that which is not perceived be recognized?

Furthermore, since a single object is grasped through both seeing and touching, it is not proper to deny the existence of a substance that is clearly perceived as being non-different from its color and touch.

In forests and the like, this conceptual construction (kalpanā) spreads by the force of subverting cognitions (*bādhaka-pratyaya*); because of distance, there is no apprehension of the intervening space, and thus the conventional usage of "apprehending non-difference" proceeds.
However, it has been explained previously that there is no subverting cognition regarding the whole (*avayavin*).
Therefore, it is established that the perception of a universal (*jāti*) is mere idle talk, due to the absence of a substance as its substratum.
And as for this which was stated— that because a universal is eternal, it cannot serve as a means of proving a universal even when producing the cognition of itself— [that is not so].
It is indeed a means of proving a universal.
Because that [universal] is not apprehended by perception.
For the configuration (*ākṛti*), however, is not an object distinct from what is cognized by the means of valid cognition that is perception; rather, it is inference alone that operates therein.
It is established as stated in the *Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa*. Furthermore, inference is not possible even against the Śākyas.
Of ghee; whereas he who is a keen observer is capable of perceiving even a subtle form;
among those who are bound—enough of this excessive detail.
He understands even birth by means of the eye alone;
he does not depend upon the apprehension of odor.
In this regard, some [hold that] "existence" (sattā) resides in substances, qualities, and actions, as expressed by the term "in cows and so forth."
Indeed, much has been studied in this way; for what basis do they then accept the nature of the *āhavanīya* fire?
For in all cases, there is indeed the cognition "it exists."

In certain rites for the accomplishment of specific goals, some have the qualification [to perform them] and others do not; thus they speak, asking, "What is the persistence [of this rule]? This, however, is because the reality of their caste has not been properly discerned.
And the establishment of the application of the word "brāhmaṇa" is [thus] explained.
To this it is replied: [this is] merely a fabrication of the opponent.
If it is granted that [the universal] conforms to its prior form,
then since in beginningless saṃsāra certain things are established through the relationship of producer and produced, the universal must indeed be accepted.
Nor [is there a commonality] among substances of diverse kinds.
O King, the continuums of women and men constitute a "continuum," and these arise from mutual transformation.
This applies to mustard seeds, mountains, and so forth, as well as to qualities such as odor and taste, which possess similar forms.
The reversal of gender applies to those denoted by the word *brāhmaṇa*;
and because they are not heedless regarding this,
existence comes to be.
However, it is by the mere word "existent" (sat) alone that [the lineage] is employed;
because all [members] belong to that continuous series, they are established as being denotable by the term "Brāhmaṇa" due to their status as his descendants.
Furthermore, even in the absence of birth (*jāti*), there is the designation of "cook," "Mīmāṃsaka," and so forth;
therefore, being born from a specific lineage alone is what is denoted by the word "Brāhmaṇa."
The application of words.
Now, even the application of a single word does not have a single basis; [there must be] a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
That the qualification for ritual action belongs only to those who possess a body is not at all untenable;
it is true that there is indeed one limiting condition (*upādhi*), namely, the connection with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It is inferior.
What, then, are those specificities of the continuum? They cannot be pointed out by being enumerated; they are simply what is called "aptitude."
In this regard, another person who considers himself wise thinks:
"Surely they can be [established], but let them be understood as being well-known from worldly usage alone."
Likewise: this improper [reading],
"the subject of inquiry" (*jijñāsāpada*), does not indicate deliberation (*vicāra*), but rather simply "doubts regarding dharma."
*Bāla*, p. 1. ⚑ The maxim *jitvarīvad upācaret* (one should treat it as in the case of *jitvarī*).
This was employed in the Mahābhāṣya on the rule *vidūrāt ñyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.80).
However, the intended meaning according to both systems (*tantra*) is this: this formulation is incorrect.
This river Maṇivindūrā does not originate from that mountain; rather, it originates from a specific feature known as Bālavāya. It flows near that mountain and is situated in the city of Vidūra.
Thus, it follows that either Bālavāya and Vidūra are distinct primary elements (*prakṛti*).

If it is argued that this is not the case there, [we reply] that by logical principle one should treat it as in the case of *iśvarī*; just as merchants address Vārāṇasī as "the conqueror," so do grammarians address Bālavāya as "Vidūra. Thus it has been said in the *Sāhasrī* (840): "The mention of 'living' is a benediction for longevity, because that is its purpose."

In the Sarvakhāra sacrifice, during the Prāyaṇīya and other rites while the sacrificer is still alive, regarding the Sūktavāka, there is no mention of the blessings for long life—specifically, the phrase "He desires long life" (*āyur āśāste*)—and it should not be recited therein. This is because that sentence is intended for that purpose, namely, the attainment of the sacrificer's long life.
However, in the Sarvakhāra, the sacrificer desires death and does not desire long life.
Therefore, it should be recited there;
or rather, because of his entitlement, the statement should be made prior to what was previously mentioned.

In the *sarvakhāra* sacrifice, beginning with the *prāyaṇīya*, while the sacrificer is still alive, the recitation of the blessing for long life—namely, "He desires long life"—must be performed within the *sūktavāka*.
The word "or" (*vā*) serves to exclude the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Because [the deity] possesses a share prior to what was stated [above],
when the commencement is undertaken, it becomes the object of prayer as one who has gone toward the direction of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
Therefore, prior to what has been stated, the *āyurāśis* (the prayer for long life) is indeed appropriate as a *bhāginī*—
that is, one that possesses a share (*bhāga*), meaning an occasion (*avasara*) [for its recitation].
Consequently, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *āyurāśis* must be recited in the *sūktavāka* at the *prāyaṇīya* and other such rites.

The mention of "living" refers to the blessing of longevity, because that is its purpose. Regarding the case where [the *sūktavāka*] is performed when [the sacrificer] is deceased, it has been stated as a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintya*) according to the principle: "Because there is no desire for action, as in the case of the *sūktavāka*" (10.2.15). Thus, even in the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice, since all the fruits of the *sūktavāka* are desired, it would follow that they should not be mentioned; however, in the phrase "the mention of living," because of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the mantra for longevity, it is understood that this specific fruit is intended as the result of the other fruits of the *sūktavāka* which are themselves desired. (Bālakrīḍā, p. 175). Living (*jīvana*) is said to mean the maintenance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

Kaṇikā, p. 364: Life, being an unexhausted cause, is not employed for its own sake in rites such as the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*), but rather it is employed in what is to be understood through the form of the injunction (*pādhaśya*).
Bāla., p. 107: As long as there is life, obligatory duty (*nityakarman*) must necessarily be performed, just like eating.
Vi. 6.3.2: The maxim that "even though one lives (*jīvan*), he would not truly live if he were censured by the world."
The meaning is clear.

*Sāhasrī*, 902. ⚑ "May Agni, being pleased, partake of the clarified butter (*ājya*)," and "May Soma, being pleased, partake of the offering of clarified butter"—these are the two introductory mantras for the *ājyabhāga* (butter-portions).
*Saṃkarṣa*, 4.3.11. ⚑ The *juhū* ladle is connected to another sacrifice that has been performed.
VI. 3.6.1: The *juhū* ladle made of *parṇa* wood is not connected by physical grasping (*anārambhavahitā*).
It finds its place in the archetype (*prakṛti*), and in the ectype (*vikṛti*) it follows from the general injunction (*codaka*).

Regarding the *juhū*: "He whose *juhū* is made of *parṇa* wood hears no evil report"—the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood is for the sake of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*), as its connection with the ritual is established by the syntactical unit (*vākya*); and the mention of a fruit is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

"Being made of *parṇa* wood" means being made of *palāśa* wood. One faces the *juhū* [ladle] with the mantra: "We yoke speech together with the sun in heaven" (Bhāṣya 12.1.5.11). With the mantras beginning with "The eye by means of the *juhū*" and so forth, one performs the anointing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
12|1|126. The form of the *juhū* ladle is twofold: worldly (*laukika*) and scriptural (*śāstrīya*).
The worldly form is that which is seen as being about one *aratni* in length, resembling a swan, and having a smooth surface, and so forth.

[The term] *haṃsamukhatva* refers to the state of having a face like the face of a swan (*haṃsa-mukha*). That which has a face like a swan's is *haṃsamukhī*; the abstract quality of that is *haṃsamukhatva*.
An *aratni* is a cubit measured from the tip of the little finger to the end [of the elbow].
That which has a cavity in its own region is "skin-piercing" (*tvagilā*); because it is unprecedented (*apūrvīyatva*), it is scriptural.
Here, this state of being unprecedented does not exist through any other specific sacrifice; therefore, it is complete and entered [into the ritual system].

VI. 3|6|5. Because the offering of the substance from the *juhū* ladle results in its contact with the fire, it serves as the primary means (*pradhānasādhana*) here; thus, there is a greater distance from the fire in relation to the primary [act]. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 626). One takes clarified butter four times into the *juhū*:
"He takes four times into the *juhū*.
In that regard, for each taking, a mantra and so forth are employed.
And the mantra is "I take you, the bright one, for the sake of the bright ones, from station to station, for the gods, for each sacrificial formula (yajus)," and so forth.
[Vi.
1.4.15] Because the *juhū* and other vessels have not been previously employed [in the context], according to Jaimini. [1775]
Because the *juhū* and other vessels are not employed [in a *satra*], when there is doubt, one should understand that the sacrificer may act according to his desire.

Since the *juhū* and other sacrificial vessels (*yajñāpātra*) are not employed in a *satra*, and because there is an absence of usage—meaning an absence of a rule stating "the performance should be carried out with one's own vessels"—there arises a doubt as to which vessels should be used for the performance. In this state of doubt, it should be understood that the sacrificer may act according to his desire;
he should do exactly as he wishes.
The performance may be carried out with one's own vessels or with those of another;
this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
However, the reading "one may act according to one's desire" (*yathākāmī*) is understood as being in accordance with the Sūtra.
However, the *bhāṣya* reads "he may act according to his desire.
Alternatively, they may use other vessels in common, because of the prohibition and because it is prescribed by scripture.
With the word "apivā" (alternatively), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), which reverses the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) reached by the sūtra.
The common vessels should be new ones, distinct from those used by other sacrificers who are similar to them; the performers of the *sattra* should prepare these as their own shared set.
However, there would be a contradiction if one were to take the vessels belonging to any one individual;
for if the vessels of a particular person were taken and he should die by fate during the middle of the *sattra*, they would have to be destroyed along with him.
If that were the case, there would be the omission of the performance of the *sattra* sacrifice;
however, if the vessels are not burnt, the cremation of the deceased would be defective—thus there is a conflict.
Furthermore, the vessels are common to all, established by the scriptures, and constitute the intended subject matter of the scriptures.
Nor should it be argued that the performance of the sacrifice may proceed with the vessels of another person while he is still alive;
for even so, because the rapidity of the ritual procedure (*prayoga-prāśubhāva*) is mandated by scripture, a deficiency in the sacrifice (*kratu-vaiguṇya*) would be unavoidable.
Therefore, due to this contradiction and because it is prescribed by scripture, the common vessels must be prepared independently.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Ke.

⚑ The *ārya* [grain] situated in the *juhū* ladle is for the purpose of the three *prayāja* offerings. Vi. 4.1.15. ⚑ The root *juhoti* signifies the act of casting [into the fire], because its nature consists of such a deposition.

The renunciation of a substance (*dravyatyāga*) intended for a deity as the result of an offering (*prakṣepa*) is what is denoted by the word *juhoti*. (Madhava, p. 102). Since the root *juhoti* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), it has been stated in the *Tantraratna*, *Tantrasāra*, and *Nyāyasudhā* that the accusative case ending on *saktūn* indicates its status as the instrument (*karaṇatva*).

In this regard, because the suffix *niṣṭhā* (past participle marker) is seen in such instances as "he turns away from the *juhū* [ladle]" (*juhotutaḥ paryāvartate*), it is established that *juhoti* is intransitive; yet, since the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would apply to the object of *hu* by the rule "the third case is used for the object of *hu*" (*tṛtīyā ca hośchandasi*, Pāṇini 2.3.13)—and by the word *ca* ("and"), the second case (*dvitīyā*) would also apply—it follows that *juhoti* is transitive according to the usage of the author of the Sūtras. (Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa, *Pradīpa*, 2.1.12, p. 78). For *juhoti*, the primary element is the act of throwing [into the fire], which constitutes the completion of the *homa* and is preceded by the renunciation [of the offering] directed toward a deity.

Su. Pṛ. 1527. ⚑ The name *darvihoma* belongs only to those acts enjoined by the root *juhoti* (to offer), because the word *homa* (offering) is used in its primary sense there, and not to those enjoined by the root *yajati* (to sacrifice). Vi. 8.4.43. ⚑ Or rather, it belongs to those enjoined by *juhoti* because of their connection with that [word].
It is understood that the term *darvihoma* is a designation for both Smārta and Śrauta rites.

Now, in the inquiry as to whether the term *darvihoma* is the name for all injunctions involving *yajati* (sacrifices) and *juhoti* (offerings), or only for those involving *juhoti*, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) says:
the word *darvihoma* is the name only for injunctions involving *juhoti*.
The word "or" (*vā*) serves to exclude [the application of] both types of injunctions.
Because of its connection with that [word *darvi*], it is a *darvihoma*; this is because of the connection with the word *homa*.
If, however, it were [connected] with *yajati*, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, the term *darvihoma* is a name for the act of *juhoti*.
In the second [section], regarding the performance of the *antarāgarbhya* rite, this is the Sūtra:
"For all those enjoined by the term *juhoti*, the designation 'Darvihoma' and their status as *apūrva* (novel rites) will be stated" (Sūtra, p.
816). A yawn (*jṛmbhā*), known as *jṛmbhikā*, is a specific modification of the vital air (*vāyu*) induced by the onset of sleep, which has the primary result of [releasing] a yawn.
Jaimini [states]: "Because of the consequence of dependence on another. (Sūtra 1.1.5).
By means of inference based on the mark of what has been known, there would be a prohibition of independence for Jaimini due to the consequence of dependence on another.

In the *paśupuroḍāśa* (the cake-offering for the animal sacrifice), the *prayāja*s and other such rites are accomplished by *prasaṅga* (extension) from the animal sacrifice's *prayāja*s and so forth; therefore, they need not be performed separately. However, it is the opinion of the teacher Jaimini that the two *ājyabhāga*s (butter-portions) must be performed in the *paśupuroḍāśa*.
This is because there would be a prohibition of one's own independent procedure (*svatantra*) due to the occurrence of another's procedure (*paratantrāpatti*).

When the procedure (*tantra*) of another occurs in place of the work of one's own procedure regarding a particular rite-element, then, due to that occurrence of another's procedure, there should be a prohibition of one's own procedure—just as the procedures of the *pauroḍāśika* (cake-offering) are prohibited when the *pāśuka* (animal-sacrifice) procedures apply.
However, where no action belonging to another is encountered, a prohibition is not appropriate, as in the case of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings. Therefore, there is no cessation of those two.

Nor is it the case that the two *ājyabhāgas* are prescribed for the animal sacrifice (*paśu*); thus, their accomplishment is achieved through the ritual procedure (*tantra*) pertaining to the animal sacrifice.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the two *ājyabhāga* offerings must be performed in the *paśupuroḍāśa*. Ke.

[This is because] in the section beginning with "Jaimini’s [view] would be a prohibition of the independent [rite], due to the occurrence of dependence on another" (12.1.2.7), it will be stated that the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavacana*) is weaker than the general rule (*codaka*).
The *Dharmamīmāṃsā* composed by Jaimini consists of sixteen chapters (*adhyāyas*), each containing four sections (*pādas*).

It begins with the sūtra "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) and concludes with the sūtra "Or rather, it exists because of the time of the Veda, as in the case of the *yājyā*-invocation and the like, as in the case of the *yājyā-saṃpreṣa*" (*vidyate vā 'mnāyakālatvād yathā yājyādyairviprayogo yathā yājyāsaṃpreṣaḥ*).
(Saṃkarṣa. 4.4.10)

The collection of sūtras proclaimed by Jaimini (consisting of twelve chapters), beginning with "Dharma is a purposeful matter characterized by an injunction" and ending with "And the anvāhārya [is performed] because it is seen," [Vi.
1.1.1]. The followers of Jaimini do not accept the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), but they do accept the intermediate dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*).
The term "pralaya" should be considered as it appears in the *Maṇi*. Ke.:
*Jopaṇa* is the determination that the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) tree is fit for service because it is characterized by the defining marks;
and that is a property of the sacrificial post (*yūpadharma*).
The scriptural passage concerning the silent recitation (*japa*) is "Agni has accepted this oblation," and so forth; [this occurs] at the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
The butter in the *jauhava* vessel is for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings, whereas the butter in the *aupabhṛta* vessel is for the sake of both the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings.
Those who know the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) follow the object of knowledge (*prameya*), [understanding it] as it has been known.
*Bṛhatī*, p. 66: Only that which is already known has the capacity to make known a remote object. *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, p.
"And the instruction [is given] regarding what is known; for one who does not know is not prescribed [as an agent]," according to the principle at *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 3.8.8.18.

It is known that the sacrificer is one who possesses knowledge. For it is only when the sacrificer is endowed with knowledge that the instruction "he causes the sacrificer to recite the *klṛpti* verses" is prescribed.
This is because one who is ignorant is not authorized for Vedic ritual action.
However, only the learned person is prescribed;
such is the literal meaning of the Nyāya-sūtra.
According to the principle that "it is when [the object] is known," the ignorant person has no entitlement even to the Āśvinī cup, just as they have none to the duties of the sacrificer (yājamāna).
Su. Pṛ. 99:
And the recitation [of formulas] occurs when [the meaning] is known, for one who is ignorant is not prescribed [for such a role].
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "He causes the sacrificer to recite the *klṛpti* formulas," and "He causes the sacrificer to recite the *ujjiti* formulas."
The mantras beginning with "May it be prepared through long life; may it be prepared through the sacrifice for breath" are called *klṛptis*.

The *ujjiti* mantras, however, are those beginning with "Agni conquered speech by means of the single syllable" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.1.11). Regarding these, since it is stated "he causes [the sacrificer] to recite," it is understood that even one who has not studied the Veda must be made to recite the *yājyā* and other formulas at the time of the ritual performance. When this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been established, the proponent of the final position (*siddhāntin*) replies.

"The knower exists; the sacrificer is known. This usage is formed with the suffix *ac* in the sense of possession (*matvarthin*), as in "the father [is] cows" (*pitā gāvaḥ*) meaning "one who possesses cows," or "the Brahmins [are] well-spoken of" (*suktā brāhmaṇāḥ*), or "the cloth [is] tied after being drunk" (*pītapratibaddhavastam*). And since the sacrificer is indeed known when he is known, the recitation of the mantras must be performed.

Alternatively, the word *jñāta* may be understood exactly as it was heard [in the original injunction]. Even when the collection of mantras has been learned by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the recitation (*vācana*) must still be performed. And this recitation may be carried out according to preference, either as a partial delivery (*khaṇḍaśaḥ samarpaṇam*) or as the command "Recite! (*brūhi*).
Now, why is there instruction only when [the text] is already known? Because one who is ignorant—that is, one who has not studied his own Veda—is neither enjoined nor authorized for ritual acts.

Therefore, even though he has already studied it, he must be instructed for the sake of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*); this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Why? Because, apart from the knowledge of the subject matter, there is a necessity for the state of being "known" [through formal instruction].

Maṇi, p. 16. In the Mīmāṃsaka school, it is accepted that the apprehension of a cognition occurs solely through inference based on the mark (*liṅga*) of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*). And "cognizedness" is a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) residing in the object of knowledge, produced by mental cognition.
And that [excellence] is mental—
The proximity characterized by cognition is the object of perception;
this is the proof for "cognizedness" (jñātatā), according to Vaidyanātha, page 33.
The term "prāmāṇyavādaḥ" should be understood as being marked with a *vindu* (anusvāra).

Maṇi, p. 16. The ancient masters [hold that] there is no relationship of agent and object (*karmatva*) for the knower, because [the object] possesses the result of manifestation (*prākaṭya*) produced by cognition.
Maṇi, p. 54. There is the maxim: "Cognition is the remover of ignorance only for one who is ignorant."
For cessation is of two kinds: by way of an opposing factor and by way of the cessation of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
For example, the destruction of a lamp by wind; or, for example, the cessation of a lamp through the exhaustion of oil, wick, and so forth.
Likewise, the first [kind of cessation] pertains to knowledge, while the second pertains to the category of effects.
The *Sāhasrī*. 378. Knowledge, because it is inherent in the self (*ātmasamavetatva*), has the self as its substratum.
*Su.* p. 660. Knowledge is not perceptible; rather, it is inferable from the "knownness" (*jñātatā*) of the object.
This is to be seen in the section titled "Prāmāṇyavāda."

The view of the proponent of the "unsupported" (nirālambanavādin)—that all knowledge has only false objects and thus no cognition is valid—and its refutation, should be seen in the *Vindī* under the section "nirālambanavādinaḥ," on pages 23–24 of the *Maṇi*. "For knowledge indeed has the person as its locus; therefore, it is not contradicted by that [knowledge].
And non-knowledge residing in another person is not sublated by it. (*Maṇi*, p. 24)
This is the logical principle (*nyāya*). *Ślokavārttika*, in the section on the refutation and resolution of objections regarding relation (35):
Ratnākara states that "the state of being known" (*jñātatva*) is relative; therefore, even for a single object, its being known or unknown is contradictory from the perspective of different persons.
For knowledge residing in one person is not contradicted by ignorance residing in another;
nor is ignorance contradicted by knowledge. Rather, the subsequent knowledge, as it arises, arises precisely by subverting its own stable prior knowledge.
"Furthermore, knowledge in its state of producing an effect is not what is known; rather, it is [known] after its causal function has ceased.

(Rjuvimalā, p. 66). Just as the knowledge that "one hundred and twelve" has arisen is sublated by the subsequent knowledge of the occasional rite involving the gift of all one's possessions and so forth.
When knowledge is not sublated, its validity is established through intrinsic validity (svataḥ-prāmāṇya) in the absence of defects.
Rahasya, p. 14: [The author] will state that knowledge is inferential.
*Bṛhatī*, p. 45: Because knowledge has as its fruit the manifestation of the object of knowledge, and no other fruit is admitted. *Vivaraṇa*, p.
271: Since knowledge is dependent upon the determination of the object of knowledge, it is differentiated by the differentiation of the objects of knowledge.

Su. Pṛ. 704: Because cognition (*jñāna*) is partless. Pṛ. 1082: The distinction of the subordinate action of cognition arises solely through the distinction of the primary actions upon which it depends. Mī. Ko. 223: Cognition is inferable.
On this point, some maintain that cognition is inferable; in their view, the very non-existence of cognition is established.

For instance, the inference of knowledge cannot arise from the mere existence of an object, because that [existence] lacks the necessary invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with it; indeed, even in the absence of objects such as Yudhiṣṭhira and others, knowledge certainly persists.

If it is argued that "knowledge of the object" is the logical mark (*liṅga*), that too is not a mark by its mere existence, because there is no distinction between indifference and non-perception regarding something that does not manifest itself; for a logical mark that does not manifest itself cannot be an inferential indicator. Nor can the manifestation of the knowledge of an object depend upon another cognition, because another cognition is not apprehended, and otherwise an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result.
Therefore, partial knowledge must be admitted to be self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*).

This follows from the principle that there is no subverting evidence against the effect [of self-luminosity] as described for knowledge and so forth, which is independent of the sense organs (*nirindriya*).

Just as among stationary beings (*sthāvara*), the culmination of the development of knowledge is the state of being free from impurity, so too must it be accepted that for those mixed with the culmination of the excellence of that [knowledge], the same applies.

At the beginning of the Kalpa, the moon and other planets were situated in a single constellation; from that time forward, due to their own specific motions characterized by swiftness or slowness, they pass into various other constellations.
And as these [planets] move within the circle of the constellations (*nakṣatracakra*), there arises a distinction in their cycles of motion due to the specific variations in their speed and slowness.

Because time is demarcated by the specific motions of the moon and the sun, and because it is expressed in terms of lunar days (*tithi*) and constellations (*nakṣatra*), the knowledge of lunar days and constellations arises from the knowledge of the divisions of the motions of the moon and the sun.

In order to understand that "this many revolutions of the movements of the moon and the sun occur in one *yuga*," and so as to know the specific divisions of the movements of the moon and the sun—such as "here now is the moon" and "here now is the sun"—within those years and other units of time contained therein, there is the utility of knowing the lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth.

Furthermore, by means of the measurement of the revolution of the *yuga*, the specific divisions of the movements of the moon, the sun, and others are known through the formula: "by this many revolutions of the *yuga*, there are this many revolutions of the movements of the moon and the sun."

Once it is known that "this many cycles of the *yuga* have elapsed," one calculates the *mahāgaṇa*—the total number of past days consisting of all those days and nights—by determining "of this *yuga* there were this many days and nights, and of that [previous *yuga*] there were this many. Having done so, knowledge arises as to "the current motion of this planet is such-and-such, and of that [other planet] it is such-and-such. Thus, the knowledge of the measure of the *yuga* cycles is useful for the purpose of discerning the motions of the Moon and the Sun.
This is the eighth *muhūrta* of the day; therefore, by the number of the *muhūrta*, one gains knowledge of the specific movement of the sun when it is at the midpoint of the sky. (Su. pp.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, when the Anuṣṭubh and Gāyatrī meters are produced through transposition (pratyayana), the singing of the Sāmans for the Śyāvāśva and Ādhīgava [verses] is performed in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
The Prāgāthika section, however, [is as follows]: 9|2|6|25, Section 3. Commentary: Or rather, it is thus.

"The *pañcacchandas* [stoma] is the *āvāpa*; the *pavamāna* has seven *sāmans*. There are two *gāyatra-saṃhita*s upon a *gāyatra* *tṛca*; the *iyāvāśva* and *adhīgava* are upon *anuṣṭubh*s; the *sappha* is upon an *uṣṇih*; the *pauṣkala* is upon a *kakubh*; and the *kāmavanta* is upon *jagatī*s.

Regarding these two *sāmans*, the *iyāvāśva* and the *adhīgava*, the former is an *anuṣṭubh*: "For you, for the exhilarating Soma, the conqueror of enemies, the pressing-stone has loosened the long-tongued serpent."
(Thus.
The next two verses are *gāyatrīs*: "He who, being pressed, looks around with his purifying stream—Indra, like a lover, makes him his own."
"Men, with skillful intellect, urge that Soma, difficult to attain, toward the sacrifice by means of the pressing stones. Thus [it is said].

In this matter, the point is doubtful: should the chanting be performed upon equal verses by bringing in two other *anuṣṭubh*s, or should one create a *tṛca* sequence by displacing that which was previously an *anuṣṭubh* and the two subsequent *gāyatrī*s, thereby beginning with an *anuṣṭubh*?
What is the prima facie view? That two other *anuṣṭubh*s should be brought in.
Why is this so? Because in this way, their origin will be purposeful.
This being the position reached, we reply:
"But it is [the] *prāgāthika*."
The *pragātha* chant must be performed.
For thus they remember: "The *pragātha* is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
The status of being a *pragātha* cannot be set aside by all [other] measures.
And [the word] "its own" (*sve*).
The commentary states: "In this way, the chanting will occur in its own [original form].
Thereby, the original model (*prakṛta*) will be maintained, and there will be no application of what is not the original model (*aprakṛtaprakriyā*)."
And regarding the *pragātha*: the Commentary states—The word *pragātha* is also observed when a verse-foot is sung repeatedly;
this is because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) and because there is no deviation from that [usage].
The Commentary states: Furthermore, there is an indicative mark (liṅga) [of this] through non-separation.
Thus it says: "Twenty-four Jagatī verses constitute the third pressing; one Kakubh verse [is also included]."

That is seen as follows: the *pañcacchanda* (five-metred) insertion consists of the *ābharmava* and the *pavamāna* with seven *sāmans*. In the *gāyatra-saṃhita*, there are two *tṛcas* in the *gāyatrī* meter; those make six *gāyatrīs*. There are three *jagatīs*.

In the *iyāvāśva* and *adhīgava*, which are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, the former is an *anuṣṭubh* and the latter two are *gāyatrīs*. When the *pramathana* (interchange) is performed there between the two *sāmans*, there are six *anuṣṭubhs*; those [six] become four *jagatīs*, and together with the former ones, they total seven.

The *uṣṇih* has thirty-two syllables, and the *kakubh* has forty-four; one is the *pauṣkala*, and another is also on a single melody (*ekasāman*). Those two, the *uṣṇih* and the *kakubh*, together with the *jagatī* and the quarter of a *gāyatrī*, make eight *jagatīs* along with the preceding ones.
In the *kāva* [section], there are three *jagatī* verses; together with those, they become eleven.
The *ekaviṃśa* [stoma] is the *yajñāyajñīya*; therein, the former is a *bṛhatī* and the latter is a *viṣṭārapaṅkti*.
Then, by making the two subsequent [verses] *kakubh*s, the *pragātha* is formed.
And when the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*stoma*) is being performed, there are seven *bṛhatī*s and fourteen *kakubh*s.
Those which are the seven *bṛhatī*s are five *jagatī*s;
together with the preceding ones, they total sixteen.
The *ekakṣatra* is one quarter of a *jagatī*; together with the preceding quarter of a *gāyatrī*, they constitute twenty characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Now, regarding the fourteen *kakubhs*: those twelve *kakubhs* are seven *jagatīs*.
In the *jyotiṣṭoma*, there are eighteen *anuṣṭubhs*.
Together with the previous ones, there are twenty-three.

Those two remaining *kakubh* verses, along with one *jagatī* foot, constitute a *gāyatrī* foot; together with the previous ones, they form twenty-four *jagatī*s. A single *kakubh* verse consists of twenty syllables, as previously stated.
When the *pragātha* is thus performed, there are twenty-four *jagatī*s and one *kakubh*.

If, however, the *pragātha* is not performed, then—due to the introduction of two *anuṣṭubh*s in the case of the *śyāvāśva* verses and so forth, and due to the introduction of a *bṛhatī* and a *kakubh* in the *yajñāyajñīya*—this numerical total is not achieved.
Therefore, the singing must be performed using the *pragātha* method.

(Note: Regarding the fact that "jagatī-hood" has been mentioned many times here, it should be understood as being merely a conceptual designation based on the count of syllables, and not because they are actually recited as such. Śā—As for the statement, "The two *tucas* of Śyāvāśva and others consist of *anuṣṭubh*s," there is a deliberation as to whether the first of those two is an *anuṣṭubh* and the latter two are *gāyatrīs*, or whether two other *anuṣṭubh*s are introduced there, or whether the three *anuṣṭubh*s are to be produced through *pragāthana* from those very verses already recited.

However, this alternative explanation (in the Bhāṣya) is for the purpose of demonstrating another indicative mark (*liṅga*); there is no further doubt to be raised here. [In the context of] Soma—the Jyotiṣṭoma—at the Āgnīdhra [station] in the Jyotiṣṭoma, such as at the *iṣṭi* and so forth...

One should perform [the rite] with the *ṛc* itself, and not with any verse from the *Daśataya*. (Vi. 3.2.8) In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Hiraṇyakeśins perform the consecration of the Āgnīdhra shed with the verse "atha no agniḥ," while the Baudhāyanas do so with "agnimūrdhā.
(Ke. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, during the worship of the Āgnīdhra, Sadas, and Havirdhāna sheds, one should respectively employ a relevant verse addressed to Agni, one to Indra, and one to Viṣṇu.
In the *āgneyī* modification (*vikṛti*), it is offered as a *nirvāpa*.

Bhāṣya 10.2.15–18, Section 1: In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, regarding the statement "the *ājyas* are fifteenfold," the word *ājya* is the name of specific recitations (*śastra*), not an injunction of a quality. 1.4.2.3: In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is said, "They praise with the *ājyas*; they praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*."
There is no sublation of the archetypal *rathaṃtara* sāman, the *devya* verses, and so forth, by the *ājyapṛṣṭha* and other stotras; rather, there is their combination (*samuccaya*).
(Vi. 10.4.9). In the Jyotiṣṭoma, is the *ātithyā* and so forth [performed] by means of the *upasat*, *mīya*, and *upayaj* offerings as a matter of incidental application (*prasaṅga*)?
Or [is it performed] in the Jyotiṣṭoma while rising? (188) In the Jyotiṣṭoma, while rising...
The *sāmidhenī* verses are enjoined as things to be recited.
What then? That [recitation] is connected to a specific *havirdhāna* cart; and that which is not enjoined does not constitute an auxiliary (*aṅga*).
Nor is it enjoined in this way: "The *havirdhāna* cart is to be taken up for those *sāmidhenī* verses being recited because they are moving together.

How then? Here, a connection with a specific *havirdhāna* is heard regarding the *sāmidhenīs*, but a general connection with a *havirdhāna* is not being enjoined. Furthermore, no connection of the *havirdhāna* with the *sāmidhenīs* has been previously established that could be restated for the sake of specifying a particular one.

With what, then, is the *havirdhāna* cart connected? For the *soma* is directly perceived as the object of the action, whereas the *havirdhāna* is not directly perceived as the object of the *sāmidhenī* verses.
However, there is a connection between the location and the *sāmidhenīs*.
By the phrase "behind the altar" (*apareṇa vedim*), a specific location is indicated as the reason; that location extends up to either the northern or the southern *havirdhāna* cart.
"In that regard, he recites what they press"—
this statement is based on logical reasoning (*upapatti*).
Therefore, the mention of the *havirdhāna* (soma-cart) is for the purpose of indicating the location.

Now, why should the connection not be as follows: "In whichever *havirdhāna* they press [the Soma], that *havirdhāna* has a connection with the *sāmidhenī* verses"? This is not possible. For in this way, two connections would have to be established:
a connection with the *havirdhāna* in general, and a connection with a specific *havirdhāna*; in that case, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Therefore, the connection is not thus. Or rather: first, the Havirdhāna shed does not depend on direct perception for its function of holding the Soma; furthermore, since the Sāmidhenī verses serve the purpose of [providing] the *nidhana* (concluding formula) in the archetype itself, they have no need for a subsidiary action (*aṅgakriyā*) as their purpose. Alternatively, if one were to assume a general connection even when the sentence is intent upon a specific connection with the Havirdhāna, then the "splitting of the sentence" (*vākyabheda*) mentioned in the *Āgneyī-adhikaraṇa* should be applied here.

For one who avoids the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*) by means of a specific [injunction] implying a general rule, an *arthāpatti* (presumption) must be demonstrated through the established position of the Siddhānta, which possesses an established general relationship.
For there is indeed the prior application of either the *havirdhāna* shed or the *āgnīdhra* shed as a characteristic of the original location;
therein, only the specific detail is easily enjoined.
Therefore, it is characterized by its location;
and its designation is likewise.
The Commentary: And its designation is exactly like that.
Just as the *sāmidhenī* verses are taught by logic [to be for the sake of the *soma*], namely, "the *havirdhāna* [is for the sake of the *soma*]";
for it is logical that that which has no other purpose is designated as being for the sake of something else.
Otherwise, it might even be called the "place for the *sāmidhenīs*."

(The term *sāmidhenīdhāna* refers to that in which the *hotṛ* priest—who is [indirectly] designated by the term *sāmidhenīs* through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—is stationed, just as the term *havirdhāna* [refers to the cart where the oblation is placed].

Soma: As before, because there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), it is stated that the *havirdhāna* is to be enjoined as the locus for the *sāmidhenīs*; this constitutes the connection (*saṃgati*). The purpose (*prayojana*) is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the recitation of the *sāmidhenīs* should be performed while standing on the southern cart called the *havirdhāna*; however, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it should be performed at that location [the *sāmidhenīdhāna*].

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: Based on the statement, "He recites the *sāmidhenī* verses there," it follows that the *havirdhāna* shed itself—in which [the southern one] the mounting occurs—that *havirdhāna* would be the locus for the *sāmidhenīs*.
As stated: "Standing at the *havirdhāna*, he should recite the *sāmidhenīs* here;
by this, the specific location of the *havirdhāna* is indicated."
[If it is argued that] its status as a subsidiary arises from syntactical connection (*vākya*), do not say so; for by the *prakṛti* [suffix], the western region has already been established.
By parsimony (*lāghava*), the proximity of the cart (*śakaṭasannidhi*) is what is to be indicated.

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the scriptural text, "And that which they pour out, he recites the *sāmidhenī* verses over it," the meaning is that wherever the pressing occurs in the southern *havirdhāna*, there one should recite the *sāmidhenī* verses for the *agnīṣomīya* and other offerings. In this regard, a deliberation arises as to whether the *havirdhāna* cart is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenīs*, or whether it is a specific location indicated by it. In considering this, just as in the previous case, because of the avoidance of both an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) and a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), the *havirdhāna*—even though its purpose is fulfilled by holding the Soma—is a subsidiary of the *sāmidhenīs* according to the logic of the sacrificial cake's potsherd (*puroḍāśa-kapāla-nyāya*).

This being the prima facie view, [we reply]: since the *havirdhāna* cart is absolutely unestablished [in this context], prescribing it as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses would result in the fault of an "original injunction" (*apūrvavidhi*). Furthermore, because the *āhavanīya* fire is transferred from the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is already established by extension (*atideśa`); and since there is no fixed rule regarding its proximity to the southern *havirdhāna*, it is already established [as being near it] by default. Therefore, in an injunction that restricts the location indicated by the term "southern *havirdhāna*," there is parsimony (*lāghava*); and thus, even the use of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in accordance with that [parsimony] is not a defect.

In reality, however, because parsimony (*lāghava*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is untenable in accordance with that [parsimony], the meaning understood is: "In whatever place they press (*su-vanti*, *abhiṣuṇvanti*), in that very place of pressing he should recite the *sāmidhenī* verses. Thus, there is no need for figurative indication even regarding the *havirdhāna* shed, since the place of pressing itself is directly enjoined by the sacred text (*śruti*).

The practical application is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the *sāmidhenīs* are to be recited over the *havirdhāna* shed; according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), they are to be recited at the place of pressing near the southern *havirdhāna*.
Maṇḍana: "The fruit of these two is designated as *bhadrapada*.
Śaṅkara: "And that would occur under another designation;
that is the fruit."
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the mantra for the *uparava* holes: "I dig the Vaiṣṇava [holes], which destroy the Rakṣas and the *valaga*.
This mantra is to be repeated for each individual *uparava* hole;
this is the principle of the *uparava* rule (*uparavanyāya*).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, one should employ a *pratipad* containing the word "upa" for that which has the *rathantara* as its *pṛṣṭha*, and one containing the word "agra" for that which has the *bṛhat* as its *pṛṣṭha*.

Here, one *pṛṣṭha* is the cause [for the application of the rule] independently of the other; specifically, the *gāyatrī* used at the commencement is "upavatī" (containing *upa*), while the verse beginning with "prayujo vāco agriyaḥ" is "agratvatī" (containing *agra*).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, because this [single] element must necessarily be enjoined and because it serves as the means for obtaining the general rule, no fault is perceived; thus, in that case, there is no Varuṇa-sacrifice for the giver.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, regarding the mere rising [from the seat]: in the Jyotiṣṭoma, when one horse rises, there is the instruction of a mantra for the release of speech.

Regarding the Udgātṛ’s cup (*udgātracamasa*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma, the opinion of the Bhāṣya is that it belongs to the Udgātṛs who have undergone the *samudbhavaṇa* ceremony; the opinion of the Vārtika is that it belongs to those excluding the Subrahmaṇya priest.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, when the simultaneous disconnection (apaccheda) of both the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ occurs, there is an option between the forfeiture of the sacrificial fee (adākṣiṇya) and the giving away of one's entire property as the fee (sarvasvadākṣiṇya).
Bhā. 6.5.18.51–53: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the *upagās* (assistant singers) are among those very same officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) already mentioned.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the uparava holes, it is heard in the scripture: "What is auspicious here, let that be with us there. Thus, the fruit belongs to the officiating priests as well.
This is explained in detail [in the *Tantravārttika*].
Furthermore, there is the indicative mark (*vyapadeśa*).
(30 ke. Commentary: Where there is a designation (*vyapadeśa*), there the fruit is produced by the meaning (*ārthija*).
Below the southern *havirdhāna* cart, there are four *uparava* holes, each a span (*prādeśa*) in width and separated from one another by a span.

Having inserted his hands there, the Adhvaryu asks the sacrificer, "What is here? He replies, "Auspiciousness. The Adhvaryu responds, "May we share therein. Thus, there occurs a designation between the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer.
In that context, the dual expression "tatrau saha" refers to both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer;

therefore, the fruit of the sacrifice belongs to the sacrificer. Furthermore, while [the principle] "on account of designation" (3.4.14) was cited there from the Brāhmaṇa, here it is cited from the mantra according to the Prastāva-veda.
Therefore, there might be a suspicion that when [the action] is conceptualized with effort, it might sometimes be impossible to conceptualize both [the agent and the object].
However, the cause for such conceptualization remains the same whether they occur simultaneously or not; thus, there is no complexity whatsoever.

Now, why are these two [terms] employed in this way? Since even by employing only one [term], it is indeed possible to manifest the result pertaining to both, then—this being established—there is no purpose in employing both agents, and thus there is a restriction to the *adhvaryu* priest.
Vi— "The phrase *'bhadraṃ tatrau saṃhita'* [is used] in what context? It is appropriate for two masters. It has two referents: the Adhvaryu and the Yajamāna.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, beneath the two wooden boards (*phalaka*) that serve as the supports for the pressing of the Soma in the Havirdhāna shed, there are four holes called *uparava*s situated in the four directions starting from the southeast (*āgneyī*). Because they are one *aratni* in measure, they meet one another at their lower parts, while at their upper parts they are separated by a distance of one *prādeśa*.
Among those, having extended his right hand over one of the uparavas, the Adhvaryu takes hold of the sacrificer’s hand from below.
At that time, the sacrificer asks a question with the mantra: "What is here? (kim atra).
The Adhvaryu priest responds with the mantra "Bhadram" (the auspicious).
Thereupon, the sacrificer accepts that fruit as belonging to both parties by means of the mantra "Tanno saha" (that, for us, together).
Maṇḍana states: "The fruit denoted by the word 'Bhadra' belongs to both."
Śaṅkara says: "And that [result] would occur through indirect indication (nyapadeśa).
