In the Jyotiṣṭoma, because this [one-day rite] must necessarily be prescribed and because it serves as the means for obtaining the general rule, no fault is perceived; thus, in that case, there is no Vāruṇī sacrifice for the giver.
Oṃ: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is an option regarding the one and other [numbers of] initiations.
The initiation lasts for twelve days, and there are exactly twelve [days].
Regarding the measure of initiation (*dīkṣā*), because there is a specific optionality according to one's desire.

The Commentary states: With reference to the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard in scripture: "One initiation, three *upasads*, and the fifth is the *prasuta*"; yet many measures of initiation are also recorded, such as "three initiations" and "twelve initiations.
Regarding these, there is a doubt: is there a restrictive rule such that any one of those measures may be adopted, or is it that twelve initiations must be taken?
What is the conclusion? Regarding the duration of initiation, one may act according to one's desire;
there is no fixed rule.
Why? Because there is no specific distinction made.

No specific [limit] is prescribed; therefore, any measure whatsoever may be adopted. This is because, regarding the measure of initiation (*dīkṣā*), there is the distinction of acting according to one's own desire.
(The author of the Bhāṣya, having accepted the unity of locus for this [sacrifice] in the subsequent sūtra, established the conclusion that its measure is twelve [days].
He objects to that: Here, the conclusion described by the author of the Bhāṣya is incorrect.

It is true that the constant injunction here is the reason, but it is not [the case that] "one who has been initiated for twelve nights should seek prosperity" (meaning: one should be joined with initiation for twelve days).
And at that time, he requests the materials required for the sacrifice.
This [request] is not for the sake of the sentence "tamu yācane" (he requests him); rather, for what then? It is for the sake of such [sentences] as "There is one initiation" (*ekā dīkṣā*).
For why are those [rites], which are permanently enjoined within the context, displaced? Furthermore, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between those that possess equal authority.
He says: "In that case, they are not permanent, because they are occasional (*pākṣikatvāt*)."
It is said:

Eternality is with respect to the original form (*prakṛti*)—that is, having established that [the elements] are eternally prescribed in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, they are called eternal; it is not with respect to the performance (*prayoga*), and thus there is no contradiction.
If it is argued that [the elements] are optional, then how is the statement regarding the sacrificial fee (*bhṛti*) to be understood? [The author] replies: Let it be transferred (*utkṛṣyatām*).
(He himself says: "What is the reason here for you, that many [details] are elevated while one is not elevated?
It would be better that many be elevated, as this accords with the context.

(In reality, however, he says that there is no elevation of anything at all—) "Furthermore, even the sentences concerning 'one' and so forth are subsidiary to the Jyotiṣṭoma by virtue of the context; the sentence regarding the payment of wages is also subsidiary."

And it is not the case that, when the context (*prakaraṇa*) is equal, one [element] is extracted from another; (here, the reading in the Ānandāśrama edition is *atulyaprakaraṇe anyatamenānyatamamutkṛṣya*;
in our manuscript it is *na ca tulye prakaraṇatvameva anyatamamutkṛṣya*;
however, in the Tantraratna it is *na ca tulye*).
The reading is "having extracted one from among [the options] in the section on the means of proof.
And this [phrase] "twelve nights" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
If it were intended as an injunction of meaning, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

How so? First, the statement regarding wages (*bhṛti*)—that is, the acquisition of materials—is already established by the purpose of the act; for by that alone, the hiring of services is not possible.
Thus, that [wages] is certainly not something to be enjoined (because it is established by the purpose).
Furthermore, the phrase "twelve nights" (referring to the duration of the initiation) is likewise not to be enjoined.

For there are indeed twelve nights for him (the initiated one), because of the scriptural statement, "twelve initiations. Furthermore, it is not possible to enjoin that there must be exactly twelve nights (and not eleven nights, etc. as if they were obligatory, for fear of rendering the statements regarding one night and so forth meaningless. Moreover, even in the word *dīkṣita*, it is not for the purpose of enjoining its own primary meaning—namely, that "initiation has occurred for this person"—for his initiation has already occurred through the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* and other rites.

What, then, is to be enjoined? [The author] states it: the connection between the word *bhṛti* ("hiring") and the *upapada* (the accompanying word) is what is enjoined. (In that case too, since there is an *upapada*, one must consider which [word] is enjoined as being connected with the word *bhṛti*.

If, first of all, it were enjoined that "whatever hiring one should perform, that should be for twelve nights," then there would be a connection between the permanent and the non-permanent (*nityānityasaṃyoga*); for the hiring would be as if permanent, while the twelve nights are non-permanent.
Now, why is it that the hiring [of priests] is prescribed specifically for the night by means of the exclusion of the day? It is said:
[If so,] the sentence would be split, as in: "One should perform the hiring during the nights, and that [should be done] in twelve [days].

Alternatively, if it is prescribed that "that which is the hiring during the nights [should be done] in twelve [days]," then there is the fault of restating a qualified [already established] fact (*viśiṣṭānuvāda*).
If, however, the alternative view is that "one who should acquire the wages for the forest [sacrificial fee] is the initiated one" (*dīkṣita*), then there is no fault.
And this must indeed be enjoined, for that acquisition of the forest [fee] does not otherwise apply to the initiated one.

Furthermore, the phrase "for twelve nights" is either a restatement of an optional [measure of time] or a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that the acquisition of the wages for the forest should be performed simultaneously with the time of initiation (the printed text reads *dīkṣitakālasambandhena*).
The reading "at the same time as the consecration" (dīkṣitasamakāle) is that of Ratna.

Therefore, this very restriction applies to the duration of the consecration: one may act according to one's desire. However, the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) should be [the rule] on account of an indicative mark (liṅga).
Commentary: The measure should be taken as twelve days alone. Why? From an indicative mark (liṅga).
This means by virtue of its inherent capacity (sāmarthya).
What is the functional capacity [of this text]?

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the single vessel, it is prescribed for many that "the initiated one should win prosperity for twelve nights"; this is a mandatory rule (nitya), not an optional one (pākṣika).
One who performs that very [twelve-day rite] constantly is able to adopt another measure.
Therefore, the measure should be restricted to the twelve-day rite itself;
other measures will apply to the modified rites (vikṛti), so there is no pointlessness in these [other measures].
"However, the twelve-day [rite] should be [the rule] because of an indicative mark.
(The *Tantraratna* states that this is a *siddhānta-sūtra* establishing the conclusion of the section.

Disregarding the *bhāṣya* on the sūtra "In regard to the measure of initiation," the author of the *Vārttika*, having explained this as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of a *pūrvapakṣa* not based on the sūtra itself, treats the sūtra "But the twelve-day [rite]" as a subtle, separate section within the *Nyāya*.)
(Thus ends the commentary on the verse. Regarding the duration of initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the Jyotiṣṭoma in the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), it is obtained according to one's desire.

In that regard, there is a doubt: is it the same here, or is there a restrictive rule (*niyama*)? Since there is no distinction [from the model sacrifice], one may act according to one's desire (the reading *yathākāmī* is found in the Ranapāṭha).
Thus it is concluded.
"But the twelve-day [sacrifice] should be [the model], on account of the indicative mark. What is the indicative mark? "This twelve-day sacrifice is indeed thirty-six days," so it is said.
And this is not an injunction,
because it is a praise of something else.

Furthermore, in the passage concerning initiation, after enumerating six sets of two— namely, "with two [verses] he shaves the hair," "with two the skin," "with two the blood," "with two the flesh," "with two the bone," and "with two the marrow"— it praises the number twelve.
Therefore, there are twelve initiations (*dīkṣā*) in the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice.
Vi— "In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, there are twelve excellent initiations and one *upasad*.
The first [number] would follow from the statement regarding the fee (*bhṛti*), while the latter follows from direct scriptural audition (*pratyakṣa-śruti*)."

Therefore, all these options are optional alternatives (*vikalpita*) in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. Bhaṭṭa: In the *Soma* sacrifice, many options regarding the initiations (*dīkṣā*) are heard in the scripture, such as "one initiation" or "three initiations.

Among these, in the *Soma* sacrifice, only the option of twelve initiations is valid, because of the conformity with the scriptural statement regarding the fee for initiation—namely, "Having been initiated for twelve nights, he should win the sacrificial fee" (*bhṛti*)—which would be impossible under the other alternative options. Consequently, the other options pertain to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).
According to the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya, [passages such as] "He chooses one" (*ekaṃ vṛṇīte*) and so forth are restatements (*anuvāda*) of what has already been established.

However, according to the author of the Vārttika, because these occur in different locations, they cannot be considered explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) like "He chooses one"; rather, there is no dispute that they are all injunctions (*vidhi*).
Nevertheless, in accordance with the context (*prakaraṇa*), the aforementioned interpretation does not apply to these.
Thus, there is the assumption of optionality for a single statement regarding the fee (*bhṛti*);
one [interpretation] refers merely to the measure of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) as lasting twelve nights,
while the other refers to the duration in which the initiation occurs over as many nights as there are Pitṛs.

In reality, however, this figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) does not apply even to the injunction, because it is the very act of begging for wages performed by the initiated sacrificer—which is either already established as an option or entirely unestablished—that must be enjoined during the performance; thus, it is logical that the term "twelve nights" is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Consequently, there is no possibility of assuming its status as a mere optional alternative.
Rather, there is simply an option between the various days of initiation, similar to the choice between rice and barley.
Or, even if there were a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding its being something to be performed, there would still be no fault. Maṇḍana [says]: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, initiation is optional."
Śaṅkara: "The option regarding initiation applies to the archetype.
Oṃ. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, when several people consume Soma from a single vessel, it must be consumed only after having obtained permission.
[The rule for] eating after being permitted by a command.

The Commentary: Now, when Soma is eaten from a single vessel by several people, should it be eaten there having been either commanded or not commanded [to do so], or only after being permitted? When the view that one may act without permission is reached on account of parsimony, it is said in reply:
"It should be eaten after having obtained permission.
Why? Because of a scriptural statement.
This scriptural statement exists: "Therefore, Soma should not be drunk without being formally accepted (anugṛhīta)."
The bringing near (*upahāna*) and the requesting permission (*anu-jñāpana*):
this is specific to each case.
Or rather—this *sūtra* is for the sake of explaining the meaning of "therefore Soma is not favored" and for the sake of the subsequent subject matter.

Soma: Even here, the connection is through the same incidental application (*prasaṅga*). Viśvarūpa: "One should not eat without having obtained permission, or one may; however, in this case, the former is preferable due to brevity. [Objection: If the first were accepted, it would be stated that "it should not be drunk"; thus, the latter [alternative] is adopted.
Bhaṭṭa: Furthermore, this consumption must be done only after having obtained permission, according to the injunction: "Soma is not to be drunk without being invited.

Even that permission is not to be sought by means of ordinary worldly speech, but rather by means of the mantra "Upahūta upahvayasva" (Invited, invite [me]), which is like the Vedic revelation itself.

There too, setting aside the syntactical connection (*vākya*) by means of the indicative power (*liṅga*), one [verse] is for the purpose of seeking permission, while the other is for the act of granting permission.
Furthermore, by the force of the prohibition, even in the case of requesting permission (*anujñāpana*), there is no assumption of an injunction, because it is a mantra.

Even in that context, setting aside the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) in favor of the order of meaning (*arthakrama*), the phrase "upahvayasva" (invite) is to be employed for first receiving permission, and "upahūtaḥ" (invited) for subsequently granting permission. (Here ends the section consisting of the three sūtras numbered 14, 15, and 16 of the Bhāṣya.)
Maṇḍana: "And drinking [should occur] after an invitation. Śaṅkara: "And eating should occur after having obtained permission.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, when many [drink] from a single vessel... in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, when many [drink] from a single vessel.
(Symbol): In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, when consuming Soma from a single vessel, the Hotṛ priest consumes first.

In a single vessel, the Adhvaryu should consume first in sequence. Commentary: Now, where many consume from one vessel, what is the sequence there? It is said: "In a single vessel... (the Sūtra). For his sequence of consumption is determined by whose hand holds the Soma. Or: it has been established that when there are multiple consumers from a single vessel...
Now, the specific details regarding the sequence of those who consume [the remnants] are being set forth.
In that regard, the Adhvaryu consumes first; there is no handing over [of the vessel], as the performance is distinguished by his direct approach.

Otherwise, if it were handed over again by the Adhvaryu after he had already offered it, there would be a distraction due to handing it back to him; thinking thus, the Adhvaryu comes first according to the sequence.
Thus says the author of the Sūtras:
"Or the Hotṛ priest, on account of the wording of the mantra.
The Commentary states: "Or rather, the Hotṛ priest should consume [the portion] first."

Because of the wording of the mantra. For the wording of the mantra is as follows: "Even before the Hotṛ priest, they have eaten the sacrificial food" (Ṛgveda 10.94.14). [The first three quarters of this verse are: "These speak with hundreds, they speak with thousands; they cry out with their golden splendors; having performed their work well, the pressing-stones, being skillful, [have acted] with good deeds. These are the first three quarters.
(Rigveda 10.94.2).
Likewise: "Like a Hotṛ-priest, drink first for us; O Adhvaryu, having prepared the honeyed, beautiful, pure [soma], bring it to Vāyu.
Like a Hotṛ-priest, drink first for us; O God, we have offered this to you for your exhilaration."
Or rather—it is established by the words of the mantra that when a stronger means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has been prescribed, the presentation of a weaker one constitutes a fault (*kilbiṣa*).
In this regard, the mantra concerned with *āśvasta* indicates the first consumption for those who perform the *hautra* ritual.
(He states the meaning of the mantra: These speak; when the pressing is being performed, the pressing-stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*) make a sound.

They cry out with a hundredfold and thousandfold voice—their speaking itself is characterized by a loud, resonant outcry. With greenish-yellow lusters—that is, with lusters that have turned blue through contact with the *soma*.
[In the word *āśvasta*, there is the substitution of *ās* for *śvas*. Regarding the act of sitting (*viṣṭvī-karman*):
the pressing-stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*) are "well-makers" (*sukṛtaḥ*), meaning they are performers of beautiful deeds.
By means of well-performed action and its excellence;
even before the Hotṛ—the oblation is worthy of the Hotṛ, that which is first to be eaten by the Hotṛ—they have reached it;
they have consumed it.

By stating "thus speaking," [the mantra] shows that the one who utters *vaṣaṭ* has the first portion for consumption. Likewise, in the phrase "like a Hotṛ, drink first for us," it is understood through the well-known analogy that the Hotṛ drinks first.

And because of the scriptural statement. The commentary states: there is this scriptural statement, "The first draught belongs to the one who utters the vaṣaṭ-call"; this is indeed a scriptural statement.
It should not be thought that primacy is interrupted because of the prescription of multiple qualities;

since primacy has not been previously established, this is not a restatement (anuvāda), but rather an injunction (vidhi). Furthermore, when expressed through a compound, it is not difficult to enjoin multiple qualities simultaneously.
Alternatively—the previously mentioned qualified injunction, "The first portion is for the one who utters *vaṣaṭ*," is established;
and because it is a novel prescription (*apūrva*), there is no fault of multiple injunctions. Furthermore, the compound is superior.
In brief, because a single *kāraka* is prescribed as having become a single unit, the rule "it should be taught for each of those" (5.1.15) does not apply;
this is due to the cause being the merit (*puṇya*).
The Bhāṣya states: "For the first utterance of *vaṣaṭ* is the occasion for the *hotṛ* priest."
Therefore, the *hotṛ* [is mentioned] first because it is the cause (*nimitta*) for the *adhvaryu*.

And because of the sequence of causes, there is a sequence of the effects (*naimittika*). For instance, since the occurrence of the effect follows the cause—as in the rule "he offers when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered"—the activity of the *hotṛ* is the cause first, and subsequently comes the oblation by the *adhvaryu*.
Nor was there a pressing [of Soma] for him alone at the very beginning.

This is true; however, he does not possess the status of being the cause [for the first consumption] by himself, nor do both together, because of the rule: "For those two, there is no manual of ritual law" (6.4.17.25), which indicates that they are the cause only when combined.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "Even before the Hotṛ, they ate the sacrificial food," which implies that the Hotṛ alone receives the first portion, it is established by these two sūtras that the word "Hotṛ" refers merely to the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* call.

Śā—Since it is established that there is eating by many [priests], the order [of eating] is now considered (this is the connection). However, the Prābhākaras hold that in the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, for the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer, [the eating is] of the *aiṣṭika* [portions].
(1794) In the Jyotiṣṭoma... [the portions belonging to the sacrifice].
The horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and the *dākṣāyaṇa* sacrifice are prescribed within the *Jyotiṣṭoma* itself, and not as separate rituals.

Bhāṣya 2.3.12.0 states: "In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*: 'This indeed is the first sacrifice, the *agniṣṭoma*; he who, having not sacrificed with this, should sacrifice with another [sacrifice], truly perishes like one falling into a pit, or he is destroyed. Here, by the words 'he who with this,' it is the *agniṣṭoma* alone that is referred to, due to the context."

By the word "other" (*anya*) in the phrase "then by another," all sacrifices that are modifications of the Soma sacrifice are included—namely, the *atyagniṣṭoma* and others, the *ekāhas*, the *ahīnas*, and the *satras*. (Vi.

5.3.123). In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is an injunction regarding the qualities of the cups (*graha*), such as "he draws the cups beginning with the Aindravāyava. This is the section concerning the Rathantara.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, among the cups dedicated to Indra-Vāyu and others, the cup for the Aśvins is recited in the third position.

However, by the statement "The cup for the Aśvins is drawn as the tenth," its status as the tenth is established; this should be understood as referring to the cup (graha), whereas its status as the third refers to its place in the sacrifice (yāga).

VI. 5.4.1: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, regarding the drinking of the cups for Indra-Vāyu and others, there is an injunction specifically for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), the parched grain (saktu), and so forth.

Bhāṣya 3.8.18.133: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, one must consume the cup for Indra-Vāyu twice; for it is stated in the scripture: "He consumes the cup for Indra-Vāyu twice, because he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call twice for it."

The *aindrāvāyavanyāya* (the principle concerning the cup for Indra and Vāyu) [3.5.1.18]. In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, there is a mantra for consuming the Soma dedicated to Indra and Agni [3.2.17.40–41]. In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the ritual acts pertaining to the *iṣṭi*—such as the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)—are to be performed after the *prātaranuvāka*, and subsequently the rites pertaining to the Soma sacrifice, such as the *pracaraṇī-homa*, are to be performed.

VI.5.1.13: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the offering pertaining to the iṣṭi (aiṣṭika-nirvāpa) must be performed on a cart distinct from the two carts that serve as the Soma-vessels (saumika-havirdhāna). It is not to be performed on either of those two Soma-vessel carts themselves.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the iṣṭi-related rites such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and so forth are to be performed first, whereas the Soma-related rites such as the Pracaraṇī-oblation (pracaraṇī-homa) and so forth are to be performed later.
[This refers to] those for whom the time is determined by the sequence of performance.

The Commentary states: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, at the time of the Prātaranuvāka, it is heard: "O Pratiprasthātṛ, cook the Savanīya oblations"—thus the time for the offering of the Savanīyas is prescribed.
Furthermore, when the Bahiṣpavamāna has been chanted, [the command is given]: "O Āgnīdhra, spread the fires; mow the sacrificial grass; prepare the sacrificial cakes."

In this regard, there is a doubt: at the time of the Prātaranuvāka, are the Saumika rites, such as the offering from the *pracaraṇī* ladle for the Savanīya animal sacrifice, to be performed, or are they the Pauroḍāśika rites [to be performed] prior to the *alaṃkaraṇa* (adornment)? What is the prima facie view? There is no fixed rule, because there is no scriptural injunction that establishes a restriction.
This being the position, we reply:
Regarding those whose time is determined by the sequence of performance:
for those items whose time is known through their position in the ritual procedure, there should be a restriction based on that sequence.
For one indeed desires to perform the preceding item while it is still being employed; since that [subsequent item] is recited after it, it must be performed subsequently.
However, because of the scriptural injunction regarding the *pracaraṇī-homa*—a ritual act belonging to the Soma sacrifice—the [original] sequence is set aside.

Furthermore, the decoration (*alaṃkaraṇa*) of the *bahiṣpavamāna* is prescribed as occurring after [the *pracaraṇī-homa*]. Therefore, the ritual act preceding that [decoration], such as the pouring out (*nirvāpaṇa*) and so forth, must be performed first; thereafter, the ritual acts pertaining to the Soma sacrifice are to be carried out.

The Ṭup-ṭīkā states: After the Adhvaryu has given the *prātaranuvāka* to the Hotṛ with the command, "Recite for the gods the morning libation (*prātaryāvanyaḥ*)," he subsequently issues the direction to the Pratiprasthātṛ, saying, "O Pratiprasthātṛ, prepare the *savanīya* offerings," and hands [the materials] over to him.
Once the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant has been recited, he again issues the command to the Agnīdhra, "O Agnīdh, spread the fires.
Thereupon, the Hotṛ, impelled by that command, proceeds with the *prātaranuvāka*.
The Adhvaryu, stationed near the Hotṛ (upāsyām), remains occupied with his duties from the command until the completion of the Prātaranuvāka.
(For, since the Hotṛ must sit near him having mentally undertaken the Prātaranuvāka, the Adhvaryu is thus engaged.
Because he is so occupied, [the Hotṛ does not participate] in the sprinkling and other rites occurring after the pouring out (nirvāpa) and prior to the decoration.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice,
for the Adhvaryu who performs the *upasthāna* (ritual attendance), the purificatory act of *nirvāpa* (the pouring out of the oblation) passes away because it has long since occurred;
therefore, he does not bring about the subsequent acts such as *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling).

The mantra "abhūd uṣā" (which serves as the concluding verse of the *prātaranuvāka*), even when connected with a specific time, is capable of making it understood that "at this time the *pracaraṇī-homa* is to be performed.
If the *pracaraṇī-homa* and other rites were not performed at this [time of dawn], the connection with the time [expressed by the word] "abhūd uṣā" (as heard in the scripture) would be contradicted.

(If it were so, then by that statement alone the *pracaraṇī-homa* would have to be performed at that time, while the *prokṣaṇa* and other rites would not; thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) would be untenable. Therefore, it is explained otherwise:
the *upāsana* of the *adhvaryu* is optional.
Consequently, it is deliberated upon in that alternative case where it does not exist.

Should [the procedure] commence with the *pracaraṇī-homa* and subsequent rites belonging to the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*), or with the *prokṣaṇa* and subsequent rites belonging to the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika*)?
In this regard, there is a determining authority [in the text]:
"Therefore, having offered the oblation, the *prokṣaṇa* and other rites are to be performed; after that, the Soma-related rites."
In the Jyotiṣṭoma,
the Mahāpātra vessel belongs specifically to the Soma-related northern altar (auccara-vedika).
The performance of the *aiṣṭika* (sacrificial) rites on the great altar (*mahāvedi*) belonging to the *saumika* (Soma sacrifice) is established by incidental application (*prasaṅga*).

(12.13) In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the choosing (*varaṇa*) of the Hotṛ for the *aiṣṭika* rites must be performed separately from the choosing for the *saumika* rites, because it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, after the carrying forward of the fire to the Uttaravedi, the Śālāmukhīya fire becomes the Gārhapatya, and the Prājahita fire [becomes the Āhavanīya].
The Śālāmukhīya fire is indeed the Āhavanīya,
because of its usage as the source [of the fire] from the Āhavanīya;
there is merely a division by means of a different altar, just as in the case of the Vaidhṛta offerings.

This being the case, regarding the injunction "one should make [the fire] into the Āhavanīya by means of carrying it forth (praṇayana) which has the Āhavanīya as its point of departure (apādāna) and the sacrificial altar (vedī) as its locus," although the status of the Āhavanīya applies to the point of departure at the moment immediately preceding the act of carrying forth—such that such a designation is possible at that time—nevertheless, from the subsequent moment onward, its status is exclusively that of the Gārhapatya, because it is the generator of that [Āhavanīya] state.
For this very reason, the designation of both the Prājahita and the Śālāmukhīya fires as "Gārhapatyas" in another Vedic text is justified.
And there is a Smṛti text stating: "From this point upward, this becomes the Gārhapatya fire.

As for the alternative exposition (*varṇaka*) found in the Bhāṣya, it is a re-presentation of this very same section through a different passage, intended to demonstrate a variation in the reading of the Siddhānta-sūtra.
(Saṃkarṣa 3.2.12). In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is a mantra for scratching: "May we be in the furrows; we have scratched."

The reading "kṛṣiṣu syasāmakṛṣe" alone is necessary; however, the Ānandāśrama reading has arisen either directly or indirectly from a scribal error in reading the original text. Furthermore, even when the original text was written as such, some scholar of the meaning raised the doubt: "The form 'kṛṣiṣu' is incorrect; why is there not a change to ṣatva?"

"May we be [prosperous]"—because the word *satya* is neuter, his conviction was that it was indeed incorrect; thus he formulated an alternative reading. When one scratches simultaneously with a single mantra, even then it should be employed only once; there is no repetition. (Bhāṣya 11.4.16.48–49). In the Jyotiṣṭoma, at the commencement of the rite, the sacrificer's own wealth is set aside upon the altar: "This is for my enjoyment, this is for the sacrifice, this is for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
And this division is extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to the Viśvajit sacrifice.

VI. 6|77: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, having taken the optional cups such as the Śukra and others, one should hold them in the hand with the formula "yuṣmad"; [one should hold] that which one desires for the sake of the one who takes [the cup]; having taken the Aindravāyava cup, one should set it down. 10|5|21: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, [it is said] "he scratches with the black antelope horn" and "when the sacrificial fees have been led forth, he throws the black antelope horn into the Cātvāla pit.
Here, regarding the scratching—
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the vessels accompanied by the *bhakṣaṇa* (consuming) are present;
in the Jyotiṣṭoma, the carrying away of the *camasins*' vessels is the motivator, whereas their disposal (*prāsanam*) is a secondary act of disposal (*pratipatti*).

The Section on the Prāsana (Throwing Away). Bhāṣya 4.2.19: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, ritual duties such as the *kyāmin* and others are to be performed only in relation to the *soma*, not in relation to the *phalacamasa*.

The section concerning the injunction for the non-wasting of the Soma-substance (Somadharmākṣāmānavidhyādhikaraṇa) [3.6.16.41–47]: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the injunction "When the Soma has not been purchased, he gives a staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa" and "Bearing the staff, recite the *preṣas*," the holding of the staff by the Maitrāvaruṇa is a primary purposeful act (*arthakarma*), not a secondary act of disposal (*pratipatti*).
This is the principle of the giving of the staff (*daṇḍadānanyāya*).

4|2|16–19. In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the mantra containing the phrase "of the Gāyatrī metre" (*gāyatracchandasaḥ*) and so forth applies only to the Soma offerings dedicated to Indra that consist of various metres, and not elsewhere. (This is a *kṛtvācintā* [hypothetical discussion]. Here, the full detailed text itself should be cited.)
Even in the case of a gift to Indra, when it is joined with the Gāyatrī meter alone, [the term] "Aindravāyava" is used;
it would likewise be used even when joined with other meters, for such is the expression regarding the mantra.

The *bahuvrīhi* compound is equal in both cases, yet there is no instance of a single meter; this deliberation (*kṛtvācintā*) was made solely with respect to the various meters. This statement regarding the purpose of the *savana* is declared to be an "extraction" (*udghātana*).
Therefore, in all the various ritual offerings (*sarvadāna*), the recitation of the mantra remains exactly as it stands.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, during the rites pertaining to the Gārhapatya fire, [the offering] is indeed at the Śālāmukhīya fire.

Regarding those duties pertaining to the *gārhapatya* fire—such as the injunctions of the *saumika* rites stating "he offers in the *gārhapatya*"—and those pertaining to the *iṣṭi* sacrifices, such as the *patnīsaṃyāja* and so forth, all of these should, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), be performed optionally at both locations without distinction. This being the position, [the conclusion is reached]: because of the scriptural statement beginning with "They carry the *praṇītā* waters forward" and ending with "Then he should take the cooking vessel for the animal sacrifice from there; thus he makes it a sharer," which declares that the *prājahita* fire has the single function of cooking the animal sacrifice, the other [duties] belong to the *śālāmukhīya* fire alone.

In the *Saṃkarṣa* (3.2.13), regarding the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the singular form in the injunction "one cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*) is not intended to be significant. Therefore, all cups (*grahas*) are to be cleansed.
This is the section concerning the cup (*grahādhikaraṇa*).

Bhāṣya 3.1.12–15: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, when the precedence of the Aindravāyava cup is prescribed among the cups, the drawing [of the cup] occurs in the place of the Aindravāyava, and not before the Upāṃśu cups.

10.5.17–64: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the mixing of the Soma contained in all the cups with milk and other substances is prescribed as follows: "He mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk, the Manthin with groats, the Āgrayaṇa with parched grains, the Śukra with gold, and the Pālīvata with clarified butter."

In this context, because substances such as milk (*payaḥ*) and others serve as sanctifying agents (*saṃskāraka*), the *soma*-related rites such as purchase (*kraya*) and so forth need not be performed; rather, the duties pertaining to the *praṇītā* water and other such items are to be followed.
(JS 4.1.13). In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, all participants, including the Grāvastut priest, are partakers in the consumption of the Hāriyojana cup.

(Bhāṣya 3.5.9.27–30). In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the scriptural passage beginning with "Clarified butter belongs to the gods" (*ghṛtaṃ devānām*) is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the injunction "anointed with clarified butter."
VI. 3.4.7. In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is no cleansing of the *camasas* with the *daśāpavitra*.
This is the section concerning the *camasas*.
A *daśāpavitra* is a certain piece of cloth.
And that word expresses [the sense] "accompanied by a tenth part. Such a rule does not apply in common worldly usage.
Bhāṣya 3.1.18.16–17: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the *camasādhvaryus* are distinct from both the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the attendants of the sacrificer (*yajamānapuruṣa*).
3|7|10|25. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, ten Camasādhvaryus are to be chosen.
This is the principle regarding the Camasādhvaryus.
Vi. 3|7|12. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, many Camasādhvaryus are to be chosen.
The Principle of the Camasādhvaryus and the Hotṛs. Bhāṣya 3.7.1.126: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is consumption [of Soma] by those designated as *camasins* according to their titles.
3.7.1.22: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is consumption of the remnants of Soma by the *camasins*.

[The conclusion follows] from the designation (*samākhyāna*) regarding the cups (*camasa*), because that connection is based upon it. *Bhāṣya*: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice itself, it is heard [in scripture]: "Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forward; let the Brahman’s go forward; let those of the Udgātṛs go forward; let the sacrificer’s go forward; let those of the Sadasyas go forward. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is there a consumption (*bhakṣa*) for the possessors of the cups (*camasin*), or not? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? We say: no.
It has been stated that eating does not apply excessively.
This being the case, we reply:
there is eating in the cups (camasa).
Why? Because of the designation (*samākhyāna*).
This is indicated by the designations "the Hotṛ’s cup," "the Brahman’s cup," and "the Udgātṛ’s cup.
Where the Hotṛ has sipped, will sip, or has sipped [Soma], that is the Hotṛ’s cup.
"In that case, the Hotṛ would not drink, nor would there be a Hotṛ's cup;
therefore, he says, 'Thou art a cup' (camasī)."
What is the means of obtaining this indicative mark?
We say it is capacity:
[the capacity] to proceed with the *hotṛ*’s cup.
Moreover, if the Hotṛ were not to drink from it here, it would be impossible for him to proceed with the Hotṛ’s cup;
nor will the Hotṛ drink anything else, such as boiled rice and so forth, for they designate that vessel as the "Soma-cup."

Furthermore, that substance does not belong to the Hotṛ; it belongs to the sacrificer (yajamāna). Therefore, the rinsing (camana) must be performed by the Hotṛ. Moreover, when the Soma is being consumed, the oblation (homa) cannot be accomplished by means of it, for Soma is pure (pavitra); once it has been consumed, the vessel is no longer pervaded by it.
In that case, it is possible to offer with the cup.
If it is argued that one may offer with the residue on the authority of the scriptural statement,
this is not so.
In the absence of an opportunity, a statement is sublated;
however, there is indeed an opportunity for the consumption of Soma.
Therefore, the Soma must be consumed by the cup-holders (camasins).
Now, if [the acts] such as carving were to depend on the material,
then by the destruction of that [material], there would be the destruction of the substance itself, or it would become a different substance altogether.
And for that reason, the text prohibits the purchase of Soma.

"If one should officiate at a sacrifice for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, and he should desire to consume Soma, one should fetch the white shoots of the Nyagrodha tree, grind them, mix them with curd, and offer that as the consumption [of Soma] to him"—this shows that the consumption [of Soma] is prohibited [for them].
This very apprehension regarding consumption is justified only if there is a consumption for those who possess the *camasins*.
Therefore, we consider that it does exist.
Or rather—we accept this as it has been taught.
However, that teaching must be followed according to its specific designations and so forth, and not merely based on the particularity of what is heard in the text.

In that regard, concerning the cups (*camasa*), although no direct instruction found within the Brāhmaṇa is perceived, nevertheless, a designation (*samākhyā*) is inferred by way of the ritual direction (*praipa*).

For the sending forth of the *anuvacana* (invocation) with the substance qualified by the status of being the *hotṛ-camasa* and so on does not arise [as a new injunction] if the Hotṛ and others do not drink the Soma from those vessels.

How so? The word *camasa* is derived from the root *cam*, meaning "to eat," with the *auṇādika* suffix *atrap* used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa-sādhana*). When the time for the *praiṣa* (direction) arrives, since a connection must be sought among the meanings of the past, future, or present, and since neither the past nor the present is observed [in this context], its future nature is inferred.
Otherwise, the performance of the direction "Let the *hotṛ-camasa* go forth" would not be possible.

Therefore, the *camasins*, beginning with the *hotṛ*, must consume [the remnant]. It is understood that the *camasa*s have been offered while still containing remnants of Soma; for the *camasa* is offered with its remnant, according to the scriptural statement: "He offers a small amount."

Furthermore, no other substance such as cooked rice (odana) is perceived, by the consumption of which the status of being a *camasa* (cup) would be established. Moreover, that [substance] could not constitute an integral part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*); in that case, the context (*prakaraṇa*) would be subverted, the injunction (*praiṣa*) would be contradicted, and the designation (*samākhyā*) "Soma-cup" would also be subverted.
And if one were to consume cooked rice and the like, then a subsequent oblation (*homa*) could not be performed with a vessel containing remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*).

In that case, if one resorts to carving and other methods for the sake of purification, since the *hotṛcamasa* whose identity has been determined would be destroyed, no other substance could bear that same name; thus, because of the injunction for a homa performed with a substance designated by that specific name, [the original cup must remain]. By this, the proposal to take up another cup is refuted. Furthermore, if such another were taken up, there would be a transgression of the number of cups explicitly stated in the scripture.
Nor can it be established by the force of the statement that,

in the Jyotiṣṭoma, the practice of consuming the Soma with the remains (ucchiṣṭa) is an auxiliary part (aṅga) common to and undifferentiated among the cup-holders (camasins), because such a practice already finds its scope elsewhere.
If it is argued that all this is the same even in the case of one who consumes the Soma, it is not so; for there is the scriptural injunction: "They do not become impure by means of the Soma.
Therefore, the Soma must be consumed by those who hold the cups (*camasin*).
The commentary (*bhāṣya*) also is to be interpreted according to this very sequence, and not as it was written.
Because other births are defiled by being separated from other births,
[the text] prohibits the drinking of Soma for one who has fallen from that state.

Furthermore, if the designation "of the sacrificer" (*yajamānasya*) did not result in the attainment of the drinking of Soma, then the mention of the prohibition "not Soma" in the *phalacamasa* rite— "if he should desire to drink Soma"— would be inexplicable.

Therefore, there is a consumption of Soma by those holding the *camasa* cups. In the *Śābarabhāṣya*, the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*, and other works, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is included within the preceding section itself. [Question: "Does the formula, 'May the Hotṛ's *camasa* come forward,' indicate that this is a non-consumption, or is it a consumption?"
"Because it is not mentioned [in the text], there is no eating; let that [eating] belong to the *hotṛ* priest through the exhaustion [of his labor].
[Objection: "The designation (*saṃjñā*) 'Maṇḍana' would imply eating.
[Reply: "That [designation] is caused by the name 'Śaṅkara'."
In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the injunction "I am austerity; indeed, I do not shine; indeed, I do not shine" pertains only to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).
According to a specific scriptural statement, it may also apply to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in certain cases.

(Bhāṣya 3.8.11–10). In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the invocation of the *havirpā* (the vessel for the oblation) should not be performed during the *tṛtīyasavana* offerings, such as the *puroḍāśa* cakes and others.

1|2|4| 12-13. Regarding the statement "one bathes at a non-tīrtha" in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, bathing at a *tīrtha* is included within the Jyotiṣṭoma section itself, because it is a duty pertaining to the person engaged in the sacrifice (*ṛtuyuktapuruṣadharma*).
3|4|15|14-16. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the cause is indeed equal and undifferentiated. In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the cause is indeed equal and undifferentiated.
For since the reason for being primary is the possession of a fruit, and that is undifferentiated and common to all sacrifices because they are all sacrifices;
therefore, all sacrifices are primary.
This is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
Because the qualities are connected by means of the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), there is a scriptural statement regarding the cause; therefore, Soma should be the primary element.
Refuting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the word "but" (*tu*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
It is "appropriate" (*upapadyate*); thus, "origin" (*utpatti*) refers to the result, and the "originative injunction" (*utpattivākya*) is the sentence that establishes it.
"Let one who desires heaven sacrifice"— this is the sentence stating the result (*phalavākya*).
The qualities (*guṇa*) are the *stomas* consisting of the forms of nine, fifteen, seventeen, and twenty-one [verses].
They are denoted by the word *jyotis*.

Since there exists a connection of the qualities (*guṇas*) with the sentence of origin (*utpattivākya*), it is possible for the scriptural mention of the cause (*kāraṇaśruti*) to signify the attainment (*bhūti*)—the connection with the fruit—of the cause mentioned in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Because the *Jyotiṣṭoma* is connected with the fruit, the qualities denoted by the word *stoma*, which are of the nature of *jyotis*, are also connected with the fruit.
And the *stomas* (hymns) have Soma as their purpose.
Therefore, in the Jyotiṣṭoma, Soma should be the primary element.
The Soma sacrifices alone are the primary elements, whereas the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other sacrifices are merely auxiliary (*aṅga*).
And likewise, there is the observation of another scriptural passage supporting this.
He states another reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), beginning with: "The initiatory rite (*dīkṣaṇīyā*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice."
There is the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) having another purpose.

Thus, [in the texts] "One should give gold weighing twenty-four *mānas* at the *dīkṣaṇīyā*" and "At the *prāyaṇīyā*, two [amounts of] twenty-four *mānas," a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) distinct from that of the *jyotiṣṭoma* is observed; that too is an indicative mark.
By this, it is established that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are subsidiary (*aṅga*), and not principal (*pradhāna*).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, [the names] are equal because the reason is not distinguished.

Since the term *jyotiṣṭoma* is applied to the *trivṛt* and other *stomas* in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"For these *stomas* of his are indeed lights"—and since it is understood from the statement, "Having taken the cup (*graha*) or having raised the bowl (*camasa*), he begins the chant (*stotra*)," that the Soma sacrifice possesses the *trivṛt* and other *stomas* in its various forms, the meaning of the sacrifice is qualified by the name according to its well-known sense.
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 724)
